He wrote two of the seventeen episodes of one of the most analyzed television series ever produced, and he's a ghost.
He wrote this episode as a possible series finale — "Number Six gets out, but has to be recaptured, in case the show continues." It was the thirteenth episode produced, originally intended to close the first filming block. ITV broadcast it seventh. That's the wrong place for it. By episode seven you've only seen one escape attempt (Chimes of Big Ben), so this reads as a retread. Placed at thirteen, after a run of increasingly abstract episodes where Number Six never comes close to leaving, the sheer physical directness of it — building a raft, fighting gunrunners, hitching on a lorry — would have landed with real force. The broadcast order buried it.
The escape itself is extraordinary. Twenty-five days at sea on a raft made of Village materials. Gunrunners steal his belongings and throw him overboard. He climbs back aboard their boat, fights them, commandeers it, is overpowered again, and washes up on a beach somewhere in southern Europe. Romani travellers who speak no English. Then a British policeman — and suddenly he's running again, because anyone in uniform might be one of them. He stows away on a truck. He reaches London. He makes his way to his own front door — 1 Buckingham Place, the house from the title sequence — and finds a woman living in it, driving his car.
Mrs. Butterworth. Georgina Cookson played her — born Antoinette Georgina Cookson on December 19, 1918, in Mevagissey, Cornwall. Her father was the racing driver Roger Cookson. Her mother, Sybil, wrote novels under the pseudonym Sydney Tremayne and contributed to The Tatler. Georgina was the great-granddaughter of Sir James Crichton-Browne, the Victorian psychiatrist who corresponded with Charles Darwin and was an early investigator of brain localization. She left Benenden School at fifteen to train at RADA. She was married four times — twice divorced, twice widowed. Her film work included John Schlesinger's "Darling" (1965), playing Carlotta Hale alongside Julie Christie, Dirk Bogarde, and Laurence Harvey. In the same year: "Catacombs," also known as "The Woman Who Wouldn't Die." She had appeared in "Danger Man" before The Prisoner, playing Miss Bishop in "The Trap" — which is how ITC shows worked: the same pool of actors circulated through the same producers' shows, and you might play a guest villain one month and a Number Two the next. In fact she appeared in The Prisoner twice: as the unnamed blonde woman in "A. B. and C." (episode three) and as Mrs. Butterworth here. She died in Sydney, Australia, on October 1, 2011, aged ninety-two.
Mrs. Butterworth feeds Number Six, gives him clothes, lends him her car — his car, really — and sends him off to report to his superiors. She mentions his birthday. He had not mentioned his birthday. That's the tell, if you're paying attention.
He goes to the underground car park from the title sequence and presents himself to the man behind the desk — who is, as always, George Markstein, the series' script editor, playing himself. This was the last episode Markstein worked on. He left after the first thirteen productions, citing irreconcilable creative differences with McGoohan over the show's direction. Markstein wanted a spy drama grounded in the real tradecraft he knew from his intelligence background — he was the one who'd heard about Inverlair Lodge, the actual wartime "village" in the Scottish Highlands where compromised agents were kept, and pitched it to McGoohan as a series premise. McGoohan wanted allegory, abstraction, philosophy. Markstein wanted to know who Number One was. McGoohan didn't think that was the point. The divorce was inevitable, and this was the last episode they made together. Markstein's appearance in the title sequence — the anonymous bureaucrat behind the desk who receives Number Six's resignation — is the most ironic piece of casting in the series. The man who conceived the show appears in every episode as the functionary who triggers the plot, but whose face is never identified. He went on to write novels: "The Cooler" (1974), whose title refers to Inverlair Lodge itself, and "The Goering Testament." He died on January 15, 1987, in Uxbridge, aged fifty-four.
The Colonel and Thorpe receive Number Six with careful suspicion. Donald Sinden played the Colonel. Born October 9, 1923, in Plymouth, Devon — the middle child of a chemist whose shop was called "The Limes" in Ditchling, East Sussex. He failed his eleven-plus. He made his first stage appearance in 1941, stepping into a part in place of his cousin Frank, who'd been called up. Rejected for naval service because of asthma, he joined a theatrical company that entertained troops along the south coast. In 1942, in Hove, he befriended Lord Alfred Douglas — "Bosie" — Oscar Wilde's lover. Douglas was seventy-one, living out his last years, and had by then converted to Catholicism, written bitter repudiations of Wilde, un-repudiated them, and settled into a quiet dotage among friends who included John Betjeman, Malcolm Muggeridge, and Terence Rattigan. Sinden is believed to have been the last surviving person to have known Douglas. He carried that connection — a handshake from Oscar Wilde through one intermediary — into a career that spanned seven decades. "The Cruel Sea" (1953) made him a star overnight. The Rank Organisation signed him for seven years. He played Benskin in the "Doctor" films. He played the Duke of York in "The Wars of the Roses" opposite Peggy Ashcroft. He won the Evening Standard Best Actor award for "King Lear" in 1977. Then, with the timing of a man who understood that gravity is optional, he reinvented himself as a sitcom star: "Two's Company" (1975-79) and "Never the Twain" (1981-91). He was knighted in 1997. His son Jeremy Sinden also became an actor and died young, in 1996, of lung cancer. His other son Marc became a producer. Sinden died September 12, 2014, at ninety, at his home in Wittersham, Kent.
Patrick Cargill played Thorpe — Number Six's former colleague who is shifty, ambiguous, and clearly knows more than he lets on. Born Edward Sydney Patrick Cargill on June 3, 1918, in Bexhill-on-Sea, Sussex. Educated at Haileybury College. Trained at Sandhurst. Served as a commissioned officer in the British Indian Army during the war. Came home to act. Joined Anthony Hawtrey's company, worked repertory at Windsor, performed in a revue seen by the Queen and twenty-six of her guests. He became the doctor who clashes with Tony Hancock in "The Blood Donor" (1961) — one of the most beloved episodes of British television comedy. His play "Ring for Catty," co-written with Jack Beale, was adapted into "Carry On Nurse" (1959), the second Carry On film. He appeared in Charlie Chaplin's final film, "A Countess from Hong Kong" (1967). He starred in "Father, Dear Father" (1968-73), which was written specifically for him. And he returned to The Prisoner as the Number Two in "Hammer Into Anvil" — which was shot before this episode but broadcast after it, creating one of the show's deepest continuity puzzles: Thorpe in "Many Happy Returns" is a colleague from Number Six's old life who seems complicit in the recapture. Number Two in "Hammer Into Anvil" is a bullying sadist whom Number Six systematically destroys. Are they the same man? If Thorpe was always Village, was his Number Two posting a promotion or a punishment? Cargill never played them as the same character, but the casting says what the script doesn't. He died May 23, 1996, in Richmond, London, aged seventy-seven.
Director credit: Joseph Serf. Which is McGoohan. The shoot began under Michael Truman — a producer-director who'd worked with Ealing Studios — but Truman dropped out after several days, citing illness. McGoohan stepped in to finish the location work himself, under his pseudonym. Since he was also the only cast member for most of the outdoor sequences, he was directing himself in silence on location in Portmeirion and London in March 1967. March 19 was McGoohan's birthday, and it's written into the script: the London scenes are set on March 18, and Number Six mentions to Mrs. Butterworth that "tomorrow is my birthday." She says she might even bake him a cake. She does. She delivers it to his cottage in the Village, wearing a Number Two badge, and says "Many happy returns." The title is the cruelty.
"Many Happy Returns" was broadcast on November 10, 1967. That day, the ATS-3 satellite took the first full-disk true-color photograph of the Earth from space — the whole planet, in actual color, for the first time. A man escapes an artificial world and makes it home, only to be returned. A camera in orbit sees the real world whole for the first time. The scale mismatch is perfect: the satellite says, look how big reality is. The episode says, it doesn't matter how big reality is if you can't stay in it.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
It was the sixth episode they shot but the sixteenth they aired, and in between those two numbers lies the entire arc of the series.
Patrick McGoohan wrote and directed this one himself, under his own name — no "Paddy Fitz," no "Joseph Serf." By the time it reached screens on January 25, 1968, eight months had elapsed since filming. In between, McGoohan had left The Prisoner entirely to shoot "Ice Station Zebra" with Rock Hudson at MGM — the Cold War submarine thriller that Howard Hughes would later watch on continuous loop in his Las Vegas penthouse, possibly 150 times. While McGoohan was away, his absence had to be concealed. "Do Not Forsake Me Oh My Darling" was hastily rewritten so that Number Six's mind could inhabit another actor's body for an entire episode. Other installments were padded with stock footage. The series was fraying. When McGoohan returned, Lew Grade informed him there would be no second series — wrap it up. McGoohan had perhaps two weeks' notice to write an ending for a show he'd conceived as a multi-year allegory about the architecture of control.
He chose to make a two-hander. Just him and Leo McKern, locked in a room for a week.
McKern was an Australian who'd lost his left eye at fifteen — not to illness or combat but to an industrial accident, a steel fragment at a factory in Sydney where he worked after dropping out of engineering studies. He wore a glass replacement for the rest of his life. Born Reginald McKern in Sydney in 1920, he'd started in engineering at Sydney Technical College, hated it, drifted into amateur theatre through the Independent Theatre company, and discovered he was better at becoming other people than at building things. He served in the Australian Army during the war, then emigrated to England in 1946 with nothing, joining the Old Vic company and working his way through Shakespeare — Iago, the Fool in King Lear. By the mid-1960s he was one of the most recognizable character actors in British film and television: Thomas More's prosecutor Cromwell in "A Man for All Seasons" (1966), the role that put him in front of the widest audience he'd ever have. He'd already played Number Two once, in "The Chimes of Big Ben," and his contract was extended by a fortnight to shoot this episode immediately afterward — the sixth produced, held back for the penultimate slot.
The working title was "Degree Absolute." The premise: a psychological technique in which therapist and patient are sealed together in a room for seven days, with the understanding that one of them may not survive. It draws on Shakespeare's Seven Ages of Man from "As You Like It," Act II Scene 7 — infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon, oblivion — and Number Two takes Number Six through each stage, playing father, headmaster, employer, commanding officer, judge. The Embryo Room is stocked with props for childhood but runs out of scenery by adulthood, so the later ages must be enacted with whatever's at hand. Boxing gloves. Fencing foils. A wine glass. A cage.
What makes this episode legendary is what happened to the actors while shooting it. According to the 2007 documentary "Don't Knock Yourself Out," both McGoohan and McKern became so consumed by their roles that they approached what multiple witnesses described as a near-psychotic state. McKern, by various accounts, suffered either a nervous breakdown or a heart attack during production — sources differ, and McKern himself was characteristically vague about which it was. Production stopped. When he returned for "Fall Out" almost a year later, he was visibly a different man — heavier, older, hollowed out. The episode had taken something from him that didn't come back.
The Butler, played by Angelo Muscat, finally receives a "featuring" credit — his only one in the entire series, despite appearing in fourteen of seventeen episodes. Muscat was born in Malta in 1930, stood four feet three inches tall, and came from a family where everyone else was of ordinary height. He worked mundane jobs in Malta before emigrating to England and joining a touring production of "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs." McGoohan cast him from a lineup of photographs shown by the casting director. Muscat never speaks a single word of dialogue across the entire run of The Prisoner, yet there was genuine fan speculation during the original broadcast that he might be Number One — the silent figure who sees everything and serves everyone and belongs to no side. After the series, Muscat appeared in the Beatles' "Magical Mystery Tour" (1967) and played an Oompa Loompa in "Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory" (1971). He died at forty-seven in 1977. George Markstein, the show's script editor, said of him: "He never said a word throughout the series, and yet in a way he was as important, or perhaps even more so, than Number Six himself. Angelo was a genial little man — he always had a smile, even on set at eight o'clock in the morning."
Peter Swanwick, the Supervisor — the man behind the console in the control room, the functionary who watches the watchers — appeared in nine of the seventeen episodes and gets his final showcase here. Born in Nottingham in 1922, Swanwick had started with a bit part in "The African Queen" (1951) and become a fixture of 1960s British television, including two episodes of McGoohan's earlier series "Danger Man." He played Herr Zeller in the original London stage production of "The Sound of Music." Multiple operations in the 1960s left him with limited time. He died on November 14, 1968, at forty-six years old — nine months after "Fall Out" aired, less than a year after the series ended. Two of the three actors who shared that Embryo Room were dead within a decade. Only McGoohan survived into old age, and he never stopped being asked why he resigned.
For Prisoner fans, there is an infamous line that sustained decades of debate: does McKern's Number Two, in headmaster mode, say "Report to my study in the morning, Drake!" — confirming that Number Six is John Drake from "Danger Man"? McKern's delivery is genuinely unclear. When the original script was eventually published, the line read: "Report to my study in the morning break." The most consequential word in Prisoner scholarship turned out to be "break," not "Drake." The mystery was a diction problem.
The episode aired on ITV on January 25, 1968 — a Thursday. Two days earlier, North Korea had seized the USS Pueblo in international waters, capturing 83 American crew members in what became the longest-held captivity of a U.S. naval vessel's crew since the War of 1812. Five days later, on January 30, the Tet Offensive began. While a fictional spy sat locked in a room being regressed to childhood, a real intelligence-gathering ship sat captured in Wonsan harbor, and 84,000 Viet Cong soldiers were massing for simultaneous assaults on every major city in South Vietnam. The number one song in America was "Judy in Disguise (With Glasses)" by John Fred and His Playboy Band — a novelty parody of the Beatles' "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds." In Britain, it was still "Hello, Goodbye" by the Beatles themselves. A song about departure. A song about not being able to tell which is which.
Degree Absolute works both ways. That is the point of the episode, the thing Number Six understands that Number Two does not. The technique requires the therapist to enter the patient's mind so completely that the boundary between them dissolves — and when it does, the patient can walk out through the therapist's door. Number Two asks "Why did you resign?" for the last time, and Number Six answers with a question: "Why don't you resign?" It is the only moment in the entire series where someone turns the central question back on the questioner. McKern's face when he hears it — delight, terror, recognition — is the finest single piece of acting in the show's run.
The cage door closes. The timer runs out. "Die, Six, die!" screams a voice. Number Two falls. The Supervisor asks Number Six what he wants. "Number One," Six replies. The Supervisor says he will take him there.
The answer was always in the room.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Patrick McGoohan had no idea how to end the show. Nobody did. Producer David Tomblin later recalled that "there had been various conversations and ideas put forward early in production, but nothing definite had been decided." The series had been conceived as an open question — why did you resign? — and McGoohan had always understood, perhaps more clearly than anyone, that the question was the point. The answer was beside the point. But television does not permit open questions. Television demands a finale.
Lew Grade had pulled the plug on a second series. McGoohan had two weeks, maybe a little more, to write the ending. Alex Cox, using production paperwork, argues the timeline was less compressed than legend suggests — shooting took place over twelve days in November 1967, two months before transmission. But the creative problem was real: McGoohan sat down to write the last episode of a show whose whole premise was that the last episode should never come.
The episode that resulted begins with a caption card. For seventeen episodes, the production had kept a secret — the identity of the Village. Now McGoohan honored his agreement with Sir Clough Williams-Ellis and finally revealed the location: Portmeirion, the Italianate fantasy village on the coast of Gwynedd in North Wales that Williams-Ellis had spent fifty years building from salvaged architectural fragments. The caption thanked him. The secret was out. The game was ending.
What follows is not a resolution. It is an exorcism.
Number Six, having defeated Number Two in the Embryo Room, is brought before an assembly in white robes and hoods — a kangaroo parliament, a Ku Klux bureaucracy — who sit in judgment of three defendants. First: Number Forty-Eight, representing rebellious youth. Second: the resurrected Number Two, representing the old guard. Third: Number Six himself, representing the individual. The President of the assembly, played by Kenneth Griffith, presides.
Griffith was a Welshman from Tenby, born Kenneth Reginald Griffiths in 1921, raised by Methodist grandparents who taught him to question everything. His headmaster suggested he drop the "s" from his surname so it would "sound less English" — an instruction Griffith followed for the rest of his life. He lasted one day at his only non-acting job, weighing nails in a Cambridge ironmonger's. He was invalided out of the RAF with scarlet fever and took up stamp collecting. He appeared in over eighty films, including "A Night to Remember" (1958) as Jack Phillips, the Titanic's wireless operator who tapped out distress signals until the ship sank beneath him — the last man at the key. His later career pivoted to documentary filmmaking of such incendiary sympathy for Irish republicanism that his 1973 film "Hang Up Your Brightest Colours" — about Michael Collins — was banned by the IBA and not broadcast until the BBC picked it up twenty years later. He made "Curious Journey" in 1974, interviewing nine surviving IRA veterans from the Irish revolutionary period. Lew Grade — the same Lew Grade who funded The Prisoner — pulled that one too. A man who made a career of being suppressed, playing the president of a suppressive assembly: McGoohan knew what he was doing with that casting.
Griffith had already appeared in "The Girl Who Was Death," the fairy-tale episode. So had Alexis Kanner, who now returns as Number Forty-Eight. Kanner was born Henri Alex Kanner in Bagneres-de-Luchon, Nazi-occupied France, in May 1942, to a Jewish family. In April 1944, shortly before his second birthday, his family escaped to Montreal on the Portuguese ship Serpa Pinto — one of the few neutral vessels still carrying refugees across the Atlantic. He attended the Montreal Children's Theatre, moved to England as a teenager, joined the Birmingham Repertory Theatre, and played Hamlet under Peter Brook's direction for the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1965. He was twenty-three.
McGoohan cast Kanner because he wanted what Kanner could not help being: volatile, unpredictable, feral. In "Living in Harmony" he had played the Kid — a mute gunslinger in circus trousers and a top hat. Both actors practiced quick-draw for the duel scene "assiduously," according to Tomblin. Now, in Fall Out, Kanner plays Youth itself — literally put on trial for the crime of rebellion. His testimony consists of singing "Dem Bones" while dancing on the assembly table. The delegates shoot him. He keeps singing. He is forcibly restrained. It does not help. "Dem Bones" continues. The episode does not explain why. The episode does not explain anything.
Leo McKern is resurrected from the dead. This is not a metaphor — Number Two died at the end of "Once Upon a Time," and in Fall Out his body is placed in a glass tube and revived. McKern's physical transformation between the two episodes is jarring: he has visibly aged, his hair is shorter and dyed for a stage role he'd been playing during the intervening year. The script accounts for none of this. McKern regarded McGoohan as "a bully" and "something of a tyrant on set," according to Robert Fairclough's "The Prisoner: Official Companion." He came back anyway.
Number Six is given a choice. "Lead us... or go." He is presented with his old clothes, a key, a passport, money, and a Lotus Seven — the same car from the opening titles. He is taken to meet Number One. The white-robed figure wears a mask. Beneath the mask is another mask, this one a monkey's face. Beneath the monkey mask is Patrick McGoohan's own face. Number One is Number Six. The prisoner is the jailer. Man is his own worst enemy, and the system that imprisons him is the one he built.
An audience that had spent seventeen weeks waiting for a Bond villain unmasking instead got a philosophical proposition. They did not take it well. ITV switchboards were overwhelmed. Viewers stormed McGoohan's house. He had to leave the country and go into hiding for several days. People had expected an answer. McGoohan had given them a mirror.
Then comes the gunfight — McGoohan's single concession to the audience expecting a thriller. Number Six, Number Two, Number Forty-Eight, and the Butler storm the underground complex with machine guns and grenades. It is pure chaos, accompanied by the Beatles' "All You Need Is Love" — licensed in perpetuity by music editor Eric Milverton for a one-off payment of sixty dollars, reportedly the cheapest Beatles licensing deal ever made. Whether Lennon was a secret fan of the show or whether someone at Northern Songs simply failed to read the contract remains unknown. But the result is that Fall Out is one of the only television productions that can still broadcast "All You Need Is Love" in its original context, while Doctor Who had to strip Beatles music from three of its stories for home release. A bureaucratic miracle disguised as a clerical error.
Rover, the white balloon that had been the show's most iconic enforcer, melts away during the chaos. According to Kanner, the visual was inspired by him dropping ice cream into his coffee and watching it bubble and dissolve. The Village is evacuated. The underground lair self-destructs. Our four fugitives escape in a lorry, driving through the English countryside to London. The evacuation footage is stitched together from unused material and shots recycled from "Arrival" and "The General" — a finale assembled from fragments of its own past, like Portmeirion itself.
The lorry reaches London. The Prisoner's car is delivered. He drives to 1 Buckingham Place — the same address from the opening titles, the door he slammed on his way out in the first scene of the first episode. The Butler follows him inside. The door closes behind them with the same automated hiss that opened the series. The title card still reads "Prisoner." The car has the same license plate. Nothing has changed. He has gone home, and home is still a cage.
Angelo Muscat — the Butler — walks through that door without speaking, as he has not spoken for seventeen episodes. He served Number Two. He served Number Six. He served Number One. He served everyone and no one. He was the only character who moved freely between all sides, the only one Rover never pursued. In the final shot, his master's door closes on him, and us.
Peter Swanwick's Supervisor delivers Number Six to the assembly and watches the revolution from behind his console. It was his last significant role. He died on November 14, 1968, nine months after this episode aired. Kanner died of a heart attack in London in 2003, at sixty-one, and was buried at his request on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem. McKern died in Bath in 2002, at eighty-two, having long since become Rumpole of the Bailey — the role that finally let him play a man who wins arguments for a living instead of losing them. McGoohan died in Los Angeles on January 13, 2009. Griffith died in London in 2006, at eighty-four, having spent his final decades the same way he spent his first: being told he could not say what he wanted to say, and saying it anyway.
The episode aired on ITV on Thursday, February 1, 1968. The day before, a meat-packing plant in Chicago exploded, killing nine and injuring sixty-nine. The Tet Offensive had begun that morning — the coordinated North Vietnamese assault on over one hundred cities and towns across South Vietnam that would shatter American confidence in the war and end Lyndon Johnson's presidency. The number one song in America was "Green Tambourine" by the Lemon Pipers. In Britain, it was "The Mighty Quinn" by Manfred Mann — a Dylan song about a man whose arrival makes everyone jump for joy, though nobody can explain why. In the R&B chart, Aretha Franklin still held the top spot with "Chain of Fools," a song about a woman who realizes that the people who control her life are connected to the people who control theirs, in an unbroken chain that goes all the way up to the top.
Be seeing you.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Patrick McGoohan was bored. That was his word for it — "boredom" — delivered without apology to Warner Troyer in Toronto in March 1977. He had made fifty-four episodes of Danger Man and decided that was an adequate amount. So he told Lew Grade, the cigar-rolling impresario who ran ITC Entertainment, that he wanted to quit. Grade, who was making good money off the spy show, did not like the idea. McGoohan pitched him something else.
They met on a Saturday morning at seven o'clock. That was always when they had their discussions. McGoohan brought photographs, a budget, and a written format for a show about a man imprisoned in a beautiful coastal village. Grade said he didn't want to read the format — claimed he couldn't read anything except accounts. "Tell me," he said. McGoohan talked for ten minutes. Grade stopped him. "I don't understand one word you're talking about, but how much is it going to be?" McGoohan produced the budget. Grade asked when he could start. McGoohan said Monday, on scripts. "The money'll be in your company's account on Monday morning," Grade replied. It was. That was how The Prisoner began.
The idea had been germinating for two years. During location work on Danger Man, the crew had filmed at Portmeirion, a fantasy village on the coast of Gwynedd in North Wales, and McGoohan had been struck by the place. It was the life's work of Sir Clough Williams-Ellis, a Welsh architect born in 1883 who spent fifty years — from 1925 to 1975 — constructing an Italianate folly on a rocky promontory overlooking Tremadog Bay. Williams-Ellis bought the site, a neglected wilderness called Aber Iâ, for less than five thousand pounds. He rescued architectural fragments from demolished buildings across Britain and reassembled them: a colonnade from a Bristol mansion, a Jacobean town hall from Flintshire, pieces of a demolished Victorian ballroom. The result was a surreal Mediterranean piazza in the Welsh rain, complete with campanile, painted cottages, and subtropical gardens thriving in the warm Gulf Stream air. It looked like nowhere in Britain. McGoohan recognized immediately that it could be the Village.
But the Village also had a darker inspiration. George Markstein, the script editor McGoohan brought onto the project, had done his own research into the Special Operations Executive. Markstein knew about Inverlair Lodge — SOE No. 6 Special Workshop School — a requisitioned country house in Glen Spean, near Inverness, where British intelligence held agents who had failed their training or been recalled from operations. The SOE couldn't simply release people who knew too much about clandestine networks, safe houses, and cover identities, so they were sent to Inverlair to "cool off" — meaning they were kept in benign captivity until their knowledge was stale enough to be harmless. The inmates didn't always know they were prisoners; their "training" would simply continue indefinitely, standards set impossibly high, while the war went on without them. French officers suspected of working for the Germans were billeted there at de Gaulle's personal request. An RAF pilot who had shared a flight with a Resistance leader was sent to a Highland country house the week before his wedding — the marriage was allowed to proceed, then he was quietly disappeared to Scotland. Markstein later turned this material into his 1974 novel "The Cooler," with a dedication that read: "This story is fiction. But there was a Cooler. Those who know about it don't have to be told any more. Those who don't can't be told any more."
Markstein and McGoohan disagreed, publicly and bitterly, about who actually conceived The Prisoner. McGoohan maintained it was entirely his creation. Markstein claimed he brought the real-world intelligence background that gave the concept its teeth. The truth appears to be collaborative: McGoohan had the Portmeirion vision and the philosophical architecture — a man reduced to a number, fighting a system designed to break individuality — while Markstein contributed the espionage framework, the understanding that governments really did this to their own people, and the bureaucratic texture that made the Village feel operational rather than purely allegorical. Markstein left the show after thirteen episodes, furious with the direction McGoohan was taking it. He never forgave him.
The first script went through multiple hands. Markstein and David Tomblin prepared an initial draft. McGoohan rewrote it. By late June 1966, a shooting script titled "The Arrival" was finalized. Principal location filming at Portmeirion began on September 5, 1966, with Don Chaffey directing. Chaffey was no journeyman — he had directed Jason and the Argonauts in 1963, the Ray Harryhausen epic with the skeleton fight that remains one of the most celebrated sequences in the history of special effects. He understood spectacle, and he understood how to shoot a landscape as though it were a character. The Portmeirion footage in "Arrival" is essentially a location documentary disguised as a thriller: the geography of the Village is established so thoroughly that every subsequent episode could take it as given.
The most famous accident in the show's production happened during these early shoots. McGoohan had commissioned an elaborate mechanical device to serve as Rover, the Village's roving guardian. It was a hovercraft-like contraption designed to go underwater, emerge on the beach, climb walls — "this marvelous piece of machinery," as McGoohan later described it, with audible sarcasm. On the first day of shooting, Rover was supposed to descend from the beach into the water, perform some maneuvers, and return. It went into the water and stayed there permanently. The mechanical Rover sank and was never recovered.
The crew stood on the beach with an entire day's shooting ruined, every scene requiring Rover. Bernard Williams, the production manager, looked up at the sky. "What's that?" he asked. McGoohan didn't know. "I think it's a meteorological balloon," Williams said. They stared at each other. "How many can you get within two hours?" McGoohan asked. Williams took an ambulance — so he could use the siren and get there faster — and drove to the nearest meteorological station. He came back with a hundred weather balloons in assorted sizes. They filled them variously with water, oxygen, or helium depending on what they needed Rover to do, and discovered that the uncanny, silent, bouncing thing was far more unsettling than any machine could have been. They used approximately six thousand balloons over the course of the series. "In the end," McGoohan told Troyer, "we could make him do anything: lie down, beg, anything."
Guy Doleman plays the first Number Two — a man accustomed to command, drawling and dangerous. Doleman was a New Zealander who had carved out a career as the go-to cold-eyed authority figure in British spy cinema: he played Colonel Ross, Harry Palmer's manipulative superior, in The Ipcress File (1965) alongside Michael Caine, and the SPECTRE operative Count Lippe in Thunderball the same year. Casting him immediately situated The Prisoner in the cultural landscape of mid-sixties espionage fiction — and then subverted it, because the Village was the thing James Bond and Harry Palmer were supposed to be protecting Britain from.
George Baker appears as the new Number Two who replaces Doleman partway through the episode — the first instance of the rotating-Number-Two structure that would become the show's signature device. Paul Eddington, thirteen years before he became Jim Hacker in Yes, Minister (Margaret Thatcher's favorite television program), plays Cobb, the apparent defector whose staged death is part of the Village's machinery.
Angelo Muscat appears as the Butler for the first time. Born in Malta on September 24, 1930, the son of a policeman, Muscat stood about four feet tall. He never speaks a word in fourteen of the seventeen episodes. McGoohan later mused to the Toronto audience that Muscat's character carried an intentional ambiguity: "There was always the possibility that he might be No. 1. Because he was such a good friend and always by the side of No. 6, there should have been an implication that perhaps he was a sinister character." Muscat died on October 10, 1977, seven months after McGoohan made those remarks. He was forty-seven.
The theme music had its own troubled path to the screen. McGoohan rejected two commissioned scores before settling on Ron Grainer's now-iconic march. Robert Farnon submitted a theme that McGoohan dismissed as a virtual copy of the score from The Big Country (1958). Wilfred Josephs was contracted next; his work was also rejected by McGoohan personally. Grainer, who had already composed the Doctor Who theme in 1963 — famously realized by Delia Derbyshire at the BBC Radiophonic Workshop — delivered the thundering, paranoid, brass-heavy piece that became inseparable from the show's identity.
"Arrival" first aired on ITV on Friday, September 29, 1967 — ATV Midlands and Grampian broadcast it first, with other ITV regions following on different dates. CBS showed it in the United States on Saturday, June 1, 1968. McGoohan had wanted seven episodes, told as a serial. Lew Grade needed at least seventeen for the CBS sale. Over a single weekend, McGoohan and his writers cooked up ten additional story outlines — seven or eight pages each — stretching a seven-episode concept to nearly two and a half times its intended length. McGoohan was never happy about this. "It should be seven," he said flatly, a decade after the fact.
Before the writers could begin, McGoohan sat down and produced a forty-page document describing every aspect of the Village: what the residents ate, the transport system, the telephones, the sewerage, the boundaries. The writers were given copies and sent away to generate ideas. "They were also prisoners of conditioning," McGoohan observed, "and they were used to writing for The Saint or the Secret Agent series." Several were lost by the wayside.
Virginia Maskell plays the Woman in the episode. Born on February 27, 1936, she had trained at the Webber Douglas School and appeared opposite Peter Sellers in Only Two Can Play (1962). Critics noted a recurring sadness in her performances. She died on January 25, 1968 — four months after "Arrival" aired — at the age of thirty-one.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
This episode was the fourth produced but the eighth broadcast, and it should have been the second or third. Number Six describes himself as relatively new to the Village. He is still aggressively resisting normalization. He has not yet been broken enough to know the shape of his captivity. Placed at eight, after two escape attempts and five interrogations, that rawness reads as regression. The broadcast order betrayed the episode twice — once by burying it, and once by making its internal logic contradict everything around it. McGoohan reportedly fell out of love with it during production. The episode under-ran. The scripted finale — Number Six destroying the Telex machine — was never shot. Film editor John S. Smith reconstructed what existed into something coherent. Smith later said, "That atmosphere was the essence of the series." He was right, and the atmosphere was an accident.
Anthony Skene wrote it — his first Prisoner script, before "Many Happy Returns." He claimed to have been offered a blank slate and to have been inspired by Jean Cocteau and Franz Kafka. The Cocteau surfaces in the radio that Number Six finds on the drowned man: it receives only static and muffled voices, like the car radio in "Orphée" that picks up transmissions from the underworld. The Kafka surfaces everywhere else — the Town Hall that is "choosy about who it allows to enter," the kangaroo court, the circular logic, the punishment without crime. But the episode's deepest source is older than either: the Danse Macabre, the medieval allegory in which Death invites all ranks of society to dance. The carnival ball is the Danse Macabre made literal. Everyone wears a costume — Peter Pan, Napoleon, Little Bo Peep, Caesar, Elizabeth I, a Jester. Number Six is given his own dinner jacket. He alone is not disguised. In the Danse Macabre, the point is that Death strips all disguises. Here, the Village gives everyone a disguise except the one man who won't accept one. His punishment is a mock trial. His sentence is death. But as Number Two tells him: "They don't know you're already dead." The outside world has been sent his corpse — a drowned man altered to look like him — so that no one will come looking. The Village has killed him by making the world believe he died. Identity theft as murder.
Mary Morris played Number Two. Born Mary Lilian Agnes Morris on December 13, 1915, in Lautoka, Fiji. Her father was Herbert Stanley Morris, an Australian-born botanist who served as District Commissioner on Fiji and aide-de-camp to the island's governor, Sir Ernest Bickham Sweet-Escott. He fought in the First World War with the Royal Flying Corps as a second lieutenant and was killed in an aircraft accident in England in 1919. Mary was three years old. She moved to Britain with her mother, Sylvia Ena de Creft-Harford, and trained at RADA.
She made her debut in "Lysistrata" at the Gate Theatre, London, in 1936. She appeared with Leslie Howard in "'Pimpernel' Smith" (1941) — the film about an archaeology professor smuggling intellectuals out of Nazi Germany, made while the real Leslie Howard was alive and two years before his BOAC flight was shot down over the Bay of Biscay by the Luftwaffe. She played Anna Petrovitch in Ealing's "Undercover" (1943), a Serbian guerrilla's wife. On television: Professor Madeleine Dawnay in "A for Andromeda" (1961) and its sequel "The Andromeda Breakthrough" — the Fred Hoyle science fiction drama about a message from space containing instructions to build a computer, then a woman, which was one of the BBC's earliest attempts at serious televised science fiction. She played Queen Margaret in "An Age of Kings" (1960), the BBC's landmark Shakespeare history cycle. Cleopatra in "The Spread of the Eagle" (1963). Lady Macbeth on radio. Elizabeth I on an EMI LP narrating the queen's own words set to contemporary music.
She played Number Two dressed as Peter Pan for the carnival masquerade. This was not an arbitrary costume. She had played Peter Pan on stage in 1946, in a production described as a "radical interpretation of the text" — twenty years before The Prisoner. The casting department did not pick Peter Pan. They picked an actress who had been Peter Pan, and let the audience who knew it feel the vertigo. The boy who never grows up, running a surveillance state. After a twenty-five-year absence from film, she reappeared in "Full Circle" (1977), a horror film about a dead child, and played the shaman Panna opposite Peter Davison in the Doctor Who serial "Kinda" (1982) — a story about a paradise corrupted by colonial contact, which rhymes with The Prisoner more than anyone involved probably intended. She died of heart failure on October 14, 1988, in Aigle, Switzerland, aged seventy-two.
Duncan Macrae played the Doctor who doubles as the Judge in the carnival court — dressed as Napoleon. Born John Duncan Macrae on August 20, 1905, in Maryhill, Glasgow, the fourth of six children of a police sergeant. He attended Allan Glen's School, entered engineering at Glasgow University in 1923, didn't graduate, trained as a schoolteacher at Jordanhill College instead. He taught in Glasgow schools for nearly two decades before turning professional actor in 1943 at thirty-eight — one of those careers that starts late because the person was doing something else entirely and then stops doing it.
He joined the Citizens' Theatre in Glasgow in its founding year, alongside the young Stanley Baxter. He played the title role in Robert McLellan's "Jamie the Saxt" — a performance that became his signature — and Flatterie in the revival of Sir David Lyndsay's sixteenth-century "Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaites," directed by Tyrone Guthrie at the Edinburgh Festival in 1948. He was Angus MacCormac in the Ealing comedy "Whisky Galore!" (1949). Inspector Mathis in "Casino Royale" (1967) — the James Bond spoof with five directors and no coherent plot, which was shooting simultaneously with The Prisoner. He played Pipe Major Maclean in "Tunes of Glory" (1960), opposite Alec Guinness and John Mills. He was a fixture of Scottish Hogmanay television, performing "The Wee Cock Sparra" in broad Glaswegian, a song every Scottish viewer of a certain age knows by heart.
He died in Glasgow on March 23, 1967 — before "Dance of the Dead" aired, before "Casino Royale" was released. He never saw either. He was sixty-one. The episode is haunted by a dead man's performance in a story about a dead man's body repurposed to kill someone else's identity.
Norma West played Number 240, Number Six's observer — his assigned watcher, a woman whose job is surveillance and who is dressed as Little Bo Peep at the carnival. The joke being: Bo Peep lost her sheep. The observer who can't keep track of her subject. West was born on November 19, 1943, in Cape Town, South Africa. She had appeared in "Danger Man" before The Prisoner — like so many of the guest cast, circulating through ITC's stable of shows. Her best-known television role after this was Queen Elizabeth of York in the BBC's "The Shadow of the Tower" (1972).
Aubrey Morris played the Town Crier who doubles as Chief Judge, dressed as Caesar. Born Aubrey Steinberg on June 1, 1926, in Portsmouth — one of nine children in a family from Kiev that fled to Britain in 1890 to escape the pogroms. His father, Morry, had appeared in Jewish vaudeville halls in the East End before the First World War left him severely wounded. His mother was a talented amateur mezzo-soprano who nursed the father for the rest of his life. Aubrey and his elder brother Wolfe both became actors and adopted the surname Morris in tribute to their father's first name. Jeremy Brett once introduced Aubrey to Noël Coward as "the finest small-part player in London."
He won the Leverhulme scholarship to RADA. His professional debut was the Clown in "The Winter's Tale" at Regent's Park Open Air Theatre in 1944. He joined the Old Vic under Tyrone Guthrie — the same Guthrie who'd directed Duncan Macrae in Edinburgh — and played Bardolph to Richard Burton's Henry V in 1955, a production that also ran on Broadway. Then television consumed him: nearly two hundred appearances. He was the Town Crier in this episode, and McGoohan liked him well enough to write a part for him in a never-made film version of The Prisoner. He went on to play Mr. Deltoid in Stanley Kubrick's "A Clockwork Orange" (1971) — the probation officer who lectures a near-naked Malcolm McDowell with unctuous menace — and the chuckling gravedigger in "The Wicker Man" (1973). The jolly captain of the B-Ark in "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" (1981), spending years luxuriating in a bubble bath while the telephone sanitizers orbit a dead planet. And finally, the dying actor Chesterton in HBO's "Deadwood" (2004), being read King Lear as he shuffles off. He moved to America in 1986 and died in Los Angeles on July 15, 2015, aged eighty-nine.
The voice you hear throughout every episode — "Good morning. Good morning. Any complaints?" — the Village's public address announcer, the telephone operator, the disembodied feminine authority that saturates the air of the Village — belonged to Fenella Fielding. Born Fenella Marion Feldman on November 17, 1927, in Whitechapel, London. She was called "England's first lady of the double entendre." She played Valeria in "Carry On Screaming!" (1966), the vampiric seductress. She voiced Madame Blue in "Dougal and the Blue Cat" (1972), the Magic Roundabout film. She was the Village's audio wallpaper — the most pervasive presence in every episode, never seen. She died on September 11, 2018, in London, aged ninety.
"Dance of the Dead" was broadcast on November 17, 1967. That same day, Régis Debray — the French intellectual who had gone to Bolivia to fight alongside Che Guevara's guerrillas — was sentenced to thirty years in prison by a Bolivian military court. Guevara himself had been executed five weeks earlier, on October 9. A man is tried by a kangaroo court in a Village carnival while wearing his own dinner jacket. A philosopher is sentenced to thirty years in a Bolivian courtroom for believing revolution was possible. Neither trial was about justice. Both were about performance. Debray was released after three years. Number Six is still there.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
This was the third episode produced — shot back-to-back with "Dance of the Dead" in September 1966. Its working title was "The Queen's Pawn," a double meaning: the chess piece Number Six is conscripted to play, and the fact that he had recently been in Her Majesty's service. The broadcast order placed it ninth, which is wrong. Number Six describes himself as new to the Village. He is still figuring out who is a prisoner and who is a guard. He hasn't yet abandoned group strategy for solitary resistance. At nine, after eight episodes of solo escapes and cynical loners, the sudden optimism about collective action reads as naïveté rather than calculation. It should have been the second or third episode. The chess game, the recruitment, the betrayal — it's the story of a man who still believes cooperation is possible. By episode nine the audience knows better, even if Number Six doesn't.
The human chess game was Gerald Kelsey's idea. He'd seen a life-size chessboard at a castle in Germany while on holiday and thought it had potential as a dramatic framework — this before he knew about the lawn at Portmeirion. Kelsey was an ITC regular, a steady professional who wrote episodes of "Dixon of Dock Green" for the BBC for twenty years between the mid-1950s and mid-1970s. The chess game in this episode is played on the Gothic Pavilion lawn at Portmeirion. The board was painted directly onto the grass and remained in place for a week during filming. When the squares were removed, the sun-bleached pattern was clearly visible in the lawn for months afterward — you can see the ghost of it in other episodes.
Number Six plays White Queen's Pawn. This is the same piece Alice plays in Lewis Carroll's "Through the Looking-Glass" — the game where Alice crosses the board from pawn to queen, never understanding the rules, never choosing her moves, pushed forward by forces she cannot see. Carroll published it in 1871. A hundred years later, Number Six makes the same crossing and arrives nowhere. His piece is moved back to its starting square by the silent Butler in the final shot — Angelo Muscat, who appears in nearly every episode, who never speaks, who repositions the pawn. The entire series compressed into one image.
The episode's thesis is in the Chess Master's observation: you can tell who is a prisoner and who is a guardian "by their disposition. By the moves they make." Number Six builds a test on this insight — he recruits people who behave like prisoners: nervous, defiant, resentful of authority. He recruits the Rook, who was subjected to Pavlovian conditioning in the hospital. The Rook helps him build a radio from pilfered parts. They hail a passing ship with a false Mayday. The escape comes closer to working than any other in the series. Then the Rook betrays him. Not because the Rook is a plant — because Number Six behaves like a guardian. He gives orders. He controls information. He tells people what to do without explaining why. His disposition is authority. By the Rook's own test — the test Number Six taught him — Number Six is a jailer, not a prisoner. The irony is structural. The qualities that make Number Six capable of leading an escape are the same qualities that make him indistinguishable from the people who run the Village.
Peter Wyngarde played Number Two — the most mysterious biography in the history of British television. His name until 1945 was Cyril Goldbert. His birthdate is genuinely unknown. He claimed not to know his own age in a 1993 interview. Official documents variously record his birth year as 1927, 1928, or 1929. He told journalists 1933. His death registration says 1927 and Singapore. He told everyone Marseilles. His biographer concluded Marseilles, 1928. He arrived in England from Shanghai on the SS Arawa on December 14, 1945, listed as eighteen years old, next of kin a Mr. H. Goldbert care of the Ministry of Shipping, London.
His father was Henry Goldbert, born 1897, a citizen of the Russian Empire naturalized as a British subject in Singapore in 1919, where his family — Marco Goldbert and Rosa Klivger — ran a hotel on North Bridge Road. The surname Goldbert is exceptionally rare: about 118 people worldwide use it, nearly half in Israel. The family likely originated in Mykolaiv, now in Ukraine, then a port of the Russian Empire whose population was roughly twenty percent Jewish in the late nineteenth century.
His mother was Marcheritta Marie Ahin, known as Madge, from a Eurasian family in Singapore. She told a newspaper she was French. She and Henry Goldbert separated by 1937. Wyngarde grew up in Shanghai, attended the Western District Public School for Boys in the French Concession, and during the Japanese occupation was interned at the Lunghua Civilian Assembly Centre — the same camp that held J.G. Ballard, the same camp that became "Empire of the Sun." Ballard was a boy; Wyngarde was a teenager. They were interned together and Ballard later named him in interviews. Wyngarde left Shanghai for England in 1945 and reinvented himself completely. Cyril Goldbert — child of Russian-Jewish and Eurasian parentage, internee of the Japanese, citizen of nowhere in particular — became Peter Wyngarde, British actor, style icon, and man of impenetrable mystery.
He played Jason King in "Department S" (1969) and its spinoff "Jason King" (1971) — the velvet-jacketed spy novelist whose flamboyance became a template for Austin Powers. General Klytus in Flash Gordon (1980). Timanov in the Doctor Who serial "Planet of Fire" (1984). In 1975 he was convicted of gross indecency at a bus station in Gloucester. His career never fully recovered. He lived alone in Chelsea and died on January 15, 2018, aged eighty-nine or ninety — nobody is certain which.
Wyngarde claimed that McGoohan originally planned a permanent Number Two and selected him for the role, before deciding that rotating the actor would add mystery. Whether this is true cannot be verified. What is visible is that his Number Two is one of the most physically distinctive in the series — meditating in his office, then abruptly shattering planks with karate chops, for reasons the episode never explains and never uses. Chekhov's karate goes unfired.
Ronald Radd played the Rook, the nervous man who becomes Number Six's most important recruit and then his betrayer. Born in Ryhope, Sunderland, on January 22, 1929. Stage debut at the Alexandra Theatre, Birmingham, in the early 1950s alongside Leslie Sands and Edward Mulhare. He appeared with Kenneth Williams in two productions at the Apollo Theatre in 1956. By 1958 he was on Broadway in "My Fair Lady." He gradually abandoned theatre for television and appeared in some sixty shows over two decades. His most important role was Hunter in the one-off "Armchair Theatre" play "A Magnum for Schneider" (1967) — the pilot that became "Callan," the spy series starring Edward Woodward about a reluctant assassin working for a morally bankrupt government department. The irony being that Radd originated the role of the spymaster and then appeared in "The Prisoner" as the man who cannot tell spymasters from prisoners. He was nominated for a Tony for "Abelard and Heloise" in 1971. He died of a brain haemorrhage in Toronto in 1976 at forty-seven.
George Coulouris played the Man with a Stick — credited as such, no number, an old man on a bench in the Village who watches the chess game. Born George Alexander Coulouris on October 1, 1903, in Manchester, of Anglo-Greek parentage. Educated at Manchester Grammar School. Stage debut in "Henry V" at the Old Vic in 1926. In 1936 he met Orson Welles in "Ten Million Ghosts" on Broadway. Welles recruited him for the Mercury Theatre, and Coulouris played Mark Antony in the company's debut production — "Caesar," the modern-dress Julius Caesar that drew explicit parallels to Fascist Italy. Then Citizen Kane. Coulouris played Walter Parks Thatcher, the guardian banker, the man who controls young Kane's fortune and tries to control Kane himself. Twenty-six years later he sat on a bench in a Welsh village playing a man with a stick, watching a chess game he understood perfectly. He played Arbitan in the 1964 Doctor Who serial "The Keys of Marinus." He appeared in "Papillon" (1973), "Murder on the Orient Express" (1974), and over eighty other films. He died in London in 1989, aged eighty-five.
Rosalie Crutchley played the Queen — the woman on the chessboard who is brainwashed into falling in love with Number Six, and whom Number Six then uses and discards. Born Rosalie Sylvia Crutchley on January 4, 1920, in London. Trained at the Royal Academy of Music. She had dark, piercing eyes and was cast as sinister or foreign women for her entire career. She played Madame Defarge in two separate "Tale of Two Cities" adaptations — the 1958 film and the 1965 BBC serial. She played Amalia Freud, Sigmund's mother, in John Huston's "Freud: The Secret Passion" (1962). Mrs Dudley, the unnerving housekeeper, in Robert Wise's "The Haunting" (1963) — the greatest haunted house film ever made. Catherine Parr in "The Six Wives of Henry VIII" (1970) and again in "Elizabeth R" (1971). Somaya in Moustapha Akkad's "The Message" (1976) — the epic about the birth of Islam. Her final role was the pilot episode of "Midsomer Murders" in 1997, shortly before her death at seventy-seven. She played queens, housekeepers, mothers, and Madame Defarge twice. In this episode she played a woman brainwashed into love, and the man she loved used her technology to try to escape and didn't look back.
"Checkmate" aired on November 24, 1967. Six days later, on November 30, the last British troops left Aden — ending 128 years of colonial occupation, handing power to the National Liberation Front, and creating the People's Republic of South Yemen. An empire was folding its chess pieces and leaving the board. "Incense and Peppermints" by the Strawberry Alarm Clock was the number one song in America. "Baby Now That I've Found You" by the Foundations was number one in Britain. Sam and Dave's "Soul Man" was number one on the R&B chart. The Graduate had just opened in theaters. Number Six was moved back to his starting square by a mute butler who never speaks. The game continued.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Leo McKern lost his left eye in a factory accident when he was fifteen years old. He was working in a Sydney factory — he hadn't wanted to; he'd wanted to act — and something went wrong, and that was that. A glass eye for the rest of his life. He went on to become an engineering apprentice, then an artist, then a sapper with the Royal Australian Engineers during the war, and finally, in 1944, he stood on a stage in Sydney for the first time. He fell in love with an Australian actress named Jane Holland, followed her to England, married her in 1946, and — despite the glass eye, despite the accent that marked him as colonial — talked his way into the Old Vic and the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre at Stratford-upon-Avon. By 1952 he was playing Iago. By 1960 he had originated the role of Common Man in Robert Bolt's "A Man for All Seasons" in the West End, then switched to Thomas Cromwell for the Broadway transfer and the 1966 film. He played Clang, the high priest, in the Beatles' "Help!" He played Bugenhagen in "The Omen." He would eventually become Horace Rumpole, the role that devoured all others — "If I get an obit in any paper," he once said, "they will say, 'of course, known to millions as Rumpole.'" He was right. He died in Bath in 2002, aged eighty-two, terrified of flying to the end, booking passage on cargo ships whenever he needed to cross an ocean. He suffered from stage fright that worsened with age.
But in the autumn of 1966, McKern was on a soundstage at MGM-British Studios in Borehamwood, playing the second Number Two in the series and the first one anyone would remember. Where Guy Doleman's Number Two in "Arrival" had been a cold instrument of bureaucratic power, McKern's is something warmer and more dangerous: a man who genuinely enjoys the contest. He treats Number Six like a chess opponent — not an enemy to be crushed but a puzzle to be solved, a mind to be cracked open for the pleasure of watching what's inside. "A man can enjoy the pleasure of his work," McKern's Number Two tells Six. He means it. The enjoyment is the point. This is the performance that established the rotating-Number-Two concept as something more than a gimmick: each new Number Two would bring a different philosophy of control, a different theory of what makes a prisoner break.
McKern would return twice — for "Once Upon a Time" and the finale, "Fall Out." The filming of "Once Upon a Time" nearly killed him. The episode required McKern and McGoohan to perform an increasingly unhinged psychological duel over seven days of shooting, locked in a cage set, improvising for stretches, pushing each other to extremes. According to Robert Fairclough's "The Prisoner: The Official Companion," the strain caused McKern to suffer either a nervous breakdown or a heart attack — accounts differ, and McKern himself never clarified publicly. Production stopped. When he recovered enough to continue, he reportedly told McGoohan he never wanted to work with him again. McGoohan convinced him to come back for one more.
The script is by Vincent Tilsley — born 1931, a television writer since the 1950s, more than a hundred scripts over twenty years. He wasn't one of the regular ITC stable writers, which is probably why McGoohan and Markstein wanted him. He'd most recently written for the BBC's "Z Cars." He wrote one more Prisoner episode — "Do Not Forsake Me Oh My Darling," the odd body-swap episode filmed while McGoohan was away shooting "Ice Station Zebra" — and continued writing through the early 1970s. When ITV cut his 1973 series "The Death of Adolf Hitler" from six hours to two, he quit television permanently and became a psychotherapist. He died in September 2013, aged eighty-one.
Don Chaffey directs again — his second of four Prisoner episodes, after "Arrival." The Portmeirion location footage was shot at the end of September 1966, with studio work at MGM Borehamwood in late November. You can tell the difference: the beach scenes and the forested area where Number Six constructs his sculpture are visibly studio-bound, the lighting too even, the backgrounds too still. The courtyard set containing the Exhibition Hall was repurposed from "The Dirty Dozen," which had been shot at the same studio earlier that year. The interior of the exhibition hall was yet another redressing of the versatile Control Room set.
Nadia Gray plays Number Eight — the beautiful, apparently frightened new arrival who tells Number Six she knows where the Village is: the Baltic coast of Lithuania, thirty miles from the Polish border. Born Nadia Kujnir-Herescu in Bucharest, she had fled Romania for Paris in the late 1940s to escape the Communist takeover. Her first husband was Constantin Cantacuzino, a Romanian fighter ace and one of the most decorated pilots of the Second World War — she met him while she was a passenger on one of his commercial flights. By the mid-1960s she had accumulated a filmography that ranged across French, Italian, and British cinema. Her most famous role was the woman who performs the striptease at the party in Fellini's "La Dolce Vita" (1960). In "The Chimes of Big Ben," she plays a woman whose entire biography is a fabrication — a Village operative posing as a fellow prisoner, deployed to earn Number Six's trust and extract his secrets through manufactured intimacy. McGoohan, characteristically, refused to allow the script to depict a full love affair between Six and Eight; the same discomfort with on-screen romance had cost him the role of James Bond and had been a perpetual source of tension on "Danger Man."
Finlay Currie appears as the General — eighty years old at the time of filming, born in Edinburgh in 1878, a veteran of over a hundred films. He had played Magwitch in David Lean's "Great Expectations" (1946), Saint Peter in "Quo Vadis" (1951), and Balthazar in William Wyler's "Ben-Hur" (1959). He died in May 1968, seven months after this episode aired.
Richard Wattis plays Fotheringay, who appears to be Number Six's friend and former superior in British intelligence. In an earlier cut of the episode, their backstory is established — they were at school together — but this was trimmed from the broadcast version. There's a connection here that the attentive viewer of "Danger Man" would have caught: Wattis had played John Drake's boss in the original thirty-minute episodes of that series. His presence in The Prisoner's fake London office is either a deliberate wink at the Drake-is-Six theory or a characteristically sly piece of McGoohan casting.
The voice you hear throughout the Village — the relentlessly cheerful announcements encouraging participation in community activities — belongs to Fenella Fielding, though she's never seen on screen. Born Fenella Feldman in Whitechapel in 1927 to Romanian Jewish and Lithuanian Jewish parents, she was famous for her husky, insinuating voice: the sound of the Carry On films at their most suggestive. Here, that voice becomes something else entirely — the purr of totalitarianism disguised as hospitality. "Good morning, good morning, good morning! Any complaints?" She recorded all her lines in a single session and never appeared on set.
The episode's central mechanism is brilliant in its simplicity. Number Six builds an abstract sculpture for the Village arts competition — every other entry is a flattering portrait of Number Two, because in a dictatorship the only sanctioned art is propaganda — and wins first prize. His sculpture is titled "Escape." It is, literally, a boat. He and Nadia sail away in it. They are packed into a crate. They travel by sea and air. They arrive in London. Number Six is reunited with his old colleagues. He is about to reveal why he resigned — the one piece of information every Number Two has sought — when he hears Big Ben chiming. He checks his borrowed watch. The time is wrong. If they had really traveled from Lithuania to London, there would be a one-hour time difference. There isn't. He opens the office door and finds himself back in the Village.
The craftsmanship of the trap is the episode's argument: the Village doesn't just imprison the body. It constructs entire realities, complete with borrowed watches and tape-recorded traffic noise, and trusts that the prisoner's own desperation to be free will do the rest. Number Six's escape was real in every way except the one that mattered. The Village gave him everything he wanted — London, his colleagues, the chance to finally speak — and then let Big Ben's chimes pull the thread. The prison is made of hope.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Patrick McGoohan wrote this episode under the name "Paddy Fitz." "Paddy" is the standard Irish diminutive of Patrick. "Fitz" is from Fitzpatrick, his mother's maiden name. He used the pseudonym because he was already starring in every frame and producing the series and didn't want to be seen writing it too — not out of modesty, but because Lew Grade's ITC might have wondered whether one man controlling a show this completely was a risk or a symptom. (He also directed episodes as "Joseph Serf," because one pseudonym apparently wasn't enough.) Don Chaffey was originally set to direct "Free for All." McGoohan took over after they had what the Episode by Episode blog calls "a huge disagreement about how to go about the filming." The Unmutual website softens it slightly: Chaffey "was responsible for some sequences." Either way, McGoohan seized the chair. This was the second episode produced — one of the earliest things shot — and he was already directing himself in his own scripts under a fake name. The pattern was set.
The episode is about elections. Made in 1966, a British election year. Number Six is invited to run for the office of Number Two. It is presented as an opportunity: if he wins, he'll finally meet Number One. He campaigns, and the campaign is a machine. The election posters announcing his candidacy are already printed before he agrees to run. The Tally Ho interview has already been written. A journalist rides alongside him in a mini-moke, and when Number Six answers every question with "No comment," the journalist simply invents answers. When Number Six finally volunteers a substantive response, it's printed as "No comment." McGoohan was not subtle about the press.
The foreign language spoken by Number Fifty-Eight — the perky, apparently dim assistant assigned to Number Six — is gibberish. Not a real Slavic language, not a dialect, not a constructed tongue: "a meaningless linguistic pastiche specially invented by the scriptwriters," as one academic study of the show phrases it. Rachel Herbert spent the entire episode performing enthusiastic nonsense syllables and physical comedy, and then, in the final scene, switched to clipped, perfect English to reveal herself as the actual incoming Number Two. The "previous" Number Two — the avuncular, seemingly powerful Eric Portman — had been a stooge the entire time. Herbert was already a regular on William Greatorex's "The Power Game" (1965–69), playing a role in a series about corporate power struggles and the unelected forces that shape British life. McGoohan, whether he knew this or not, had cast someone who was already working inside a show about hidden power structures and put her in a role about hidden power structures. The casting rhyme is almost too neat.
Eric Portman was sixty-five when he filmed this, and visibly unwell. Born in Halifax, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, in 1901, the son of a wool merchant. Educated at Rishworth School. At twenty-one he was selling menswear at the Marshall & Snelgrove department store in Leeds and performing in the Halifax Light Opera Society. His professional debut came in 1924 with Henry Baynton's company; the same year he made his West End debut as Antipholus of Syracuse in "The Comedy of Errors" at the Savoy Theatre. Lilian Baylis hired him for the Old Vic. By 1928 he was playing Romeo. By 1933 he was on stage with Gerald du Maurier and Basil Rathbone.
His film career was defined by Powell and Pressburger. He played Lieutenant Hirth, a Nazi on the run through Canada, in "49th Parallel" (1941), and the role made him a star overnight. He followed it with "One of Our Aircraft Is Missing" (1942) and then "A Canterbury Tale" (1944), Powell's strange, lyrical meditation on England and landscape, in which Portman played Thomas Colpeper, the local magistrate who pours glue in women's hair at night — one of the most unsettling sympathetic characters in British cinema. The BFI called him "an unlikely box-office attraction" whose audiences "admired his polished, distinctive voice (both gritty and reedy) and portrayals of disturbed, complex characters." In 1945 and 1946, exhibitors voted him the tenth most popular star at the British box office.
He crossed to Broadway for Terence Rattigan's "Separate Tables" in 1956, playing the bogus Major Pollock — a man pretending to be something he isn't, clinging to a fraudulent identity in a residential hotel — and received a Tony nomination for Best Actor. He played Rochester in "Jane Eyre" on Broadway (it flopped), then had a long run in Eugene O'Neill's "A Touch of the Poet." He claimed — through his assistant, the screenwriter Norman Hudis — that in 1937, Joachim von Ribbentrop, then the German Ambassador to Britain, had told him over dinner in London that "when Germany wins the war, Portman would be installed as the greatest English star in the New Europe" at a purpose-built film studio in Berlin.
By 1966, Portman was nearing the end. On the Portmeirion location shoot for "Free for All," held in mid-September, he couldn't remember his dialogue. McGoohan solved this by placing large "idiot boards" — cue cards — out of shot for Portman to read from. The speedboat chase sequence was filmed with doubles, the stunt work handled by Brian Axworthy, a local man from Porthmadog who owned the jet boat used in the scene. The Rover balloon was released from the bottom of the estuary by Axworthy, diving. Portman died in December 1969, at sixty-eight, of heart disease, at his home in St Veep, Cornwall. He was buried in the parish church. Decades after his death it emerged that he had been gay; his partner was Knox Laing, an assistant director, who died in 1974.
The episode's thesis is simple and brutal: democracy in a controlled system is indistinguishable from theater. Number Six wins the election. Every citizen votes for him. He walks into the Green Dome, the seat of power, and attempts to broadcast to the Village that they are free. "You are free to go!" he shouts. "Obey me and be free!" And in that sentence — "Obey me" — he becomes the thing he fought. The mechanics in coveralls beat him senseless. Number Fifty-Eight, who has been babbling in fake Slavic all episode, addresses him in perfect English. She is Number Two. The election was a script. He performed his role. The establishment didn't just survive his rebellion; it wrote it.
McGoohan was not optimistic about democracy. He thought voting was a ritual that pacified populations into believing they had agency while power remained where it always was. This isn't cynicism dressed as art; it's a conviction the episode earns through structure. Every institution Number Six encounters — the press, the Labour Exchange, the Council, the cave where a supposedly rebellious Number Two drowns his sorrows in illegal liquor — is a layer of the same apparatus. Even the underground alternative is managed. The counterculture is a franchise. The opposition is a subsidiary.
"Free for All" got 11.1 million viewers on its first UK broadcast. In Wales, they didn't see it until January 1970.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
The first twenty minutes of this episode contain no dialogue. None. Number Six wakes up, discovers the Village is empty, builds a raft out of timber and oil drums, and puts to sea. He says nothing because there is no one to talk to, and Patrick McGoohan was not the kind of actor who would talk to himself for the benefit of an audience. The silence is the episode's thesis: the absence of other people is the absence of language. Language is a social technology. Alone, you don't need it. Twenty minutes of a network television drama in 1967 with no words — just a man working with his hands, the sound of wood and rope and wind. It is the most radical sequence in the entire series, and nobody fought it.
Anthony Skene wrote it. Born September 17, 1924, in Brentford, Middlesex. He also wrote "Dance of the Dead" for The Prisoner — the only writer to contribute two scripts to the series besides McGoohan himself and Lewis Greifer. Before television he wrote pulp fiction and comic books. His television credits include "Journey to the Unknown" (the 1968 Hammer Films anthology series), Brian Clemens' "Thriller" (the 1973 series, not the later American one), and "Doris Lessing's Each His Own Wilderness" for ITV's "Sunday Night Theatre." He died February 27, 2000. Almost nothing is written about him. No Wikipedia article. No interviews. No obituary I can find. He wrote two of the seventeen episodes of one of the most analyzed television series ever produced, and he's a ghost.
He wrote this episode as a possible series finale — "Number Six gets out, but has to be recaptured, in case the show continues." It was the thirteenth episode produced, originally intended to close the first filming block. ITV broadcast it seventh. That's the wrong place for it. By episode seven you've only seen one escape attempt (Chimes of Big Ben), so this reads as a retread. Placed at thirteen, after a run of increasingly abstract episodes where Number Six never comes close to leaving, the sheer physical directness of it — building a raft, fighting gunrunners, hitching on a lorry — would have landed with real force. The broadcast order buried it.
The escape itself is extraordinary. Twenty-five days at sea on a raft made of Village materials. Gunrunners steal his belongings and throw him overboard. He climbs back aboard their boat, fights them, commandeers it, is overpowered again, and washes up on a beach somewhere in southern Europe. Romani travellers who speak no English. Then a British policeman — and suddenly he's running again, because anyone in uniform might be one of them. He stows away on a truck. He reaches London. He makes his way to his own front door — 1 Buckingham Place, the house from the title sequence — and finds a woman living in it, driving his car.
Mrs. Butterworth. Georgina Cookson played her — born Antoinette Georgina Cookson on December 19, 1918, in Mevagissey, Cornwall. Her father was the racing driver Roger Cookson. Her mother, Sybil, wrote novels under the pseudonym Sydney Tremayne and contributed to The Tatler. Georgina was the great-granddaughter of Sir James Crichton-Browne, the Victorian psychiatrist who corresponded with Charles Darwin and was an early investigator of brain localization. She left Benenden School at fifteen to train at RADA. She was married four times — twice divorced, twice widowed. Her film work included John Schlesinger's "Darling" (1965), playing Carlotta Hale alongside Julie Christie, Dirk Bogarde, and Laurence Harvey. In the same year: "Catacombs," also known as "The Woman Who Wouldn't Die." She had appeared in "Danger Man" before The Prisoner, playing Miss Bishop in "The Trap" — which is how ITC shows worked: the same pool of actors circulated through the same producers' shows, and you might play a guest villain one month and a Number Two the next. In fact she appeared in The Prisoner twice: as the unnamed blonde woman in "A. B. and C." (episode three) and as Mrs. Butterworth here. She died in Sydney, Australia, on October 1, 2011, aged ninety-two.
Mrs. Butterworth feeds Number Six, gives him clothes, lends him her car — his car, really — and sends him off to report to his superiors. She mentions his birthday. He had not mentioned his birthday. That's the tell, if you're paying attention.
He goes to the underground car park from the title sequence and presents himself to the man behind the desk — who is, as always, George Markstein, the series' script editor, playing himself. This was the last episode Markstein worked on. He left after the first thirteen productions, citing irreconcilable creative differences with McGoohan over the show's direction. Markstein wanted a spy drama grounded in the real tradecraft he knew from his intelligence background — he was the one who'd heard about Inverlair Lodge, the actual wartime "village" in the Scottish Highlands where compromised agents were kept, and pitched it to McGoohan as a series premise. McGoohan wanted allegory, abstraction, philosophy. Markstein wanted to know who Number One was. McGoohan didn't think that was the point. The divorce was inevitable, and this was the last episode they made together. Markstein's appearance in the title sequence — the anonymous bureaucrat behind the desk who receives Number Six's resignation — is the most ironic piece of casting in the series. The man who conceived the show appears in every episode as the functionary who triggers the plot, but whose face is never identified. He went on to write novels: "The Cooler" (1974), whose title refers to Inverlair Lodge itself, and "The Goering Testament." He died on January 15, 1987, in Uxbridge, aged fifty-four.
The Colonel and Thorpe receive Number Six with careful suspicion. Donald Sinden played the Colonel. Born October 9, 1923, in Plymouth, Devon — the middle child of a chemist whose shop was called "The Limes" in Ditchling, East Sussex. He failed his eleven-plus. He made his first stage appearance in 1941, stepping into a part in place of his cousin Frank, who'd been called up.
