Rejected for naval service because of asthma, he joined a theatrical company that entertained troops along the south coast. In 1942, in Hove, he befriended Lord Alfred Douglas — "Bosie" — Oscar Wilde's lover. Douglas was seventy-one, living out his last years, and had by then converted to Catholicism, written bitter repudiations of Wilde, un-repudiated them, and settled into a quiet dotage among friends who included John Betjeman, Malcolm Muggeridge, and Terence Rattigan. Sinden is believed to have been the last surviving person to have known Douglas. He carried that connection — a handshake from Oscar Wilde through one intermediary — into a career that spanned seven decades. "The Cruel Sea" (1953) made him a star overnight. The Rank Organisation signed him for seven years. He played Benskin in the "Doctor" films. He played the Duke of York in "The Wars of the Roses" opposite Peggy Ashcroft. He won the Evening Standard Best Actor award for "King Lear" in 1977. Then, with the timing of a man who understood that gravity is optional, he reinvented himself as a sitcom star: "Two's Company" (1975-79) and "Never the Twain" (1981-91). He was knighted in 1997. His son Jeremy Sinden also became an actor and died young, in 1996, of lung cancer. His other son Marc became a producer. Sinden died September 12, 2014, at ninety, at his home in Wittersham, Kent.
Patrick Cargill played Thorpe — Number Six's former colleague who is shifty, ambiguous, and clearly knows more than he lets on. Born Edward Sydney Patrick Cargill on June 3, 1918, in Bexhill-on-Sea, Sussex. Educated at Haileybury College. Trained at Sandhurst. Served as a commissioned officer in the British Indian Army during the war. Came home to act. Joined Anthony Hawtrey's company, worked repertory at Windsor, performed in a revue seen by the Queen and twenty-six of her guests. He became the doctor who clashes with Tony Hancock in "The Blood Donor" (1961) — one of the most beloved episodes of British television comedy. His play "Ring for Catty," co-written with Jack Beale, was adapted into "Carry On Nurse" (1959), the second Carry On film. He appeared in Charlie Chaplin's final film, "A Countess from Hong Kong" (1967). He starred in "Father, Dear Father" (1968-73), which was written specifically for him. And he returned to The Prisoner as the Number Two in "Hammer Into Anvil" — which was shot before this episode but broadcast after it, creating one of the show's deepest continuity puzzles: Thorpe in "Many Happy Returns" is a colleague from Number Six's old life who seems complicit in the recapture. Number Two in "Hammer Into Anvil" is a bullying sadist whom Number Six systematically destroys. Are they the same man? If Thorpe was always Village, was his Number Two posting a promotion or a punishment? Cargill never played them as the same character, but the casting says what the script doesn't. He died May 23, 1996, in Richmond, London, aged seventy-seven.
Director credit: Joseph Serf. Which is McGoohan. The shoot began under Michael Truman — a producer-director who'd worked with Ealing Studios — but Truman dropped out after several days, citing illness. McGoohan stepped in to finish the location work himself, under his pseudonym. Since he was also the only cast member for most of the outdoor sequences, he was directing himself in silence on location in Portmeirion and London in March 1967. March 19 was McGoohan's birthday, and it's written into the script: the London scenes are set on March 18, and Number Six mentions to Mrs. Butterworth that "tomorrow is my birthday." She says she might even bake him a cake. She does. She delivers it to his cottage in the Village, wearing a Number Two badge, and says "Many happy returns." The title is the cruelty.
"Many Happy Returns" was broadcast on November 10, 1967. That day, the ATS-3 satellite took the first full-disk true-color photograph of the Earth from space — the whole planet, in actual color, for the first time. A man escapes an artificial world and makes it home, only to be returned. A camera in orbit sees the real world whole for the first time. The scale mismatch is perfect: the satellite says, look how big reality is. The episode says, it doesn't matter how big reality is if you can't stay in it.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Terence Feely sold a script to Alfred Hitchcock in 1955. He was twenty-seven, a Fleet Street journalist who'd come to London from Liverpool's Jesuit College, where the Jesuits had taught him English and psychology — not a bad curriculum for someone who would spend the next forty-five years writing television about surveillance, paranoia, and women who are smarter than the systems that employ them. He'd started at a small paper in Middlesbrough and worked his way to the Sunday Graphic. Then television swallowed him. By 1961 he was writing for "The Avengers." By 1967 he was co-director of Everyman Films alongside Patrick McGoohan and David Tomblin — "The Prisoner" was partly his company's production. He wrote two episodes. This is the first.
"The Schizoid Man" is about the theft of identity through conditioning. Number Six is drugged, subjected to electroshock therapy, his handedness reversed from right to left, his tastes in food and cigarettes altered, his hair restyled and dyed. He wakes up believing it is the next morning. It has been weeks. He is told he is Number Twelve — a Village agent assigned to impersonate Number Six. The real Number Six, he is informed, is already here. And there he is: same face, same build, same voice, wearing a negative-image blazer (black piping on white where Number Six wears white piping on black). The double knows things only Number Six would know. The double passes tests Number Six now fails. The double is, by every metric the Village can devise, more Number Six than Number Six.
McGoohan plays both roles, and the performance is surgical. Number Six is bewildered, then furious, then quietly desperate. Number Twelve is smooth, amused, precise — a man entirely at home in someone else's life. The technical apparatus was primitive: split-screen photography and Frank Maher, McGoohan's regular stunt double since "Danger Man," standing in for whichever Number was facing away from camera. The fight between the two McGoohans — Number Six grappling with his own stolen self — was choreographed to hide the seams, and it works. You forget you're watching one man and a trick.
The identity theft fails because of a bruised fingernail. In the episode's opening scene, before the conditioning begins, Number Twenty-Four — Alison, a young woman practicing a mind-reading act for the Village festival — accidentally damages Number Six's left thumbnail while photographing him. The bruise is still growing out weeks later when Number Six awakens as "Number Twelve." Neither Number Two nor the real Number Twelve noticed it. The entire apparatus of conditioning, electroshock, taste alteration, and handedness reversal is defeated by a thumbnail. McGoohan understood that identity doesn't live in preferences or habits or even handedness. It lives in the body's own calendar: the slow, biological fact of a bruise working its way to the edge of a nail.
This is also the only episode in the entire run where the white balloon is called by name. Number Two orders "Deactivate Rover." Later, when Curtis — the real Number Twelve, who has been impersonating Number Six — is killed trying to escape, the report comes back: "Rover got him." Across 17 episodes and 197 more appearances, the balloon is never named again. The show felt no need to explain what it was. It was simply there — vast, white, suffocating, bouncing across the beach like a nursery toy designed by a totalitarian state.
Anton Rodgers played Number Two. Born Anthony Rodgers in London in 1933, he was on stage by fourteen — his West End debut was in "Carmen" at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, in 1947. He was a boy in the chorus. The same year he toured as Pip in "Great Expectations" and then took the title role in a revival of Rattigan's "The Winslow Boy." He trained at the Italia Conti Academy and then LAMDA. By the mid-1960s he'd been through Birmingham rep, Northampton rep, Hornchurch rep, and a Broadway run of the musical "Pickwick" (he played Mr Jingle at the Saville Theatre in 1963, then took it to the 46th Street Theatre in New York in 1965). He played Vladimir in "Waiting for Godot" in Manchester, directed "The Fantasticks" at Hampstead, played Macheath in "The Threepenny Opera" at Stratford Ontario, Dr Rank in "A Doll's House" at the Criterion, Henry V in Coventry, Lord Henry Wotton in "The Picture of Dorian Gray" at Greenwich, and Astrov in "Uncle Vanya" at the Oxford Playhouse. His film career included "The Day of the Jackal" (1973) and "Dirty Rotten Scoundrels" (1988), where he played Andre, the comically corrupt French policeman who enables Michael Caine's schemes. He sang "Thank You Very Much" in "Scrooge" (1970), which got an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song. But television audiences knew him as the warm, exasperated husband in "Fresh Fields" (1984–86) and the gentle solicitor in "May to December" (1989–94) — the kind of actor who spent decades doing Ibsen, Shaw, and Wilde on stage while becoming famous for sitcoms. His second wife was the actress Elizabeth Garvie, who had played Elizabeth Bennet in the 1980 BBC "Pride and Prejudice." They toured together doing Jane Austen readings. He died in Reading, Berkshire, in December 2007, aged seventy-four. He was a patron of the Angles Theatre in Wisbech, the town where his family had been evacuated during the war — his father had worked for Balding and Mansell, printers of ration books, permits and passes.
Jane Merrow played Alison, Number Twenty-Four. Born Jane Josephine Meirowsky in Hertfordshire in 1941, daughter of an English mother and a German-Jewish refugee father — "My father's side of the family were ethnically Jewish, but not practising," she said later. She studied at RADA, won the Shakespeare Cup at the Kent Drama Festival, and by 1963 was starring in the BBC's "Lorna Doone." Then the ITC circuit absorbed her: "Danger Man," "The Saint," "The Baron," "The Avengers." After her penultimate-episode appearance in the 1967 series of "The Avengers" ("Mission... Highly Improbable"), she was considered as Diana Rigg's replacement. The role went to Linda Thorson instead. In 1965 she had played Julia in a Theatre 625 adaptation of Orwell's "Nineteen Eighty-Four." The following year she was in "Night of the Big Heat" with Peter Cushing and Christopher Lee. Then came "The Prisoner," and then the role that should have made her a star: Alais, the mistress of Henry II, opposite Peter O'Toole in "The Lion in Winter" (1968). She received a Golden Globe nomination for Best Supporting Actress. She lost to Ruth Gordon for "Rosemary's Baby." After that, Hammer's "Hands of the Ripper" (1971), then America — guest spots on "Mission: Impossible," "Mannix," "The Six Million Dollar Man," "Magnum, P.I.," "MacGyver," "Airwolf," the entire grid of 1970s and '80s American television procedurals. She returned to Britain in the 1990s to run a family business. In 2006 and 2008, she went back to Portmeirion for Prisoner conventions.
Earl Cameron played the Supervisor. He was born in Pembroke, Bermuda, in 1917, the youngest of six children. He joined the merchant navy, landed in Britain, became a song-and-dance man with ENSA during the war, worked in repertory, and then in 1951 was cast in "Pool of London," an Ealing Studios film noir directed by Basil Dearden. He played a West Indian merchant seaman in a relationship with a young white woman — the first time an interracial romance had been sensitively handled in a British film. The BFI calls it a milestone. From there: "Simba" (1955) with Dirk Bogarde, "Thunderball" (1965) as Bond's local contact Pinder, four episodes of "Danger Man" with McGoohan, "Doctor Who" (1966, "The Tenth Planet" — the First Doctor's regeneration story), and then "The Prisoner." In 2005, at eighty-eight, he played a dictatorial president opposite Nicole Kidman in Sydney Pollack's "The Interpreter." In 2010, at ninety-three, he appeared in Christopher Nolan's "Inception." He was appointed CBE in 2009. He died in 2020, aged 102.
Pat Jackson directed. Born Patrick Douglas Selmes Jackson in Eltham in 1916, he joined the GPO Film Unit on his seventeenth birthday as a messenger boy — his mother had persuaded her MP, Sir Kingsley Wood (who also happened to be the Postmaster General), to find work for her son after his father's early death. He worked on "Night Mail" (1936); the voice narrating W.H. Auden's poem ("This is the Night Mail crossing the border, bringing the cheque and the postal order") was Jackson himself. He directed "Western Approaches" (1944), a semi-documentary about merchant seamen that took three years to complete, with six months of lifeboat sequences shot at sea. After the war, three years under contract at MGM in Hollywood. He directed four episodes of "The Prisoner" — more than anyone except McGoohan. He died in 2011, aged ninety-five.
"The Schizoid Man" was broadcast on October 27, 1967. That same day in Baltimore, four men — Philip Berrigan, Thomas Lewis, David Eberhardt, and James Mengel — walked into a Selective Service office on South Gay Street and poured their blood over draft files. Berrigan was a Josephite priest. He had brought duck blood mixed with his own. The "Baltimore Four" action was the first in what would become a series of increasingly dramatic draft-file destructions — seven months later, Berrigan and eight others would burn 378 files with homemade napalm in Catonsville, Maryland, an act that would define the Catholic antiwar left for a generation. In London, "Hair" had just opened off-Broadway six days earlier. "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead" was in its second week on Broadway. The March on the Pentagon had happened six days before — fifty thousand people, Norman Mailer among them, besieging the military headquarters for two days. The Patterson-Gimlin Bigfoot film had been shot a week earlier at Bluff Creek, California. And Walt Disney's "The Jungle Book" had been in theaters for nine days, the last film Walt personally supervised before his death eleven months earlier. In the Village, Number Six was fighting a man who looked exactly like him for the right to be himself.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Lewis Greifer was born in London's East End on December 19, 1915, into a poor Jewish family. He was orphaned at fourteen and raised by his grandmother. He started in journalism, became editor of the Hampstead News in 1947, then moved to the London Evening Standard as a reporter from 1952 to 1956. Between the orphaning and the reporting, the war had happened — he served in the Royal Air Force, was posted to Palestine, and met his wife Nan there. They married in 1947 and had two sons, Adam and Josh. He named his pseudonym after them: Joshua Adam.
Under that name he wrote "The General." It was instigated by a concern any parent of school-age children in the 1960s would recognize: his boys were being taught to memorize and regurgitate, not to think. Rote learning was in vogue — the acquisition of simple facts, endlessly reproducible, testable, efficient. Kings and Queens, dates of reign, battles won and lost. The meaning was missing. Greifer took that anxiety and fed it through the apparatus of The Prisoner, where the absence of meaning isn't a pedagogical failure but a design feature.
Speed Learn is a subliminal education program transmitted through television. A three-year university course in three minutes. The Village broadcasts it; the population absorbs it; and afterward every resident can recite, with perfect fidelity, every date and name and treaty in the History of Europe. What they cannot do is interpret any of it. The Professor — an elderly academic played by Peter Howell — fronts the program. He delivers televised lectures with the serene authority of a man who has been doing this for decades. Behind him, unseen, is "the General" — the real power behind Speed Learn, the machine that generates the curriculum. Nobody has seen the General. Number Six assumes it is a person. It is not.
The episode's trick is that Number Six destroys the General not with force or cunning but with epistemology. Number Two, confident that the General can answer any question instantaneously, invites Number Six to test it. Number Six feeds the machine a single question on a strip of paper: WHY? The General cannot process it. It overloads and self-destructs, killing the Professor and Number Twelve in the explosion. A computer that can store and transmit every fact in human civilization is annihilated by a three-letter word that asks for meaning. Greifer, the man whose sons were being taught to memorize without understanding, wrote a machine that dies of the same disease.
Harold Wilson's "white heat of technology" speech had been delivered at the Labour Party conference in 1963 — four years before this episode aired. It was one of the most famous political speeches of the twentieth century: a vision of Britain remade by science, efficiency, automation. Wilson won the election. One of his first projects was the Open University — "a University of the Air," announced in 1966, which would use television broadcasts to deliver higher education to anyone, anywhere, without entry qualifications. The Open University's founding committee was meeting while Greifer was writing this script. Speed Learn is the Open University's evil twin: same delivery mechanism (television), same promise (education without barriers), opposite intent. The Open University wanted to democratize knowledge. Speed Learn wants to standardize it — to produce a population that all know the same facts, in the same order, with the same words, and none of them know why.
Colin Gordon played Number Two for the second time — or the first, depending on who you believe about the viewing order. In the transmitted sequence, "A. B. and C." aired third and "The General" sixth, but the internal evidence runs the other way: the Number Two of "The General" is nervous but functional, still believing his projects will succeed. The Number Two of "A. B. and C." is sweating, desperate, expecting punishment from above if he fails again. The implication is that "The General" comes first — the computer project that seemed so promising, the triumph that turned to ash — and "A. B. and C." is the aftermath, the same man given one more chance and feeling the noose tighten.
Gordon was born in British Ceylon on April 27, 1911, the son of William Arthur Gordon and his wife Lily Vera, née Troup. He was educated at Marlborough College and Christ Church, Oxford. His first professional stage appearance, in 1934, was as the hind legs of Alfred the carthorse in a production of "Toad of Toad Hall" at the Royalty Theatre. The hind legs. He spent forty years working his way forward from there. By 1936 he was directing the Fred Melville Repertory Company in Brixton. Then six years in the army during the war. Then back to work: "The Man in the White Suit" (1951), "Laughter in Paradise" (1951), "The Mouse That Roared" (1959) as the BBC announcer, "The Pink Panther" (1963) with Peter Sellers — he appeared in five Sellers films altogether. He played Templeton-Green, the Whitehall civil servant, in "The Baron," opposite Steve Forrest. He played government officials the way other actors played heavies: with an air of permanent, slightly wounded bureaucratic authority. In 1961, he appeared as the doctor in the "The Lift" episode of "Hancock's Half Hour." In 1967, the same year as The Prisoner, he played the airport commandant in the "Doctor Who" serial "The Faceless Ones." And in 1969, two years before his death, he hosted "The Complete and Utter History of Britain" — a London Weekend Television sketch show written by Michael Palin and Terry Jones, the pre-Monty Python collaboration that rehearsed many of the historical parodies that would later become Python's stock-in-trade. The show is mostly lost. Gordon's presence in it means that the man who played The Prisoner's most anxious Number Two spent his final working years doing comedy sketches about British history with the future Monty Python team. He died in Haslemere, Surrey, on October 4, 1972, aged sixty-one. He had been taken ill while working in South Africa and was brought home. He was buried with his wife at St Andrew's Church, Didling, West Sussex.
Peter Howell played the Professor. Born Peter Norman Bulmer Howell in London on October 25, 1919, he was educated at Winchester College and began reading law at Christ Church, Oxford, but left in 1939 when the war called him up. He served as a second lieutenant in the Rifle Brigade and was invalided out with dysentery during the North Africa Campaign in 1943. Shortly after, he made his professional stage debut with the Old Vic company. His West End plays included "The Affair," "The Doctor's Dilemma," "Little Boxes," and "Conduct Unbecoming." But television audiences knew him as Dr. Peter Harrison in "Emergency Ward 10" — the long-running hospital drama that was a fixture of ITV from 1957 to 1967. He appeared in it from 1958 to 1964, returned briefly in 1966, and came back one last time for the show's final episode in 1967. He also played the prison governor in Alan Clarke's "Scum" (1979) — the film so bleak the BBC banned its own version — and Sir William Lucas in the 1980 BBC "Pride and Prejudice," the one starring Elizabeth Garvie (who, in the small world of 1960s British acting, would later marry Anton Rodgers, who had played Number Two in the previous episode of this show). On BBC Radio 4, Howell voiced Saruman in the 1981 adaptation of "The Lord of the Rings" and played the Bishop of Felpersham in "The Archers" from 1987 to 2006. His close friend was Ian McKellen, who was godfather to his daughter Tamara. Howell was an active Labour Party member who campaigned against the planned 1968–69 England cricket tour of apartheid-era South Africa. He died at Denville Hall — a home for retired actors in Northwood, London — on April 20, 2015, aged ninety-five.
John Castle played Number Twelve, the sympathetic Village functionary who helps Number Six and dies in the General's explosion. Born John Michael Frederick Castle in Croydon on January 14, 1940, he was educated at Brighton College and Trinity College Dublin, then trained at RADA. His screen debut was in Michelangelo Antonioni's "Blowup" (1966) — he played Bill, the artist friend of David Hemmings' photographer, in the film that broke every rule of conventional narrative and somehow became a box-office hit. The following year, "The Prisoner." The year after that, "The Lion in Winter" (1968), in which he played Geoffrey, Duke of Brittany — the cold, manipulative fourth son of Peter O'Toole's Henry II. (Jane Merrow, who had played Alison in "The Schizoid Man" the episode before this one, played Alais in the same film. The Prisoner's casting pool and "The Lion in Winter's" casting pool were the same pool.) Castle went on to play Octavius Caesar in Charlton Heston's "Antony and Cleopatra" (1972), Postumus Agrippa in "I, Claudius" (1976), and the villain McDaggett in "RoboCop 3" (1993). On stage, he played Oswald in the Royal Shakespeare Company's revival of Ibsen's "Ghosts" in 1967 and Gandhi at the Tricycle Theatre in 1982.
Peter Graham Scott directed. Born in East Sheen, Surrey, on October 27, 1923, he attended the Italia Conti Academy as a child. As a teenager during the war, he worked in the films division of the Ministry of Information until he was called up. Commissioned as a Royal Artillery officer, his military career ended abruptly in a training accident. He went back to filmmaking and by 1947 was editing "Brighton Rock" — the Boulting Brothers' adaptation with a young Richard Attenborough as Pinkie Brown. He directed seven episodes of "Danger Man" with McGoohan in the early 1960s, which is how he ended up on "The Prisoner" — "I was quick and I was cheap!" he said later. After "The Prisoner," he produced and directed "Children of the Stones" (1977), a seven-part children's serial set in a village ringed by megalithic stones where time folds in on itself — widely regarded as one of the most unsettling pieces of children's television ever broadcast. In 1984, he won the Royal Television Society's Sir Ambrose Fleming Award for Outstanding Contribution to Television. In 1999, he published his memoirs: "British Television: An Insider's History." He died in Windlesham, Surrey, on August 5, 2007.
"The General" was broadcast on November 3, 1967. That same day in the Central Highlands of South Vietnam, the Battle of Dak To began — one of the bloodiest engagements of the war, which would last twenty-two days and kill nearly 400 Americans and an estimated 1,644 North Vietnamese. Che Guevara had been executed in Bolivia four weeks earlier. In London, the pirate radio stations had been silenced by the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act four months before, and the BBC had launched Radio 1 in their place — Kenny Everett and Tony Blackburn replacing the outlaws. The Wilson government was preparing to devalue the pound, which it would do two weeks later on November 18 (Wilson's famous "the pound in your pocket" broadcast). And in the Village, a machine that knew everything was destroyed by the only question it couldn't answer.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Pat Jackson joined the GPO Film Unit on his seventeenth birthday as a messenger boy. His mother had persuaded her MP — Sir Kingsley Wood, who happened also to be the Postmaster General — to find work for her son after his father's long illness and early death had ended the family's money and the boy's formal education. Within a few years he was a production assistant on "Night Mail" (1936), the celebrated documentary about the postal train from London to Scotland. The voice narrating W.H. Auden's poem over the final sequence — "This is the Night Mail crossing the border / Bringing the cheque and the postal order" — was Jackson himself. He was twenty years old.
His first feature was "Western Approaches" (1944), a semi-documentary about merchant seamen made for the Crown Film Unit over three years, much of it shot on actual lifeboats at sea with non-professional actors. The lifeboat sequences alone took six months. After the war, MGM brought him to Hollywood under contract, but he directed only one film there — "Shadow on the Wall" (1950) — before returning to Britain. His "Encore" (1951) competed at Cannes. By the mid-1960s he had moved largely to television, and it was his stage work with Patrick McGoohan — he seems to have been involved in casting McGoohan for "Danger Man" — that brought him to The Prisoner, where he directed four episodes. He died in 2011, aged ninety-five.
Jackson's Prisoner episodes are the ones that go inside Number Six's head. "A. B. and C." is the first and most literal of these: Number Two, with the help of a scientist called Number Fourteen, drugs Number Six through his evening tea, wheels him to a laboratory, injects him with an experimental compound, hooks his brain to a machine, and watches his dreams on a cinema screen. The premise is pharmacological science fiction; the execution is something closer to theater of the absurd. Number Two and Number Fourteen sit in the dark watching a projected dream the way studio executives watch dailies — cueing up pre-recorded film clips of foreign agents to insert into the sleeping man's narrative, arguing about dosage and timing, narrating what they see. It's television about watching television, surveillance about the dream of surveillance.
Colin Gordon plays this episode's Number Two — the second of his two appearances in the role, though it was broadcast first. (He had already played Number Two in "The General," the tenth episode produced, but that wouldn't air until sixth. The production-versus-broadcast order confusion runs through the entire series like a structural fracture.) Gordon was born in British Ceylon in 1911, educated at Marlborough and Christ Church, Oxford, and first appeared on the professional stage in 1934 — in the hind legs of Alfred the carthorse in a production of "Toad of Toad Hall" at the Royalty Theatre. He went on to a three-decade career playing government officials, solicitors, bureaucrats, and BBC announcers in over sixty films, including five with Peter Sellers: "The Mouse That Roared," "The Pink Panther," "Casino Royale," and two others. He was a regular in ITC's "The Baron," played the airport commandant in the 1967 Doctor Who serial "The Faceless Ones," and hosted "The Complete and Utter History of Britain," the 1969 pre-Monty Python collaboration between Michael Palin and Terry Jones.
His Number Two is the series' first portrait of a middle manager under pressure. Where McKern's Number Two in "Chimes" was a philosophical adversary who relished the game, Gordon's is a man visibly losing control: nervous, sleepless, subsisting on milk to calm his stomach, flinching every time an oversized red telephone rings with calls from someone above him — Number One, or whoever occupies that rank. He knows he is failing. He knows the consequences. By the episode's end he is threatening Number Fourteen with her own drug. Colin Gordon was taken ill while working in South Africa and died in October 1972, aged sixty-one. He was buried with his wife at St Andrew's Church, Didling, in West Sussex.
Sheila Allen plays Number Fourteen, the scientist who built the dream machine and who serves as the episode's conscience — the technician who warns that the drug can only be used three times, that they must wait a day between sessions, that they are risking Number Six's life. Allen had a long career in British television, including Z-Cars and later Children of the Stones, but here she's playing something rare for 1960s genre television: a female scientist whose expertise drives the plot, who argues back against her superior, and whose professional ethics are the episode's moral baseline. When Number Two orders her to enter Number Six's dream and speak through one of the characters — manipulating the dreamer's reality in real time — it's Fourteen who understands the violation this represents, even as she carries it out.
The three suspects — A, B, and C — are agents Number Two believes Number Six may have been planning to defect to. "A" is played by Peter Bowles, born in London in 1936, who would become famous two decades later as the debonair Richard DeVere in "To the Manor Born" and as Guthrie Featherstone in "Rumpole of the Bailey" — the same series that consumed Leo McKern. Here he's a smooth defector, charming and dangerous. "B" is Annette Carell, a German-born British actress. "C" remains unknown: no photograph, no film clip, just a dossier with a name blacked out. That gap is where the episode lives.
Katherine Kath plays Madame Engadine, the hostess of the glamorous party that recurs in each dream iteration. Born Rose Marie Lily Faess in Berck, in the Pas-de-Calais, she had been a prima ballerina at the Théâtre du Châtelet in Paris until an injury ended her dance career and she turned to acting. She appeared in French films from 1947 and eventually crossed into English-language cinema, including "Moulin Rouge" (1952) alongside José Ferrer. In The Prisoner, her role is structurally essential: Engadine's party is the recurring social environment into which Number Two injects his suspects, the petri dish in which he hopes to culture betrayal.
The writer is Anthony Skene, making the first of his three Prisoner contributions (he also wrote "Many Happy Returns" and "Dance of the Dead"). Skene was an experienced television writer who had worked on "Armchair Mystery Theatre" and "Haunted." The Counterstrike connection is worth noting: in 1969, Skene wrote an episode called "Nocturne" for the BBC alien invasion series "Counterstrike" that told an eerily similar story about dream manipulation. But the "Counterstrike" script was actually written in 1966, before "A. B. and C." — meaning the Prisoner episode was the recycled version, and the earlier script wasn't broadcast until two years later due to production delays on "Counterstrike." The idea came first for a show about aliens; it found its better home in a show about paranoia.
The episode is a bottle show. Very little Portmeirion footage; almost everything shot on standing sets at MGM Borehamwood. Skene said as much: "I wrote it around the church door, the street from The Dirty Dozen and other bits, too, which were all leftovers." The laboratory where Number Six's dreams are projected is a redressed version of the Control Room / Number Two's office set from "Arrival." Budget constraints made the episode claustrophobic, and claustrophobia made it better.
Scottish Television was supposed to broadcast the episode on Friday, October 19th, 1967, one week after "The Chimes of Big Ben." A power cut hit the station that evening, knocking it off the air. The following Friday, Scottish continued with "Free for All" instead, skipping this episode entirely. "A. B. and C." didn't air in Scotland until Thursday, November 23rd, as the seventh episode — meaning Scottish viewers saw it after "Many Happy Returns," completely out of sequence. In Wales, the episode didn't air until January 21, 1970 — more than two years after the rest of the UK.
The episode's turning point is the moment Number Six becomes aware inside his own dream. He has followed Number Fourteen to the laboratory, studied the equipment, found the needle marks on his arm, figured out the mechanism. On the third night, he dilutes the drug. Then he does something the show has never done before: he straightens a crooked mirror in the dream — the camera has been shooting in Dutch angles throughout, and now the frame levels — and takes control of the narrative. He walks through his own dream to the laboratory set, addresses Number Two directly through the screen, and hands him an envelope that was supposed to contain the secrets he'd been selling. It contains holiday brochures. "I was not selling out. That was not the reason I resigned."
Then he turns to the camera. "We mustn't disappoint them," he says, "the people who are watching."
He means Number Two. He means the audience at home. He means us. In 1967, on a Friday-night ITC adventure show, a character inside a dream inside a surveillance feed broke the fourth wall and told the viewers they were complicit in the watching. Nobody on television was doing this. Most shows couldn't even manage continuity between episodes.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
The one CBS refused to air. The Western. The episode that got banned from American television in 1968 because a man wouldn't pick up a gun.
It aired in Britain on December 29, 1967 — the Friday between Christmas and New Year. "Hello Goodbye" by the Beatles was the number one song. "The Graduate" was in cinemas. Gladys Knight and the Pips were topping the R&B charts with "I Heard It Through the Grapevine." The Tet Offensive was four weeks away.
There is no title sequence. The episode opens cold. A sheriff turns in his badge and his gun. His reasons are his own. He rides out of town. Men drag him back to a place called Harmony. A judge runs the town. A kid with a gun runs the streets. A woman works in the saloon. The sheriff will not pick up a gun. This is the entire premise. It is also, structurally, The Prisoner. The badge is the resignation. The town is the Village. The Judge is Number Two. The refusal to carry a weapon is the refusal to conform. Everything else — every episode, every escape attempt, every interrogation — is contained inside this one Western.
CBS broadcast seventeen of the seventeen Prisoner episodes when the show aired in the United States in the summer of 1968. They skipped this one. Only sixteen aired. The network's official reason has never been clearly documented, but the consensus is straightforward: a hero who refuses to carry a gun, in a recognizably American setting, during the height of the Vietnam War, in the summer of the draft card burnings and the Chicago convention and the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. and Bobby Kennedy. CBS executives looked at a man turning in his badge and his weapon and walking away, and they saw an anti-war statement. They were probably right. McGoohan's pacifism was real — not just a character trait but a personal conviction. He had refused to do love scenes and violent scenes throughout his career. He had turned down James Bond because he objected to the character's morality. The refusal of the gun was not subtext. It was text. CBS read it correctly and pulled the episode.
The episode was the fourteenth produced and the fourteenth broadcast. It took five weeks to shoot instead of the usual two. David Tomblin wrote and directed it — his story, from a concept by assistant editor Ian Rakoff. Tomblin was McGoohan's partner in Everyman Films, the company that made The Prisoner. Born October 18, 1930, in Borehamwood, Hertfordshire — the town where the studios were. He started in film as a runner at fourteen. National Service with the Royal Marines. First Assistant Director by 1954. He and McGoohan met on "Danger Man" and decided to make their own show. After The Prisoner, Tomblin became one of the most prolific first assistant directors in cinema history: "The Empire Strikes Back," "Return of the Jedi," all three original Indiana Jones films, "Superman," "Gandhi" — for which he directed 250,000 extras in the reconstruction of Gandhi's funeral in Delhi — "A Bridge Too Far," "Out of Africa," "Empire of the Sun," "Never Say Never Again," "The Adventures of Baron Munchausen." He received a BAFTA Michael Balcon Award in 2003 and an OBE in 1994. When he applied for a US work permit during "Return of the Jedi," he had to list every film he'd worked on and stopped at 478, deciding that was probably enough. He died July 20, 2005, aged seventy-four. The man who wrote and directed the Western episode of The Prisoner went on to first-AD every major franchise of the next three decades. He started by building a fake Western town in the grounds of the Village and ended by building the Death Star.
Alexis Kanner played the Kid — Number Eight, the mute enforcer in circus trousers and a top hat who dies in a duel with Number Six. Born Henri Alex Kanner, May 2, 1942, in Bagnères-de-Luchon, France, to a Jewish family under Nazi occupation. In April 1944, shortly before his second birthday, his family escaped to Montreal on the Portuguese ship Serpa Pinto. He attended the Montreal Children's Theatre. Moved to England in the late 1950s and joined the Birmingham Repertory Theatre. Royal Shakespeare Company — "The Tempest" in 1961, Hamlet under Peter Brook in 1965. He met David Tomblin on "Reach for Glory" (1962), a film about the brutal war games of evacuated teenage boys. That connection brought him to The Prisoner.
McGoohan was planning the final four episodes when he cast Kanner. There was opposition. McGoohan was looking for someone with genuinely rebellious and maverick qualities, and Kanner had them — on and off screen. To prepare for the duel scene, both actors practiced quick-draw obsessively. McGoohan reportedly took lessons from Steve McQueen and sent Kanner a telegram about it, prompting Kanner to double his own practice. McGoohan was so impressed that he wrote Kanner a second role: Number Forty-Eight in "Fall Out," the final episode, where Kanner would stand trial as the representative of rebellious youth. And he gave him an uncredited third part — the photographer in "The Girl Who Was Death," where Kanner performed his own stunts on a roller coaster.
After The Prisoner, Kanner starred opposite Roger Moore in "Crossplot" (1969), opposite Bette Davis and Michael Redgrave in "Connecting Rooms" (1970). He moved back to Canada and made "Kings and Desperate Men" (1981) — a hostage drama he wrote, produced, directed, and starred in alongside McGoohan. He later sued the producers of "Die Hard," claiming they stole the concept from his film. He lost. His final acting role was in "Nightfall" (1988), based on Isaac Asimov. He settled back in London in 1996, working on a film project called "J R Profitt" that never came to fruition. He died of a heart attack at his London home on December 13, 2003, aged sixty-one. He had requested that his body be buried in Jerusalem, at the Mount of Olives. The Jewish child who escaped Nazi France on a Portuguese ship, who played a mute killer in a fake Western town, who was put on trial for the crime of youth in the final episode of the most paranoid show ever made — he asked to be buried on the hill where tradition says the resurrection of the dead will begin.
David Bauer played the Judge — Number Two in all but name. But his name wasn't David Bauer. It was Herman Bernard Waldman. Born March 6, 1917, in Chicago. Washington University in St. Louis, class of 1938, where he won the Dramatic Club Prize and a scholarship to the Berkshire Playhouse in Stockbridge, Massachusetts. There he met Jane Wyatt, Sinclair Lewis, and Fred Stone. After the war, he joined the Actors' Laboratory Theatre in Los Angeles. Radio credits in "Big Town" and "Those We Love." Over a hundred stage and radio credits by 1948. He changed his name to David Wolfe and appeared in "The Undercover Man," "5 Fingers," "Wait Till the Sun Shines, Nellie." And then "Salt of the Earth" — Herbert Biberman's 1954 film about a New Mexico miners' strike, produced by blacklisted Hollywood professionals, crewed by blacklisted technicians, starring blacklisted actors. It was the most blacklisted film in American history. Herman Waldman appeared in it.
Following his appearance before the House Un-American Activities Committee, Wolfe was blacklisted. The name changed again — David Wolfe became David Bauer. He was being billed as Bauer by no later than the 1956 New York Shakespeare Festival revival of "Titus Andronicus." He left America in November 1958 and never went back. He worked in Britain for the rest of his life: "The Saint," "The Avengers," "The Baron," "The Champions," "Department S," "Randall and Hopkirk (Deceased)." He appeared in "You Only Live Twice," "Patton," "Diamonds Are Forever," "The Spy Who Came in from the Cold." He narrated every episode of "The Champions." He married British actress Stella Tanner in 1960. He died of a heart attack at his London home on February 8 or 13, 1973, aged fifty-five. The exact date is disputed.
This is the thing about this episode that nobody planned but everybody should notice: a HUAC blacklist fugitive — a man who had his name taken from him by the American government, who fled his own country, who could not go home — played the Judge in a story about a man trapped in a town he cannot leave, ruled by a power structure that demands conformity. The episode that CBS banned for its pacifism was partly performed by a man whom America had already banned for his politics. Herman Waldman knew what the Village was. He had lived in one.
Valerie French played Kathy — the Saloon Girl, Number Twenty-Two. Born Valerie Harrison, March 11, 1928, in London. Her father was an accountant who had served as a Lieutenant with the Artists' Rifles in the First World War. Theatre Royal, Windsor. Then Hollywood: "Jubal" (1956) opposite Glenn Ford, "Decision at Sundown" (1957) opposite Randolph Scott — real Westerns, Budd Boetticher Westerns, the very films this episode was deconstructing. She appeared in John Osborne's "Inadmissible Evidence" on Broadway in 1965. She caused a minor sensation appearing nude in "The Mother Lover" at the Booth Theatre in 1969 — only her back was visible. Her first husband was the playwright Michael Pertwee, brother of Jon Pertwee, the Third Doctor Who. Her second husband was Thayer David, who played Professor Stokes on "Dark Shadows." They divorced. They got back together. They were planning to remarry when he died in 1978. She died of leukemia in New York in 1990, aged sixty-two. The woman who played the saloon girl in a deconstructed Western had actually appeared in the real ones being deconstructed.
The method by which Number Six is immersed in Harmony is never fully explained. Drugs, microphones, a theme-park backlot adjacent to the Village. The blog reviewer notes the resemblance to "Westworld" — Michael Crichton's 1973 film about a fully immersive Western theme park, and later the HBO series. Crichton may have seen "Living in Harmony" when it aired in Britain. The episode predates his film by six years.
The cardboard cutouts are Tomblin's idea. When the simulation breaks — when Number Six pulls himself out of Harmony and back into the Village — the characters from the Western appear as flat cardboard standees. Their avatars. The Kid and the Saloon Girl cannot survive the transition from fiction to reality. Number Eight (the Kid's real identity) hangs himself. Number Twenty-Two (the Saloon Girl's real identity) throws herself from a balcony. The virtual-reality Western kills its supporting cast. Only Number Six walks away, because Number Six has always known which world is real. The people who believed in Harmony died when Harmony ended.
December 29, 1967. Four days until 1968. The last Friday of the last full year of the 1960s that still felt like the 1960s. In four months, Martin Luther King Jr. would be dead. In six months, Bobby Kennedy. In eight months, the Democratic Convention in Chicago would turn into a police riot. CBS would look at this episode — a man in a Western town who will not carry a gun, who refuses to be sheriff, whose pacifism is treated as a form of resistance rather than weakness — and decide that America could not watch it. They were not wrong about what it meant. They were wrong about whether people should see it.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
The eighth episode produced. The first where McGoohan seized control of the production from the director. It was filmed in January 1967 and the shoot was, by multiple accounts, a catastrophe. The director Robert Asher was a comedy specialist — five Norman Wisdom films, a Morecambe and Wise film, "Make Mine Mink" with Terry-Thomas. He'd moved into ITC television work and was competent, professional, and entirely unprepared for Patrick McGoohan. On set, McGoohan overrode him, screamed at him, and eventually took over direction of the episode while Asher stood aside. The cast watched it happen. Annette Andre, interviewed decades later for the 2007 DVD documentary "Don't Knock Yourself Out," strongly criticized McGoohan's behavior. Mark Eden recalled McGoohan losing control during a fight scene and nearly strangling him. A crew member stated his belief that McGoohan experienced a nervous breakdown during production. The episode that emerged from this wreckage is, structurally, the most complex of the series: a triple-layered conspiracy involving two Number Twos, a bomber watchmaker, "jammers" who create fake plots to waste the authorities' time, and a false-flag assassination designed to justify a crackdown — all filtered through Number Six's justified paranoia about whether the information he's being fed is real or planted.
The concept of "jamming" is drawn from actual resistance practice in 1960s Eastern Europe. Dissidents in Communist states created and disseminated details of fake plots — fabricated conspiracies that intelligence services were obliged to investigate, tying up surveillance resources and eroding institutional trust. The Situationists called it "radio jamming." By the 1980s it evolved into "culture jamming" — the subversive alteration of billboard advertising — a term popularized by the band Negativland. Woddis's "Hammer into Anvil" had a Communist writer exploring paranoia within authority; Cramoy's "It's Your Funeral" has an American writer exploring how a surveillance state drowns in its own noise. The two episodes are companion pieces. Together they describe the complete failure mode of totalitarianism: paranoia eating itself from both directions.
Michael Cramoy was American. He had written for "Dragnet" — the Jack Webb police procedural, the most procedural show in television history. Webb's mantra was "just the facts." Cramoy then moved to England and wrote for ITC: "The Invisible Man" in the 1950s, "The Saint" in the 1960s. His task on this episode was peculiar: write a script incorporating pre-existing location footage already shot at Portmeirion plus the standing MGM Borehamwood studio sets, with a later Portmeirion shoot using stand-ins for both McGoohan and Andre. He was building a story around footage that already existed. Fitting narrative to pre-existing images. The episode's plot, in which truth and fabrication become indistinguishable, was constructed by the same method.
Derren Nesbitt played the new Number Two — the ambitious young replacement planning to assassinate his predecessor. Born Derren Michael Horwitz, June 19, 1935, in London. Jewish. RADA-trained. He is best known as Major von Hapen in "Where Eagles Dare" (1968) — the Gestapo officer interrogating Richard Burton and Clint Eastwood. While filming in Austria, Nesbitt requested a meeting with a former Gestapo officer to understand the character. During the scene where von Hapen is shot, the blood squib attached to Nesbitt exploded with such force that he was temporarily blinded. He recovered.
For "The Prisoner" he chose to play Number Two as a bleach-blond dandy in oversized spectacles — an image so distinctive that the Episode by Episode blog notes its uncanny resemblance to Joe 90, Gerry Anderson's child puppet spy, which wouldn't appear until a year later. Whether Anderson took inspiration is unknown. Nesbitt was never told what the show was about. He played Number Two in a state of genuine confusion, which may be the most honest performance any actor delivered on the series. He later played Sandy Youth, a predatory blackmailer of gay men, in "Victim" (1961) — one of the first major British films to address homosexuality sympathetically. He played DCI Jordan in "Special Branch" (1969). He wrote, directed, and produced "The Amorous Milkman" (1975), a sex comedy starring Julie Ege and Diana Dors, based on his own novel. He has been married four times. In 1973 he was fined £250 for assaulting his first wife, the actress Anne Aubrey, with a leather strap after she told him about an affair. In 2018, aged eighty-three, he played a drag queen in the independent film "Tucked." As of 2026, he is ninety and still living in Worthing, West Sussex.
André van Gyseghem played the retiring Number Two — the "permanent" one who claims to have been on holiday during all of Number Six's previous encounters. Born August 18, 1906, in Eltham, Kent — the same Eltham where Pat Jackson, who directed the previous episode, was born a decade later. RADA-trained. After Hull Repertory Theatre, he directed at the Embassy Theatre throughout the early 1930s. In 1933 he directed Paul Robeson and Flora Robson in Eugene O'Neill's "All God's Chillun Got Wings." He directed Robeson again in "Stevedore" in 1935. Between 1933 and 1935 he made several trips to the Soviet Union, spending a year working at Nikolay Okhlopkov's Realistic Theatre in Moscow. He became a member of the Communist Party of Great Britain and president of Unity Theatre's Management Committee — the same Unity Theatre where Roger Woddis, who wrote the previous episode, had cut his teeth a decade later. Van Gyseghem attributed much of his acting expertise to his Soviet training. A Communist directed Paul Robeson. A Communist wrote "Hammer into Anvil." The retiring Number Two who represents institutional permanence was played by a Communist Party member who trained in Stalin's Moscow. Nobody in the audience knew any of this. Van Gyseghem appeared in over fifty British television dramas between 1951 and his death in 1979 at seventy-three.
Annette Andre played the Watchmaker's Daughter. Born Annette Christine Andreallo, June 24, 1939, in Drummoyne, New South Wales, Australia. Her father was an upholsterer. She trained as a ballet dancer from age four at an academy linked to the Australian Ballet. At fifteen she quit dance for acting. She was too young to work legally as an actress — not yet sixteen — so she enrolled in a radio training school, and her first role was in a serial called "Kid Grayson Rides the Range." She moved to the UK in 1963. She played Philia, a beautiful virgin concubine, in the 1966 film of "A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum" — opposite Phil Silvers, Zero Mostel, and Buster Keaton in his final film role. Her most famous part was Jeannie Hopkirk in "Randall and Hopkirk (Deceased)" (1969) — the ghost detective show where she plays the widow of a murdered private eye who returns as a ghost only she and his partner can see. She turned down a proposal of marriage from Benny Hill. She was romantically linked with George Best. In 2018 she published her memoir "Where Have I Been All My Life," with a foreword by Roger Moore. She is now semi-retired and works in animal welfare.
In the 2007 DVD documentary, Andre said she did not enjoy her time on "The Prisoner." She strongly criticized McGoohan for screaming at Asher and taking over the production. She is one of the few people who worked on the series to say so publicly.
Wanda Ventham played the Computer Attendant — a small role. Born August 5, 1935, in Brighton. Trained at the Central School of Speech and Drama as a contemporary of Judi Dench. She appeared in "Carry On Cleo" and "Carry On Up the Khyber." She played Colonel Virginia Lake in the Gerry Anderson series "UFO." She appeared in "Doctor Who" three times across three decades: Jean Rock in "The Faceless Ones" (1967), Thea Ransome in "Image of the Fendahl" (1977), and Faroon in "Time and the Rani" (1987). She played Pamela Parry in "Only Fools and Horses." In 1976 she married Timothy Carlton. Their son is Benedict Cumberbatch.
Mark Eden played Number 100, the operative who manages the assassination plot on the ground. Born Douglas John Malin, February 14, 1928, in St Pancras, London. He played Marco Polo in the 1964 "Doctor Who" serial of the same name — one of the great lost stories, all episodes missing from the BBC archive. He played Inspector Parker in the 1970s Lord Peter Wimsey adaptations. His most famous role was Alan Bradley in "Coronation Street" (1986–1989), the villain killed by a Blackpool tram in one of the most-watched moments in British soap opera history. In 2009 he unveiled a plaque at the tram stop where the scene was filmed. After Coronation Street he said he received many offers for "psycho" roles. His first wife was Joan Long, who later married John Le Mesurier — Sergeant Wilson in "Dad's Army." His third wife was Sue Nicholls, who plays Audrey Roberts in "Coronation Street" — the daughter of Baron Harmar-Nicholls. During filming of this episode, McGoohan lost control during a fight scene and nearly strangled him. He developed Alzheimer's disease and died on January 1, 2021, aged ninety-two.
"It's Your Funeral" aired on December 8, 1967. That same day, the Beatles released "Magical Mystery Tour" — a film about a bus trip to nowhere, directed by nobody, structured around confusion and whimsy, received with bewilderment by a public that expected coherence. A few days earlier, on December 3, Dr. Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant in Cape Town. A man's heart was removed and replaced with a stranger's. "Daydream Believer" by the Monkees was number one in America. "Hello, Goodbye" by the Beatles was number one in Britain. The retiring Number Two left by helicopter. The new Number Two sat down in his chair. Number Six congratulated him, and told him that something equally suitable would be arranged when his time came. The system replaces the man and continues. "It's your funeral," he said. He was talking to everyone.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.sub-title: Do Not Forsake Me Oh My Darling
programme.desc:
The episode without Patrick McGoohan. He appears for approximately ninety seconds.
This is the fourteenth episode produced and the thirteenth broadcast. It aired on December 22, 1967, the last Friday before Christmas. ITV had skipped The Prisoner the previous week — deemed unsuitable for Christmas Eve week — but apparently a body-swap episode about identity theft and an absent protagonist was considered appropriate holiday viewing.
McGoohan was in the Arctic. Not literally, but professionally: he was in Hollywood filming "Ice Station Zebra" for John Sturges at MGM. A Cold War submarine thriller based on Alistair MacLean's novel, shot in Super Panavision 70 and released in Cinerama — Rock Hudson, Ernest Borgnine, Jim Brown, and McGoohan. The budget was eight to ten million dollars. It earned four point six. Mixed reviews. Two Oscar nominations (cinematography, visual effects). A commercial failure by every reasonable metric. And then Howard Hughes happened. In the final years of his life, Hughes lived on the top floor of the Desert Inn in Las Vegas, a recluse in a darkened penthouse. He had a private print of "Ice Station Zebra" on a continuous loop. He watched it an estimated one hundred and fifty times. When he bought the television station KLAS-TV, he ordered it broadcast repeatedly. Nobody knows why. The film that McGoohan left The Prisoner to make became the favorite movie of the most famous madman in America — a man who had made himself a prisoner in a room at the top of a building, watching the same story on repeat, attended by handlers who controlled his access to the outside world. McGoohan went to Hollywood to escape the Village and walked into a film that would become the private obsession of a man who had built his own.
McGoohan claimed he took the role partly to finance the final four episodes of The Prisoner through his company Everyman Films. This may or may not be true. What is true is that with the star absent, the production had to continue — Lew Grade's money was on the clock.
Vincent Tilsley wrote the script. Born June 3, 1931. He wrote "The Chimes of Big Ben" — the second episode broadcast, one of the finest hours — and "The General." He was not a regular ITC writer. He came from serious television drama: he'd been writing for the BBC and ITV since the 1950s. The original draft of this episode was significantly different from what aired. In his version, Number Six storms back to his office in a fury to resign again, only realizing his appearance has changed when he sees an unfamiliar face. His fiancée Janet features more prominently. There is a kiss — an intimate one, enough to make her recognize her vanished lover inside a stranger's body. McGoohan would have cut that kiss even if he'd been present. Vincent Tilsley was writing a love story inside a spy thriller. McGoohan wanted neither.
The fiancée is the problem. Her name is Janet Portland. Her father is Sir Charles Portland, Number Six's former employer. This episode, and only this episode, tells us that Number Six was engaged. That his boss was his prospective father-in-law. That he had been missing for a year. None of this information appears in any other episode. None of it is ever mentioned again. The blog reviewer's question is the right one: are these people real, or are they constructions planted by the Village to make the Colonel feel comfortable in Number Six's skin? The show never answers. It never asks again. The fiancée exists for forty-nine minutes and then vanishes from the series forever.
Zena Walker played Janet Portland. Born Zena Cecilia Walker, March 7, 1934, in Selly Oak, Birmingham. Her father was a grocer. RADA-trained. She was Ophelia opposite Paul Scofield's Hamlet. She won the 1968 Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Play for "A Day in the Death of Joe Egg" — Peter Nichols's black comedy about parents of a severely disabled child, a play so unflinching that audiences walked out during its original run and then came back and gave it standing ovations. She appeared in "The Dresser" (1983) with Albert Finney and Tom Courtenay. Her first husband was Robert Urquhart, the actor. Her second was Julian Holloway, the actor — son of Stanley Holloway, who played Alfred Doolittle in "My Fair Lady." Her third husband was John French, a theatrical agent, who survived her. She died August 24, 2003, in Brockenhurst, Hampshire, aged sixty-nine. Her last role was as the messenger in "Oedipus." The woman who played Number Six's fiancée — the only person in the entire series shown to love him as a private individual rather than a political subject — ended her career delivering the news in a Greek tragedy about a man who cannot escape his identity.
Nigel Stock played the Colonel — the body Number Six's mind inhabits. Born September 21, 1919, in Malta, the son of an Army captain. Grew up in India. Attended St Paul's School, London, then RADA, where he won the Leverhulme Exhibition, the Northcliffe Scholarship, and the Principal's Medal — the full sweep. He served in the Second World War with the London Irish Rifles and the Assam Regiment of the Indian Army, in Burma, China, and Kohima. Twice mentioned in dispatches. Discharged as a Major. He was Dr. Watson. The BBC's Sherlock Holmes from 1964 to 1968 cast Stock as Watson alongside Douglas Wilmer and then Peter Cushing — he played the same Watson to two different Holmeses, an identity problem of its own. He appeared in "Brighton Rock" (1947), "The Dam Busters" (1955), "The Great Escape" (1963), and "The Lion in Winter" (1968). He was in "Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy" (1979) and "Yes Minister" (1982). His final film was "Young Sherlock Holmes" (1985), in which he played — naturally — Holmes's mentor. He had started as Watson and ended training Holmes. He married three times. He and his third wife, Richenda Carey, had just appeared together on stage in the world premiere of "Mumbo Jumbo" in May 1986 when he died of a heart attack on June 23, 1986, aged sixty-six. The man whose body Number Six inhabited was a decorated war hero, a three-time Watson, and a man who died one month after his last opening night.
Clifford Evans played Number Two. Born Clifford George Evans, February 17, 1912, in Senghenydd, Glamorgan, Wales. Senghenydd. The name carries weight if you know Welsh mining history: the Senghenydd colliery disaster of October 14, 1913 — an underground coal dust explosion that killed 439 miners and one rescuer. It remains the worst mining accident in British history. Evans was born one year before the disaster, in the same village. He grew up in a place that had buried four hundred and forty of its men in a single morning. He became an actor. During the Second World War, he was a conscientious objector — refused to fight — and served in the Non-Combatant Corps. This was not a popular position in wartime Britain. He continued to act. After the war, he found his niche at Hammer Studios: Don Alfredo Carledo in "The Curse of the Werewolf" (1961) and Professor Zimmer, "an often inebriated vampire-hunter," in "Kiss of the Vampire" (1963). He played Caswell Bligh, the building tycoon, in "The Power Game" (1965-1969) — and Rachel Herbert, who appeared in that same show, had already appeared in "Free for All" as Number Two's aide. He married Hermione Hannen, an actress and wartime radio announcer, in 1943. She predeceased him in 1983. He died June 9, 1985, in Aberaeron, Dyfed, Wales, aged seventy-three. He went home.
Hugo Schuster played Professor Seltzman — the scientist who invented the mind-swap process, who engineers the three-way switch at the climax, who escapes the Village in the Colonel's body while the Colonel dies in his. Almost nothing is known about Hugo Schuster outside this role. He has no Wikipedia page. He appears in no other well-documented production. The man who played the inventor of a technology that puts one person's mind into another's body is himself nearly untraceable — a ghost in the archive, a man who exists on screen for a few minutes and then vanishes, much like Seltzman himself.
The title comes from "The Ballad of High Noon" — "Do Not Forsake Me, O My Darlin'" — Tex Ritter's 1952 Oscar-winning song from "High Noon." The song is about a man who must face a gunfight alone while his new bride considers leaving him. It plays throughout the episode. In "High Noon," the wife stays. In The Prisoner, the fiancée exists for one episode and is never mentioned again. The show took the title from a love song and used it for an episode about the irrelevance of love.
Pat Jackson directed — his second Prisoner episode after "Hammer into Anvil." Born Patrick Douglas Selmes Jackson, March 26, 1916, in Eltham. He was the voice on "Night Mail" (1936) — "This is the Night Mail crossing the border, bringing the cheque and the postal order" — reading Auden's poem. He directed "Western Approaches" (1944), a three-year production about merchant seamen, shot on location at sea with non-professional actors. He spent three years under contract at MGM after the war. He died June 3, 2011, aged ninety-five. The man who read Auden's poem about connection and correspondence directed an episode about a man who cannot prove to anyone — not his fiancée, not his employer, not himself — that he is who he says he is.
George Markstein had quit by this point. His replacement appears in the title sequence — someone else sits behind the desk in the underground office where Number Six resigned. Markstein left over one too many conflicts with McGoohan, and David Tomblin took a larger hand in the creation of the remaining episodes. The last four would go somewhere completely different. McGoohan was coming back from the Arctic, and he was done with escape-and-recapture. The Prisoner had three episodes left and it was about to stop making sense on purpose.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
The ninth episode produced and the twelfth broadcast. It is the second episode from which Patrick McGoohan fired the director. Roy Rossotti lasted one day. McGoohan took over under his pseudonym "Joseph Serf" — the same name he'd used on "Free for All." The pattern was now established: McGoohan had hired professional television directors, found them inadequate to his vision, sacked them mid-production, and finished the episodes himself. Rossotti directed episodes of "The Saint," "Randall and Hopkirk (Deceased)," "Department S," and "Jason King" — competent ITC journeyman work. He was not incompetent. He was simply not McGoohan. Nobody was.
The episode is about lobotomy as social policy. The Village declares Number Six "unmutual" — a diagnosis by committee, enforced by mob, resolved by surgery. Roger Parkes wrote it. Born 1933. Died May 2, 2008, aged seventy-five. He was a crime reporter who became a trainee story editor at the BBC, assigned to "Compact" — the daily serial about a women's magazine, broadcast live from 1962 to 1965, now almost entirely wiped from the archive. "Compact" was the BBC's first attempt at a soap opera aimed at adults. It was cancelled because the BBC thought soap operas were beneath them. Parkes moved from documenting real crime to scripting fictional soap to writing one of the most explicitly political episodes of "The Prisoner." His subsequent career confirmed the political instinct: he wrote for "Doombolt Chase," Terry Nation's "Survivors" (1975), and "Blake's 7" (1978) — three separate visions of collapsed or totalitarian Britain. He also wrote for "Doombwatch," "Juliet Bravo," "Boon," and "Campion." He published several novels. He wrote the foreword to the published script of this episode in 2006, two years before his death.
His first draft had Number Eighty-Six aggressively pursuing Number Six romantically. McGoohan cut every page of it. The no-romance edict was absolute. McGoohan believed that sexuality in the series would reduce Number Six from an archetype to a character. The Prisoner was not about a man. It was about Man. Desire would make it personal. McGoohan wanted it universal.
John Sharp played Number Two — an oleaginous functionary who delegates the dirty work to a woman and then blames her when it fails. Born John Herbert Sharp, August 5, 1920, in Bradford, Yorkshire. The name confusion is real: he was credited as "John Sharpe" on this episode, which is either a production office error (per Rick Davy's "The Essential Guide") or a deliberate choice he later reversed (per Robert Fairclough's "Official Companion"). Wikipedia and IMDb both list him as "John Sharp." Whatever his billing, he was a character actor of extraordinary range across forty-two years. Over 130 television appearances. He played Ezra Biggins — the parsimonious, awkward Yorkshire dairy farmer — in "All Creatures Great and Small," and Peter Davison remembered him as "a wonderful raconteur who would tell you these long stories." Christopher Timothy, who played James Herriot, said: "I found myself getting quite moved when I watched an episode recently, not because of what we were doing, but because all those lovely people are no longer with us. John Sharp was a lovely, lovely man." He played the Bishop in Franco Zeffirelli's "Brother Sun, Sister Moon" (1972). He appeared in "The Wicker Man" (1973). He played the Publican in "The Avengers" episode "Murdersville" (1967). He appeared in Lindsay Anderson's "The White Bus" (1967) and in "Night and the City" (1950) — Jules Dassin's noir masterpiece, uncredited. He died November 26, 1992, aged seventy-two.
Angela Browne played Number Eighty-Six — the woman who administers the fake lobotomy, who drugs Number Six's tea, who is then hypnotized and turned against Number Two. Born June 14, 1938, in Walton-on-Thames, Surrey. RADA-trained. She had already worked with McGoohan — she played the Girl in the "Danger Man" episode "The Girl in Pink Pyjamas." Her career was a catalogue of ITC and BBC prestige: "Ghost Squad," "The Saint," "The Avengers," "Man in a Suitcase," "Upstairs, Downstairs," "Minder." She appeared in Rumer Godden's "Kizzy" (1976), an adaptation of "The Diddakoi" about a Romany girl, fondly remembered by a generation of British children. She was in "Carry On Nurse" (1959), uncredited, and in Norman Wisdom's "Press for Time" (1966) — connecting her to the man whose director McGoohan had just fired, Robert Asher, who had directed five Norman Wisdom films.
She married Francis Matthews in 1963. Matthews was the voice of Captain Scarlet. Born September 2, 1927, in York. His father was a shop steward at the Rowntree's chocolate factory. Matthews trained at St Michael's Jesuit College in Leeds, then became a stagehand at the Theatre Royal before his national service in the Royal Navy. He played Dr. Hans Kleve in Hammer's "The Revenge of Frankenstein" (1958) and the heroes of "Dracula: Prince of Darkness" and "Rasputin the Mad Monk" (both 1966). He was Paul Temple in the BBC's Francis Durbridge adaptations from 1969 to 1971. Gerry Anderson cast him as Captain Scarlet specifically because Matthews could do an impeccable Cary Grant impression — the entire vocal characterization of Captain Scarlet is an imitation of Cary Grant. Matthews and Browne co-starred in "The Dark Island" (1962) and "Paul Temple" (1970). She gave up acting in 1990. She died June 20, 2001, aged sixty-three. He died June 14, 2014 — which would have been her seventy-sixth birthday — aged eighty-six.
George Pravda played the Doctor. Born Jiří Pravda, June 19, 1916, in Prague, Austria-Hungary. He emigrated to Britain in 1956 — the year of the Hungarian Uprising, the year Czechoslovakia's brief post-Stalin thaw began to freeze again. He appeared in "Thunderball" (1965) as Ladislav Kutze, the reluctant SPECTRE scientist who ultimately helps Bond. He played three different roles across three different serials of "Doctor Who": Doland in "The Enemy of the World" (1968), Jaeger in "The Mutants" (1972), and Castellan Spandrell in "The Deadly Assassin" (1976). He appeared in "Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy" (1979), "I, Claudius" (1976), and Clint Eastwood's "Firefox" (1982). His wife was Hana Pravda — also a Czech actress, also an emigrée. "Pravda" means "truth" in Czech. The Doctor who administers a fake lobotomy was played by a man whose name means Truth. Nobody in the audience knew this. Pravda died May 1, 1985, aged sixty-eight.
Among the uncredited Social Group members: Michael Chow. Born Zhou Yinghua, March 7, 1939, in Shanghai. His father was Zhou Xinfang, one of the most famous Peking Opera performers in Chinese history. His sister is Tsai Chin — the actress who played the Bond girl in "You Only Live Twice" (1967), released six months before this episode aired. Chow was sent to an English boarding school at twelve and never spoke to his father again. He studied at Saint Martin's School of Art. His first wife was Grace Coddington, the legendary Vogue creative director. Two months after this episode aired, in February 1968, he opened Mr Chow in Knightsbridge — Chinese food served by Italian waiters, with Peter Blake and David Hockney paintings on the walls. It became one of the most famous restaurants in the world. He opened locations in Beverly Hills, New York, Las Vegas, Miami. In this episode, he was an extra. An uncredited face in a crowd scene about social conformity. Within two months he would become one of the most celebrated restaurateurs in London. Within a decade, one of the most famous in the world.
"A Change of Mind" aired on December 15, 1967 — a Friday. That afternoon, at 5:04 PM local time, the Silver Bridge collapsed. It connected Point Pleasant, West Virginia, to Gallipolis, Ohio — an eyebar chain suspension bridge built in 1928, the only one of its kind in America. A single eyebar, number 330, had developed a microscopic crack through fretting wear at the bearing. The crack grew through internal corrosion over thirty-nine years. At rush hour on a Friday ten days before Christmas, the eyebar failed and the entire bridge fell into the Ohio River in less than a minute. Forty-six people died. Twenty-one vehicles went into the water. The NTSB investigation established that no inspection protocol in existence at the time could have detected the flaw. The bridge had been carrying loads it was never designed for. Everyone who drove across it assumed it was safe because it had always been there.
In Point Pleasant, the collapse was preceded by thirteen months of reported sightings of a creature with large red eyes and enormous wings — the Mothman. John Keel documented the sightings in "The Mothman Prophecies" (1975). Whether or not one believes in the Mothman, the metaphor is hard to ignore: a community haunted by an incomprehensible warning it could not interpret, followed by a catastrophic structural failure caused by an invisible defect in a system everyone trusted because it had never failed before.
"Daydream Believer" by the Monkees was number one in America. "Hello, Goodbye" by the Beatles was number one in Britain. ITV did not broadcast the next episode on December 22 — "The Prisoner" was deemed not suitable for Christmas Eve week. The series would not return until the new year. The bridge had always been there. And then it wasn't.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
The title is from Goethe. "Du mußt Amboß oder Hammer sein" — "You must be anvil or hammer." Number Two quotes it in the original German. This is the twelfth episode produced and the tenth broadcast. It is, by nearly unanimous agreement, one of the two or three best episodes of the entire series. It is also the only episode where Number Six wins.
Not escapes. Not survives. Wins. He destroys a man using nothing but theater.
Roger Woddis wrote it. Born May 17, 1917, in London. A Communist — literally. He was a member of the Communist Party of Great Britain, confirmed by his obituary in The Times. He worked at the Little Unity Theatre in King's Cross during the 1930s and 1940s. Unity Theatre was the explicitly political London theatre founded by the Left Book Club and the Communist Party in 1936 — it staged "Waiting for Lefty" and premiered Sean O'Casey's "The Star Turns Red." Woddis wrote revue material there before moving into print. He became the New Statesman's weekly poet from 1970 until months before his death, following in the footsteps of "Sagittarius" (Olga Katzin). He wrote a column for Radio Times called "Woddis On." Throughout the 1980s he wrote "Subverse" for Punch — a weekly political poem, humorously subversive, covering miners' strikes and Vietnam and apartheid in rhyming couplets.
His most famous poem was "Ethics for Everyman." Note the name of McGoohan's production company: Everyman Films. The poem's lines map directly onto this episode. "Terror, no need to add / Depends on who's wearing the hood." "Social morality / Has a duality / One for each side of the tracks." And the one that matters here: "Discipline by the strong / Is fair, if your collar is white." A Communist poet wrote a script about a man who defeats a totalitarian regime by making it paranoid — by exploiting the inherent fragility of any system built on suspicion. The irony is multiple. Woddis believed in a political system historically famous for purges driven by exactly this kind of paranoia. Whether he intended the script as self-critique is unknowable. He died in 1993, aged seventy-six.
Woddis had no prior ITC experience. He'd written one episode of the now-lost 1967 ABC paranormal series "Haunted," some material for "Armchair Theatre," and later a contribution to "Churchill's People." "Hammer into Anvil" is an outlier in his career — the one piece of genre television by a man whose natural medium was the political couplet. It is the most literary episode of the series. The script incorporates Goethe, Bizet, Cervantes, and Vivaldi. Not as decoration. As plot.
The Bizet is L'Arlésienne — specifically, Number Six buys six identical copies of the recording from the Village shop and plays them while timing something on his watch. The music is not random. L'Arlésienne is Alphonse Daudet's story of Frédéri, a young Provençal peasant who discovers his bride's infidelity and kills himself by jumping from a hayloft. A man driven to self-destruction by learning his lover has betrayed him. The episode opens with Number Seventy-Three, a young woman interrogated by Number Two about her husband's infidelity, who kills herself by jumping from a hospital window. Bizet's music plays throughout the episode as underscore. Woddis is using L'Arlésienne as a structural rhyme — the suicide that opens the episode and the Bizet that soundtracks it are telling the same story, and Number Six is using the music itself as a weapon, making Number Two hear betrayal everywhere.
Number Six also places an advertisement in the Village newspaper quoting Don Quixote in the original Spanish. He sends a meaningless numerical message by pigeon. He transmits a nursery rhyme in Morse code from the beach to nobody. He hides blank pages in a stone boat as though dead-dropping intelligence. He buys the cuckoo clock. Every act is a performance. Every performance is meaningless. And because Number Two believes Number Six would never do anything without purpose, every meaningless act acquires sinister significance in Number Two's mind. The paranoid leader builds his own conspiracy from nothing. Number Six doesn't even have to lie. He just has to act.
Patrick Cargill played Number Two — the second time in the series. He'd already appeared as Thorpe, one of Number Six's real-world colleagues, in "Many Happy Returns" (episode seven).
