The Embryo Room is stocked with props for childhood but runs out of scenery by adulthood, so the later ages must be enacted with whatever's at hand. Boxing gloves. Fencing foils. A wine glass. A cage.
What makes this episode legendary is what happened to the actors while shooting it. According to the 2007 documentary "Don't Knock Yourself Out," both McGoohan and McKern became so consumed by their roles that they approached what multiple witnesses described as a near-psychotic state. McKern, by various accounts, suffered either a nervous breakdown or a heart attack during production — sources differ, and McKern himself was characteristically vague about which it was. Production stopped. When he returned for "Fall Out" almost a year later, he was visibly a different man — heavier, older, hollowed out. The episode had taken something from him that didn't come back.
The Butler, played by Angelo Muscat, finally receives a "featuring" credit — his only one in the entire series, despite appearing in fourteen of seventeen episodes. Muscat was born in Malta in 1930, stood four feet three inches tall, and came from a family where everyone else was of ordinary height. He worked mundane jobs in Malta before emigrating to England and joining a touring production of "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs." McGoohan cast him from a lineup of photographs shown by the casting director. Muscat never speaks a single word of dialogue across the entire run of The Prisoner, yet there was genuine fan speculation during the original broadcast that he might be Number One — the silent figure who sees everything and serves everyone and belongs to no side. After the series, Muscat appeared in the Beatles' "Magical Mystery Tour" (1967) and played an Oompa Loompa in "Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory" (1971). He died at forty-seven in 1977. George Markstein, the show's script editor, said of him: "He never said a word throughout the series, and yet in a way he was as important, or perhaps even more so, than Number Six himself. Angelo was a genial little man — he always had a smile, even on set at eight o'clock in the morning."
Peter Swanwick, the Supervisor — the man behind the console in the control room, the functionary who watches the watchers — appeared in nine of the seventeen episodes and gets his final showcase here. Born in Nottingham in 1922, Swanwick had started with a bit part in "The African Queen" (1951) and become a fixture of 1960s British television, including two episodes of McGoohan's earlier series "Danger Man." He played Herr Zeller in the original London stage production of "The Sound of Music." Multiple operations in the 1960s left him with limited time. He died on November 14, 1968, at forty-six years old — nine months after "Fall Out" aired, less than a year after the series ended. Two of the three actors who shared that Embryo Room were dead within a decade. Only McGoohan survived into old age, and he never stopped being asked why he resigned.
For Prisoner fans, there is an infamous line that sustained decades of debate: does McKern's Number Two, in headmaster mode, say "Report to my study in the morning, Drake!" — confirming that Number Six is John Drake from "Danger Man"? McKern's delivery is genuinely unclear. When the original script was eventually published, the line read: "Report to my study in the morning break." The most consequential word in Prisoner scholarship turned out to be "break," not "Drake." The mystery was a diction problem.
The episode aired on ITV on January 25, 1968 — a Thursday. Two days earlier, North Korea had seized the USS Pueblo in international waters, capturing 83 American crew members in what became the longest-held captivity of a U.S. naval vessel's crew since the War of 1812. Five days later, on January 30, the Tet Offensive began. While a fictional spy sat locked in a room being regressed to childhood, a real intelligence-gathering ship sat captured in Wonsan harbor, and 84,000 Viet Cong soldiers were massing for simultaneous assaults on every major city in South Vietnam. The number one song in America was "Judy in Disguise (With Glasses)" by John Fred and His Playboy Band — a novelty parody of the Beatles' "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds." In Britain, it was still "Hello, Goodbye" by the Beatles themselves. A song about departure. A song about not being able to tell which is which.
Degree Absolute works both ways. That is the point of the episode, the thing Number Six understands that Number Two does not. The technique requires the therapist to enter the patient's mind so completely that the boundary between them dissolves — and when it does, the patient can walk out through the therapist's door. Number Two asks "Why did you resign?" for the last time, and Number Six answers with a question: "Why don't you resign?" It is the only moment in the entire series where someone turns the central question back on the questioner. McKern's face when he hears it — delight, terror, recognition — is the finest single piece of acting in the show's run.
The cage door closes. The timer runs out. "Die, Six, die!" screams a voice. Number Two falls. The Supervisor asks Number Six what he wants. "Number One," Six replies. The Supervisor says he will take him there.
The answer was always in the room.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
Terence Feely sold a script to Alfred Hitchcock in 1955. He was twenty-seven, a Fleet Street journalist who'd come to London from Liverpool's Jesuit College, where the Jesuits had taught him English and psychology — not a bad curriculum for someone who would spend the next forty-five years writing television about surveillance, paranoia, and women who are smarter than the systems that employ them. He'd started at a small paper in Middlesbrough and worked his way to the Sunday Graphic. Then television swallowed him. By 1961 he was writing for "The Avengers." By 1967 he was co-director of Everyman Films alongside Patrick McGoohan and David Tomblin — "The Prisoner" was partly his company's production. He wrote two episodes. This is the first.
"The Schizoid Man" is about the theft of identity through conditioning. Number Six is drugged, subjected to electroshock therapy, his handedness reversed from right to left, his tastes in food and cigarettes altered, his hair restyled and dyed. He wakes up believing it is the next morning. It has been weeks. He is told he is Number Twelve — a Village agent assigned to impersonate Number Six. The real Number Six, he is informed, is already here. And there he is: same face, same build, same voice, wearing a negative-image blazer (black piping on white where Number Six wears white piping on black). The double knows things only Number Six would know. The double passes tests Number Six now fails. The double is, by every metric the Village can devise, more Number Six than Number Six.
McGoohan plays both roles, and the performance is surgical. Number Six is bewildered, then furious, then quietly desperate. Number Twelve is smooth, amused, precise — a man entirely at home in someone else's life. The technical apparatus was primitive: split-screen photography and Frank Maher, McGoohan's regular stunt double since "Danger Man," standing in for whichever Number was facing away from camera. The fight between the two McGoohans — Number Six grappling with his own stolen self — was choreographed to hide the seams, and it works. You forget you're watching one man and a trick.
The identity theft fails because of a bruised fingernail. In the episode's opening scene, before the conditioning begins, Number Twenty-Four — Alison, a young woman practicing a mind-reading act for the Village festival — accidentally damages Number Six's left thumbnail while photographing him. The bruise is still growing out weeks later when Number Six awakens as "Number Twelve." Neither Number Two nor the real Number Twelve noticed it. The entire apparatus of conditioning, electroshock, taste alteration, and handedness reversal is defeated by a thumbnail. McGoohan understood that identity doesn't live in preferences or habits or even handedness. It lives in the body's own calendar: the slow, biological fact of a bruise working its way to the edge of a nail.
This is also the only episode in the entire run where the white balloon is called by name. Number Two orders "Deactivate Rover." Later, when Curtis — the real Number Twelve, who has been impersonating Number Six — is killed trying to escape, the report comes back: "Rover got him." Across 17 episodes and 197 more appearances, the balloon is never named again. The show felt no need to explain what it was. It was simply there — vast, white, suffocating, bouncing across the beach like a nursery toy designed by a totalitarian state.
Anton Rodgers played Number Two. Born Anthony Rodgers in London in 1933, he was on stage by fourteen — his West End debut was in "Carmen" at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, in 1947. He was a boy in the chorus. The same year he toured as Pip in "Great Expectations" and then took the title role in a revival of Rattigan's "The Winslow Boy." He trained at the Italia Conti Academy and then LAMDA. By the mid-1960s he'd been through Birmingham rep, Northampton rep, Hornchurch rep, and a Broadway run of the musical "Pickwick" (he played Mr Jingle at the Saville Theatre in 1963, then took it to the 46th Street Theatre in New York in 1965). He played Vladimir in "Waiting for Godot" in Manchester, directed "The Fantasticks" at Hampstead, played Macheath in "The Threepenny Opera" at Stratford Ontario, Dr Rank in "A Doll's House" at the Criterion, Henry V in Coventry, Lord Henry Wotton in "The Picture of Dorian Gray" at Greenwich, and Astrov in "Uncle Vanya" at the Oxford Playhouse. His film career included "The Day of the Jackal" (1973) and "Dirty Rotten Scoundrels" (1988), where he played Andre, the comically corrupt French policeman who enables Michael Caine's schemes. He sang "Thank You Very Much" in "Scrooge" (1970), which got an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song. But television audiences knew him as the warm, exasperated husband in "Fresh Fields" (1984–86) and the gentle solicitor in "May to December" (1989–94) — the kind of actor who spent decades doing Ibsen, Shaw, and Wilde on stage while becoming famous for sitcoms. His second wife was the actress Elizabeth Garvie, who had played Elizabeth Bennet in the 1980 BBC "Pride and Prejudice." They toured together doing Jane Austen readings. He died in Reading, Berkshire, in December 2007, aged seventy-four. He was a patron of the Angles Theatre in Wisbech, the town where his family had been evacuated during the war — his father had worked for Balding and Mansell, printers of ration books, permits and passes.
Jane Merrow played Alison, Number Twenty-Four. Born Jane Josephine Meirowsky in Hertfordshire in 1941, daughter of an English mother and a German-Jewish refugee father — "My father's side of the family were ethnically Jewish, but not practising," she said later. She studied at RADA, won the Shakespeare Cup at the Kent Drama Festival, and by 1963 was starring in the BBC's "Lorna Doone." Then the ITC circuit absorbed her: "Danger Man," "The Saint," "The Baron," "The Avengers." After her penultimate-episode appearance in the 1967 series of "The Avengers" ("Mission... Highly Improbable"), she was considered as Diana Rigg's replacement. The role went to Linda Thorson instead. In 1965 she had played Julia in a Theatre 625 adaptation of Orwell's "Nineteen Eighty-Four." The following year she was in "Night of the Big Heat" with Peter Cushing and Christopher Lee. Then came "The Prisoner," and then the role that should have made her a star: Alais, the mistress of Henry II, opposite Peter O'Toole in "The Lion in Winter" (1968). She received a Golden Globe nomination for Best Supporting Actress. She lost to Ruth Gordon for "Rosemary's Baby." After that, Hammer's "Hands of the Ripper" (1971), then America — guest spots on "Mission: Impossible," "Mannix," "The Six Million Dollar Man," "Magnum, P.I.," "MacGyver," "Airwolf," the entire grid of 1970s and '80s American television procedurals. She returned to Britain in the 1990s to run a family business. In 2006 and 2008, she went back to Portmeirion for Prisoner conventions.
Earl Cameron played the Supervisor. He was born in Pembroke, Bermuda, in 1917, the youngest of six children. He joined the merchant navy, landed in Britain, became a song-and-dance man with ENSA during the war, worked in repertory, and then in 1951 was cast in "Pool of London," an Ealing Studios film noir directed by Basil Dearden. He played a West Indian merchant seaman in a relationship with a young white woman — the first time an interracial romance had been sensitively handled in a British film. The BFI calls it a milestone. From there: "Simba" (1955) with Dirk Bogarde, "Thunderball" (1965) as Bond's local contact Pinder, four episodes of "Danger Man" with McGoohan, "Doctor Who" (1966, "The Tenth Planet" — the First Doctor's regeneration story), and then "The Prisoner." In 2005, at eighty-eight, he played a dictatorial president opposite Nicole Kidman in Sydney Pollack's "The Interpreter." In 2010, at ninety-three, he appeared in Christopher Nolan's "Inception." He was appointed CBE in 2009. He died in 2020, aged 102.
Pat Jackson directed. Born Patrick Douglas Selmes Jackson in Eltham in 1916, he joined the GPO Film Unit on his seventeenth birthday as a messenger boy — his mother had persuaded her MP, Sir Kingsley Wood (who also happened to be the Postmaster General), to find work for her son after his father's early death. He worked on "Night Mail" (1936); the voice narrating W.H. Auden's poem ("This is the Night Mail crossing the border, bringing the cheque and the postal order") was Jackson himself. He directed "Western Approaches" (1944), a semi-documentary about merchant seamen that took three years to complete, with six months of lifeboat sequences shot at sea. After the war, three years under contract at MGM in Hollywood. He directed four episodes of "The Prisoner" — more than anyone except McGoohan. He died in 2011, aged ninety-five.
"The Schizoid Man" was broadcast on October 27, 1967. That same day in Baltimore, four men — Philip Berrigan, Thomas Lewis, David Eberhardt, and James Mengel — walked into a Selective Service office on South Gay Street and poured their blood over draft files. Berrigan was a Josephite priest. He had brought duck blood mixed with his own. The "Baltimore Four" action was the first in what would become a series of increasingly dramatic draft-file destructions — seven months later, Berrigan and eight others would burn 378 files with homemade napalm in Catonsville, Maryland, an act that would define the Catholic antiwar left for a generation. In London, "Hair" had just opened off-Broadway six days earlier. "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead" was in its second week on Broadway. The March on the Pentagon had happened six days before — fifty thousand people, Norman Mailer among them, besieging the military headquarters for two days. The Patterson-Gimlin Bigfoot film had been shot a week earlier at Bluff Creek, California. And Walt Disney's "The Jungle Book" had been in theaters for nine days, the last film Walt personally supervised before his death eleven months earlier. In the Village, Number Six was fighting a man who looked exactly like him for the right to be himself.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
The eighth episode produced. The first where McGoohan seized control of the production from the director. It was filmed in January 1967 and the shoot was, by multiple accounts, a catastrophe. The director Robert Asher was a comedy specialist — five Norman Wisdom films, a Morecambe and Wise film, "Make Mine Mink" with Terry-Thomas. He'd moved into ITC television work and was competent, professional, and entirely unprepared for Patrick McGoohan. On set, McGoohan overrode him, screamed at him, and eventually took over direction of the episode while Asher stood aside. The cast watched it happen. Annette Andre, interviewed decades later for the 2007 DVD documentary "Don't Knock Yourself Out," strongly criticized McGoohan's behavior. Mark Eden recalled McGoohan losing control during a fight scene and nearly strangling him. A crew member stated his belief that McGoohan experienced a nervous breakdown during production. The episode that emerged from this wreckage is, structurally, the most complex of the series: a triple-layered conspiracy involving two Number Twos, a bomber watchmaker, "jammers" who create fake plots to waste the authorities' time, and a false-flag assassination designed to justify a crackdown — all filtered through Number Six's justified paranoia about whether the information he's being fed is real or planted.
The concept of "jamming" is drawn from actual resistance practice in 1960s Eastern Europe. Dissidents in Communist states created and disseminated details of fake plots — fabricated conspiracies that intelligence services were obliged to investigate, tying up surveillance resources and eroding institutional trust. The Situationists called it "radio jamming." By the 1980s it evolved into "culture jamming" — the subversive alteration of billboard advertising — a term popularized by the band Negativland. Woddis's "Hammer into Anvil" had a Communist writer exploring paranoia within authority; Cramoy's "It's Your Funeral" has an American writer exploring how a surveillance state drowns in its own noise. The two episodes are companion pieces. Together they describe the complete failure mode of totalitarianism: paranoia eating itself from both directions.
Michael Cramoy was American. He had written for "Dragnet" — the Jack Webb police procedural, the most procedural show in television history. Webb's mantra was "just the facts." Cramoy then moved to England and wrote for ITC: "The Invisible Man" in the 1950s, "The Saint" in the 1960s. His task on this episode was peculiar: write a script incorporating pre-existing location footage already shot at Portmeirion plus the standing MGM Borehamwood studio sets, with a later Portmeirion shoot using stand-ins for both McGoohan and Andre. He was building a story around footage that already existed. Fitting narrative to pre-existing images. The episode's plot, in which truth and fabrication become indistinguishable, was constructed by the same method.
Derren Nesbitt played the new Number Two — the ambitious young replacement planning to assassinate his predecessor. Born Derren Michael Horwitz, June 19, 1935, in London. Jewish. RADA-trained. He is best known as Major von Hapen in "Where Eagles Dare" (1968) — the Gestapo officer interrogating Richard Burton and Clint Eastwood. While filming in Austria, Nesbitt requested a meeting with a former Gestapo officer to understand the character. During the scene where von Hapen is shot, the blood squib attached to Nesbitt exploded with such force that he was temporarily blinded. He recovered.
For "The Prisoner" he chose to play Number Two as a bleach-blond dandy in oversized spectacles — an image so distinctive that the Episode by Episode blog notes its uncanny resemblance to Joe 90, Gerry Anderson's child puppet spy, which wouldn't appear until a year later. Whether Anderson took inspiration is unknown. Nesbitt was never told what the show was about. He played Number Two in a state of genuine confusion, which may be the most honest performance any actor delivered on the series. He later played Sandy Youth, a predatory blackmailer of gay men, in "Victim" (1961) — one of the first major British films to address homosexuality sympathetically. He played DCI Jordan in "Special Branch" (1969). He wrote, directed, and produced "The Amorous Milkman" (1975), a sex comedy starring Julie Ege and Diana Dors, based on his own novel. He has been married four times. In 1973 he was fined £250 for assaulting his first wife, the actress Anne Aubrey, with a leather strap after she told him about an affair. In 2018, aged eighty-three, he played a drag queen in the independent film "Tucked." As of 2026, he is ninety and still living in Worthing, West Sussex.
André van Gyseghem played the retiring Number Two — the "permanent" one who claims to have been on holiday during all of Number Six's previous encounters. Born August 18, 1906, in Eltham, Kent — the same Eltham where Pat Jackson, who directed the previous episode, was born a decade later. RADA-trained. After Hull Repertory Theatre, he directed at the Embassy Theatre throughout the early 1930s. In 1933 he directed Paul Robeson and Flora Robson in Eugene O'Neill's "All God's Chillun Got Wings." He directed Robeson again in "Stevedore" in 1935. Between 1933 and 1935 he made several trips to the Soviet Union, spending a year working at Nikolay Okhlopkov's Realistic Theatre in Moscow. He became a member of the Communist Party of Great Britain and president of Unity Theatre's Management Committee — the same Unity Theatre where Roger Woddis, who wrote the previous episode, had cut his teeth a decade later. Van Gyseghem attributed much of his acting expertise to his Soviet training. A Communist directed Paul Robeson. A Communist wrote "Hammer into Anvil." The retiring Number Two who represents institutional permanence was played by a Communist Party member who trained in Stalin's Moscow. Nobody in the audience knew any of this. Van Gyseghem appeared in over fifty British television dramas between 1951 and his death in 1979 at seventy-three.
Annette Andre played the Watchmaker's Daughter. Born Annette Christine Andreallo, June 24, 1939, in Drummoyne, New South Wales, Australia. Her father was an upholsterer. She trained as a ballet dancer from age four at an academy linked to the Australian Ballet. At fifteen she quit dance for acting. She was too young to work legally as an actress — not yet sixteen — so she enrolled in a radio training school, and her first role was in a serial called "Kid Grayson Rides the Range." She moved to the UK in 1963. She played Philia, a beautiful virgin concubine, in the 1966 film of "A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum" — opposite Phil Silvers, Zero Mostel, and Buster Keaton in his final film role. Her most famous part was Jeannie Hopkirk in "Randall and Hopkirk (Deceased)" (1969) — the ghost detective show where she plays the widow of a murdered private eye who returns as a ghost only she and his partner can see. She turned down a proposal of marriage from Benny Hill. She was romantically linked with George Best. In 2018 she published her memoir "Where Have I Been All My Life," with a foreword by Roger Moore. She is now semi-retired and works in animal welfare.
In the 2007 DVD documentary, Andre said she did not enjoy her time on "The Prisoner." She strongly criticized McGoohan for screaming at Asher and taking over the production. She is one of the few people who worked on the series to say so publicly.
Wanda Ventham played the Computer Attendant — a small role. Born August 5, 1935, in Brighton. Trained at the Central School of Speech and Drama as a contemporary of Judi Dench. She appeared in "Carry On Cleo" and "Carry On Up the Khyber." She played Colonel Virginia Lake in the Gerry Anderson series "UFO." She appeared in "Doctor Who" three times across three decades: Jean Rock in "The Faceless Ones" (1967), Thea Ransome in "Image of the Fendahl" (1977), and Faroon in "Time and the Rani" (1987). She played Pamela Parry in "Only Fools and Horses." In 1976 she married Timothy Carlton. Their son is Benedict Cumberbatch.
Mark Eden played Number 100, the operative who manages the assassination plot on the ground. Born Douglas John Malin, February 14, 1928, in St Pancras, London. He played Marco Polo in the 1964 "Doctor Who" serial of the same name — one of the great lost stories, all episodes missing from the BBC archive. He played Inspector Parker in the 1970s Lord Peter Wimsey adaptations. His most famous role was Alan Bradley in "Coronation Street" (1986–1989), the villain killed by a Blackpool tram in one of the most-watched moments in British soap opera history. In 2009 he unveiled a plaque at the tram stop where the scene was filmed. After Coronation Street he said he received many offers for "psycho" roles. His first wife was Joan Long, who later married John Le Mesurier — Sergeant Wilson in "Dad's Army." His third wife was Sue Nicholls, who plays Audrey Roberts in "Coronation Street" — the daughter of Baron Harmar-Nicholls. During filming of this episode, McGoohan lost control during a fight scene and nearly strangled him. He developed Alzheimer's disease and died on January 1, 2021, aged ninety-two.
"It's Your Funeral" aired on December 8, 1967. That same day, the Beatles released "Magical Mystery Tour" — a film about a bus trip to nowhere, directed by nobody, structured around confusion and whimsy, received with bewilderment by a public that expected coherence. A few days earlier, on December 3, Dr. Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant in Cape Town. A man's heart was removed and replaced with a stranger's. "Daydream Believer" by the Monkees was number one in America. "Hello, Goodbye" by the Beatles was number one in Britain. The retiring Number Two left by helicopter. The new Number Two sat down in his chair. Number Six congratulated him, and told him that something equally suitable would be arranged when his time came. The system replaces the man and continues. "It's your funeral," he said. He was talking to everyone.

programme.title: The Prisoner
programme.desc:
The ninth episode produced and the twelfth broadcast. It is the second episode from which Patrick McGoohan fired the director. Roy Rossotti lasted one day. McGoohan took over under his pseudonym "Joseph Serf" — the same name he'd used on "Free for All." The pattern was now established: McGoohan had hired professional television directors, found them inadequate to his vision, sacked them mid-production, and finished the episodes himself. Rossotti directed episodes of "The Saint," "Randall and Hopkirk (Deceased)," "Department S," and "Jason King" — competent ITC journeyman work. He was not incompetent. He was simply not McGoohan. Nobody was.
The episode is about lobotomy as social policy. The Village declares Number Six "unmutual" — a diagnosis by committee, enforced by mob, resolved by surgery. Roger Parkes wrote it. Born 1933. Died May 2, 2008, aged seventy-five. He was a crime reporter who became a trainee story editor at the BBC, assigned to "Compact" — the daily serial about a women's magazine, broadcast live from 1962 to 1965, now almost entirely wiped from the archive. "Compact" was the BBC's first attempt at a soap opera aimed at adults. It was cancelled because the BBC thought soap operas were beneath them. Parkes moved from documenting real crime to scripting fictional soap to writing one of the most explicitly political episodes of "The Prisoner." His subsequent career confirmed the political instinct: he wrote for "Doombolt Chase," Terry Nation's "Survivors" (1975), and "Blake's 7" (1978) — three separate visions of collapsed or totalitarian Britain. He also wrote for "Doombwatch," "Juliet Bravo," "Boon," and "Campion." He published several novels. He wrote the foreword to the published script of this episode in 2006, two years before his death.
His first draft had Number Eighty-Six aggressively pursuing Number Six romantically. McGoohan cut every page of it. The no-romance edict was absolute. McGoohan believed that sexuality in the series would reduce Number Six from an archetype to a character. The Prisoner was not about a man. It was about Man. Desire would make it personal. McGoohan wanted it universal.
John Sharp played Number Two — an oleaginous functionary who delegates the dirty work to a woman and then blames her when it fails. Born John Herbert Sharp, August 5, 1920, in Bradford, Yorkshire. The name confusion is real: he was credited as "John Sharpe" on this episode, which is either a production office error (per Rick Davy's "The Essential Guide") or a deliberate choice he later reversed (per Robert Fairclough's "Official Companion"). Wikipedia and IMDb both list him as "John Sharp." Whatever his billing, he was a character actor of extraordinary range across forty-two years. Over 130 television appearances. He played Ezra Biggins — the parsimonious, awkward Yorkshire dairy farmer — in "All Creatures Great and Small," and Peter Davison remembered him as "a wonderful raconteur who would tell you these long stories." Christopher Timothy, who played James Herriot, said: "I found myself getting quite moved when I watched an episode recently, not because of what we were doing, but because all those lovely people are no longer with us. John Sharp was a lovely, lovely man." He played the Bishop in Franco Zeffirelli's "Brother Sun, Sister Moon" (1972). He appeared in "The Wicker Man" (1973). He played the Publican in "The Avengers" episode "Murdersville" (1967). He appeared in Lindsay Anderson's "The White Bus" (1967) and in "Night and the City" (1950) — Jules Dassin's noir masterpiece, uncredited. He died November 26, 1992, aged seventy-two.
Angela Browne played Number Eighty-Six — the woman who administers the fake lobotomy, who drugs Number Six's tea, who is then hypnotized and turned against Number Two. Born June 14, 1938, in Walton-on-Thames, Surrey. RADA-trained. She had already worked with McGoohan — she played the Girl in the "Danger Man" episode "The Girl in Pink Pyjamas." Her career was a catalogue of ITC and BBC prestige: "Ghost Squad," "The Saint," "The Avengers," "Man in a Suitcase," "Upstairs, Downstairs," "Minder." She appeared in Rumer Godden's "Kizzy" (1976), an adaptation of "The Diddakoi" about a Romany girl, fondly remembered by a generation of British children. She was in "Carry On Nurse" (1959), uncredited, and in Norman Wisdom's "Press for Time" (1966) — connecting her to the man whose director McGoohan had just fired, Robert Asher, who had directed five Norman Wisdom films.
She married Francis Matthews in 1963. Matthews was the voice of Captain Scarlet. Born September 2, 1927, in York. His father was a shop steward at the Rowntree's chocolate factory. Matthews trained at St Michael's Jesuit College in Leeds, then became a stagehand at the Theatre Royal before his national service in the Royal Navy. He played Dr. Hans Kleve in Hammer's "The Revenge of Frankenstein" (1958) and the heroes of "Dracula: Prince of Darkness" and "Rasputin the Mad Monk" (both 1966). He was Paul Temple in the BBC's Francis Durbridge adaptations from 1969 to 1971. Gerry Anderson cast him as Captain Scarlet specifically because Matthews could do an impeccable Cary Grant impression — the entire vocal characterization of Captain Scarlet is an imitation of Cary Grant. Matthews and Browne co-starred in "The Dark Island" (1962) and "Paul Temple" (1970). She gave up acting in 1990. She died June 20, 2001, aged sixty-three. He died June 14, 2014 — which would have been her seventy-sixth birthday — aged eighty-six.
George Pravda played the Doctor. Born Jiří Pravda, June 19, 1916, in Prague, Austria-Hungary. He emigrated to Britain in 1956 — the year of the Hungarian Uprising, the year Czechoslovakia's brief post-Stalin thaw began to freeze again. He appeared in "Thunderball" (1965) as Ladislav Kutze, the reluctant SPECTRE scientist who ultimately helps Bond. He played three different roles across three different serials of "Doctor Who": Doland in "The Enemy of the World" (1968), Jaeger in "The Mutants" (1972), and Castellan Spandrell in "The Deadly Assassin" (1976). He appeared in "Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy" (1979), "I, Claudius" (1976), and Clint Eastwood's "Firefox" (1982). His wife was Hana Pravda — also a Czech actress, also an emigrée. "Pravda" means "truth" in Czech. The Doctor who administers a fake lobotomy was played by a man whose name means Truth. Nobody in the audience knew this. Pravda died May 1, 1985, aged sixty-eight.
Among the uncredited Social Group members: Michael Chow. Born Zhou Yinghua, March 7, 1939, in Shanghai. His father was Zhou Xinfang, one of the most famous Peking Opera performers in Chinese history. His sister is Tsai Chin — the actress who played the Bond girl in "You Only Live Twice" (1967), released six months before this episode aired. Chow was sent to an English boarding school at twelve and never spoke to his father again. He studied at Saint Martin's School of Art. His first wife was Grace Coddington, the legendary Vogue creative director. Two months after this episode aired, in February 1968, he opened Mr Chow in Knightsbridge — Chinese food served by Italian waiters, with Peter Blake and David Hockney paintings on the walls. It became one of the most famous restaurants in the world. He opened locations in Beverly Hills, New York, Las Vegas, Miami. In this episode, he was an extra. An uncredited face in a crowd scene about social conformity. Within two months he would become one of the most celebrated restaurateurs in London. Within a decade, one of the most famous in the world.
"A Change of Mind" aired on December 15, 1967 — a Friday. That afternoon, at 5:04 PM local time, the Silver Bridge collapsed. It connected Point Pleasant, West Virginia, to Gallipolis, Ohio — an eyebar chain suspension bridge built in 1928, the only one of its kind in America. A single eyebar, number 330, had developed a microscopic crack through fretting wear at the bearing. The crack grew through internal corrosion over thirty-nine years. At rush hour on a Friday ten days before Christmas, the eyebar failed and the entire bridge fell into the Ohio River in less than a minute. Forty-six people died. Twenty-one vehicles went into the water. The NTSB investigation established that no inspection protocol in existence at the time could have detected the flaw. The bridge had been carrying loads it was never designed for. Everyone who drove across it assumed it was safe because it had always been there.
In Point Pleasant, the collapse was preceded by thirteen months of reported sightings of a creature with large red eyes and enormous wings — the Mothman. John Keel documented the sightings in "The Mothman Prophecies" (1975). Whether or not one believes in the Mothman, the metaphor is hard to ignore: a community haunted by an incomprehensible warning it could not interpret, followed by a catastrophic structural failure caused by an invisible defect in a system everyone trusted because it had never failed before.
"Daydream Believer" by the Monkees was number one in America. "Hello, Goodbye" by the Beatles was number one in Britain. ITV did not broadcast the next episode on December 22 — "The Prisoner" was deemed not suitable for Christmas Eve week. The series would not return until the new year. The bridge had always been there. And then it wasn't.

programme.title: Citizen Kane
programme.desc: Orson Welles was twenty-five years old and had never made a film. RKO gave him a contract unprecedented in Hollywood history: develop his own story, cast his own actors, crew his own production, and retain final cut. No studio executive could see footage until Welles chose to show it. No cuts without his approval. The deal was so resented in the industry that the Hollywood press mocked RKO for months. Welles called the movie studio "the greatest electric train set a boy ever had." His first project, Heart of Darkness shot entirely in first person, collapsed when he couldn't trim $50,000 from the budget. A political thriller stalled next. Then he and screenwriter Herman Mankiewicz — who had been writing Mercury radio scripts and who hated William Randolph Hearst after being exiled from his social circle — began arguing, inventing, discarding, thrashing toward Kane. Mankiewicz wrote a draft under John Houseman's supervision on 300 pages of Welles's notes. Welles drastically condensed and rearranged it, added scenes of his own. Mankiewicz's contract stipulated no credit; when the film neared release he threatened full-page trade paper ads and an exposé in the Saturday Evening Post. Welles himself circled Mankiewicz's name on the guild form and drew an arrow putting it first. The official credit reads "Screenplay by Herman J. Mankiewicz and Orson Welles." The argument over authorship lasted decades — Pauline Kael's 50,000-word essay "Raising Kane" in 1971 damaged Welles's reputation, but later scholarship by Robert Carringer, reviewing all seven drafts still intact at RKO, concluded that "Welles's contribution was not only substantial but definitive." Cinematographer Gregg Toland — "just then, the number-one cameraman in the world" — walked into Welles's office and said "I want you to use me on your picture." He'd seen the Mercury stage productions and wanted to work with someone who didn't know the rules. Together they invented deep focus photography where foreground and background are both razor sharp, something no Hollywood camera had achieved. They built sets with ceilings — unheard of, because that's where the lights went — so they could shoot from floor level. They cut holes in the concrete floor to get the camera even lower. Welles learned filmmaking by watching John Ford's Stagecoach forty times, often with a different department head, asking "How was this done? Why was this done?" His entire cast was new to motion pictures. He brought the Mercury Theatre company — Joseph Cotten, Agnes Moorehead, Everett Sloane, Ray Collins — none of whom had acted on screen. Dorothy Comingore was recommended by Charlie Chaplin. To start filming without executive interference, Welles began on a Saturday morning when few would be around, labeling everything "Orson Welles Tests" on the paperwork. The first "test" was the projection room scene, shot for $809 against a budget of $528 — "one of the most famous scenes in movie history." When executives showed up unannounced, the entire cast and crew would start playing softball until they left. Welles worked sixteen to eighteen hours a day, starting at 4 AM for the special effects makeup that aged him. The contact lenses to make him look elderly were so painful a doctor had to place them. He badly cut his wrist shooting the scene where Kane destroys Susan's bedroom. He fell ten feet during the Gettys staircase scene, chipping two ankle bones, and directed from a wheelchair for two weeks before strapping on a steel brace to resume acting — it's visible in the low-angle shot after the election. For the final scene, the Rosebud sled was burned in a working furnace on a Selznick stage. On the ninth take, the Culver City Fire Department arrived in full gear because the flue had caught fire. "Orson was delighted with the commotion." Bernard Herrmann was given twelve weeks for the score — most Hollywood composers got two or three. He composed complete musical pieces for the montages and Welles edited scenes to match their length. Robert Wise, roughly Welles's age, edited the film; he and Mark Robson both became successful directors. Hearst tried to have every print destroyed. He prohibited any mention of the film in his newspapers. RKO couldn't get theaters to book it. Budget: $839,727. It lost money on first run. It lost Best Picture to How Green Was My Valley. Won only Best Original Screenplay. Then it grew. French critics championed it. André Bazin wrote that "even if Welles did not invent the cinematic devices, one should credit him with the invention of their meaning." D.W. Griffith said "I loved Citizen Kane and particularly loved the ideas he took from me." For forty consecutive years — five decennial polls — it stood at number one in Sight and Sound's greatest films list. AFI No. 1 in 1998 and 2007. National Film Registry, 1989. When asked where the confidence came from to make something so radical, Welles answered: "Ignorance. Sheer ignorance. There's no confidence to equal it."

programme.title: FALLING LEAVES — Interstitial
programme.desc: Told her sister will die when the last leaf falls, little Trixie ties the leaves to the trees. From cinema's first woman director.

programme.title: Falling Leaves
programme.desc:
Little Trixie Thompson overhears the family doctor tell her parents that her older sister Winifred, gravely ill with consumption, will die when the last leaf falls from the tree outside her window. Taking the warning literally, Trixie slips into the garden after dark with a spool of string and ties the fallen leaves back onto the bare branches, determined to hold off autumn itself. A passing doctor, Earl Headley, finds her at this task, learns what she is trying to do, and, once he sees Winifred, treats her with an experimental serum of his own devising. The leaves stay tied; Winifred recovers.
The picture is a loose, considerably softened adaptation of O. Henry's 1907 short story "The Last Leaf," in which an old painter saves a dying woman by forging a leaf on the wall outside her window, at the cost of his own life to pneumonia. Alice Guy-Blaché, credited on some prints simply as director and on others as director-scenarist, kept the central conceit — a leaf standing between a sick woman and death — but replaced O. Henry's fatal irony with a child's earnestness and a happy ending secured by medicine rather than art. Sets were designed by Henri Ménessier, who had worked with Guy-Blaché since her days at Gaumont in Paris. Magda Foy, billed by Solax as "The Solax Kid," plays Trixie; Marian Swayne plays Winifred; Mace Greenleaf plays Dr. Headley.
Guy-Blaché had directed what is generally regarded as the first narrative fiction film, La Fée aux Choux (The Cabbage Fairy), in 1896, while running the production side of Gaumont in Paris — making her, by most film-historical accounts, the first woman to direct a film and, for roughly a decade afterward, the only one working anywhere. In 1910 she and her husband Herbert Blaché formed the Solax Company in Flushing, New York, with Alice as president — the first woman to found and head her own film studio. Falling Leaves was released March 15, 1912, from Solax's Flushing plant, shortly before the company's move to a larger, purpose-built studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey. Guy-Blaché directed and produced hundreds of films for Solax and earlier at Gaumont; only a small fraction are known to survive.
A print is held by the Library of Congress, and the film circulates today in more than one form: a black-and-white release with piano accompaniment and a tinted release with orchestral scoring have both been issued on home video. This file appears untinted, with English-language intertitles bearing the Solax sunburst logo and the studio's own credit line ("Falling Leaves, Solax 135-3"); the surviving elements show the scratches and softened contrast typical of an early-surviving public-domain print, but the image remains clean enough to follow Guy-Blaché's staging in depth, particularly in the multi-plane interior compositions of the sickroom scenes.

programme.title: CASABLANCA — Interstitial
programme.desc: Made during the actual war, the ending wasn’t even decided on set. Ingrid Bergman was told to play it both ways. The airport is a painted backdrop with a cardboard airplane and midget extras forced in perspective.

programme.title: Casablanca
programme.desc: Warner Bros. story analyst Stephen Karnot read an unproduced play called Everybody Comes to Rick's and called it "sophisticated hokum." Story editor Irene Diamond convinced producer Hal B. Wallis to buy it for $20,000 — the most anyone in Hollywood had ever paid for an unproduced play. The original was written by Murray Burnett, inspired by a trip he and his wife took through Europe in 1938. In Vienna shortly after the Anschluss they saw antisemitism firsthand. In the south of France they found a nightclub full of exiles and refugees, with a Black pianist — the prototype of Sam. Twins Julius and Philip Epstein were assigned to the screenplay but left to work on Frank Capra's Why We Fight series. Howard Koch filled in, producing thirty to forty pages. The Epsteins returned after a month and were reassigned; Koch's pages were not used. The three writers were never in the same room at the same time. The Epsteins were paid $30,416; Koch got $4,200. Casey Robinson did three uncredited weeks of rewrites, contributing every scene where Rick and Ilsa meet in the café. Nobody knew the ending. They were shooting in sequence because only the first half of the script was ready when filming began on May 25, 1942. Casey Robinson wrote to Wallis that the ending was "set up for a swell twist when Rick sends her away on the plane with Laszlo. For now, in doing so, he is not just solving a love triangle. He is forcing the girl to live up to the idealism of her nature." Ingrid Bergman asked Michael Curtiz which man her character was really in love with. He told her to play it both ways. Julius Epstein said he and Philip were driving when they simultaneously came up with "Round up the usual suspects," after which the entire resolution fell into place, including the farewell and "a suddenly noble Bogart." The last line — "Louis, I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship" — was chosen by Wallis from a telegram on August 7 and dubbed by Bogart a month after shooting ended. "Here's looking at you, kid" was not in any draft; Bogart said it to Bergman while she played poker between takes with her English coach. The airport finale used a cardboard cutout Lockheed Electra with little person extras to force the perspective, shrouded in fog to hide the fakery. The entire picture was shot on Warner Bros. soundstages in Burbank except for close-ups of the plane at Van Nuys Airport. Bergman was two inches taller than Bogart; Curtiz had him stand on blocks. Arthur Edeson, who had shot The Maltese Falcon and Frankenstein, photographed Bergman mainly from her preferred left side with a softening gauze filter and catch lights to make her eyes sparkle. Dooley Wilson was a drummer, not a pianist — he mimed the keyboard while Jean Plummer played off-screen, but his singing voice is his own. Max Steiner wanted to replace "As Time Goes By" with an original composition, but Bergman had already cut her hair for For Whom the Bell Tolls and couldn't reshoot, so Steiner wove the song through the entire score as a leitmotif alongside "La Marseillaise." The duel of the anthems was originally meant to pit "La Marseillaise" against the "Horst-Wessel-Lied," but that was still under copyright in non-Allied countries, so "Die Wacht am Rhein" was substituted. During the filming of that sequence, a witness saw many of the extras crying and "realized that they were all real refugees." Of the credited cast, only three were born in America. Conrad Veidt, who played Major Strasser, was a refugee German actor who had fled the Nazis with his Jewish wife; he was the highest-paid member of the cast and died shortly after the film's release. Marcel Dalio, who played the croupier, had been a star in French cinema — La Grande Illusion, La Règle du Jeu — before fleeing with his wife Madeleine Lebeau, who played Yvonne. Lebeau was the last surviving cast member, dying in 2016. Budget: $1,039,000. Shot in less than three months. Rushed into release on November 26, 1942, to capitalize on the Allied invasion of North Africa. Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay. Roger Ebert: "If there is ever a time when they decide that some movies should be spelled with an upper-case M, Casablanca should be voted first." 99% on Rotten Tomatoes. 100 on Metacritic — a perfect score. AFI No. 3 all-time. No. 1 on AFI's list of great screen passions. Six lines in the AFI top 100 quotes — more than any other film. The Writers Guild voted it the greatest screenplay ever written. National Film Registry, 1989. Julius Epstein: "More corn than in the states of Kansas and Iowa combined. But when corn works, there's nothing better."

programme.title: THE INSECTS' CHRISTMAS — Interstitial
programme.desc: A tiny Father Christmas climbs down from the tree to celebrate with the beetles and frogs of the forest — stop-motion puppetry from its first master.

programme.title: The Insects' Christmas
programme.desc:
A Father Christmas ornament climbs down from a tinsel-hung tree, makes his way into the winter forest, and dresses a small fir there with lights and gifts for the creatures who live among the snow. Beetles, grasshoppers and their neighbors accept the invitation, gather at the tree, and see out the night skating and playing in the snow before the toy climbs back to its place. It is a slight, gentle scenario, closer to a nursery pantomime than to the domestic comedies Starevich was also making in these years, and its charm rests entirely on the puppetry rather than on plot incident.
The director was Władysław Starewicz (Ladislas Starevich in most Western catalogues), a Polish naturalist working in the Russian film industry. His stop-motion technique had begun almost by accident three years earlier: as a museum curator in Kaunas making documentary shorts on Lucanus cervus, the stag beetle, he found the insects went inert under studio lighting and could not be filmed fighting from life. He rigged dead specimens with wire-jointed legs and animated their combat frame by frame instead, producing The Battle of the Stag Beetles (1910) and, in short order, the first puppet film with an actual plot, The Beautiful Leukanida (1912). Aleksandr Khanzhonkov, the Moscow producer who released Leukanida, brought Starevich onto his studio's payroll, and it was for Khanzhonkov's Trading House that The Insects' Christmas was made and released.
Sourcing on this title is thinner than on Starevich's better-known insect comedies, and the record is not perfectly settled. English-language filmographies and film databases catalogue the picture as a 1913 Russian release running roughly seven minutes; a cluster of Russian-language sources instead dates the Khanzhonkov premiere to December 31, 1912, and gives a shorter runtime nearer five minutes, which may reflect a different surviving cut or simply projection-speed variance common to hand-cranked silent material — this print runs 7 minutes at its transfer speed. The film should not be confused with Starevich's other, unrelated 1913 Christmas subject, a much longer live-action adaptation of Gogol's "The Night Before Christmas."
This copy carries Polish intertitles rather than the original Russian cards — "Boże Narodzenie w Lesie" ("Christmas in the Forest"), crediting "Scenariusz i reżyseria: Władysław Starewicz, Moskwa 1913" — indicating a later Polish-market or archival reissue rather than a first-run print. The image is uniformly cyan-toned throughout in the manner used for silent-era night exteriors, and the film carries a modern, non-original recorded score (excerpts of Vivaldi's "Winter" and Pachelbel's Canon) synchronized for this transfer, confirming it is a later restoration or compilation reissue rather than a raw nitrate scan.

programme.title: KID AUTO RACES AT VENICE — Interstitial
programme.desc: The Little Tramp's first appearance on any screen: Chaplin, in a costume assembled that morning, ruins a newsreel crew's day by refusing to get out of the shot.

programme.title: Kid Auto Races at Venice
programme.desc:
Keystone shot this split-reel farce on location at the second annual junior "pushmobile" race in Venice, California, on Sunday, January 11, 1914, folding a comedy into an actual public event rather than staging one on a lot. Henry Lehrman directed and plays the newsreel cameraman on-site to film the race; Chaplin plays the interloper who keeps wandering into his shot. There is almost no plot beyond that premise and almost no editing: a fictional cameraman films a real crowd watching a real race, while Chaplin mugs, preens, and gets shoved out of frame, only to wander back in. Much of the crowd was not in on the joke — spectators can be seen glancing at the camera and at Chaplin with open curiosity rather than playing along, which is precisely what made the film a novelty: it captured, unrehearsed, the public's first sight of a character it did not yet have a name for.
That distinction matters and is worth stating precisely. Chaplin had already assembled the tramp costume a few days earlier on the Mabel's Strange Predicament set, where Mack Sennett had told him to find "a comedy makeup, anything will do" — Chaplin came back in a small derby, a cane, a tight coat, baggy trousers, and shoes several sizes too large, worn on the wrong feet for the splayed walk. Mabel's Strange Predicament was filmed first but held for release; Kid Auto Races at Venice was shot afterward, cut quickly, and rushed out first, on February 7, 1914, two days ahead of it. So the character was born on one set and introduced to the public on another: Kid Auto Races is the Tramp's first appearance before an audience, not his first time in front of a camera. Keystone's own publicity later dressed up the costume's origin as a grab-bag of borrowed wardrobe — Fatty Arbuckle's trousers, Chester Conklin's tiny coat, Ford Sterling's oversized shoes are the names usually attached to the story — but the specific attributions come from studio promotion rather than a verified fitting-room account, so they are best treated as color rather than settled fact; the broader point, that the outfit was improvised on the spot from whatever the wardrobe department had lying around, is not in dispute.
The film survives only in worn dupe prints struck down through decades of 16mm reduction and public-domain reissue, which is the source of the scratches, contrast loss, and jumpy splices visible in most circulating copies, including this one; no tinting is present, and being a 1914 actuality-style one-reeler it carries no intertitles beyond the opening Keystone credit card, so what plays out is close to what a 1914 nickelodeon audience saw. No original release score is known to survive; accompaniment on modern prints is a later addition, not a period one. Contemporary trade notice was enthusiastic out of proportion to the film's simplicity — The Cinema called it "about the funniest film we have ever seen" — and it was reissued around 1918 on a states-rights basis as The Pest once Chaplin's fame had grown. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 2020, citing it as the first public sighting of the most recognized character in film history.

programme.title: THE RED SHOES — Interstitial
programme.desc: A ballerina is torn between love and an impresario who demands total devotion to dance. The 17‑minute Ballet of the Red Shoes sequence is one of cinema’s great Technicolor set pieces.

programme.title: The Red Shoes
programme.desc: Victoria Page wants to dance. Boris Lermontov wants to own the greatest ballet company in the world. Julian Craster wants to compose. Lermontov asks Vicky the question that defines the film: "Why do you want to dance?" She answers: "Why do you want to live?" He hires her on the spot. When she falls in love with Julian, Lermontov forces a choice: the ballet or the man. She chooses the man. It destroys all three of them. Vicky runs from her dressing room in the red shoes and throws herself in front of a train. As she dies, she whispers to Julian: "Take off the red shoes." Lermontov walks onto the stage and tells the audience: "Miss Page is unable to dance tonight — nor indeed any other night." The company performs The Ballet of the Red Shoes with a spotlight on the empty space where she would have been. Michael Powell conceived the film in the 1930s with producer Alexander Korda as a vehicle for Merle Oberon, but Oberon couldn't dance, and the project was shelved for a decade. When Powell and his partner Emeric Pressburger finally made it, they decided on dancers who could act rather than actors who could dance. They recruited from the Royal Ballet. Moira Shearer, a Scottish ballerina who was just beginning to ascend at Sadler's Wells, was recommended by Robert Helpmann. She said no. She fought for a year to avoid the film. "Red Shoes was the last thing I wanted to do. I fought for a year to get away from that film, and I couldn't shake the director off." She was right to worry — the film made her the most famous ballerina in the world and she spent the rest of her career trying to be taken seriously as a dancer again rather than a movie star. Ninette de Valois, her director at Sadler's Wells, finally told her to just do it. Boris Lermontov was based on Sergei Diaghilev, the impresario who founded the Ballets Russes. The specific moment was Diaghilev seeing fourteen-year-old Diana Gould partnering Frederick Ashton in the premiere of his first ballet and inviting her to join his company — he died before it could happen. The cinematographer was Jack Cardiff, who may be the greatest color photographer in the history of cinema. Cardiff was born in 1914 to vaudeville parents, was a child film star by age four, and was a camera assistant by fourteen. When a German cinematographer shouted "Hey you!" and told the boy to rotate a lens between two pencil marks on command, Cardiff asked afterward what he'd done. "You followed focus, sonny." When he interviewed for a job learning Technicolor, the interviewers asked technical questions about polarizing light and film negatives. Cardiff told them they were wasting their time talking to him. Shocked silence. How did he hope to become a cinematographer? "I told them I studied the works of painters — Vermeer, the Old Masters, and the Impressionists. I could also describe and match how the light fell in a subway, in my house, or on the street at night." They asked about a face in a Rembrandt painting. He said the light was on the right side. He got the job. He shot travelogues on top of Mount Vesuvius during a volcanic eruption — lava burned the tripod and their shoes, one crew member was hospitalized, and the film was magnificent. He spent six months in a lifeboat filming a documentary about the Merchant Navy during WWII. For The Red Shoes, a giant 300-amp water-cooled arc spotlight was custom-built by Mole-Richardson and Taylor Hobson specifically for the ballet sequence. Cardiff won the Oscar for Black Narcissus the year before; Natalie Kalmus, the daughter of Technicolor's inventor, was asked to name the best color film ever made and answered without hesitation: The Red Shoes. The seventeen-minute ballet at the center of the film was choreographed by Robert Helpmann. It uses dissolves, superimpositions, and special effects that were unprecedented — a swirling newspaper transforms into a dancer, the conductor's face melts into the impresario's, the stage floor becomes an ocean. Art director Hein Heckroth said: "When the girl is dancing, she feels she is a bird, a flower, a cloud." Gene Kelly saw it and the ballet sequence in An American in Paris (1951) was a direct response. Michael Powell said the film is "about dying for art, that art is worth dying for." But film scholar Adrienne McLean saw something darker: Vicky "seems pushed by those she loves who would rather possess her than support her." When A Chorus Line was created in the early 1970s, dancer after dancer cited The Red Shoes as the reason they became dancers. Marvin Hamlisch paid homage to it in "At the Ballet" and "What I Did for Love." The film was the first British production to gross over $5 million in American theatrical rentals. Martin Scorsese saw it as a child and it changed his life. He championed Powell's entire body of work, married Powell's editor Thelma Schoonmaker, and when Powell died in 1990, Scorsese spearheaded the restoration of The Red Shoes from the original three-strip Technicolor nitrate negatives through the Film Foundation and UCLA Film Archive. The restored version screened at Cannes in 2009. It directly influenced Darren Aronofsky's Black Swan. It was voted the ninth greatest British film ever made by the BFI and fifth by Time Out. Powell himself left a bank clerk job to join Rex Ingram's production unit in Nice, France — the same pattern as Nilsson, as Juster, as so many: the bank job, then the art.

programme.title: THE TANTALIZING FLY — Interstitial
programme.desc: Koko the Clown climbs out of a real inkwell and battles a real fly for control of the drawing board. The rotoscope era begins.

programme.title: The Tantalizing Fly
programme.desc:
The Tantalizing Fly is an early entry in Max Fleischer's Out of the Inkwell series, made for J. R. Bray's studio and released in the fall of 1919 — by most accounts the second Inkwell short to reach audiences, distributed as part of the Goldwyn-Bray Pictograph program rather than as a stand-alone release. The premise is the one the series would run for years: Fleischer, seated at his drawing board, is needled by a live fly that keeps landing on his paper and his hand. When he swats at it he misses the fly and strikes his own drawing instead, and the clown he is inking stirs to life on the page. The clown then tries his own hand at the problem, sketching a bald, seated figure as a helper against the fly, with no better luck — the blows keep landing on the wrong target. It is a slight premise stretched over a few minutes, but the film is really an advertisement for a piece of hardware: the collision of a real insect, a real hand, and a hand-drawn figure occupying the same frame, sold as one continuous space.
That illusion was the rotoscope, which Fleischer had patented a few years earlier and was still proving out commercially in these Bray one-reelers. Live-action film was projected frame by frame onto a glass-covered easel and traced by hand, giving the animated figure the weight and timing of a photographed performer rather than the rubbery bounce of drawn-from-scratch cartooning of the period. The character being traced was modeled on Fleischer's younger brother Dave, a former Coney Island clown who performed the movements in costume for the camera; the drawn figure built from that footage is the character now generally known as Koko the Clown, though the name itself is a later addition to the series — animator Dick Huemer is credited with formally christening the character in the mid-1920s, well after this short was made. In 1919 the figure on screen is simply "the clown," an unnamed proof of concept for a new way of putting a cartoon and a person in the same shot.
The Bray Studios production this print carries in its titles is the outfit run by pioneering animation producer J. R. Bray, whose company employed and distributed several of the era's key animators — Fleischer among them — before Max and Dave struck out on their own a couple of years later as Out of the Inkwell Films and, later, Fleischer Studios. The Tantalizing Fly is a small document of that Bray-era apprenticeship: the hybrid live-action/animation format, the rotoscope as a selling point rather than a mature house style, and a title-card credit that spells the director's name "Fleicher," a misprint on the card itself rather than an error in this description.
The surviving print carries the usual wear of a hand-processed 1919 negative — scratches, speckling, and contrast that shifts a little scene to scene — and no restoration credit appears on screen; digital copies in circulation, including this one, run a little under four minutes, close to contemporary catalog listings of roughly three and a half to four minutes for the film. Intertitles are in English throughout, and the print shows no tinting.

programme.title: THE TEN COMMANDMENTS — Interstitial
programme.desc: DeMille was seventy‑three and suffered a heart attack mid‑production, returning to set the next morning. For the Red Sea, they poured 300,000 gallons into a tank and ran the footage backward—then composited it with location plates.

programme.title: The Ten Commandments
programme.desc: Cecil B. DeMille was seventy-three years old and had been making movies since 1913 — silents, hand-cranked through the camera. For twenty years after the war, letters arrived from around the world asking him to remake his 1923 silent Ten Commandments. The studio hesitated. One Paramount executive asked, "You won't call it The Ten Commandments, of course." Adolph Zukor leapt from his chair and made clear there would be no other title. DeMille sailed for Egypt on September 23, 1954. Near Cairo, between Saqqara and the Giza pyramids, his crew built the Per-Rameses gate — 107 feet high, 325 feet long, the biggest exterior set ever constructed for a motion picture, costing a quarter million dollars alone. Behind it: a mess tent, wardrobe department, horse stables. He met Nasser. He had tablets of the Ten Commandments hewn from actual Mount Sinai granite, inscribed in ancient Canaanite letters by Dr. Ralph Marcus of the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute. He cast Charlton Heston as Moses because Heston resembled Michelangelo's sculpture in Rome. Heston's three-month-old son Fraser played the infant Moses in the basket — Henry Wilcoxon's suggestion the moment Heston announced his wife was pregnant. Heston also voiced God at the Burning Bush, toned to a softer register. DeMille saw Yul Brynner in The King and I on Broadway. During intermission, he went backstage, told Brynner the story from Rameses' point of view, and offered him the role. Brynner: "It all happened in seven and a half minutes." He wanted Audrey Hepburn for Nefretiri but her figure wasn't curvaceous enough for the form-fitting Egyptian gowns. Edward G. Robinson had been blacklisted. Someone suggested him for Dathan but thought he couldn't be hired. DeMille coldly reviewed the matter, felt Robinson had been done an injustice, and cast him anyway. Robinson later wrote: "Cecil B. DeMille returned me to films. Cecil B. DeMille restored my self-respect." Yvonne De Carlo's brown contact lenses kept popping out. DeMille let her keep her natural gray eyes, calling them "a God-given treasure." During production, DeMille suffered a massive heart attack. His doctor ordered two weeks flat on his back in an oxygen tent. He was back on set three days later. John P. Fulton spent months on the Red Sea sequence — Paramount built a huge tank split by a U-shaped trough, into which 360,000 gallons of water were released from the sides, then the footage was printed in reverse. They composited it with location footage shot at the actual Red Sea, added animation, matte paintings, and pyrotechnics. It won the film's only Oscar. Henry Noerdlinger, the researcher, consulted Philo, Josephus, the Midrash Rabbah, and Eusebius, studying 950 books, 984 periodicals, and 2,964 photographs. Four screenwriters worked for three years. Five costume designers planned 25,000 costumes; 125 tailors took over a year to make them. 70,000 props. Seven casting directors hired 53 star and featured roles, 488 speaking parts, and 100 dancers. Shot in VistaVision, Technicolor. Elmer Bernstein's score. Anne Bauchens' editing — she'd been cutting DeMille's films since 1918. The most expensive film ever made at the time. Highest-grossing film of 1956. It has aired annually on American network television during Passover and Easter since 1973 — the longest-running annual broadcast of a single film in television history. Selected for the National Film Registry in 1999. DeMille never directed another picture. He died in 1959.

programme.title: FELIX IN HOLLYWOOD — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first animation superstar goes to the studios and meets Chaplin, Keaton's hat, and the censor's scissors. Felix at the top of his fame.

programme.title: Felix in Hollywood
programme.desc:
Felix and his down-and-out owner are evicted for back rent and set out for Hollywood to make their fortune, Felix riding along disguised as a suitcase. Broke on arrival, Felix schemes his way into a shoe-store job — hawking gum to lure in customers — before wandering onto a studio lot billed as "Static Studio," where the picture turns from a road story into a walk through the industry's own gallery of faces. The cartoon threads Felix through caricatures of the era's biggest names: censor Will H. Hays turns up as a moon-headed office boss, Ben Turpin's crossed eyes and William S. Hart's cowboy stare get sight gags of their own, and Felix's own inside joke arrives when he apes Charlie Chaplin's walk — cane, waddle and all — only for the caricatured Chaplin to spin around and accuse him of "stealing my stuff."
The film was produced at Pat Sullivan's New York studio and released through M.J. Winkler on July 15, 1923, credited on-screen, as all Felix cartoons of the period were, to Pat Sullivan alone. The credit was not accurate. Sullivan ran the business side of the operation and, by his own later accounts and those of staffers who worked under him, contributed little to the day-to-day drawing; the cartoons were directed, written and largely animated by Otto Messmer, who had created the character for Sullivan's studio in 1919 and continued to shape Felix's stories and gags through the decade. Messmer only began receiving public credit for his authorship after Sullivan's death in 1933, when former colleagues — among them Sullivan's own attorney — corroborated his account. Animation historians, including John Canemaker, whose research forms the basis of the modern understanding of the studio's working methods, now credit Messmer as Felix's creator and the animating hand behind films like this one.
Felix in Hollywood arrived at the character's commercial peak. By the mid-1920s Felix was the most recognized cartoon star in the world, licensed onto toys, ceramics, songs and a Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade balloon years before Mickey Mouse existed, and this short trades directly on that fame, treating Felix as a celebrity roaming among celebrities rather than an anonymous gag figure. The joke lands because audiences of 1923 knew both Felix and the stars he was rubbing shoulders with; a Wikipedia-sourced anecdote has Chaplin himself telling Sullivan that Felix was his only rival, but that line cannot be traced to a citable primary source and is omitted here as unverified. The short was later voted one of the 50 Greatest Cartoons of all time in a 1994 poll of animators and historians conducted by Jerry Beck, the only Felix cartoon on the list.
The surviving print used here runs roughly 8 minutes at the file's transfer speed, against catalogued lengths of one reel (commonly listed near 9 minutes); silent-era cartoons were shot for hand-cranked or variable-speed projection, and small runtime differences between prints and modern digital transfers are expected rather than a sign of missing footage. The transfer is black-and-white with English-language intertitles and visible print wear consistent with a surviving theatrical or early-generation dupe rather than a fresh photochemical restoration.

programme.title: NORTH BY NORTHWEST — Interstitial
programme.desc: Hitchcock’s ultimate wrong‑man thriller sends Cary Grant from the United Nations to Mount Rushmore. It is equal parts espionage, comedy, and pure cinematic geometry.

programme.title: North by Northwest
programme.desc: Ernest Lehman wanted to write "the Hitchcock picture to end all Hitchcock pictures." He and Hitchcock had been assigned to adapt The Wreck of the Mary Deare for MGM, but after two weeks Lehman offered to quit — he couldn't crack it. Hitchcock told him they got along great and they'd just write something else. Lehman said he wanted to make the ultimate Hitchcock film. Hitchcock thought for a moment and said he'd always wanted to do a chase across Mount Rushmore. They brainstormed: a murder at the United Nations, a chase through a Detroit car plant, a showdown in Alaska. Then Hitchcock remembered something an American journalist named Otis Guernsey had told him — inspired by Operation Mincemeat, the wartime British scheme of planting false documents on a corpse — about spies creating a fictitious agent as a decoy. Perhaps their hero could be mistaken for this nonexistent man. They bought Guernsey's sixty-page treatment for $10,000. The tornado came from Hitchcock. The hero stranded in the middle of nowhere, and the villains send a cyclone to kill him. "But they're trying to kill him. How are they going to work up a cyclone?" Lehman said. Somewhere that afternoon the cyclone became the crop duster. The plane was a Naval Aircraft Factory N3N "Yellow Peril," a wartime Navy trainer converted for dusting, piloted by Bob Coe from Wasco, California. The "Indiana" highway was actually central California; Hitchcock placed replica square Indiana signs. Empire magazine voted it the greatest movie moment of all time. Cary Grant had been working with Hitchcock since Suspicion. MGM wanted Cyd Charisse for the female lead. Hitchcock insisted on Eva Marie Saint, whom he'd met at a dinner. Days later her mother reminded her that Hitchcock loved casting women in beige with white gloves. She wore exactly that to the next meeting. For Martin Landau, Hitchcock attended a Broadway play to watch Edward G. Robinson but was struck by the young unknown. He showed Landau the entire project — storyboards and all — then turned and said, "You're now Leonard." Hitchcock insisted on shooting in Paramount's VistaVision even though this was an MGM picture — the only other VistaVision film MGM ever made was High Society. Saul Bass designed the opening titles, the first extended use of kinetic typography in cinema. Bernard Herrmann composed the score. Robert Burks shot it. George Tomasini edited it. The U.N. sequence was filmed illicitly — after reviewing the script, the United Nations denied permission. After two failed attempts, Hitchcock had Grant pull up in a taxi right outside the General Assembly Building while a hidden camera crew filmed from across the plaza. Vandamm's mountaintop house was designed in the style of Frank Lloyd Wright by art director Robert Boyle — a cantilevered living room in limestone that never existed outside matte paintings and a Culver City soundstage. MGM wanted fifteen minutes cut to get the film under two hours. Hitchcock had his agent check the contract, found he had final cut, and refused. One line was redubbed: Eva Marie Saint originally said "I never make love on an empty stomach," which the censors changed to "I never discuss love on an empty stomach." The final shot — the train entering a tunnel after a romantic embrace — Hitchcock called "probably one of the most impudent shots I ever made." The title has no compass bearing. "Northwest by north" exists; "north by northwest" does not. Hitchcock told Peter Bogdanovich: "It's a fantasy. The whole film is epitomized in the title — there is no such thing as north-by-northwest on the compass." GQ convened a panel in 2006 and declared Grant's gray suit the greatest suit in film history. It has been called "the first James Bond film." The crop duster inspired the helicopter chase in From Russia with Love. South by Southwest takes its name from it. $9.8 million worldwide on a $4.3 million budget. National Film Registry, 1995. 97% on Rotten Tomatoes, 98 on Metacritic. Time Out named it the greatest thriller ever made.

programme.title: PLANE CRAZY — Interstitial
programme.desc: Mickey's true first outing, made silent months before Steamboat Willie and released after it with a soundtrack added.

programme.title: Plane Crazy
programme.desc:
Mickey Mouse's first cartoon was, chronologically, this one. Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks built it in a rush in the spring of 1928, riding the wave of aviation mania that followed Charles Lindbergh's solo Atlantic crossing the previous May: a barnyard photo of "Lindy" inspires Mickey to cobble together a rickety biplane out of a Model T, a washtub and assorted farm junk, then press Minnie and a coop's worth of livestock into service as passengers and parts. Iwerks animated the picture essentially alone, working from Walt's story sketches at a punishing pace to have a print ready for a trade screening within weeks. Disney previewed the finished silent film for a Hollywood theater audience, and for prospective distributors, on May 15, 1928 — the true birthday of Mickey Mouse, months before the character most audiences would come to know him from. No distributor bit; an MGM executive who saw the screening reportedly liked the mouse but passed on the picture.
That commercial failure redirected the studio. Disney had already been trying to crack synchronized sound, and rather than shop the silent Plane Crazy further, he shelved it and built a new short, Steamboat Willie, around a Cinephone sound track from the outset. Steamboat Willie's November 1928 New York opening was a sensation, and Walt went back to the earlier films to retrofit them for the format that had actually sold Mickey to the public. Plane Crazy was rescored and re-cut with a synchronized soundtrack — dialogue grunts, barnyard effects, a jaunty musical bed, but no character speech to speak of, in keeping with the crude but electrifying "Mickey Mousing" style of the moment — and released on March 17, 1929, through Pat Powers's Celebrity Pictures using the Powers Cinephone system credited on the reissue's own title card. It went out as the third Mickey short to reach audiences, behind Steamboat Willie and The Gallopin' Gaucho, even though it was the first one made.
The title card on this print reads "Mickey Mouse Sound Cartoon — Plane Crazy — A Walt Disney Comic by Ub Iwerks, Recorded by Cinephone System," identifying it unambiguously as the 1929 sound reissue rather than the lost-to-most-audiences 1928 silent original; the image is plain black-and-white throughout, with no tinting, hand-coloring, or restoration card, and no live-action prologue. Gags familiar from the character's later run are already present in embryonic form: Mickey improvises a parachute from Minnie's bloomers when the plane goes into a spin, and the short ends on the chase-and-kiss beat — Minnie bailing out rather than accept Mickey's advances — that recurs across the early cartoons. Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks share directing credit; no cast is credited on the print, consistent with the era, before Disney and his stable of actors began regularly voicing Mickey, Minnie, and Pete later in 1929.
Because the American copyright terms for the silent and sound versions were registered separately, the two prints of Plane Crazy left copyright on different dates: the 1928 silent version entered the U.S. public domain on January 1, 2024, alongside Steamboat Willie, but the sound version carried on this file — bearing an on-screen 1929 date, with its copyright registered and later renewed under Pat Powers's Celebrity Pictures — is treated by the U.S. Copyright Office as a separate work and did not enter the public domain until January 1, 2025. Caution is warranted in describing this file's rights status: it is the sound reissue, not the 1928 original, and the two should not be conflated.

programme.title: STEAMBOAT WILLIE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Mickey Mouse arrives, whistling in synchronized sound — the cartoon that made sound animation the industry standard.

programme.title: Mickey Mouse - Steamboat Willie
programme.desc:
Steamboat Willie was not Mickey Mouse's first cartoon but his third: Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks had already animated Plane Crazy and The Gallopin' Gaucho as silent pictures earlier in 1928, only to find no distributor would take them. Sound was the gamble that changed that.
