Disney had heard Al Jolson in The Jazz Singer the year before and, cut off from the Alice Comedies and Oswald the Lucky Rabbit he had lost to Charles Mintz and Universal, staked what was left of his small studio on a synchronized-sound cartoon built around the new mouse character. The title and premise parody Buster Keaton's Steamboat Bill, Jr., released by United Artists that same year, though Willie's plot of a bullying riverboat captain, a stowaway mouse, and a deckhand's improvised barnyard orchestra owes little to Keaton beyond the name and the setting.
The film was animated largely by Iwerks himself, at a reported pace of hundreds of drawings a day, with assistance from Les Clark, Johnny Cannon, Dick Lundy and Wilfred Jackson, none of them credited on screen. Its claim to history rests on sound: Disney and his brother Roy financed a trip to New York to record a synchronized track using Pat Powers's Cinephone system, a variant of Lee de Forest's Phonofilm process that Powers controlled outside Western Electric and RCA's patent pools. Getting picture and soundtrack to line up was the hard problem, and it was Wilfred Jackson, an assistant animator whose mother had taught music, who proposed conducting the recording session to a metronome and drawing up a bar sheet mapping actions to beats — the direct ancestor of the animation exposure sheet and click track still used in the industry. Disney himself provided Mickey's falsetto voice and vocal effects, alongside Iwerks and other staff on the incidental sound; the soundtrack leans on two public-domain tunes, "Steamboat Bill" and "Turkey in the Straw," the latter the source of the mouse's famous pot-and-pan-and-livestock performance in the film's second half.
Steamboat Willie premiered on November 18, 1928, at the Colony Theatre on Broadway in New York, on a bill with a live-action feature, Gang War, playing the Colony's Western Electric sound system. Trade reviews, including in Variety and Film Daily, singled out the novelty and precision of the synchronization rather than the character himself, and the date has since been adopted by Disney as Mickey Mouse's official birthday. The film's success let Disney secure regular distribution and finally release the two shelved silent Mickey cartoons with added soundtracks; it also set off a scramble among rival studios, Fleischer and Van Beuren among them, to reverse-engineer Disney's synchronization method before Jackson's bar-sheet technique became common knowledge.
The short was among the first twenty-five films named to the Library of Congress National Film Registry in 1998, cited for its historical and aesthetic significance as the first cartoon released with a fully synchronized soundtrack recorded to match the action rather than played live or added as a rough afterthought. Its US copyright, held by Disney since 1928, expired on January 1, 2024, placing this earliest screen version of Mickey and Minnie Mouse — round-eyed, long-nosed, more rodent than the character Disney would later refine — into the American public domain, though Disney retains trademark rights over the character's use in commerce. This print carries no restoration or tinting; it is the plain black-and-white Cinephone release, title card and Copyright MCMXXVIII notice intact.

programme.title: C’ÉTAIT UN RENDEZ‑VOUS — Interstitial
programme.desc: The car is a Mercedes‑Benz 450SEL 6.9; the engine sound is dubbed from a Ferrari 275 GTB V12. Landmark‑timing analyses give an average around 50–56 mph, with a disputed short spike near 136 mph. Treat the spike as likely measurement error; the run is mostly far slower.

programme.title: C'Était un Rendez-vous
programme.desc:
A car races through the empty streets of Paris just after dawn, the camera fixed low on the bumper, the drive rendered as a single unbroken take with no cuts. It runs a real route — out of a tunnel at Porte Dauphine, up the Avenue Foch, around the Arc de Triomphe, down the Champs-Élysées, past the obelisk at the Place de la Concorde and the Palais Garnier, through a blind corner at the Louvre, and up into Montmartre — before the car stops at the base of the steps below Sacré-Cœur, where a woman is waiting. A man gets out, crosses to her, and the image freezes on the embrace. An opening title card states the film was made "sans aucun trucage ni accéléré" — without trickery or fast motion.
Claude Lelouch shot it in August 1976 on film stock left over from his feature Si c'était à refaire, which had just wrapped with Catherine Deneuve. Roughly nine and a half minutes of 35mm remained on the reel, and Lelouch used it to realize an idea he had been carrying for some time: a single-shot race across the city built around the sensation of being dangerously late for someone. A Caméflex camera was rigged low on the front of his own Mercedes-Benz 450 SEL 6.9, chosen, by Lelouch's account, because its suspension held the shot steadier than a sports car's would have. He drove the car himself before dawn on a Sunday morning to keep the streets as clear as the film claims; a cinematographer riding in the passenger seat adjusted focus and aperture by remote control as they went, and Elie Chouraqui was posted as a safety spotter at the blind tunnel exit by the Louvre, one of the route's more hazardous points. No permission was sought from the city or the police, since a legal closure of that much of central Paris would have been unthinkable.
The engine on the soundtrack is not the Mercedes'. Lelouch dubbed in the sound of his own Ferrari 275 GTB, a V12 with a note the 450 SEL's V8 could not produce, and it plays under the picture at a pitch that suggests speeds well beyond anything the car was actually doing for most of the run. Timing analyses of the visible landmarks against the reel have generally put the car's average speed in the region of 50 to 60 mph, well short of the folklore figure of 200 km/h Lelouch himself has claimed for the short straight of the Avenue Foch, and any single instant reconstructed at that speed should be treated as extrapolation from a few seconds of footage rather than a measured fact about the whole drive. Red lights and oncoming traffic are visible at several points and were, per Lelouch, real hazards rather than staged obstacles.
The woman at the end is Gunilla Fridh, a Swedish former beauty-pageant finalist and, at the time, Lelouch's companion; she is the only face shown in the film and was simply told to be waiting at the steps when he arrived. After the film screened, Lelouch was summoned by the Paris police prefecture. He has recounted being told that if the drive really had been filmed without cuts or effects, the red lights caught on camera were genuine violations enough to justify pulling his license outright — and that the prefect then took the license, looked at it, and handed it straight back, remarking that his own children had loved the film.
The film was produced under Lelouch's own company, Les Films 13, and carries French visa number 46,452. It has since been cited by other filmmakers working with practical, unbroken car sequences, including the makers of Mission: Impossible – Fallout, and has been revived in retrospective screenings of Lelouch's work, including by La Cinémathèque française.

programme.title: LA DOLCE VITA — Interstitial
programme.desc: Fellini’s portrait of Roman nightlife gave the world the word “paparazzi.” The Trevi Fountain scene made Anita Ekberg an icon and sealed the film’s reputation as a portrait of decadent modernity.

programme.title: La Dolce Vita
programme.desc: Fellini said the inspiration was a sack dress — gorgeous on the outside, possibly a skeleton of squalor underneath. The film grew from there into a panoramic descent through Rome's café society, structured as seven episodes from evening to dawn, each one a downward spiral triggered by Marcello descending another staircase. The producer wanted Paul Newman for the lead. Fellini told Mastroianni he preferred him because he had "the face of normal." Mastroianni asked to read the script; Flaiano brought it over and it was blank pages — except for a sketch of a man swimming with an enormous phallus, surrounded by dancing mermaids. Mastroianni signed immediately. Over eighty locations were built at Cinecittà by Piero Gherardi, including a full reconstruction of Via Veneto and the dome of St. Peter's with its staircase. The Trevi Fountain scene was shot over a week in winter. Ekberg stood in the freezing water for hours without complaint; Mastroianni needed a wetsuit under his clothes and still couldn't take it — Fellini only got the scene after the actor polished off a bottle of vodka. The character Paparazzo, the news photographer played by Walter Santesso, was modeled on real-life photojournalist Tazio Secchiaroli, whose famous shots of Aïché Nana's striptease at Rugantino in 1958 had already scandalized Rome. The name itself likely comes from George Gissing's 1901 travel book "By the Ionian Sea," where a Signor Paparazzo appears — co-writer Flaiano pulled it from there. The word entered every language on earth. Pier Paolo Pasolini contributed uncredited to the screenplay. The Steiner subplot — the intellectual who murders his children and himself — came from co-writer Tullio Pinelli, who had watched his school friend Cesare Pavese's over-intellectualism curdle into the emotional sterility that led to Pavese's suicide in a Turin hotel in 1950. Won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, the Academy Award for Best Costume Design, and three additional Oscar nominations including Best Director. The Vatican condemned it; the Italian right tried to ban it; audiences made it a worldwide sensation.

programme.title: 8½ — Interstitial
programme.desc: Fellini turned his own creative crisis into a film about a director who cannot make his film. Reality, memory, and fantasy collapse into one another; it remains the definitive movie about making movies.

programme.title: 8½
programme.desc: Federico Fellini nearly killed this film before it existed. By April 1962, he had signed deals with producer Angelo Rizzoli, cast Mastroianni, built sets at Cinecittà, hired cinematographer Gianni Di Venanzo — and still had no idea what his protagonist did for a living. Sitting in his office, he began drafting a letter to Rizzoli confessing he had "lost his film." The chief machinist interrupted to invite him to toast the production's launch. Standing before his crew, glass raised, Fellini was overwhelmed by shame — and then everything fell into place: he would make a film about a director who no longer knows what film he wants to make. Shooting began May 9, 1962, with a strip of brown tape stuck near the camera viewfinder reading "Ricordati che è un film comico" — Remember that this is a comic film. Like nearly all Italian productions of the era, the entire film was shot without live sound; all dialogue was dubbed in post-production, and Fellini shouted direction at his actors during takes. Claudia Cardinale was allowed to dub her own voice for the first time — previously her Tunisian accent had been deemed undesirable. Fellini originally shot an ending set in a train's restaurant car, with Guido and his wife surrounded by all the film's characters as the train enters a tunnel — an implicit suicide. Co-writer Tullio Pinelli persuaded him to use the alternative beach sequence instead, giving the film its exuberant, circular finale. After shooting wrapped October 14, Nino Rota composed the circus marches and fanfares that would become Fellini's signature sound. The title is Fellini's own count of his filmography — six features, one co-direction, two short segments: eight and a half. The working title, proposed by Ennio Flaiano, was "La bella confusione" — The Beautiful Confusion. Released in Italy on February 13, 1963, the film won Academy Awards for Best Foreign Language Film and Best Costume Design, took the Grand Prize at Moscow, and screened at Cannes to near-universal acclaim. Truffaut wrote simply: "Fellini's film is complete, simple, beautiful, honest." It was Fellini's last work in black and white.

programme.title: ALI BABA AND THE FORTY THIEVES — Interstitial
programme.desc: Hand‑colored by Segundo de Chomón using the stencil process later known as Pathécolor. One of the longest narrative films of its era.

programme.title: Ali Baba And The Forty Thieves
programme.desc:
Ali Baba et les quarante voleurs is a Pathé Frères production credited to Ferdinand Zecca, though some accounts hold that Albert Capellani directed under Zecca's supervision — the Fondation Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé, which now holds the Pathé archive, lists Zecca alone. It dramatizes the Arabian Nights tale added to European editions of the collection in the eighteenth century by Antoine Galland's translator-successors, and it is generally cited as the story's first film adaptation. The Pathé catalogue described the film as running twelve scenes; the historian Henri Bousquet, working from surviving prints, counts seven, each introduced by an intertitle: "Sésame, ouvre-toi !", "Le trésor des voleurs", "Enfin riche !", "Cassim est surpris et exécuté", "Brigands découverts par la servante", "Le faux marchand d'huile", and "Triomphe d'Ali Baba — Apothéose."
The surviving frames follow that structure. A woodcutter is startled at a rocky grotto mouth as mounted brigands ride up; the wall opens on the password and reveals the treasure cave. Ali Baba's brother Cassim, told the secret, is later caught inside by the thieves and killed. A servant discovers the raiders and, in the tale's best-known set-piece, a disguised oil merchant's jars conceal the gang before their discovery. The film closes with a courtyard celebration — dancers moving in ranks before Moorish arcades — and a gold-and-starburst apotheosis tableau of the kind Pathé used to cap its féerie subjects.
The color is hand-applied stencil work by Segundo de Chomón, the Spanish filmmaker and colorist then running his own laboratory in Barcelona for Pathé, using the frame-by-frame stencil method the company would shortly mechanize and market as Pathécolor. The palette is built from a handful of dyes — rose, blue, ochre, gold — laid over black-and-white release prints to pick out costumes, architecture, and the final tableau's radiant background, characteristic of the soft-edged, non-naturalistic look of stencil color before Pathé's later industrialized process.
Zecca returned to the story in 1907 with a longer version, again for Pathé. The 1902 film predates Georges Méliès's own fairy-tale spectacles of the period and stands with them as an early instance of French studios building multi-scene fantasy narratives, rather than single-shot actualities, for a mass audience.

programme.title: RACE HORSE — Interstitial
programme.desc: A sequence of photographs that proved all four hooves leave the ground at a gallop. Not a film yet, but the direct ancestor of motion pictures.

programme.title: Race Horse
programme.desc:
In 1872 the railroad magnate and former California governor Leland Stanford put up money to settle a wager, or at least a standing argument, about how a horse actually moves at a gallop: was there a moment when all four hooves left the ground at once? Stanford believed there was and hired the English-born photographer Eadweard Muybridge to prove it. It took years of experimentation with cameras, shutters, and trip-wires before Muybridge had an answer. On 19 June 1878, at Stanford's Palo Alto stock farm, he set up a bank of cameras with threads stretched across the track, so that a horse galloping past would trip each shutter in succession. The subject was Sallie Gardner, a mare owned by Stanford, ridden by a jockey identified in Muybridge's own caption only as G. Domm, "running at a 1:40 gait." The resulting sequence of photographs showed exactly what Stanford had wagered on: a phase of the gallop in which the horse is fully airborne, all four legs drawn beneath it, touching nothing.
The photographs made Muybridge's name and settled the "unsupported transit" question that had nagged horsemen and painters for a generation, but the pictures were stills, printed in newspapers and later plates. The animation that survives on this file is a further step. In 1879 Muybridge built the zoopraxiscope, a hand-cranked projector that spun a glass disc around its rim, onto which the individual gallop positions had been hand-traced as silhouettes by a hired artist rather than reproduced photographically. Muybridge used the device in his lecture tours through the early 1880s, under titles such as "The Attitudes of Animals in Motion," to project a horse that appeared to run in a continuous loop for an audience for the first time. It is on the strength of the zoopraxiscope, not the raw sequential photographs, that Muybridge is often credited as the first person to project a moving image to a paying audience, years ahead of Edison or the Lumières.
The footage here is a modern digitization of that looping gallop cycle, drawn from the Palo Alto sequence and its zoopraxiscope silhouette rendering: a jockey low over a horse's neck, the animal's legs cycling through the gallop, shot in the flat black-and-white of the original glass-disc artwork. It has no plot beyond the motion itself. Its historical claim rests entirely on priority: this is not a film in the narrative sense but the empirical demonstration, and then the mechanical projection, that made the idea of motion pictures thinkable a decade before cameras could record and project photographic movement directly.

programme.title: ROUNDHAY GARDEN SCENE — Interstitial
programme.desc: The oldest surviving motion‑picture film, shot in Leeds, England. Le Prince vanished mysteriously in 1890 before he could debut his camera.

programme.title: Roundhay Garden Scene
programme.desc:
On 14 October 1888, the French-born inventor Louis Aimé Augustin Le Prince set up a wood-and-brass camera of his own construction in the garden of Oakwood Grange, the Roundhay, Leeds home of his in-laws Joseph and Sarah Whitley. He filmed his son Adolphe, the Whitleys, and a family friend, Harriet Hartley, circling on the garden path — walking in a loop to stay within the small frame the camera could cover. Shot at roughly 12 frames per second on Eastman Kodak paper-base photographic film, the resulting fragment runs about two seconds. It is, on present evidence, the oldest surviving motion picture.
Le Prince's single-lens camera used unperforated roll film about 2⅜ inches wide, with a second lens above the taking lens for viewing and a brass shutter to control exposure — a working solution built with far fewer resources than Edison or the Lumière brothers had behind them. The same day he also filmed his son playing an accordion and traffic crossing Leeds Bridge, but only the garden footage survives. Sarah Whitley died ten days after the filming, which makes the scene, incidentally, the last surviving record of her.
Le Prince never lived to demonstrate the camera publicly. In September 1890, en route to Paris to arrange a demonstration of his work, he boarded a train at Dijon after visiting his brother and was never seen again — no luggage, no body, and no resolution despite searches by French police, Scotland Yard, and his own family. His widow and son later pressed his claim to have invented motion pictures before Edison or the Lumières, but with no public screening on record and Le Prince gone, the field passed to others. The original paper negatives survived long enough for the Science Museum in London to photograph a run of surviving frames onto glass copy negatives in the 1930s, before the fragile paper originals degraded further; those glass negatives and a period paper print are now held by the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford, and it is from that preserved run of frames that the film is known today.

programme.title: Roundhay Garden Scene
programme.desc:
On 14 October 1888, the French-born inventor Louis Aimé Augustin Le Prince set up a wood-and-brass camera of his own construction in the garden of Oakwood Grange, the Roundhay, Leeds home of his in-laws Joseph and Sarah Whitley. He filmed his son Adolphe, the Whitleys, and a family friend, Harriet Hartley, circling on the garden path — walking in a loop to stay within the small frame the camera could cover. Shot at roughly 12 frames per second on Eastman Kodak paper-base photographic film, the resulting fragment runs about two seconds. It is, on present evidence, the oldest surviving motion picture.
Le Prince's single-lens camera used unperforated roll film about 2⅜ inches wide, with a second lens above the taking lens for viewing and a brass shutter to control exposure — a working solution built with far fewer resources than Edison or the Lumière brothers had behind them. The same day he also filmed his son playing an accordion and traffic crossing Leeds Bridge, but only the garden footage survives. Sarah Whitley died ten days after the filming, which makes the scene, incidentally, the last surviving record of her.

programme.title: A TRIP TO THE MOON — Interstitial
programme.desc: The rocket‑in‑the‑Moon’s‑eye image defined early cinema. A hand‑colored print was rediscovered in 2011 and restored.

programme.title: A Trip to the Moon
programme.desc:
An assembly of astronomers, presided over by Professor Barbenfouillis, debates a proposal to travel to the Moon. Over the objections of a few skeptics, six of them agree to go. Workmen in a foundry forge a bullet-shaped capsule and cast an enormous cannon to fire it, and a chorus line of women in sailor's uniforms load the astronomers aboard and ram the shell home. The cannon fires, and the capsule strikes the Man in the Moon squarely in the eye — the single image, more than any other, by which the film is remembered. The astronomers land, sleep through a snowfall and a vision of comets and planets, then descend into a mushroom-forested cavern where they are set upon by the Selenites, insectoid lunar inhabitants who vanish in a puff of smoke when struck. Captured and brought before the Selenites' king, Barbenfouillis and his colleagues fight free, flee back to their capsule, and tip it off a lunar cliff. They fall through space, splash down in the ocean, and are towed ashore to a hero's welcome, a parade, and the unveiling of a commemorative statue.
Méliès directed, wrote, produced, and starred in the film for his own Star Film Company, drawing on a tangle of contemporary sources he later acknowledged: Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon and its sequel Around the Moon, Adolphe d'Ennery's stage adaptation of Verne, the recent French translation of H.G. Wells's The First Men in the Moon, Jacques Offenbach's operetta on the same premise, and the "Trip to the Moon" walk-through attraction at the 1901 Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo. Méliès had already spent several years building trick films out of stage illusion and stop-motion substitution at his glass-walled studio in Montreuil; A Trip to the Moon scaled that workshop practice up to an unprecedented length and cast, with acrobats from the Folies-Bergère engaged to tumble and vanish as the Selenites, Bleuette Bernon appearing as the goddess seated in a crescent moon, and Henri Delannoy as the capsule's pilot.
The film survives in two very different forms. Most reference prints, including the version restored by film historian and animator Lobster Films with financial backing that eventually reached theaters worldwide, are black and white. A hand-colored print, however, was applied frame by frame in the Paris workshop of Elisabeth Thuillier, who supervised some two hundred colorists, each responsible for a single color across the entire run — dyes applied directly to the emulsion with a fine brush, one frame at a time. A print of this hand-colored version surfaced in 1993 in a donation to the Filmoteca de Catalunya in Barcelona, badly decomposed and fused at the edges into what conservators initially judged a lost cause. Lobster Films' Serge Bromberg and Éric Lange found that the core of most frames remained intact beneath the ruined edges, and between 2002 and 2005 the print was painstakingly separated and captured frame by frame with a digital camera. A full photochemical and digital restoration, undertaken jointly by the Groupama Gan Foundation for Cinema, the Technicolor Foundation for Cinema Heritage, and Lobster Films, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May 2011 with a new score by the French band Air, under the title The Extraordinary Voyage.
A Trip to the Moon premiered in France in September 1902 and quickly became one of the most widely seen and pirated films of the young medium, copied and distributed abroad without payment to Méliès in ways that contributed to his later financial ruin. Its stagecraft — model work, superimposition, and above all the substitution splice used to make objects and figures appear or vanish — set a benchmark for what trick photography on film could do, and the bullet-in-the-eye Moon remains one of the most reproduced single images in all of cinema.

programme.title: TRAFFIC CROSSING LEEDS BRIDGE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Among the earliest films ever shot: a single view of horse‑drawn traffic on Leeds Bridge. Only fragments survive.

programme.title: Traffic Crossing Leeds Bridge
programme.desc:
Louis Le Prince filmed this view of horse-drawn carts, carriages, and pedestrians crossing Leeds Bridge over the River Aire in late October 1888, a few weeks after shooting Roundhay Garden Scene in the garden of his in-laws' house nearby. He and his son Adolphe set up the camera at an upper window of Hick Brothers, an ironmonger's premises at the bridge's south-east end and one of his own equipment suppliers, and pointed it down at the ordinary traffic of the street below: carts, a horse-drawn omnibus, and men and women on foot, all moving on the left in the manner of British road use of the day.
Le Prince shot the scene on his single-lens camera, patented in Britain that November, using unperforated sensitized Kodak paper roll film rather than the glass plates or multi-lens rigs other inventors were still experimenting with. The original paper negative did not survive intact. In the 1930s the Science Museum in London made glass copy negatives from what remained of it, preserving twenty consecutive frames — numbered 110 to 129 on the surviving negative — which is the entirety of the footage now known to exist. Those twenty frames are what any modern print or reconstruction of the film consists of.
Le Prince never lived to publicly demonstrate this or any of his moving-picture work. In September 1890, while travelling from Dijon to Paris ahead of a planned demonstration of his camera, he vanished from a train and was never seen again; no body or luggage was ever found, and the disappearance remains unresolved. Whether he had shown the Leeds Bridge footage to anyone before then is disputed by historians, but the frames themselves, held today by the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford alongside Le Prince's cameras, stand with Roundhay Garden Scene as the oldest surviving motion picture material, made years before Edison's Kinetoscope shorts or the Lumières' first Paris screenings.

programme.title: ALICE IN WONDERLAND — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first Alice ever filmed, and Britain's longest film at the time. Restored by the BFI from the sole surviving, partly damaged print.

programme.title: Alice in Wonderland
programme.desc:
Cecil Hepworth and his staff director Percy Stow made Alice in Wonderland in the spring of 1903 at Hepworth's own studio in Walton-on-Thames, using his family, his staff, and his gardens as the whole production apparatus. It was the first film adaptation of Lewis Carroll's book, made just thirty-seven years after the novel was published and only eight years into the life of projected cinema, and its scenes were staged as a direct translation of John Tenniel's illustrations rather than as fresh invention — the rabbit hole, the Hall of Many Doors, the Duchess's kitchen, the Mad Hatter's tea party, and the trial of the Knave of Hearts, each set up to echo a specific engraving. At around 800 feet and roughly twelve minutes, it was, by a wide margin, the longest film yet produced in Britain, at a time when most story films ran two or three minutes. Distributors judged the full length unwieldy for a single programme slot, so Hepworth sold the picture's sixteen scenes both as a complete reel and piecemeal, letting a showman buy just the Mad Tea-Party or the March of the Card Soldiers if that was all his programme needed.
The cast was drawn almost entirely from the Hepworth household and payroll. May Clark, then a teenage employee at the studio who did everything from splicing negative to developing prints, played Alice; she went on to a long career at Hepworth's company as one of the industry's first film editors before emigrating to the United States. Hepworth's wife, Margaret Hepworth, took the doubled roles of the White Rabbit and the Queen, and Hepworth himself appears as the Frog Footman. The Duchess's cat was played by a Hepworth family pet. The production leaned on trick photography that was already a Hepworth specialty — stop-motion substitution to shrink and enlarge Alice at the Hall of Many Doors and inside the White Rabbit's house, and a garden path standing in for Wonderland itself, with the wooden stage set built in the grounds of the nearby Mount Felix estate for interiors and exteriors alike.
Only a single print of Alice in Wonderland is known to survive, and it reached the archive in poor condition: the nitrate had suffered heavy chemical decomposition, tearing, and emulsion loss across long stretches of the reel. The British Film Institute National Archive restored the surviving material, publishing a restoration in 2010 that recreated the film's original tinting scheme where the source allowed it, while leaving the extensive physical damage — scratches, blotching, and the missing frames that account for the difference between the original twelve-minute length and the roughly nine minutes that now survive — visibly intact rather than digitally erased. The print gathered here preserves that damage: the emulsion staining and tearing visible through the garden and tea-party scenes, and the darkened, sometimes near-illegible passages toward the reel's end, are the authentic condition of the one surviving copy, not an artifact of this transfer.
Alice in Wonderland occupies a founding place in two lineages at once: it is the first of what would become one of cinema's most frequently adapted stories, predating every subsequent screen Alice by decades, and it is one of the earliest surviving instances of a British studio building a multi-scene story film long enough, and popular enough, to be sold and exhibited as a stand-alone attraction rather than a single item on a mixed bill.

programme.title: PAUVRE PIERROT — Interstitial
programme.desc: Animation before cinema existed: 500 hand-painted images on a ribbon, projected by Reynaud's own Théâtre Optique in Paris three years before the Lumières.

programme.title: Pauvre Pierrot
programme.desc:
Charles-Émile Reynaud painted Pauvre Pierrot directly onto a long strip of shellac-protected gelatin, frame by frame, no camera involved anywhere in its making. Some five hundred individual images went onto the band, which Reynaud fed through his Théâtre Optique, a projector he had patented in 1888 as an elaboration of his earlier praxinoscope: a system of rotating mirrors that threw the painted images, in registered sequence, onto a screen for a seated audience. He opened the show at the Musée Grévin in Paris on 28 October 1892, under the umbrella title Pantomimes Lumineuses, pairing Pauvre Pierrot with two companion reels, Un bon bock and Le Clown et ses chiens. He kept performing it there for years afterward, well past a thousand shows, with a score by Gaston Paulin played live to accompany the picture. The run predates the Lumière brothers' first paid public film screening by more than three years, which is why Reynaud's strip is routinely cited as the first instance of a story told in projected, sequential images before an audience, animated rather than photographed.
The pantomime itself is simple stock company material: Pierrot arrives at a garden balustrade beneath Colombine's window to serenade her with a mandolin, only to be undercut by Arlequin, who has already been let in and who mocks, trips, and finally kicks Pierrot out of the garden so that he can have Colombine to himself. Reynaud staged it as broad, wordless clowning, in keeping with the commedia dell'arte stock triangle the title borrows its characters from, and hand-colored the figures directly on the strip — Pierrot in his white, black-dotted suit, Colombine in orange, Arlequin in his diamond patchwork, against a painted garden set with an urn of flowers, a balustrade, and a rising moon that tracks the passage of the night across the scene.
None of Reynaud's original hand-painted strips for Pauvre Pierrot survive intact; the family lent, then in 1928 donated, what remained to the Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers, and Reynaud himself had already destroyed and discarded other reels of his own work in a fit of despair around 1910. What circulates today, including this file, descends from a 1996 35mm reconstruction undertaken by Julien Pappé with the Centre National de la Cinématographie and the CNAM, rebuilding the pantomime from the surviving original band; the Bibliothèque nationale de France holds it for consultation, and the reconstruction has since been distributed on disc and online. That process is also why any modern print runs a few minutes rather than the reported quarter-hour of Reynaud's live 1892 performance, which depended on hand-cranked pacing and repeated or extended passages that a fixed-speed film reconstruction does not reproduce.
Reynaud never made the leap from his painted strips to photographic filmmaking, and Pantomimes Lumineuses lost its audience to the Lumière cinematograph within a few years of its Grévin debut. He died in poverty in 1918, but Pauvre Pierrot's status as the oldest surviving projected animated film, made before "cinema" had a name, is undisputed in the standard animation histories, and its two surviving companion strips and the Gaston Paulin scores were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2015.

programme.title: A TRIP DOWN MARKET STREET — Interstitial
programme.desc: A camera on a cable car glides down San Francisco's Market Street, four days before the great earthquake destroyed everything in view.

programme.title: A Trip Down Market Street
programme.desc:
The film is a single continuous shot: a camera bolted to the front of a San Francisco cable car as it runs the length of Market Street from Eighth Street to the Ferry Building, the whole 1.55-mile trip compressed into about ten minutes of hand-cranked film and now presented at roughly fourteen. It was made by the Miles Brothers, a San Francisco film exchange and production outfit run by four siblings — Harry, Herbert, Earle, and Joseph Miles — who had gone into independent production in 1905 after building the first coast-to-coast film distribution business in the country. Harry J. Miles cranked the camera, a Bell & Howell mounted on an open platform, so that the streetcar's own forward motion supplied the shot: automobiles, horse carts, pedestrians, newsboys, and other streetcars weave directly at and around the lens in a continuous stream of unstaged traffic, with the Ferry Building's clock tower growing larger in frame as the car approaches it. It is an actuality film in the purest sense, a genre common to the period, but almost never executed with this much sustained ambition or this much incidental information packed into the frame.
For decades the film was catalogued as an 1905 production, filed as a fairly ordinary piece of pre-earthquake San Francisco street footage. That dating was overturned by David Kiehn, a historian at the Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum, who cross-referenced details visible in the frame against outside records. Kiehn noticed standing puddles in the gaps beside the cable car tracks and checked San Francisco weather reports, finding no rain heavy enough to leave them until late March and early April of 1906; he also traced the license plate on one of the automobiles in the shot, number 4867, to a registration issued in early 1906. Combined with other period detail — building construction, advertising signage, the specific model years of the automobiles — Kiehn's research redated the film to April 14, 1906. That is four days before the earthquake and fire that leveled the street the camera had just recorded, which makes the film, whatever the Miles Brothers intended it to be, an accidental and nearly exact time capsule of the city in its last days before catastrophe.
The footage survived by coincidence. Harry and Joseph Miles left San Francisco by train on April 17 with a print of the film, bound for New York; en route they learned of the earthquake, sent the film ahead, and turned back toward the city. The Miles Brothers' studio at 1139 Market Street, itself visible in the film's opening moments, survived the quake but was later destroyed by the fires that followed, and the brothers never rebuilt their San Francisco production operation. Surviving prints eventually circulated in small numbers; one, held by Rick Prelinger's archive after being acquired from a newsreel cameraman, was used to strike a new 35mm duplicate negative via Film Technology Company in 2010 and later given a 4K scan in 2018, and it is this Prelinger print that underlies most modern viewing copies, including restorations screened with newly commissioned musical accompaniment. The film was added to the National Film Registry by the Library of Congress in 2010, the same year of its dating correction and preservation work, cited for its documentary value as a record of daily street life in early twentieth-century San Francisco in the days immediately preceding its destruction.

programme.title: FRED OTT'S SNEEZE — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first film ever copyrighted in America: an Edison worker takes a pinch of snuff and sneezes. Deposited at the Library of Congress as paper prints.

programme.title: Fred Ott's Sneeze
programme.desc:
In January 1894, Harper's Weekly asked Thomas Edison's laboratory for a photograph illustrating the new Kinetoscope process, and the request was specifically for a sneeze — an action assumed to be too fast for still photography to catch cleanly. W.K.L. Dickson, the Scottish-born engineer who had built Edison's motion-picture apparatus and ran the Black Maria studio in West Orange, New Jersey, staged the shot with Fred Ott, a skilled machinist who had worked in Edison's shops since the 1870s and turned up as an on-camera subject in several of the lab's earliest test films. Ott, mustached and in a suit and tie, takes a pinch of snuff, works up to it, and sneezes into the frame — a demonstration film with no plot beyond the act itself, shot on Edison's 35mm Kinetograph stock.
The film's documentary status is unusual: it was never exhibited publicly as a Kinetoscope subject and no projected or peep-show release is recorded. Instead, Dickson deposited two sets of still photographic enlargements, printed on gelatin printing-out paper from the negative, with the Library of Congress on 9 January 1894 under the title Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze — copyright registration number 2887. Because the 1894 copyright statute had no category for motion pictures, the Copyright Office registered the deposit as a photograph, which is how the film survived at all: the deposit card of 45 frames sat in the Library's paper-print holdings for decades, and a separate, longer 81-frame sequence ran as a halftone grid in the 24 March 1894 issue of Harper's Weekly under the title "Fred Ott's Sneeze," the caption that stuck. It is routinely described, including by the Library of Congress itself, as the earliest surviving motion picture registered for copyright in the United States, though the Library's own records elsewhere rank it as the second-oldest surviving copyrighted example — a discrepancy the sourcing has never fully resolved, so the claim is best stated as "among the very first," not asserted flatly as "the first."
The version on this file descends from a genuine restoration rather than an old dupe. Kemp R. Niver's studio made the first transfer of the paper deposit to 16mm film in the 1950s as part of the Library of Congress Paper Print Collection recovery project, and every prior circulating copy — including the one long carried on the National Film Registry — was struck from that 45-frame card alone. In 2013, Library of Congress moving-image staff, prompted by research for the Orphans Midwest film symposium, went back to the original Harper's Weekly halftone plate and found 36 frames of the sequence that had never been included in any reanimated version, revealing that Ott sneezes twice in one continuous take. The Library's lab in Culpeper, Virginia combined the 45-frame copyright deposit with the additional Harper's frames into a new 81-frame, 35mm internegative — the most complete reconstruction of the original negative attempted to date — which premiered at Indiana University in September 2013. At 24 frames per second the reconstructed take runs a little over five seconds; exhibition prints of the restoration repeat it in sequence to fill a reel, which is consistent with this file's one-minute length. The image is black-and-white throughout, with no tinting, hand-coloring, or added titles beyond what the restoration itself carries — heavy grain and print damage are native to the surviving paper-print source, not compression artifacting.
The film was inducted into the National Film Registry in 2015 for its cultural and historical significance, and it is now most often cited as the founding document of American film copyright — the moment motion pictures, not yet legally a medium of their own, first passed through the Copyright Office by masquerading as a photograph.

In January 1894, Harper's Weekly asked Thomas Edison's laboratory for a photograph illustrating the new Kinetoscope process, and the request was specifically for a sneeze — an action assumed to be too fast for still photography to catch cleanly. W.K.L. Dickson, the Scottish-born engineer who had built Edison's motion-picture apparatus and ran the Black Maria studio in West Orange, New Jersey, staged the shot with Fred Ott, a skilled machinist who had worked in Edison's shops since the 1870s and turned up as an on-camera subject in several of the lab's earliest test films. Ott, mustached and in a suit and tie, takes a pinch of snuff, works up to it, and sneezes into the frame — a demonstration film with no plot beyond the act itself, shot on Edison's 35mm Kinetograph stock.
The film's documentary status is unusual: it was never exhibited publicly as a Kinetoscope subject and no projected or peep-show release is recorded. Instead, Dickson deposited two sets of still photographic enlargements, printed on gelatin printing-out paper from the negative, with the Library of Congress on 9 January 1894 under the title Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze — copyright registration number 2887. Because the 1894 copyright statute had no category for motion pictures, the Copyright Office registered the deposit as a photograph, which is how the film survived at all: the deposit card of 45 frames sat in the Library's paper-print holdings for decades, and a separate, longer 81-frame sequence ran as a halftone grid in the 24 March 1894 issue of Harper's Weekly under the title "Fred Ott's Sneeze," the caption that stuck. It is routinely described, including by the Library of Congress itself, as the earliest surviving motion picture registered for copyright in the United States, though the Library's own records elsewhere rank it as the second-oldest surviving copyrighted example — a discrepancy the sourcing has never fully resolved, so the claim is best stated as "among the very first," not asserted flatly as "the first."
The version on this file descends from a genuine restoration rather than an old dupe. Kemp R. Niver's studio made the first transfer of the paper deposit to 16mm film in the 1950s as part of the Library of Congress Paper Print Collection recovery project, and every prior circulating copy — including the one long carried on the National Film Registry — was struck from that 45-frame card alone. In 2013, Library of Congress moving-image staff, prompted by research for the Orphans Midwest film symposium, went back to the original Harper's Weekly halftone plate and found 36 frames of the sequence that had never been included in any reanimated version, revealing that Ott sneezes twice in one continuous take. The Library's lab in Culpeper, Virginia combined the 45-frame copyright deposit with the additional Harper's frames into a new 81-frame, 35mm internegative — the most complete reconstruction of the original negative attempted to date — which premiered at Indiana University in September 2013. At 24 frames per second the reconstructed take runs a little over five seconds; exhibition prints of the restoration repeat it in sequence to fill a reel, which is consistent with this file's one-minute length. The image is black-and-white throughout, with no tinting, hand-coloring, or added titles beyond what the restoration itself carries — heavy grain and print damage are native to the surviving paper-print source, not compression artifacting.
The film was inducted into the National Film Registry in 2015 for its cultural and historical significance, and it is now most often cited as the founding document of American film copyright — the moment motion pictures, not yet legally a medium of their own, first passed through the Copyright Office by masquerading as a photograph.

programme.title: DICKSON EXPERIMENTAL SOUND FILM — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first film with live-recorded sound. Dickson plays violin into a giant recording horn while two colleagues dance in Edison's Black Maria studio.

programme.title: Dickson Experimental Sound Film
programme.desc:
Shot at Edison's Black Maria studio in West Orange, New Jersey, sometime in late 1894 or early 1895, this brief test film shows William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, the Edison laboratory engineer most responsible for inventing the Kinetoscope, playing a barcarolle from Robert Planquette's operetta Les Cloches de Corneville on a violin directly into the recording horn of a wax-cylinder phonograph while two of his Edison lab colleagues dance together in front of the camera; a fourth man crosses briefly behind the horn near the end. It was made to test the Kinetophone, an experimental attempt to run a Kinetoscope and a phonograph together so that picture and sound could be seen and heard at the same time. William Heise operated the camera. The device never achieved true mechanical synchronization and was abandoned within a few years, but the film survives as the earliest known attempt to marry moving image and recorded sound.
The wax cylinder recorded that day was long assumed lost. In the early 1960s, staff cataloguing the Edison National Historic Site's collection found a metal canister in the laboratory's music room labeled "Dickson - Violin by W.K.L. Dickson with Kineto." When the canister was opened in 1964 the cylinder inside was found broken in two, and it sat unplayable for more than three decades while the film itself was preserved separately at the Library of Congress. The connection between the two artifacts was not acted upon until 1998, when Library of Congress curator Patrick Loughney and Edison site sound curator Jerry Fabris arranged for the cylinder to be repaired and re-recorded at the Rodgers and Hammerstein Archive of Recorded Sound at Lincoln Center in New York, work carried out by cylinder specialist Peter Dilg and audio engineer Adrian Cosentini on June 3, 1998.
Loughney, on the suggestion of producer Rick Schmidlin, then sent the footage and the recovered audio to film editor Walter Murch, who had worked with Schmidlin earlier that year restoring Orson Welles's Touch of Evil. Murch and his team, working with Industrial Light & Magic and Skywalker Sound and in cooperation with the Library of Congress and the Edison National Historic Site, had to reconcile a film shot at roughly 40 frames per second with sound running at an uneven, cracked-cylinder speed; the synchronized restoration premiered on May 23, 1998, at the Domitor early-cinema conference in Washington, D.C., giving audiences the first opportunity in over a century to see and hear the test as Dickson and his Edison colleagues had. This print, credited as a work in progress, repeats the sequence three times with explanatory title cards, the final pass presented with the cylinder's surface noise cleaned up; an early moment preserves an off-camera voice instructing, "Are the rest of you ready? Go ahead!" The film was added to the National Film Registry of the Library of Congress in 2003.
The identity of the violinist was debated for years, with some early accounts proposing Edison studio musician Charles D'Almaine; Loughney's own 2001 research into the restoration, along with a surviving photograph of D'Almaine, weighs against that identification in favor of Dickson himself, consistent with the cylinder's own label crediting "W.K.L. Dickson with Kineto." The two dancers and the man who crosses behind the horn remain unidentified Edison employees. As a recording, it predates the commonly cited synchronized-sound landmarks of the 1920s by a quarter century, though its significance is as a laboratory test rather than a public entertainment.

programme.title: EL HOTEL ELÉCTRICO — Interstitial
programme.desc: In the hotel of the future, luggage unpacks itself and brushes groom the guests — Chomón's stop-motion masterpiece.

programme.title: El Hotel Eléctrico
programme.desc:
A couple, Laure and Bertrand, check into a hotel wired so that every service is performed by electricity rather than staff. Left alone in their room, they discover that a control panel on the wall commands the furniture and their own luggage: trunks unpack themselves, shoes fly across the room to be brushed and buffed and fly back, a hairbrush and comb style Laure's hair unassisted, and Bertrand is shaved by a razor working on its own. The gag escalates when a hotel electrician, drunk, stumbles into the machine room in the basement and starts throwing switches at random, sending the room's objects into chaos before the couple manage to write home that they are "installés confortablement" for "un voyage des plus" comfortable — the joke undercut, in the surviving print, by the wreckage still going on around them.
The film was directed by Segundo de Chomón for Pathé Frères and shot in Paris in 1908, with Chomón and his wife Julienne Mathieu playing Bertrand and Laure. Some later filmographies and video reissues date the film to 1905 and place it in Barcelona, but that earlier date predates Chomón's documented adoption of true frame-by-frame stop-motion, which he only began developing at Pathé's Paris studio from about 1906 onward; the 1908 Paris dating is the one supported by Pathé's own production records and is treated as settled by silent-era filmographers including silentera.com. The film is sometimes catalogued under its French title, Hôtel électrique, and sometimes under the Spanish title used here, a reflection of Chomón's dual French/Spanish career and of Pathé's practice of issuing prints under locally adapted titles for different markets.
The effect that makes the film a landmark is achieved by pixilation: live actors and real props were shot one frame, or a few frames, at a time, with the performers and objects repositioned slightly between exposures so that on projection the luggage appears to pack itself and the boots march off unaided. It is among the earliest surviving demonstrations of the technique, predating its widespread use by decades — the same frame-by-frame animation of real objects and people later associated with Willis O'Brien's and Ray Harryhausen's model work, and, later still, with the Pixilation shorts of the mid-20th century. Chomón had already used stop-substitution and other in-camera trick work in earlier Pathé shorts; El Hotel Eléctrico marks a more ambitious step, animating an entire hotel room's worth of objects in continuous, sustained motion rather than single transformations.
Mathieu, credited here as Laure, worked in French cinema before Chomón did, with earlier experience at Méliès's Star-Film company, and by most accounts of Chomón's career it was she who drew him into the business after his military service; she went on to act in dozens of his Pathé films and is credited by historians with contributing to his scripts and trick-effects work. The film survives complete and has circulated widely on public-domain film platforms and in silent-era retrospectives; no tinting is visible on the print held here, which appears to be a black-and-white duplicate typical of the surviving copies in circulation, unlike the Pathécolor-stencilled prints of some of Chomón's other Pathé Frères shorts from the same years.

programme.title: THE SEA — Interstitial
programme.desc: A static shot of waves—pure observation as cinema. Part of the first Lumière screenings in 1895.

programme.title: The Sea
programme.desc:
A fixed camera looks down a wooden breakwater jutting into open water at La Ciotat, on the Mediterranean coast near Marseille. Bathers climb out along the jetty and jump or dive into the waves below, surfacing and swimming while others wade and splash closer to shore. There is no story beyond the repeated action of the jump itself — the camera simply records bodies entering water, over and over, from a single unmoving vantage point.
Louis Lumière shot the film at Le Clos des Plages, the family's seaside property in La Ciotat, sometime between July and September 1895. It carries the number 11 in the Lumière operators' catalogue under the title Baignade en mer, and was first shown locally at Le Clos des Plages before travelling to Paris. There, on December 28, 1895, it closed the program of ten films the Lumière brothers projected for a paying public in the basement Salon Indien of the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines — the screening now generally treated as the birth of commercial cinema exhibition. The other nine films that night included La Sortie de l'Usine Lumière à Lyon and Le Repas de bébé; Baignade en mer, being the last, sent the audience out with an image of pure holiday movement rather than industry or domestic life.
Like the rest of the earliest Lumière output, the film belongs to the actuality genre the operators favored before fiction took hold of the medium: a fixed frame, a single uncut shot, and unstaged or lightly arranged everyday activity offered as a demonstration of the Cinématographe's ability to capture motion itself. La Ciotat's shoreline became one of the Lumière company's most-used locations in these first years, best known today for the same jetty seen here and for the arriving train that would soon make the town's station famous in its own right.

programme.title: LITTLE NEMO — Interstitial
programme.desc: McCay bet his newspaper colleagues he could make four thousand drawings move. The result astonished audiences and began character animation.

programme.title: Little Nemo
programme.desc:
Winsor McCay, the New York Herald's star cartoonist, made his first film for the Vitagraph Company of America, released April 8, 1911, under the unwieldy title Winsor McCay, the Famous Cartoonist of the N.Y. Herald and His Moving Comics — a title that survives on the print's own opening card. The picture opens not with animation but with live action: McCay, playing himself at a table with a circle of newspaper colleagues, wagers that he can produce drawings that move on a screen, and that he can turn out four thousand of them inside a month to do it. The framing scenes were staged at Vitagraph's Brooklyn studio under the supervision of J. Stuart Blackton, the studio's leading director and himself a pioneer of trick and lightning-sketch films; McCay's fellow Herald cartoonist George McManus (creator of Bringing Up Father) and the popular Vitagraph comedian John Bunny appear among the colleagues taking the bet, with Blackton also visible in the sequence. A comic aside shows a messenger boy sent for supplies making a hash of delivery, spilling and mixing the barrels of ink and crates of drawing paper McCay has ordered — a bit of slapstick padding out the live-action frame before a title card announces "One month later."
The animation proper, roughly four minutes of the reel, delivers on the wager: McCay's hand is shown at the drawing board inking a figure, followed by the completed sequence in motion — Little Nemo, the green cigar-smoking clown Flip, the Imp, Doctor Pill and the Princess of Slumberland stretching, shrinking, and reshaping themselves in the loose, elastic gag-drawing style of early animation, distinct from narrative continuity. The characters are drawn from Little Nemo in Slumberland, the full-page Sunday strip McCay had been running in the Herald since October 1905, in which a boy's elaborate dreams are undone each week by his waking in bed; the film borrows the strip's cast rather than adapting a specific storyline. McCay drew the four thousand images himself on rice paper, mounted them onto cardboard for photographing frame by frame at Vitagraph, and by his own and his son's later accounts did the enormous labor essentially alone, well before any division-of-labor animation studio system existed. The film closes by returning to live action, McCay presenting the finished reel to his now-astonished colleagues.
The print surviving here carries hand coloring on the animated frames — Nemo, Flip, and the dragon-drawn chariot rendered in reds, greens, and yellows brushed frame by frame onto the black-and-white base, the labor-intensive tinting process common to specialty prints of the period rather than a mechanical stencil process. The Museum of Modern Art holds a comparably hand-colored nitrate print, among the rarest surviving artifacts of the release; other prints, black-and-white, are held by archives including the Cinémathèque québécoise. McCay debuted the film in theaters on April 8, 1911, and folded it into his vaudeville act within days, projecting it as the capstone of a chalk-talk act in which he appeared to converse with his drawn characters live on stage. Trade press response was strong — Moving Picture World praised it as "an admirable piece of work" — and its favorable reception is credited with pushing McCay toward the more ambitious character animation of Gertie the Dinosaur three years later. In 2009 the Library of Congress selected Little Nemo for the National Film Registry as culturally, historically, and aesthetically significant.

programme.title: FISHING FOR GOLDFISH — Interstitial
programme.desc: An early home‑movie moment: baby Auguste Lumière fishing in a bowl. Shown at the Lumières’ first public screening on Dec 28, 1895.

programme.title: Fishing For Goldfish
programme.desc:
A man stands behind a table holding a small child steady on the tabletop while she leans forward, again and again, trying to get her hand into a large glass bowl of goldfish. That is the entire film: no story beyond the repeated, thwarted reach, filmed in a single static shot at roughly waist height. The subjects are Auguste Lumière and his daughter Andrée, filmed by his brother Louis at Monplaisir, the family's house and factory grounds in Lyon, in the spring of 1895. It carries the number 69 in the Lumière production catalogue.
The scene belongs to a small cluster of Lumière home movies shot on the same grounds around the same months — babies being fed, a garden being watered, a wall being demolished — the earliest instances of a camera turned on domestic life rather than on public spectacle. Louis Lumière first screened this view in Lyon on 10 June 1895, well before the Cinématographe went public, and it was later folded into the program the brothers took to Paris. On 28 December 1895, in the basement Salon Indien of the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines, it ran as one of the ten films shown at the first paying, publicly advertised exhibition of projected motion pictures — the screening now conventionally cited as the birth of commercial cinema.
There is no trick of editing or camera here, only the patience of a fixed lens: the film's interest is entirely in watching an infant's small, failed grabs at something bright and just out of reach, and in the father's hands doing the steadying work at the edge of the frame. A related but distinct Lumière subject, Bocal aux poissons rouges (catalogue No. 18), frames the same goldfish bowl in close-up with no child present and was made separately; the two are sometimes confused. The print here is black-and-white, undecorated by tinting, exactly as the Lumière negative survives.

programme.title: GERTIE THE DINOSAUR — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first cartoon character with a personality. McCay performed alongside her on stage, and Gertie obeyed — or sulked — on cue.

programme.title: Gertie the Dinosaur
programme.desc:
Winsor McCay was already the most technically accomplished cartoonist in America — the newspaper strip Little Nemo in Slumberland had made his reputation for architectural, shifting dream imagery, and his 1911 film Little Nemo had already proven that his characters could be animated rather than merely drawn. For his next film, made with the help of a twenty-year-old neighbor and art student, John A. Fitzsimmons, who spent months tracing McCay's master drawings onto rice paper with Higgins ink, McCay set out to give an animated figure something no cartoon character had shown before: a personality. The two men produced roughly ten thousand drawings between the summer of 1913 and early 1914. McCay used a stopwatch to time an elephant's breathing at the Bronx Zoo as a model for Gertie's, then economized the enormous labor by cycling: sixty-four drawings of an inhale and thirty-two of an exhale, re-photographed in sequence more than a dozen times rather than redrawn. He is also generally credited with originating registration marks — fixed reference points on each sheet to keep the backgrounds and the moving figure aligned frame to frame — a bookkeeping innovation that made animation by a studio of hands, rather than a single obsessive, thinkable.
Gertie premiered not in a movie theater but on a vaudeville stage, at the Palace Theater in Chicago on February 8, 1914. McCay appeared in a black cutaway tuxedo, cracking a bullwhip like an animal trainer, bantering with the audience, and commanding the projected dinosaur to bow, dance, and weep on cue; at the finish he stepped offstage and a small animated McCay walked into the frame to climb onto Gertie's back and ride off, the audience watching the live performer vanish into his own drawing. The act was a sensation on the Hearst-affiliated vaudeville circuit through 1914, until Hearst curtailed McCay's stage engagements to keep him at the drawing board. That November, William Fox's Box Office Attraction Company offered to distribute the film to theaters outright, and McCay obliged by shooting a live-action prologue to substitute for the patter he could no longer deliver in person. The added footage, copyrighted September 15, 1914 and released in cinemas from late December, shows McCay and fellow cartoonist George McManus — later famous for the strip Bringing Up Father — held up by a flat tire outside the American Museum of Natural History; the museum granted the crew rare permission to film its brontosaurus skeleton on the condition that only natural light be used and the institution not be made an object of ridicule. Over dinner with a table of colleagues, McCay wagers he can bring a dinosaur back to life through a series of drawings, and the film cuts to his studio — mountains of paper, an assistant (McCay's own son Robert, in a small cameo) sorting drawings — before settling into the cartoon itself, now framed by intertitles rather than a barker's voice.
The result is a hybrid object: part demonstration film, part vaudeville souvenir, part promotional short for McCay's own showmanship. Within the cartoon, Gertie is coy, disobedient, food-motivated, and wounded by scolding — a set of behaviors keyed entirely to timing and drawn expression rather than to any mechanical trick, which is what separated her from the "lightning sketch" and trick-film animation of Blackton and Cohl that preceded him. The theatrical intertitle version circulating today — with the museum prologue, the wager, and the dinner-party audience McCay draws for on-screen rather than in a live house — is the print most commonly preserved and screened, since McCay's original hand-cranked stage performances, patter and all, could not be filmed and survive only in eyewitness description. The Library of Congress added Gertie to the National Film Registry in 1991, citing its role in establishing personality-driven character animation as an art form; animation historians from Donald Crafton onward have traced a direct line from Fitzsimmons's tracing table through Gertie to the Fleischer brothers, Otto Messmer's Felix the Cat, and the Disney studio's own early insistence on characters with drawn, legible feeling.

programme.title: L’ARROSEUR ARROSÉ — Interstitial
programme.desc: Cinema’s first narrative comedy: a boy steps on a gardener’s hose and gets his comeuppance. The first documented film gag.

programme.title: L'Arroseur Arrosé
programme.desc:
A gardener waters flower beds with a hose in a single static shot at Monplaisir, the Lumière family's house and factory grounds in Lyon. A boy creeps up behind him, plants a foot on the hose, and stops the flow. When the gardener bends down to peer into the nozzle, the boy lifts his foot; the water hits the gardener full in the face, knocking his hat askew. He drops the hose, gives chase, catches the boy, and spanks him before returning to his watering. It is a complete comic scene told in one uninterrupted take, with a setup, a reversal, and a punishment — the earliest surviving film built around a staged sight gag rather than a recorded actuality.
Louis Lumière shot the scene in the spring of 1895, using his own gardener, François Clerc, and a young factory apprentice, variously recorded as Benoît Duval, in the roles. It entered the Lumière catalogue as No. 99, Arroseur et arrosé, and was first projected in Lyon on 10 June 1895, at a congress of the Société française de photographie, ahead of the Cinématographe's public debut later that year. The Lumière catalogue in fact lists three separate camera negatives under this same title and number, shot at different times over roughly two years and differentiated mainly by minor staging details — a reminder that "the first comedy" was popular enough with the Lumière operators themselves to be restaged more than once.
The film is widely credited as the first fiction film shown to a paying public and the first film comedy — a piece of slapstick construction, cause and payback, rather than a simple record of a train or a factory gate. It also has an odd footnote in the history of film marketing: when the Lumières mounted their first commercial screening at the Grand Café in Paris that December, one of the two posters made for the event, illustrated by Marcellin Auzolle, depicted an audience laughing at the exact moment of the gardener's soaking projected on the screen behind them — the first poster made to advertise a specific film by showing a scene from it.
The surviving print is black-and-white, undecorated by tinting or hand-coloring, exactly as photographed.

programme.title: ANNABELLE SERPENTINE DANCE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Annabelle Whitford swirls yards of silk, each frame painted by hand — the closest thing the 1890s had to color film.

programme.title: Annabelle Serpentine Dance
programme.desc:
Annabelle Moore, born Annabelle Whitford, was a Chicago-born dancer who made her professional debut at fifteen during the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition and went on to become one of the Edison Manufacturing Company's most frequently filmed performers. Between August 1894 and May 1897 she was brought before William Heise's camera in the Black Maria studio in West Orange, New Jersey, at least four separate times to perform variations on her Butterfly, Sun, and Serpentine dances, with W.K.L. Dickson credited alongside Heise on the earliest sessions. Because Edison and its distributors reissued and recut this material repeatedly under the same title across those years, "Annabelle Serpentine Dance" refers to a small family of films rather than one single negative, and surviving prints and catalog listings do not always agree on which session a given copy descends from; the silentera.com filmography, for instance, lists a February 1895 Edison version of roughly fifty feet distributed through the Continental Commerce Company as a direct replacement for the 1894 original, itself later followed by at least one more remake.
The dance itself was not Annabelle's invention. It belonged to Loie Fuller, who had developed and sought to patent the "Serpentine Dance" a few years earlier, dancing in voluminous silk that she manipulated with concealed wands so that it billowed and coiled around her under stage light, evoking flame and flower petals as much as any serpent. Annabelle's version, performed in the cramped tar-paper-walled Black Maria under raw sunlight admitted through the studio's roof slot, was by contemporary account a more modest rendering than some of her rivals attempted, with the swirl of fabric kept above ankle and knee even as it filled the frame.
What survives on this print is a hand-tinted copy, and the coloring is the historically important part of the artifact: frame-by-frame application of dye or transparent paint directly onto the black-and-white positive, done by colorists working print by print rather than through any photographic or mechanical process. The film has long been cited, including by the Library of Congress, as among the earliest surviving examples of hand-color applied to motion-picture film, predating the later stencil systems such as Pathecolor by roughly a decade. In this print the coloring plays across Annabelle's gown as gold and yellow through most of the dance, shifting to rose and magenta as she draws the fabric up and out, with the surrounding stage and backdrop left in untinted black and white, the effect contemporary viewers described as the costume seeming to change color as it moved. It was exactly this kind of sensory novelty, alongside the underlying eroticism of watching a solitary woman dance through a Kinetoscope's peephole viewer, that made Annabelle's films reliable earners for Edison in the medium's first commercial years.
The film was inducted into the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress in December 2024, cited as an example of how the earliest film industry worked to "entice and enchant audiences" during a decade when actuality subjects like this one, rather than staged narrative, were the dominant form. It has since surfaced repeatedly in film-history compilations, including Chuck Workman's centennial retrospective "100 Years at the Movies," as a founding image of cinema's relationship to spectacle, color, and the dancing body.

programme.title: ONE WEEK — Interstitial
programme.desc: Newlyweds build a mail-order house. A rival renumbers the crates. The house that results — and what the railroad does to it — made Keaton a star in one reel.

programme.title: One Week
programme.desc:
One Week was the first film Buster Keaton released under his own name after three years apprenticing in Roscoe "Fatty" Arbuckle's Comique troupe. Joseph Schenck had set Keaton up with his own production unit, Buster Keaton Comedies, and rather than lead with the picture he'd shot first — The High Sign, which he considered too weak and held back — Keaton opened his independent career with this two-reeler, co-written and co-directed with Edward F. Cline. It premiered September 1, 1920, through Metro Pictures.
The premise parodies a specific piece of promotional filmmaking: Home Made, a 1919 Ford Motor Company short extolling the virtues of prefabricated, mail-order housing that a buyer could assemble in a week from numbered crates. Keaton kept the calendar-page structure marking off the days and the general shape of the pitch, then handed his newlywed couple — Keaton's groom and Sybil Seely's bride, on screen together for the first time — a kit house sabotaged by a jilted rival who has switched all the crate numbers. What follows is less a story than an escalating catalogue of sight gags built from a single design idea: a house that is subtly, then wildly, wrong. Windows sit above where doors should be, floors tilt, a piano crashes through a wall, and in the film's best-known passage the entire structure spins on its foundation in a windstorm while Keaton rides it like a fairground attraction. Special-effects work by Fred Gabourie put the house on a real turntable for that sequence rather than relying on models, and cameraman Elgin Lessley, who had shot for Keaton since the Arbuckle days, filmed the collapses and falls in unbroken takes.
The stunts were not trick photography. Keaton's fall through the second story onto his back was real, and accounts of the shoot describe him treating the resulting swelling with hot and cold water and liniment rather than losing shooting days to it — the kind of physical risk-taking that became his signature rather than an exception to it. The film's other lasting gag is its ending: having finally finished the house, the couple discovers they built it on the wrong lot and haul it, on rollers, to the correct address — only to strand it on a railroad crossing, where a train appears to obliterate it before a second train, from the opposite direction, reveals the joke was on the audience as much as the couple. Keaton leaves a "For Sale" sign on the wreckage.
One Week established the template Keaton would follow through his independent shorts and into his features: a plain, almost documentary shooting style in service of gags that were engineered like small machines, performed by their director at real physical risk, and paced without a wasted setup. It was added to the National Film Registry in 2008 for cultural, historical, and aesthetic significance, and the essay accompanying its Registry entry singles out the two-story fall as a feat few other performers of the period would have attempted. Modern transfers commonly run in the low twenties of minutes, against period trade listings of roughly 19 minutes at silent projection speed — a function of projection-speed conversion rather than missing footage.

programme.title: THE HAUNTED CASTLE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Often cited as the first horror film. Méliès used a stop‑trick substitution splice to transform a bat into the Devil.

programme.title: The Haunted Castle
programme.desc:
A bat flies into the courtyard of a medieval castle, circles, and settles on a cauldron before transforming into Mephistopheles. From there the demon conjures a run of apparitions — skeletons, witches, ghosts draped in sheets, cavaliers who arrive to confront him with swords and pitchforks — until one of the men produces a crucifix and the devil vanishes in a burst of smoke. Méliès shot it outdoors in the garden of his property at Montreuil, using a painted backdrop to stand in for the castle wall, and released it through his own Star Film Company, where it was cataloged among the earliest numbers in the company's list.
Méliès had bought the Théâtre Robert-Houdin in Paris in 1888 and spent the mid-1890s folding the conjuring and stage-illusion tricks of that house into the new medium of film. Le Manoir du diable is the clearest early result: its transformations rely on the stop-trick, a substitution splice in which the camera is stopped, the scene rearranged with a figure added, removed, or swapped for a prop, and the camera restarted, so that the change appears instantaneous on screen. Méliès had stumbled onto the effect by accident not long before, when his camera jammed while filming a Paris street scene and the resulting splice appeared to turn a bus into a hearse. Here the same principle turns a bat into a man, a cauldron's contents into ghosts, and a devil into smoke.
The film runs just over three minutes, a considerable length for 1896, when most exhibited films ran under a minute. It played at the Théâtre Robert-Houdin on Christmas Eve of that year. Méliès himself takes the role of Mephistopheles; Jehanne d'Alcy, who appears throughout his early catalog and later became his second wife, is among the other performers, though the individual roles in the cast are not firmly documented beyond Méliès's own.
Nothing in the film's staging asks to be taken as frightening. The pantomime is broad and theatrical, closer to a conjuring act translated to celluloid than to a ghost story meant to unsettle, and Méliès intended it as comic spectacle in the tradition of his stage magic shows. Its later reputation as the first horror film, and sometimes the first vampire film for its bat-to-man transformation, is a retrospective label applied by historians looking back at its subject matter rather than a description of how contemporary audiences experienced it.
The film was long presumed lost. The only known surviving print had been bought in a Christchurch, New Zealand junk shop sometime in the 1930s or 1940s and sat unidentified until a film archivist recognized it in 1985; it now survives through the collection now known as Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision. Because it predates the Berne-era copyright regime that would later cover such works, it circulates freely today, and its rediscovery is cited in film history as one of the pivotal early recoveries that let scholars examine Méliès's stagecraft directly rather than through secondhand description. It should not be confused with Méliès's own 1897 film Le Château hanté, released in some markets under the same English title, The Haunted Castle, and sometimes mistaken for a reissue of this earlier work rather than a separate production.

programme.title: THE PLAYHOUSE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Keaton plays the whole theater: the band, the audience, the minstrels, the stagehands — dozens of Busters at once, by double exposure nobody could explain.

programme.title: The Playhouse
programme.desc:
The Playhouse opens on a full night at a vaudeville house — orchestra, minstrel act, dancing girls, stagehands, and an audience packed into the boxes — and every single figure on screen is Buster Keaton. He is the conductor and each musician under him, all nine members of a blackface minstrel line, the trapeze act, and the men and women watching from the seats, one of whom leans over to remark, "This fellow Keaton seems to be the whole show." The gag was aimed squarely at the era's star-billing conceit, reportedly needling producer Thomas Ince, whose name papered every credit on his pictures.
