The sequence was the work of Keaton's regular cameraman, Elgin Lessley, using a custom matte box fitted with independently adjustable metal shutters: Lessley hand-cranked the same stretch of film up to nine times, exposing one sliver of frame per pass while masking the rest, holding the crank speed dead level on every pass so the multiplied Keatons would line up and move in step. Keaton called him "a human metronome." The effect went unexplained by Keaton for decades and remains one of the most technically demanding in-camera composites of the silent era.
The film was made under duress. Keaton had broken his ankle shooting the escalator gag for The Electric House, and with that production shelved for his recovery, he and co-director Edward F. Cline turned out The Playhouse in the meantime, built around sight gags and camera trickery rather than the falls and stunt work an intact ankle would normally supply. Once the minstrel-show dream sequence resolves — Keaton is roused awake by stage manager Joe Roberts and discovers even his bedroom is a stage set — the picture shifts into a more conventional backstage plot, with Keaton as a stagehand-turned-performer chasing a girl (Virginia Fox, in a dual role as twins) while contending with a mishandled trained monkey act, a diving tank, and a minstrel number he must perform himself. Cline, credited as co-writer and co-director, also appears unbilled as the monkey trainer whose escaped animal Keaton impersonates on stage.
Working titles aside, the film has circulated under both The Playhouse and The Play House; period trade material and the 1921 release generally favor the two-word form. It was produced by Keaton's own unit at the Comique Film Corporation for Joseph M. Schenck and released by Associated First National on October 6, 1921, with technical direction by Fred Gabourie, who built the trick stage machinery seen in the second half. At standard silent projection speed the two-reel picture runs close to twenty-two minutes; this file, transferred at a brisker rate, comes in around twenty.
The minstrel-show sequence preserves blackface performance conventions typical of American vaudeville and early film comedy of the period and is presented here as filmed, without alteration. The multiple-exposure opening remains the film's calling card and a touchstone for later films built on the same trick, including Keaton's own The Playhouse influencing generations of split-screen and self-multiplication gags that followed it.

programme.title: ADMIRAL CIGARETTE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Considered the first film made purely as an advertisement. Twenty‑eight seconds of costumed figures selling Admiral Cigarettes.

programme.title: Admiral Cigarette
programme.desc:
Admiral Cigarette is a half-minute advertising tableau shot by cameraman William Heise for the Edison Manufacturing Company at the Black Maria studio in West Orange, New Jersey, in the summer of 1897. It was made to promote Admiral Cigarettes, a brand of the National Cigarette and Tobacco Company, and survives because Edison deposited it for copyright as a paper print — a positive image printed onto a photographic paper roll, the method the company used at the time to secure federal protection for its films before formal motion-picture copyright registration existed. The Library of Congress transferred that paper print back to 35mm film in 1995, which is the source of the copy in circulation today.
The film stages a painted backdrop lettered "ADMIRAL CIGARETTE" fronted by a small company of costumed figures drawn from period print advertising for the brand: a uniformed admiral, an Uncle Sam type in star-and-stripe trousers, and companions meant to read as stock national emblems. A showgirl steps out and moves along the group, gesturing and distributing cigarettes, before the assembled figures unfurl a banner reading "WE ALL SMOKE" to close the scene. The staging matches the brand's contemporary magazine advertising, in which the same showgirl character appeared on trade cards.
Admiral's advertising leaned on the slogan "Not made by a trust," pitching the brand as the underdog against the American Tobacco Company combine — a pitch that did not save it: the National Cigarette and Tobacco Company was bought by Union Tobacco, which was itself absorbed into American Tobacco in 1899. The film is counted among the earliest surviving films made expressly to advertise a consumer product, produced in the same year Edison and other New York producers were also turning out ad films for Dewar's Scotch, Pabst beer, and local cigar shops. Rooftop screenings of these early advertising shorts drew large nightly crowds on Broadway in 1897, popular enough that projectionist Edwin S. Porter was reportedly detained by police for the crowds and traffic they caused.

programme.title: CINDERELLA — Interstitial
programme.desc: The fairy tale in hand-cut silhouettes, four years before Reiniger's Prince Achmed — every figure scissored from black card and animated frame by frame.

programme.title: Cinderella
programme.desc:
Lotte Reiniger made her Aschenputtel at the Institut für Kulturforschung in Berlin, the experimental film workshop where she had landed a few years earlier as a teenager who could cut silhouettes with astonishing speed. The technique was already hers: black cardboard figures, jointed with wire at the elbows and knees, laid flat under glass and lit from below, animated a fraction of a movement at a time. The film opens on that method rather than hiding it — a pair of scissors cuts Cinderella's shape from a sheet of black paper before the story proper begins, so the audience watches the medium declare itself. Rhyming intertitles narrate the action in short "Snip!" couplets, echoing the same scissors-and-paper conceit throughout.
Reiniger followed the Brothers Grimm telling rather than Perrault's, which gives the film a harder edge than the softer, fairy-godmother version more familiar in English-language nurseries. There is no fairy godmother; a hazel tree planted on the mother's grave provides the gowns and coach. And the story keeps the Grimm ending: when the golden slipper is brought to the stepsisters, one slices off her heel and the other her toes trying to force the fit, both readable here as small, sharp silhouette gestures rather than anything graphic, and the prince is tipped off each time by blood welling in the shoe. It is a piece of the tale most adaptations for children quietly drop.
The film was produced and photographed by Carl Koch, whom Reiniger had met at the Institut and married in 1921; he would remain her cameraman and closest collaborator for the rest of his life, working out the technical problems — focus, exposure, multiplane depth — that her increasingly ambitious silhouette work demanded. That partnership reached its first major test four years later with Die Abenteuer des Prinzen Achmed (The Adventures of Prince Achmed, 1926), the feature-length silhouette film now credited as the oldest surviving animated feature; Aschenputtel is the short, self-contained dry run for the technique that film would carry to an hour and change. The print held here carries English-language intertitles rather than the original German cards, an export version made for English-speaking audiences rather than a later dub or reconstruction.

programme.title: LE SQUELETTE JOYEUX — Interstitial
programme.desc: A dancing skeleton created with early trick photography—macabre comedy in the infancy of cinema.

programme.title: Le Squelette Joyeux
programme.desc:
A skeleton, lit against a bare dark backdrop, capers and staggers through a frantic solo dance before it comes apart at the joints, tumbling into a heap of loose bones, and then reassembles itself to carry on dancing. The film is catalogued by the Lumière company as Vue N° 831, "Danse d'une marionnette à fils" — the dance of a string-operated marionette. The performer is a puppet worked on strings from above rather than a hand-articulated model, and the disassembly-and-reassembly trick that gives the film its punchline was produced the way many Lumière and early Méliès effects were: by stopping the camera, altering the puppet or its rig between the two halves of the shot, and starting the camera again. The catalogue records the effect plainly as "2 plans par arrêt caméra" — two takes joined by a camera stop.
The operator who shot it is unrecorded; the Lumière catalogue lists it as "opérateur inconnu," and the 2000 Cinémathèque française retrospective of early trick and fantasy film catalogued it the same way, crediting only the company and a Lyon origin. The film's earliest documented public screening was March 20, 1898, in Lyon, though the Lumière catalogue and later filmographies date the shooting itself to 1897, consistent with the year long attached to the title.
The subject sits in the same vein as Méliès's skeleton gag in Le Manoir du diable the year before, and skeletal marionettes were a familiar fairground and magic-lantern turn well before either company put a camera on one. Whether the Lumière operator borrowed the idea from Méliès, from the stage, or simply from a puppet already on hand is not established by the surviving record. What the catalogue does establish is the film's place among the Lumière company's "Numéros d'adresse" series — filmed performance acts, here classed alongside acrobats and equilibrists — a small, functional trick film rather than a narrative one, built to show a single sustained sight gag from start to finish.

programme.title: THE ASTRONOMER’S DREAM — Interstitial
programme.desc: A fantasist astronomer beset by celestial visions. Méliès’ elaborate sets and substitutions foreshadow *A Trip to the Moon*.

programme.title: The Astronomer's Dream
programme.desc:
An astronomer sits at his desk in a vaulted observatory tower, a long telescope angled up through the window beside him. He dozes, and the room fills with apparitions: Satan appears and is banished in turn by Phoebe, goddess of the moon, who vanishes just as suddenly herself. The astronomer chalks a globe on a blackboard; it sprouts a face and limbs and comes to life on its own. Then the Moon itself intrudes into the tower as an enormous grinning face, swallowing the astronomer's telescope whole and belching smoke. Small clown-devils tumble out of its mouth and are shoved back in by the flustered astronomer; a woman reclines in the crook of a crescent moon overhead; and when the astronomer reaches for her, the Moon's face lunges forward and swallows him too, spitting him back out in pieces before he is reassembled.
The film is Georges Méliès's La Lune à un mètre — literally "the moon at one metre," referring to the telescope's power rather than any distance travelled. It was shot at Méliès's glass-roofed studio at Montreuil and issued through his Star Film Company, catalogued under numbers 160–162, spanning three reels' worth of Star Film stock for what runs only a few minutes. Méliès plays the astronomer himself, reworking a comic magic sketch he had performed on the stage of his own Théâtre Robert-Houdin earlier in the decade; the moon-headed apparition and the swallowing gag are stage illusions translated directly into substitution splices and pyrotechnic smoke. Jehanne d'Alcy, a Robert-Houdin stage actress since the 1880s, plays Phoebe; she and Méliès would marry roughly three decades later.
The film sits in the run of trick fantasies Méliès made in the years just after Un Escamotage d'une dame, when he was refining the stop-substitution and multiple-exposure techniques that let a figure vanish, a drawing animate itself, or a painted moon-face open its mouth on camera. Those same devices — the man swallowed by a leering moon, the reassembly of a dismembered body, the observatory setting itself — reappear four years later, considerably expanded, in Le Voyage dans la Lune; La Lune à un mètre is routinely cited as its direct rehearsal piece, right down to the man-in-the-moon face taking a projectile (here a telescope, there a capsule) in the eye or mouth.

programme.title: SAFETY LAST! — Interstitial
programme.desc: A country boy fakes big-city success until he must climb a twelve-story building himself. The clock-face dangle is the most famous image in silent comedy.

programme.title: Safety Last!
programme.desc:
Harold Lloyd plays a small-town boy, identified in the titles only as "The Boy," who leaves his sweetheart behind in Great Bend to make good in the city, promising to send for her once he has proven himself. He lands a clerk's job at the De Vore department store and, to keep up appearances in his letters home, lets her believe he is already a rising executive. When she turns up unannounced to see his success for herself, Lloyd is forced to improvise: he recruits his roommate, a steeplejack known as "Limpy" Bill, to climb the store's building as a publicity stunt for a thousand-dollar prize, intending to take the credit while someone else takes the risk. A run-in with a policeman sends Bill into hiding, and Lloyd ends up making the climb himself, one story at a time, while his friend promises to take over at the next floor and never quite manages to.
The film was Lloyd's fourth "thrill picture" and the one that fixed the formula for good, produced at Hal Roach Studios and credited to directors Fred C. Newmeyer and Sam Taylor, working from a story by Hal Roach, Taylor, and Tim Whelan. Lloyd got the idea after watching Bill Strother, a real steeplejack billed as "the Human Spider," scale the side of the International Bank Building in downtown Los Angeles in September 1922 while a crowd gathered below. Lloyd introduced himself, hired him, and wrote the climb into the picture, casting Strother as Limpy Bill and using him to double for the wide shots of the ascent. Lloyd himself performed the closer shots, including the climactic clock sequence, on facades built on the rooftops of several downtown buildings — principally 908 South Broadway — with the camera positioned low against the parapet edge so that ordinary street traffic several stories below Lloyd's actual platform read on film as many more floors down. It was an optical trick built from platform height, building selection, and camera angle rather than any single gimmick, and it held up because Lloyd, unlike his double, was genuinely climbing and genuinely exposed for every shot in which his face is visible.
Lloyd performed these climbs three years after an accident that should have ended his career. On August 24, 1919, during a photo session at the Witzel studio in Los Angeles, he picked up what he believed was a prop bomb, lit it to pose for a publicity still, and it turned out to be live — mixed in, apparently, with a batch of dummies left over from another production's test shots. The explosion took his right thumb and forefinger and damaged his eye and chest. Lloyd went back to work within months, performing physical comedy in a specially built prosthetic glove made to disguise the injury on camera, well enough that most contemporary audiences never noticed. The building climbs of Safety Last!, filmed with that hand, are why the sequence has never played as a mere special effect: the danger in the wide shots is Strother's, but the danger in the close-ups, floor by floor, is Lloyd's own, missing fingers and all.
Mildred Davis plays the girl, "The Girl" in the credits, whom Lloyd's character is trying to impress. Davis had appeared opposite Lloyd in more than a dozen shorts and features since 1919, and the two married on February 10, 1923, shortly before Safety Last! reached theaters that April; it was her last picture before she retired from the screen. Noah Young appears as the policeman whose pursuit of Limpy Bill sets the climb in motion, and Westcott B. Clarke plays the store's officious floorwalker. The picture was shot by Walter Lundin, Lloyd's regular cameraman through the silent period, and edited by Thomas J. Crizer.
Safety Last! was an enormous commercial success on its 1923 release and remains the film most identified with Lloyd's screen persona, the bespectacled go-getter whose ambition keeps outrunning his nerve. The clock-face shot, in which Lloyd hangs from the hands of a giant street clock as they begin to give way beneath him, has circulated so widely as a still image that it now stands, with Chaplin's tramp and Keaton's stone face, among the handful of pictures that summarize silent comedy to people who have never seen a silent film. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 1994. The version in most circulation today, including the widely used Harold Lloyd Trust restoration with Carl Davis's orchestral score, runs a few minutes longer than contemporary trade listings for the original release, the difference accounted for by modern main and end titles rather than any missing footage.

programme.title: LA PETITE FILLE ET SON CHAT — Interstitial
programme.desc: An intimate domestic scene—an early “actuality” capturing everyday life rather than spectacle.

programme.title: La Petite Fille Et Son Chat
programme.desc:
A young girl sits at a table in a garden, offering scraps of meat to a large, long-haired cat. The cat wants the food more than it wants to cooperate: it lunges and paws at her hand, climbs onto the table and onto her lap, and by the end of the shot is wrestling with her outright while she tries to fend it off and keep hold of the treat. It is a plain piece of domestic life set up for the camera, with no trick, no edit, and no larger point to make beyond the spectacle of a child and an unruly animal sharing a frame for under a minute.
The girl is Madeleine Koehler, niece of Auguste and Louis Lumière, and the setting is the Koehler family home in the Monplaisir district of Lyon, where a number of the Lumière operators' home-movie subjects were shot. The Lumière company's own catalogue lists the film as vue no. 1100 and credits no specific operator by name — a reminder that many of the roughly 1,400 Lumière actualities were shot by staff cameramen sent out under the company's banner rather than by Louis or Auguste personally, even when family members appear on screen.
The catalogue entry, and the Cinémathèque française's own record of the film, date it to 1900 rather than 1899, the dating derived from Madeleine Koehler's apparent age in the shot. The 1899 date attached to this print is the one that has circulated widely online and in some secondary listings, but it does not match the two primary institutional sources for the film.
Like other Lumière actualities of the period, it survives because the operators treated everyday incident — a meal, a train, a baby, a cat refusing to behave — as sufficient subject matter for the new medium, with the camera doing nothing more than holding still and recording what happened in front of it.

programme.title: SHERLOCK JR. — Interstitial
programme.desc: A projectionist falls asleep and walks into the movie he is showing. Keaton broke his neck making it and didn't find out for years.

programme.title: Sherlock Jr.
programme.desc:
A small-town movie projectionist, moonlighting as a would-be detective while he saves for a ring, is framed for the theft of a watch by a rival for his girl's affections. Falling asleep at the projector after being thrown out of her house, he dreams himself literally into the picture he is screening, stepping off the theater floor and into the frame as the immaculate master detective Sherlock Jr., who solves the case his waking self could not. Buster Keaton directed, produced, and starred, working from a story and scenario credited to Jean Havez, Joseph Mitchell, and Clyde Bruckman. Roscoe Arbuckle, hired as co-director and the man who had given Keaton his start in pictures a decade earlier, is also billed on the credits, though accounts differ sharply on how much of his work survived into the finished film; Keaton later said Arbuckle had grown difficult on set in the wake of the 1921 scandal that ended his own starring career, and that he arranged for Arbuckle to move to another picture so he could finish this one alone. Joseph M. Schenck produced for Buster Keaton Productions, released through Metro Pictures.
The film's best-known passage is the sequence in which the dreaming projectionist walks down the aisle and into the screen itself. The already-edited film does not accommodate him: he steps off a porch into a busy street, dives off a rock into a snowbank, and is stranded on a traffic island a beat ahead of an oncoming train, the cuts landing on his body with no regard for where his environment has gone. Keaton and cameramen Elgin Lessley and Byron Houck worked out the geometry with a surveyor's transit, marking precise camera positions and sightlines so that Keaton's figure would register at exactly the same size and screen position across each transposed setting — a technical problem with no real precedent in 1924, solved by hand and by tape measure rather than by trick photography of the sort audiences of the day expected. Keaton told historian Kevin Brownlow that after the film's release "every cameraman in the business went to see that picture more than once trying to figure out how the hell we did some of that."
Two stunts from the picture have become touchstones of Keaton's reputation as his own most reckless stuntman. In the railway chase, Keaton grabs the rope of a moving train's water tower to swing himself off; the tower's spout let go with far more force than anticipated, and he was slammed to the tracks below, the back of his neck striking the rail. He finished the scene and complained only of headaches afterward. It was not until a routine physical examination roughly a decade later that an X-ray turned up a healed fracture in his upper spine — he had been performing and touring for years with a broken neck he never knew he had. Later in the same chase, Keaton is thrown up onto the handlebars of a motorcycle whose driver has already fallen off; unaware the machine is now unmanned, he rides on, weaving through cross-traffic, road crews, and a washed-out bridge for a continuous run of real Los Angeles streets, entirely without a driver, timed by instinct against traffic that was not part of the gag.
Kathryn McGuire plays the girl at the center of the frame story, sharing the screen with Keaton's own father, Joe Keaton, as her father, and with Ward Crane as the "local sheik," the well-dressed rival who frames the projectionist for theft and, inside the dream, becomes the villain the master detective unmasks. Erwin Connelly appears as a butler doubling as accomplice. Keaton shot for roughly five months, previewed the picture and cut it down, and the release version ran five reels, about 44 to 45 minutes depending on the projection speed used to time it — the same picture clocked at slightly different lengths by contemporary and modern sources purely as an artifact of variable silent-era projection rates, not of missing footage.
Sherlock Jr. opened in New York in May 1924 to respectful but not rapturous notices; it did solid, unspectacular business for Keaton at the time, overshadowed in the popular imagination by The General two years later. Its reputation has grown steadily since with the historical rediscovery of Keaton's work from the 1950s onward, and it is now routinely cited, including by the Library of Congress in its National Film Registry essay, as one of the most technically accomplished and self-reflexive comedies of the silent era — a film about the act of watching and making films, built by a man who did his own falling.

programme.title: THE ONE MAN BAND — Interstitial
programme.desc: Méliès appears seven times in one frame using multiple exposures, one of the earliest compositing effects in cinema.

programme.title: The One Man Band
programme.desc:
A bare stage, framed by a theatrical curtain, holds nothing but a row of chairs. Georges Méliès walks on alone and, chair by chair, multiplies himself into an entire ensemble: musicians with violins and horns, a man brandishing a cymbal overhead, a conductor keeping time, until seven identical figures occupy the frame at once, all played by Méliès, all moving independently and in step with one another.
The illusion required seven separate exposures of the same strip of film. Méliès masked off every chair but the one currently in use, ran that portion of the scene, wound the film back to the start, unmasked the next chair, and repeated the process until the whole band had been recorded in sequence on a single reel. He later described the strain of the method in blunt terms: "you go into a rage when after three quarters of an hour of work and attention, a sprocket rips forcing you to start all over again, repair being impossible." Only one other film in his output, Le Mélomane, pushed the same trick to as many simultaneous exposures; contemporaries and later historians alike treated the result as a high-water mark for the technique. John Frazer, in his study of Méliès's films, called it "a Méliès tour de force, unchallenged for years."
The performance itself is simple theater dressed up as a magic act: the seven Méliès figures play together, fold back down to one, and the lone performer takes his bow before an enormous fan that rises up behind him and closes the scene. The trick is entirely in the camera and the darkroom rather than in any stage machinery, and the film survives as one of the clearest surviving demonstrations of how far Méliès had already taken multiple exposure by 1900, two years after his first ventures into substitution splicing.
Star Film catalogued the picture under numbers 262-263. It has no plot beyond the act itself; its interest is the performer's control over the mechanics of the exposure, repeated seven times without a visible seam.

programme.title: PETER PAN — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first film of Barrie's play, made with the author's blessing — Betty Bronson flies, Tinker Bell glows, and the crocodile ticks.

programme.title: Peter Pan
programme.desc:
Peter Pan was the first film adaptation of J. M. Barrie's 1904 stage play, produced by Famous Players-Lasky and released through Paramount at the end of 1924. Barrie himself controlled the film rights and, unusually for an author dealing with Hollywood, kept a hand in the production: he wrote a treatment suggesting how the play might be opened out for the screen, and director Herbert Brenon followed the stage text closely enough that most of the intertitles are lifted directly from Barrie's own dialogue. The result plays less like a free adaptation than a filmed record of the play's spirit, complete with a title card of Barrie's own words on the nature of the story addressed straight to the audience.
The casting of Peter went through months of screen tests before Barrie made his choice. Established stars including Mary Pickford and Gloria Swanson were known to want the part, but Barrie picked Betty Bronson, a teenager with only bit parts to her name, after seeing her test footage. It made her a star overnight. Ernest Torrence, a Scottish stage actor who had recently made his name as the villainous Luke Hatburn in Tol'able David, played Captain Hook, and Mary Brian was cast as Wendy. Anna May Wong, already a familiar screen presence after The Toll of the Sea and The Thief of Bagdad, appeared as Tiger Lily, one of the more prominent roles given to an Asian American actress in a major studio production of the period. Cinematographer James Wong Howe, early in a career that would make him one of Hollywood's most respected camera artists, shot the picture; Roy Pomeroy, later an Oscar winner for sound and special effects work, served as assistant director.
Nana the dog and the crocodile were both played, in costume, by George Ali, a veteran vaudeville and pantomime animal impersonator who had performed the same roles on stage for years, including opposite Barrie's own productions. Ali's Nana suit combined real dog fur on the head with caracul for the body and a system of internal strings that let him work the eyes, ears, and tail from inside; contemporary accounts single out the performance as uncannily convincing for what was, mechanically, a man in a fur suit. Peter and Wendy's flights over London and through Neverland were achieved with wire rigging concealed by careful lighting and camera placement, a technique already established in stage productions of the play and adapted here for the camera; Tinker Bell was rendered partly as a point of light on a wire and partly, in closer shots, by an actress.
Peter Pan was believed lost for decades after Paramount, like most studios, let its silent negatives lapse once sound arrived. A 35mm nitrate print turned up in 1971 among the holdings later catalogued at the George Eastman Museum, and the film was restored in full in 1995 with funding from the Walt Disney Corporation, premiering in its restored form at the Pordenone silent film festival in 1996. It was added to the National Film Registry by the Library of Congress in 2000. The film has long since fallen into the public domain in the United States, and prints in circulation vary in length according to the projection speed used in transfer; the studio's own release figures list the picture at ten reels, roughly 9,593 feet, which runs somewhat longer than this file's 102 minutes when projected at silent-era speeds rather than the sound-era standard.

programme.title: THE HAUNTED CURIOSITY SHOP — Interstitial
programme.desc: A British trick film produced by Robert W. Paul. Apparitions torment a curio dealer in a showcase of optical effects.

programme.title: The Haunted Curiosity Shop
programme.desc:
An elderly antique dealer, alone among the crowded shelves of his shop, finds the bric-a-brac coming to life around him. A skull materialises out of nowhere; a suit of medieval armour becomes an animated knight; a tall urn on a pedestal issues a column of smoke from which further apparitions emerge. The dealer is prodded, startled, and harried from one end of the set to the other as each new trick supersedes the last, until the shop itself seems to have turned against him.
The film was directed by Walter R. Booth for producer Robert W. Paul, the pairing that had already built a reputation for effects-driven novelty films such as Upside Down, or The Human Flies (1899) and Railway Collision (1900). Where those earlier films had generally been built around a single trick, The Haunted Curiosity Shop is a showcase piece: stop-motion substitution, matte work, and in-camera editing (halting the camera to swap or remove performers and props between exposures) are strung together in rapid succession, each apparition dissolving into the next. Booth, a former stage conjuror, supplied the trick sense; Paul supplied the apparatus and the production backing, as he did for the run of fantastical films coming out of his New Southgate studio in this period.
BFI Screenonline's Michael Brooke has called it "an effective and engrossing experience," noting the sheer density of transformation packed into its short running time. The film sits alongside contemporary work by Georges Méliès in Paris as part of the same turn-of-the-century vogue for the trick film, in which the camera's capacity for substitution and superimposition was treated as an attraction in itself, with no more narrative scaffolding than a haunted setting required. The print held here runs a single minute, shorter than the roughly two-minute length in which the film has otherwise survived.

programme.title: PROLIFIC MAGIC EGG — Interstitial
programme.desc: A conjurer produces gigantic eggs and living figures—stage magic translated into screen trickery.

programme.title: Prolific Magic Egg
programme.desc:
A skeleton propped on a table by an assistant is left alone in the room, kicks its legs, flails its arms, and rises up transformed into a conjurer in evening dress — Georges Méliès himself, playing the magician as he so often did in his own trick films. He picks up an egg, dashes a crude face onto its shell with a few strokes, and sets it on a stand, where under his passes it swells from a hand-sized prop to the size of a human head. The egg's shape dissolves away and in its place hangs the head of a young woman; two more heads matching it bloom on either side, so that three faces float in a row where a single egg had stood. The triad closes together into one head, which in turn gives way to the leering, oversized head of a hobgoblin. The transformation reverses itself, the goblin fades back into a plain egg at its ordinary size, and the magician plucks it from the stand and swallows it whole.
The film is a Star Film production, shot in the glass studio Méliès had built at Montreuil, with the painted proscenium arch, backing flat, and side stools that furnish nearly every Méliès subject of the period — visible in this print, along with the "Star Film Paris" trademark worked into the set dressing to deter the duping of his negatives by rival distributors, a running problem for him in the American market. The trick itself belongs to a run of "head" and "growth" films Méliès made across 1901-1903, in which substitution splices (arrêt de caméra) let a prop swell, multiply, or change identity between cuts invisibly to the eye — the same stop-camera technique underlying his beheadings, multiplications, and appearing/vanishing acts elsewhere in his catalog. The premise of an egg yielding faces recurs in his output; he returned to eggs again a few years later in The Easter Eggs (1907).
The film was distributed in France as L'Œuf du sorcier ou L'Œuf magique prolifique and reached American screens under the Star Film imprint as The Prolific Magical Egg / Prolific Magic Egg, with a US release in early 1903, which is the date by which the film is generally catalogued in English-language listings and the reason for this year against a title made in Méliès's 1902 production run. It survives today through Lobster Films' preservation elements, restored and issued on the Flicker Alley/Lobster Films set Georges Méliès Encore: New Discoveries (1896-1911), alongside dozens of other rediscovered Star Film subjects. No color-tinted print is known to survive; the surviving elements, including the one behind this transfer, are black and white.

programme.title: THE GOLD RUSH — Interstitial
programme.desc: The Tramp goes to the Klondike: the boiled boot, the dance of the dinner rolls, the cabin teetering on the cliff. Chaplin said this was the film he wanted to be remembered by.

programme.title: The Gold Rush
programme.desc:
Charlie Chaplin's Lone Prospector wanders into the Klondike gold fields during the Alaskan stampede of 1898, drifting unaware past a hunted murderer and a bear, until a blizzard drives him into the cabin of the fugitive Black Larsen and the good-natured giant Big Jim McKay. Trapped by the storm and out of food, the three draw straws for who will go out into the snow; the loser's fate turns the cabin into a study of hunger and suspicion before Big Jim stumbles onto a mountain of gold and the Prospector wanders into a boomtown, where he falls for the dance-hall girl Georgia and contrives, with a borrowed cabin and a New Year's Eve dinner nobody comes to, to win her attention.
Chaplin conceived the film from two sources he kept on his desk while developing the story: a stereoscope set of photographs of prospectors toiling up the Chilkoot Pass during the actual Klondike gold rush of 1896-99, and a book on the Donner Party, the emigrant company stranded in the Sierra Nevada in the winter of 1846-47 whose survivors ate their moccasins and, in the extremity of starvation, one another. Chaplin fused the two: the Chilkoot Pass photographs gave him the opening image of hundreds of men strung in a line up a snowbound mountain trail, which he restaged with several hundred extras above Truckee, California, not far from the Donner Party's own campsite; the Donner Party's ordeal gave him the film's most famous sequence, in which the starving Prospector boils and eats his boot with the manners of a diner at a fine restaurant, twirling laces onto a fork like spaghetti and sucking the nails clean like bones. The boot and its laces were cast from black licorice by the American Licorice Company, which supplied roughly twenty candy pairs for the scene; shooting it took three days and, by assistant director Eddie Sutherland's count, 63 takes, and both Chaplin and his co-star Mack Swain were reportedly laid up afterward from having eaten so much licorice.
Production was disrupted at its midpoint by Chaplin's personal life. His original leading lady was Lita Grey, sixteen years old, cast as the dance-hall girl; when she became pregnant during filming, Chaplin married her in Mexico that November to forestall a statutory rape prosecution, and shooting halted for roughly three months. Grey did not return to the role — she survives in the finished film only as an unbilled extra among the climbers on the Chilkoot Pass — and Chaplin replaced her with Georgia Hale, a Chicago beauty-contest winner he had noticed in a Josef von Sternberg picture. Hale plays Georgia in the release version, including the sequence, added after Grey's departure, in which the Prospector dreams he has hosted his New Year's dinner guests to great acclaim, only to wake alone; and the dance of the rolls, in which Chaplin animates two dinner rolls speared on forks into a pair of kicking legs, a bit later credited to him alone though a similar table gag had appeared years earlier in a Fatty Arbuckle short. The teetering cabin in the film's climax, blown by a fresh storm to the lip of a precipice so that every step by its two occupants rocks it further over the edge, was built as a hinged, counterweighted model by Chaplin's studio technicians and shot in forced perspective.
The Gold Rush was written, produced, directed, and edited by Chaplin for his own company, released through United Artists, the distributor he had co-founded in 1919 with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks, and D. W. Griffith. He shot roughly 230,000 feet of film over more than a year and cut it down to just under 10,000 feet. It premiered at Grauman's Egyptian Theatre in Hollywood on June 26, 1925, with a live prologue staged by Sid Grauman, and went into general release that August at a trimmed length of around 8,500 feet, running about 95 minutes at silent projection speed; this print, sourced from the original 1925 silent version rather than the 1942 reissue Chaplin later re-edited, scored, and narrated himself at a tighter 72 minutes, runs 87 minutes, a difference attributable to the platform's projection speed rather than to missing footage. Chaplin named The Gold Rush more than once, including in his own autobiography, as the film by which he most wished to be remembered. It was among the first twenty-five films selected for the National Film Registry by the Library of Congress in 1989, cited for its fusion of slapstick with pathos drawn from Chaplin's own memories of poverty.

programme.title: JUPITER’S THUNDERBALLS — Interstitial
programme.desc: Mythology as spectacle: Jupiter hurls thunderbolts from the heavens using pyrotechnics and substitution splices.

programme.title: Jupiter's Thunderballs
programme.desc:
High on a cloud-wreathed Olympus, Jupiter holds court in a painted temple set, a comic, corpulent figure attended by Mercury and a retinue of gods and muses. Méliès's American catalogue sold the film as "a mythological burlesque," and the action bears that out: Jupiter tries to conjure the nine Muses by hurling his thunderbolts, only to find the bolts have stopped working. Mercury is sent to fetch Vulcan, the forge god, to repair them, and the film's final passages play out around a smoking, flame-lit altar as the bolts are restored and the Muses are finally, triumphantly produced.
Méliès plays Jupiter himself, leaning into the role's girth for comic effect, and the film pokes at the classical education French schoolboys of his generation would have shared — the gods reduced to bumbling stagehands of their own mythology. Mercury's darting, knock-kneed run across the set echoes the same character's send-up in Offenbach's operetta Orpheus in the Underworld, a piece of shared cultural reference Méliès's Paris audiences would have caught immediately.
The trick effects are built from the same repertoire Méliès had spent the previous decade refining at his glass-walled Montreuil studio: stop-motion substitution splices make gods and pedestals appear and vanish, stage flash-powder pyrotechnics stand in for thunder and lightning, and a working fire effect animates Vulcan's forge in the closing scene. None of the surviving printed material for this title indicates hand or stencil tinting, and the print sampled here is black and white throughout.
The film was issued by Méliès's own Star Film Company under the American release title Jupiter's Thunderbolts, or the Home of the Muses, and carries the consecutive Star Film catalogue numbers 503-505, reflecting its length across multiple reels of stock. It belongs to the extraordinarily productive stretch of 1903, when Méliès was turning out mythological and fairy-tale spectacles at a rapid clip for both French and export markets, and it survives today as one of the more overtly comic entries in that run, closer in spirit to burlesque stage pantomime than to the wonder-voyage fantasies for which he is now best remembered.

programme.title: THE LOST WORLD — Interstitial
programme.desc: Willis O'Brien's stop-motion dinosaurs — a brontosaurus loose in London, three years before he built King Kong. The first creature feature.

programme.title: The Lost World
programme.desc:
Professor George Edward Challenger returns from the Amazon claiming to have found a plateau where prehistoric animals still survive, a claim London's scientific establishment greets with open scorn. To settle the argument he assembles an expedition: the skeptical Professor Summerlee, the big-game hunter Sir John Roxton, the reporter Edward Malone, and Paula White, daughter of the explorer whose diary first pointed to the plateau. What they find, once native bearers desert them and strand the party on top, is a world of living dinosaurs — brontosaurs grazing in the mist, an allosaurus stalking the camp, pterodactyls overhead — and an ape-man who stalks the humans in turn. The film adapts Arthur Conan Doyle's 1912 novel The Lost World, scripted by Marion Fairfax, and was directed by Harry O. Hoyt for First National Pictures, produced by Watterson R. Rothacker with cinematography by Arthur Edeson.
The reason the picture still matters is Willis H. O'Brien's animation. O'Brien had been experimenting with stop-motion dinosaurs since the mid-1910s, and Rothacker brought him in to build The Lost World around the technique rather than treat it as a novelty insert — the first time a Hollywood feature had done so. O'Brien and his crew built miniature armatured models, photographed them frame by frame against miniature and glass-shot sets, and combined the results with the live-action cast through split-screen and matte work supervised by Fred Jackman. It was, in effect, the dry run for King Kong eight years later, made with several of the same technicians and much of the same armature-and-latex method O'Brien would refine for that film.
Conan Doyle himself helped manufacture the film's publicity before it existed as a finished picture. In 1922, while in New York on a lecture tour, he brought a reel of O'Brien's dinosaur test footage to a dinner meeting of the Society of American Magicians — a group that included Harry Houdini — and screened it without explaining how it was made. The New York Times ran the story on its front page the next day, reporting that Doyle's "monsters" were either real or "masterpieces" of fakery, and the resulting stir did much to sell the eventual feature before First National had even finished it. The film premiered at the Astor Theatre in New York on February 2, 1925, and went into general release that June, running ten reels — contemporary references list its release length at roughly 9,700 feet, on the order of 100-110 minutes at silent projection speed.
Wallace Beery plays Challenger under heavy padding and a false beard, opposite Bessie Love as Paula White, Lloyd Hughes as Malone, Lewis Stone as Roxton, and Bull Montana, unrecognizable under makeup, as the Ape-Man. The climax — in which the expedition's captured brontosaurus is shipped to London for exhibition, breaks loose, rampages through the streets, and finally collapses Tower Bridge before swimming off down the Thames — was the picture's most talked-about set piece and anticipates the finale of King Kong in shape as well as spirit.
Like a great many silent features, The Lost World survives only in fragments of its original negative; much of what circulated for decades came down through 16mm Kodascope reduction prints assembled for home and non-theatrical rental, running roughly an hour to little over an hour, missing footage, scene order sometimes reshuffled, and title cards re-set. That abbreviated version, not the original ten-reel release cut, is what fell into the public domain and is most commonly seen. Beginning with a George Eastman Museum-supervised reconstruction in the 1990s and continuing through Lobster Films' 2016 restoration overseen by Serge Bromberg — which combined some ten surviving international source prints, including material recovered from Czech and French archives, and restored the original tinting scheme — closer-to-complete versions approaching 90-100 minutes have been reassembled. This transfer is the older, widely-circulated short cut, not the full restoration.

programme.title: THE UNTAMABLE WHISKERS — Interstitial
programme.desc: A man’s facial hair grows uncontrollably despite shaving—classic Méliès stop‑trick comedy.

programme.title: The Untamable Whiskers
programme.desc:
Georges Méliès plays showman and subject at once. Standing in medium shot before a painted backdrop of rooftops and a river — an unusually close, static framing for a director normally given to deep, busy tableaux — he greets the audience directly, then snatches up a stick of chalk and dashes off a rapid sketch of his own bald head crowned with a long, flowing wig. He strikes a pose, and the wig appears on him in fact, the substitution splice timed to slip past the eye. He repeats the trick again and again: a hasty chalkboard portrait of a white-bearded elder, then Méliès himself wearing the beard; a monocled gentleman with heavy side-whiskers; the words "comic excentric" scrawled on the board, followed by a clown. He sketches a naval officer in a bicorne hat and becomes him in turn. The performance closes on a final transformation into a horned, robed figure of the Devil, who vanishes from the set as abruptly as he arrived.
The film revives a specialty Méliès had performed on the Paris variety stage before he ever owned a camera: the "lightning sketch" act, in which a quick-change artist draws a face and then instantly becomes it. He had already filmed a version of the routine, generally cited under the English title A Lightning Sketch, sometime earlier in his career; that film is now lost, which leaves Le Roi du maquillage as the surviving record of how he staged the trick for the screen. The mechanics are the plainest in his repertoire — chalk drawings, a change of wig, whiskers, or hat, and a dissolve or substitution splice to cover the join — but the film asks nothing more of its effects than that they disappear, so the eye reads only a man's face endlessly remaking itself.
Star Film catalogued the picture as numbers 552-553. It reached English-language markets under two different titles: American distributors sold it as The Untamable Whiskers, while in Britain it circulated as The King of the Mackerel Fishers, a title with no evident connection to the on-screen action beyond the pun on "maquillage." Both English titles obscure the film's actual subject, which the French original states plainly: a king, or master, of stage makeup.
The film survives in the paper-print holdings deposited at the Library of Congress for copyright registration, the route by which a great many early Star Film titles were preserved after their nitrate negatives perished. It is a minor entry next to Méliès's fantastical voyages, but a direct record of the music-hall skill — fast drawing, faster costume changes — that he brought with him into filmmaking and that underlies the transformation scenes of his more famous trick films.

programme.title: THE GENERAL — Interstitial
programme.desc: A Southern engineer chases his stolen locomotive through the Civil War. The train wreck was the most expensive shot of the silent era, done once, for real.

programme.title: The General
programme.desc:
Johnnie Gray loves two things: his locomotive, the General, and Annabelle Lee. When Fort Sumter falls he rushes to enlist, only to be turned away — the recruiting officers judge him more valuable to the Confederacy as an engineer than as a soldier, but no one tells him why, and Annabelle, humiliated by what looks like cowardice, will not speak to him. A year later Union raiders led by Captain Anderson steal the General from a station stop, with Annabelle trapped aboard the attached boxcar, and Johnnie takes off after his engine and his girl in a single-minded chase that never lets up: on foot, on a handcar, on a bicycle, and finally at the throttle of another locomotive, deep into Union-held Georgia and back out again with the whole Northern army on his tail. The film is credited to Buster Keaton and Clyde Bruckman as directors, with the scenario by Keaton and Bruckman adapted by Al Boasberg and Charles Henry Smith from William Pittenger's 1863 memoir The Great Locomotive Chase, an account of the 1862 Andrews Raid, in which a party of Union soldiers and civilian scouts under James J. Andrews seized a Confederate train near Big Shanty, Georgia, and tried to run it north while tearing up track and cutting telegraph wire behind them, only to be run down and captured; several raiders, Andrews among them, were later hanged as spies. Keaton's film inverts the history it draws on: where Andrews's raiders were the Union men and the pursuit was Confederate, Johnnie Gray chases as a Southerner recovering his own stolen engine, a reversal Keaton made because it let his character spend the picture as the pursuer rather than the pursued, and because a Confederate engineer triumphing gave the ending its shape. Buster Keaton Productions financed the film, with Joseph M. Schenck producing and United Artists distributing.
Keaton shot the picture largely around Cottage Grove, Oregon, where the production built a stand-in for wartime Marietta along the town's parallel rail lines and where a fleet of vintage narrow- and standard-gauge locomotives, borrowed from the Oregon, Pacific and Eastern Railroad, stood in for the General, the Texas, and the other engines of the story. The film's set-piece is the collapse of a wooden trestle under the full weight of a moving locomotive: Keaton's crew built a 215-foot bridge roughly 34 feet above the Row River at Culp Creek, set it alight, and sent an engine across as the structure gave way beneath it, dropping engine and tender into the water below in a single unrepeatable take shot with multiple cameras. It is routinely cited as the most expensive single shot of the silent era, budgeted at around $42,000, a substantial fraction of the film's roughly $750,000 total cost — at the time the most expensive film Keaton had made. The wrecked engine was left where it fell; it became a minor local attraction sitting in the river for more than a decade before being pulled out and cut up for scrap during a Second World War metal drive. In the finished film the river is called the Rock River, a name invented for the story; the location itself is the Row River, and present-day accounts of the shoot sometimes elide the two.
Marion Mack, a Mack Sennett-trained comedienne making one of her few starring features, plays Annabelle Lee opposite Keaton's Johnnie Gray, and the film gives her comic business of her own rather than treating her purely as cargo to be rescued — she sweeps out the cab of a moving locomotive and discards a piece of firewood for being "got a knot hole in it," and Keaton lets the joke run rather than cutting away from her. Glen Cavender plays the Union Captain Anderson who steals the engine, Jim Farley appears as the Union general, and Charles Henry Smith plays Annabelle's father. Keaton's own father, Joe Keaton, has a bit part among the Confederate soldiers. As with Keaton's other silent features of the period, there was no synchronized score at the time of release; theaters supplied their own musical accompaniment, and modern video and restoration releases have carried a range of newly composed or compiled scores, none of them original to 1926.
The General opened commercially in early 1927 to reviews that found it uneven and its Civil War subject matter an odd fit for comedy — Life magazine and other contemporary critics singled out gags involving battlefield dead as being in poor taste for what audiences expected of a Keaton picture, and it did not recoup its cost outright on first release. Its failure to turn the profit Schenck and United Artists expected was a significant factor in Keaton's loss of creative independence soon after, when he was folded into the more heavily supervised production system at Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer. The film's reputation was rebuilt slowly, alongside the broader rediscovery of Keaton's silent work from the 1940s and 1950s onward championed by historians including Kevin Brownlow, and it was among the first twenty-five films selected by the Library of Congress for the National Film Registry in 1989. It is now widely ranked among the finest American films of the silent era, admired for the way its physical comedy is staged in and organized around real landscape and real, unfaked machinery rather than trick photography.
The print transferred for this file runs 79 minutes, longer than the roughly 67-to-75-minute lengths common to many home-video transfers of the same eight-reel, 7,500-foot original; the difference is consistent with a slower, more era-appropriate silent projection speed rather than any added or missing footage. The transfer carries the period-typical tinting convention of amber-toned exteriors and blue-toned night scenes, with plain white serif intertitles on black.

programme.title: A DREADFUL NIGHT — Interstitial
programme.desc: Chomón’s early trick film for Pathé—Spain’s answer to Méliès, built on surreal nighttime terrors.

programme.title: A Dreadful Night
programme.desc:
A traveler settles in for the night at a cheap inn, only to find his room will not let him rest. His bed tips, folds, and pitches him onto the floor; a ghost rises from the wardrobe; furniture rearranges itself when his back is turned. He fights back against the room itself, wrestling the bedclothes and grappling with the sheeted spirit, before the whole building comes down around him. The last shot shows him picking himself out of the rubble of the collapsed inn.
The film is the work of Segundo de Chomón, shot for Pathé Frères in 1905. Chomón, a Spaniard who had joined Pathé a few years earlier hand-tinting release prints frame by frame, moved into direction as the studio pushed to compete with Georges Méliès's Star-Film trick pictures, and by 1905 he was directing and photographing his own fantasy shorts using the same stop-substitution splicing Méliès had popularized: the camera halts, the set or actor is altered, and the camera resumes, so that objects appear to vanish, swap, or move under their own power. The haunted-room-at-an-inn setup was already a stock premise on the Paris trick-film circuit; Chomón's version strips it down to a rapid sequence of gags culminating in the building's destruction, rather than the more discursive dream-logic of Méliès's own inn films.
The print carries the tinted PATHÉ rooster trademark on its title card, standard practice for the company's releases of the period as a guard against duplication by rival studios. In Britain the film circulated as "A Dreadful Night" and, under a separate release title, "Robert Macaire and Bertrand"; in the United States it was distributed as "A Terrible Night."
Chomón would go on to become one of early cinema's most technically inventive figures, developing stop-motion and matte work later used on productions as prominent as Cabiria (1914), but this Pathé short belongs to his first years as a director, when the haunted-inn trick film was standard fare for the studios racing to fill programs with novelty.

programme.title: THE MAGIC TABLE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Objects animate themselves on a table—early stop‑motion and object animation from a pioneer of the technique.

programme.title: The Magic Table
programme.desc:
A family sits down to dinner in a single dressed room — a table laid with a cloth, wall clocks and plates for decoration, chairs drawn up for the meal — and the meal will not stay put. The table empties itself, refills, shrinks, grows, and drops away beneath the diners; the servant sent to lay it again is thwarted by the furniture itself, and the household ends up in a small slapstick riot of falls, snatches, and startled exits. The trick is built entirely from stop-motion substitution splices and, almost certainly, a trapped platform of the kind Pathé's effects shops built for exactly this purpose — a table fitted with springs and trap doors so it could be made to sink, rise, or vanish under a cloth without a visible cut. The print carries no tinting; it survives in plain black-and-white photography.
The film is attributed to Segundo de Chomón, the Aragonese-born director whom Pathé Frères brought from Barcelona to Paris specifically to compete with Georges Méliès's trick-film business. Chomón had been a Pathé agent and colorist before he ever pointed a camera at a magic act, and by the time he settled in Paris he was running one of the studio's stencil-coloring workshops alongside his directing work — the split between craftsman and director shows in how mechanically precise this film's gags are next to Méliès's more theatrical showmanship. Attribution and dating for this particular title are not fully settled: some archives and databases place it in 1905, others in 1908, and the resemblance to Méliès's own dinner-table trick films is close enough that at least one commentator has wondered whether the reels were simply mislabeled somewhere along the way. Chomón's documented run of prolific trick-film output for Pathé is usually dated from 1907 onward, which leans against the earlier date, but no single source settles the question decisively.
Whatever its exact year, the film belongs to a small, well-populated genre of the 1900s: the "haunted dinner" or "uncooperative furniture" trick film, in which the joke is entirely mechanical and the actors exist to react to props behaving impossibly. It asks nothing of its performers beyond comic timing and a willingness to be knocked about by unseen stagehands, and it delivers its entire premise, complication, and resolution inside a single minute of running time — the format's usual scale for the period.

programme.title: MAN WITH A MOVIE CAMERA — Interstitial
programme.desc: A day in the Soviet city, filmed by a cameraman we watch filming it. A movie about making movies, edited faster than anything before it.

programme.title: Man with a Movie Camera
programme.desc:
Man with a Movie Camera opens with a printed statement of intent rather than a story: the film declares itself "an experiment in the cinematic communication of visible events" made "without the help of intertitles," without a script, without actors, and without sets, in pursuit of "a truly international absolute language of cinema" separated from theatre and literature. What follows is a single constructed day — dawn to night — in a city that is really three cities spliced into one: Odesa, where most of the footage was shot, along with Kyiv and Moscow. Streets wake up, shops open, trams and factories start moving, couples marry and divorce, a woman gives birth, workers labor at looms and switchboards, and the city later empties into sport, drink, and evening leisure. There is no plot and no named character, only the recurring figure of a cameraman with a tripod slung over his shoulder, climbing onto moving trains and scaling towers to get his shot.
The film was produced by VUFKU, the All-Ukrainian Photo Cinema Administration, the state studio through which Soviet Ukraine ran its film industry in the 1920s and which gave Dziga Vertov the resources to pursue his most uncompromising work after friction with Moscow-based production bodies. Vertov, born David Abelevich Kaufman, had spent the decade making newsreel compilations under the Kino-Pravda banner and arguing in manifestos for a cinema built from unstaged observation and montage rather than drama. Man with a Movie Camera was the fullest statement of that argument: a film about the act of filming and editing itself, made by what Vertov called the "Council of Three."
The other two members of that council were his brother and his wife. Mikhail Kaufman, the cinematographer, is the man of the title, filmed at his camera in trains, on rooftops, in traffic, and — through double exposure — apparently standing inside a giant beer glass and straddling a camera perched atop another camera. He and Vertov had worked together since the Kino-Pravda newsreels, and this film represents the peak of Kaufman's daredevil, documentary-verite camera style before the brothers' working relationship broke down soon afterward. Yelizaveta Svilova, Vertov's wife and a trained editor, cut the footage down from well over a thousand meters of negative and appears repeatedly on screen at her own splicing bench, sorting strips of film and physically assembling the sequences the audience has just watched or is about to watch. Her presence turns the film into a demonstration of its own construction: shots of a movie camera, shots of an editor cutting the shots, and shots of an audience watching the finished result are folded into one continuous argument about how cinema makes meaning.
Stylistically the film is a compendium of what silent cinema could do by 1929: split screens, superimpositions, Dutch angles, extreme slow and fast motion, freeze frames, stop-motion animation of a camera walking on its own tripod legs, and match cuts that jump between unrelated cities as if they were one place. None of it is explained by a title card, because none was permitted; meaning is built entirely through the ordering of images, in keeping with Vertov's theoretical writing on montage as the foundation of a specifically cinematic language. The film premiered in Kyiv in January 1929, followed by screenings in Moscow that April and in the United States that May, where it met a mixed critical reception before its reputation grew over subsequent decades. Because prints were subsequently duplicated and distributed at inconsistent speeds, its rhythm was altered for much of the twentieth century; archival reconstructions, including work by the Austrian Film Museum and EYE Filmmuseum drawing on a surviving nitrate print, have since restored a running time close to the original, though exact figures vary by source and transfer.
Man with a Movie Camera entered the American public domain on January 1, 2025, along with other works first published in 1929. Long absent from mainstream circulation, it has since become a fixture of critical and historical polling: it topped Sight & Sound's inaugural critics' poll of the greatest documentaries ever made and has placed within the top ten of the magazine's decennial all-time greatest-films poll, the only nonfiction film to do so. It is now widely taught as a foundational text of Soviet montage theory and of documentary self-reflexivity, and its imagery — the cameraman scaling a factory chimney, the eye superimposed over a camera lens, Svilova at her editing table — remains among the most reproduced in silent-film history.

programme.title: RESCUED BY ROVER — Interstitial
programme.desc: A collie leads his master to a kidnapped baby. Its shot-to-shot storytelling invented film editing as suspense — and made Rover the first canine film star.

programme.title: Rescued by Rover
programme.desc:
Rescued by Rover was made on a budget Cecil Hepworth himself later itemized down to the shilling: seven pounds, thirteen shillings and sixpence. It was shot in and around Hepworth's own studio and home at Walton-on-Thames, using his own family as the cast. His wife, Margaret Hepworth (billed as Mrs. Hepworth), wrote the scenario and played the mother; Hepworth played the father; their infant daughter, Barbara Hepworth, played the kidnapped baby; and the family's collie, Blair, played Rover. Sebastian Smith and his wife played the gypsy beggar-woman who steals the baby from its pram and the tramp who shelters her, and May Clarke played the nursemaid who loses the child while flirting with a soldier in the park. Direction is credited in most contemporary and archival listings to Lewin Fitzhamon, who worked as Hepworth's principal staff director in this period, though Hepworth's own hand in the production — as producer, cinematographer, and performer — was substantial enough that many sources list the two men jointly.
The story is simple and told without a single explanatory intertitle: a nursemaid's inattention lets a beggar woman make off with the baby in its pram; Rover notices, gives chase along the towpath, swims a canal, and tracks the pair to a slum lodging; finding the door shut to him, he runs home to fetch the father, leading him back over the same route the dog had just covered. What made the film a landmark was not the plot but the cutting. Rather than staging the chase as a single continuous shot or a static tableau, Hepworth and Fitzhamon broke it into a sequence of locations — street, towpath, riverbank, doorway — cut together to imply continuous motion across real geographical space, and then repeated the same string of locations in reverse as Rover leads the father back, and a third time as the father and dog retrace the route to the rescue. It is this systematic use of parallel, geographically coherent editing to build tension — cutting on action and repeating settings to orient the viewer rather than confuse them — that later historians, notably Michael Brooke for BFI Screenonline, point to when calling the film a foundational document in the development of narrative film grammar, made at a moment Brooke describes as possibly the only point in film history when British cinema unambiguously led the world.
Commercially, Rescued by Rover was a sensation out of proportion to its cost. Hepworth's own figures put its circulation at around 400 prints sold at £8 each, circulating in exhibition for four or five years, at a time when even a hit American film of the period might sell only a couple of hundred copies. Demand was heavy enough that the original camera negative wore out from the repeated printing; Hepworth had his cast and dog re-stage the picture shot-for-shot to strike a second negative, and when that one also wore out, they filmed it a third time — the same actors, the same dog, the same locations, redone twice more simply to keep prints in circulation. Blair the collie, credited only as "Rover" on release, became popular enough on the strength of the film that the name Rover saw a marked revival as a dog's name in Britain in the years that followed, and Hepworth built a small run of sequel and imitation "Rover" pictures on the back of it, including a version of the same story remade around 1908.
The print gathered here derives from a modern black-and-white digital transfer of a surviving 35mm print; no tinting, hand-coloring, or restoration overlay is present, and there is no added live-action prologue. Frame-grabs from the file show the fireplace nursery opening with Barbara Hepworth and Blair, the nursemaid's flirtation and the pram theft in the park, Rover's run along the towpath and swim across the canal, the low lean-to interior where the kidnappers hide the child, and the father's search and reunion in the final shots — matching the documented shot list for the film. Along with Hepworth's other Walton-on-Thames pictures of the period, it survives as one of the clearest surviving demonstrations of how quickly, and how locally, the language of narrative cinema was assembled in the first decade of the twentieth century.

programme.title: DUCK SOUP — Interstitial
programme.desc: The Marx Brothers set their anarchic satire in the fictional nation of Freedonia, where Rufus T. Firefly declares war for no reason at all. The film flopped in 1933 and was later recognized as one of the greatest comedies ever made.

programme.title: Duck Soup
programme.desc: The bankrupt nation of Freedonia appoints the insufferable Rufus T. Firefly as its leader, and he promptly declares war on neighboring Sylvania for no good reason. It is the most dangerous comedy ever made, and in 1933 nobody wanted it. The Marx Brothers at their most anarchic — a film so corrosive to authority that Mussolini personally banned it in Italy because he thought it was about him. The Brothers were ecstatic. The project went through four titles before release. Paramount, riding high on Horse Feathers (their biggest hit of 1932), wanted a quick follow-up. The first treatment was called "Oo La La," set in a mythical kingdom. Ernst Lubitsch was briefly attached to direct. By October 1932 it became "Firecrackers," then "Cracked Ice" by December, then briefly "Grasshoppers" ("because animal stories are so popular," the studio explained). On May 11, 1933, the brothers' father Sam "Frenchie" Marx died in Los Angeles. A week later, the contract dispute with Paramount was settled and Leo McCarey signed on to direct. He named the picture after an old Laurel and Hardy short he'd directed in 1927, continuing the animal-title tradition. "Duck soup" was 1930s slang for something easy. When asked what the title meant, Groucho said: "Take two turkeys, one goose, four cabbages, but no duck, and mix them together. After one taste, you'll duck soup for the rest of your life." The uncredited producer was Herman J. Mankiewicz — six years before he'd write Citizen Kane. Many of the best gags were recycled from "Flywheel, Shyster, and Flywheel," Groucho and Chico's 1932 radio show written by Nat Perrin and Arthur Sheekman, who got an "additional dialogue" credit. Groucho's character was originally "Rufus T. Firestone." The ambassador was "Ambassador Frankenstein of Amnesia." Zeppo's part was written as Firefly's son, not his secretary. Harpo's name in the pressbook was "Brownie," not Pinky. The mirror scene — Harpo, dressed as Groucho, pretending to be his reflection in a missing mirror — is the most famous sequence in the film, and McCarey revived it from the brothers' old vaudeville act. The gag traces back through Max Linder's "Seven Years Bad Luck" (1921) and Harold Lloyd's "The Marathon" (1919) to Chaplin's "The Floorwalker" (1916). Harpo and Groucho's timing is so precise that when they swap positions mid-scene, you genuinely lose track of which is the reflection. Harpo later reprised it with Lucille Ball on "I Love Lucy," both in his fright wig and trench coat. The battle sequence has been called "the funniest of all of cinema." Firefly wears a different costume in every shot — Union, Confederate, British palace guard, Boy Scout Scoutmaster, Davy Crockett coonskin cap — while the building itself keeps changing from bunker to fort between cuts. Pinky carries a sandwich board reading "Join the Army and see the Navy." When Chicolini volunteers Pinky to carry a message through enemy lines, Firefly tells him: "And remember, while you're out there risking life and limb through shot and shell, we'll be in here thinking what a sucker you are." Thomas Doherty wrote that this single line sums up the entire Great War cynicism toward patriotism. The war production number features "All God's Chillun Got Guns" — a parody of the spiritual — and at one point Groucho mutters "and that's why darkies were born," a reference to a popular song of the era. When Universal released the DVD, columnist Marilyn Beck reported the racial material would be edited out. It wasn't. Breaking all convention, neither Harpo's harp nor Chico's piano gets a solo — the only Marx Brothers film where this is true. Harpo pretends to play harp on a piano's strings instead. Disney sued Paramount for using "Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf" without permission, and won. Zeppo's last film with the brothers — he retired from acting after this. Margaret Dumont, whom Groucho called "practically the fifth Marx Brother," absorbs abuse with the regal obliviousness that made her perhaps the greatest straight woman in cinema history. The film was a commercial disappointment in the depths of the Depression. Irving Thalberg told the brothers the problem was "no story and nothing to root for — you can't root for the Marx Brothers because they're a bunch of zany kooks." He convinced them to add love stories to future films. When critics asked Groucho about the film's political significance, he shrugged: "What significance? We were just four Jews trying to get a laugh." But he corresponded with T.S. Eliot, Antonin Artaud, and Salvador Dalí — all of whom praised the brothers' work — so he was at least aware of the readings. Danel Griffin argues it belongs beside Chaplin's Great Dictator and Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove, "only slightly more unnerving in that Duck Soup doesn't seem to realize it is anything more than innocent fluff." The film was rediscovered by 1960s college students and the counterculture. Harold Bloom called its ending one of the greatest works of American art of the twentieth century. In Woody Allen's "Hannah and Her Sisters," a chance screening of Duck Soup convinces Allen's character that life is worth living. The Beatles cited it as a major influence on "Help!" Animaniacs spoofed it as "King Yakko." The residents of Fredonia, New York, wrote to the Marx Brothers protesting that the film would hurt their town's reputation. The brothers replied: "Change the name of your town. It is hurting our picture." National Film Registry, 1990. AFI's 5th funniest film of all time.

programme.title: A FUNNY SHAVE — Interstitial
programme.desc: A barber’s tools take on a life of their own, powered by substitution tricks and playful object animation.

programme.title: A Funny Shave
programme.desc:
A man settles in front of his bedroom mirror to lather up and shave. Each time he raises his razor, the reflection looking back at him has changed: a leering, white-maned face, a wild-eyed grey head in spectacles, a pink, big-eared goblin mask baring its teeth. He recoils, gestures his fright straight at the camera, tries again, and gets another monstrosity for his trouble. Pathé's own trademark rooster stamps the Spanish-market title card, "La Barba Rebelde" ("The Rebellious Beard"), under which the film also circulated — the English release title on this print is "A Funny Shave."
The film is the work of Segundo de Chomón, a Spanish filmmaker who came up through Pathé's Barcelona operation hand-coloring prints alongside his wife, the actress Julienne Mathieu, before relocating to Paris around 1905 to work as a trick-film specialist under the Pathé banner. The gag here runs on the same substitution splice Méliès had popularized — stop the camera, swap what's in front of it, resume — but de Chomón shoots tighter and closer on the mirror than Méliès typically bothered to, so the switched faces read as a magic trick played directly on the audience rather than a staged tableau viewed from the stalls.
De Chomón spent these Pathé years mastering the stencil-and-hand-tint coloring process the company would market internationally as Pathécolor, work that shows here in the warm tinting applied to the substituted mask faces against the otherwise cooler-toned bedroom set. He would go on to far more elaborate fantasy shorts for Pathé — using the same substitution tricks in more sustained arrangements — before his stop-motion work in Turin and, at the end of his career, camera work on Abel Gance's Napoléon (1927).
Sources disagree on the exact year of release, with some archival listings giving 1905 and others 1906; the print here carries the later date.

programme.title: THE SCARLET PIMPERNEL — Interstitial
programme.desc: During the Reign of Terror, a seemingly foppish English aristocrat leads a secret double life rescuing French nobles from the guillotine. Leslie Howard’s dual performance made this the original superhero story decades before Batman.

programme.title: The Scarlet Pimpernel
programme.desc: Sir Percy Blakeney is the richest fool in England — a preening dandy who cares about nothing but his clothes and the cut of his cravat. He is also the Scarlet Pimpernel, the masked rescuer who smuggles French aristocrats out from under Robespierre's guillotine. Not even his wife Marguerite knows. The genius of the story is the double life: a hero who hides behind incompetence. A man so committed to the performance of stupidity that his own wife holds him in contempt. This was the first superhero. Stan Lee, who created Spider-Man and the X-Men, said so explicitly: "The Scarlet Pimpernel was the first superhero I had read about, the first character who could be called a superhero." The dual identity — the aristocratic fop who is secretly the daring avenger — directly spawned Zorro (1919), the Shadow (1930), the Green Hornet (1936), Batman (1939), and Superman (1938). Every masked hero in popular culture descends from a Hungarian baroness standing on a London Underground platform in 1903. Baroness Emmuska Orczy — born Emma Magdalena Rozalia Maria Jozefa Barbara Orczy de Orci in Tarnaors, Hungary, 1865 — was the daughter of a baron who was also a composer and conductor. Her family fled their estate when she was three, afraid of a peasant uprising. They moved through Budapest, Brussels, and Paris before settling in London when she was fourteen. She studied art, married an English illustrator named Montagu Barstow, and was desperately poor. She conceived the Scarlet Pimpernel while waiting for a train. She wrote the novel in five weeks. It was rejected by twelve publishers. While the rejection letters piled up, her husband co-wrote the stage play, which opened at the New Theatre in the West End on January 5, 1905, starring Fred Terry. It ran for four years and over 2,000 performances. The publishers changed their minds. Alexander Korda, the Hungarian-born producer who was building the British film industry single-handedly, chose to adapt it. Korda was born in a town not far from the Orczy family estate — two Hungarians separated by decades and class, reunited in England through the same story. He first offered the role to Charles Laughton, fresh from The Private Life of Henry VIII. The public erupted — the pug-nosed Laughton as the suave Sir Percy? Korda recast with Leslie Howard. The original American director, Rowland Brown, was directing the period piece like a gangster film.
