Raymond Massey (who played the villain Chauvelin) witnessed the confrontation: "Brown announced he would direct the way he liked or walk out. Alex said very sweetly, 'Please walk.'" Brown was left unemployed and stranded in England. Harold Young replaced him. Howard's performance — languid, effete, suddenly dangerous — became the definitive Pimpernel and the template for every secret-identity hero who followed. Then the story bled into reality. In 1941, Howard directed and starred in "Pimpernel" Smith, transplanting the plot to pre-war Germany — a Cambridge archaeologist secretly rescuing concentration camp prisoners. Goebbels was furious. The film directly inspired Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who saved tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews from the Nazi death camps in Budapest during the last months of the war. And then Leslie Howard was killed. On June 1, 1943, BOAC Flight 777, a civilian DC-3 flying from Lisbon to Bristol, was shot down over the Bay of Biscay by eight Luftwaffe Junkers Ju-88s. All seventeen passengers and crew were killed. Howard was aboard. The Luftwaffe targeted a clearly marked civilian aircraft. The reason has never been definitively established — theories range from a mistaken belief that Winston Churchill was on the plane to targeted retaliation against Howard for his anti-Nazi propaganda work. The man who played the hero who rescued innocents from state terror was murdered by the state he had spent his career opposing. He was 50 years old. The Scarlet Pimpernel — the character — lives in every superhero comic, every masked vigilante, every secret identity. The Scarlet Pimpernel — the man who played him — died for the role.

programme.title: THE MERRY FROLICS OF SATAN — Interstitial
programme.desc: One of Méliès’ most ambitious films, culminating in a wild ride through space in a skeleton‑horse carriage.

programme.title: The Merry Frolics Of Satan
programme.desc:
An engineer named William Crackford and his servant John are visited by an old man who leads them to his master, the alchemist Alcofrisbas — Satan himself, played by Georges Méliès. Alcofrisbas supplies magic pills that grant instant wishes when thrown to the ground, and Crackford unwittingly signs away his soul to get them. The pills set off a chain of transformations: the Crackford household is converted into a train for a round-the-world journey, the travelers pass a disastrous night at a devil-run inn, and their coach is ultimately hitched to a horse that turns inside-out into a rearing skeleton. Satan drives the skeletal team up the slope of an erupting volcano and the carriage is blasted into the heavens, sailing past a ringed planet, a comet, and a man-in-the-moon on its way to a fiery, infernal finale.
Méliès built the film from his own recent stage work rather than starting fresh. In 1905 the producer Victor de Cottens had commissioned him to supply film inserts for a Théâtre du Châtelet revival of "Les Pilules du diable," a féerie dating to an 1839 premiere at the same house; Méliès contributed a sequence called "The Space Trip," which he folded into this picture along with the magic-pill device from the original play. To sidestep a rival stage update of the same material that had opened in 1905 under the title "Les Quatre Cents Coups du diable," Méliès altered his own film's French title to "Les Quat'Cents Farces du diable" — same pun, different noun, no infringement.
The production leaned harder on stagecraft than on camera trickery: trapdoors, rolling and hinged backdrops, pyrotechnic flashes, and a large scale model volcano Méliès had already built and filmed once before, for his 1902 actuality "The Eruption of Mount Pelée." Onto that stage machinery he layered his usual battery of substitution splices and multiple exposures, so that the coach horse's mid-shot transformation into a skeleton reads as a single unbroken action. Star Film catalogued the finished picture as a "grande pièce fantastique en 35 tableaux," numbers 849 through 870 in its listings — a scale of production, in tableaux and in expense, that placed it among the largest Méliès ever mounted.
The surviving print carries the elaborate stencil hand-coloring typical of Star Film's prestige releases, applied frame by frame by the coloring house Méliès contracted in Paris; the volcano's reds and oranges and the gold of the transforming carriage are original to that process rather than a later tinting pass. A hand-colored restoration was issued by film preservationist David Shepard in 2008 and is the version in wide circulation today. Along with "A Trip to the Moon," the film represents the summit of Méliès's studio-bound fantastical style before the French cinema industry's shift toward narrative realism and location shooting left his brand of théâtre filmé behind.

programme.title: HUMOROUS PHASES OF FUNNY FACES — Interstitial
programme.desc: Often credited as the first animated film. Blackton’s chalkboard drawings come alive and transform on screen.

programme.title: Humorous Phases of Funny Faces
programme.desc:
A hand enters the frame and chalks two profiles onto a blackboard — a bald, bespectacled man and a woman with an elaborate pile of hair — and then the drawings begin to move on their own: the man puffs a cigar, blowing a ring of smoke into the woman's face; her hair unspools and coils into a spiral before the two faces turn to bicker in profile. The board is wiped clean and redrawn several times over, closing with a chalk "Professor" figure in a conical cap who juggles, cracks a whip, and puts a dog through a hoop. It is a vaudeville chalk-talk transplanted onto film stock: static gag drawings, exposed one frame at a time, that appear to animate themselves once the artist's hand withdraws.
The film was made by James Stuart Blackton, an English-born former newspaper illustrator who had worked in the U.S. as a "lightning sketch" performer — a vaudeville turn in which a cartoonist produced rapid comic drawings live before an audience while patter accompanied the pad. Blackton's own account was that a reporting assignment brought him to interview Thomas Edison in 1896; Edison turned the tables and filmed Blackton performing a lightning portrait of him, on the spot, in the Black Maria studio. The encounter left Blackton with a print of the resulting film and a Vitascope projector, which he and his vaudeville partner Albert E. Smith used to tour the act — the beginning of the Vitagraph Company of America, which the two founded in 1897 and built into one of the major studios of the silent era.
Blackton had already put chalk drawings in motion once before, in The Enchanted Drawing (copyrighted 1900), a single-shot novelty in which he appeared to pull objects out of a drawn face. Humorous Phases of Funny Faces, copyrighted by Vitagraph on April 6, 1906, goes further: after the opening title card and a few seconds of the artist's hand at work, the drawings carry on by themselves, redrawing and erasing without a visible hand — achieved by stopping the camera between single-frame exposures and altering the chalk lines (and, for some passages, jointed paper cutouts) a fraction at a time before resuming. That technique — single-frame exposure used to fake continuous motion in a drawing with no artist visibly present — is why film historians generally credit the film as the earliest surviving animated film shot on standard picture stock, a claim usually offered with the caveat that "animation" existed already in other media and that Blackton's own prior film had dabbled in the same trick on a smaller scale.
The film's success is credited with helping establish trick and cartoon films as a viable studio product rather than a novelty aside, feeding directly into the wave of American character animation that followed within the decade, from Winsor McCay's Little Nemo and Gertie the Dinosaur onward. Blackton himself went on to a long career as a Vitagraph director and producer before the studio's sale to Warner Bros. in 1925; the chalk-talk film, only a few minutes long and never intended as more than a supporting reel, survives as the point historians point to when dating the start of American theatrical animation.

programme.title: TOPPER — Interstitial
programme.desc: A reckless socialite couple dies in a car crash and returns as ghosts to liberate their buttoned-up banker friend. Roland Young earned an Oscar nomination, and the invisible special effects were groundbreaking for 1937.

programme.title: Topper
programme.desc: Hal Roach had spent decades producing comedy shorts — Laurel and Hardy, Our Gang — and wanted to break into features. He found his property in Thorne Smith's risqué 1926 novel about a pair of charming ghosts who haunt their stiff banker friend into having fun. Smith specialized in sexy comic fantasies that Depression-era readers devoured; he died in 1934 and never saw Hollywood touch his work. Roach wanted W. C. Fields for Topper and Jean Harlow as the female lead. Fields turned it down. Harlow was dying. Roach pivoted to Cary Grant, who was freelancing and skeptical — he worried the supernatural elements wouldn't work. Roach pitched it as a screwball comedy and offered $50,000. Grant signed as a one-picture deal to justify the salary demands he was making to Columbia and RKO. Constance Bennett was so impressed with the material she agreed to work below her usual $40,000 fee. The opening shot tells you everything: Bennett dozing in a gorgeous streamline Deco roadster while Grant sits on the back of the car, driving with his feet, both in rumpled evening clothes from an all-nighter. On the way to a Wall Street board meeting, they stop for more cocktails and sing "Old Man Moon" with Hoagy Carmichael at the piano — his first screen appearance. Then Grant crashes the car, and they're ghosts. Roy Seawright, Roach's resident effects man, handled the invisibility gags with split screens, wire work, and stop-motion animation. The results were groundbreaking for 1937 and still play. Roland Young's physical performance — talking to nobody, riding in a driverless car, being drunkenly carried through a hotel lobby by invisible hands — earned him his only Academy Award nomination. Young is the whole movie's center of gravity: every scene of spectral chaos lands because his bewilderment is so precise and so dignified. Billie Burke is the perfectly horrible wife. Eugene Pallette is the baffled hotel detective. Hedda Hopper — the gossip columnist herself — plays a snooty neighbor. A nineteen-year-old Lana Turner appears uncredited as a nightclub patron. The Kerbys' car was a custom body built on a 1936 Buick Roadmaster chassis by Bohman and Schwartz, designed to resemble a Cord or Duesenberg, with non-functional supercharger exhaust pipes. The trunk had hidden compartments for camera equipment. After filming, the Gilmore Oil Company bought it for promotions. It was the biggest hit of the summer of 1937, grossing $2 million in domestic rentals against a $500,000 budget. Grant stepped directly from this into The Awful Truth, Bringing Up Baby, and Holiday — the run that made him Cary Grant. Bennett got the best notices of her career. It spawned two sequels and a television series. In 1985 it became the first black-and-white film to be digitally colorized — Roach's studio chose it because it represented their entry into major feature production, and they wanted it on the cutting edge again.

programme.title: DREAM OF A RAREBIT FIEND — Interstitial
programme.desc: A man eats too much Welsh rarebit and his bed flies over the city. Edison's trick-film answer to Méliès, from the Winsor McCay comic strip.

programme.title: Dream of a Rarebit Fiend
programme.desc:
By early 1906 Winsor McCay's newspaper feature Dream of the Rarebit Fiend, which had been running in the New York Evening Telegram since September 1904, was popular enough that its basic joke needed no introduction: a different unlucky soul each week overeats Welsh rarebit — melted cheese sauce over toast, a dish widely blamed at the time for giving diners nightmares — and suffers a lurid, escalating dream before waking with a jolt in the final panel. Edwin S. Porter, the Edison Manufacturing Company's leading director and the man behind The Great Train Robbery three years earlier, adapted the strip's premise for the screen with Wallace McCutcheon, the two sharing directing credit on the resulting film, which Edison catalogued and released in February 1906. There is no documented evidence that McCay himself worked on the production; Edison licensed the idea and the title, not McCay's labor.
The film opens on a diner, played by the stage actor Jack Brawn (billed in Edison's own catalog as John P. Brawn), gorging himself on rarebit and beer at a restaurant table crowded with chafing dishes and bottles. Turned out into the night, he weaves down the street, wraps himself around a lamppost that seems to spin and buckle under him, and is walked home to bed by a companion. What follows is the dream proper: his bedroom furniture comes alive and marches off on its own, and a swarm of pitchfork-wielding imps climbs out of a hovering chafing dish to torment him in bed. The bed itself then breaks loose from the room, sails out through the window, and flies over a miniature nighttime cityscape with the sleeper still clinging to it, before he is pitched off, comes down astride a weathervane atop a church spire, and is finally shaken awake in his own bed, the ordeal revealed as a dream.
Edison's own promotional copy at the time claimed the picture contained photographic effects "never before attempted," and on the technical side that was not far off. Porter built the sequence from in-camera double exposure — the imps and the animated furniture layered over the live-action bedroom plate — combined with miniature sets for the aerial flight over the city and a rotating or tilted camera setup to sell the drunk's spinning point of view at the lamppost. It was an ambitious escalation of the trick-film vocabulary Porter and Georges Méliès had each been developing since the turn of the century, applied for the first time to an American newspaper property rather than an original scenario, and it anticipated by two decades the idea that a popular comic strip could be a ready-made source for a motion picture. Edison's sales figures bore out the gamble: the film reportedly sold around 192 prints in 1906, making it one of the company's strongest sellers of the year during the nickelodeon boom.
The print gathered here runs the film's original single reel straight through in black and white, matching Edison's release; there is no tinting, hand-coloring, or added live-action prologue on this transfer, and the surviving elements show the expected wear of a century-plus-old negative rather than any credited modern restoration. McCay would return to the same dream-logic material himself a few years later as an animator, and the imagery here — a man borne bodily out a window and over a sleeping city, his nightclothes betraying him at every turn — reappears, refined and self-drawn, in his own Winsor McCay/Little Nemo cartoons and in the character's later screen revivals. The Library of Congress selected Dream of a Rarebit Fiend for the National Film Registry in 2015, citing its historical and aesthetic significance as an early landmark of trick photography and one of the first true adaptations of a comic strip to film.

programme.title: BRINGING UP BABY — Interstitial
programme.desc: A mild-mannered paleontologist is derailed by a scatterbrained heiress and her pet leopard. Howard Hawks pushed screwball comedy to maximum speed; audiences in 1938 didn’t know what hit them.

programme.title: Bringing Up Baby
programme.desc: Howard Hawks read a short story by Hagar Wilde in Collier's Weekly in April 1937 and it made him laugh out loud. RKO bought the screen rights for $1,004. The story had no dinosaur, no intercostal clavicle, no museum — just a woman, her brother's pet panther, and a man she dragged to Connecticut. Wilde and screenwriter Dudley Nichols built a 202-page script around it, falling in love during the process and co-writing the Astaire-Rogers film Carefree a few months later. The script was written specifically for Hepburn. Hawks initially wanted Harold Lloyd for the male lead. Producer Pandro Berman rejected Lloyd and Ronald Colman, then offered the role to Robert Montgomery, Fredric March, and Ray Milland — all turned it down. Hawks's friend Howard Hughes finally suggested Cary Grant, who had just finished The Awful Truth and was hesitant about playing an intellectual. Hawks promised to coach him and told him to study Harold Lloyd films. Grant took two weeks to accept, but his manager used the casting to renegotiate his contract from $50,000 to $75,000 per picture. They couldn't find a panther that would cooperate, so Baby became a leopard — a trained animal named Nissa who had worked eight years in B-movies. Nissa's trainer Olga Celeste stood just off camera with a whip during every scene. When Hepburn spun around and her skirt twirled, Nissa lunged at her; Celeste cracked the whip just in time. Hepburn was unafraid and wore heavy perfume to keep the cat calm. Grant was terrified. Most of his scenes with Nissa are close-ups with a stand-in. Hepburn tormented him by throwing a toy leopard through the roof of his dressing room. Hepburn struggled early with comedy — she overacted, tried too hard to be funny. Hawks brought in Walter Catlett, a vaudeville veteran, to coach her. Catlett acted out scenes with Grant for Hepburn, showing her that the comedy worked when he played it straight. Hepburn understood immediately, played herself for the rest of the shoot, and was so grateful she insisted Catlett play Constable Slocum. Grant and Hepburn ad-libbed constantly and delayed production with uncontrollable laughing fits. The scene where Grant frantically asks about his bone was shot from ten in the morning until after four because neither could keep a straight face. The gag of the dog burying a dinosaur bone was borrowed from the comic strip Professor Dinglehoofer and His Dog — RKO paid King Features $1,000 for the idea. Grant's famous ad-lib — "Because I just went gay all of a sudden!" while wearing a woman's negligee — was not in the script. The original line had him stammering about how he doesn't usually wear one of these. Whether Grant meant "gay" in its modern sense or its older one has been debated for decades; Vito Russo argued in The Celluloid Closet that people in Grant's Hollywood circles certainly knew the slang. Hawks went twelve days on the jail scene instead of five, shut down production to attend a horse race, and came in forty days behind schedule and $330,000 over budget. Final cost: $1,096,796.23. Hepburn's salary doubled from $72,500 to $122,000. Grant's from $75,000 to $123,000. Hawks's from $88,000 to $203,000. The film broke even on first run and was branded a failure. Hepburn had already been declared "box office poison" by Harry Brandt of the Independent Theatre Owners of America. She bought out her RKO contract for $22,000. Hawks was released from his deal. He later said the film had "a great fault — there were no normal people in it." But it grew. Television in the 1950s found it. The Cahiers du Cinéma critics championed it in the 1960s. A. O. Scott called it astonishing after sixty-five years. Leonard Maltin named it "the definitive screwball comedy." Stanley Cavell placed it in a tradition running from ancient Rome through Shakespeare. AFI ranked it the fourteenth funniest American film ever made. 97% on Rotten Tomatoes. National Film Registry, 1990. The fastest, most anarchic screwball comedy ever made, and it cost someone their career to make it.

programme.title: THE EASTER EGGS — Interstitial
programme.desc: Eggs transform into dancers and fantastical figures—an early showcase of Chomón’s stencil‑color mastery.

programme.title: The Easter Eggs
programme.desc:
A woman in an ornate, flower-hung proscenium — playing a sorceress or fairy figure rather than any character with a name — receives a succession of oversized eggs, seemingly from nowhere. She sets each on a low table and opens it, and each yields a tiny costumed dancer who performs a brief turn before the frame; the last eggs give up not dancers but infants, cradled and held up to close the act. A card reading "Fin" ends the film. The whole of it plays out inside a single decorated set built to look like a miniature stage-within-the-stage, the woman controlling the illusion from just outside its border.
The film is the work of Segundo de Chomón, a Spanish-born filmmaker who by 1907 was one of Pathé Frères' most valued trick-film directors, working out of the company's Vincennes studios in a rivalry of technique, if not of temperament, with Georges Méliès. Chomón had come to filmmaking through his wife, the actress Julienne Mathieu, who worked in Parisian special-effects and coloring workshops before introducing him to the trade; she appears here, as she does in a great many of his Pathé shorts from this period, both acting before the camera and contributing to the effects work behind it. The scale tricks that let the eggs disgorge miniature performers rely on split-screen and superimposition techniques Chomón used across his output of these years, executed with a steadiness that period critics and later historians alike have singled out as cleaner than Méliès's own, more visibly unsteady mattes.
The color on the print is not an afterthought but the point of the production. Chomón was concurrently in charge of Pathé's stencil-coloring atelier, the department that hand-tinted release prints frame by frame through cut stencils — a process the company would soon patent and market as Pathéchrome. Easter Eggs was made as a showcase for that process as much as for any trick photography: the gold proscenium, the woman's costume, and the small dancers are all built around bands of color meant to be laid in by the stencil line rather than left to a tinting bath, and the surviving prints carry that hand-applied color rather than a uniform dye.
Pathé's own records place the film's Paris premiere at the Omnia Pathé cinema on 25 July 1907, with a Lyon booking at the Pathé Grolée following on 9 August of that year — an ordinary release pattern for a Pathé short of the period, distributed as one title among the firm's frequent slate of trick and féerie films timed to the spring holiday it depicts. Beyond that commercial life, the film has no larger claim on history than any other of Chomón's numerous Pathé shorts from these years; its interest for historians rests specifically in the stencil coloring and in Chomón's continuing experiments with the scale and superimposition tricks that would culminate, a few years later, in more ambitious work such as El Hotel Eléctrico.

programme.title: HIS GIRL FRIDAY — Interstitial
programme.desc: The dialogue averages 240 words per minute—nearly three times normal speech. Hawks gender‑swapped the play The Front Page after hearing a woman read one of the male roles. Rosalind Russell secretly hired a writer to punch up her lines.

programme.title: His Girl Friday
programme.desc:
Ace reporter Hildy Johnson walks into the newsroom of the Morning Post to tell her editor — and ex-husband — Walter Burns that she's quitting the paper to marry a nice, dull insurance man named Bruce Baldwin. Walter has no intention of letting either thing happen. A condemned man is about to be executed, the mayor is corrupt, the story is enormous, and Walter knows Hildy can't resist a scoop any more than she can resist him.
The film is Howard Hawks's reworking of The Front Page, the 1928 newspaper play by Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur. Hawks hit on his transformation almost by accident: reading the play aloud at a party with a woman taking one of the male roles, he realised the crackling banter between editor and reporter worked even better as a romance. He had Hildy Johnson rewritten as a woman and Charles Lederer adapt the script. The other innovation was the sound. Hawks wanted dialogue that overlapped the way real speech does, and with his sound crew worked out how to record several voices at once — the actors talk over one another, step on lines, and ad-lib at a clip of roughly 240 words a minute, nearly three times the era's norm. It is often called the first film to use overlapping dialogue by design, and the technique influenced filmmakers for generations.
Hawks's licence to improvise produced the film's best backstage story: Rosalind Russell, certain Cary Grant had been handed the better lines, secretly hired her own writer — through her brother-in-law — to punch up Hildy's dialogue. Hawks never noticed; Grant did, and took to greeting her each morning with "What have you got today?" Grant slipped in a private joke of his own, too: Walter, describing how he would deal with a man, says he is the sort who would end up like one "Archie Leach" who cut his throat — Archie Leach being Grant's own real name. Ralph Bellamy plays the hapless fiancé Bruce, the decent bore no screwball heroine ever actually marries. The film opened in January 1940 and has only grown in stature — routinely named the definitive screwball comedy — and, because Columbia never renewed the copyright, it long ago passed into the public domain, which is why it circulates so freely today.

programme.title: THE ENCHANTED POND — Interstitial
programme.desc: A fairy‑tale tableau built on hand‑colored effects and trick‑film choreography at Chomón’s peak.

programme.title: The Enchanted Pond
programme.desc:
At the edge of a woodland pond, a woman comes to draw water and finds the place is not what it seems. Figures appear and vanish behind a stretched cloth and in bursts of splash, naiads and satyrs surfacing and dissolving around her as the pond itself begins to bubble and steam. The trick work is built from the simplest materials available outdoors — a hung sheet for a cutaway substitution, timed dousing for the appearance gags, smoke pots for the vapor over the water — cut together so the transformations read as continuous and unbroken.
The film was directed by Segundo de Chomón for Pathé Frères, credited on the surviving print as "Fantasmagorie de Mr Secondo de Chomon." Chomón had come up through Pathé's Barcelona operation as a hand-colorist before being brought to Paris in 1905, where Charles Pathé backed him as an in-house answer to Georges Méliès's Star Film trick pictures. What set L'Étang enchanté apart from most of that house style, Méliès's included, is that it was shot outdoors on natural water rather than built on a studio stage — the pond, the tree line, and the daylight are all real, and the trick effects had to be staged against them rather than painted around them.
The cast is built around Julienne Mathieu, Chomón's wife, who plays the central figure at the pond. Mathieu had worked in the French film industry before Chomón did — for Pathé and, earlier, for Méliès's own company — and by most accounts it was she who drew him into pictures in the first place after his military service. Beyond acting in dozens of his films between 1907 and 1909, she is credited with contributing to his scripts and to the special-effects work, and with introducing him to the Pathécolor stencil process that tints prints like this one.
The surviving print carries that Pathécolor treatment: the image throughout is toned a uniform green, consistent with contemporary Pathé stencil and dye-tinting practice for outdoor and fantastical subjects. The film was originally issued at roughly 60 meters, running about a minute and a half; what survives and circulates today is a Pathé-Baby reduction print — the abridged home-projection format Pathé sold for domestic 9.5mm viewing beginning in the 1920s — identifiable by the Pathé-Baby rooster trademark that closes the reel. The full original negative is presumed lost; only this later, shorter home-market edition is known to survive.

programme.title: FANTASMAGORIE — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first fully animated cartoon: 700 drawings of a stick figure morphing through surreal transformations.

programme.title: Fantasmagorie
programme.desc:
A hand enters the frame and sketches a ringmaster figure on a sheet of paper; from that first mark the drawing comes loose from its maker and begins to move on its own. What follows is a continuous chain of transformations: a clownish little man — Cohl's recurring character Fantoche — wanders through a world where every object is unstable, changing from a wine bottle to a flower to an elephant, from a window to a spinning wheel, with no scene held for more than a few seconds before it dissolves into the next. There is no plot in the ordinary sense, only the logic of one drawing metamorphosing into another, which is itself the film's subject.
Fantasmagorie was made by Émile Cohl (born Emile Eugène Jean Louis Courtet), a veteran caricaturist and member of the Paris Incohérents circle who came to the Gaumont film company around 1908 already in his fifties. Working from a background in newspaper cartooning rather than photography, Cohl drew roughly 700 individual images on paper, tracing each new position from the last on a light box and photographing them one at a time. The finished negative was printed in reverse, turning his black pencil lines on white paper into white lines racing across a black field — the "blackboard" look the film is known for, achieved entirely as a printing effect rather than by drawing on slate. Some prints, including scans made from a 16mm source held by Gaumont, show this negative image tinted rather than pure black-and-white.
Gaumont released the film in Paris on 17 August 1908. It is widely credited by animation historians as the first fully hand-drawn animated cartoon, predating the wider adoption of drawn animation as a commercial form by several years, and Fantoche is generally cited as the medium's first recurring animated character, reappearing in Cohl's subsequent films for Gaumont. The film's method — continuous, unmotivated metamorphosis rather than a fixed set of characters acting out a story — set a template that Cohl himself repeated through more than a decade of subsequent shorts and that later animators would return to as one of animation's foundational tricks.

programme.title: THE THIEF OF BAGDAD — Interstitial
programme.desc: This Technicolor fantasy was made by six directors across three countries as war closed studios around them. Its special effects—flying carpet, genie, mechanical horse—won the Academy Award and influenced fantasy cinema for decades.

programme.title: The Thief of Bagdad
programme.desc: Abu is a boy thief in Baghdad. Ahmad is the deposed king, blinded by the sorcerer Jaffar. Together they flee, fall in love (Ahmad with a princess), get separated by magic, and find their way back through a genie in a bottle, a magic carpet, and an all-seeing eye. Abu kills Jaffar with a magic crossbow and flies off on the carpet, alarmed by Ahmad's plan to educate him. It is the most purely joyful adventure film ever made. Roger Ebert put it in his Great Movies list and said it was "on a level with The Wizard of Oz." It has a perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes. It premiered at Radio City Music Hall on December 5, 1940, and Bosley Crowther wrote that it "ranks next to Fantasia as the most beguiling and wondrous film of this troubled season." The film invented the bluescreen. Lawrence Butler created the first proper chroma key process for the special effects — the traveling matte technique that would become the foundation of all visual effects compositing for the next eighty years. It won three Academy Awards: Cinematography, Art Direction, and Special Effects. It was the first British film ever nominated for Original Score. Disney's Aladdin (1992) is essentially this film redrawn. The villain Jafar is named after Conrad Veidt's character, who is himself named after the historical vizier Ja'far ibn Yahya. The Sultan's obsession with toys is lifted directly. The thieving monkey Abu is named after Sabu's character. Jordan Mechner cited this film as a primary inspiration for the Prince of Persia games. The production was chaos. Alexander Korda, the Hungarian producer who had made The Scarlet Pimpernel, hired German director Ludwig Berger, then undermined him by secretly bringing in Michael Powell to shoot scenes behind Berger's back. Korda installed a rival composer, Miklos Rozsa, in the office next to Berger's with a piano. Berger was "persuaded to walk away." American director Tim Whelan was brought in to augment Powell. Then war broke out in September 1939 and Powell was pulled off to make propaganda films. Korda ran out of money and moved the entire production to Hollywood in the spring of 1940, where his brothers Zoltan and Vincent took over along with William Cameron Menzies. The heroes were filmed in the Grand Canyon, Monument Valley, Bryce Canyon, and the Painted Desert. Sabu had grown three inches in the year since filming began and had to reshoot scenes. Six directors worked on the film. It should have been a disaster. Instead it was perfect. Conrad Veidt, who played Jaffar, was one of the great silent film stars of Germany — Cesare in The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, the disfigured man in The Man Who Laughs whose permanent rictus grin became the visual template for Batman's Joker. When the Nazis took power in 1933 and imposed a racial questionnaire on the film industry requiring everyone to declare their race, Veidt — who was not Jewish — wrote "Jude" (Jew). His wife Ilona Prager was Jewish. He was told he could keep working in Germany if he divorced her and declared support for the regime. He refused. Goebbels declared he would never work in Germany again. The British government had to intervene diplomatically to get Veidt out of the country after he was placed under house arrest. In England and then Hollywood, his contract stipulated that if he played a Nazi, the character must be a villain. His last great role was Major Strasser in Casablanca — the man who played the most elegant villain in Arabian fantasy also played the most elegant villain in wartime drama. He noted the irony: he was praised "for portraying the kind of character who had forced him to leave his home country." Before leaving Britain for America, Veidt and Ilona donated their life savings to the British government to help finance the war. He died of a heart attack on a golf course in Los Angeles in 1943, at fifty years old. He was the highest-paid member of the Casablanca cast. Sabu was discovered at thirteen by documentary filmmaker Robert Flaherty in Mysore, India, where his father was a mahout — an elephant keeper. Flaherty cast him in Elephant Boy (1937) and Korda adopted him as a star. He became "Britain's first above-the-title film star of Indian origin." After The Thief of Bagdad, Sabu became an American citizen in 1944 and immediately enlisted. He served as a tail gunner and ball-turret gunner on B-24 Liberators with the 370th Bombardment Squadron in the Pacific, flying dozens of combat missions. He was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for valor. The boy who played the thief who flew on a magic carpet went to war in a bomber. His career declined after the war. Hollywood didn't know what to do with an Indian actor. He was denied a work permit for a film in India and never appeared in a movie made in his native country. In 1952 he was performing with an elephant act in a circus. He died of a heart attack in 1963 at thirty-nine. John Prine wrote a song about him: "Hey look, Ma, here comes the elephant boy / Bundled all up in his corduroy / Headed down south towards Illinois / From the jungles of East St. Paul." The Criterion Collection released the film with a commentary track by Martin Scorsese and Francis Ford Coppola, recorded separately and edited together — two of the greatest directors in history, talking over each other about a film made by six directors that somehow turned out to be one of the most beautiful things ever put on screen.

programme.title: THE ACROBATIC FLY — Interstitial
programme.desc: A fly juggles a matchstick, a dumbbell, and another fly. Smith's microscope cinematography showed audiences a world no one had ever seen moving.

programme.title: The Acrobatic Fly
programme.desc:
F. Percy Smith was a clerk at the Board of Education whose spare-time hobby was photographing insects and plants through a microscope. A photograph he took of a bluebottle's tongue caught the attention of Charles Urban, the American-born producer who had built a business in Britain filming scientific and travel subjects under his Kineto brand. Urban lent Smith a camera and, in 1908, the result was The Balancing Bluebottle, a short built entirely around a fly tethered in place and made, through patient trial and the fly's own instinctive grip-and-brace reflexes, to appear to juggle a cork, a blade of grass, and a miniature dumb-bell. Smith re-edited and reissued the footage in 1910 under the title The Acrobatic Fly, and a further variant, close to identical but longer, followed in 1911 as The Strength and Agility of Insects. All three drew on the same home-laboratory methods Smith would use for the rest of his career: adapting microscope optics to a cine camera, working alone or with his wife Kate and their collaborator Phyllis Bolté, and relying on painstaking preparation rather than any camera trick to make the ordinary look extraordinary.
The film's premise plays as vaudeville rather than biology lecture. A fly, held fast at a fixed point, is presented with small objects — a stick, a ball, and finally what reads as a tiny trapeze or chair — and appears through sheer strength and balance to manipulate and mount them, with a second fly joining for the closing gag atop the ball. Smith first demonstrated the underlying technique to the Royal Photographic Society in November 1908, establishing to a skeptical audience that the effect was achieved practically, with no insects harmed, before Urban's outfit put it before the public. The magnification of a housefly's minute movements into a legible comic performance was, at the time, effectively unprecedented outside the still photograph, and the film is now cited as an early landmark of micro-cinematography — using the camera not to record a story but to make visible a scale of action the naked eye could not otherwise follow.
Smith's arrangement with Urban's company became full-time in 1910, the same year this reissue appeared, beginning a partnership in nature and scientific filmmaking that would run for decades and eventually produce Smith's better-known time-lapse work, including The Birth of a Flower. The Acrobatic Fly and its companion titles are held by the BFI National Archive, which has made the film available directly through its own channels for modern viewing; the print carries no color, no spoken or intertitle language beyond the original English main title, and shows the wear typical of a surviving 35mm negative of its age, without any added tinting visible in this transfer.

programme.title: CITIZEN KANE — Interstitial
programme.desc: Orson Welles was twenty‑five and had never made a film. Cinematographer Gregg Toland volunteered to work with someone who didn’t know the rules; they built sets with ceilings and shot from floor trenches. William Randolph Hearst tried to destroy every print.

programme.title: Citizen Kane
programme.desc: Orson Welles was twenty-five years old and had never made a film. RKO gave him a contract unprecedented in Hollywood history: develop his own story, cast his own actors, crew his own production, and retain final cut. No studio executive could see footage until Welles chose to show it. No cuts without his approval. The deal was so resented in the industry that the Hollywood press mocked RKO for months. Welles called the movie studio "the greatest electric train set a boy ever had." His first project, Heart of Darkness shot entirely in first person, collapsed when he couldn't trim $50,000 from the budget. A political thriller stalled next. Then he and screenwriter Herman Mankiewicz — who had been writing Mercury radio scripts and who hated William Randolph Hearst after being exiled from his social circle — began arguing, inventing, discarding, thrashing toward Kane. Mankiewicz wrote a draft under John Houseman's supervision on 300 pages of Welles's notes. Welles drastically condensed and rearranged it, added scenes of his own. Mankiewicz's contract stipulated no credit; when the film neared release he threatened full-page trade paper ads and an exposé in the Saturday Evening Post. Welles himself circled Mankiewicz's name on the guild form and drew an arrow putting it first. The official credit reads "Screenplay by Herman J. Mankiewicz and Orson Welles." The argument over authorship lasted decades — Pauline Kael's 50,000-word essay "Raising Kane" in 1971 damaged Welles's reputation, but later scholarship by Robert Carringer, reviewing all seven drafts still intact at RKO, concluded that "Welles's contribution was not only substantial but definitive." Cinematographer Gregg Toland — "just then, the number-one cameraman in the world" — walked into Welles's office and said "I want you to use me on your picture." He'd seen the Mercury stage productions and wanted to work with someone who didn't know the rules. Together they invented deep focus photography where foreground and background are both razor sharp, something no Hollywood camera had achieved. They built sets with ceilings — unheard of, because that's where the lights went — so they could shoot from floor level. They cut holes in the concrete floor to get the camera even lower. Welles learned filmmaking by watching John Ford's Stagecoach forty times, often with a different department head, asking "How was this done? Why was this done?" His entire cast was new to motion pictures. He brought the Mercury Theatre company — Joseph Cotten, Agnes Moorehead, Everett Sloane, Ray Collins — none of whom had acted on screen. Dorothy Comingore was recommended by Charlie Chaplin. To start filming without executive interference, Welles began on a Saturday morning when few would be around, labeling everything "Orson Welles Tests" on the paperwork. The first "test" was the projection room scene, shot for $809 against a budget of $528 — "one of the most famous scenes in movie history." When executives showed up unannounced, the entire cast and crew would start playing softball until they left. Welles worked sixteen to eighteen hours a day, starting at 4 AM for the special effects makeup that aged him. The contact lenses to make him look elderly were so painful a doctor had to place them. He badly cut his wrist shooting the scene where Kane destroys Susan's bedroom. He fell ten feet during the Gettys staircase scene, chipping two ankle bones, and directed from a wheelchair for two weeks before strapping on a steel brace to resume acting — it's visible in the low-angle shot after the election. For the final scene, the Rosebud sled was burned in a working furnace on a Selznick stage. On the ninth take, the Culver City Fire Department arrived in full gear because the flue had caught fire. "Orson was delighted with the commotion." Bernard Herrmann was given twelve weeks for the score — most Hollywood composers got two or three. He composed complete musical pieces for the montages and Welles edited scenes to match their length. Robert Wise, roughly Welles's age, edited the film; he and Mark Robson both became successful directors. Hearst tried to have every print destroyed. He prohibited any mention of the film in his newspapers. RKO couldn't get theaters to book it. Budget: $839,727. It lost money on first run. It lost Best Picture to How Green Was My Valley. Won only Best Original Screenplay. Then it grew. French critics championed it. André Bazin wrote that "even if Welles did not invent the cinematic devices, one should credit him with the invention of their meaning." D.W. Griffith said "I loved Citizen Kane and particularly loved the ideas he took from me." For forty consecutive years — five decennial polls — it stood at number one in Sight and Sound's greatest films list. AFI No. 1 in 1998 and 2007. National Film Registry, 1989. When asked where the confidence came from to make something so radical, Welles answered: "Ignorance. Sheer ignorance. There's no confidence to equal it."

programme.title: FALLING LEAVES — Interstitial
programme.desc: Told her sister will die when the last leaf falls, little Trixie ties the leaves to the trees. From cinema's first woman director.

programme.title: Falling Leaves
programme.desc:
Little Trixie Thompson overhears the family doctor tell her parents that her older sister Winifred, gravely ill with consumption, will die when the last leaf falls from the tree outside her window. Taking the warning literally, Trixie slips into the garden after dark with a spool of string and ties the fallen leaves back onto the bare branches, determined to hold off autumn itself. A passing doctor, Earl Headley, finds her at this task, learns what she is trying to do, and, once he sees Winifred, treats her with an experimental serum of his own devising. The leaves stay tied; Winifred recovers.
The picture is a loose, considerably softened adaptation of O. Henry's 1907 short story "The Last Leaf," in which an old painter saves a dying woman by forging a leaf on the wall outside her window, at the cost of his own life to pneumonia. Alice Guy-Blaché, credited on some prints simply as director and on others as director-scenarist, kept the central conceit — a leaf standing between a sick woman and death — but replaced O. Henry's fatal irony with a child's earnestness and a happy ending secured by medicine rather than art. Sets were designed by Henri Ménessier, who had worked with Guy-Blaché since her days at Gaumont in Paris. Magda Foy, billed by Solax as "The Solax Kid," plays Trixie; Marian Swayne plays Winifred; Mace Greenleaf plays Dr. Headley.
Guy-Blaché had directed what is generally regarded as the first narrative fiction film, La Fée aux Choux (The Cabbage Fairy), in 1896, while running the production side of Gaumont in Paris — making her, by most film-historical accounts, the first woman to direct a film and, for roughly a decade afterward, the only one working anywhere. In 1910 she and her husband Herbert Blaché formed the Solax Company in Flushing, New York, with Alice as president — the first woman to found and head her own film studio. Falling Leaves was released March 15, 1912, from Solax's Flushing plant, shortly before the company's move to a larger, purpose-built studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey. Guy-Blaché directed and produced hundreds of films for Solax and earlier at Gaumont; only a small fraction are known to survive.
A print is held by the Library of Congress, and the film circulates today in more than one form: a black-and-white release with piano accompaniment and a tinted release with orchestral scoring have both been issued on home video. This file appears untinted, with English-language intertitles bearing the Solax sunburst logo and the studio's own credit line ("Falling Leaves, Solax 135-3"); the surviving elements show the scratches and softened contrast typical of an early-surviving public-domain print, but the image remains clean enough to follow Guy-Blaché's staging in depth, particularly in the multi-plane interior compositions of the sickroom scenes.

programme.title: CASABLANCA — Interstitial
programme.desc: Made during the actual war, the ending wasn’t even decided on set. Ingrid Bergman was told to play it both ways. The airport is a painted backdrop with a cardboard airplane and midget extras forced in perspective.

programme.title: Casablanca
programme.desc: Warner Bros. story analyst Stephen Karnot read an unproduced play called Everybody Comes to Rick's and called it "sophisticated hokum." Story editor Irene Diamond convinced producer Hal B. Wallis to buy it for $20,000 — the most anyone in Hollywood had ever paid for an unproduced play. The original was written by Murray Burnett, inspired by a trip he and his wife took through Europe in 1938. In Vienna shortly after the Anschluss they saw antisemitism firsthand. In the south of France they found a nightclub full of exiles and refugees, with a Black pianist — the prototype of Sam. Twins Julius and Philip Epstein were assigned to the screenplay but left to work on Frank Capra's Why We Fight series. Howard Koch filled in, producing thirty to forty pages. The Epsteins returned after a month and were reassigned; Koch's pages were not used. The three writers were never in the same room at the same time. The Epsteins were paid $30,416; Koch got $4,200. Casey Robinson did three uncredited weeks of rewrites, contributing every scene where Rick and Ilsa meet in the café. Nobody knew the ending. They were shooting in sequence because only the first half of the script was ready when filming began on May 25, 1942. Casey Robinson wrote to Wallis that the ending was "set up for a swell twist when Rick sends her away on the plane with Laszlo. For now, in doing so, he is not just solving a love triangle. He is forcing the girl to live up to the idealism of her nature." Ingrid Bergman asked Michael Curtiz which man her character was really in love with. He told her to play it both ways. Julius Epstein said he and Philip were driving when they simultaneously came up with "Round up the usual suspects," after which the entire resolution fell into place, including the farewell and "a suddenly noble Bogart." The last line — "Louis, I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship" — was chosen by Wallis from a telegram on August 7 and dubbed by Bogart a month after shooting ended. "Here's looking at you, kid" was not in any draft; Bogart said it to Bergman while she played poker between takes with her English coach. The airport finale used a cardboard cutout Lockheed Electra with little person extras to force the perspective, shrouded in fog to hide the fakery. The entire picture was shot on Warner Bros. soundstages in Burbank except for close-ups of the plane at Van Nuys Airport. Bergman was two inches taller than Bogart; Curtiz had him stand on blocks. Arthur Edeson, who had shot The Maltese Falcon and Frankenstein, photographed Bergman mainly from her preferred left side with a softening gauze filter and catch lights to make her eyes sparkle. Dooley Wilson was a drummer, not a pianist — he mimed the keyboard while Jean Plummer played off-screen, but his singing voice is his own. Max Steiner wanted to replace "As Time Goes By" with an original composition, but Bergman had already cut her hair for For Whom the Bell Tolls and couldn't reshoot, so Steiner wove the song through the entire score as a leitmotif alongside "La Marseillaise." The duel of the anthems was originally meant to pit "La Marseillaise" against the "Horst-Wessel-Lied," but that was still under copyright in non-Allied countries, so "Die Wacht am Rhein" was substituted. During the filming of that sequence, a witness saw many of the extras crying and "realized that they were all real refugees." Of the credited cast, only three were born in America. Conrad Veidt, who played Major Strasser, was a refugee German actor who had fled the Nazis with his Jewish wife; he was the highest-paid member of the cast and died shortly after the film's release. Marcel Dalio, who played the croupier, had been a star in French cinema — La Grande Illusion, La Règle du Jeu — before fleeing with his wife Madeleine Lebeau, who played Yvonne. Lebeau was the last surviving cast member, dying in 2016. Budget: $1,039,000. Shot in less than three months. Rushed into release on November 26, 1942, to capitalize on the Allied invasion of North Africa. Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay. Roger Ebert: "If there is ever a time when they decide that some movies should be spelled with an upper-case M, Casablanca should be voted first." 99% on Rotten Tomatoes. 100 on Metacritic — a perfect score. AFI No. 3 all-time. No. 1 on AFI's list of great screen passions. Six lines in the AFI top 100 quotes — more than any other film. The Writers Guild voted it the greatest screenplay ever written. National Film Registry, 1989. Julius Epstein: "More corn than in the states of Kansas and Iowa combined. But when corn works, there's nothing better."

programme.title: THE INSECTS' CHRISTMAS — Interstitial
programme.desc: A tiny Father Christmas climbs down from the tree to celebrate with the beetles and frogs of the forest — stop-motion puppetry from its first master.

programme.title: The Insects' Christmas
programme.desc:
A Father Christmas ornament climbs down from a tinsel-hung tree, makes his way into the winter forest, and dresses a small fir there with lights and gifts for the creatures who live among the snow. Beetles, grasshoppers and their neighbors accept the invitation, gather at the tree, and see out the night skating and playing in the snow before the toy climbs back to its place. It is a slight, gentle scenario, closer to a nursery pantomime than to the domestic comedies Starevich was also making in these years, and its charm rests entirely on the puppetry rather than on plot incident.
The director was Władysław Starewicz (Ladislas Starevich in most Western catalogues), a Polish naturalist working in the Russian film industry. His stop-motion technique had begun almost by accident three years earlier: as a museum curator in Kaunas making documentary shorts on Lucanus cervus, the stag beetle, he found the insects went inert under studio lighting and could not be filmed fighting from life. He rigged dead specimens with wire-jointed legs and animated their combat frame by frame instead, producing The Battle of the Stag Beetles (1910) and, in short order, the first puppet film with an actual plot, The Beautiful Leukanida (1912). Aleksandr Khanzhonkov, the Moscow producer who released Leukanida, brought Starevich onto his studio's payroll, and it was for Khanzhonkov's Trading House that The Insects' Christmas was made and released.
Sourcing on this title is thinner than on Starevich's better-known insect comedies, and the record is not perfectly settled. English-language filmographies and film databases catalogue the picture as a 1913 Russian release running roughly seven minutes; a cluster of Russian-language sources instead dates the Khanzhonkov premiere to December 31, 1912, and gives a shorter runtime nearer five minutes, which may reflect a different surviving cut or simply projection-speed variance common to hand-cranked silent material — this print runs 7 minutes at its transfer speed. The film should not be confused with Starevich's other, unrelated 1913 Christmas subject, a much longer live-action adaptation of Gogol's "The Night Before Christmas."
This copy carries Polish intertitles rather than the original Russian cards — "Boże Narodzenie w Lesie" ("Christmas in the Forest"), crediting "Scenariusz i reżyseria: Władysław Starewicz, Moskwa 1913" — indicating a later Polish-market or archival reissue rather than a first-run print. The image is uniformly cyan-toned throughout in the manner used for silent-era night exteriors, and the film carries a modern, non-original recorded score (excerpts of Vivaldi's "Winter" and Pachelbel's Canon) synchronized for this transfer, confirming it is a later restoration or compilation reissue rather than a raw nitrate scan.

programme.title: KID AUTO RACES AT VENICE — Interstitial
programme.desc: The Little Tramp's first appearance on any screen: Chaplin, in a costume assembled that morning, ruins a newsreel crew's day by refusing to get out of the shot.

programme.title: Kid Auto Races at Venice
programme.desc:
Keystone shot this split-reel farce on location at the second annual junior "pushmobile" race in Venice, California, on Sunday, January 11, 1914, folding a comedy into an actual public event rather than staging one on a lot. Henry Lehrman directed and plays the newsreel cameraman on-site to film the race; Chaplin plays the interloper who keeps wandering into his shot. There is almost no plot beyond that premise and almost no editing: a fictional cameraman films a real crowd watching a real race, while Chaplin mugs, preens, and gets shoved out of frame, only to wander back in. Much of the crowd was not in on the joke — spectators can be seen glancing at the camera and at Chaplin with open curiosity rather than playing along, which is precisely what made the film a novelty: it captured, unrehearsed, the public's first sight of a character it did not yet have a name for.
That distinction matters and is worth stating precisely. Chaplin had already assembled the tramp costume a few days earlier on the Mabel's Strange Predicament set, where Mack Sennett had told him to find "a comedy makeup, anything will do" — Chaplin came back in a small derby, a cane, a tight coat, baggy trousers, and shoes several sizes too large, worn on the wrong feet for the splayed walk. Mabel's Strange Predicament was filmed first but held for release; Kid Auto Races at Venice was shot afterward, cut quickly, and rushed out first, on February 7, 1914, two days ahead of it. So the character was born on one set and introduced to the public on another: Kid Auto Races is the Tramp's first appearance before an audience, not his first time in front of a camera. Keystone's own publicity later dressed up the costume's origin as a grab-bag of borrowed wardrobe — Fatty Arbuckle's trousers, Chester Conklin's tiny coat, Ford Sterling's oversized shoes are the names usually attached to the story — but the specific attributions come from studio promotion rather than a verified fitting-room account, so they are best treated as color rather than settled fact; the broader point, that the outfit was improvised on the spot from whatever the wardrobe department had lying around, is not in dispute.
The film survives only in worn dupe prints struck down through decades of 16mm reduction and public-domain reissue, which is the source of the scratches, contrast loss, and jumpy splices visible in most circulating copies, including this one; no tinting is present, and being a 1914 actuality-style one-reeler it carries no intertitles beyond the opening Keystone credit card, so what plays out is close to what a 1914 nickelodeon audience saw. No original release score is known to survive; accompaniment on modern prints is a later addition, not a period one. Contemporary trade notice was enthusiastic out of proportion to the film's simplicity — The Cinema called it "about the funniest film we have ever seen" — and it was reissued around 1918 on a states-rights basis as The Pest once Chaplin's fame had grown. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 2020, citing it as the first public sighting of the most recognized character in film history.

programme.title: THE RED SHOES — Interstitial
programme.desc: A ballerina is torn between love and an impresario who demands total devotion to dance. The 17‑minute Ballet of the Red Shoes sequence is one of cinema’s great Technicolor set pieces.

programme.title: The Red Shoes
programme.desc: Victoria Page wants to dance. Boris Lermontov wants to own the greatest ballet company in the world. Julian Craster wants to compose. Lermontov asks Vicky the question that defines the film: "Why do you want to dance?" She answers: "Why do you want to live?" He hires her on the spot. When she falls in love with Julian, Lermontov forces a choice: the ballet or the man. She chooses the man. It destroys all three of them. Vicky runs from her dressing room in the red shoes and throws herself in front of a train. As she dies, she whispers to Julian: "Take off the red shoes." Lermontov walks onto the stage and tells the audience: "Miss Page is unable to dance tonight — nor indeed any other night." The company performs The Ballet of the Red Shoes with a spotlight on the empty space where she would have been. Michael Powell conceived the film in the 1930s with producer Alexander Korda as a vehicle for Merle Oberon, but Oberon couldn't dance, and the project was shelved for a decade. When Powell and his partner Emeric Pressburger finally made it, they decided on dancers who could act rather than actors who could dance. They recruited from the Royal Ballet. Moira Shearer, a Scottish ballerina who was just beginning to ascend at Sadler's Wells, was recommended by Robert Helpmann. She said no. She fought for a year to avoid the film. "Red Shoes was the last thing I wanted to do. I fought for a year to get away from that film, and I couldn't shake the director off." She was right to worry — the film made her the most famous ballerina in the world and she spent the rest of her career trying to be taken seriously as a dancer again rather than a movie star. Ninette de Valois, her director at Sadler's Wells, finally told her to just do it. Boris Lermontov was based on Sergei Diaghilev, the impresario who founded the Ballets Russes. The specific moment was Diaghilev seeing fourteen-year-old Diana Gould partnering Frederick Ashton in the premiere of his first ballet and inviting her to join his company — he died before it could happen. The cinematographer was Jack Cardiff, who may be the greatest color photographer in the history of cinema. Cardiff was born in 1914 to vaudeville parents, was a child film star by age four, and was a camera assistant by fourteen. When a German cinematographer shouted "Hey you!" and told the boy to rotate a lens between two pencil marks on command, Cardiff asked afterward what he'd done. "You followed focus, sonny." When he interviewed for a job learning Technicolor, the interviewers asked technical questions about polarizing light and film negatives. Cardiff told them they were wasting their time talking to him. Shocked silence. How did he hope to become a cinematographer? "I told them I studied the works of painters — Vermeer, the Old Masters, and the Impressionists. I could also describe and match how the light fell in a subway, in my house, or on the street at night." They asked about a face in a Rembrandt painting. He said the light was on the right side. He got the job. He shot travelogues on top of Mount Vesuvius during a volcanic eruption — lava burned the tripod and their shoes, one crew member was hospitalized, and the film was magnificent. He spent six months in a lifeboat filming a documentary about the Merchant Navy during WWII. For The Red Shoes, a giant 300-amp water-cooled arc spotlight was custom-built by Mole-Richardson and Taylor Hobson specifically for the ballet sequence. Cardiff won the Oscar for Black Narcissus the year before; Natalie Kalmus, the daughter of Technicolor's inventor, was asked to name the best color film ever made and answered without hesitation: The Red Shoes. The seventeen-minute ballet at the center of the film was choreographed by Robert Helpmann. It uses dissolves, superimpositions, and special effects that were unprecedented — a swirling newspaper transforms into a dancer, the conductor's face melts into the impresario's, the stage floor becomes an ocean. Art director Hein Heckroth said: "When the girl is dancing, she feels she is a bird, a flower, a cloud." Gene Kelly saw it and the ballet sequence in An American in Paris (1951) was a direct response. Michael Powell said the film is "about dying for art, that art is worth dying for." But film scholar Adrienne McLean saw something darker: Vicky "seems pushed by those she loves who would rather possess her than support her." When A Chorus Line was created in the early 1970s, dancer after dancer cited The Red Shoes as the reason they became dancers. Marvin Hamlisch paid homage to it in "At the Ballet" and "What I Did for Love." The film was the first British production to gross over $5 million in American theatrical rentals. Martin Scorsese saw it as a child and it changed his life. He championed Powell's entire body of work, married Powell's editor Thelma Schoonmaker, and when Powell died in 1990, Scorsese spearheaded the restoration of The Red Shoes from the original three-strip Technicolor nitrate negatives through the Film Foundation and UCLA Film Archive. The restored version screened at Cannes in 2009. It directly influenced Darren Aronofsky's Black Swan. It was voted the ninth greatest British film ever made by the BFI and fifth by Time Out. Powell himself left a bank clerk job to join Rex Ingram's production unit in Nice, France — the same pattern as Nilsson, as Juster, as so many: the bank job, then the art.

programme.title: THE TANTALIZING FLY — Interstitial
programme.desc: Koko the Clown climbs out of a real inkwell and battles a real fly for control of the drawing board. The rotoscope era begins.

programme.title: The Tantalizing Fly
programme.desc:
The Tantalizing Fly is an early entry in Max Fleischer's Out of the Inkwell series, made for J. R. Bray's studio and released in the fall of 1919 — by most accounts the second Inkwell short to reach audiences, distributed as part of the Goldwyn-Bray Pictograph program rather than as a stand-alone release. The premise is the one the series would run for years: Fleischer, seated at his drawing board, is needled by a live fly that keeps landing on his paper and his hand. When he swats at it he misses the fly and strikes his own drawing instead, and the clown he is inking stirs to life on the page. The clown then tries his own hand at the problem, sketching a bald, seated figure as a helper against the fly, with no better luck — the blows keep landing on the wrong target. It is a slight premise stretched over a few minutes, but the film is really an advertisement for a piece of hardware: the collision of a real insect, a real hand, and a hand-drawn figure occupying the same frame, sold as one continuous space.
That illusion was the rotoscope, which Fleischer had patented a few years earlier and was still proving out commercially in these Bray one-reelers. Live-action film was projected frame by frame onto a glass-covered easel and traced by hand, giving the animated figure the weight and timing of a photographed performer rather than the rubbery bounce of drawn-from-scratch cartooning of the period. The character being traced was modeled on Fleischer's younger brother Dave, a former Coney Island clown who performed the movements in costume for the camera; the drawn figure built from that footage is the character now generally known as Koko the Clown, though the name itself is a later addition to the series — animator Dick Huemer is credited with formally christening the character in the mid-1920s, well after this short was made. In 1919 the figure on screen is simply "the clown," an unnamed proof of concept for a new way of putting a cartoon and a person in the same shot.
The Bray Studios production this print carries in its titles is the outfit run by pioneering animation producer J. R. Bray, whose company employed and distributed several of the era's key animators — Fleischer among them — before Max and Dave struck out on their own a couple of years later as Out of the Inkwell Films and, later, Fleischer Studios. The Tantalizing Fly is a small document of that Bray-era apprenticeship: the hybrid live-action/animation format, the rotoscope as a selling point rather than a mature house style, and a title-card credit that spells the director's name "Fleicher," a misprint on the card itself rather than an error in this description.
The surviving print carries the usual wear of a hand-processed 1919 negative — scratches, speckling, and contrast that shifts a little scene to scene — and no restoration credit appears on screen; digital copies in circulation, including this one, run a little under four minutes, close to contemporary catalog listings of roughly three and a half to four minutes for the film. Intertitles are in English throughout, and the print shows no tinting.

programme.title: THE TEN COMMANDMENTS — Interstitial
programme.desc: DeMille was seventy‑three and suffered a heart attack mid‑production, returning to set the next morning. For the Red Sea, they poured 300,000 gallons into a tank and ran the footage backward—then composited it with location plates.

programme.title: The Ten Commandments
programme.desc: Cecil B. DeMille was seventy-three years old and had been making movies since 1913 — silents, hand-cranked through the camera. For twenty years after the war, letters arrived from around the world asking him to remake his 1923 silent Ten Commandments. The studio hesitated. One Paramount executive asked, "You won't call it The Ten Commandments, of course." Adolph Zukor leapt from his chair and made clear there would be no other title. DeMille sailed for Egypt on September 23, 1954. Near Cairo, between Saqqara and the Giza pyramids, his crew built the Per-Rameses gate — 107 feet high, 325 feet long, the biggest exterior set ever constructed for a motion picture, costing a quarter million dollars alone. Behind it: a mess tent, wardrobe department, horse stables. He met Nasser. He had tablets of the Ten Commandments hewn from actual Mount Sinai granite, inscribed in ancient Canaanite letters by Dr. Ralph Marcus of the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute. He cast Charlton Heston as Moses because Heston resembled Michelangelo's sculpture in Rome. Heston's three-month-old son Fraser played the infant Moses in the basket — Henry Wilcoxon's suggestion the moment Heston announced his wife was pregnant. Heston also voiced God at the Burning Bush, toned to a softer register. DeMille saw Yul Brynner in The King and I on Broadway. During intermission, he went backstage, told Brynner the story from Rameses' point of view, and offered him the role. Brynner: "It all happened in seven and a half minutes." He wanted Audrey Hepburn for Nefretiri but her figure wasn't curvaceous enough for the form-fitting Egyptian gowns. Edward G. Robinson had been blacklisted. Someone suggested him for Dathan but thought he couldn't be hired. DeMille coldly reviewed the matter, felt Robinson had been done an injustice, and cast him anyway. Robinson later wrote: "Cecil B. DeMille returned me to films. Cecil B. DeMille restored my self-respect." Yvonne De Carlo's brown contact lenses kept popping out. DeMille let her keep her natural gray eyes, calling them "a God-given treasure." During production, DeMille suffered a massive heart attack. His doctor ordered two weeks flat on his back in an oxygen tent. He was back on set three days later. John P. Fulton spent months on the Red Sea sequence — Paramount built a huge tank split by a U-shaped trough, into which 360,000 gallons of water were released from the sides, then the footage was printed in reverse. They composited it with location footage shot at the actual Red Sea, added animation, matte paintings, and pyrotechnics. It won the film's only Oscar. Henry Noerdlinger, the researcher, consulted Philo, Josephus, the Midrash Rabbah, and Eusebius, studying 950 books, 984 periodicals, and 2,964 photographs. Four screenwriters worked for three years. Five costume designers planned 25,000 costumes; 125 tailors took over a year to make them. 70,000 props. Seven casting directors hired 53 star and featured roles, 488 speaking parts, and 100 dancers. Shot in VistaVision, Technicolor. Elmer Bernstein's score. Anne Bauchens' editing — she'd been cutting DeMille's films since 1918. The most expensive film ever made at the time. Highest-grossing film of 1956. It has aired annually on American network television during Passover and Easter since 1973 — the longest-running annual broadcast of a single film in television history. Selected for the National Film Registry in 1999. DeMille never directed another picture. He died in 1959.

programme.title: FELIX IN HOLLYWOOD — Interstitial
programme.desc: The first animation superstar goes to the studios and meets Chaplin, Keaton's hat, and the censor's scissors. Felix at the top of his fame.

programme.title: Felix in Hollywood
programme.desc:
Felix and his down-and-out owner are evicted for back rent and set out for Hollywood to make their fortune, Felix riding along disguised as a suitcase. Broke on arrival, Felix schemes his way into a shoe-store job — hawking gum to lure in customers — before wandering onto a studio lot billed as "Static Studio," where the picture turns from a road story into a walk through the industry's own gallery of faces. The cartoon threads Felix through caricatures of the era's biggest names: censor Will H. Hays turns up as a moon-headed office boss, Ben Turpin's crossed eyes and William S. Hart's cowboy stare get sight gags of their own, and Felix's own inside joke arrives when he apes Charlie Chaplin's walk — cane, waddle and all — only for the caricatured Chaplin to spin around and accuse him of "stealing my stuff."
The film was produced at Pat Sullivan's New York studio and released through M.J. Winkler on July 15, 1923, credited on-screen, as all Felix cartoons of the period were, to Pat Sullivan alone. The credit was not accurate. Sullivan ran the business side of the operation and, by his own later accounts and those of staffers who worked under him, contributed little to the day-to-day drawing; the cartoons were directed, written and largely animated by Otto Messmer, who had created the character for Sullivan's studio in 1919 and continued to shape Felix's stories and gags through the decade. Messmer only began receiving public credit for his authorship after Sullivan's death in 1933, when former colleagues — among them Sullivan's own attorney — corroborated his account. Animation historians, including John Canemaker, whose research forms the basis of the modern understanding of the studio's working methods, now credit Messmer as Felix's creator and the animating hand behind films like this one.
Felix in Hollywood arrived at the character's commercial peak. By the mid-1920s Felix was the most recognized cartoon star in the world, licensed onto toys, ceramics, songs and a Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade balloon years before Mickey Mouse existed, and this short trades directly on that fame, treating Felix as a celebrity roaming among celebrities rather than an anonymous gag figure. The joke lands because audiences of 1923 knew both Felix and the stars he was rubbing shoulders with; a Wikipedia-sourced anecdote has Chaplin himself telling Sullivan that Felix was his only rival, but that line cannot be traced to a citable primary source and is omitted here as unverified. The short was later voted one of the 50 Greatest Cartoons of all time in a 1994 poll of animators and historians conducted by Jerry Beck, the only Felix cartoon on the list.
The surviving print used here runs roughly 8 minutes at the file's transfer speed, against catalogued lengths of one reel (commonly listed near 9 minutes); silent-era cartoons were shot for hand-cranked or variable-speed projection, and small runtime differences between prints and modern digital transfers are expected rather than a sign of missing footage. The transfer is black-and-white with English-language intertitles and visible print wear consistent with a surviving theatrical or early-generation dupe rather than a fresh photochemical restoration.

programme.title: NORTH BY NORTHWEST — Interstitial
programme.desc: Hitchcock’s ultimate wrong‑man thriller sends Cary Grant from the United Nations to Mount Rushmore. It is equal parts espionage, comedy, and pure cinematic geometry.

programme.title: North by Northwest
programme.desc: Ernest Lehman wanted to write "the Hitchcock picture to end all Hitchcock pictures." He and Hitchcock had been assigned to adapt The Wreck of the Mary Deare for MGM, but after two weeks Lehman offered to quit — he couldn't crack it. Hitchcock told him they got along great and they'd just write something else. Lehman said he wanted to make the ultimate Hitchcock film. Hitchcock thought for a moment and said he'd always wanted to do a chase across Mount Rushmore. They brainstormed: a murder at the United Nations, a chase through a Detroit car plant, a showdown in Alaska. Then Hitchcock remembered something an American journalist named Otis Guernsey had told him — inspired by Operation Mincemeat, the wartime British scheme of planting false documents on a corpse — about spies creating a fictitious agent as a decoy. Perhaps their hero could be mistaken for this nonexistent man. They bought Guernsey's sixty-page treatment for $10,000. The tornado came from Hitchcock. The hero stranded in the middle of nowhere, and the villains send a cyclone to kill him. "But they're trying to kill him. How are they going to work up a cyclone?" Lehman said. Somewhere that afternoon the cyclone became the crop duster. The plane was a Naval Aircraft Factory N3N "Yellow Peril," a wartime Navy trainer converted for dusting, piloted by Bob Coe from Wasco, California. The "Indiana" highway was actually central California; Hitchcock placed replica square Indiana signs. Empire magazine voted it the greatest movie moment of all time. Cary Grant had been working with Hitchcock since Suspicion. MGM wanted Cyd Charisse for the female lead. Hitchcock insisted on Eva Marie Saint, whom he'd met at a dinner. Days later her mother reminded her that Hitchcock loved casting women in beige with white gloves. She wore exactly that to the next meeting. For Martin Landau, Hitchcock attended a Broadway play to watch Edward G. Robinson but was struck by the young unknown. He showed Landau the entire project — storyboards and all — then turned and said, "You're now Leonard." Hitchcock insisted on shooting in Paramount's VistaVision even though this was an MGM picture — the only other VistaVision film MGM ever made was High Society. Saul Bass designed the opening titles, the first extended use of kinetic typography in cinema. Bernard Herrmann composed the score. Robert Burks shot it. George Tomasini edited it. The U.N. sequence was filmed illicitly — after reviewing the script, the United Nations denied permission. After two failed attempts, Hitchcock had Grant pull up in a taxi right outside the General Assembly Building while a hidden camera crew filmed from across the plaza. Vandamm's mountaintop house was designed in the style of Frank Lloyd Wright by art director Robert Boyle — a cantilevered living room in limestone that never existed outside matte paintings and a Culver City soundstage. MGM wanted fifteen minutes cut to get the film under two hours. Hitchcock had his agent check the contract, found he had final cut, and refused. One line was redubbed: Eva Marie Saint originally said "I never make love on an empty stomach," which the censors changed to "I never discuss love on an empty stomach." The final shot — the train entering a tunnel after a romantic embrace — Hitchcock called "probably one of the most impudent shots I ever made." The title has no compass bearing. "Northwest by north" exists; "north by northwest" does not. Hitchcock told Peter Bogdanovich: "It's a fantasy. The whole film is epitomized in the title — there is no such thing as north-by-northwest on the compass." GQ convened a panel in 2006 and declared Grant's gray suit the greatest suit in film history. It has been called "the first James Bond film." The crop duster inspired the helicopter chase in From Russia with Love.
