When it discovers a toy piano marked "$1.98" and begins to play, the entire shop comes alive — dolls dance and sing, a marionette springs into motion, teddy bears make music. The revelry turns to chaos when the spider, still clutching a lit candle, lands in a box of fireworks. The ensuing explosion sends it fleeing back through the keyhole, preferring the snowstorm to the pyrotechnic pandemonium within. Originally announced for July 3 but postponed to August 16 due to the studio's ongoing production delays. Director Wilfred Jackson helmed the entry, with Walt Disney voicing the black doll and Marcellite Garner the spider. Motion Picture Herald (May 2, 1931) praised its "merit of lightness and general amusement" and predicted "the youngsters should enjoy it very much, and the oldsters will be entertained." The toy shop setting would echo in later Disney works, most notably Geppetto's workshop in Pinocchio (1939).

programme.title: Peculiar Penguins
programme.desc: Peculiar Penguins, directed by Wilfred Jackson, turns a courtship comedy into a survival chase as a shy penguin suitor competes for his mate and then fights to save her from a sea lion attack. Disney artists reportedly observed live penguins to capture group movement and behavior, which gives the film's crowd scenes a natural rhythm beneath the caricatured expressions. Leigh Harline's song "The Penguin Is a Very Funny Creature" sets a playful tone before the action tightens, and later critics have singled out the short's music-and-animation craft as stronger than most cute-animal shorts of the period. The result is an underrated mid-1930s Silly Symphony that balances observational animal study with romance, slapstick, and genuine peril in under ten minutes.

programme.title: Interjections!
programme.desc: "Interjections! Show excitement! Or emotion! They're generally set apart from a sentence by an exclamation point, or by a comma when the feeling's not as strong." A rapid-fire series of dramatic vignettes — a kid getting a shot, finding a dollar, being surprised at a party — each punctuated by interjections (Darn! Wow! Ouch! Hey!). The energy is relentless and perfectly captures what interjections actually do: interrupt the flow with raw feeling. Part of Grammar Rock. Performed with breathless enthusiasm by Essra Mohawk.

programme.title: Victory Vehicles
programme.desc:
Wartime gas rationing has eliminated the automobile, so the narrator demonstrates alternative transportation methods: roller skates, stilts, piggyback, pole-vaulting, a trained kangaroo, and ultimately the pogo stick — which the short proposes as America's definitive Victory Vehicle. Every citizen (all played by Goofy) bounces to work, to school, to church on pogo sticks while the narrator maintains that this is perfectly practical.
One of Disney's WWII home front shorts. By 1943, rubber and gasoline rationing had made civilian driving nearly impossible — "Victory Vehicles" was the government's actual term for car alternatives. Jack Kinney plays the absurdity straight, treating the pogo stick transportation network with the same earnest narrator authority as a genuine War Department information film. The satire only works because the format is indistinguishable from the real propaganda Disney was making next door. Released July 30, 1943 by RKO.

programme.title: Exercise and Health
programme.desc:
Three teenagers carry three different problems into the school gym: Ernie is run-down and out of shape, Jean is shy and withdrawn, Hal is tense and quick to snap. A physical-education instructor points all three toward the school's Acrobatics Club, and the film spends most of its ten minutes on the resulting workouts — spotted handstands and vaults off a partner's shoulders, tumbling on mats, chin-ups on a bar, badminton and archery out on the lawn. Two printed title cards carry the argument the pictures only illustrate: one notes that the sedentary worker, "bound by rules of business diplomacy," needs a physical outlet, and that the "pleasant tiredness" following exercise "promotes complete relaxation"; the other credits teamwork with building "balance and poise, along with skill, strength, and general physical fitness." By the last reel Ernie has traded the doctor's office for the tumbling mat, Jean is talking easily with the other girls on the archery line, and Hal has swapped his clenched jaw for a game of catch — three complaints answered by the same prescription of regular, cooperative exercise.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films, the picture opens with its only screen credit: educational collaborator Erwin F. Beyer of the Department of Physical Education at the University of Chicago, recorded on the RCA Sound System, with a copyright date of MCMXLIX (1949) under Coronet's founder David A. Smart. Coronet's house director Ted Peshak is credited with the film on Letterboxd and TMDB, consistent with his work on the studio's other social-guidance shorts of the period, though as with most Coronet one-reelers the on-screen credits name only the academic collaborator, not the director or cast.
The Prelinger Archives catalog summarizes the film in a single line — "How exercise will make you healthy and popular" — which is a fair, if blunter, restatement of the same argument the picture makes at length: that organized physical activity is a fix for the loosely related ailments of poor health, poor sociability, and poor nerves alike. It belongs to the same wave of postwar Coronet guidance shorts, tailored for physical-education classes rather than homeroom, and it survives today through Prelinger/Internet Archive prints rather than any particular later reputation of its own; no reliable cast credits have surfaced for Ernie, Jean, or Hal.

programme.title: Springtime
programme.desc: The third Silly Symphony, released five days before the 1929 stock market crash, and the first in a four-seasons cycle that would continue with Summer, Autumn, and Winter the following year. Directed by Ub Iwerks. Flowers, ladybugs, centipedes, birds, and frogs dance and devour each other to a medley of light classics — Grieg's "Morning Mood," Ponchielli's "Dance of the Hours," Offenbach's "Gaîté Parisienne." The centerpiece: a chain of frogs graduated in size swallow each other one by one until only the biggest remains, who is then swallowed by a long-legged bird so weighted down it flops into a pond and drowns. The Film Daily called it "a fine satire on the survival of the fittest in the animal world." Motion Picture News called it "A Panic." Variety praised the timing as so perfect that "the rhythm alone imparts rare entertainment value." The short later appeared on a television screen in 101 Dalmatians (1961).

programme.title: Who Killed Cock Robin?
programme.desc: The 54th Silly Symphony takes an 18th-century nursery rhyme and turns it into a celebrity courtroom spoof. Released June 29, 1935, David Hand stages a murder trial after Cock Robin collapses mid-serenade to Jenny Wren, with an owl judge, a fast-talking parrot prosecutor, and a lineup of rattled bird suspects. The short's real hook is caricature: Jenny Wren plays as a Mae West send-up, while other birds echo contemporary stars including Bing Crosby and a Harpo Marx-style cuckoo. Frank Churchill keeps the tempo brisk, and Disney pushed the title tune hard enough that bandleader Ben Bernie performed an expanded radio arrangement that summer. The ending flips the "murder" into a Cupid gag, but the short had a notable afterlife: Alfred Hitchcock used it in Sabotage (1936) to intensify the theater sequence. It was nominated for the Academy Award, losing to Disney's own Three Orphan Kittens.

programme.title: Three Blind Mousketeers
programme.desc: Released September 26, 1936, this short drops the nursery-rhyme mice into a Dumas-style swashbuckler and lets the animators stage pure action-comedy around blindness as both handicap and superpower. Captain Cat, backed by his feline guards, storms a Parisian courtyard and kidnaps a mouse maiden, only to meet three tiny musketeers who fight by sound, touch, and fearless momentum while shouting "all for one and one for all." Under David Hand, the film runs on escalating sight gags: capes and rapiers tangling in panic, cannon fire gone sideways, and a final firecracker launch that sends Captain Cat rocketing away in humiliation. Albert Hay Malotte's score keeps the pace clipped and theatrical, and the cartoon stands out in late-period Symphonies for replacing pastoral whimsy with brisk adventure choreography.

programme.title: Naughty Number Nine
programme.desc: A film noir-styled episode where the number nine is a pool-hustling troublemaker. "He was naughty number nine — he was a mean little dude." Teaches the nines times table and the finger trick (hold down the nth finger, the remaining fingers show the answer). The dark, smoky pool-hall animation is unlike anything else in the series. Part of Multiplication Rock. Sung by Grady Tate.

programme.title: Interplanet Janet
programme.desc: A girl named Janet zooms through the solar system visiting each planet in order. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto — the whole tour set to a disco beat. One of the most popular Science Rock episodes, both for its earworm melody and for the sheer joy of its space animation. Pluto was still a planet. Part of Science Rock. Performed by Lynn Ahrens.

programme.title: Family Life
programme.desc:
"Family Life" opens the way most Coronet council-of-family films do: with everybody a little frayed. The Miller household is a small chaos of overlapping errands — grocery bags fought over on the front step, a stalled car raising its hood in the driveway while father, mother, and their two teenagers crowd around it, a run out and back that solves nothing. Cut inside, and it's the mother who is left holding the kitchen together while the rest of the family goes its separate, quietly resentful ways. She decides the house needs running "like a business," and gathers everyone around the dinner table to lay out the plan on an actual placard: Guides to Home Management — Schedule, Responsibilities, Privileges, Finances. Chores get assigned (the daughter at the sink, the son drying and putting away), a weekly family council is scheduled to keep everyone honest, and by the last reel the Millers are eating together, laughing, and heading out the door as a unit — teenage son Harold, whose deadpan asides are the film's one real comic asset, getting the best lines along the way.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' Glenview, Illinois studio and copyrighted in 1949 to David A. Smart, the picture follows the house formula down to the credit block: the only person named on screen is the academic backing the script, here Florence M. King, M.S., Assistant Professor of Home Economics at the University of Illinois, billed as "Educational Collaborator." No director, writer, or performer receives a card — Coronet's postwar shorts routinely credited the consulting expert and nobody else, a practice meant to sell the film to school boards as sound applied psychology rather than as entertainment. The print carries the RCA Sound System mark seen on Coronet's 16mm classroom prints of the period and runs a lean nine minutes and forty-six seconds, per the Prelinger Archives' own cataloging of the surviving print.
"Family Life" belongs to the same wave of Coronet "systems" shorts that treated the household as a small enterprise to be managed with schedules and minutes, alongside titles like "Sharing Work at Home" and "Your Thrift Habits" — home economics extension thinking translated into 16mm melodrama for junior-high homerooms. It survives today through the Prelinger Archives and the Internet Archive, in the public domain like most of Coronet's late-1940s output, one of dozens of the studio's domestic-guidance shorts urging the same lesson: harmony at home is a matter of organization, not luck.

programme.title: Bugs in Love
programme.desc: The final black-and-white Silly Symphony, Bugs in Love turns discarded junk into an insect city where romance and slapstick share equal space. Bucky Bug and June Bug skate over a broken mirror and exchange handwritten love notes until a predatory crow crashes the courtship, trapping Bucky in a bottle and forcing the whole bug community into a miniature urban war. Production drafts show the short began as Bug Symphony around March 1932, while Disney's Sunday comic strip was simultaneously naming its little hero through a reader contest that landed on Bucky. The film and strip fed each other: Squire Cawker-style villainy, Junkville worldbuilding, and Bucky's popularity all spilled into later comics and eventually into Walt Disney's Comics and Stories runs through the 1940s. Historically, this is the line in the sand before the series went fully color, with old monochrome craftsmanship pushed to its limit just before Technicolor took over.

programme.title: The Cookie Carnival
programme.desc: Released May 25, 1935, The Cookie Carnival is Disney doing Cinderella as a confection parade, complete with beauty-pageant satire lifted from Atlantic City boardwalk culture. Ben Sharpsteen directs a world of marching pastries and vaudeville suitors until a hobo cookie refashions a ragged girl into the dazzling Miss Bon Bon, who is crowned queen and chooses her rescuer as king. The technical story sits under the sugar: animators including Grim Natwick, Bill Tytla, and a young Frank Thomas push subtler acting and fuller figure construction, especially as the heroine shifts from flat cookie design toward a more human silhouette. Historians often treat that transformation as one more step toward believable human animation before Snow White. Leigh Harline's score supports the pageant mood, including "The Sweetest One of All," while the short balances charm with period caricature that modern viewers read very differently.

programme.title: The Tale of Mr. Morton
programme.desc: A shy man named Mr. Morton has a crush on his neighbor Pearl. Each verse advances his love story while teaching subject-predicate sentence structure. Written and performed by Jack Sheldon. The last Grammar Rock episode, produced during the 1993 revival — twenty years after the original run. Gentler and more narrative than the 1970s episodes, telling a complete short story through grammar lessons. Mr. Morton gets the girl.

programme.title: Tax Man Max
programme.desc: Taxes — what they are, where they go, and why we pay them. Tax Man Max collects a portion of everything and uses it to build roads, fund schools, and run the government. A surprisingly even-handed explanation of taxation for kids, neither demonizing nor celebrating it. Part of Money Rock.

programme.title: Mickey Mouse - Steamboat Willie
programme.desc:
Steamboat Willie was not Mickey Mouse's first cartoon but his third: Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks had already animated Plane Crazy and The Gallopin' Gaucho as silent pictures earlier in 1928, only to find no distributor would take them. Sound was the gamble that changed that. Disney had heard Al Jolson in The Jazz Singer the year before and, cut off from the Alice Comedies and Oswald the Lucky Rabbit he had lost to Charles Mintz and Universal, staked what was left of his small studio on a synchronized-sound cartoon built around the new mouse character. The title and premise parody Buster Keaton's Steamboat Bill, Jr., released by United Artists that same year, though Willie's plot of a bullying riverboat captain, a stowaway mouse, and a deckhand's improvised barnyard orchestra owes little to Keaton beyond the name and the setting.
The film was animated largely by Iwerks himself, at a reported pace of hundreds of drawings a day, with assistance from Les Clark, Johnny Cannon, Dick Lundy and Wilfred Jackson, none of them credited on screen. Its claim to history rests on sound: Disney and his brother Roy financed a trip to New York to record a synchronized track using Pat Powers's Cinephone system, a variant of Lee de Forest's Phonofilm process that Powers controlled outside Western Electric and RCA's patent pools. Getting picture and soundtrack to line up was the hard problem, and it was Wilfred Jackson, an assistant animator whose mother had taught music, who proposed conducting the recording session to a metronome and drawing up a bar sheet mapping actions to beats — the direct ancestor of the animation exposure sheet and click track still used in the industry. Disney himself provided Mickey's falsetto voice and vocal effects, alongside Iwerks and other staff on the incidental sound; the soundtrack leans on two public-domain tunes, "Steamboat Bill" and "Turkey in the Straw," the latter the source of the mouse's famous pot-and-pan-and-livestock performance in the film's second half.
Steamboat Willie premiered on November 18, 1928, at the Colony Theatre on Broadway in New York, on a bill with a live-action feature, Gang War, playing the Colony's Western Electric sound system. Trade reviews, including in Variety and Film Daily, singled out the novelty and precision of the synchronization rather than the character himself, and the date has since been adopted by Disney as Mickey Mouse's official birthday. The film's success let Disney secure regular distribution and finally release the two shelved silent Mickey cartoons with added soundtracks; it also set off a scramble among rival studios, Fleischer and Van Beuren among them, to reverse-engineer Disney's synchronization method before Jackson's bar-sheet technique became common knowledge.
The short was among the first twenty-five films named to the Library of Congress National Film Registry in 1998, cited for its historical and aesthetic significance as the first cartoon released with a fully synchronized soundtrack recorded to match the action rather than played live or added as a rough afterthought. Its US copyright, held by Disney since 1928, expired on January 1, 2024, placing this earliest screen version of Mickey and Minnie Mouse — round-eyed, long-nosed, more rodent than the character Disney would later refine — into the American public domain, though Disney retains trademark rights over the character's use in commerce. This print carries no restoration or tinting; it is the plain black-and-white Cinephone release, title card and Copyright MCMXXVIII notice intact.

programme.title: Marriage Is a Partnership
programme.desc:
Dotty rides an eastbound train alone and lets her mind drift back over the year just past. In flashback, Coronet reconstructs the small, cumulative friction of a first year of marriage: she and her husband Pete move into their first apartment together and work out, meal by meal, who does the dishes and who irons the shirts, redividing chores neither of them wanted the first time around. A furniture-buying trip turns into an argument about what they can actually afford; an older female relative arrives to help hang curtains and wash windows and, in the course of helping, quietly second-guesses how Dotty is keeping house; an afternoon spent minding a friend's baby gives the young couple an uneasy preview of a stage still ahead of them. The seasons turn — a yard filling with fallen leaves marks the year passing — and the flashback resolves the way Coronet's guidance shorts usually do: not with one partner winning an argument, but with Pete and Dotty at the kitchen table, going over the household budget together and deciding, out loud, as partners. The film closes back on the train, Dotty's face settled rather than troubled.
The card that opens the print reads "A Coronet Film," followed by a copyright date of MCMLI — 1951 — under the name of David A. Smart, the Chicago publisher who owned Coronet Instructional Films, and the RCA Sound System trademark Coronet ran on its negatives through the period. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance catalog, no director or performer is named on screen; the only credited contributor is the educational collaborator, Lemo D. Rockwood, Ph.D., billed as Professor of Family Relationships at the New York State College of Home Economics at Cornell University.
Rockwood's own class at Cornell, known on campus as the Marriage Course, was one of the most sought-after electives of the late 1940s, open to students across every college and taught with an unusual mix of historical and anthropological background alongside frank discussion of courtship, mate selection, and the daily mechanics of married life — an approach that, per Cornell University Library's own retrospective on Rockwood, drew real anxiety from more conservative faculty and administrators even as students filled her lecture hall. That same practical, unsentimental voice is what Coronet put on screen here: a Pete-and-Dotty story with no villain, only two people learning to negotiate. The film survives today through Prelinger Archives' donation of Coronet's negatives to the Internet Archive, where it continues to circulate in classroom-print form.

programme.title: Hell's Bells
programme.desc: The fourth Silly Symphony, directed by Ub Iwerks and released the day before Halloween 1929. Set entirely in Hell. Fire consumes the screen to reveal a cavern with a pit of flames, where a spider swings until the fire drags it down, an alligator crawls into the abyss, and a three-headed Cerberus snarls at the viewer. A bat blows a raspberry at a snake, gets swallowed, and the snake sprouts wings and flies away. An orchestra of demons performs — one plays a stringed spine and pelvis in place of a cello. Satan presides, ringing a bell for food: servants squeeze a cow-like creature for milk hot as fire. He feeds a small demon to Cerberus and reaches for a second, who revolts and kicks Satan off the cliff of Hell to the strains of Grieg's "In the Hall of the Mountain King." Stalling's score also weaves in Gounod's "Funeral March of a Marionette" — later famous as the Alfred Hitchcock Presents theme — and the opening of Mendelssohn's "Hebrides" overture.

programme.title: The Bird Store
programme.desc: In a pet shop, caged birds chirp along in their distinctive styles — including four birds caricatured as the Marx Brothers. When a hungry black cat sneaks through an open transom and attacks a baby canary, the birds organize a dramatic counterattack, working together to trap the feline predator inside a cage that they hoist outside to land atop a flagpole in the city dog pound. The final Silly Symphony distributed by Columbia Pictures before the series moved to United Artists, this short marked the first recorded voice work of Clarence Nash for Walt Disney Productions — the man who would become the iconic voice of Donald Duck two years later. Motion Picture Herald praised it as "very good."

programme.title: The Big Bad Wolf
programme.desc: Directed by Burt Gillett, The Big Bad Wolf extends Disney's Three Little Pigs phenomenon by dropping the same Wolf into a Little Red Riding Hood setup and then circling back to the earlier short's theme song. The cartoon plays like a deliberate attempt to bottle 1933's lightning: Frank Churchill's music and familiar pig personalities drive the rhythm while new fairy-tale business expands the cast. Production histories note that it was made in direct response to the runaway success of Three Little Pigs, and reception at the time was respectable but not as explosive as its predecessor. Even so, it locked in the studio's pig-and-wolf mini-cycle, leading to The Three Little Wolves and The Practical Pig, and shows Disney testing how far recurring cartoon characters could carry story momentum inside the still-experimental Silly Symphonies format.

programme.title: Tyrannosaurus Debt
programme.desc: The national debt as a dinosaur that keeps growing and growing. Borrowing money to pay for things the country wants but cannot afford, and the interest that piles up. A surprisingly sophisticated topic for a kids show — the animation shows the debt-dinosaur stomping through Washington getting bigger with each budget cycle. Part of Money Rock.

programme.title: Walkin' on Wall Street
programme.desc: The stock market for kids. Buying shares means owning a piece of a company. Stocks go up, stocks go down. Bulls and bears. The last Money Rock episode, rounding out the economics series with the most abstract financial concept: equity markets. Part of Money Rock.

programme.title: How Do You Know It's Love?
programme.desc:
Nora is on the phone in her bedroom, turning over the same argument she's had all evening: this time, with Jack, it really is love. Her mother — reprising, almost word for word, the counsel Coronet had already handed down in Are You Ready for Marriage? — reminds her that conviction alone proves nothing, that most people fall in love more than once, and sometimes with more than one person at a time. Nora keeps seeing Jack anyway, and the two of them double-date with Jack's older brother Bob and Bob's fiancée Jean, out for dinner and back afterward to look through a photo scrapbook, where a joke snapshot turns up captioned "Whoops, caught you!!!" — a gag that only sharpens the contrast next to it. Measured against Bob and Jean, who share real interests, feel at ease together, take pride in each other, and have already worked out where they stand on religion, children and money, Nora's feeling for Jack starts to look more like a crush than the real thing. Common sense wins out, and, in the genre's usual fashion, everyone ends up happy.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films — copyright MCML under founder David A. Smart — and recorded on the RCA Sound System, the print carries a single credit: educational collaborator Reuben Hill, Ph.D., identified on the title card as a research professor in family life at the University of North Carolina, whose research on courtship and marital adjustment underlies the film's four-question test for "mature love." No director is named on screen; Letterboxd's listing for this specific title credits Ted Peshak, the house director behind most of Coronet's postwar guidance catalog, though the print itself is silent on the point.
Ken Smith, whose shot-list notes for the Prelinger Archives accompany the Internet Archive print, calls out the film as one of the few Coronet productions to carry a recurring background theme — a "wistful" musical cue used as a bridge between scenes — and rates it a film that "grows on you," a rare compliment inside a genre built mostly on cautionary conformity. It has circulated since as public-domain classroom ephemera through the Prelinger Collection, one of dozens of Coronet social-guidance shorts preserved there alongside it.

programme.title: Babes in the Woods
programme.desc: Disney's third color Silly Symphony folds several dark folk traditions into one streamlined fairy-tale nightmare: the old English Babes in the Wood ballad fused with Hansel and Gretel, then filtered through a candy-house witch story that leans surprisingly gothic for 1932. Hansel and Gretel find safety with cheerful dwarfs, then walk straight into a trap where children are transformed into vermin and caged like trophies. Behind the scenes, production drafts show a deep bench of future Disney talent, with Norm Ferguson, Les Clark, Jack King, Dick Lundy, and Tom Palmer handling major sequences and younger animators learning under Ben Sharpsteen. The short was released November 19, 1932 and functioned as a clear bridge toward Disney's later feature fairy tales, especially the tonal mix of whimsy and menace that would define Snow White. It also marked the end of an audio era: one of the last Disney shorts recorded with Powers Cinephone before the studio moved to RCA Photophone.

programme.title: Broken Toys
programme.desc: Broken Toys, released December 14, 1935, was moved ahead in production so Disney could land a Christmas-season Silly Symphony, and it shows unusual story discipline for the series. In a junk heap of discarded playthings, a sailor doll rallies damaged toys for a repair mission that can return them to children by morning. Ben Sharpsteen stages the short as part rescue picture, part Hollywood caricature revue: dolls modeled on W.C. Fields, ZaSu Pitts, Ned Sparks, and Stepin Fetchit pass through the operation line while the score shifts between tenderness and march-time urgency. Cartoon Research documents unusually strict character assignment among animators, including Dick Huemer on the sailor boy, Art Babbitt on several caricature toys, Bill Tytla on the Stepin Fetchit marionette and Jemima rag doll, and Grim Natwick on the blind girl doll whose softer acting points toward Snow White-era character work. It remains one of Disney's key 1930s holiday shorts, though its period stereotypes now read as overtly offensive.

programme.title: Verb: That's What's Happening
programme.desc: A superhero called Verb flies through the city demonstrating action words. "I get my thing in action — VERB! To be, to sing, to feel, to live — VERB! That's what's happening." Zachary Sanders delivers the vocal with disco-era energy. The animation puts Verb in a cape, soaring over buildings while performing every action he names. One of the most beloved Grammar Rock episodes. Written by Bob Dorough.

programme.title: Conjunction Junction
programme.desc: The most famous Schoolhouse Rock episode. A train conductor at Conjunction Junction hooks up boxcars labeled "and," "but," and "or" to demonstrate how conjunctions connect words, phrases, and clauses. "Conjunction Junction, what's your function? Hooking up words and phrases and clauses." Written and performed by Bob Dorough. The train metaphor is so perfectly matched to the concept — conjunctions literally couple things together — that it became the definitive example of the series' genius. Four-time Daytime Emmy winner. Part of Grammar Rock.

programme.title: The Body Machine
programme.desc: Your body is a machine that needs fuel (food), maintenance (exercise), and rest (sleep). The heart pumps, the lungs breathe, the stomach digests — all the major systems explained as mechanical processes in a biological factory. The animation cross-cuts between a real machine and the human body doing the same work. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: Solar Power to the People
programme.desc: Solar energy — the sun as an infinite, clean power source. Solar panels on rooftops, solar farms in deserts, and the science of photovoltaic cells turning sunlight into electricity. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Ways to Settle Disputes
programme.desc:
Two boys in a quiet suburban front yard come to blows over whose turn it is on the tricycle, and a knot of neighborhood kids pulls them apart — the film's first lesson, illustrated with a simple chalkboard-style cartoon of two riders sharing one trike, is COMPROMISE. From there the film moves to the schoolyard, where a shoving match breaks out during a pickup ballgame; the animated card this time reads OBEY THE RULES, with a batter squaring up beneath the words. Indoors, the same children — the film follows three of them by name, Alice, Jerry, and Eddie — argue over a mislaid notebook at their desks, settled once a teacher walks them through FIND THE FACTS. The last dispute is a classroom election for playground representative: the candidates' names go up on the blackboard with a tally beside them, and the lesson this time is FIND OPINIONS, weighing what classmates actually think rather than assuming it.
Coronet Instructional Films produced the short at its own studio outside Chicago, in the same house style as its other social-guidance shorts of the period. The only credit on screen, after the copyright card for company principal David A. Smart, is the educational collaborator: Carter Davidson, Ph.D., identified as President of Union College and Chancellor of Union University. Davidson was, in fact, president of Union College in Schenectady, New York, from 1946 to 1965, having previously spent a decade as president of Knox College in Illinois — a genuine academic credential lent to the studio's classroom-conduct pictures, in keeping with Coronet's practice of pairing its writer-director staff with an outside consultant's name for the title card.
"Ways to Settle Disputes" belongs to the wave of postwar Coronet social-guidance shorts distributed to schools on 16mm reels, teaching a single practical procedure — compromise, rule-following, fact-finding, opinion-gathering — through small, staged neighborhood and classroom conflicts rather than a single continuous story. Like most of Coronet's output from this period, the print carries no other on-screen cast credit; the child performers playing Alice, Jerry, and Eddie go unnamed. It has since passed into the public domain and circulates through the Prelinger Archives and the Internet Archive as an artifact of American classroom media, catalogued there by its Coronet reel description.

programme.title: Three Is a Magic Number (Nike Commercial)
programme.desc: Nike licensed Bob Dorough's "Three Is a Magic Number" for a television commercial, animating it in a style that pays homage to the original Schoolhouse Rock episode. A cultural artifact showing how deeply the series penetrated American popular culture — its songs became valuable enough for major brand advertising.

programme.title: Pastushka i Trubochist
programme.desc:
Two porcelain figures on a mantelpiece — a shepherdess and a chimney sweep — fall in love and decide to escape into the wide world. A carved mahogany satyr wants the shepherdess for himself. The china figures flee up the chimney, see the stars, grow afraid of the vastness, and return to their shelf. Hans Christian Andersen's 1845 fairy tale is one of his most bittersweet: the lovers gain freedom and surrender it, and the story lets you decide whether that's cowardice or wisdom.
Lev Atamanov directed this at Soyuzmultfilm in 1965. Born Levon Atamanyan in Moscow in 1905 to an Armenian Jewish family from Nakhichevan-on-Don, Atamanov studied with Lev Kuleshov at VGIK (the man who invented the Kuleshov effect, the foundation of film editing theory). His debut was a traffic safety PSA in 1931. In 1936 he moved to Yerevan and directed the first Armenian animated films — Dog and Cat (1938) from a Tumanyan fairy tale. He served in the Red Army during the war. Returning to Moscow and Soyuzmultfilm, he made The Scarlet Flower (1952, a plea against Soviet antisemitism disguised as a fairy tale), The Golden Antelope (1954) from Indian folk tales, and The Snow Queen (1957).
The Snow Queen is where the threads converge. Hayao Miyazaki has called it his favorite film — the work that defined what animation could be. Atamanov was making his own adaptation of the same Hans Christian Andersen story that another director, Paul Grimault, had already turned into the most influential European animated film ever made.
Grimault's The Shepherdess and the Chimney Sweep (La Bergère et le Ramoneur, 1952) — a very different, loose adaptation of the same Andersen tale — was released incomplete against Grimault's wishes and toured the world. When it reached Japan in 1955, it detonated. Isao Takahata wrote: "If I had not seen this film, I would have never imagined entering the world of animation." At Toei Doga, the young Miyazaki, Takahata, and animator Yasuo Otsuka studied it frame by frame until the print tore vertically. They taped the soundtrack and played it in the studio. They drew pose collections from it. Takahata copied the entire script by hand from borrowed airmail paper. It became the origin point of everything that would become Studio Ghibli.
So here is Atamanov — whose Snow Queen made Miyazaki want to animate — making his OWN version of the exact story whose French adaptation made Takahata want to animate. Two parallel lines from the same Andersen fairy tale, one Soviet and one French, converging in Tokyo to create modern Japanese animation.
The film features Ole Lukoye (Andersen's sandman figure) as narrator — a character Atamanov had first used in The Snow Queen. Voice cast includes Lyudmila Gnilova, Nina Gulyaeva, Sergey Martinson, and Anatoly Papanov — the voice of the Wolf in Nu, pogodi! (Well, Just You Wait!), the Soviet Tom and Jerry.
Atamanov continued working at Soyuzmultfilm until his death on February 12, 1981. He made over 30 films. A commemorative star was placed at Charles Aznavour Square in Yerevan in 2023. He is buried at the Moscow Armenian Cemetery.

programme.title: Social Courtesy
programme.desc:
Bill primps in front of his bedroom mirror, getting ready for a costume party with his girlfriend Carol, and grumbles that all this fuss over manners is old-fashioned. An unseen narrator disagrees, and makes Bill live with the consequences: every time the boy is rude, the narrator freezes the scene, "takes a picture" of it — the moment dissolves into a photograph hanging on the wall of the next shot — and rewinds Bill back to try again, a little more friendly this time. At the party itself, a teenage rec room dressed up as a hobo jungle, with hand-lettered signs reading "To Train," "Track 1," "Keep Out," and "Baggage Checked" strung up among the decorations, Bill argues under his breath with a voice nobody else can hear, until one of the girls asks if he's talking to himself. Bit by bit he tries doing what he's told — standing when an adult speaks to him, sitting up instead of slouching, actually listening to his friends — and by the last reel the chaperone is remarking on what a changed, courteous boy he's become; Bill leaves already holding an invitation to the next party.
The only screen credit belongs to the educational collaborator: the opening title cards name Mary E. Weathersby, Head of the Homemaking Education Department at Mississippi State College, in the standard Coronet slot for the psychologist or home-economics consultant behind the lesson plan. The copyright card reads MCMLI under the name of Coronet founder David A. Smart, and the print carries the RCA Sound System mark seen across the line. The finished film runs ten minutes sixteen seconds, and the Prelinger Archives catalog credits the camera work to Bruce Colling. No director or performer is named on screen, and none has turned up in any reliable secondary source for this particular title.
Social Courtesy belongs to the same wave of early-1950s Coronet social-guidance shorts as Are You Popular? and Shy Guy, but it handles the genre's usual show-and-correct formula more strangely than most: an audibly bickering, fourth-wall-breaking narrator, freeze-frames that turn into snapshots on a wall, and a scene structure that keeps backing up and starting over. Ken Smith singled it out in his 1999 study of the genre, Mental Hygiene: Classroom Films 1945-1970, as one of the most inventive films Coronet ever made. It has since passed into the public domain and is preserved in the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive.

programme.title: Night
programme.desc: The ninth Silly Symphony and a masterful marriage of classical music and pioneering animation. The personified moon hums Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata as owls and insects waltz by moonlight on shimmering water. In what Variety (May 14, 1930) called a groundbreaking first, fireflies illuminate in precise cadence with the music — "the first time in any cartoon for this effect" — performing to the well-known "Glow Worm" tune. Mosquitoes dance alongside a bullfrog whose elastic tongue proves their undoing, and a frog orchestra of croaking brethren provides the score for an amphibian romance on the lily pads. Motion Picture News found it "extremely diverting," praising the "owls performing jazz steps on water lilies, wasps turning collegiate, and even the man in the moon going in for the shimmy." Originally scheduled for April 10 but postponed to July 31 due to production delays following the departures of Ub Iwerks and Carl Stalling, the film was originally released with atmospheric blue tinting to enhance its nocturnal ambiance. Variety concluded that "old folks, as well as the kids, have evidenced a strong liking for this series. They won't be disappointed in Night."

programme.title: Mother Goose Melodies
programme.desc: The sixteenth Silly Symphony and a turning point in the series' ambition. An enormous Old King Cole commands entertainment at his court. When Mother Goose presents her storybook, its pages come magically to life — the "fiddlers three" are revealed as the Three Blind Mice, Little Miss Muffet flees her spider, Jack and Jill encounter Simple Simon atop their hill, Humpty Dumpty takes his tumble, Little Jack Horner sits in his corner, and the Cat fiddles while the Cow jumps over the Moon. What distinguishes the entry is its narrative sophistication: the stories don't simply appear in sequence but overlap and interact, one nursery rhyme flowing seamlessly into the next. The film may mark the debut of composer Frank Churchill at Disney, who would go on to write "Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf?" and the songs for Snow White. Motion Picture Herald (May 9, 1931) proclaimed it "Great," noting "almost the illusion of real life in some of the figures, so fine is the animation." The Film Daily (September 13, 1931) agreed: "Walt Disney and his assistants have turned out a synchronized cartoon comedy that will be hard to beat." Disney would revisit the concept with the Technicolor semi-remake Old King Cole (1933) and later Mother Goose Goes Hollywood (1938).

programme.title: Egyptian Melodies
programme.desc: A curious spider explores the Great Sphinx, descending into a torch-lit tomb where dancing mummies spring to life and animated hieroglyphics depict chariot races and ancient Egyptian scenes. The spider flees in terror back to daylight. Notable for its innovative camera-perspective animation through corridors — a technique ahead of its time — the short incorporated Alexandre Luigini's 1875 "Ballet égyptien" into Frank Churchill's score. Background animation was later reused in Mickey Mouse's "The Mad Doctor." Variety gave a lukewarm review, calling it "just fair filler matter" with good animation but criticizing it for falling into "the usual ghost and mummy stuff" after a promising opening.

programme.title: The Night Before Christmas
programme.desc: A direct follow-up to Santa's Workshop, this December 1933 Silly Symphony adapts Clement Clarke Moore with less narration and more mechanical wonder. Santa lands on the roof, slips down the chimney, and unloads a roomful of toys that wake up and stage their own nocturnal parade while the children sleep. Wilfred Jackson keeps the staging brisk and musical, with toy-soldier precision from animators including Les Clark and Ed Love under Leigh Harline's score. Contemporary response was strong: in January 1934, The New York Times singled the cartoon out in its holiday-season coverage as one of Disney's best recent shorts. Like several early Disney holiday titles, later reissue and TV versions circulated with edits that removed racially offensive gag material from original prints, making surviving complete versions important as historical records of both craft and period attitudes.

programme.title: How Friendly Are You
programme.desc:
Ray moves through a run of small social tests over the course of the film — wheeling his bike alongside another boy, brushing off a girl who's delighted to show him something wrapped in paper, working alongside his older brother Phil at Mr. Martin's shop, squaring off with another boy in the park over a piece of trash left on the grass — and gets nearly all of them wrong: offhand, closed off, quick to take offense. Phil eventually sits him down and talks through what friendliness actually costs and what it returns, the "responsibility of friendship" the film's own catalog description names directly. Ray works back through the same round of situations correcting himself one by one, and the film closes with him at a piano surrounded by a room full of grinning classmates — the reward Coronet's guidance shorts always hand out for good behavior: being liked.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' Glenview, Illinois studio and directed by Ted Peshak, from a script by Robert Chapin and Dick Creyke, photographed by Dale Sharkey and cut by editor George Wilbern, with narration by George Stone. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance line, the only credit that appears on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Harl R. Douglass, Ph.D., director of the College of Education at the University of Colorado, a life-adjustment educator whose papers are held today in that university's own archives. Prelinger Archives, whose print of the film circulates today, catalogs the release as 1952; Letterboxd and IMDb's short-film index both list 1951 instead, a year's discrepancy common to Coronet's undated 16mm classroom prints.
Phil is played by Dick York — five years past his screen debut in the title role of Coronet's own Shy Guy (1947), and a dozen years before he became Darrin Stephens on Bewitched — while Mr. Martin, whose shop gives Phil his after-school job, is played by Carl Kroenke. Ray and the film's other roles went uncredited on screen, in keeping with Coronet's practice of naming only its academic consultant. The short is one of dozens Coronet turned out during its postwar guidance cycle and survives today as a plain, commercial-free classroom print through the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive.

programme.title: Autumn
programme.desc: The seventh Silly Symphony and the third in Disney's four-seasons cycle, following Springtime and Summer. Directed by Ub Iwerks, the short depicts forest animals preparing for winter. Squirrels gather and hoard nuts and pine cones in a tree hollow, playing with them until crows swoop in to steal the cache. A hedgehog shakes apples from a tree. Beavers construct a dam and dance on the riverbank. Ducks paddle in the stream, then take flight. As the first snow begins to fall, beaver, skunk, crows, and hedgehog all retreat to shelter. This was the last Silly Symphony completed before Ub Iwerks and Carl Stalling abruptly resigned from the Disney studio in January 1930. Iwerks, who had animated nearly the entire first Silly Symphony — The Skeleton Dance — in six weeks and had co-created Mickey Mouse with Walt Disney, left to start his own studio under a side deal with distributor Pat Powers. His departure triggered a business crisis and months of acrimonious negotiations. Stalling, the studio's music director, followed him out the door. The sudden loss of Disney's two most important collaborators caused severe production delays on subsequent cartoons. Motion Picture News (August 2, 1930) called it "Well done, but constructed along the same lines as most cartoons, the majority of which depend on fantastic stepping by the animal characters to put it over. The musical renditions are splendid." Autumn marked the end of an era — never again would Iwerks animate for Disney until his return a decade later in a technical, rather than creative, capacity.

programme.title: Just Dogs
programme.desc: Dogs imprisoned in the city pound howl Vernon Dalhart's melancholic "The Prisoner's Song." A resourceful small dog engineers a mass breakout, liberating all the canines including a distinctly ungrateful Pluto. Once free, the small dog devotedly follows Pluto, who shows little appreciation for his benefactor. When the helpful pup discovers a massive bone, every escaped dog descends in a chaotic chase. Using an army of fleas as unlikely allies, the small dog reclaims the prize and generously offers it back to Pluto, whose selfish heart finally softens. Historically significant as Pluto's first solo starring role without Mickey Mouse, directed by Burt Gillett with an unusually large animation team including Fred Moore, whose work on character expression was reshaping the studio's approach to personality animation.

programme.title: The Golden Touch
programme.desc: Walt Disney stepped back into the director's chair for this King Midas retelling, then never officially directed another short. Released March 22, 1935, The Golden Touch runs longer than most Symphonies and follows Midas from greedy triumph to panic as food, water, and even comfort turn to metal in his hands. Billy Bletcher voices the king with broad theatrical weight, while Norm Ferguson and Fred Moore animate the two leads: Midas and the taunting elf Goldie. The cartoon is remembered inside Disney history as a costly lesson. Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston later wrote that the film proved a punch line cannot land until the character is truly defined, citing Midas begging for a hamburger and Goldie answering, "with or without onions?" The short did not connect at preview, but it sharpened Disney's story priorities before the feature era.

programme.title: The Great American Melting Pot
programme.desc: Immigration to America from the colonial era through the early 20th century, told as ingredients going into a great melting pot. Pilgrims, Germans, Irish, Chinese, Italians, Jews — all arriving with their cultures, blending into something new. The animation shows the Statue of Liberty stirring the pot. A product of its Bicentennial-era optimism about pluralism. Part of America Rock. Performed by Lori Lieberman.

programme.title: Fireworks
programme.desc: The Declaration of Independence and the Fourth of July. The Continental Congress debates, Jefferson writes, and the colonies declare independence from Britain. The title refers both to the celebratory fireworks and to the explosive political act itself. Released during the American Bicentennial. Part of America Rock.

programme.title: Attitudes and Health
programme.desc:
Marvin Baker is introduced as "an average fellow from an average home in an average town," and the film wastes no time showing what a sour mood has done to him: a shoving match with the boys he used to walk with, a cold shoulder from the same group at the school lockers, and a mother at home who watches him mope without knowing quite why. The picture's real interest, though, is what that attitude does to the body, not just the friendships. It cuts away more than once to generalized stock scenes of grown men stewing over a setback — one anxiously dialing a phone, another pressing a hand to his temple, another scowling in a doorway — offered as proof that a bad outlook can sour an adult's fortunes (a passed-over promotion is the example given) just as easily as a teenager's. Marvin's own case ends up in a doctor's office, where a physical exam turns up nothing wrong; instead the doctor lectures Marvin and his worried mother together, telling them that attitude, not illness, is behind more than half the complaints he sees in his practice. Marvin takes the lesson to heart, is shown working alone with a basketball in the yard rather than sulking, and by the last reel has made the first team.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films at the company's studio in Glenview, Illinois, with a copyright card reading "MCMXLIX, David A. Smart" — Coronet's founder. As in the rest of Coronet's postwar output, none of the actors are credited on screen; the only title card naming a person identifies the outside experts who vetted the film's content: "Educational Collaborators, Dean F. Smiley, M.D., and Fred V. Hein, Ph.D., Consultants in Health and Fitness, Bureau of Health Education, American Medical Association." That AMA affiliation is doing real work here, lending institutional authority to the film's central, slightly startling claim that a doctor's waiting room is full of patients whose real trouble is attitude. Sound is credited to the RCA Sound System, standard for Coronet's 16mm classroom prints of the period.
At under ten minutes, Attitudes and Health sits with Coronet's other late-1940s social guidance shorts — the same house style seen in Are You Popular? and Shy Guy — though its stated audience runs wider than most, "high school, college, and adult groups" rather than teenagers alone. It circulated for classroom rental for years before lapsing out of commercial distribution, and it survives today through the Prelinger Archives' scan at the Internet Archive, one of thousands of educational one-reelers preserved there after their original market disappeared.

programme.title: Three Little Pigs
programme.desc: The Silly Symphony that exploded past "cartoon short" and became a national event. Premiering at Radio City Music Hall in May 1933, Burt Gillett's adaptation cost about $22,000 and reportedly earned roughly $250,000, then stayed in theaters so long some exhibitors joked it outranked the features it played with. Walt Disney later said, "At last we have achieved true personality in a whole picture," and that's the breakthrough you feel: Fifer, Fiddler, and Practical move like three distinct temperaments, not one model sheet in triplicate. Frank Churchill's "Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf?" escaped the screen and became a Depression-era anthem. The short won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short, launched three direct sequels, and remains one of the clearest turning points in character animation history.

programme.title: Music Land
programme.desc: A battle-of-the-bands allegory with no spoken dialogue, Music Land premiered October 5, 1935 and imagines diplomacy as orchestration. Across the Sea of Discord, the Land of Symphony and Isle of Jazz go to war when a saxophone prince courts a violin princess and gets locked in a metronome tower. Wilfred Jackson turns the rescue into an artillery duel of organ pipes, brass barrages, and Wagner blasts, then resolves it with a bridge literally named Harmony. Leigh Harline's score is the engine: Beethoven and Wagner collide with bugle calls, two original jazz pieces ("The Saxes Have It" and "Jazz Fireworks"), and the prince's coded note set to "The Prisoner's Song." J.B. Kaufman and Russell Merritt note Disney initially underestimated the short, but its design and musical wit aged into classic status. In 1937 it won the first animation prize at the Venice International Film Festival.

programme.title: Merbabies
programme.desc: The only Silly Symphony ever farmed out to another studio — and the studio that made it was founded by Walt Disney's oldest colleagues. Hugh Harman and Rudolf Ising had worked alongside Disney and Ub Iwerks at the Laugh-O-Gram Studio in Kansas City before going on to create Looney Tunes for Warner Bros. and the cartoon division at MGM. By 1937, their MGM contracts had lapsed. Disney, drowning in Snow White production, struck a deal: Harman-Ising would lend their ink and paint staff to finish Snow White; in return, Disney contracted three Silly Symphonies. He accepted only this one — RKO refused to distribute the other two. Scored by Scott Bradley (later famous for Tom and Jerry), it's a plotless underwater circus: redheaded merbabies materialize from ocean spray, descend to the seafloor, and stage a full big-top spectacle with seahorse parades, an octopus trained like an elephant, and a shark lion-taming act. A whale's sneeze launches them all skyward in bubbles. The underwater effects work — light refraction, caustics, the physics of bubbles — fed directly into Pinocchio's ocean sequences two years later.

programme.title: The Energy Blues
programme.desc: A blues song about the energy crisis. Oil, coal, gas — they are running out, and we need to conserve and find alternatives. Written during the actual 1970s energy crisis when gas lines and oil embargoes were daily reality. One of the few Schoolhouse Rock episodes that feels explicitly political, reflecting the national anxiety of its era. Part of Science Rock. Performed by Jack Sheldon.

programme.title: Lunchroom Manners
programme.desc:
A puppet theater dominates the front of an elementary classroom, flag hanging behind it, as a fumbling marionette named Mr. Bungle blunders in and out of a little door marked "BOYS ROOM," and the watching class laughs at exactly the behavior the film means to stamp out. The cartoonish object lesson gives way to a live-action follow-through: a boy scrubs his hands at the washroom sink, joins the line filing into the cafeteria, and works his way down a hot line loaded with cake, franks, and trimmings. Left to his own habits he eats carelessly — shoveling, slurping a straw, leaving his tray a mess — while a watching teacher looks on from the doorway unimpressed. A tidier classmate is held up as the counter-example, and the short closes on trays properly scraped and stacked, its lesson in "beginning responsibility" delivered the way Coronet always delivered it: gently, repetitively, and entirely without dialogue that isn't a teacher's.
The title card reads "Beginning Responsibility: Lunchroom Manners," placing it in the same Coronet strand as Shy Guy and its kin, and carries a copyright date of MCMLX — 1960 — a year later than the date this print is commonly catalogued under. As with the rest of the series, the only credit on screen is the educational collaborator: Ross L. Allen, Dr.P.H., Director of Education for the Division of Health, Physical Education and Recreation at the College of Education, Cortland State University of New York. No writer or director is named on the print itself, and none has been reliably attributed to this particular title elsewhere. The trademark card underneath identifies Coronet Instructional Films as, at the time, "a division of Esquire, Inc."
The film's afterlife has outrun its classroom career by a wide margin. Its puppet antagonist gave the experimental rock band Mr. Bungle, formed by Mike Patton and friends in Northern California in the mid-1980s, its name. Excerpts also turned up on an HBO Pee-wee Herman special, introducing the short to an audience of a very different age and temperament than the one it was built for. Coronet's straight-faced cafeteria etiquette lesson, uncredited actors and all, has proven considerably stickier than its intended nine-and-a-half-minute classroom slot.

programme.title: Three Orphan Kittens
programme.desc: Winner of the 1935 Academy Award for Best Short Subject (Cartoons), Three Orphan Kittens opened October 26, 1935 and proved Disney could build a hit almost entirely on behavior animation. Directed by David Hand, it follows three stray kittens who duck in from a snowstorm and turn a house into chaos, then into the famous player-piano set piece where they scamper over the keys to a variation on Zez Confrey's "Kitten on the Keys." The short is also a craft milestone: the tracking run past table legs, chairs, and piano was redrawn frame by frame to sell depth, a training-ground exercise for artists heading toward Snow White. Contemporary trade response was rapturous: The Film Daily called the piano sequence a "laugh riot," while Boxoffice predicted broad audience appeal. Disney reissued it in the 1937 Academy Award Review and brought the trio back the next year in More Kittens.

programme.title: Elmer Elephant
programme.desc: Released March 28, 1936, Elmer Elephant arrived while Disney was reorganizing the studio into specialized units during the Snow White buildup, and the short uses that extra polish on broad comedy and surprisingly tender character acting. Story artist Dick Huemer recycled Elmer and giraffe classmate Tillie from an unfinished 1934 project, then built a schoolyard romance around Elmer's stage fright and oversized trunk. At a birthday party, a mean trio of pranksters loads Elmer with peanuts, setting up the film's signature sneeze barrage as his trunk blasts cake, guests, and eventually a burning house. Elmer redeems himself by turning the same gag into a fire hose rescue. The short was popular enough to spin into the Sunday Silly Symphony comic strip as "Elmer and Tillie" later in 1936, briefly positioning Elmer as Disney's next breakout personality.

programme.title: My Hero, Zero
programme.desc: A love song to the number zero — the placeholder that makes our number system work. "My hero, zero, such a funny little hero, but till you came along we counted on our fingers and toes." Bob Dorough explains how zero as a placeholder lets you write ten, a hundred, a thousand, and beyond. Part of Multiplication Rock. The animation features a caped zero flying through cascading digits.

programme.title: Lucky Seven Sampson
programme.desc: The sevens times table told through the story of Lucky Seven Sampson, a cat with seven lives who keeps getting into scrapes. Bob Dorough sings through the notoriously difficult sevens (7×8=56, the hardest multiplication fact for most kids) with a bluesy shuffle. Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: Do the Circulation
programme.desc: Blood circulation as a dance. The heart pumps, arteries carry oxygen-rich blood out, veins bring it back, lungs re-oxygenate — and the whole cycle is choreographed as a funky dance number. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: The Little Things We Do
programme.desc: Small daily actions that help the environment — turning off lights, recycling, using less water, walking instead of driving. The message: environmental stewardship starts with individual habits, not grand gestures. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Am I Trustworthy?
programme.desc:
Eddie Johnson wants to be treasurer of his hobby club, and he's stung when the members nominate another boy instead and put him on the clean-up committee. He tells his father the other kids just don't like him, but his father redirects the question: trustworthy isn't the same thing as popular, it's whether people can count on you to do what you said you'd do. Pressed on it, Eddie has to admit the evidence is against him — a lamp he promised to fix sits forgotten in the corner, homework gets left to the last minute, a model kit lies half-built on the table. He draws up a chart to track himself against his word, then works through it scene by scene: fixing the lamp, finishing assignments on time, helping around the house and at the grocery store, and taking on a small job at the school library's book charge-out desk. By the end his kept promises have done what his campaign speech couldn't, and the treasurer's job he wanted looks within reach after all.
The only credit on screen, in keeping with Coronet's house practice of naming the classroom consultant rather than the filmmakers, is "Educational Collaborator Elizabeth B. Carey, Ph.D., Supervisor, Bureau of Instructional Supervision, The University of the State of New York," under a copyright dated MCML (1950) to Coronet's publisher, David A. Smart, with an RCA Sound System credit. A contemporary DVD review of the film corroborates that it was made for that same New York State office, meaning Carey's department was not just a lending credit but the body the film was produced to serve. No director is credited on the print, and none is reliably documented for this specific title elsewhere, so none is listed here.
"Am I Trustworthy?" belongs to the "social guidance" genre of postwar classroom shorts that Ken Smith catalogued in his 1999 book Mental Hygiene: Classroom Films 1945-1970, where he notes that trustworthiness in the film functions as something close to a synonym for obedience and conformity, and quotes its closing moral: "People have to show they can be trusted with little things if they want to be trusted with big things." A 16mm print was donated to the Internet Archive's Prelinger Collection in 2002 and remains in the public domain, and the film was later remastered for Kino Lorber's 2009 DVD anthology "How to Be a Man, Volume 1," drawn from Skip Elsheimer's A/V Geeks film library alongside eleven other classroom shorts of the era — a fairly ordinary, "stagey and confined" example of the genre, by one reviewer's account, but a representative one.

programme.title: Birds In The Spring
programme.desc: One of Disney's early Technicolor flexes: a spring nursery comedy that turns into a miniature survival thriller. Directed by David Hand, the short follows a pair of parent birds from nest-building to hatch day, then leaps forward to flying lessons for their three chicks. One rebellious baby wanders off, gets mesmerized by a rattlesnake, then blunders into a hornets' nest before the parents dive in for a rescue and drag him home for a stern feathered spanking. The color work drew immediate notice. On March 21, 1933, The Film Daily called it one of the "niftiest little numbers" around, praising its "height of color cartoon art" and ending with a simple verdict: "For kids or grownups, it's a pip." Frank Churchill and Bert Lewis's score keeps the whole thing bouncing between lullaby sweetness and panic comedy.

programme.title: The Tortoise And The Hare
programme.desc: The cartoon that gave Disney another Oscar and turned an old fable into a personality showcase. Released January 5, 1935, this Technicolor Silly Symphony introduces Toby Tortoise and Max Hare, with Max animated as a rubber-limbed show-off who can sprint, preen, and flirt in the same breath. The race follows Aesop, but the fun is in the detours: Max stops to clown for a crowd of girl bunnies while Toby keeps grinding forward, stretching his body to steal inches at the line. Frank Churchill's score drives the pace, while animators like Dick Lundy and Eric Larson sell Max's swagger and Toby's stubborn calm. The short won the Academy Award for Best Short Subject (Cartoon) and was popular enough to get a sequel, Toby Tortoise Returns, the next year.

programme.title: The Robber Kitten
programme.desc: Released April 20, 1935, this Silly Symphony starts as a child's outlaw fantasy and ends as a hard scare about consequences. Ambrose the kitten renames himself Butch, skips his bath, steals cookies, and tries to play highwayman until he meets Dirty Bill, a genuinely dangerous bulldog voiced by Billy Bletcher. Dave Hand stages the short as a tonal shift from pretend bravado to real fear, with Ham Luske and Bill Roberts animating Bill's heavy jowls, knife flashes, and Ambrose's panic sprint home. Frank Churchill even gives the pair a comic bonding tune, "Dirty Bill," before the threat turns serious. Trade reaction was not entirely playful: Motion Picture Daily reported that Pennsylvania censors briefly withheld the short for showing kittens as gangsters. That tension is exactly what makes The Robber Kitten memorable.

programme.title: Elementary, My Dear
programme.desc: A Sherlock Holmes-styled detective investigates the mystery of the fours times table. "Elementary, my dear — two times two is four, four times two is eight..." Sung by Blossom Dearie with her distinctive wispy vocal style. Part of Multiplication Rock. Teaches the fours multiplication table through a detective narrative of clue-finding and deduction.

programme.title: Rufus Xavier Sarsaparilla
programme.desc: Rufus Xavier Sarsaparilla finds a kangaroo, his sister Rafaella Gabriela Sarsaparilla finds a rhinoceros, and their friend Albert Andreas Armadillo finds an aardvark. Without pronouns, every sentence becomes an exhausting mouthful of proper nouns. Jack Sheldon sings this comic masterpiece about why pronouns exist — because nobody wants to say the full name fourteen times in a paragraph. Part of Grammar Rock.

programme.title: Developing Friendships
programme.desc:
Bob McGraw used to walk home from school by himself, keeping to his own thoughts and not much minding the company. Then the other fellows start talking about the baskets Joe has been sinking, and Bob can't see what the excitement is about — after all, he'd been the one they used to call the best player, and he decides he doesn't need a rival crowding him out. But Joe keeps being decent in ways that are hard to resent: he credits his teammates instead of taking the bow himself, he goes out of his way for a floundering, awkward classmate named Eddie, and he treats a girl named Marie with the same plain courtesy he shows everyone else. Won over more or less against his will, Bob starts falling in with Joe and the circle of friends who gather around him, and when Joe enters — and wins — a statewide essay contest on Junior Citizenship, earning himself a trip to the capital, Bob is one of the gang who piles into a car and races to the station to welcome him home. That homecoming is the film's frame: the whole account of how the group came together unfolds as Bob's recollection while the friends wait together on the depot benches.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films out of Glenview, Illinois, and released to classrooms on August 19, 1950, with Ted Peshak directing, as he did much of Coronet's postwar guidance output. Coronet's usual practice was to reserve its one on-screen credit for the psychology consultant attached to a film, but the print circulating today opens directly on the station-platform scene, with no title or collaborator card surviving in it to transcribe; the young cast, drawn from the same pool of Chicago-area teenagers who turn up across the studio's other 1950 shorts, likewise goes unbilled on screen.
"Developing Friendships" belongs to a cluster of Coronet titles from the same year — Developing Leadership, The Fun of Making Friends, How Friendly Are You? — built around the same basic civics-class argument: that popularity and belonging are skills to be learned rather than traits you either have or don't, with a model classmate on hand to demonstrate the technique. Where a companion film like Are You Popular? measures its heroine against a cautionary rival, this one works by simple contrast between Bob's early standoffishness and Joe's easy generosity. The film survives in the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive, part of the large body of Coronet's classroom output that passed into the public domain and now circulates as the same plain print schools once rented by mail.

programme.title: The Cat's Out
programme.desc: A house cat chases a bird onto a weathervane and is knocked unconscious, plunging into a surreal nightmare where everything comes alive to torment him — giant owls, a dancing scarecrow, menacing bats, spiders, and grasping trees. Upon waking and realizing it was all a dream, the relieved cat is promptly thrown out of the cottage and marches away in defiance. Originally copyrighted as "The Cat's Nightmare," the working title survived on vault prints. Variety called it "one of Walt Disney's Silly Symphony series and a beaut," praising its snappy penmanship and new ideas. Music weaves in "For He's a Jolly Good Fellow" and "Listen to the Mockingbird" throughout the nocturnal ordeal.

programme.title: The Bears and the Bees
programme.desc: Two mischievous bear cubs raid a beehive for honey, triggering a furious counterattack from the swarm. The cubs flee through the forest in a series of escalating slapstick encounters, their rear ends bearing the brunt of the bees' wrath. Physical comedy and musical choreography drive the action as the bears discover that stealing from nature has painful consequences. Historically significant as the first Silly Symphony distributed by United Artists, which doubled the per-cartoon budget from $7,500 to $15,000 — the financial boost that would enable Disney's landmark transition to three-strip Technicolor just weeks later with Flowers and Trees. Pinto Colvig, later famous as Goofy, voiced the bear cubs. The cubs themselves resurfaced in 1940s-50s Disney comics as Cubby and Tubby.

programme.title: Water Babies
programme.desc: One of Disney's most sugar-sweet and technically polished 1935 Symphonies, Water Babies turns Charles Kingsley's Victorian fantasy into pure movement and color. Released May 11, 1935, the short opens on lilies unfolding at dawn, each flower revealing a tiny child before the film shifts into parades, swan rides, frog rodeos, and a miniature bullfight with a belligerent bullfrog. Contemporary prints and later home-video versions differed, with some bottom-exposure gags removed in censored edits. Music is central: animation historian J.B. Kaufman notes the title song was written as a vocal number but used instrumentally in the short, giving the whole cartoon a floating, ballet-like rhythm. Directed by Wilfred Jackson, it became popular enough to inspire a follow-up, Merbabies, in 1938.

programme.title: I Got Six
programme.desc: A funky soul number about the sixes times table. "I got six — that's all, and that's been my lucky number since I was very small." Grady Tate brings a warm, grooving vocal to the multiplication facts that feel the least intuitive to kids (6×7, 6×8, 6×9). Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: Electricity, Electricity (Goodness)
programme.desc: The band Goodness covers Electricity, Electricity for the Schoolhouse Rock Rocks! tribute compilation. A grunge-influenced take on the Science Rock classic. Part of the 2002 tribute album series.

programme.title: The Fun of Being Thoughtful
programme.desc:
Jane Proctor is a cheerful teenager who is, in archivist Ken Smith's later phrase, "slavishly devoted" to her family's happiness, and the film catalogues one evening of it: she tidies her room, helps get dinner on the table amid a bit of kitchen panic over the mashed potatoes, and — the plot's real engine — works to fix up her awkward brother Eddie with a date for the following night. Eddie, whose voice keeps threatening to crack, gripes along the way that he "hasn't a thing to wear" either. Jane's persistent thoughtfulness pays off in the last scene: she comes down the stairs in a new dress to her parents' and Eddie's evident delight, and the household settles back into its usual harmony.
Produced at Coronet's studio in Glenview, Illinois and copyrighted in 1950 (the title card reads MCML) by David A. Smart, who had founded the company with his brother Alfred as an offshoot of their Esquire magazine business. As with the rest of Coronet's postwar social-guidance catalog, the teenage cast goes uncredited; the only name in the titles belongs to the psychology consultant, credited on screen as Educational Collaborator Ernest M. Ligon, Ph.D., director of the Character Research Project at Union College in Schenectady, New York. Ligon had founded the Character Research Project in 1935 and would direct it for over four decades, building its work on ideas he had laid out in his earlier book The Psychology of Christian Personality. Directing credit likewise appears nowhere on screen, but Ted Peshak — the Glenview house director credited with roughly 350 educational films for Coronet — lists Fun of Being Thoughtful among his 1950 directing credits. The uncredited actor playing Eddie Proctor was a Coronet regular: a retrospective tracing faces across the studio's uncredited teen stock company notes that the same performer's voice had not yet finished cracking a year earlier in The Meaning of Pi (1949), and that he turns up again later in 1950 as Eddie in Developing Friendships and as Ed Parker in How to Get Cooperation.
The print survives through the Prelinger Archives on the Internet Archive, in the public domain along with the rest of that collection. Prelinger's cataloguer Ken Smith, whose notes on Coronet's output were later folded into his book Mental Hygiene: Better Living Through Classroom Films, 1945-1970, flagged the script's habit of chasing several morals inside ten minutes as "fun but a little hard to follow" — a fair description of a film that covers housework, dating, dress shopping, and hospitality all in one sitting. It belongs to the postwar "social guidance" genre Coronet all but defined for American classrooms, in which ordinary household courtesy is treated as a small-scale rehearsal for the larger civic virtues — responsibility, cooperation, good citizenship — that the studio's other shorts preached more directly.

programme.title: More Kittens
programme.desc: More Kittens, released December 19, 1936, brings back the trio from Three Orphan Kittens for a looser backyard sequel. After being thrown outside by the housekeeper, the kittens turn a garden into chaos: a run-in with a tortoise, a scuffle with a bluebird, and laundry-line havoc that floods the yard. Their main ally is Bolivar, a massive St. Bernard who serves as reluctant shelter from punishment before finally embracing the tiny troublemakers. Contemporary trade notices praised the short's lively feline business, while modern viewers also read its period domestic caricatures as part of its historical context.

programme.title: The Moth And The Flame
programme.desc: Burt Gillett's return to Disney after the collapse of Van Beuren Studios — the director of Flowers and Trees and Three Little Pigs closing out his Disney career with another story about fire. Moths invade a costume shop at night and feast on fabric while a boy moth ignores his girl to gorge on a hat. A candle flame springs to life as a suave seducer — face modeled on Clark Gable — and lures the neglected girl moth toward disaster. The Flame character required two animators working in tandem: Ed Love handled movement and expression while John McManus independently animated fire effects overlaid on Love's drawings, producing a figure that reads simultaneously as charming villain and convincing conflagration. When the boy moth accidentally douses the blaze with benzene and makes everything catastrophically worse, the swarm mobilizes — water-filled bagpipes as hoses, aerial drops from funnels, cotton-ball bombardments — until an old top hat smothers the Flame for good. Gustaf Tenggren, then shaping the visual identity of Pinocchio, provided the inspirational art. Reviewers noted the fire here burns with greater intensity than anything in Snow White.

programme.title: Busy Prepositions
programme.desc: A kid runs through a park demonstrating prepositions by physically acting them out — in, on, under, over, through, between, beside, behind. The animation follows the kid climbing over fences, crawling under bridges, and running between trees. The physicality is the whole lesson: prepositions describe spatial relationships, and the best way to learn them is to move your body through space. Part of Grammar Rock.

programme.title: Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips: Introduction
programme.desc: The introduction to the Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips series — the 1980s addition to Schoolhouse Rock teaching kids about personal computers. Scooter is a skateboarding kid, Mr. Chips is a friendly computer. Together they explain the digital revolution to a generation that was about to live through it. The weakest era of Schoolhouse Rock by consensus, but historically fascinating as a time capsule of early computer literacy education.

programme.title: Where the Money Goes
programme.desc: Tracking a dollar from your pocket through the economy — spending, business revenue, wages, taxes, government spending, and back around again. The circular flow of money visualized as a literal journey that a dollar bill takes through shops, banks, and government buildings. Part of Money Rock.

programme.title: Don't Be a Carbon Sasquatch
programme.desc: Carbon footprints — every action has an environmental cost measured in carbon emissions. Driving, flying, heating your house, even eating certain foods. A Carbon Sasquatch leaves giant footprints everywhere. The goal: shrink your footprint. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Developing Leadership
programme.desc:
Developing Leadership opens on a printed title card posing five questions the film means to answer — how to be a good member of a group, how to help as a follower, how to become a leader, what qualities leadership requires, and how a leader helps the group along — before cutting to a shot of a town half-submerged in floodwater.
