"Snap Out of It!" — its full on-screen title carries the subtitle "Emotional Balance" — belongs to the mental-hygiene wave of classroom shorts that dominated homeroom film projectors through the 1950s, alongside Coronet stablemates like "Are You Popular?," "Overcoming Fear," and "Control Your Emotions." Its short running time still finds room for three separate cautionary vignettes orbiting Howard's central story, a structure typical of the genre's habit of restating one lesson across several interchangeable teenagers. Like most of Coronet's early catalog, the film lapsed into the public domain and survives today chiefly through the Prelinger Archives, which preserved and digitized the Coronet library, transcript and all, for research and reuse.

programme.title: Lullaby Land
programme.desc: One of the strangest dream-logic entries in the series: a baby and a toy dog drift into a patchwork nursery world where rattles grow on trees, bottles and safety pins march in formation, and comfort objects can flip into menace without warning. Wilfred Jackson directs it like a musical fever dream, with Frank Churchill and Leigh Harline alternating lullaby sweetness and sudden threat as the pair wander into a "Forbidden Garden" full of scissors, knives, tacks, and giant matches that come alive and hunt them. Dick Huemer and Leonard Sebring's animation leans hard into shape-shifting object comedy before the Sandman resets the whole nightmare and returns the child to the cradle. Disney later echoed this imagery in Disneyland's Storybook Land Canal Boats, whose quilt-garden section directly traces back to this short's visual design.

programme.title: Mother Pluto
programme.desc: Released on November 14, 1936, Mother Pluto folds a marquee Disney character into the Silly Symphonies format. A hen hides her eggs in Pluto's doghouse; the chicks hatch under him, immediately imprint on him, and follow him across the farm. Pluto tries to escape, then softens into a reluctant guardian, battling first a furious mother hen and then a rooster before the chicks return to him anyway. Disney's archives note this as the first cartoon where Pluto is the central star rather than supporting Mickey, a direct bridge to his dedicated Pluto series that began the following year with Pluto's Quin-puplets.

programme.title: Them Not-So-Dry Bones
programme.desc: The skeletal system, riffing on the old spiritual. The toe bone connects to the foot bone, the foot bone connects to the ankle bone — but with actual anatomical names and real science about what bones do (support, protect, produce blood cells, store minerals). The animation builds a skeleton bone by bone. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: The Worm Turns
programme.desc:
Mickey, in full mad-scientist regalia, pores over a volume of Ancient Formulae and brews the "Courage Builder" — a super-strength tonic mixed from Tigerus Marrow, Spiritu Bravado, Stimuli Valorus and Lionus Tonicio that turns the food chain on its head. One spritz from his flit-gun and the meek become mighty, in an escalating chain of reversals: a fly trapped in a web thrashes the spider and ties him up in his own silk, a cornered mouse flattens the cat, the sprayed cat routs Pluto, and when dogcatcher Pete corners Pluto at the pound, Mickey's spray turns the dog into a one-pup wrecking crew who sends Pete crashing through the fence. The last word goes to a fire hydrant, which gets a dose of the formula and gives Pluto a soaking.
Released on January 2, 1937, under the supervision of Ben Sharpsteen, from a story by Otto Englander — both men deep in Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs at the time, and it shows: the short was made in part as a working test of the laboratory effects being developed for the witch's dungeon transformation scene, which reached theaters eleven months later. The bubbling beakers, colored vapors and electrical apparatus of Mickey's lab were the proving ground. Walt Disney himself voices Mickey, as he still did in this era; Billy Bletcher growls Pete, Pinto Colvig plays Pluto, Clarence Nash — Donald's voice — supplies the cat, mouse, spider and assorted roars, and Jimmy MacDonald, who would inherit Mickey's voice from Walt a decade later, squeaks the fly. Paul Smith's score is built on Franz von Suppé's Light Cavalry Overture, galloping along under the mayhem.
The title is the old proverb — "even a worm will turn" — and the title card runs with the idiom, showing a worm rounding on a bird; neither animal appears in the cartoon. The premise carries more than a whiff of Jekyll and Hyde, and animation historians have noted that Tom and Jerry's "Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Mouse" trod remarkably similar ground a decade later. The cat's nine lives, depicted as a procession of little angels, reprise a gag from Pluto's Judgement Day; Pete's bellowed "I knew I'd get ya!" was dusted off 76 years later for the 2013 short Get a Horse! This copy is taken from the Walt Disney Cartoon Classics: Limited Gold Edition "Mickey" VHS (1984), where the short sat third in the lineup between Mickey's Grand Opera and Mickey's Parrot.

programme.title: Shy Guy
programme.desc:
Phil Norton is new in town and new at school, and he spends his lunch hours alone and his evenings in the basement, building radios and record players. His father — finding him down there again — puts the problem in Phil's own language: a component has to fit in, so it can work with all the other parts. So Phil goes back to school and does what an engineer would do. He observes. He watches the popular kids to work out what actually makes them liked, and the data surprises him: it isn't looks or money or noise, it's that they pay attention to other people. Phil tries it — asks questions, listens, offers to help a classmate fix a broken record player — and by the final reel the basement workshop is full of friends.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and directed by Ted Peshak, the house director behind many of Coronet's postwar guidance films. In keeping with Coronet practice, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Alice Sowers, Ph.D., director of the Family Life Institute at the University of Oklahoma. Released to classrooms in August 1947, it became one of the most widely shown of all the social guidance shorts — the genre's usual prescription of conformity delivered, for once, with a certain sweetness: the film never asks Phil to stop building radios, only to look up from the workbench occasionally.
Two people made their film debuts in these thirteen minutes, and both became fixtures of American television. Phil is a nineteen-year-old Dick York, then a busy Chicago radio actor, seventeen years before he became Darrin Stephens on Bewitched; educational and industrial films like this one were his bread and butter for years. And the narrator's voice belongs to a young Chicago announcer named Myron Wallace — who, as Mike Wallace, would spend nearly four decades asking harder questions on 60 Minutes.

programme.title: Birds Of A Feather
programme.desc: The seventeenth Silly Symphony — a pastoral celebration of avian life and Bert Lewis's final score for the series. Swans glide across a tranquil lake, a proud peacock displays its plumage in glorious monochrome, a passing duck jeers, lyrebirds play each other's tails, songbirds fill the air, a woodpecker pursues a caterpillar, and owls croon at dusk. A mother hen busily hunts worms while neglecting her chicks, until a menacing hawk circles overhead. When the raptor snatches a chick, the entire bird community forms an attack squadron, swarming and dive-bombing the hawk in remarkably fluid animation. Variety (April 15, 1931) was unimpressed: "This subject suffers from too much similarity with previous cartoons of this and other series... a concoction of rhythmic gyration by various fowl." But the film earned admiration from an unexpected quarter: Soviet filmmaker Sergei Eisenstein cited it in his influential book The Film Sense as an exemplary case of audio-visual synchronization, specifically praising the peacock display sequence. A three-month Sunday comic strip adaptation ran from March to June 1934.

programme.title: Woodland Café
programme.desc: Released March 13, 1937, Woodland Café stages a full insect nightclub revue: a bustling arrival sequence, an Apache-style spider-and-fly floor show, and a packed finale set to "Truckin'" in a Cab Calloway-inspired groove. Story artist Bianca Majolie and director Wilfred Jackson turn bugs, flowers, and leaves into bandstands and dance props, with caricature nods to contemporary celebrity culture. The short is one of Disney's pure rhythm-and-gag Silly Symphonies, while surviving prints and scholarship also document era-specific racialized performance imagery that later edits trimmed in some versions.

programme.title: Figure Eight
programme.desc: An ice skater traces figure eights on the ice while Blossom Dearie sings the eights times table in her unmistakable breathy style. "Figure eight as double four, figure four as half of eight — if you skate, you would be great, if you could make a figure eight." One of the most beautiful Schoolhouse Rock episodes — the animation of the skater gliding through multiplication is genuinely graceful. Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: Lolly, Lolly, Lolly, Get Your Adverbs Here
programme.desc: A father-and-sons street vendor operation sells adverbs from a cart. Bob Dorough and his real-life sons performed this one together. The sales-pitch framing is clever — adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs, and the vendors demonstrate each use case like hawkers showing off their wares. Part of Grammar Rock.

programme.title: Conjunction Junction (Better Than Ezra)
programme.desc: Better Than Ezra covers Conjunction Junction for the Schoolhouse Rock Rocks! tribute album. A pop-rock reimagining of the classic grammar lesson with updated production and new animation. Part of the 2002 compilation where various artists recorded their own versions of Schoolhouse Rock songs.

programme.title: My Hero, Zero (Lemonheads)
programme.desc: The Lemonheads (Evan Dando) cover My Hero, Zero for the Schoolhouse Rock Rocks! tribute compilation. Power-pop take on the Multiplication Rock classic about the number zero as placeholder. Part of the 2002 tribute album series.

programme.title: The Golden Rule
programme.desc:
The film opens with the maxim itself rather than a single character: a carved relief accompanies the King James wording of Luke 6:31, "As ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise," and a teacher then chalks the plainer classroom version - "The Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you" - on the blackboard for a room of young pupils. A world map follows, with hands pinning flags marking the Holy Land and China, showing the same rule recurring in cultures on opposite sides of the globe. From there the lesson moves into ordinary childhood settings rather than a single continuous story: a family sits down to dinner together, two girls stop to talk at a backyard fence and then walk on down the sidewalk, boys play in the street on a bicycle and a tricycle, and in the closing minutes a boy folds and flies a paper airplane, then carries it down the block to share with a girl waiting at her door. Onscreen captions - "as you would have them," "what you would like" - punctuate the vignettes, restating the lesson each time the setting changes.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio on the Smart family estate in Glenview, Illinois, the picture is copyrighted 1953 to John Smart, who took over Coronet's productions after his brother and the company's founder, David A. Smart, died in 1952. The subtitle "A Lesson for Beginners" marks it as one of Coronet's primary-grade releases rather than the junior- and senior-high guidance shorts the studio is best remembered for. As on those films, the only credited participant is the educational collaborator named on the title card: A. M. Johnston, Ph.D., Associate Professor of Education at the University of Tennessee, recorded on the RCA Sound System. No director or cast is credited on screen.
The film belongs to the broad run of postwar "social guidance" shorts Coronet produced through the late 1940s and 1950s, which leaned on local nonprofessional performers rather than name actors to model behavior for classroom audiences. "The Golden Rule" is thinly documented outside its own print: it has no IMDb entry, and no Letterboxd or TMDb page could be located for it. The surviving copy has circulated through the stock-footage archive A.V. Geeks, whose catalogue description likewise characterizes the film as a series of everyday vignettes illustrating the rule - matching what the print itself shows.

programme.title: A Victim of Gravity
programme.desc: Newton's apple, falling objects, and the universal force that keeps us stuck to the Earth. The first Science Rock episode introduces gravity through a kid who keeps dropping things and wondering why everything falls down, never up. The animation visualizes gravitational pull as an invisible hand. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: Report from the North Pole
programme.desc: Climate change is melting the polar ice caps. A report from the North Pole about rising temperatures, shrinking glaciers, and what it means for polar bears and the planet. The first Earth Rock episode, part of the 2009 direct-to-video revival focused on environmental education.

programme.title: Fat Cat Blue: The Clean Rivers Song
programme.desc: River pollution and the importance of clean waterways. A bluesy cat laments what has happened to the rivers — industrial runoff, sewage, and litter turning clear water murky. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Khalif-Aist
programme.desc:
A bored, beautiful Caliph of Baghdad buys a magic powder from a peddler: sniff it, say "Mutabor," and you become any animal you wish. Say "Mutabor" again and you change back. One rule: never laugh while transformed. The Caliph and his Vizier become storks — graceful, long-necked, free — and then they laugh, and the word vanishes from their minds, and they are trapped.
The story comes from Wilhelm Hauff, a German writer who died of typhoid at twenty-four in 1827, leaving behind a shelf of fairy tales that remain staples in German-speaking countries. "Kalif Storch" was published in his first Märchen Almanach in 1826, written for the children of a Württemberg general whose family he tutored. Hauff had studied theology at Tübingen, but his gift was for the exotic and the strange — Arabian settings, cursed transformations, moral fables wrapped in spectacle.
Valeriy Ugarov's 1981 animation for Soyuzmultfilm translates Hauff's tale into something hallucinatory. The art style is dense and psychedelic — ornamental Islamic patterns that breathe and shift, a Caliph drawn as a languid, androgynous figure whose transformation into a stork is both beautiful and disturbing. Letterboxd reviewers call it "body horror before body horror was mainstream" and describe an out-of-body experience watching it. The film sits at the intersection of fairy tale and fever dream.
The voice cast is staggering. The Caliph is voiced by Innokenty Smoktunovsky — the greatest actor in Russian cinema history, the man Laurence Olivier called the most brilliant Hamlet he had ever seen (Kozintsev's 1964 film, Lenin Prize). Smoktunovsky was born in a Siberian village in 1925, fought at Kursk and the Dnieper, started in provincial theatre in Krasnoyarsk, and stunned Leningrad with his Prince Myshkin. He voiced the narrator of Tarkovsky's Mirror. He played Tchaikovsky, Salieri, and Uncle Vanya. He appears as a cameo in Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears. A minor planet is named after him. Here, his voice is soft and insinuating — "bewitching with its iridescent intonations," as one reviewer wrote.
The evil wizard is Vasily Livanov — the definitive Russian Sherlock Holmes, also the voice of Karlsson-on-the-Roof and Gena the Crocodile, two of the most beloved characters in Soviet animation. The Vizier is Yuri Yakovlev, another giant of Soviet cinema. The fairy is Inna Churikova. Even the animator Garri Bardin, himself a legendary figure in Russian stop-motion, voices a minor role.
Ugarov directed from Soyuzmultfilm, where he had worked since the early 1970s. He would later direct The Magic Flute for the Operavox series — a Welsh-Russian co-production with S4C — and contributed to Animated Tales of the World. His connection to Wales started even earlier, with "The Quest for Olwen" (1990), a Soyuzmultfilm/S4C adaptation of Welsh Mabinogion mythology that established the pipeline. He died in 2007.

programme.title: How To Be Well-Groomed
programme.desc:
Don and Sue are a well-scrubbed brother and sister whose entire day, it turns out, is organized around looking presentable. The morning starts with an alarm clock and a made bed, then moves through the sink and the mirror: washing, combing, cleaning fingernails. Sue skips red nail polish because, the narrators explain, it would only call attention to her stubby hands, and Don works through his own ritual of shaving and picking a tie in front of the glass, a Rice pennant tacked up on his wall behind him. Evenings run the same machinery in reverse — an iron on the board, shoes buffed to a shine, blouses and skirts hung with care in a closet barely large enough to hold them. The family sits down to breakfast together, mother included, and the dual narrators — a man and a woman trading lines — keep tallying the payoff: good habits that, they insist, make Don and Sue "the kind of people you'd like to know." The week's grooming builds to Friday night, when Sue chooses a dress and Don straightens his jacket, and the two head out the door turned out for their dates.
The film's title card carries a copyright date of MCMXLVIII — 1948 — under producer David A. Smart's name, though the Prelinger Archives and A.V. Geeks catalogs both list it under 1949, evidently the year the short actually reached classrooms. As was Coronet's standard practice, no director is credited on screen; the sole named contributor is the subject-matter consultant, billed on her own card as "Educational Collaborator Mary E. Weathersby, Head, Homemaking Education Department, Mississippi State College." Coronet Instructional Films, the Chicago-area studio David Smart built out of his Coronet and Esquire magazine ventures, supplied schools with hundreds of these shorts, and the recurring formula — an authority figure's name up front, an anonymous director behind the camera — appears here exactly as it does elsewhere in the catalog.
"How To Be Well-Groomed" belongs to the wave of postwar social-guidance shorts that scholar Michelle Boulé has dated to a 1947-1957 heyday, films built to model "preferred behaviors" for teenagers through tidy, repeatable rituals rather than drama. The two-narrator technique on display here — a man's voice and a woman's trading observations about Don and Sue's choices — was one of the genre's stock devices for making conformity sound like friendly advice. The film has been preserved and made publicly available through the Prelinger Archives, where cataloger Ken Smith (whose own reference book on the genre, "Mental Hygiene," draws on prints like this one) noted the shot list's small, telling details, and separately through the A/V Geeks 16mm Archive, which digitized its own surviving copy for continued classroom-history use.

programme.title: The China Plate
programme.desc: The eighteenth Silly Symphony, based on the classic Willow pattern legend traditionally depicted on blue-and-white pottery. An oriental scene painted on a decorative china plate comes magically to life: two young lovers whose romance is disrupted by an angry, corpulent Emperor — the girl's father — who pursues them relentlessly for disturbing his rest. The chase escalates when a fearsome fire-breathing dragon joins the hunt. In a darkly humorous twist, the Emperor mistakes the dragon's gaping maw for a cave entrance and is promptly devoured, allowing the lovers to escape. Notable for the complete absence of dialogue — just sound effects and Frank Churchill's musical score. The Film Daily (June 14, 1931) called it "real and different entertainment all the way," highlighting novelty over humor. Variety (June 30, 1931) noted it had earned prime placement at the Roxy Theatre: "The biggest arena of 'em all has gone cartoon for the last couple of shows. Pen and ink reels aren't being restricted to the supper hour, but are flashing at the deluxe performances right after the newsreel... good enough to fit any big house layout." Directed by Wilfred Jackson, one of Disney's most prolific directors who would go on to helm classics from Cinderella to Lady and the Tramp.

programme.title: The Busy Beavers
programme.desc: A colony of beavers works through the night building a dam, gnawing trees in rhythmic unison and floating logs downstream in an elaborate construction effort synchronized to music. When a sudden storm breaks the dam and sends floodwaters surging through their work, the beavers rally together in a frantic race to repair the breach before everything is lost. Their coordinated teamwork saves the day, and the colony celebrates with a triumphant dance. One of the final black-and-white Silly Symphonies before Disney embraced Technicolor, the short showcases the studio's growing mastery of naturalistic animal animation and synchronized musical choreography.

programme.title: Father Noah's Ark
programme.desc: Released just weeks before Three Little Pigs, this is Disney's first animated pass at Noah: part Biblical pageant, part slapstick weather report. Wilfred Jackson stages the Ark as a full production line, with Ham, Shem, and Japheth hammering from dawn to dark while their wives stack provisions and Noah keeps the chaos moving. When the flood finally hits, the short pivots into pure Silly Symphony business: waves battering the ship, lightning chasing Noah from porthole to porthole, and animal pairs packed wall-to-wall in rhythmic motion. Leigh Harline builds the score around Beethoven's 12 Contredanses, giving the picture a formal dance backbone even when gags are flying. It also left a long Disney afterimage: decades later, Fantasia 2000's Pomp and Circumstance segment would revisit the same Ark setup with a different visual style and scale.

programme.title: I'm Just a Bill
programme.desc: A piece of legislation sits on the steps of Capitol Hill explaining how a bill becomes a law. Jack Sheldon voices the weary, hopeful Bill who must survive committee, floor votes, filibusters, and presidential veto to become a law. Arguably the single most culturally impactful Schoolhouse Rock episode — referenced in The Simpsons, Saturday Night Live, and countless civics classes. It taught more Americans about the legislative process than any textbook. Part of America Rock.

programme.title: You Oughta Be Savin' Water
programme.desc: Water conservation — shorter showers, fixing leaky faucets, not running the tap while brushing teeth. Fresh water is finite and precious. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Your Thrift Habits
programme.desc:
Jack is broke, and he knows exactly why: a nickel here for a Berry Supreme sundae at the corner soda fountain, three dollars there for a ticket to the State College-All Stars game at Folger Stadium, and the rest gone to movies and odds and ends he can't quite account for. What he wants is a camera like the one his friend Ralph already owns, and he can't see how he'll ever get there on the money he has. Sitting down with an older advisor to work out where his allowance actually goes, Jack draws his income as a pie sliced into lunches, carfare, snacks, and personal spending, then writes himself a plain warning on a sheet of paper: "Watch these expenses!" From there it's a matter of engineering rather than willpower — a weekly budget, a savings line charted week over week, and a homemade progress gauge built around the shape of the camera he's saving for. The line climbs toward twenty-five dollars, and by the last reel Jack is signing his own name to the purchase.
Coronet Instructional Films copyrighted the picture in 1948 (MCMXLVIII, per the title card, under founder David A. Smart), produced with the company's usual RCA sound system billing. As with the rest of Coronet's guidance line, the only credit on screen belongs to the educational collaborator: Paul L. Salsgiver, director of the School of Business at Simmons College, whose academic standing was meant to give the budgeting lesson classroom authority. No actors are credited on screen, and no cast for this specific title could be corroborated in outside sources, so none is listed here.
Released to schools on 31 August 1948, Your Thrift Habits belongs to Coronet's long run of postwar social-guidance shorts, this one aimed squarely at consumer economics rather than manners or dating etiquette: a teenager's income, once it's actually itemized, turns out to be manageable if not exactly generous. It survives today through the Prelinger Archives, cataloged there as a lesson in budgeting and the choice between immediate and future satisfactions — a small, plainly made document of how postwar American schools tried to teach thrift to a generation raised on installment plans and drugstore sodas.

programme.title: The Merry Dwarfs
programme.desc: The fifth Silly Symphony — and the first to feature humans, however diminutive. Released as Prohibition still gripped America, the film opens with a band of identical bearded dwarfs hammering anvils to Verdi's "Anvil Chorus" from Il trovatore in their woodland village. They shoe a grasshopper and a centipede by playing their many feet like xylophones. Then the beer flows. They dance with barrels, jump through hoops, leap into beer steins, drink heavily, and dance some more. The finale: two dwarfs pirouetting atop a flower tumble into a barrel of beer, emerge soused, and stagger through a world gone wavy and distorted — the entire screen warps in sympathy with their inebriation. Motion Picture News called it "the first of the series in which humans are introduced," noting the "rollicking band of gnomes filled with the spirit of music and dance." The Film Daily declared it would "cop the glory from a number of features," while Variety, comparing it to The Skeleton Dance and Springtime, admitted it was "not as good, but almost." Eight years later Disney returned to dwarfs for Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the transformation revealing just how far the studio's artistry had evolved. The dwarfs made a cameo in Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) during "Smile Darn Ya Smile." The film entered the US public domain on January 1, 2025.

programme.title: Winter
programme.desc: The fourteenth Silly Symphony and the climactic finale to Disney's ambitious four-seasons cycle begun with Springtime. Snow blankets the forest. When icy winds howl, the creatures take shelter — bears attempt to hibernate, though a playful cub refuses to stay asleep. When the wind subsides, raccoons sneeze from the cold, moose brave the frozen waters, and an enchanting menagerie of woodland animals glide across the ice in an elaborate skating ballet, dancing in pairs and elaborate group formations. The film culminates with animals gathering around a groundhog to divine spring's return before the winds send them scurrying back to shelter. The Film Daily (December 28, 1930) offered a notably tepid review: "This Disney Silly Symphony doesn't stand up with previous releases. The synchrony is well done and the animation up to the average but it lacks gags for laughs. Much snow, skating and sliding, with the usual animal antics for nothing particularly clever." A fair assessment — the seasons cycle had grown formulaic — but the four-film arc nonetheless demonstrated Disney's ambition to explore thematic serialization within the Silly Symphonies, laying groundwork for the narrative-driven shorts that would follow.

programme.title: Funny Little Bunnies
programme.desc: Disney's only Easter-themed cartoon, released March 24, 1934, and one of the studio's most elaborate assembly-line fantasies. At rainbow's end, rabbit crews run an entire confectionery operation: eggs are molded, painted in plaid and polka dots, packed, and rolled out with military efficiency while chickens and chorus voices keep the factory humming. The score blends Frank Churchill and Leigh Harline, giving the short both nursery-song charm and rhythmic industrial momentum. Wilfred Jackson assigns distinct rabbit business to different animators, and the production is notable as the earliest known Disney animation work by future Nine Old Men director Wolfgang Reitherman. The result feels like a pastel cousin to Santa's Workshop: same fascination with process, same delight in synchronized labor, but built around springtime candy engineering instead of Christmas toys.

programme.title: I'm Gonna Send Your Vote to College
programme.desc: The Electoral College explained. Your vote goes to college — the Electoral College — where electors cast the actual ballots for President. A revival-era America Rock episode that tackles one of the most confusing parts of American democracy. The surround-sound remix suggests this is from a later home video release. Jack Sheldon returns to voice the befuddled voter trying to understand why his vote takes a detour through 538 electors.

programme.title: The Weather Show
programme.desc: How weather works — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and the water cycle. Sun heats the ocean, water evaporates, clouds form, rain falls, rivers flow back to the ocean, repeat. The last of the original Science Rock episodes, wrapping up the 1970s run with the biggest system of all: the atmosphere. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: The Rainforest
programme.desc: Tropical rainforests — their biodiversity, their role as the lungs of the planet, and the threat of deforestation. Millions of species live in rainforests, many not yet discovered. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Mind Your Manners
programme.desc:
A hand draws a cartoon on a blackboard — a couple bumping into each other, tempers fraying — under the chalked warning "Watch it! Your manners are showing!" That gag sets up the day the film then follows: a teenager named Jack moving from the breakfast table to school to the soda shop, with his manners tested at every stop. At home he minds his appearance before a hallway mirror and sits down to a family dinner with his mother, father, and sister. At school he waits his turn in a hallway lined with lockers, ducks into the library, and settles into a crowded classroom. After hours he catches a Glenview Bus Co. coach across town and lands with friends at a windmill-themed soda fountain, where a waitress in Dutch cap and apron works the booths while the kids talk, share, and needle a stalled car with its hood up out at the curb. The film's thesis is practical rather than moralizing: it drills the same short list of courtesies — greetings, waiting, sharing, tidy dress, table manners — through one ordinary day's worth of settings, trusting repetition over lecture.
Coronet Instructional Films of Glenview, Illinois copyrighted the picture in 1953 (the title card reads "Copyright MCMLIII, John Smart") and recorded it on the RCA Sound System, standard for the studio's output at the time. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance cycle, the only name that appears on screen belongs to the educational collaborator: Margaret M. Justin, Ph.D., Dean of the School of Home Economics at Kansas State College, who vetted the etiquette lessons for classroom use. No director is credited on the print, and none is attested for this specific title elsewhere, so none is listed here. The Glenview Bus Co. coach visible mid-film is a nice bit of incidental local color, consistent with the studio's home base outside Chicago.
Like Coronet's other manners-and-conduct shorts of the era, Mind Your Manners was built for classroom rental rather than theatrical release, one entry in a long run of social-guidance titles the company issued through the 1940s and '50s. It has since passed into the public domain and circulates through the Internet Archive and preservation outlets such as A/V Geeks, which catalogue it as a straightforward etiquette lesson built around a teenage character the site names Jack Connor. Seen today, it holds up as a plain, earnest artifact of postwar classroom instruction — a checklist of small courtesies dramatized rather than a story anyone would mistake for entertainment.

programme.title: The Fox Hunt
programme.desc: An English fox hunt erupts across the countryside as aristocratic riders and their hounds pursue a wily fox who consistently outwits the bumbling hunters through comic reversals. The chase careens through fields and hedgerows, the fox exploiting every opportunity to humiliate his pursuers while the music drives the frenetic pace. Dawn-breaking silhouette sequences showcase the studio's growing command of atmospheric backgrounds. A lesser-remembered entry in the black-and-white Silly Symphonies, the short nonetheless demonstrates Disney's increasingly confident integration of music-driven action and personality animation, with George Voelker Jr.'s "A Hunt in the Black Forest" woven into Frank Churchill's lively score.

programme.title: The Wise Little Hen
programme.desc: Wilfred Jackson's The Wise Little Hen adapts The Little Red Hen into a farm-economy parable where laziness gets a castor-oil punchline, but the short's larger place in animation history is Donald Duck's screen debut. Clarence Nash's voice performance, discovered after Jackson heard his duck impression and took it to Walt Disney, gives Donald immediate comic identity even before the character's design fully settles. Leigh Harline's "Help Me Plant My Corn" keeps the film moving as Mrs. Hen outworks Donald and Peter Pig, and later scholarship has read the cartoon's labor-and-reward logic against Great Depression and New Deal anxieties around self-sufficiency. With that mix of topical subtext and durable character introduction, this Silly Symphony is both a period document and the launch point for one of Disney's defining personalities.

programme.title: Ready or Not, Here I Come
programme.desc: A game of hide-and-seek teaches the fives times table. "Five, ten, fifteen, twenty — ready or not, here I come!" Counting by fives is the most natural skip-counting pattern (it mirrors how we read clocks and count coins), and this episode leans into that intuition. Part of Multiplication Rock. Sung with a playful energy that captures the excitement of the chase.

programme.title: The Three Rs
programme.desc: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle — the three Rs of environmental responsibility. The most recognizable Earth Rock episode, featuring a live-action pop-punk performance that is a significant stylistic departure from the hand-drawn animation of the classic series. Originally aired on Disney Channel. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Thru the Mirror
programme.desc:
Mickey falls asleep reading Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass and dreams himself through his bedroom mirror into a topsy-turvy world where furniture is alive and playing cards have tempers. He shrinks to tabletop size after eating a magic walnut, then performs a Fred Astaire tap dance routine with a pair of living gloves — one of the most celebrated dance sequences in Disney animation. When he waltzes with the Queen of Hearts, the jealous King rallies his cards for a chase sequence that ends with Mickey blown back through the mirror by an electric fan.
The 83rd Mickey Mouse short. Directed by David Hand, story by William Cottrell and Joe Grant. The card marching sequence uses a jazzed-up arrangement of Schubert's Military March in D Major. Music by Frank Churchill, Leigh Harline, and Paul J. Smith — the same team scoring Snow White simultaneously. The animation of Mickey's tap dance was studied frame-by-frame from live-action footage of professional dancers, making it an early example of Disney's rotoscope-adjacent reference technique before it was formalized for Snow White. Released May 30, 1936 by United Artists. Later featured on Walt Disney Treasures: Mickey Mouse in Living Color (2001) and as a bonus on the Alice in Wonderland DVD.

programme.title: Act Your Age
programme.desc:
Jim is working an algebra problem in a crowded classroom when the lead in his prized mechanical pencil snaps. He doesn't ask to borrow a spare; instead he takes the pencil to the top of his desk and starts carving his initials into the wood. That gets him sent to the principal, Mr. Edmonds, who confiscates the pencil but skips the lecture on vandalism and asks Jim to think instead about why he did it. Cutaways recast the outburst as childish rather than criminal: teenagers behaving badly dissolve into five-year-olds throwing the same tantrums, and a grown man on a sandlot diamond drops to the ground kicking and pulling his hair after a bad play, exactly like a scolded toddler. The school janitor adds his own complaint about kids "acting like babies," and Jim, talked into grading himself rather than just apologizing, builds a chart of his own: "How Old Am I?", rating his reactions when someone disagrees with him, pokes fun at him, or won't give him what he wants, scored against columns for today, next month, and next year, with his parents and friends filling in marks alongside his own. He gets the pencil back, and the film closes on Jim owning that the chart, not the excuse, is the honest answer.
Produced at Coronet's Glenview, Illinois studio and copyrighted in 1949 to the studio's founder, Esquire publisher David A. Smart, the picture carries the parenthetical subtitle "(Emotional Maturity)" on its own title card — the actual guidance-curriculum heading Coronet was selling to school boards under a catchier classroom title. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance line, the only credit on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: Wendell W. Wright, Ph.D., Dean of the School of Education at Indiana University, billed as "Educational Collaborator," with an RCA Sound System credit underneath. Coronet's regular postwar staff director, Ted Peshak, is credited with the film; the cast, in keeping with studio practice, goes unnamed on screen and unconfirmed elsewhere, so no actors are listed here.
Act Your Age sits in the same wave of Coronet "social guidance" shorts as Shy Guy and Are You Popular?, aimed at the same classroom hygiene-and-citizenship curricula, but working the material from the disciplinarian's side of the desk rather than the peer group's. Its "How Old Am I?" self-rating chart, turning an abstract scolding about maturity into a homework assignment Jim can fill out and hand back, is the device later viewers of the print have most often singled out as the quintessential Coronet touch — reducing a psychological problem to a worksheet with a solution built in. The film was preserved through Rick Prelinger's ephemeral-film salvage work, catalogued into the Prelinger Collection and digitized for the Internet Archive in 2002, and remains in the public domain today as the same plain classroom print Coronet released in 1949.

programme.title: Santa's Workshop
programme.desc: Originally titled Santa's Toy Shop, this fourth color Silly Symphony was rushed through production for the 1932 holiday season and became a showcase for what Disney's new United Artists budgets could buy: denser crowd animation, richer color design, and assembly-line toy choreography timed to Schubert's Military March. Santa reads children's letters while a floor full of gnomes tune reindeer, weld toys, and feed a parade of wind-up animals into his sack, with Walt Disney himself voicing one of the helpers. Production notes tie the short to Disney's technical transition year: though Powers Cinephone is still credited onscreen, the studio was already shifting toward higher-fidelity RCA Photophone recording. The short also sits in Disney's complicated "From the Vault" history, later edited for some TV and home-video releases because of offensive ethnic caricatures. As pure staging and motion design, though, it is one of the clearest early blueprints for Disney's Christmas iconography.

programme.title: The Old Mill
programme.desc: Released November 5, 1937, The Old Mill is one of Disney's key technical milestones: the first cartoon shot with the multiplane camera and the first Silly Symphony distributed by RKO. With almost no dialogue, it tracks birds, mice, bats, and frogs inside an abandoned windmill as a summer storm escalates from wind and rain into near-catastrophe, then passes by dawn. The short functioned as a proving ground for effects and depth staging that immediately fed Snow White and later Disney features. It won the Academy Award for Best Short Subject (Cartoon), and in 2015 the Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry.

programme.title: Wynken, Blynken And Nod
programme.desc: Graham Heid had co-directed The Old Mill with Wilfred Jackson the previous year; this was his sole outing as lead director, and he made it count. Adapted faithfully from Eugene Field's 1889 poem "Dutch Lullaby," with Leigh Harline setting Field's words to music sung by a soprano throughout. Three babies sail a wooden shoe through the night sky, fishing for stars with candy canes. The multiplane camera — debuted in The Old Mill just months earlier — creates extraordinary depth as the shoe glides through painted cloudbanks and luminous starfields. The babies hook a comet that tows them on a wild ride before a storm breaks their mast and sends them tumbling. They slide home on moonbeams, and the reveal lands: three children are really one sleeping boy, Wynken and Blynken his two eyes, Nod his nodding head, the wooden shoe his trundle-bed. Leonard Maltin called it "as extravagant as any Disney feature," and he was right — the effects animation alone, handled by George Rowley and Ugo D'Orsi, bursts from every frame. A direct precursor to Fantasia.

programme.title: Sufferin' Till Suffrage
programme.desc: The fight for women's right to vote, from the Seneca Falls Convention through the 19th Amendment. One of the more substantive America Rock episodes, covering real history with real stakes. The wordplay in the title — suffering until suffrage — captures the patience and pain of a 72-year movement in three words. Part of America Rock. Performed by Essra Mohawk.

programme.title: The Trash Can Band
programme.desc: Recycling and reuse through music — a band that makes instruments out of trash. Cans become drums, bottles become flutes, junk becomes art. The message is that waste is a failure of imagination. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Date Etiquette
programme.desc:
A boy at the lockers works up to asking a classmate out, and the film follows the date start to finish exactly the way its own catalog description promises: the asking and the accepting, the call at her house, the evening out, and the goodnight at the door. He arrives to collect her properly and is walked into the parlor to meet her parents, seated and watching him make the right impression before he's allowed to take their daughter anywhere. The two of them join a crowd of classmates at a school affair built around a hallway soda fountain, all charm bracelets and small talk over paper cups, before pairing off to a restaurant booth, where the real lesson plays out in miniature: what to order, how to make conversation, who looks after the check. The night winds down the way it started, on a porch in near-darkness, with a goodnight exchanged in the same careful, rehearsed register as everything that came before it.
Coronet Instructional Films' only screen credit is its usual one: "Educational Collaborator Evelyn M. Duvall, Ph.D., Consultant, National Council on Family Relations," over the RCA Sound System card. The copyright record filed with the Library of Congress lists the short at 354 feet of 16mm, registered to David A. Smart on April 7, 1952 — a length that runs almost exactly the ten minutes Coronet built its classroom reels to fit. Duvall was no rented name for the title card: she had stepped down in 1951 after six years as executive secretary of the National Council on Family Relations and had just published Facts of Life and Love for Teenagers (1950), one of the first mainstream dating guides aimed at teenagers themselves rather than their parents. Date Etiquette plays like that book's table of contents staged with a cast of unbilled teenagers, each beat of the evening — invitation, parents, the affair, the restaurant, the doorstep — treated as a discrete skill to be gotten right.
It belongs to a run of Coronet dating shorts from the period, alongside titles like What to Do on a Date (1950), that walked the same courtship through in careful procedural order, with Duvall or another family-life consultant standing in for the studio's actual authorship. No director or performer is named on the print, and none has turned up attached to this particular title with any confidence — the film's teenagers are meant to be interchangeable models of correct behavior, not characters. The surviving print comes down through the Gordon Elgart Collection at Prelinger Archives, cataloged with its original one-line description from a 1953 Educational Film Guide entry, the same synopsis this note draws from.

programme.title: Cock O' The Walk
programme.desc: Released November 30, 1935, Cock O' The Walk reframes barnyard romance as prizefight spectacle. A championship rooster arrives to cheering hens, steals another rooster's sweetheart, and humiliates his rival in the ring, until a photo exposing his hidden family flips the crowd and the match. Ben Sharpsteen directs it as a parody of both boxing melodrama and Busby Berkeley-style choreography, with the comeback kiss triggering one of Disney's most shamelessly crowd-pleasing reversals. The major story is musical: more than half the short is built on Vincent Youmans's recent hit "The Carioca" from Flying Down to Rio, unusual for Silly Symphonies, which generally quoted outside tunes only in brief fragments. J.B. Kaufman and Russell Merritt note the score is split around that centerpiece: Frank Churchill handles the pre-Carioca material, and Albert Hay Malotte takes over afterward for his Symphony debut.

programme.title: The Country Cousin
programme.desc: An Aesop adaptation that Disney staff later singled out as one of the studio's strongest shorts, The Country Cousin premiered October 31, 1936 and won the Academy Award for Animated Short at the 9th Oscars. Wilfred Jackson stages the city-mouse banquet as a social nightmare: the visiting country mouse Monty can barely survive cocktails, loud jazz, and predatory housecats while his slick cousin Abner treats danger as nightlife. The centerpiece is Monty's accidental champagne binge, animated as a full drunk routine with floating hiccup bubbles and rubbery balance shifts that animation historians have linked to the delirium style Disney would revisit in Dumbo's "Pink Elephants on Parade." Art Babbitt, Les Clark, and Dick Lundy push dense acting in tiny gestures, especially Monty's panic responses to every urban hazard. The moral lands hard: he flees home to plain crackers, choosing safety and quiet over glamorous terror.

programme.title: Little Hiawatha
programme.desc: Inspired by Longfellow's The Song of Hiawatha, this May 15, 1937 short follows a would-be young hunter whose bravado collapses into empathy. Little Hiawatha cannot bring himself to shoot a rabbit, then needs rescue from an enraged mother bear; the same woodland animals he spared help him escape. Disney's archives note Walt briefly explored expanding Hiawatha into a feature before shelving the idea. The short was the final Silly Symphony released through United Artists, and it remains both a technically polished animal-action cartoon and a clear example of 1930s Hollywood's simplified, ahistorical Native imagery.

programme.title: Unpack Your Adjectives
programme.desc: A girl goes on a camping trip and unpacks adjectives from her backpack to describe everything she encounters. Blossom Dearie returns with her whispery delivery, turning grammar into a nature hike. The camping frame makes abstract description concrete — you need adjectives to tell someone what the bear looked like. Part of Grammar Rock.

programme.title: Control Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Jeff Moore is seventeen and having a bad Friday. He's the designated driver for a triple date that night, and everything conspires against him along the way: the car won't start in the garage, his kid brother Roger is underfoot and easy to frighten, his mother and his sister Joan want things from him at exactly the wrong moments, and his friends needle him at the drugstore soda fountain while he waits on a stalled engine. A psychologist in a white coat keeps interrupting from behind a desk to sort Jeff's afternoon into three labeled blocks — RAGE, FEAR, LOVE — treating each flare-up as a case study in how those basic emotions get triggered, and how they can be managed instead of vented. By evening Jeff has stopped slamming doors and started thinking before he reacts; the film closes on the same picnic-ground bonfire it opened with, the whole group gathered around it roasting marshmallows, dates delivered and temper intact.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio on David A. Smart's estate in Glenview, Illinois — Smart, the Esquire magazine publisher, had set up Coronet in 1946 as a dedicated producer of 16mm classroom shorts — and copyrighted 1950 (the title card reads "Copyright MCML David A. Smart"). As with the rest of the line, the only person named on screen is the psychology consultant: the card credits Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College. Lauer's usual specialty at Iowa State was traffic safety — he headed the college's Driver Training Laboratory and is credited on Coronet's driver-education shorts of the same period — so his appearance here, consulting on temper rather than turn signals, is a small crossover into the studio's general social-guidance catalog. Letterboxd and TMDB both credit the direction to Ted Peshak, Coronet's regular postwar house director.
The film sits in Coronet's long run of postwar social guidance, or "mental hygiene," shorts made for classroom use, alongside titles like Are You Popular? and Shy Guy — all built on the same premise, that an adolescent's raw feeling is a problem to be labeled, explained, and brought under control rather than simply expressed. The Prelinger Archives, which preserved and catalogs this print, summarize it in a single line: well-balanced emotions help to create a well-rounded personality, especially in teenagers. Like most of Coronet's guidance output, the film has long since passed into the public domain and survives today chiefly through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Paddle to the Sea
programme.desc: A boy in Nipigon country, north of Lake Superior, carves a small wooden figure of an Indian in a canoe. On the bottom he scratches: "Please put me back in the water. I am Paddle to the Sea." He sets it in the snow. When spring comes, the meltwater carries the tiny canoe into a creek, then a river, then the Great Lakes themselves. Over what feels like years, Paddle survives sawmills, forest fires, Niagara Falls, ocean freighters, and the frozen surface of Lake Erie — carried always by the current, always toward the sea. Bill Mason was a commercial artist in Winnipeg when the National Film Board of Canada finally agreed to let him adapt Holling C. Holling's 1941 children's book. Mason — who would later be called "the patron saint of canoeing" — directed, shot, and edited the film himself, on a budget of $70,913. He taught himself to carve in order to make the tiny boats, and had to replace them when they drifted off at sea or were lost over Niagara Falls. For the Niagara Falls sequence, Mason and his colleague Blake James did not ask permission to climb over the safety fence at Horseshoe Falls. They rappelled down to the water's edge, James cast the boat into the current, and Mason filmed it going over. There was no Plan B. The film differs from Holling's book in one significant way: Mason added a sequence where the tiny boat must endure polluted waters, shot on Lake Superior near Marathon, Ontario. In 1966, environmentalism was not yet a mainstream concern; Mason was ahead of his time, and spent his career making films about wolves, wilderness, and the fragility of the Canadian landscape. The launch scene was actually filmed in Gatineau Park, not Nipigon. For the forest fire sequence, Mason installed spruce trees along the shoreline of Meech Lake and set them on fire, with the local fire department standing by. Louis Applebaum composed the score. Stanley Jackson narrated. The film was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film at the 40th Academy Awards in 1968. To attend the ceremony, Mason drove from Canada to Los Angeles with a canoe strapped to the roof of his car, stopping at rivers along the way to paddle. He did not win. He didn't care. Today, one of his hand-carved canoe replicas is on display at the Canadian Museum of History. His red Chestnut Prospector — the 16-foot canvas-covered canoe he considered the most versatile design ever manufactured — was donated to the Canadian Canoe Museum in Peterborough, Ontario, after his death from cancer in 1988. He was 59. A rock spire in the midst of Virginia Falls in Nahanni National Park is informally called "Mason's Rock." A 72-acre outdoor classroom in Ottawa bears his name. His children, Paul and Becky, are both canoeists and artists. The film is 28 minutes long. It is one of the most beautiful things you will ever see. It asks nothing of you except to watch a tiny carved figure travel from snow to sea, helped along by strangers who read the message on the bottom and put him back in the water.

programme.title: Overcoming Fear
programme.desc:
At a busy municipal swimming pool, a teenage boy named Bill hangs back while the rest of the gang runs for the water. The opening shots track a crowd of kids racing past the diving boards and pool chairs, then settle on Bill alone at the water's edge and again by the locker-room doors, in his trunks but not going in. Mr. Barker, the pool's swimming coach, doesn't order him in; he sits down with Bill, first at poolside and then on a locker-room bench, and gets him to name what actually scares him about the water. The film then leaves the pool for a run of short vignettes on other, smaller fears — a backyard talk near the clothesline, a girl coaxing a small dog she's wary of, a scene in a book-lined room — before bringing Bill back to the water for a deliberately paced sequence of steps: standing in the shallow end, floating, finally diving from the board on his own. By the last reel he is swimming freestyle across the pool and crouching at the steps to help a smaller child in, one of the crowd he had been avoiding at the start.
Produced at Coronet's studio in Glenview, Illinois — the estate David A. Smart, the Esquire magazine publisher, converted into a 16mm production facility for his instructional-film business — and copyrighted MCML under the Coronet trademark, with the RCA Sound System credit that runs across the studio's postwar output. As with the rest of that catalog, no actors or director are named on screen; the only credit in the title cards is the educational collaborator, Herbert Sorenson, Ph.D., professor of educational psychology at the University of Kentucky and author of textbooks in the field, brought in to keep Barker's breakdown of Bill's fear grounded in contemporary psychology rather than simple reassurance.
Overcoming Fear belongs to the same run of Coronet social-guidance shorts as Shy Guy and Are You Popular?, made for classroom health units rather than theatrical release. The Prelinger Archives catalog description matches the print scene for scene: Bill's fear of the water, Barker's coaching, and the gradual buildup of swimming skill and confidence. No director or cast credits for this specific title turn up in any accessible filmography — Coronet's own credits stop at the consultant, and surviving catalog entries do not even agree on the running time of the print, some logging it under twelve minutes and others closer to thirteen. What holds constant across every source is the premise: fear treated as a nameable, solvable problem, worked through with the same brisk manner Coronet brought to its other studies of adolescent anxiety.

programme.title: The Clock Store
programme.desc: At midnight in a clock shop, timepieces of every variety spring to life — grandfather clocks waltz, cuckoo birds emerge for a chorus, alarm clocks jitter and bounce, and a tiny clock couple dances a romantic duet. The revelry builds into an elaborate synchronized musical number before dawn approaches and every clock scrambles back to its shelf, frozen and innocent when the shopkeeper arrives. Wilfred Jackson directed what became one of the most popular Silly Symphonies of the black-and-white era, its premise of objects coming alive after hours establishing a template Disney would revisit throughout the decade.

programme.title: King Neptune
programme.desc: The second color Silly Symphony after Flowers and Trees, King Neptune was designed for three-strip Technicolor from the outset rather than retrofitted mid-production. Neptune holds an operetta-style underwater court until drunken pirates kidnap a mermaid, triggering a full marine counterattack: sawfish become living weapons, eels fire like electric artillery, and sea creatures improvise a cartoon naval war. Production records place the story meeting on May 10, 1932, with animation assignments in June; veteran animators handled the personality scenes while younger artists trained under Ben Sharpsteen and Dave Hand took on the battle-heavy crowd action. The short also seeded a durable Disney archetype: the same broad, bearded character design was reused for Santa in Santa's Workshop and for Father Noah the next year. A 1933 Blue Ribbon pop-up book paired King Neptune with Babes in the Woods, showing how quickly the short became merchandising material.

programme.title: The Preamble
programme.desc: The Preamble to the United States Constitution, set to music and sung in its entirety. Generations of Americans learned the Preamble not from school but from this three-minute cartoon. The melody is so effective as a mnemonic that adults who watched this as children can still sing it decades later but cannot recite it without the tune. Part of America Rock. Performed by Lynn Ahrens.

programme.title: I'm Just a Bill (Folk Implosion)
programme.desc: Folk Implosion (Lou Barlow of Dinosaur Jr/Sebadoh) covers the iconic civics lesson. A lo-fi indie rock version of the most famous Schoolhouse Rock song. Part of the 2002 Schoolhouse Rock Rocks! tribute compilation.

programme.title: Brave Little Tailor
programme.desc:
Mickey the tailor kills seven flies at once and brags about it within earshot of villagers discussing a giant terrorizing the kingdom. Gossip inflates "seven with one blow" into seven giants. The king offers Princess Minnie's hand and vast riches to whoever can subdue the giant. Smitten, Mickey accepts — then realizes he has no idea how to catch a giant.
What follows is nine minutes of the best physical comedy Disney ever animated: Mickey gets scooped into the giant's mouth with a handful of pumpkins, latches onto his uvula, gets smoked inside a haystack-cigar, pokes the giant's nose with scissors, and finally sews him up with needle and thread. The defeated giant is chained down and turned into an amusement park ride powered by his own snoring.
Nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film at the 11th Academy Awards — lost to Ferdinand the Bull, also Disney. Ranked 26th on the 50 Greatest Cartoons list compiled by 1,000 animation professionals. The animation team is staggering: Les Clark, Ollie Johnston, Fred Moore, Frank Thomas, and Bill Tytla — four of Disney's Nine Old Men plus Tytla, who animated Chernabog in Fantasia. Joe Grant wrote the story. Music by Albert Hay Malotte, who later composed "The Lord's Prayer." Walt Disney voices Mickey. The 103rd Mickey Mouse short. Released September 23, 1938 by RKO.
This film was part of Disney's deliberate campaign to revive Mickey's fading popularity — by the late 1930s, Donald Duck, Goofy, Popeye, and Porky Pig had all surpassed him. The other rescue attempt was The Sorcerer's Apprentice, which became the centerpiece of Fantasia.

programme.title: Better Use of Leisure Time
programme.desc:
Ken Michaels is flat on his bed doing nothing, and an unseen narrator won't let him get away with calling it rest — "moping" is the word used. Ken protests that there's nothing to do and no more free time than anyone else has, so the narrator takes him somewhere no ordinary Coronet short bothers to go: backward. First to a version of his own father a hundred years back, a farmer working a 72-hour week who orders young Ken off the bed to muck the stable and build new porch steps; then to a version fifty years back, a ten-hour-a-day, six-day-a-week father whose one indulgence is an evening with the stereoscope. Only then does the narrator return Ken to the present, where his real father works a 40-hour week, sneaks in a round of golf before supper, and is building a bookcase for the house in his spare time. The same time-trip is run on Ken's mother — scrubbing clothes, hauling water, baking bread and feeding chickens from dawn to dark fifty years ago, versus a washing machine and an evening spent planning the women's club program today. Sent to find out what his friends do with their own leisure, Ken discovers Dave identifying birds, Bill clerking part-time at the bookstore, Alice learning to sew, Marge at the piano, and a knot of boys in group sports. The narrator distills his father's bookcase hobby into a formula — a pleasant change from work, a chance to learn something, and a long-range goal — and Ken, rummaging out the camera he got for Christmas, decides photography might fill all three and maybe even a job someday.
The only screen credit is the customary Coronet consultant title card: Educational Collaborator Paul H. Landis, Ph.D., Professor of Sociology at State College of Washington. The picture itself is copyrighted, per its titles, to David A. Smart, the Esquire publisher whose Coronet Instructional Films turned out these classroom shorts by the hundreds from its Glenview, Illinois studio. What sets this one apart from its stablemates is the framing device: rather than a flat classroom-camera address, an argumentative off-screen narrator walks Ken through a series of staged historical vignettes to make its point about work, leisure and the modern 40-hour week. The Prelinger Archives catalog note on the print, written by film historian Ken Smith, calls it "more imaginative than most" Coronet titles "when it comes to visual gimmickry" — a fair description of the back-in-time device carrying the argument.
Ken's mother, credited on no title card but identified in later filmography listings as "Mrs. Michaels," is an early and uncredited screen role for Hope Summers, long before she became a familiar television face as Clara Edwards on The Andy Griffith Show and Mayberry R.F.D. Smith's same catalog note records that the boy playing Ken went on to headline another Coronet short, appearing as "Chuck-of-the-future" in Good Table Manners — one small thread connecting two entries in Coronet's social-guidance run. The film survives today through the Prelinger Archives holdings at the Internet Archive, cataloged as one of the more visually resourceful entries in a genre usually content to let its narrator simply talk over a static scene.

programme.title: Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips: Number Cruncher
programme.desc: Computers are number crunchers — they do math faster than any human can. Mr. Chips demonstrates calculations, sorting, and data processing at speeds that amaze Scooter. The last of the Scooter Computer series. Part of Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips.

programme.title: The Prince and the Pauper
programme.desc:
Two identical Mickeys — one a beggar, one a prince — swap places on a lark in Tudor England and discover that Pete, the captain of the guard, has been terrorizing the kingdom in the dying king's name. The pauper Mickey gets trapped playing prince while the real prince, out in the streets for the first time, sees what his people are suffering. When Pete figures out the switch, the race is on: coronation, sword fight, chandelier crash, and Pluto sniffing out his real master.
Based on Mark Twain's 1881 novel. The last Disney theatrical production made with traditional ink-and-paint and camera — every cel was hand-painted and photographed on a physical camera stand. After this, Disney switched permanently to the CAPS digital system that debuted on The Rescuers Down Under, which this short accompanied in theaters on November 16, 1990. The animation deliberately evokes Disney's late-1930s style, influenced by Fred Moore's round, expressive character designs.
The story team reads like a preview of Disney's 1990s renaissance: Roger Allers (went on to direct The Lion King), Gary Trousdale and Kirk Wise (Beauty and the Beast), and Burny Mattinson (Disney's longest-serving employee, joined in 1953 at age 18, worked there until his death in 2023). Directed by George Scribner, who had just finished Oliver & Company. Wayne Allwine voices Mickey — he inherited the role from Jimmy MacDonald, who inherited it from Walt Disney himself. Allwine married Russi Taylor (the voice of Minnie Mouse) in 1991, making Mickey and Minnie married in real life. Roy Dotrice narrates.

programme.title: Going Steady?
programme.desc:
Marie and Jeff are the couple everyone else has already decided is going steady — their friends assume it and their families discuss it, and the film opens by promising not to settle the question for either the characters or the audience. What follows plays out less as a story than as a string of conversations: Jeff works the question over by phone with a friend while his father hovers nearby waiting his turn to weigh in; Marie takes her own calls at home, then sits having her hair set by a girlfriend, turning the same question over out loud in front of a hand mirror; a parent on each side gets a scene alone with one of the teenagers, making a case neither Marie nor Jeff asked to hear. There is no crisis to resolve and no villain to blame, only the accumulating pressure of everyone around the two of them having an opinion about their relationship. The picture ends the way it began, on a title card handing the question back to the viewer: "What are the advantages -- and the disadvantages -- of going steady?"
Produced at Coronet's Glenview, Illinois plant and copyrighted MCMLI (1951) to Coronet founder David A. Smart, Going Steady? follows the studio's standard practice of naming only its academic consultant on screen: the title card credits Judson T. Landis, Ph.D., family sociologist at the University of California, Berkeley, whose survey work on adolescent courtship fed several Coronet scripts of the period. The Prelinger Archives catalog record for the surviving print — drawn from the production's own credit sheet rather than the screen titles — lists Gil Altschul as director, Hartley Pfeil as writer, Bruce Colling on camera, Ace Moore editing, and Sanford Singer in the role of Jeff. In place of a narrator, the film carries its exposition entirely on title cards, a structural choice the same catalog record notes explicitly.
Going steady itself was still a fairly new fixture of American high-school life in 1951, and a good deal of adult opinion regarded it warily, worried that pairing off early pushed teenagers toward premature marriage or worse. Coronet built much of its postwar catalog on that same anxiety, turning out dozens of comparable shorts on dating and getting along under its "social guidance" banner. Writing about the genre, film historian Ken Smith observed dryly that there would have been no need for these classroom mental-hygiene films at all if the young had actually behaved so pleasantly — and Going Steady? is typical of the type in refusing to resolve the argument it stages, closing on the same title card that opened it and leaving the discussion to the classroom rather than to the screenwriter.

programme.title: Midnight In A Toyshop
programme.desc: The twelfth Silly Symphony and a charming entry that casts a spider — typically the villain in earlier entries like "Summer" and "Hell's Bells" — as a sympathetic protagonist. Caught in a snowstorm, the enterprising arachnid slips through a toy shop's keyhole into a world of wonders. It mimics a cuckoo clock, tumbles through alphabet blocks, dodges a wind-up car and a barking toy dog, and startles at a jack-in-the-box. When it discovers a toy piano marked "$1.98" and begins to play, the entire shop comes alive — dolls dance and sing, a marionette springs into motion, teddy bears make music. The revelry turns to chaos when the spider, still clutching a lit candle, lands in a box of fireworks. The ensuing explosion sends it fleeing back through the keyhole, preferring the snowstorm to the pyrotechnic pandemonium within. Originally announced for July 3 but postponed to August 16 due to the studio's ongoing production delays. Director Wilfred Jackson helmed the entry, with Walt Disney voicing the black doll and Marcellite Garner the spider. Motion Picture Herald (May 2, 1931) praised its "merit of lightness and general amusement" and predicted "the youngsters should enjoy it very much, and the oldsters will be entertained." The toy shop setting would echo in later Disney works, most notably Geppetto's workshop in Pinocchio (1939).

programme.title: Peculiar Penguins
programme.desc: Peculiar Penguins, directed by Wilfred Jackson, turns a courtship comedy into a survival chase as a shy penguin suitor competes for his mate and then fights to save her from a sea lion attack. Disney artists reportedly observed live penguins to capture group movement and behavior, which gives the film's crowd scenes a natural rhythm beneath the caricatured expressions. Leigh Harline's song "The Penguin Is a Very Funny Creature" sets a playful tone before the action tightens, and later critics have singled out the short's music-and-animation craft as stronger than most cute-animal shorts of the period. The result is an underrated mid-1930s Silly Symphony that balances observational animal study with romance, slapstick, and genuine peril in under ten minutes.

programme.title: Interjections!
programme.desc: "Interjections! Show excitement! Or emotion! They're generally set apart from a sentence by an exclamation point, or by a comma when the feeling's not as strong." A rapid-fire series of dramatic vignettes — a kid getting a shot, finding a dollar, being surprised at a party — each punctuated by interjections (Darn! Wow! Ouch! Hey!). The energy is relentless and perfectly captures what interjections actually do: interrupt the flow with raw feeling. Part of Grammar Rock. Performed with breathless enthusiasm by Essra Mohawk.

programme.title: Victory Vehicles
programme.desc:
Wartime gas rationing has eliminated the automobile, so the narrator demonstrates alternative transportation methods: roller skates, stilts, piggyback, pole-vaulting, a trained kangaroo, and ultimately the pogo stick — which the short proposes as America's definitive Victory Vehicle. Every citizen (all played by Goofy) bounces to work, to school, to church on pogo sticks while the narrator maintains that this is perfectly practical.
One of Disney's WWII home front shorts. By 1943, rubber and gasoline rationing had made civilian driving nearly impossible — "Victory Vehicles" was the government's actual term for car alternatives. Jack Kinney plays the absurdity straight, treating the pogo stick transportation network with the same earnest narrator authority as a genuine War Department information film. The satire only works because the format is indistinguishable from the real propaganda Disney was making next door. Released July 30, 1943 by RKO.

programme.title: Exercise and Health
programme.desc:
Three teenagers carry three different problems into the school gym: Ernie is run-down and out of shape, Jean is shy and withdrawn, Hal is tense and quick to snap. A physical-education instructor points all three toward the school's Acrobatics Club, and the film spends most of its ten minutes on the resulting workouts — spotted handstands and vaults off a partner's shoulders, tumbling on mats, chin-ups on a bar, badminton and archery out on the lawn. Two printed title cards carry the argument the pictures only illustrate: one notes that the sedentary worker, "bound by rules of business diplomacy," needs a physical outlet, and that the "pleasant tiredness" following exercise "promotes complete relaxation"; the other credits teamwork with building "balance and poise, along with skill, strength, and general physical fitness." By the last reel Ernie has traded the doctor's office for the tumbling mat, Jean is talking easily with the other girls on the archery line, and Hal has swapped his clenched jaw for a game of catch — three complaints answered by the same prescription of regular, cooperative exercise.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films, the picture opens with its only screen credit: educational collaborator Erwin F. Beyer of the Department of Physical Education at the University of Chicago, recorded on the RCA Sound System, with a copyright date of MCMXLIX (1949) under Coronet's founder David A. Smart. Coronet's house director Ted Peshak is credited with the film on Letterboxd and TMDB, consistent with his work on the studio's other social-guidance shorts of the period, though as with most Coronet one-reelers the on-screen credits name only the academic collaborator, not the director or cast.
The Prelinger Archives catalog summarizes the film in a single line — "How exercise will make you healthy and popular" — which is a fair, if blunter, restatement of the same argument the picture makes at length: that organized physical activity is a fix for the loosely related ailments of poor health, poor sociability, and poor nerves alike. It belongs to the same wave of postwar Coronet guidance shorts, tailored for physical-education classes rather than homeroom, and it survives today through Prelinger/Internet Archive prints rather than any particular later reputation of its own; no reliable cast credits have surfaced for Ernie, Jean, or Hal.

programme.title: Springtime
programme.desc: The third Silly Symphony, released five days before the 1929 stock market crash, and the first in a four-seasons cycle that would continue with Summer, Autumn, and Winter the following year. Directed by Ub Iwerks. Flowers, ladybugs, centipedes, birds, and frogs dance and devour each other to a medley of light classics — Grieg's "Morning Mood," Ponchielli's "Dance of the Hours," Offenbach's "Gaîté Parisienne." The centerpiece: a chain of frogs graduated in size swallow each other one by one until only the biggest remains, who is then swallowed by a long-legged bird so weighted down it flops into a pond and drowns. The Film Daily called it "a fine satire on the survival of the fittest in the animal world." Motion Picture News called it "A Panic." Variety praised the timing as so perfect that "the rhythm alone imparts rare entertainment value." The short later appeared on a television screen in 101 Dalmatians (1961).

programme.title: Who Killed Cock Robin?
programme.desc: The 54th Silly Symphony takes an 18th-century nursery rhyme and turns it into a celebrity courtroom spoof. Released June 29, 1935, David Hand stages a murder trial after Cock Robin collapses mid-serenade to Jenny Wren, with an owl judge, a fast-talking parrot prosecutor, and a lineup of rattled bird suspects. The short's real hook is caricature: Jenny Wren plays as a Mae West send-up, while other birds echo contemporary stars including Bing Crosby and a Harpo Marx-style cuckoo. Frank Churchill keeps the tempo brisk, and Disney pushed the title tune hard enough that bandleader Ben Bernie performed an expanded radio arrangement that summer. The ending flips the "murder" into a Cupid gag, but the short had a notable afterlife: Alfred Hitchcock used it in Sabotage (1936) to intensify the theater sequence. It was nominated for the Academy Award, losing to Disney's own Three Orphan Kittens.

programme.title: Three Blind Mousketeers
programme.desc: Released September 26, 1936, this short drops the nursery-rhyme mice into a Dumas-style swashbuckler and lets the animators stage pure action-comedy around blindness as both handicap and superpower. Captain Cat, backed by his feline guards, storms a Parisian courtyard and kidnaps a mouse maiden, only to meet three tiny musketeers who fight by sound, touch, and fearless momentum while shouting "all for one and one for all." Under David Hand, the film runs on escalating sight gags: capes and rapiers tangling in panic, cannon fire gone sideways, and a final firecracker launch that sends Captain Cat rocketing away in humiliation. Albert Hay Malotte's score keeps the pace clipped and theatrical, and the cartoon stands out in late-period Symphonies for replacing pastoral whimsy with brisk adventure choreography.

programme.title: Naughty Number Nine
programme.desc: A film noir-styled episode where the number nine is a pool-hustling troublemaker. "He was naughty number nine — he was a mean little dude." Teaches the nines times table and the finger trick (hold down the nth finger, the remaining fingers show the answer). The dark, smoky pool-hall animation is unlike anything else in the series. Part of Multiplication Rock. Sung by Grady Tate.

programme.title: Interplanet Janet
programme.desc: A girl named Janet zooms through the solar system visiting each planet in order. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto — the whole tour set to a disco beat. One of the most popular Science Rock episodes, both for its earworm melody and for the sheer joy of its space animation. Pluto was still a planet. Part of Science Rock. Performed by Lynn Ahrens.

programme.title: Family Life
programme.desc:
"Family Life" opens the way most Coronet council-of-family films do: with everybody a little frayed. The Miller household is a small chaos of overlapping errands — grocery bags fought over on the front step, a stalled car raising its hood in the driveway while father, mother, and their two teenagers crowd around it, a run out and back that solves nothing. Cut inside, and it's the mother who is left holding the kitchen together while the rest of the family goes its separate, quietly resentful ways. She decides the house needs running "like a business," and gathers everyone around the dinner table to lay out the plan on an actual placard: Guides to Home Management — Schedule, Responsibilities, Privileges, Finances.
