The scientific advisor was Dr. Heinz Haber, a German physicist who'd arrived in the United States through Operation Paperclip — the same postwar program that brought Wernher von Braun. Before coaching Donald through the golden ratio, Haber had co-hosted Disney's "Man in Space" with von Braun and hosted "Our Friend the Atom," the Eisenhower-commissioned film that explained nuclear fission to primetime television audiences using mousetraps and ping-pong balls. He'd proposed parabolic flights for simulating weightlessness. Now he was making sure a cartoon duck got Pythagoras right. Donald stumbles through a doorway into Mathmagic Land — a place where trees have square roots, rivers brim with cascading numbers that split into smaller numbers when they hit rocks, and a pencil-headed bird recites the first fifteen digits of pi (almost correctly — it fumbles the last one). A disembodied voice called the True Spirit of Adventure, performed by Paul Frees — who a decade later would welcome foolish mortals into the Haunted Mansion — guides Donald through a journey that connects ancient Greek mathematics to music, art, nature, games, and the shape of the future. Pythagoras and his Pythagoreans hold a jam session; Donald joins on a vase used as a bongo drum. The golden rectangle appears in the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo, the United Nations building. A live-action billiards player demonstrates the diamond system while Donald spectacularly overcalculates, hitting ten cushions in a single shot. Lewis Carroll appears as both writer and mathematician. Donald tries to suggest checkers and tiddlywinks for the chess sequence; the Spirit declines both. The film's visual artists included John Hench, who'd joined Disney in 1939 as a sketch artist on Fantasia, built the giant squid for 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea, designed the original Tomorrowland, and would go on to paint Mickey Mouse's official portrait every decade for fifty years — still working full-time at Disney when he died at 95. Collin Campbell, another Disney Legend, contributed visual work. Buddy Baker composed the score. The four directors — Hamilton Luske supervising, with Wolfgang Reitherman, Les Clark, and Joshua Meador on sequences — spanned the studio's history. Les Clark had started at Disney in the Oswald the Lucky Rabbit era. The voice of Donald was Clarence "Ducky" Nash, marking Donald's 125th theatrical appearance. Released June 26, 1959 on a bill with Darby O'Gill and the Little People, the featurette was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject. Two years later it had the honor of appearing in the very first episode of Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color on NBC, September 24, 1961, with an introduction by Ludwig Von Drake. But its real life began in classrooms. Disney made it available on 16mm filmstrip, then VHS, then DVD, and it became the most popular educational film ever released by the Walt Disney Educational Media Company. For decades, the appearance of the AV cart meant one of two things: you were watching a filmstrip about dental hygiene, or you were watching Donald in Mathmagic Land. As Walt himself said: "The cartoon is a good medium to stimulate interest. We have recently explained mathematics in a film and in that way excited public interest in this very important subject." Its cultural afterlife keeps growing: Ted Lasso's 2023 hallucination sequence directly homages it, complete with the Spirit of Adventure's voice; Futurama's "The Numberland Gap" features it in the opening and builds the entire episode's plot from it. The film closes with Galileo: "Mathematics is the alphabet with which God has written the universe."

programme.title: Understand Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Mr. Brent, a high-school biology teacher, opens by springing a jack-in-the-box on his class to make a simple point: the same jolt doesn't hit everybody the same way. From there the lesson turns diagnostic. Working with three students — among them a boy named Larry — Brent lifts a plastic brain off his desk and traces the thalamus as the switching point where a stimulus becomes a feeling, then wires a student's fingers to a gauge to record the body's own evidence: racing pulse, tightened stomach, sweating palms, each mapped onto a cutaway silhouette on the wall chart. He walks the class through a wired maze holding a white mouse, using shock and cheese to demonstrate conditioning directly, then chalks the idea up as an equation: S¹, a dentist, produces only curiosity; S², his drill, produces fear. The blackboard closes the period the way it opened, as a formula — fear, rage, and love as raw material, conditioning as the process that shapes them, emotional maturity as the goal.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and copyrighted 1950 ("Copyright MCML David A. Smart," per the title card, naming Coronet's founder and the publisher of Esquire and Coronet magazines), recorded on the RCA Sound System. As with the rest of the line, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College — in real life the head of Iowa State's driver-research program and author of The Psychology of Driving, lending his credentials here to classroom emotion theory rather than his usual traffic-safety work. None of Coronet's young actors are named on screen; period research into the studio's stock company has since identified the boy playing Larry as John Galvarro, who played the same character, Larry, in Coronet's Are You Ready for Marriage? the same year and went on to small roles in Service and Citizenship (1951) and the Encyclopaedia Britannica short Drug Addiction.
The film belongs to Coronet's early-1950s run of shorts built around the vocabulary of behaviorist psychology — Control Your Emotions, made the same year, dramatizes the same three emotions through a teenager's bad Friday, while this one drops the story in favor of the lab: mice, wiring, and a plastic brain standing in for a plot. Ken Smith, whose capsule notes for the Prelinger Archives remain the standard reference for the genre, filed it as "even more Skinnerist than Control Your Emotions, and much less entertaining" — a fair verdict on a film that treats its teenage subjects less as characters than as case studies. Like most of the Coronet guidance catalog it has long since lapsed into the public domain and survives today through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Cannibal Capers
programme.desc: The eighth Silly Symphony — and the first directed by Burt Gillett, marking a crucial transition after both Ub Iwerks and Carl Stalling departed Disney in January 1930. A tribe of cannibals gather in the jungle for a ceremonial dance, drumming on skulls and preparing one of their own in a bubbling pot. Their ritual is shattered when a ferocious lion bursts in, scattering the dancers. But the intended victim leaps from the cauldron and flips the script: he snatches the lion's false teeth and waves them like a talisman, reducing the jungle beast to hysterical terror. The cannibals swarm the cowering cat as the cartoon ends. Bert Lewis scored it — his first major assignment after joining Disney only a month before Stalling's exit — weaving in Schubert's "Moments Musicaux, Op. 94, No. 3" and the Habanera from Bizet's Carmen. The Film Daily called it "one of Walt Disney's best Silly Symphonies to date." Billboard praised the "byplays sparkling with originality and cleverness" and the "skillful animation," singling out the lion battle as the "strongest risibility tickler." Released on December 19, 2006 as part of the "From the Vault" section of Walt Disney Treasures: More Silly Symphonies, Volume Two with historical context addressing its racial caricatures — a reminder that even Disney's training ground had growing pains. The copyright was renewed in 1957.

programme.title: The Spider and the Fly
programme.desc: In a bustling kitchen, houseflies frolic carefree until a menacing spider awakens and plays his web like a harp to lure victims. When a female fly becomes ensnared, her brave suitor rallies an insect cavalry — mounted on horseflies wielding pins as lances, with dragonfly bomber squadrons dropping pepper bombs and champagne bottles as artillery. The climactic battle sees the insects set the spider's web ablaze, sending the villain plummeting onto flypaper. Motion Picture Herald called it "An Animated Pinnacle," noting the opening night audience at New York's Criterion burst into applause. The Film Daily deemed it "A Knockout," praising its ingenious workmanship. One of Disney's earliest clear good-versus-evil narratives, foreshadowing the studio's legendary villain tradition.

programme.title: The Grasshopper And The Ants
programme.desc: Aesop as Depression-era musical: released February 10, 1934, with Pinto Colvig voicing Hop the grasshopper as a carefree busker who fiddles through summer while the ants stockpile food. He sings The World Owes Me a Living, mocks the workers, then nearly freezes when winter finally hits. Disney artists turn weather into character acting: Hop shivers, starves, and famously shifts blue from cold before collapsing at the ants' door. The queen ant lets him stay only if he contributes, so the same fiddle that sold laziness now earns his supper and the lyric flips to I Owe the World a Living. The song became one of the studio's durable motifs, and the short remains one of the clearest Silly Symphonies where social message, music, and personality animation all lock together without losing the comic rhythm.

programme.title: Farmyard Symphony
programme.desc: Jack Cutting's directorial debut — his very next short, The Ugly Duckling, would win the Academy Award and close the Silly Symphonies series for good. A farmyard wakes at dawn to Beethoven's Pastoral Symphony, the same piece Disney would build an entire Fantasia segment around two years later. A rooster struts into the henhouse, scatters the hens, and pursues a coy white pullet across the yard until the two perch on a fence and cluck their way through Verdi's "La donna e mobile" — an aria about the fickleness of women, repurposed as a barnyard love duet. The chorus builds: Billy Bletcher's booming bull, Florence Gill's clucking hens, ducks, a donkey, a foal — the whole farm joining in over Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 and Wagner's Tannhauser overture. Then the farmer appears with feed buckets, and every animal instantly abandons high art for dinner. The realistic animal movement — guided by Bernard Garbutt, the studio's resident anatomy expert, and animated by future Nine Old Man Milt Kahl and Bambi specialist Ken Hultgren — was a direct proving ground for Bambi.

programme.title: What To Do On A Date
programme.desc:
Nick and his friend Jeff are tossing a ball along the sidewalk when Nick spots a girl, Kay, walking home, and loses track of the game watching her go. Back at the house, her number is already penciled into the margin of Nick's notebook, right next to an unfinished book report on Nathaniel Hawthorne, and it's Jeff — leaning over the banister, needling him along — who finally gets Nick to pick up the phone and ask. Once Kay says yes, the two of them skip the expensive, ready-made idea of just taking a girl to the movies and instead throw themselves into the school's "Knick-Knacks" scavenger sale: painting signs, hanging a paper elephant from a ladder, stringing bunting and lanterns across the yard. Kay and her friend Phyllis turn up that afternoon to pitch in alongside them, sorting donated goods and tacking up notices on the club bulletin board, and by evening the sale has become a small carnival, the two couples working booths and finishing the night together over sandwiches and cold drinks — precisely the supervised, low-cost, group-built evening Coronet is holding up as the answer to the title's question.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films — the print's copyright card reads MCMLI, 1951, under founder David A. Smart, over the RCA Sound System mark. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance line, the only name in the picture itself is the consulting educator: the title card credits "Educational Collaborator Evelyn M. Duvall, Ph.D., Consultant, National Council on Family Relations," the family-life researcher whose dating and courtship studies underpin several Coronet guidance shorts of the period. No director or performer is named on screen. The Prelinger Archives catalog record for the film credits Ted Peshak as director, cameraman Dale Sharkey, writers George Tychsen and (George T.) Bradford, editor Dick Kirschner, and narrator George Stone — Peshak's credit for this specific title is echoed by Letterboxd's own listing, though, again, the print is silent on all of it.
The film sits alongside Are You Popular? and Date Etiquette in Coronet's cycle of postwar dating shorts, all pitching group activity and modest spending as the cure for an awkward date. Oddly, the Prelinger Archives catalogs this same title under 1950, a year earlier than the MCMLI copyright stamped on the print — likely a gap between production and the copyright's formal registration, but worth noting since it puts the film's actual copyright date a year later than its most common listing. Letterboxd and IMDb both credit Robert Casey as the lead of the teenage cast, though which of the two boys he played isn't attested anywhere reliable enough to print, and the film itself names no performers at all. It survives today as an unaltered classroom print, held and circulated through the Prelinger Collection along with dozens of other Coronet social-guidance shorts from the same run.

programme.title: The Skeleton Dance
programme.desc: The first Silly Symphony — and the cartoon that launched the series. Carl Stalling pitched the idea to Walt Disney during a Kansas City stopover in 1928, while Disney was heading to New York to arrange distribution for Steamboat Willie. Ub Iwerks animated nearly the entire film in six weeks, drawing inspiration from English cartoonist Thomas Rowlandson's skeleton illustrations. Four skeletons emerge from graves at midnight, dance a danse macabre, play each other's spines as xylophones, and use a cat's tail as a violin. At the rooster's crow they scramble back underground, their bones tangling together in the rush. Stalling's score weaves in Grieg's "March of the Trolls." The original xylophone used for the sound effects survives at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. Some theaters held it over for weeks.

programme.title: Monkey Melodies
programme.desc: The thirteenth Silly Symphony and one of the few early entries to extensively feature popular songs rather than classical compositions. A hero monkey swings through the treetops picking flowers for his sweetheart, their courtship set to Ethelbert Nevin's "Narcissus." Parrots squawk "Aba Daba Honeymoon" (1914), a simian trio joins in, and two crocodiles perform an elaborate cakewalk routine with canes to "At a Georgia Camp Town Meeting" (1897). A menacing crocodile pursues the sweethearts through the jungle before the couple escapes to safety. Produced in just three weeks between July 31 and August 19, 1930, the film showcased distinct animator styles — Wilfred Jackson drew the monkeys with lanky, graceful proportions for their slow dance; Tom Palmer rendered them cuddly; Johnny Cannon animated them naturalistically in the chase. No model sheets existed yet. Walt Disney voiced the male monkey, Marcellite Garner the female. Variety (October 15, 1930) called it "just a wee bit better than the usual run of cartoon shorts." Motion Picture News declared it "Foolishly Clever," noting Disney "has fairly outdone himself in the assortment of ridiculous postures." The Film Daily commended it as "entirely well done both in action and in synchronized score."

programme.title: Mother Goose Goes Hollywood
programme.desc: The third-to-last Silly Symphony and Disney's most ambitious celebrity caricature short. Two shelved concepts — "The Hollywoods" and "Mother Goose Land" — merged in 1937, with caricaturist T. Hee designing every star and pitching the short to Walt through live enactments of the impressions. The result is a nursery rhyme revue performed entirely by 1930s Hollywood: Katharine Hepburn wanders through as Little Bo Peep in a running gag, the Marx Brothers tear apart "Old King Cole" as his three fiddlers, W.C. Fields perches atop a wall as Humpty Dumpty alongside his real-life radio nemesis Charlie McCarthy, and Laurel and Hardy shuffle in as Simple Simon and the Pieman to the strains of their own theme. Charles Laughton, Spencer Tracy, and Freddie Bartholomew crowd into a tub dressed as their most famous roles. The finale packs Fred Astaire, Shirley Temple, Mae West, and Clark Gable into the Old Woman's shoe for a swing number. Dave Barry and Sara Berner voiced nearly every caricature between them. Variety found the running time "not long enough." Nominated for the Academy Award but lost to Disney's own Ferdinand the Bull — four of the five nominees that year were Disney productions.

programme.title: A Noun Is a Person, Place, or Thing
programme.desc: The first Grammar Rock episode. "Well, every person you can know, and every place that you can go, and anything that you can show — you know they're nouns." Lynn Ahrens wrote the lyrics for this and most of the Grammar Rock series, bringing a Broadway sensibility to three-minute educational shorts. A straightforward, catchy definition song that drills the concept through rapid-fire examples. Premiered September 1973 on ABC.

programme.title: The Shot Heard Round the World
programme.desc: The American Revolution told through the eyes of a minuteman at Lexington and Concord. From taxation without representation through the Declaration of Independence to Yorktown. The animation captures the chaos of colonial rebellion with surprising energy for a three-minute educational short. Part of America Rock.

programme.title: Save the Ocean
programme.desc: Ocean pollution and marine conservation. Plastic, oil spills, and runoff are killing marine life. The ocean covers 70% of the Earth and produces much of our oxygen. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: The Fun of Making Friends
programme.desc:
Joey is a solitary boy, first seen alone at his own front window while the neighborhood kids have a snowball fight out in the yard; instead of joining in, he stays inside working quietly at a table with paper and scissors. Walking to school by himself down a snowy sidewalk, he keeps the same distance from his classmates. At home, though, his mother sits him down and reduces the problem to a checklist the film puts right on screen: Smile and Talk to People. Find Good Things in People. Tell Them the Good Things. Do This All the Time. Joey tries the rules out at his school desk, sharing a look and then a bag of something with a classmate, and by the next scene the two boys are paired off at a shared table; a girl is drawn into the circle outside in the snow soon after. The film closes back at Joey's house, now full of friends and a family dog sprawled on the rug — the boy who started the picture alone at the glass now has the room crowded around him.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films and copyrighted in 1950, the picture runs a little over nine minutes. The film's own catalogued production credits, preserved with the Prelinger Archives print, list Ted Peshak as director — the studio's regular hand on its postwar social-guidance line — with camera by Dale Sharkey, script by George Tychsen, and editing by Ace Moore. In keeping with Coronet's usual practice of naming only the outside expert who vetted the content, the credits identify the consulting authority as Elizabeth B. Carey, Ph.D., Supervisor of the Bureau of Instructional Supervision for the University of the State of New York.
The film belongs to the large body of social-guidance shorts Coronet supplied to classrooms through the late 1940s and 1950s: a simple problem, a numbered rule card, and a tidy resolution inside ten minutes. Distributed for decades on the 16mm educational circuit, it survives today through the Prelinger Archives and small footage libraries like A.V. Geeks, and it still turns up on retro-media blogs as an example of the genre's plain, unfussy way of talking to a lonely kid — reach out, the film tells him, and the loneliness just ends.

programme.title: El Terrible Toreador
programme.desc: The second Silly Symphony — a tabloid-scale burlesque of Bizet's Carmen set in Spain. A barmaid carries beer overhead, walking to the Toreador Song. A man in a white suit tips her; a jealous toreador sees them together and the two fight over her. In the bullfighting ring, the toreador and a bull (bearing a suspicious resemblance to Clarabelle Cow) chase each other around until the matador finishes things by pulling the bull completely inside out. That ending was graphic enough that Disney filed it under "From the Vault" on the 2006 DVD release. Stalling's score threads in "Yankee Doodle Dandy," "Ciribiribin," and Mendelssohn's "Spring Song" alongside the Carmen melodies. Motion Picture News called it "O.K. For Laughs." The Film Daily said "almost a continuous riot from start to finish."

programme.title: Flowers and Trees
programme.desc: Disney had already started Flowers and Trees in black-and-white when Herbert Kalmus finished the first three-strip Technicolor camera in May 1932 and began shopping the process around Hollywood. Walt Disney took the gamble, restarted the short in color, and turned a routine Silly Symphony into a watershed moment: the first commercially released film in full three-strip Technicolor. Onscreen, a jealous hollow tree attacks a younger rival for a female tree's affection, then ignites a wildfire that nearly destroys the forest before birds pierce the clouds to make rain. Offscreen, the short's runaway success justified bigger color budgets and helped lock Disney's exclusive Technicolor advantage through 1935, leaving rivals to inferior systems. It won the first Academy Award for animated short subjects and was later selected for the National Film Registry.

programme.title: Elbow Room
programme.desc: Manifest Destiny and westward expansion. Lewis and Clark, the Louisiana Purchase, the Oregon Trail, the Gold Rush — America pushing west because it needed elbow room. The song is catchy enough that you almost miss how it glosses over what westward expansion cost the people already living there. A time capsule of how the 1970s taught this history. Part of America Rock.

programme.title: Mother Necessity
programme.desc: American invention and innovation, from Ben Franklin to Thomas Edison to Alexander Graham Bell. Necessity is the mother of invention, and America has always been full of necessities. The cotton gin, the steamboat, the telephone, the light bulb — each invention animated as it springs from its creator's need. Part of America Rock. Performed by Essra Mohawk.

programme.title: Electricity, Electricity
programme.desc: Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Edison, and the nature of electrical current. From lightning rods to light bulbs, the episode traces how humans learned to harness electrons. The animation crackles with literal sparks. Part of Science Rock. Performed by Zachary Sanders.

programme.title: Goofy Gymnastics
programme.desc:
Goofy comes home exhausted from work, spots a fitness ad in his newspaper, and mail-orders a home gym set. Following the instructions on a record player, he attempts barbells, chin-up bars, and cable expanders — destroying his apartment floor, launching himself out a window, and ending up slammed against the muscular diagram on the equipment chart, where he finally looks like the physique he was promised.
This is the short playing inside the movie theater in Who Framed Roger Rabbit — the one that makes Roger Rabbit laugh so hard he blows his cover and praises Goofy's "timing and finesse," calling him a genius. (Though it's an anachronism: Roger Rabbit is set in 1947 and this was released in 1949.) Directed by Jack Kinney with a story by his brother Dick Kinney. Pinto Colvig voices Goofy — the original voice since 1932, a man who was also a circus clown, vaudeville performer, and the voice of both Sleepy and Grumpy in Snow White. Animation by John Sibley and Wolfgang Reitherman (one of the Nine Old Men). Released September 23, 1949 by RKO.

programme.title: Appreciating Our Parents
programme.desc:
Tommy comes home from school to a room that looks like magic: bed made, toys shelved, a torn cowboy shirt mended, a missing jacket button replaced. The film doubles back to show what he never sees — the mess he actually left that morning, and the hours of washing, ironing, mending, and dish-clearing that erased it while he was at school. That evening his father comes home with Tommy's weekly allowance, and Tommy, thinking only that he'd like more of it, follows his parents downstairs and sits in on their evening instead: his mother recounting a day of cooking, laundry, and straightening his room, his father working through the family budget at the kitchen table and then mending a broken chair rather than buying a new one. Tommy reframes the household as a football team that only wins if every player does his job, and sets out to do his: he fixes his own broken toy train track, keeps his room tidy without being asked, and banks his allowance instead of asking for more. His reward in the closing scene is not just his parents' approval but a bigger allowance, his mother and father agreeing he's earned a share of what his help has saved — appreciation paid out in cash as plainly as it is felt.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois and copyrighted 1950 (MCML) to Coronet publisher David A. Smart. As with other Coronet guidance shorts, the only credit on the print itself is the classroom consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Reuben Hill, Ph.D., Research Professor in Family Life at the University of North Carolina. Direction is attested elsewhere as Ted Peshak, who joined Coronet's Glenview studio in 1947 and, alternating projects with fellow staff director Gil Altschul, directed roughly half the company's output through the late 1950s, at his fastest turning out a finished one-reeler in a single day. Tommy is played by Skip Peshak, Ted's own son, one of several Coronet shorts in which the director cast his boy rather than one of the studio's regular Chicago performers.
Reuben Hill brought an unusually credentialed pedigree to the picture. By 1950 he had already co-written the marriage-education bestseller When You Marry (1945) and was partway through the University of North Carolina professorship (1949-1957) during which he developed what became the ABC-X model of family stress, drawn from his wartime research on military families; he went on to chair the International Sociological Association's family research committee and later served as the ISA's president. His name on the title card reflects a broader Coronet practice of enlisting university researchers to lend classroom authority to shorts on manners, thrift, and family duty. "Appreciating Our Parents" sits in that social-guidance cycle's domestic-economy strand, chores and thrift dramatized as filial love, and survives today through a 16mm print in the Prelinger Archives on the Internet Archive.

programme.title: The Practical Pig
programme.desc: The fourth and final Three Little Pigs cartoon — billed on its title card not as a Silly Symphony but as a standalone "Three Little Pigs" short, the only entry in the series to receive that treatment. Practical Pig has moved beyond brick houses and now tinkers in his basement with a Rube Goldberg lie detector: a chair rigged with brushes, paddles, and rulers that punishes each fib with escalating slapstick. The Big Bad Wolf, meanwhile, disguises himself as a mermaid — seashell bra, fish tail, harp — and lures Fiddler and Fifer to capture with a rendition of "Frankie and Johnny." When Practical straps the Wolf into the machine and demands his brothers' whereabouts, each lie earns a mouth-soaping or a spanking until the Wolf cracks. The final gag lands hardest: Practical tells his rescued brothers "This hurts me more than it does you" while punishing them for disobedience, and the machine catches him in the lie and spanks him too. Frank Churchill's "Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf?" runs throughout — by 1939 the song had shifted from Depression anthem to something darker, a nervous joke about wolves gathering at Europe's borders.

programme.title: The Ugly Duckling
programme.desc: The seventy-fifth and final Silly Symphony — and a deliberate bookend. Walt Disney had already told Hans Christian Andersen's story in 1931 as entry No. 25, a crude black-and-white effort made before Technicolor, before the multiplane camera, before Snow White taught his animators to make audiences cry. Eight years later he ordered it remade as proof of how far the studio had come. Gustaf Tenggren painted the inspirational art; Eric Larson and Milt Kahl — two future members of Disney's legendary Nine Old Men — animated the duckling with a naturalism that reviewers compared to feature-quality work. Not a word of dialogue: Clarence Nash provides only quacks and chirps over Albert Hay Malotte's orchestral score. A duckling hatches wrong — too white, too gangly — and his own mother shakes him off her back in the water. He nuzzles a wooden decoy for comfort and gets bonked for the trouble. Then a passing swan recognizes him, and when the duck family calls him back, he turns away and swims on with his real kind. Chuck Jones called it "one of the best short subjects ever made." Won the Academy Award. The laboratory had done its work.

programme.title: Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips: Hardware
programme.desc: What is computer hardware? The keyboard, the monitor, the CPU, the disk drive — the physical parts you can touch. Mr. Chips explains his own anatomy to Scooter. A snapshot of 1983 computing: floppy disks, CRT monitors, and CPUs the size of toasters. Part of Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips.

programme.title: The Check's in the Mail
programme.desc: How checks and banking work — writing a check, what happens at the bank, how money moves between accounts. The title plays on the classic excuse for late payment. Part of Money Rock.

programme.title: Plane Crazy
programme.desc:
Mickey Mouse's first cartoon was, chronologically, this one. Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks built it in a rush in the spring of 1928, riding the wave of aviation mania that followed Charles Lindbergh's solo Atlantic crossing the previous May: a barnyard photo of "Lindy" inspires Mickey to cobble together a rickety biplane out of a Model T, a washtub and assorted farm junk, then press Minnie and a coop's worth of livestock into service as passengers and parts. Iwerks animated the picture essentially alone, working from Walt's story sketches at a punishing pace to have a print ready for a trade screening within weeks. Disney previewed the finished silent film for a Hollywood theater audience, and for prospective distributors, on May 15, 1928 — the true birthday of Mickey Mouse, months before the character most audiences would come to know him from. No distributor bit; an MGM executive who saw the screening reportedly liked the mouse but passed on the picture.
That commercial failure redirected the studio. Disney had already been trying to crack synchronized sound, and rather than shop the silent Plane Crazy further, he shelved it and built a new short, Steamboat Willie, around a Cinephone sound track from the outset. Steamboat Willie's November 1928 New York opening was a sensation, and Walt went back to the earlier films to retrofit them for the format that had actually sold Mickey to the public. Plane Crazy was rescored and re-cut with a synchronized soundtrack — dialogue grunts, barnyard effects, a jaunty musical bed, but no character speech to speak of, in keeping with the crude but electrifying "Mickey Mousing" style of the moment — and released on March 17, 1929, through Pat Powers's Celebrity Pictures using the Powers Cinephone system credited on the reissue's own title card. It went out as the third Mickey short to reach audiences, behind Steamboat Willie and The Gallopin' Gaucho, even though it was the first one made.
The title card on this print reads "Mickey Mouse Sound Cartoon — Plane Crazy — A Walt Disney Comic by Ub Iwerks, Recorded by Cinephone System," identifying it unambiguously as the 1929 sound reissue rather than the lost-to-most-audiences 1928 silent original; the image is plain black-and-white throughout, with no tinting, hand-coloring, or restoration card, and no live-action prologue. Gags familiar from the character's later run are already present in embryonic form: Mickey improvises a parachute from Minnie's bloomers when the plane goes into a spin, and the short ends on the chase-and-kiss beat — Minnie bailing out rather than accept Mickey's advances — that recurs across the early cartoons. Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks share directing credit; no cast is credited on the print, consistent with the era, before Disney and his stable of actors began regularly voicing Mickey, Minnie, and Pete later in 1929.
Because the American copyright terms for the silent and sound versions were registered separately, the two prints of Plane Crazy left copyright on different dates: the 1928 silent version entered the U.S. public domain on January 1, 2024, alongside Steamboat Willie, but the sound version carried on this file — bearing an on-screen 1929 date, with its copyright registered and later renewed under Pat Powers's Celebrity Pictures — is treated by the U.S. Copyright Office as a separate work and did not enter the public domain until January 1, 2025. Caution is warranted in describing this file's rights status: it is the sound reissue, not the 1928 original, and the two should not be conflated.

programme.title: How Quiet Helps at School
programme.desc:
The film opens in a school hallway lined with lockers, then pushes into a first-grade classroom where the ordinary business of the day — passing papers, moving chairs, calling out — plays as a small racket. Next door, under a teacher the narration calls Miss Bradley, the same tasks unfold in near-total silence: children whisper instead of talk, a boy sharpens a pencil and crosses the room to a supply closet without a sound, and the class works through an assignment while the wall clock ticks audibly in the quiet. Miss Bradley tells the room that keeping things this hushed is good practice because a classroom, like an office, runs better without noise, and that knowing when to be quiet is simply part of growing up. The film does not ask for silence everywhere — it closes on the same children loose and loud on the playground swings, the noise they were asked to hold indoors now given somewhere to go.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films on RCA's sound system and copyrighted MCMLIII to John Smart, the standard Coronet registration of the period. As with the studio's other social guidance shorts, the only credited collaborator on screen is the psychology consultant: the title card names Henry Bonner McDaniel, Ph.D., Professor of Education and Psychology at Stanford University. McDaniel was a real fixture of Stanford's education faculty in these years — Stanford's Graduate School of Education dates his work building out the university's guidance-counseling program to 1947–1968 — lending the film's classroom-management message the same applied-psychology backing Coronet leaned on across the genre. No director is credited on the print, and none is attested specifically for this title.
The film survives through the Prelinger Archives, whose catalog twice describes it in almost identical terms: a demonstration of "how a class can study and work better if the room is quiet," with noise given its proper place on the playground rather than banished outright. Later commentary on the Coronet social-guidance cycle has singled this one out as unusually serene even by the genre's own standards — one retrospective review calls the hushed classroom a room of "well-behaved, conscientious" children and notes the almost suspenseful quiet of watching a pupil cross the room without making a sound. Seen today, it reads less as an outlier than as a fairly ordinary specimen of the classroom-discipline instructionals Coronet turned out through the 1950s for use in American schools.

programme.title: Mickey and the Beanstalk
programme.desc:
Mickey, Donald, and Goofy are starving farmers in Happy Valley — a kingdom that fell into famine when its magical singing golden harp was stolen. Down to one loaf of bread and a single bean, Mickey trades their cow for magic beans. Donald, furious, throws them through a hole in the floor. Overnight they sprout into a beanstalk that lifts the house to a giant's castle in the clouds. Inside, they find the harp — and Willie the Giant, who can fly, turn invisible, and shapeshift (though when Mickey asks him to become a fly, he becomes a pink bunny instead). The trio's escape down the beanstalk with the harp is one of Disney's great chase sequences.
The second half of Fun and Fancy Free (1947), narrated by Edgar Bergen with Charlie McCarthy and Mortimer Snerd in live-action wraparound segments. Walt Disney's last regular voice performance as Mickey Mouse — he recorded most of the dialogue in spring and summer 1941, then handed the role to Jimmy MacDonald in 1948. Disney only returned to voice Mickey once more, for The Mickey Mouse Club introduction in 1955.
Originally conceived in 1940 as a standalone feature called "The Legend of Happy Valley." Bill Cottrell and T. Hee pitched it to Walt, who "burst out laughing with tears rolling down his cheeks with joy" — then refused to greenlight it because they had "murdered his characters." He was eventually talked into it. Production began May 2, 1940 but was interrupted by the Disney animators' strike and Pearl Harbor. The military commandeered the studio for propaganda films. When it was finally completed, Disney judged the animation insufficient for a solo feature and paired it with Bongo (based on a Sinclair Lewis short story) as a package film. An early draft had Honest John and Gideon from Pinocchio conning Mickey at the market.
Billy Gilbert — the comedian who sneezed his way through vaudeville and voiced Sneezy in Snow White — voices Willie the Giant. Directed by Hamilton Luske, who would later supervise Donald in Mathmagic Land. Music by Oliver Wallace, Paul Smith, Eliot Daniel, and Charles Wolcott.

programme.title: One More Year on the Family Farm?
programme.desc:
"One More Year on the Family Farm?" opens on the shot it will return to at the end: an aerial pass over a two-lane road threading a green valley down past a cluster of barns and silos. Rather than following one family through a plot, the film is built as an issue-documentary — an entry in Coronet's Changing Scene Series — that lets members of two real dairy-farming households speak for themselves about whether to keep at it. One farm has modernized: cows stand in row after row of freestall housing, a milking parlor is threaded with steel line, and a bulk tanker truck idles in the yard, while a young man in glasses works through figures at an office desk rather than working a field. The other keeps to older ways — a man in a stocking cap forks manure out of a wood-sided barn by hand, walks cattle single file up a hillside pasture, and turns a narrow furrow behind a small tractor. Interspersed are direct-to-camera moments with the people themselves — an older farmer, a young woman, the men in caps and glasses — weighing the debt, the machinery, the hours, and the pull of a life some were born into and some are choosing to leave. The film never resolves which choice is right; it ends where it began, looking down at the valley from the air.
The on-screen credit is unusually specific for a Coronet short. Following the title card and its tag "(The Changing Scene Series)," a further title reads "©1977 Coronet Instructional Media, a division of Esquire, Inc." Two consultants are named — Content Consultant Jack L. Nelson, Ed.D., Professor of Education at Rutgers University, and Classroom Consultant William B. Stanley, Teacher of Social Studies at Cranford Senior High School in Cranford, New Jersey — followed by the studio's standard closing notice, "This film may not be copied or televised without written permission." As with Coronet's classic postwar shorts, no director, writer, or on-camera participant is credited; the film speaks in the voice of its consultants rather than its filmmakers.
The title card's own series tag marks this as part of a later, more issue-driven strand of the Coronet catalog, trading the scripted teenage leads of the studio's postwar shorts for real adults talking about their own livelihoods. The print survives today through the Internet Archive's educational-film holdings, part of the same circle of ephemeral prints preserved and scanned by collectors such as A.V. Geeks, and is cataloged there under a copyright still held by Phoenix Learning Group, Inc., the successor distributor of the Coronet library.

programme.title: Frolicking Fish
programme.desc: The tenth Silly Symphony plunges into a whimsical underwater world, originally printed on green-tinted stock for atmospheric effect. Fish of all varieties engage in elaborate performances — riding seahorses, playing conch shells, dancing around treasure chests. A fish skeleton shakes maracas. Starfish and clams join the choreography. The menace comes from an angry octopus who terrorizes the revelers until a clever fish lures the villain beneath a sunken boat's anchor, crushing the cephalopod in a triumphant finale. Beyond entertainment, the film holds genuine historical importance: it was on this picture that animator Norman Ferguson discovered the revolutionary "follow-thru" technique, allowing characters to move with unprecedented naturalism — an innovation that would profoundly influence Disney's subsequent productions. Originally announced for May 8, production delays from Iwerks and Stalling's departures pushed actual release to June 21. The Film Daily (September 28, 1930) called it "an undersea exhibition that keeps the patrons chuckling all the way" and "one of the best in the Silly Symphonies series." Motion Picture News struck a sour note, reporting the film "didn't get a chuckle out of a New York audience" — a reminder that even Disney's experimental series faced skepticism.

programme.title: The Point!
programme.desc: In the Land of Point, everyone and everything has a point — except Oblio, the only round-headed boy in a kingdom of pointed heads, who has worn a pointed hat since birth to hide his difference. When the son of an evil count loses to Oblio at Triangle Toss (a game where you catch triangles on your head), the count demands enforcement of the law: pointless things must be banished. Oblio and his dog Arrow are sent into the Pointless Forest, where they discover that even the Pointless Forest has a point. They meet a man pointing in all directions who declares: "A point in every direction is the same as no point at all." They meet a rock man, dancing fat sisters, and a tree who helps Oblio see that everyone has a point. When Oblio returns and tells the kingdom what he's learned, the furious count rips off his hat — and finds a point on top of Oblio's bare head. Upon this revelation, the points of everyone else disappear and the pointed buildings become round. Harry Nilsson wrote, produced, and performed all the music. He was born in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn in 1941. His father abandoned the family when Harry was three — his song "1941" opens: "Well, in 1941, a happy father had a son / And by 1944, the father walked right out the door." Due to poverty, he dropped out after ninth grade and lied about graduating high school to get a job as a computer programmer at a bank. He worked the night shift on bank computers and spent his days writing songs. His uncle in San Bernardino gave him singing lessons. When his songs started getting recorded — by the Monkees, by Phil Spector, by Glen Campbell — Nilsson still didn't quit the bank. He never performed live concerts, one of the only major pop artists in history to achieve fame without touring. When the Beatles were asked at a 1968 Apple Corps press conference to name their favorite American artist, John Lennon said "Nilsson." Paul McCartney was asked to name his favorite American group. He also said "Nilsson." Lennon had listened to Nilsson's album Pandemonium Shadow Show for 36 straight hours. The two became close friends. During Lennon's "Lost Weekend" separation from Yoko in the mid-1970s, he and Nilsson were members of the Hollywood Vampires drinking club, notorious for alcohol-fueled incidents at the Troubadour. They made one album together, Pussy Cats (1974). After Lennon's murder in 1980, Nilsson left the music industry to campaign for gun control. He died of heart failure in 1994 at 52. The inspiration for The Point came to Nilsson on LSD: "I was on acid and I looked at the trees and I realized that they all came to points, and the little branches came to points, and the houses each came to a point. I thought, 'Oh! Everything has a point, and if it doesn't, then there's still a point to it.'" He wrote a twelve-page illustrated treatment and first pitched it to Hanna-Barbera, who passed. Fred Wolf of Murakami-Wolf Films took it on. Wolf skipped pencil tests entirely and went straight to ink-and-paint, giving the film its loose, handmade look. He worked nights and slept days through the entire production. The original story collaborator, Carole Beers, started steering the narrative toward science fiction; Nilsson, protective of his concept, was not pleased, so Wolf brought in Norm Lenzer to write the screenplay. Production began before a script existed. Mike Lookinland — Bobby Brady — voiced Oblio. In a waiting room before a recording session, young Lookinland was making car noises when his mother told him to be quiet. A man stood up, walked over, and said: "Lady, don't ever tell your kid to be quiet. I make my living on sound." The man was Mel Blanc. The film first aired February 2, 1971 on ABC's Movie of the Week — the first animated feature ever broadcast in prime time on American television. Dustin Hoffman, a friend of Nilsson's, agreed to narrate for $20,000 on the condition that his voice be used for one broadcast only. For later airings, the narration had to be completely re-recorded — first by Alan Barzman, then by Alan Thicke for cable, and finally by Ringo Starr for the home video release. Our version has the Alan Thicke narration, the third telecast restoration. The album's art director was Dean Torrance — of Jan and Dean ("Surf City"). Nilsson instructed that the design have points but no circles. The sales sticker on the shrink-wrap was a triangle. The cover illustration was hand-stitched in needlepoint by Torrance's wife Kathy. The album's arranger, George Tipton, was Nilsson's equivalent of George Martin — the last Nilsson album he arranged. Tipton had invested his life savings of $2,500 to finance Nilsson's first four recordings. The song "Me and My Arrow" became a hit single and, in the way of the early 1970s, ended up in a television commercial. The London stage adaptation at the Mermaid Theatre in 1977 starred Davy Jones and Micky Dolenz of the Monkees — who had been among the first artists to record Nilsson's songs, and who remained his close friends until his death. Nilsson also inspired the name Aerosmith: drummer Joey Kramer was listening to Nilsson's album Aerial Ballet, started riffing on the word "aerial," someone said "smith," and a band was born.

programme.title: The Adventures of Mark Twain
programme.desc: Mark Twain pilots an airship to meet Halley's Comet, accompanied by stowaways Tom Sawyer, Huck Finn, and Becky Thatcher. Along the way, they encounter animated versions of Twain's stories — the Jumping Frog, Adam and Eve's diaries, Captain Stormfield's Visit to Heaven, and, in one of the most disturbing sequences in the history of children's cinema, The Mysterious Stranger. This is the first and only feature-length film made entirely in Will Vinton's patented Claymation technique. Everything on screen — every character, every cloud, every starry sky — is made of clay. The backgrounds were clay-painted in multiple passes and layers to create depth and transparencies. The film required 130,000 individual figure changes and took three and a half years to make, on a budget of $1.5 million. It was shot in the converted bedrooms of a house behind a barbershop in Portland, Oregon. The animators worked in the basement. The producer pored over Mark Twain's writings in one bedroom. Vinton's then-wife, Susan Shadburne, wrote the screenplay in another. They called it the Barbershop Studio. The crew was seventeen people. The concept comes from one of the most extraordinary coincidences in literary history. Samuel Clemens was born on November 30, 1835 — two weeks after Halley's Comet reached perihelion. In 1909, he said: "I came in with Halley's Comet in 1835. It is coming again next year, and I expect to go out with it. It will be the greatest disappointment of my life if I don't go out with Halley's Comet. The Almighty has said, no doubt: Now here are these two unaccountable freaks; they came in together, they must go out together." He died on April 21, 1910 — one day after the comet reached perihelion. He delivered his own punch line. The Mysterious Stranger sequence is the one that broke the internet. The children enter a dark world where they meet a being who calls himself Satan — not the devil, he explains, but an angel named Satan, "Number 44." He creates tiny clay people, gives them life, makes them build a castle, watches them fight a war, and then casually destroys them all. "They were of no value," he says. He shapes one last figure from clay, crushes it in his hand, and says: "Life itself is only a vision, a dream. Nothing exists save empty space and you. And you are but a thought." His clay face shifts through a dozen masks — smiling, anguished, serene, terrifying — and then dissolves into nothing. Children who saw this in 1985 are still talking about it. The scene became a viral YouTube sensation decades later, partly through an erroneous claim that it had been censored from the TV version. Vinton said he was mystified by the rumor. It was never cut. It was always there. Will Vinton was the son of a car dealer and a bookkeeper from McMinnville, Oregon. He went to Berkeley in 1966, fell in love with Gaudí, started experimenting with clay in his apartment. He and his roommate Bob Gardiner made a film called Closed Mondays — it was rejected outright at its first local festival, then won first prize at nearly a hundred international screenings, including Cannes, and then won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short in 1975. The first stop-motion film to ever win in that category. Portland's first Oscar. He coined the word "Claymation" and trademarked it. He created the California Raisins — singing Marvin Gaye's "I Heard It Through the Grapevine" — which became so famous they landed on the Billboard Hot 100. He created the Noid for Domino's Pizza. He animated the M&Ms characters. He won six Emmys. He built Vinton Studios into a $28-million-a-year enterprise. Then Phil Knight, co-founder of Nike, staged a hostile takeover. In 2002, Knight forced Vinton out of his own company, installed his son Travis Knight — a failed rapper who performed under the name Chilly Tee — as head of the studio. Knight poured $180 million into the shell of Vinton Studios and rebranded it as Laika. Yes — THAT Laika. Coraline, ParaNorman, Kubo and the Two Strings. All built on the foundation of the man who was pushed out of his own basement. Vinton sued. The case was dismissed. He lost ownership of the California Raisins, the M&Ms, and the legal trademark to the word "Claymation" — the word he invented. He died in 2018 at age 70. James Whitmore, who voiced Twain, was Yale class of '44 and came within one award of an EGOT: Emmy, Grammy, Tony, and two Oscar nominations. Released in the UK as Comet Quest. The film tested well with teenagers and college students. Its distributor, Atlantic Releasing, ignored this and released it under their children's matinee label, Clubhouse Pictures. It grossed $849,915 and disappeared. Then the internet found it.

programme.title: Feeling Left Out
programme.desc:
Mike Hanlon is a popular type on paper — a football player with a letter jacket of his own — but the picture keeps returning to him standing at the edge of the same locker-lined hallway, watching a knot of letter-sweater boys trade jokes without him. He follows them into gym class, gripping the same chin-up bar, working the same jump rope, matching them stride for stride physically, and none of it earns him a way in; the group simply isn't built to admit one more. A coach notices him hanging back and makes the turn explicit: cliques form and close for reasons that have nothing to do with a boy's worth, and chasing one closed circle is a poor way to spend a school year. By the last reel Mike has stopped angling for the group and started talking to people one at a time — a girl bent over her books in study hall, a boy blowing a saxophone at a school function, a classmate he simply falls into step with in the hall. The film ends not with Mike joining the clique but with him no longer needing to.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films, Feeling Left Out follows the house formula of putting only one name in front of the camera — the collaborating academic. The distributor's own catalog credits Paul H. Landis, Ph.D., professor of sociology at the State College of Washington (today Washington State University), as the film's educational collaborator, the standard Coronet arrangement of borrowing a working social scientist to vouch for the lesson on screen. Coronet released the picture in 1951 as a classroom-rental 16mm sound short, part of the same wave of adolescent social-adjustment titles as Shy Guy and Are You Popular. As with most Coronet shorts of the period, the students playing Mike and his classmates went uncredited, and no director is named in surviving prints or distributor records for this title specifically.
The film survives through the A/V Geeks ephemeral-film collection, which placed its 16mm print on the Internet Archive under a Public Domain Mark; the distributor's own synopsis there — a boy who "wants friends but... concentrates on becoming friendly with a certain group of boys" rather than individuals — matches the picture beat for beat. It sits comfortably alongside Coronet's other clique-anxiety shorts of the era, all working from the same premise: that adolescent unhappiness is a solvable technical problem, and exclusion a symptom a level-headed adult and a change of strategy can fix before the closing titles.

programme.title: The Flight of Dragons
programme.desc:
Peter Dickinson did not set out to write a story. In 1979 the British novelist published a slim, lavishly illustrated book called The Flight of Dragons — a piece of mock-scholarship that took the existence of dragons seriously and answered it with chemistry. His reasoning began with the artwork: the wings medieval illustrators gave dragons were far too stubby to lift such enormous bodies, so the lift, he decided, had to come from the body itself — "some kind of gas-bag." He proposed that a dragon's rapidly growing skeleton was continuously dissolved by stomach acid, releasing hydrogen that filled the great chambers of its frame and carried it aloft like a living dirigible; the surplus gas, vented through the throat and ignited, accounted for the fire. Around this single idea he assembled the whole inheritance of dragon lore — the cave-dwelling, the hoarded gold, the taste for princesses, the one vulnerable spot, the blood that melts a sword — and made every legend a consequence of the biology. Wayne Anderson supplied the misty, otherworldly paintings. By Dickinson's own account the project began as a modest Christmas pamphlet and ballooned when a packager demanded a longer manuscript; he had to "invent a dozen extra pages with only a week to do it in," after which the publisher went bankrupt.
What happened next was, in Dickinson's telling, faintly absurd. An animation company bought the book "sight unseen, without apparently realising that there was no kind of a story or plot" — it was an essay, not a narrative. Needing an actual plot, Rankin/Bass then acquired Gordon R. Dickson's 1976 novel The Dragon and the George and grafted the two properties together. The film keeps Dickinson's science-versus-magic framing and his dragon physiology, and it names its hero Peter Dickinson after the author — recast as a Boston scientist and game designer whose mind is flung into the body of the young dragon Gorbash by a wizard's misfired spell. The real Dickinson had no involvement in the production and was never paid for the use of his name, though he noted, dryly, that the book itself had already made him a comfortable sum.
The animation came from Topcraft, the Tokyo studio that served as Rankin/Bass's hand-drawn workshop throughout this period. Founded in the early 1970s by former Toei producer Toru Hara, Topcraft had already drawn The Hobbit (1977) and The Return of the King (1980), and in 1982 it delivered both The Last Unicorn and The Flight of Dragons. The studio's afterlife is the more famous chapter: two years later Topcraft animated Hayao Miyazaki's Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, went bankrupt in 1985, and split in two — Hara and the core staff became the founding nucleus of Studio Ghibli, while the remainder formed Pacific Animation Corporation and carried on with Rankin/Bass on ThunderCats and SilverHawks. The Flight of Dragons thus belongs to the last handful of films made by the studio that would, almost immediately afterward, become Ghibli.
The voice cast is a deep bench of American character actors. John Ritter, then at the height of Three's Company, plays the displaced Peter; James Earl Jones supplies the apocalyptic menace of Ommadon, the Red Wizard who would sooner let the modern world drown in greed and fear than cede it to reason; Harry Morgan is the Green Wizard Carolinus; James Gregory voices the old dragon Smrgol; and Victor Buono, in his final role before his death in January 1982, plays the wolf Aragh. The title song was written by Jules Bass and the studio's longtime composer Maury Laws and sung by Don McLean of "American Pie" fame, who also appears in the film as the Balladeer.
The film had an unusually quiet debut — issued to home video in 1982 and not broadcast in the United States until ABC ran it as a Saturday-night movie in 1986 — and built its following slowly, through repeat television airings and word of mouth, into a touchstone for a generation of fantasy fans.

programme.title: How Friendly Are You
programme.desc:
Ray moves through a run of small social tests over the course of the film — wheeling his bike alongside another boy, brushing off a girl who's delighted to show him something wrapped in paper, working alongside his older brother Phil at Mr. Martin's shop, squaring off with another boy in the park over a piece of trash left on the grass — and gets nearly all of them wrong: offhand, closed off, quick to take offense. Phil eventually sits him down and talks through what friendliness actually costs and what it returns, the "responsibility of friendship" the film's own catalog description names directly. Ray works back through the same round of situations correcting himself one by one, and the film closes with him at a piano surrounded by a room full of grinning classmates — the reward Coronet's guidance shorts always hand out for good behavior: being liked.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' Glenview, Illinois studio and directed by Ted Peshak, from a script by Robert Chapin and Dick Creyke, photographed by Dale Sharkey and cut by editor George Wilbern, with narration by George Stone. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance line, the only credit that appears on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Harl R. Douglass, Ph.D., director of the College of Education at the University of Colorado, a life-adjustment educator whose papers are held today in that university's own archives. Prelinger Archives, whose print of the film circulates today, catalogs the release as 1952; Letterboxd and IMDb's short-film index both list 1951 instead, a year's discrepancy common to Coronet's undated 16mm classroom prints.
Phil is played by Dick York — five years past his screen debut in the title role of Coronet's own Shy Guy (1947), and a dozen years before he became Darrin Stephens on Bewitched — while Mr. Martin, whose shop gives Phil his after-school job, is played by Carl Kroenke. Ray and the film's other roles went uncredited on screen, in keeping with Coronet's practice of naming only its academic consultant. The short is one of dozens Coronet turned out during its postwar guidance cycle and survives today as a plain, commercial-free classroom print through the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive.

programme.title: The Return of the King
programme.desc:
The working title was Frodo, The Hobbit II. That tells you everything about what Rankin/Bass thought they were making: not an adaptation of the third volume of The Lord of the Rings, but a sequel to their 1977 Hobbit television special. The fact that two entire books stood between The Hobbit and The Return of the King was treated as a logistical problem, not a structural one. Romeo Muller solved it by framing the film as a story told at Bilbo Baggins's 129th birthday party in Rivendell, with the Minstrel of Gondor singing the tale while Frodo fills in the gaps. Everything in The Fellowship of the Ring and The Two Towers is summarized in the first few minutes. Helm's Deep, Moria, the breaking of the Fellowship — disposed of in a montage. The film begins where it wants to begin: Sam carrying the Ring into Cirith Ungol.
This was not, despite decades of confusion, a sequel to Ralph Bakshi's 1978 animated Lord of the Rings. Bakshi's film covered the first half of Tolkien's trilogy and ended abruptly at Helm's Deep, never receiving its planned second part. Rankin/Bass had always intended to follow The Hobbit with this film, independently of Bakshi. The confusion arose when Warner Bros. acquired both properties and marketed them as a trilogy — Rankin/Bass Hobbit, Bakshi Lord of the Rings, Rankin/Bass Return of the King — despite the three films sharing no continuity, no consistent character designs, and fundamentally incompatible tones. Bakshi's rotoscoped warriors look nothing like Topcraft's illustrated hobbits. The packaging was a lie, but it sold VHS tapes.
The Tolkien Estate sued. Unlike The Hobbit, where a publication mishap had placed the book in the American public domain, The Lord of the Rings was under copyright. The Estate and Fantasy Films argued that Rankin/Bass had not properly secured the U.S. and Canadian television rights. The lawsuit was settled "amicably" — a word that in entertainment law means someone wrote a check — and the film aired on ABC on Sunday, May 11, 1980.
The returning cast was remarkable for who came back and who didn't. Orson Bean returned, now playing both Bilbo and Frodo — the same gentle, befuddled voice carrying the weight of the Ring's corruption. John Huston was back as Gandalf, still reading Tolkien as if he'd written it himself. Brother Theodore returned as Gollum, three years older and no less terrifying. Glenn Yarbrough returned as the Minstrel, his role expanded from occasional balladeer to near-constant narrator — singing "Frodo of the Nine Fingers and the Ring of Doom" with the earnest folk sincerity that either redeems or ruins the film depending on your tolerance for hobbits breaking into song every twelve minutes. Thurl Ravenscroft was back in the chorus. Paul Frees, the Rankin/Bass utility player who had voiced Boris Badenov and narrated half of American television, replaced Cyril Ritchard as Elrond — Ritchard had died shortly after completing The Hobbit.
The new additions were, if anything, more improbable than the original cast. Roddy McDowall played Samwise Gamgee. McDowall had been a child star in How Green Was My Valley at thirteen, then became Cornelius and Caesar in four Planet of the Apes films, then built a second career as one of the most prolific voice actors in animation history — the Mad Hatter, Snowball in Pinky and the Brain, half a dozen other roles that used his precise, slightly anxious diction. His Sam is loyal and frightened and absolutely certain that Mr. Frodo is worth dying for.
Theodore Bikel voiced Aragorn. Bikel had originated the role of Captain von Trapp in The Sound of Music on Broadway, was one of the founders of the Newport Folk Festival alongside Pete Seeger, spoke six languages, and had been nominated for an Academy Award for The Defiant Ones. He played Aragorn as a weary commander who has been waiting too long for a crown he isn't sure he wants, which is closer to the book than most adaptations manage.
William Conrad was Denethor. Conrad had been the original Marshal Matt Dillon on radio's Gunsmoke — the role that went to James Arness on television because CBS decided Conrad didn't look the part — then starred in Cannon and Jake and the Fatman, narrated The Fugitive and Buck Rogers in the 25th Century, and possessed a voice so deep and authoritative that it made Denethor's madness sound like the inevitable conclusion of a lifetime spent staring into a palantir.
Casey Kasem played Merry. The host of American Top 40, the voice of Shaggy in Scooby-Doo, the man who ended every countdown with "keep your feet on the ground and keep reaching for the stars" — that Casey Kasem — voiced the hobbit who helps Eowyn kill the Witch-king of Angmar. His given name was Kemal Amin Kasem. He was Lebanese-American and a vocal advocate for Arab-American representation in media, which makes his participation in a Tolkien adaptation — a story whose debt to Northern European mythology Tolkien himself sometimes complicated with Orientalist undertones — worth noting without resolving.
The animation was again produced by Topcraft in Tokyo under Toru Hara. Arthur Rankin designed the characters and storyboards in New York. Maury Laws composed the score. Jules Bass wrote the songs. The visual style is continuous with The Hobbit — the same Arthur Rackham-influenced linework, the same watercolor backgrounds — though the subject matter forced darker imagery: the Dead Marshes, Shelob's lair, the siege of Minas Tirith. The Nazgul riding fell beasts over the Pelennor Fields is genuinely frightening in a way that the film's gentler moments don't prepare you for. Five years after this production, Topcraft would become Studio Ghibli.
The critical reception was lukewarm. The Tolkien scholars who had despised The Hobbit treated this as confirmation of their fears. The compression is severe — Faramir is absent, Saruman is absent, the Scouring of the Shire is absent, and the songs sometimes substitute for scenes that needed to be dramatized. But the framing device is clever, the voice performances are uniformly excellent, and the final sequence — Frodo leaving from the Grey Havens, giving Sam the Red Book of Westmarch, Gandalf assuring them that hobbits will have descendants among men — is played with a quiet sincerity that the Peter Jackson films, for all their craft, never quite matched in their version of the same scene.
Ninety-eight minutes. A lawsuit settled amicably. The voice of Shaggy fighting the Witch-king. The star of Planet of the Apes carrying a hobbit up a mountain. The host of American Top 40 and the founder of the Newport Folk Festival and the man CBS thought was too fat to play a cowboy, all gathered around a microphone in New York to finish a story about the end of an age.

programme.title: Self-Conscious Guy
programme.desc:
Marty is a self-conscious high school student who freezes at the moments that matter most — reciting at the blackboard in English class, asking a girl out from a corner payphone, waiting through a tryout for the school play — because, as he explains it, he feels "as if there was a spotlight on me." Coronet gives the metaphor a literal form: a spotlight lands on Marty whenever his nerves take over, cutting him off from the room around him. He wants the play's leading role and loses it to nerves, ending up instead among the stagehands working the curtain. From the wings he starts noticing that his classmates — even Jack, the confident boy who won the part he wanted — carry the same private unease, and it's an ordinary game of ping-pong in the school rec room, not the stage, where Marty finally out-plays Jack and discovers the poise he'd assumed he didn't have.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films under founder David A. Smart and copyrighted in 1951 — MCMLI on the print's own title card — the film follows Coronet's standard practice of crediting only its outside expert on screen: the title card names Judson T. Landis, Ph.D., a family sociologist at the University of California, Berkeley, as educational collaborator. Landis was, by 1951, a familiar name to health and hygiene teachers; he and his wife Mary Green Landis had already co-authored the widely used high-school textbook Building Your Life, and Coronet leaned on that classroom credibility the way it leaned on university psychologists and sociologists across its whole social-guidance line.
Film historian Ken Smith, surveying the classroom-hygiene genre, judged it a lesser cousin of Coronet's own Shy Guy — "cheap, but effective" — singling out the spotlight device as the one inventive touch in an otherwise plain ten minutes, and noting that the young actor cast as Marty also turned up as the lead in Coronet's How to Say No the same year. That actor's name never made it onto any print or catalog card; cataloging Coronet's recurring faces at the Tralfaz blog, film historian Yowp lists him simply as "actor unknown" with "a specialty in big-lip anguish." Self-Conscious Guy survives today through the Prelinger Archives holdings at the Internet Archive, in the public domain like most of Coronet's postwar guidance shorts.

programme.title: Fantastic Planet
programme.desc: On the planet Ygam, giant blue humanoids called Draags keep tiny human-like Oms as pets. Some are loved. Most are exterminated. When a young Om named Terr escapes with a stolen Draag learning device, he sparks a revolution — but what makes this film extraordinary is not its allegory. It is the circumstances of its creation. René Laloux learned animation in a psychiatric hospital. In the late 1950s he was working as a counselor at La Borde, a radical clinic in Cour-Cheverny, France, where patients were unconfined, free to roam the grounds, and participated in their own treatment decisions. Laloux was a trained woodcarver who used art therapy — then revolutionary — to work with the residents. He staged puppet shows, made shadowgraphs, and in 1960 directed his first film, "Les dents du singe" (The Monkey's Teeth), written and animated entirely by the psychiatric patients themselves. His collaborator on Fantastic Planet was Roland Topor, one of the most unsettling artists of the twentieth century. Topor was a French illustrator, novelist, and actor of Polish-Jewish descent whose family had survived the Nazi occupation by hiding in Savoy. His work is suffused with casual brutality and dark absurdism — he wrote the source novel for Polanski's "The Tenant" and played Renfield in Herzog's "Nosferatu." Together, Laloux and Topor made short films that dealt with collective postwar trauma: "Les temps morts" (Dead Times, 1965) opens with the narration "The world is a vicious circle." Their visual approach — paper cutouts animated under glass, with a tactile handmade quality that evokes etchings more than cartoons — was perfected in these collaborations. The co-production contract with the Jiří Trnka Studio in Prague was signed in 1967, during the political thaw of the Prague Spring. In Czechoslovakia, animation was generously funded by the Ministry of Culture and taken more seriously as art than anywhere in the West. Production began in spring 1968. Then in August, Soviet tanks rolled into Prague. Everything stopped for a year. Filming resumed in summer 1969, during what the Czechs call "Normalization" — the systematic crushing of the cultural freedoms the Prague Spring had briefly allowed. The paradox is staggering: one of the most subversive animated films ever made — a story about a giant civilization that treats smaller beings as vermin, gasses them, and crushes them like insects — was produced inside a Soviet satellite state during the very period when that state was being re-subjugated. A special section, independent within Krátký film Praha, was carved out for the production. The Czech authorities tolerated it because they needed the foreign currency from the French co-production contract. Laloux commuted regularly to Prague. In later years he came only once a month for a few days, leading some to credit Czech animator Josef Kábrt as co-director — but the storyboard discovered in the Bibliothèque du cinéma François Truffaut shows every shot hand-drawn by Laloux, with shot lengths marked. He also created most of the layouts. Topor, despite designing the entire visual world, spent only two weeks in Czechoslovakia at the start. Kábrt developed the character animation while Josef Váňa painted the backgrounds. The film was cut short. Three sequences were never completed, including a ten-minute passage of the Oms building their own civilization, and a dream sequence that would have given the character Tiwa a psychoanalytic arc. The reason may involve Kamil Pixa, a Normalization-era director of Krátký film Praha who was also a former State Security officer. Research in the Security Services Archive revealed that Pixa had been arrested by French secret police in 1972 for his role in persecuting foreign diplomats in the 1950s. He may have curtailed the production in retaliation. The Czech version of the film differs significantly from the French: different opening and ending sequences, more voiceover narration, and a crucially different ending — in the Czech version, reconciliation comes at the human protagonist's initiative, while in Laloux's version, it comes from within the Draag senate itself, a far more complex political statement. Alain Goraguer's score — psychedelic jazz-funk with mellotron, harpsichord, and wah-wah guitar, compared by AllMusic to Pink Floyd's "Atom Heart Mother Suite" — has become a cult object in its own right. The original French vinyl pressings command enormous prices. The soundtrack has been sampled by Madlib, Mac Miller used it in "Insomniak," and the band Failure named their 1996 album after the film. The film premiered at Cannes on May 11, 1973 and won the Grand Prix special jury prize. Gene Siskel gave it one and a half stars and said its publicists claimed "the visuals begin to make sense if your mind is chemically altered." Sean Axmaker of TCM called it "nothing if not allegorical" and wrote that "it's not a stretch to see the fight against oppression reflected in the civil rights struggle, the French in Algeria, apartheid in South Africa, and the Holocaust itself." It inspired the world design of Pikmin. James Cameron's Avatar borrows from it openly. Scavengers Reign is its direct spiritual descendant. Rolling Stone ranked it the 36th greatest animated film ever. The Criterion Collection released a restored edition in 2016. Based on Stefan Wul's 1957 novel "Oms en série" — the title is a pun on "hommes" (men) rendered as a commodity, and "Ygam" anagrammed from "imagi." A film born in a psychiatric hospital, forged inside a Soviet occupation, about what happens when the small learn to read what the large would keep from them.

programme.title: How to Say No
programme.desc:
The film opens on a bare stage behind a drawn curtain. A spotlight finds a teenager named Bill, who steps out to address the audience directly, the way a discussion leader might open a school assembly, then pulls the curtain back to show a living room set where his panel is waiting: Marty, Lucy, Nora, and Howie, sitting around as if the four of them had simply stopped by after school. Their conversation carries the rest of the picture. Marty starts things off describing what happens with "the fellows" after a game or practice, when the group usually stops somewhere and somebody starts passing bottles around; from there the panel works through a pajama-party scene where Lucy and Nora feel the pull to light up along with everyone else, and a couch scene about how far a date is allowed to go. Each vignette resolves the same way: know your own standards before the moment arrives, say no plainly instead of delivering a lecture to the group, and have something else ready to offer in its place — a sandwich and French fries after the game, a joke instead of a cigarette — so that turning something down doesn't cost anybody a friendship.
Coronet Instructional Films copyrighted the picture in 1951 under David A. Smart, and, as with the studio's other guidance shorts, the only name on screen belongs to the consultant rather than any performer: the title card credits Evelyn M. Duvall, Ph.D., of the National Council on Family Relations, as educational collaborator. Duvall was a working family-life researcher, not a studio hire in name only — she had published Facts of Life and Love for Teenagers the year before and would go on to a long career studying adolescent development. Rather than dramatize a single morality tale the way some Coronet shorts do, How to Say No is built almost entirely around the panel's own talk, staged as an informal living-room discussion in front of a studio audience implied by Bill's opening address — a format Coronet leaned on repeatedly in its early-1950s slate of teen guidance titles.
The film belongs to the cycle of "social guidance" shorts Coronet distributed to junior high and high school classrooms through the 1950s, teaching poise and peer resistance around drinking, smoking, and necking through calm, matter-of-fact talk rather than scare tactics. It survives today through the Prelinger Archives, which catalogued it under its full title, How to Say No (Moral Maturity), and the print is in the public domain.

programme.title: Fehérlófia
programme.desc:
In this hallucinatory masterpiece of Hungarian animation, a horse goddess nurses her third son Fanyűvő (Treeshaker) on her milk until he grows strong enough to descend into the Underworld, where three monstrous dragons hold three princesses captive and the power of the ancient Forefather lies in ruins. Together with his brothers Kőmorzsoló (Stonecrumbler) and Vasgyúró (Ironrubber), he must outwit the seven-winged gnome Hétszűnyű Kapanyányi Monyók, forge a sword from the creature's enchanted beard, and fight his way through three underground kingdoms to restore the cosmic order their ancestors lost.
