Marcell Jankovics spent two years (1979–1981) at Hungary's Pannónia Filmstúdió creating what IndieWire would later call "the greatest psychedelic animated movie ever made." Working under Communist-era state funding — which paradoxically gave Hungarian animators more creative freedom than their Western commercial counterparts — Jankovics drew from László Arany's narrative poem and ancient Hunnic, Avaric, and Hungarian steppe mythology to build something that looks like nothing else in cinema: pure abstract color fields that pulse and shift like living organisms, figures that dissolve into suns and reform as trees, a visual language closer to Kandinsky or Aboriginal dreamtime paintings than to any animation tradition.
The film became an underground legend. Animation historian Charles Solomon first saw it at an Academy screening in 1983 and named it one of the best animated films of the decade. Disney animator Roger Allers was so struck by it that he hired Jankovics for Kingdom of the Sun (later reworked into The Emperor's New Groove). Aeon Flux creator Peter Chung discovered it in 1984 and absorbed its influence. It premiered in the US as "The White Mare" at the Los Angeles International Animation Celebration in September 1985, then essentially vanished from American screens for decades.
In 2019, Arbelos Films completed a 4K restoration that premiered at the Fantasia International Film Festival. COVID cancelled the planned theatrical run, so the film went to Vimeo in August 2020 — the first American distribution in decades. A limited-edition Blu-ray followed in June 2021, bundled with Jankovics's earlier works including his Oscar-nominated short Sisyphus (1974) and his first feature Johnny Corncob (1973). It placed #49 on the Olympiad of Animation in 1984 and holds a 90 Metacritic score from five critics — universal acclaim for a film most Western audiences have never heard of.

programme.title: Understand Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Mr. Brent, a high-school biology teacher, opens by springing a jack-in-the-box on his class to make a simple point: the same jolt doesn't hit everybody the same way. From there the lesson turns diagnostic. Working with three students — among them a boy named Larry — Brent lifts a plastic brain off his desk and traces the thalamus as the switching point where a stimulus becomes a feeling, then wires a student's fingers to a gauge to record the body's own evidence: racing pulse, tightened stomach, sweating palms, each mapped onto a cutaway silhouette on the wall chart. He walks the class through a wired maze holding a white mouse, using shock and cheese to demonstrate conditioning directly, then chalks the idea up as an equation: S¹, a dentist, produces only curiosity; S², his drill, produces fear. The blackboard closes the period the way it opened, as a formula — fear, rage, and love as raw material, conditioning as the process that shapes them, emotional maturity as the goal.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and copyrighted 1950 ("Copyright MCML David A. Smart," per the title card, naming Coronet's founder and the publisher of Esquire and Coronet magazines), recorded on the RCA Sound System. As with the rest of the line, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College — in real life the head of Iowa State's driver-research program and author of The Psychology of Driving, lending his credentials here to classroom emotion theory rather than his usual traffic-safety work. None of Coronet's young actors are named on screen; period research into the studio's stock company has since identified the boy playing Larry as John Galvarro, who played the same character, Larry, in Coronet's Are You Ready for Marriage? the same year and went on to small roles in Service and Citizenship (1951) and the Encyclopaedia Britannica short Drug Addiction.
The film belongs to Coronet's early-1950s run of shorts built around the vocabulary of behaviorist psychology — Control Your Emotions, made the same year, dramatizes the same three emotions through a teenager's bad Friday, while this one drops the story in favor of the lab: mice, wiring, and a plastic brain standing in for a plot. Ken Smith, whose capsule notes for the Prelinger Archives remain the standard reference for the genre, filed it as "even more Skinnerist than Control Your Emotions, and much less entertaining" — a fair verdict on a film that treats its teenage subjects less as characters than as case studies. Like most of the Coronet guidance catalog it has long since lapsed into the public domain and survives today through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Twice Upon a Time
programme.desc:
John Korty spent twenty years developing a form of cutout animation he called Lumage. The technique involved prefabricated shapes moved by hand on large glass fields lit from below, producing images that looked like stained glass windows come to life. He used it for segments on Sesame Street and The Electric Company, refining the process in a studio he had built in Marin County, where he had become the first independent filmmaker to settle in Northern California. His neighbors included George Lucas and Francis Ford Coppola. In 1979, Korty decided to make a feature film.
He raised a hundred and thirty thousand dollars to produce a sample reel. He screened it for Lucas. Lucas watched ten minutes of footage and suggested that the Ladd Company might finance it. Alan Ladd Jr. — the man who had greenlit Star Wars — agreed. Lucas took an executive producer credit. That was the extent of Lucasfilm's involvement, despite the prominent billing on the poster. It was, technically, the first animated film George Lucas ever produced.
Korty moved his entire animation team into his three-story house for the duration of production. He described the arrangement as "cheerful, despite many sleepless nights." The budget was three million dollars, which Korty noted was a fraction of what traditional cel animation cost — ninety minutes of Lumage came in under four million, while seventy-five minutes of cel ran fifteen million. The savings came from the technique itself: cutout animation on backlit glass required fewer frames, fewer artists, and no ink-and-paint department.
The cast was built from improvisational comedians, because Korty did not want to use scripted dialogue. Lorenzo Music — who was already the voice of Carlton the Doorman on Rhoda and would soon become the voice of Garfield for twelve years of television specials — played Ralph, the All-Purpose Animal, with the drowsy, philosophical warmth that made everything he touched sound like it was happening at three in the morning. Marshall Efron played the villain Synonamess Botch with what turned out to be a problem: Efron thought his lines were perfect as written on the page, and played up the raunchier aspects of the character. Paul Frees — who had voiced Boris Badenov for Rocky and Bullwinkle, and Bombur in Rankin/Bass's Hobbit four years earlier — narrated.
This is where the story fractures. There are two versions of this film, and neither is definitively the original.
Producer Bill Couturie, without Korty's knowledge, supervised a cut in which Efron's profanity was left in — Botch cursing his way through the Murkworks like a cartoon Scarface. Couturie believed the raunchier version would appeal to older teenagers and college audiences. Korty did not learn about this cut until opening night. He was furious.
Most theaters that showed the film played the profanity version. It didn't matter, because almost no theaters showed the film at all. The Ladd Company was collapsing — hemorrhaging money, choosing which of its remaining productions to sacrifice. They had the same problem with The Right Stuff, Philip Kaufman's three-hour epic about the Mercury astronauts. Both films got limited releases. Twice Upon a Time opened on August 5, 1983, and earned five thousand dollars at the box office. Five thousand dollars against three million. The Ladd Company shut down the following year.
A few years later, HBO picked up the film. They received — and broadcast — the profanity cut. When Korty found out, he threatened legal action. HBO switched to the theatrical version. When viewers who had seen the HBO broadcast complained that the film had been "censored," HBO dropped it from their schedule entirely. The film vanished. A full-frame, incomplete laserdisc was issued and forgotten. For nearly thirty years, Twice Upon a Time existed primarily as a rumor passed between animation enthusiasts who had caught it on cable at two in the morning sometime in the mid-eighties.
What those people remembered was the look: the Lumage technique produced something that resembled no other animated film before or since. The city of Din — filmed in live-action black and white in the Bay Area, populated by crew members and their families — sat between two animated worlds, the bright kingdom of Frivoli and the industrial nightmare factory of the Murkworks, and the transitions between live action, cutout animation, and stop motion felt less like technique and more like dreaming. Yellow Submarine is the closest comparison, but Korty's stained-glass aesthetic has a handmade quality that George Dunning's pop-art psychedelia did not.
The crew was young. Henry Selick, who would later direct The Nightmare Before Christmas and Coraline, was a sequence director. David Fincher — nineteen years old — worked as the special effects photographer, earning the job through his dexterity with a Mitchell camera. Harley Jessup, the art director, went on to work at Pixar, where he won an Academy Award for his production design on Ratatouille. The film was made by people who did not yet know what they would become, in a three-story house in Marin County, for a studio that would not survive the year.
The Warner Archive eventually released both versions on DVD in 2015, with a commentary track reuniting Korty with Jessup, Selick's fellow sequence directors, and several animators. Korty fills the gaps with prepared notes. Nobody says a bad word about anyone. The mood is fond and puzzled, the way people talk about something they poured their lives into that the world barely noticed.
Seventy-five minutes. Three million dollars. Five thousand at the box office. A nineteen-year-old David Fincher behind the camera. The future director of Nightmare Before Christmas moving cutout shapes on glass. The voice of Garfield improvising his lines in a house in Marin County. An animation technique that took twenty years to develop, was used for one feature film, and has never been replicated.

programme.title: Improve Your Personality
programme.desc:
Improve Your Personality opens on a school walkway and quickly settles into the device it returns to for the rest of its ten minutes: a black silhouette head in profile, flanked by two labels, "OTHER PEOPLE" and "ENVIRONMENT," under the caption "YOUR PERSONALITY." The diagram states the film's whole thesis in one image — personality isn't something a person is simply born with, it's built out of how they treat others and how they answer to their surroundings — and the picture keeps cutting back to it between two contrasted case studies. A teenage boy who starts out sullen and closed-off is shown coming around: setting the table, hanging up the wash, pitching in at home instead of leaving the chores to the woman of the house. Cut hard against him is a teenage girl who does nothing in her scenes but admire her own reflection in a bedroom mirror, the diagram card reappearing each time to underline the moral. Along the way, one boy sizes up a girl walking past him on the same path from the opening and tells a friend, "Boy, has she got personality!" — about as flatly as the film could put its own pun. By the closing reel the same young people turn up dressed for a formal dance, in tuxedos and gowns, and a final card spells out the takeaway in script lettering: "Concentrate on the other person."
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films and copyrighted in 1951 (the opening card reads "MCMLI," credited to David A. Smart), the short follows Coronet's standard practice for the period: not one performer is named on screen, and the film's only title-card credit goes to its "educational collaborator," billed as Clifford R. Adams, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at the Pennsylvania State College. Adams held that post in fact as well as on the card — he was Penn State's real director of its Marriage Counseling Service and a member of the American Association of Marriage Counselors — and five years earlier had co-written the marriage-advice bestseller "How to Pick a Mate" with Vance O. Packard, then a staff writer for The American Magazine and later the author of "The Hidden Persuaders." Coronet drew on a small, recurring bench of writers, directors, and consultants across its guidance catalog — Melvin Waskin as house writer, Ted Peshak as its most frequent director among them — but this particular print names none of them; Adams alone appears on screen.
The film belongs to Coronet's postwar "mental hygiene" cycle, the run of guidance shorts the company produced through the late 1940s and 1950s for direct sale to schools. David Smart, who had toured Nazi Germany before the war, later told the Chicago Tribune that seeing Hitler's use of film as an "indoctrination tool" convinced him the same medium could be turned toward education instead, and Coronet ran with the idea hard enough to release a new title, on average, every three and a half working days. Against that backdrop, Improve Your Personality is a mild entry — no car crash, no scandal, just a civics-class gloss on manners dressed up as psychology, delivered with Adams' academic authority and Coronet's usual well-lit, tidy midcentury classrooms and living rooms. A 2010 Cineaste survey of the genre singled the film out as one of the era's less common entries not narrowly aimed at one sex, pitching its lesson at boys and girls alike.

programme.title: Donald in Mathmagic Land
programme.desc: In the late 1950s, the Disney Studio faced a peculiar challenge: how to make American schoolchildren care about mathematics. They needed a protagonist the audience could identify with — someone skeptical, impatient, allergic to abstraction. The directors found their man in-house: the irascible Donald Duck. If Donald could become interested in math, the logic went, who couldn't? The scientific advisor was Dr. Heinz Haber, a German physicist who'd arrived in the United States through Operation Paperclip — the same postwar program that brought Wernher von Braun. Before coaching Donald through the golden ratio, Haber had co-hosted Disney's "Man in Space" with von Braun and hosted "Our Friend the Atom," the Eisenhower-commissioned film that explained nuclear fission to primetime television audiences using mousetraps and ping-pong balls. He'd proposed parabolic flights for simulating weightlessness. Now he was making sure a cartoon duck got Pythagoras right. Donald stumbles through a doorway into Mathmagic Land — a place where trees have square roots, rivers brim with cascading numbers that split into smaller numbers when they hit rocks, and a pencil-headed bird recites the first fifteen digits of pi (almost correctly — it fumbles the last one). A disembodied voice called the True Spirit of Adventure, performed by Paul Frees — who a decade later would welcome foolish mortals into the Haunted Mansion — guides Donald through a journey that connects ancient Greek mathematics to music, art, nature, games, and the shape of the future. Pythagoras and his Pythagoreans hold a jam session; Donald joins on a vase used as a bongo drum. The golden rectangle appears in the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo, the United Nations building. A live-action billiards player demonstrates the diamond system while Donald spectacularly overcalculates, hitting ten cushions in a single shot. Lewis Carroll appears as both writer and mathematician. Donald tries to suggest checkers and tiddlywinks for the chess sequence; the Spirit declines both. The film's visual artists included John Hench, who'd joined Disney in 1939 as a sketch artist on Fantasia, built the giant squid for 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea, designed the original Tomorrowland, and would go on to paint Mickey Mouse's official portrait every decade for fifty years — still working full-time at Disney when he died at 95. Collin Campbell, another Disney Legend, contributed visual work. Buddy Baker composed the score. The four directors — Hamilton Luske supervising, with Wolfgang Reitherman, Les Clark, and Joshua Meador on sequences — spanned the studio's history. Les Clark had started at Disney in the Oswald the Lucky Rabbit era. The voice of Donald was Clarence "Ducky" Nash, marking Donald's 125th theatrical appearance. Released June 26, 1959 on a bill with Darby O'Gill and the Little People, the featurette was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject. Two years later it had the honor of appearing in the very first episode of Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color on NBC, September 24, 1961, with an introduction by Ludwig Von Drake. But its real life began in classrooms. Disney made it available on 16mm filmstrip, then VHS, then DVD, and it became the most popular educational film ever released by the Walt Disney Educational Media Company. For decades, the appearance of the AV cart meant one of two things: you were watching a filmstrip about dental hygiene, or you were watching Donald in Mathmagic Land. As Walt himself said: "The cartoon is a good medium to stimulate interest. We have recently explained mathematics in a film and in that way excited public interest in this very important subject." Its cultural afterlife keeps growing: Ted Lasso's 2023 hallucination sequence directly homages it, complete with the Spirit of Adventure's voice; Futurama's "The Numberland Gap" features it in the opening and builds the entire episode's plot from it. The film closes with Galileo: "Mathematics is the alphabet with which God has written the universe."

programme.title: Am I Trustworthy?
programme.desc:
Eddie Johnson wants to be treasurer of his hobby club, and he's stung when the members nominate another boy instead and put him on the clean-up committee. He tells his father the other kids just don't like him, but his father redirects the question: trustworthy isn't the same thing as popular, it's whether people can count on you to do what you said you'd do. Pressed on it, Eddie has to admit the evidence is against him — a lamp he promised to fix sits forgotten in the corner, homework gets left to the last minute, a model kit lies half-built on the table. He draws up a chart to track himself against his word, then works through it scene by scene: fixing the lamp, finishing assignments on time, helping around the house and at the grocery store, and taking on a small job at the school library's book charge-out desk. By the end his kept promises have done what his campaign speech couldn't, and the treasurer's job he wanted looks within reach after all.
The only credit on screen, in keeping with Coronet's house practice of naming the classroom consultant rather than the filmmakers, is "Educational Collaborator Elizabeth B. Carey, Ph.D., Supervisor, Bureau of Instructional Supervision, The University of the State of New York," under a copyright dated MCML (1950) to Coronet's publisher, David A. Smart, with an RCA Sound System credit. A contemporary DVD review of the film corroborates that it was made for that same New York State office, meaning Carey's department was not just a lending credit but the body the film was produced to serve. No director is credited on the print, and none is reliably documented for this specific title elsewhere, so none is listed here.
"Am I Trustworthy?" belongs to the "social guidance" genre of postwar classroom shorts that Ken Smith catalogued in his 1999 book Mental Hygiene: Classroom Films 1945-1970, where he notes that trustworthiness in the film functions as something close to a synonym for obedience and conformity, and quotes its closing moral: "People have to show they can be trusted with little things if they want to be trusted with big things." A 16mm print was donated to the Internet Archive's Prelinger Collection in 2002 and remains in the public domain, and the film was later remastered for Kino Lorber's 2009 DVD anthology "How to Be a Man, Volume 1," drawn from Skip Elsheimer's A/V Geeks film library alongside eleven other classroom shorts of the era — a fairly ordinary, "stagey and confined" example of the genre, by one reviewer's account, but a representative one.

programme.title: Le Roi et l'Oiseau
programme.desc:
In the kingdom of Takicardia, a cross-eyed tyrant king falls in love with the painting of a shepherdess who loves the chimney sweep in the painting opposite. The portraits escape. The king pursues. A mockingbird — whose wife the king shot — helps the lovers flee through a castle that rises into the clouds above a sunless lower city where the people have never seen daylight. A giant robot is unleashed. The castle falls. In the final scene, added thirty years after the first, the robot sits alone in the ruins. A small bird is trapped in a cage. The robot reaches down and frees it, then crushes the cage. End of film.
That ending took Paul Grimault thirty-two years to find.
Grimault was born in Neuilly-sur-Seine on March 23, 1905. He met Jacques Prévert through Groupe Octobre, the agitprop theater company where Surrealists and communists collided in 1930s Paris. Prévert was already famous — his screenplays for Marcel Carné (Quai des brumes, Le Jour se lève, Les Visiteurs du soir) had defined poetic realism. Their first collaboration was Le Petit Soldat (1947), an adaptation of Andersen's "The Steadfast Tin Soldier" that won the Grand Prix at Venice and Prague.
They began their second Andersen adaptation, La Bergère et le Ramoneur, in 1948. It would be the first feature-length French animated film. In 1936, Grimault had founded Les Gémeaux with his business partner André Sarrut — the second significant French animation studio, following Émile Cohl's work decades earlier. During the war, with American films unavailable, Les Gémeaux found a captive audience. But the expense of the Shepherdess feature was crushing. In 1950, Sarrut wrested control from Grimault and released the film unfinished in 1952, against both Grimault and Prévert's wishes. Les Gémeaux collapsed. The partnership shattered.
The incomplete film toured the world anyway. When it reached Japan in 1955, something detonated.
At Toei Doga, the young animators Isao Takahata and Yasuo Otsuka studied it obsessively. They screened it until the print tore vertically. They taped the soundtrack and played it in the studio. They drew pose collections from individual frames. Takahata copied the entire script by hand from borrowed airmail paper. He later wrote: "If I had not seen this film, I would have never imagined entering the world of animation." Miyazaki studied it too — particularly Grimault's use of vertical space in the castle, which he called a revelation: "It was through watching Le Roi et l'Oiseau that I understood how it was necessary to use space in a vertical manner." The Castle of Cagliostro (1979) openly echoes its castle architecture. On the Japanese deluxe DVD, Miyazaki and Takahata discuss taking frame-by-frame photographs of sequences — like the king elbowing aside the court painter — to study the animation technique. When the completed film was finally dubbed into Japanese for Ghibli Museum Library release in 2007, the bird was voiced by Gorō Naya, who had played Inspector Zenigata in The Castle of Cagliostro.
But the 1952 version that changed Japan was a film its creators disowned.
Grimault spent fifteen years recovering the rights. In 1967 he finally got possession. Then he spent another decade finding financing. By 1977 he had it — from producer Robert Dorfmann and the television network Antenne 2. He hired back the original animators alongside younger ones. The completed film uses 42 of the original 62 minutes but adds significant new animation, including the entirely new opening sequences, a different lion pit scene (the simpler, more abstract lions are the new work — you can see the two styles within a single scene), and the revolutionary ending.
The music changed completely. Joseph Kosma had scored the 1952 version. For the completed film, Grimault turned to Wojciech Kilar — the Polish composer who would later score The Pianist and Bram Stoker's Dracula. Grimault gave Kilar no instructions whatsoever. He simply showed him the film. Kilar went to Poland, recorded the score, and returned with the finished music. It was accepted unchanged.
The film is dense with cultural reference. The castle evokes Neuschwanstein and Carcassonne (with its real ville basse — lower city). The industrial undercity recalls Fritz Lang's Metropolis. The king's proclamation that "work is liberty" alludes to "Arbeit macht frei" over concentration camp gates. His appearance emerging from water — mustache and hair — unmistakably evokes Hitler. The twin police officers recall Thomson and Thompson from Tintin. The robot's chest-pounding echoes King Kong; its final posture is Rodin's Thinker. The bird was inspired by Jean Mollet (secretary to Guillaume Apollinaire) and by Pierre Brasseur's performance as Robert Macaire in Les Enfants du Paradis — Prévert's own masterpiece screenplay.
Prévert himself did not live to see the completed film. He died of lung cancer on April 11, 1977, in Omonville-la-Petite, while working on the final scenes. When Le Roi et l'Oiseau premiered on March 19, 1980 — having received the Louis Delluc Prize in December 1979 — it was dedicated to his memory. Grimault kept the seat beside him empty on opening night.
In Prévert's poetry collection Paroles (1945), the poem "Pour faire le portrait d'un oiseau" contains the lines: "Parfois l'oiseau arrive vite / mais il peut aussi bien mettre de longues années / avant de se décider" — Sometimes the bird arrives quickly / but he can also take many years / before he decides himself.
It took thirty-two years. But the bird decided.
Note: This is the 2003 digital restoration of the definitive 1980 version, in French. The English-language 1952 version — retitled "The Curious Adventures of Mr. Wonderbird," narrated by Peter Ustinov with Claire Bloom as the Shepherdess and Denholm Elliott as the Chimney Sweep — is in the public domain but is the unfinished film Grimault disowned. The 1980 version was re-released in French cinemas in 2013, in UK cinemas in 2014 by the Independent Cinema Office, and was available on The Criterion Channel. Rialto Pictures released it in select US theaters. Grimault died on March 29, 1994, aged 89.

programme.title: Marriage Is a Partnership
programme.desc:
Dotty rides an eastbound train alone and lets her mind drift back over the year just past. In flashback, Coronet reconstructs the small, cumulative friction of a first year of marriage: she and her husband Pete move into their first apartment together and work out, meal by meal, who does the dishes and who irons the shirts, redividing chores neither of them wanted the first time around. A furniture-buying trip turns into an argument about what they can actually afford; an older female relative arrives to help hang curtains and wash windows and, in the course of helping, quietly second-guesses how Dotty is keeping house; an afternoon spent minding a friend's baby gives the young couple an uneasy preview of a stage still ahead of them. The seasons turn — a yard filling with fallen leaves marks the year passing — and the flashback resolves the way Coronet's guidance shorts usually do: not with one partner winning an argument, but with Pete and Dotty at the kitchen table, going over the household budget together and deciding, out loud, as partners. The film closes back on the train, Dotty's face settled rather than troubled.
The card that opens the print reads "A Coronet Film," followed by a copyright date of MCMLI — 1951 — under the name of David A. Smart, the Chicago publisher who owned Coronet Instructional Films, and the RCA Sound System trademark Coronet ran on its negatives through the period. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance catalog, no director or performer is named on screen; the only credited contributor is the educational collaborator, Lemo D. Rockwood, Ph.D., billed as Professor of Family Relationships at the New York State College of Home Economics at Cornell University.
Rockwood's own class at Cornell, known on campus as the Marriage Course, was one of the most sought-after electives of the late 1940s, open to students across every college and taught with an unusual mix of historical and anthropological background alongside frank discussion of courtship, mate selection, and the daily mechanics of married life — an approach that, per Cornell University Library's own retrospective on Rockwood, drew real anxiety from more conservative faculty and administrators even as students filled her lecture hall. That same practical, unsentimental voice is what Coronet put on screen here: a Pete-and-Dotty story with no villain, only two people learning to negotiate. The film survives today through Prelinger Archives' donation of Coronet's negatives to the Internet Archive, where it continues to circulate in classroom-print form.

programme.title: Time Masters
programme.desc:
The second collaboration between René Laloux and novelist Stefan Wul, whose 1958 book L'Orphelin de Perdide provided the source material just as his earlier novel Oms en série had provided the basis for Fantastic Planet. Wul was the pen name of Pierre Pairault, a dentist from the Paris suburbs who wrote eleven science fiction novels in three years between 1956 and 1959, then stopped writing for nearly two decades. His novels were considered minor pulp at the time. Laloux saw something in them that nobody else had.
The production designer was Jean Giraud — Moebius — who by 1982 was arguably the most influential science fiction artist alive. He had contributed conceptual designs for Ridley Scott's Alien, animated sequences for Heavy Metal, and drawn the storyboards for Alejandro Jodorowsky's legendary unproduced Dune. According to Hungarian VFX artist Peter Eszenyi, Moebius chose Time Masters over continued work on Blade Runner, which was being produced simultaneously. Whether he truly turned it down or simply reduced his involvement is unclear, but the choice tells you where Moebius's heart was: not with Syd Mead's chrome Los Angeles but with Laloux's organic alien worlds, the kind of landscapes he'd been drawing in Arzach and The Airtight Garage since the mid-seventies.
The dialogue was written by Jean-Patrick Manchette, France's most important crime novelist of the 1970s — the man who reinvented French noir fiction with books like Nada and The Prone Gunman. An improbable hire for a children's science fiction film, and exactly the kind of decision Laloux made.
The animation was done at Pannonia Film Studio in Budapest. Laloux outsourced to Hungary because his budget was tiny but he needed a studio capable of high-quality work. Pannonia was world-class — Hungary's premier animation workshop — but the money still wasn't enough. The result is a film of wildly fluctuating quality: some sequences are gorgeously rendered, with Moebius's organic alien landscapes given full justice, while others clearly show the seams of a production running out of resources. Eszenyi, who saw it as a child in Hungary, remembers the state censors assuming anything animated must be for children. Hundreds of thousands of Hungarian kids sat down expecting Disney and got faceless angels with tentacles, brain-eating giant hornets, existential time paradoxes, and a planet called Perdide — which means "lost."
Moebius designed spaceships that looked like silver insects, forests that resembled deep-sea coral, and a cast of characters ranging from a chivalrous space captain to a pair of telepathic oval creatures called gnomes who read minds and find human thoughts physically painful. The favored themes are anarchy, individualism, nature, and love. On one planet, a race of identical faceless beings preach "unity" and "the beatitude of indifference" by eliminating individuality — a sequence that plays like Laloux's answer to the conformity anxieties of both Huxley and Orwell, rendered in pastel watercolors.
The connection to Hayao Miyazaki is direct and documented. Miyazaki said that reading Moebius's Arzach in 1980 was "a big shock" and that he "directed Nausicaä under Moebius' influence." Moebius returned the admiration — he named his daughter Nausicaä. In 2004, a joint exhibition in Paris displayed three hundred works from both artists' careers, including a drawing of Nausicaä by Moebius and one of Arzach by Miyazaki. Time Masters and Nausicaä were being made at the same time — both feature alien ecological worlds rendered with obsessive botanical detail, both treat nature as dangerous and beautiful and worth protecting from human stupidity. The line from Moebius's Perdide to Miyazaki's Valley of the Wind is not a metaphor. It's a direct inheritance.
Federico Fellini, asked about Moebius: "He disturbs and consoles. He has the ability to transport us into unknown worlds where we encounter unsettling characters. My admiration for him is total. I consider him a great artist, as great as Picasso and Matisse."
Time Masters was a commercial disappointment and a critical oddity — Laloux's only children's film, awkwardly straddling cutesy song sequences and genuinely unsettling imagery. It remained largely unknown outside France and Hungary for decades. A 4K restoration finally gave it a proper US theatrical release in 2024, starting at New York's IFC Center. Eighty minutes long, packed with enough alien worlds to fill a graphic novel, and designed by the man Fellini compared to Picasso.

programme.title: How Quiet Helps at School
programme.desc:
The film opens in a school hallway lined with lockers, then pushes into a first-grade classroom where the ordinary business of the day — passing papers, moving chairs, calling out — plays as a small racket. Next door, under a teacher the narration calls Miss Bradley, the same tasks unfold in near-total silence: children whisper instead of talk, a boy sharpens a pencil and crosses the room to a supply closet without a sound, and the class works through an assignment while the wall clock ticks audibly in the quiet. Miss Bradley tells the room that keeping things this hushed is good practice because a classroom, like an office, runs better without noise, and that knowing when to be quiet is simply part of growing up. The film does not ask for silence everywhere — it closes on the same children loose and loud on the playground swings, the noise they were asked to hold indoors now given somewhere to go.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films on RCA's sound system and copyrighted MCMLIII to John Smart, the standard Coronet registration of the period. As with the studio's other social guidance shorts, the only credited collaborator on screen is the psychology consultant: the title card names Henry Bonner McDaniel, Ph.D., Professor of Education and Psychology at Stanford University. McDaniel was a real fixture of Stanford's education faculty in these years — Stanford's Graduate School of Education dates his work building out the university's guidance-counseling program to 1947–1968 — lending the film's classroom-management message the same applied-psychology backing Coronet leaned on across the genre. No director is credited on the print, and none is attested specifically for this title.
The film survives through the Prelinger Archives, whose catalog twice describes it in almost identical terms: a demonstration of "how a class can study and work better if the room is quiet," with noise given its proper place on the playground rather than banished outright. Later commentary on the Coronet social-guidance cycle has singled this one out as unusually serene even by the genre's own standards — one retrospective review calls the hushed classroom a room of "well-behaved, conscientious" children and notes the almost suspenseful quiet of watching a pupil cross the room without making a sound. Seen today, it reads less as an outlier than as a fairly ordinary specimen of the classroom-discipline instructionals Coronet turned out through the 1950s for use in American schools.

programme.title: The Phantom Tollbooth
programme.desc: Bored young Milo finds a mysterious tollbooth in his room that transports him from live action into a hand-drawn Kingdom of Wisdom, where idioms are literal landscapes, mathematics and words are at war, and two exiled princesses named Rhyme and Reason must be rescued from the Castle in the Air. He is accompanied by Tock the watchdog — a dog with an actual alarm clock in his body — and the pompous Humbug. Together they cross the Doldrums, visit Dictionopolis (where you eat your words, served on plates), ascend to Digitopolis, and battle demons in the Mountains of Ignorance including the Terrible Trivium (an exquisitely tailored dandy without a face who wastes your time with pointless tasks) and the Triple Demons of Compromise — one tall and thin, one short and fat, and the third exactly like the other two. Norton Juster was an architect living in Brooklyn Heights. In 1960 he received a $5,000 Ford Foundation grant to write a children's book about cities. Instead, wracked with guilt over his lack of progress, he started writing something else entirely — a story about a boy who asked too many questions. His downstairs neighbor was the cartoonist Jules Feiffer, who could hear Juster pacing above him at night. When Feiffer learned the insomnia was caused not by the cities book but by a story about a boy, he asked to see the manuscript. Unbidden, he began drawing illustrations. It became a game: Juster would describe things impossible to draw (like the Triple Demons), and Feiffer would try to draw them anyway. Feiffer got revenge by depicting Juster as the Whether Man, wearing a toga. Since Juster did the cooking and Feiffer wanted to eat, Feiffer had to do the drawings. Jason Epstein at Random House bought the book based on seven chapters and a three-page outline. Some editors thought the vocabulary was too difficult — at the time, educators warned against words children didn't already know. Epstein disagreed. Nearly five million copies later, he was right. Juster also wrote The Dot and the Line: A Romance in Lower Mathematics (1963), a love story between a line, a dot, and a squiggle. Chuck Jones adapted that into an Oscar-winning animated short — and when MGM optioned Phantom Tollbooth in January 1966, Jones and his production designer Maurice Noble were the natural choice. Jones came to this project fresh from reinventing Tom and Jerry for MGM after leaving Warner Bros., where he had created Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, the Road Runner, Pepé Le Pew, and Wile E. Coyote. He had added the character Ralph — reasoning that "it had to be a boy named Ralph. Anybody called Steve or Mike would have called with something to do. Ralph sounds like a wet tennis shoe." Butch Patrick — Eddie Munster himself — plays Milo in the live-action bookend sequences. The voice cast is the golden age of American voice acting: Mel Blanc (Officer Short Shrift, the Dodecahedron, the Demon of Insincerity), Daws Butler (the Whether Man, the Senses Taker, the Terrible Trivium, the Gelatinous Giant), Hans Conried (both King Azaz AND the Mathemagician — because they are brothers), June Foray (Ralph, Princess of Pure Reason, Faintly Macabre), and Thurl Ravenscroft — the voice of Tony the Tiger — as a Lethargarian. Completed in 1968, MGM sat on it for two years due to internal turmoil, then dumped it into children's matinee slots. It flopped. The animation studio closed shortly after. It was the last significant project of MGM Animation/Visual Arts. Juster never liked the film: "It was a film I never liked. I don't think they did a good job on it. It's been around for a long time. It was well reviewed, which also made me angry." He was perhaps too close to his creation. Chuck Jones brought to it exactly what he brought to everything — impeccable comic timing, bold color, and characters who vibrate with personality even when standing still. Maurice Noble's backgrounds are stunning: stylized, geometric, and deeply weird in the way that only Noble could make weird. It is 100% on Rotten Tomatoes. C.P. Snow's 1959 lecture "The Two Cultures" — about the widening divide between humanities and sciences — directly influenced the book's central conflict between Dictionopolis and Digitopolis. Juster told an interviewer: "I didn't lay it out as a thesis or anything, but it was fun having it in there. And it doesn't get in the way of the story." Maurice Sendak, in his introduction to later editions, quoted a critic comparing Phantom Tollbooth to Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress: "As Pilgrim's Progress is concerned with the awakening of the sluggardly spirit, The Phantom Tollbooth is concerned with the awakening of the lazy mind." Juster died on March 8, 2021, at 91. Feiffer, remarkably, is still alive. The documentary about their collaboration has been made available free at phantomtollboothdoc.com.

programme.title: What To Do On A Date
programme.desc:
Nick and his friend Jeff are tossing a ball along the sidewalk when Nick spots a girl, Kay, walking home, and loses track of the game watching her go. Back at the house, her number is already penciled into the margin of Nick's notebook, right next to an unfinished book report on Nathaniel Hawthorne, and it's Jeff — leaning over the banister, needling him along — who finally gets Nick to pick up the phone and ask. Once Kay says yes, the two of them skip the expensive, ready-made idea of just taking a girl to the movies and instead throw themselves into the school's "Knick-Knacks" scavenger sale: painting signs, hanging a paper elephant from a ladder, stringing bunting and lanterns across the yard. Kay and her friend Phyllis turn up that afternoon to pitch in alongside them, sorting donated goods and tacking up notices on the club bulletin board, and by evening the sale has become a small carnival, the two couples working booths and finishing the night together over sandwiches and cold drinks — precisely the supervised, low-cost, group-built evening Coronet is holding up as the answer to the title's question.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films — the print's copyright card reads MCMLI, 1951, under founder David A. Smart, over the RCA Sound System mark. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance line, the only name in the picture itself is the consulting educator: the title card credits "Educational Collaborator Evelyn M. Duvall, Ph.D., Consultant, National Council on Family Relations," the family-life researcher whose dating and courtship studies underpin several Coronet guidance shorts of the period. No director or performer is named on screen. The Prelinger Archives catalog record for the film credits Ted Peshak as director, cameraman Dale Sharkey, writers George Tychsen and (George T.) Bradford, editor Dick Kirschner, and narrator George Stone — Peshak's credit for this specific title is echoed by Letterboxd's own listing, though, again, the print is silent on all of it.
The film sits alongside Are You Popular? and Date Etiquette in Coronet's cycle of postwar dating shorts, all pitching group activity and modest spending as the cure for an awkward date. Oddly, the Prelinger Archives catalogs this same title under 1950, a year earlier than the MCMLI copyright stamped on the print — likely a gap between production and the copyright's formal registration, but worth noting since it puts the film's actual copyright date a year later than its most common listing. Letterboxd and IMDb both credit Robert Casey as the lead of the teenage cast, though which of the two boys he played isn't attested anywhere reliable enough to print, and the film itself names no performers at all. It survives today as an unaltered classroom print, held and circulated through the Prelinger Collection along with dozens of other Coronet social-guidance shorts from the same run.

programme.title: The Last Unicorn
programme.desc:
Peter Beagle started writing the novel at twenty-two years old, in a cabin in Cheshire, Massachusetts. He has called it "the hardest, least fun thing I've ever had to write." Published in 1968, it became a cult classic — and immediately attracted Hollywood interest. Even the team behind A Charlie Brown Christmas wanted to animate it. By 1972 a production company called Balaban and Quine had optioned the rights. Nothing happened. That pattern would repeat for a decade. "Always almost getting made," Beagle said.
In 1974, a young independent producer named Michael Chase Walker fell in love with the novel. He spent two years prying the rights away from Balaban and Quine, finally buying a year-and-a-half option in 1976. Then he discovered how Hollywood really works: "If they like the idea and you have the option, the biggest strategy is that they'll wait for the option to run out and then option it themselves. Because they know you can't pour constant money into it." Studio after studio took meetings and never called back. Two weeks before his option expired, Walker gambled everything and bought the film rights outright — roughly two hundred thousand dollars in today's money. Beagle received "the biggest check I'd ever seen."
For a brief, giddy moment it looked like it would work. In 1978, riding the hype around Ralph Bakshi's animated Lord of the Rings (which Beagle himself had written the screenplay for), Warner Bros. signed a development deal at twenty-five thousand dollars per month. Walker went "from living in a lean-to in my brother's back yard to a gorgeous house in the hills in less than a month." Then Lord of the Rings posted mediocre numbers and Warner dropped The Last Unicorn instantly. Walker's payments became debt.
Desperate, Walker made the connection that saved the project. Around early 1979, Marble Arch Productions introduced him to Arthur Rankin and Jules Bass, who wanted a follow-up to their animated Hobbit. A deal was struck. Walker was relieved but not thrilled — Rankin/Bass was essentially his last option. "I really couldn't stand their animation." Beagle was worse: "I hated everything Rankin and Bass had ever done. Everything. Didn't like what they'd done to Tolkien. I hated Frosty the flipping snowman, let alone Rudolph the whatsit." He screamed at Walker: "Why don't you go all the way and sell it to Hanna-Barbera?!" Walker replied solemnly: "They were next."
Then something unexpected happened. Jules Bass asked Beagle to write the screenplay close to his novel — not the stripped-down version Beagle had preemptively written, assuming they'd want something simple. "They were surprisingly easy to work with, they respected the material, and they did better with it than really anything of theirs I had ever seen."
Rankin/Bass, as always, sent the actual animation to Japan. Tokyo's Topcraft — the same studio that would produce Hayao Miyazaki's Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind two years later — did the bulk of the work. The numbers tell the story of how seriously they took it: seventy-five thousand drawings and two hundred sixty colors, at a time when a typical anime production used eighty to one hundred thirty. They avoided static held-frame shots common in Japanese animation. Topcraft's legendary artist Tsuguyuki Kubo co-designed the characters and co-storyboarded the film. The forest backgrounds were influenced by the art of Kay Nielsen — Topcraft spent two million yen on a single artbook to study his work. For King Haggard's castle, they built a clay model and photographed it under different colored lights as reference. Several of the key animators — Tadakatsu Yoshida, Kazuyuki Kobayashi, Yoshiko Sasaki, Hidekazu Ohara — went directly from this film to Nausicaa. When Topcraft dissolved after Nausicaa, its president Toru Hara founded Studio Ghibli. The Last Unicorn is, in a real sense, a proto-Ghibli film.
The voice cast was extraordinary. Christopher Lee played King Haggard. When Beagle first met him at a Los Angeles recording studio, Lee had just finished Haggard's speech about his first sight of unicorns and immediately wanted to know, "Well, did I do it properly?" Lee called the novel one of his favorite books and the film one of the movies he was most proud of making. When it was dubbed into German, Lee re-recorded his entire performance in German for no additional fee — "I simply couldn't resist a chance to play King Haggard one more time, even in another language." Then he looked into an Austrian television camera and said, "After all, it's the closest they'll ever let me get to playing King Lear." Jeff Bridges volunteered to voice Prince Lir for free.
During the Munich dubbing sessions, Beagle and Walker went to Dachau. They returned to the hotel in silence. Lee took one look at them: "You've been to Dachau." They nodded. He lowered his voice: "Still smells, doesn't it?" Lee had been there in 1945, assigned to Special Forces to hunt and interrogate Nazi war criminals.
Jimmy Webb composed and arranged the soundtrack, performed by the band America and the London Symphony Orchestra. The distribution was cursed to the end: Universal was set as distributor but was "less than enthusiastic" about the finished film and dropped it. Rankin/Bass ended up with a tiny distributor from Utah. Box office returns were "not too good." Arthur Rankin later admitted, "We should've had more money to make it; we could've made a better film — with more production. Not the script, but the depth of animation." But VHS and television airings grew the audience over years. It became a cult film in America and a genuine phenomenon in Germany, partly thanks to Lee's German-language performance. Budget: approximately three and a half million dollars.

programme.title: Are You Ready For Marriage
programme.desc:
Larry and Sue are a young couple who have all but decided to elope, since Sue's parents object to the match. Before they run off, they agree to talk it over with Mr. Hall, the marriage counselor at their church. Sitting across the desk from him, the two realize how little they actually know about each other, and Mr. Hall walks them through what he calls Cupid's Checklist: do they come from similar backgrounds, are they real friends, do they understand what marriage actually involves? He illustrates the point with props straight out of a classroom — a board of tiny wooden figures wired together at different "psychological distances," and a hand-drawn curve charting a couple's chance for happiness against how long they've been engaged and how old the groom is when he marries. By the end, Larry and Sue haven't been told no; they've just been shown how much groundwork a lasting marriage takes; the film closes on the two of them, warmer with each other than when they walked in.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films and directed by Gil Altschul, with camera work by Bruce Colling, script by Chuck Probst and Harriette Smith, and editing by George Wilbern. As with other Coronet guidance shorts, the only credential named on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: the title card introduces Reuben Hill, Ph.D., Research Professor in Family Life at the University of North Carolina, who also appears in the film itself playing the counselor, Mr. Hall. Hill was a genuine pioneer of family-life research — long affiliated with the National Council on Family Relations — and the checklist-and-chart approach on screen is a fairly direct translation of his academic work on courtship and marital readiness into a classroom short.
The trade press noticed the effort: Educational Screen's September 1950 review praised the picture for avoiding "stereotyped characters, stale and trite expressions" and judged it well suited to high-school counseling, in group settings or one-on-one. The Coronet catalog framed the film's purpose bluntly, as an attempt to stem what it called the postwar "epidemic of youthful, impetuous, and unsuccessful marriages." Whatever its era-bound charts and lapels look like now, the short is of a piece with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance line: a real family sociologist's checklist, dressed up as a date-night crisis, aimed squarely at the study hall.

programme.title: The Hobbit
programme.desc:
Arthur Rankin Jr. contacted the Tolkien Estate about adapting The Hobbit for television. They refused. Rankin pointed out that due to a mishap in the original American publication, the books were in the public domain in the United States. The Estate and their licensee Saul Zaentz could do nothing about it. Rankin made the film anyway. It cost three million dollars, aired on NBC the Sunday after Thanksgiving in 1977, and won a Peabody Award. The Tolkien scholars hated it. Douglas Anderson called it "execrable." Baird Searles called it "an abomination." Millions of children watched it and picked up the book for the first time. Tolkien fandom has been arguing about which of those reactions matters more ever since.
The voice cast is the kind of thing that only happened in 1970s television, when Hollywood legends would show up for voice work the way they might show up for a dinner party. John Huston — who had directed The Maltese Falcon, The African Queen, and The Treasure of the Sierra Madre — read Gandalf as if he were narrating his own autobiography. He was a fan of the book, which is audible. His reading of "Far over the Misty Mountains Cold" is performed without cutting a single line from Tolkien's original poem, over a montage of Smaug's destruction of Erebor that keeps the dragon almost entirely hidden: a shadow over Dale, a roiling ball of fire, blasts of heat searing trees. It is still spine-tingling.
Otto Preminger voiced the Elvenking. The director of Laura, Anatomy of a Murder, and Exodus, playing a wood elf. Richard Boone — Paladin from Have Gun, Will Travel — gave Smaug a gravelly, predatory rumble that the Black Gate review correctly identified as generating "genuine suspense" in the conversation with Bilbo, aided by effects animation that turned Smaug's searching eyes into spotlights sweeping over the treasure hoard. Hans Conried, who had been Captain Hook for Disney in 1953, played Thorin Oakenshield and delivered the death scene — "There is more in you of good than you know, child of the kindly West" — with a sincerity that the compressed runtime had not earned but that Conried's voice made you believe anyway.
Then there was Brother Theodore as Gollum. Theodore Isidore Gottlieb, born in Dusseldorf in 1906, had been imprisoned at Dachau until he signed over his family's fortune for one Reichsmark. After being deported from Switzerland for chess hustling, he emigrated to the United States with help from Albert Einstein, a family friend. He worked as a janitor at Stanford, where he beat thirty professors at chess simultaneously. He invented a performance style he called "stand-up tragedy" — rambling, stream-of-consciousness monologues that someone once described as "Boris Karloff, Salvador Dali, Nijinsky, and Red Skelton, simultaneously." He was seventy-one years old when he voiced Gollum. His reading of "what has it got in its pocketses" sounds like something dredged from a place no cartoon character should be able to reach.
The goblin songs — "Clap! Snap! the Black Crack!" and "Fifteen Birds in Five Fir-Trees" — were performed by Thurl Ravenscroft, whose bass voice was already in the ears of every American alive whether they knew it or not. He had been Tony the Tiger for Kellogg's Frosted Flakes since 1954 and had sung "You're a Mean One, Mr. Grinch" uncredited for the 1966 Dr. Seuss special. In The Hobbit, his rumble gave the goblins a genuine menace that the animation alone could not have achieved.
The sole original song, "The Greatest Adventure (The Ballad of the Hobbit)," was written by Jules Bass and composed by Maury Laws, Rankin/Bass's in-house composer-conductor. It was performed by folk singer Glenn Yarbrough, formerly of The Limeliters, whose warm tenor became the film's emotional backbone. The rest of the musical interludes were drawn directly from Tolkien's own verse, adapted by Bass, and they work because the childlike wonder of the songs matches the tone of the source material in a way that Rankin/Bass's later Return of the King never quite managed.
Romeo Muller wrote the teleplay. He had written Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, Frosty the Snowman, and most of the other Rankin/Bass holiday specials. Rankin's instruction was absolute: add nothing to the story that is not in the original book. Muller obeyed. Beorn is the most prominent casualty. The Battle of Five Armies is compressed. But nothing was invented, and several of Muller's compressions are elegant — the Unexpected Party condenses smoothly into the opening minutes, and Bilbo's moment atop the Mirkwood canopy, surrounded by black emperor butterflies, becomes a centerpiece that captures the character's transformation in a single image. Muller added first-person narration from Bilbo over a slow rendition of "The Greatest Adventure" mixed with Tolkien's "Roads Go Ever On and On," and it is the closest the film comes to literature.
The animation was produced at Topcraft in Tokyo, founded in 1972 by Toru Hara and other former Toei Animation staff. Arthur Rankin designed the characters and concept art in New York; Topcraft executed the animation in Japan. Rankin's visual style drew from Arthur Rackham's turn-of-the-century book illustrations — finely detailed lines, rich textures, characters that look like they were drawn with a calligraphy pen. Rhode Island artist Lester Abrams did the initial character designs after Rankin saw his illustrations for a Hobbit excerpt in Children's Digest.
Seven years after animating Bilbo's journey through the Misty Mountains, Topcraft would animate Hayao Miyazaki's Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind. The film was a success. The studio was not. Topcraft went bankrupt on June 15, 1985. Miyazaki took seventy percent of the staff — along with Toru Hara, who became the first manager — and founded Studio Ghibli on the same day. Another ten percent of the departing animators included Hideaki Anno, who would go on to create Neon Genesis Evangelion. The remaining staff formed Pacific Animation Corporation, which Disney later absorbed. The hands that drew Gandalf's fireworks drew Totoro's forest. The same studio pipeline that produced a holiday TV special from a public-domain book in New York became the most celebrated animation studio in the world.
Rankin/Bass and Topcraft would collaborate twice more before the end: The Return of the King in 1980 and The Last Unicorn in 1982. All three films share the same aesthetic DNA — the detailed linework, the watercolor backgrounds, the sense that you are watching an illustrated book come to life. The Last Unicorn was Topcraft's final major production before the dissolution.
The original 1977 broadcast included ambient sound effects — background sounds, atmospheric details — that were stripped from subsequent home video releases and never restored by the rights holders. For decades, every version available was missing audio that viewers who recorded the original broadcast on VHS could still hear. Fan restorations have attempted to sync preserved original audio back onto higher-quality video transfers, producing versions closer to what thirty million Americans heard on the Sunday after Thanksgiving, 1977.
Seventy-eight minutes. A public-domain loophole. Two legendary film directors doing voice work for a cartoon. A Dachau survivor playing a cave monster. The voice of Tony the Tiger singing goblin war chants. A Japanese animation studio seven years away from becoming Studio Ghibli. A Peabody Award that the Tolkien scholars thought was undeserved, and a generation of readers who know better.

programme.title: How to Study
programme.desc:
Jim is a schoolboy handed a civics assignment: the teacher chalks up three current-events questions — should the federal government control medicine, should there be state control of radio and television, should labor unions be required to incorporate — and each student picks one to turn into a written report. Jim takes the labor-union question, and the film follows him treating the job like research rather than homework: he pencils a work schedule onto a wall calendar, then works through a stack of reference books — a general encyclopedia and a bound volume of the Readers' Guide to Periodical Literature — reading each one at a different speed depending on the job at hand, from a fast scan to find what's relevant to a slow, careful pass through the dense print on incorporation law and old court cases like Coronado Coal Company v. United Mine Workers. He boils what he finds down to three study questions, re-reads to check them, and writes the report up with time to spare on his pocket watch.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, the picture follows the house formula: the only credit on screen is the educational collaborator, here William G. Brink, Ph.D., Professor of Education at Northwestern University, named on the same title card as the RCA sound-system credit and nowhere else. Brink's own published work of the period concerned the study of classroom teaching materials, which tracks with the film's close attention to differentiated reading speeds — presented less as moralizing than as a plain set of techniques, the scan/skim/read-closely/re-read sequence that library and study-skills instruction would keep teaching for decades. As with much of Coronet's early-1940s output, the surviving print is black-and-white 16mm.
How to Study sits in the study-skills wing of Coronet's guidance catalog, a smaller cousin to the social-guidance shorts the company became better known for — the same brisk, under-ten-minute run time, aimed here at library and study-hall habits rather than dating or popularity. The Prelinger Archives catalog entry for the film describes exactly this: Jim preparing a civics report on labor unions using four kinds of reading — scanning, rapid reading, careful slow reading, and re-reading — to organize his research and write it up. Public domain since its educational-market rights lapsed, it now circulates chiefly through the Prelinger collection at the Internet Archive, alongside the rest of Coronet's postwar schoolroom output.

programme.title: The Mouse and His Child
programme.desc: A wind-up father mouse and his child — two tin figures joined at the hands, sharing one clockwork mechanism — are bought from a toy shop at Christmas and eventually discarded. They end up in a garbage dump ruled by Manny the Rat (his full name: Emmanuel Wolfington Rat III), a tyrant who enslaves broken toys to work in his casino. They escape with the help of a philosophizing frog and embark on a quest to become "self-winding" — to find autonomy, a family, and a home. Along the way they encounter a territorial muskrat, a fortune-telling crow, and an avant-garde theatrical troupe called the Caws of Art (they are crows), performing C. Serpentina's experimental play "The Last Visible Dog." The title of the play comes from a can of dog food whose label shows a dog carrying a can of dog food whose label shows a dog carrying a can of dog food — an infinite regression that becomes the story's central philosophical image. "Nothing," says the mouse child, peering between the dots of the label. "I can see nothing." "Nothing is the ultimate truth," replies the turtle. But then the label peels away and the child says: "There's nothing on the other side of nothing but us." Adapted from Russell Hoban's 1967 novel, which has been called the darkest and most philosophical children's book ever written. Hoban was the son of Jewish immigrants from Ostrog, Ukraine. His father was the advertising manager of the Yiddish-language Jewish Daily Forward and died when Russell was eleven. After briefly attending Temple University, Hoban enlisted in the Army at 18 and served in the Philippines and Italy as a radio operator, earning a Bronze Star. After the war he became an illustrator — his Time cover portrait of Joan Baez now hangs in the National Portrait Gallery — and then a children's book writer. He created Frances the Badger, one of the most beloved series in children's literature. His first wife, Lillian Hoban, illustrated the Frances books. The Mouse and His Child was his first novel and his masterpiece. After finishing it, Hoban took his family to London for what was supposed to be a short trip. The marriage dissolved. Lillian and the children returned to America. Hoban stayed in London for the rest of his life — forty-two years, until his death in 2011. He would go on to write Riddley Walker (1980), a post-apocalyptic novel written entirely in a degraded future English, which is considered one of the greatest works of twentieth-century science fiction. Harold Pinter adapted his novel Turtle Diary into a film. The Royal Shakespeare Company staged The Mouse and His Child in their 2012-13 winter season. He once ruefully observed that death would be a good career move: "People will say, Yes, Hoban, he seems an interesting writer, let's look at him again." His papers are now at the Beinecke Library at Yale. The film was a US-Japan co-production between Murakami-Wolf Productions and Sanrio — the Hello Kitty company, making one of the darkest animated films of the 1970s. Co-directed by Fred Wolf (who later became known as the producer of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles animated series) and Charles Swenson. Budget $1.6 million. Peter Ustinov voices Manny the Rat with magnificent villainy. Andy Devine plays the Frog. Cloris Leachman plays Euterpe the Parrot. Sally Kellerman plays the Seal. John Carradine appears as the Tramp. The music by Roger Kellaway is achingly beautiful — including a plaintive song sung in a waveringly broken, off-key child's voice over the credits that is almost unbearably moving. The film has never been released on DVD in the United States. It existed only on VHS until a Japanese DVD was released. The version preserved here combines the Japanese DVD's picture with the original English audio and has been restored with AI upscaling. Janet Maslin of the New York Times praised the direction and writing but noted that "83 minutes is a long time for an adult to think about mice." Leonard Maltin rated it BOMB — his lowest rating — calling it "boring" with "talk, talk, talk, and no action." They were both wrong. It is a film about whether a wind-up toy can choose its own path. It is a film about whether consciousness requires a body or just a question. It is a film about the infinite regression of meaning and whether there's anything on the other side of nothing. The Guardian's Stuart Kelly called it "comforting and devastating" in the same breath and said it was the equal of the Alice books. Released in some territories as The Extraordinary Adventures of the Mouse and His Child.

programme.title: Better Use of Leisure Time
programme.desc:
Ken Michaels is flat on his bed doing nothing, and an unseen narrator won't let him get away with calling it rest — "moping" is the word used. Ken protests that there's nothing to do and no more free time than anyone else has, so the narrator takes him somewhere no ordinary Coronet short bothers to go: backward. First to a version of his own father a hundred years back, a farmer working a 72-hour week who orders young Ken off the bed to muck the stable and build new porch steps; then to a version fifty years back, a ten-hour-a-day, six-day-a-week father whose one indulgence is an evening with the stereoscope. Only then does the narrator return Ken to the present, where his real father works a 40-hour week, sneaks in a round of golf before supper, and is building a bookcase for the house in his spare time. The same time-trip is run on Ken's mother — scrubbing clothes, hauling water, baking bread and feeding chickens from dawn to dark fifty years ago, versus a washing machine and an evening spent planning the women's club program today. Sent to find out what his friends do with their own leisure, Ken discovers Dave identifying birds, Bill clerking part-time at the bookstore, Alice learning to sew, Marge at the piano, and a knot of boys in group sports. The narrator distills his father's bookcase hobby into a formula — a pleasant change from work, a chance to learn something, and a long-range goal — and Ken, rummaging out the camera he got for Christmas, decides photography might fill all three and maybe even a job someday.
The only screen credit is the customary Coronet consultant title card: Educational Collaborator Paul H. Landis, Ph.D., Professor of Sociology at State College of Washington. The picture itself is copyrighted, per its titles, to David A. Smart, the Esquire publisher whose Coronet Instructional Films turned out these classroom shorts by the hundreds from its Glenview, Illinois studio. What sets this one apart from its stablemates is the framing device: rather than a flat classroom-camera address, an argumentative off-screen narrator walks Ken through a series of staged historical vignettes to make its point about work, leisure and the modern 40-hour week. The Prelinger Archives catalog note on the print, written by film historian Ken Smith, calls it "more imaginative than most" Coronet titles "when it comes to visual gimmickry" — a fair description of the back-in-time device carrying the argument.
Ken's mother, credited on no title card but identified in later filmography listings as "Mrs. Michaels," is an early and uncredited screen role for Hope Summers, long before she became a familiar television face as Clara Edwards on The Andy Griffith Show and Mayberry R.F.D. Smith's same catalog note records that the boy playing Ken went on to headline another Coronet short, appearing as "Chuck-of-the-future" in Good Table Manners — one small thread connecting two entries in Coronet's social-guidance run. The film survives today through the Prelinger Archives holdings at the Internet Archive, cataloged as one of the more visually resourceful entries in a genre usually content to let its narrator simply talk over a static scene.

programme.title: The Dark Crystal
programme.desc:
In 1975, Jim Henson was paging through an illustrated edition of Lewis Carroll's "The Pig-Tale" when he stopped at a Leonard B. Lubin drawing of two crocodiles lounging in a sumptuous Victorian palace. "It was the juxtaposition of this reptilian thing in this fine atmosphere that intrigued me," he said later. He began writing a treatment called Mithra — a wooded world with talking mountains and walking boulders, where a malevolent race called the Reptus group had seized power from the peaceful Eunaze. The last survivor was a boy named Brian, adopted by mystical wizards called the Bada. The three races, the quest, the Crystal, and the Great Conjunction were all there in embryonic form. "Mithra" was later shortened to "Thra" after someone pointed out the similarity to the Persian deity.
Two years later Henson met Brian Froud, whose fairy and goblin illustrations in the book Once Upon a Time made him scrap the entire Mithra concept to start fresh. "GREAT FILM," he wrote in his diary, insisting on building the world before tying anything down with a script. Then, in early 1978, Henson and his sixteen-year-old daughter Cheryl were stranded at a Howard Johnson's during a snowstorm. The two of them wrote a sixteen-page treatment they called The Crystal. "I had a delightful time working on the concept and talking it over with Cheryl," he wrote, "and it all jelled during that time."
The philosophical backbone came from an unlikely source. Henson kept multiple copies of Jane Roberts's channeled metaphysical text Seth Speaks and insisted that both Froud and screenwriter David Odell read it before collaborating. Odell later explained: "The idea of perfect beings split into a good mystic part and an evil materialistic part which are reunited after a long separation is Jim's response to the teachings of that book." He noted that Aughra's line upon hearing the Master has died — "He could be anywhere then" — could not have been written without Roberts's material.
Before cameras rolled, Henson got a crucial technical dry run. George Lucas was filming across the street at Elstree Studios and needed help developing a small, wizened Jedi master for The Empire Strikes Back. Yoda was built and performed by the Henson team — Frank Oz performed both Yoda and Aughra, with Kathy Mullen and Wendy Midener operating Yoda's additional controls. Three puppeteers for one character. "It was just the sort of thing that needed a lot of research, a lot of time, and experimentation," Henson said. What they learned went directly into the far more complex creatures of The Dark Crystal, where the Gelflings alone required four puppeteers each.
The creature work was punishing. Wendy Midener sculpted the Gelflings, whose performers walked on their knees during off-camera leg shots to make the gait convincing. Jen was originally meant to be blue, in homage to the Hindu deity Rama. The Skeksis were built around the seven deadly sins — though with ten Skeksis, some sins had to be invented or doubled. Froud initially designed them as deep-sea fish before settling on "part reptile, part predatory bird, part dragon." The Chamberlain puppet contained twenty-one electronic components. The performers, their arms extended overhead to operate the faces, had monitors strapped to their chests because they were completely blind inside the suits. The Mystics were the hardest of all — performers walked on their haunches with their right arms thrust forward bearing the full weight of the head. Henson could hold the position for only five to ten seconds.
Aughra was originally called Habeetabat. Froud vetoed the name because it sounded too much like Habitat, a British retailer he despised. Her voice was inspired by Zero Mostel. Henson and Oz declined to voice any characters themselves, afraid audiences would recognize them from the Muppets.
Henson wanted the Skeksis to speak a constructed language with no subtitles — "like an opera," his daughter Lisa explained. Accounts differ on who built the language: Gary Kurtz says author Alan Garner based it on Ancient Egyptian; David Odell says he created it from Indo-European roots. Either way, it died at a March 1982 sneak preview in Washington, DC. "Not great," Henson wrote in his journal. Creative director Mike Frith told him flatly: "I have no idea what that scene was about." Odell was dispatched to write English dialogue matching the existing mouth movements. The Podling language — based on Serbo-Croatian, with Polish and Russian speakers reportedly catching individual words — survived intact.
The funding story is equally dramatic. Lord Lew Grade at ITC initially promised fourteen million; David Lazer sweet-talked him up to twenty-five million at Cannes, which Frank Oz called "the money that saved the film." But Grade then sold ITC to Australian businessman Robert Holmes à Court, who disliked Henson and the film. Holmes à Court's lawyers and bankers started telling Henson how to "fix" his movie — less Mystics, more Skeksis. "I can't work like this," Henson said. "I've got to get these guys out of here." His solution: buy The Dark Crystal back with his own money, risking nearly all his capital.
Shot at Elstree Studios from April to September 1981, with exteriors in the Scottish Highlands, Gordale Scar in North Yorkshire, and Twycross in Leicestershire. Photographed by Oswald Morris — the same cinematographer who shot Oliver!, Fiddler on the Roof, and The Man Who Would Be King — using the Panaflex camera system with anamorphic lenses and the Lightflex system, processed in Technicolor. Trevor Jones composed the score, recorded at CTS Studios and Abbey Road.
The first major live-action film with no human characters on screen. Frank Oz said Henson's intention was to "get back to the darkness of the original Grimms' Fairy Tales" — he believed it was unhealthy for children to never be afraid. Many of the puppeteers went directly from this production to Return of the Jedi. Mixed reviews on release; now a cult classic. The Netflix prequel series Age of Resistance won an Emmy in 2019 before being cancelled after one season. Budget: twenty-five million dollars. Box office: forty-one million.

programme.title: Overcoming Fear
programme.desc:
At a busy municipal swimming pool, a teenage boy named Bill hangs back while the rest of the gang runs for the water. The opening shots track a crowd of kids racing past the diving boards and pool chairs, then settle on Bill alone at the water's edge and again by the locker-room doors, in his trunks but not going in. Mr. Barker, the pool's swimming coach, doesn't order him in; he sits down with Bill, first at poolside and then on a locker-room bench, and gets him to name what actually scares him about the water. The film then leaves the pool for a run of short vignettes on other, smaller fears — a backyard talk near the clothesline, a girl coaxing a small dog she's wary of, a scene in a book-lined room — before bringing Bill back to the water for a deliberately paced sequence of steps: standing in the shallow end, floating, finally diving from the board on his own. By the last reel he is swimming freestyle across the pool and crouching at the steps to help a smaller child in, one of the crowd he had been avoiding at the start.
Produced at Coronet's studio in Glenview, Illinois — the estate David A. Smart, the Esquire magazine publisher, converted into a 16mm production facility for his instructional-film business — and copyrighted MCML under the Coronet trademark, with the RCA Sound System credit that runs across the studio's postwar output. As with the rest of that catalog, no actors or director are named on screen; the only credit in the title cards is the educational collaborator, Herbert Sorenson, Ph.D., professor of educational psychology at the University of Kentucky and author of textbooks in the field, brought in to keep Barker's breakdown of Bill's fear grounded in contemporary psychology rather than simple reassurance.
Overcoming Fear belongs to the same run of Coronet social-guidance shorts as Shy Guy and Are You Popular?, made for classroom health units rather than theatrical release. The Prelinger Archives catalog description matches the print scene for scene: Bill's fear of the water, Barker's coaching, and the gradual buildup of swimming skill and confidence. No director or cast credits for this specific title turn up in any accessible filmography — Coronet's own credits stop at the consultant, and surviving catalog entries do not even agree on the running time of the print, some logging it under twelve minutes and others closer to thirteen. What holds constant across every source is the premise: fear treated as a nameable, solvable problem, worked through with the same brisk manner Coronet brought to its other studies of adolescent anxiety.

programme.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed
