The same time-trip is run on Ken's mother — scrubbing clothes, hauling water, baking bread and feeding chickens from dawn to dark fifty years ago, versus a washing machine and an evening spent planning the women's club program today. Sent to find out what his friends do with their own leisure, Ken discovers Dave identifying birds, Bill clerking part-time at the bookstore, Alice learning to sew, Marge at the piano, and a knot of boys in group sports. The narrator distills his father's bookcase hobby into a formula — a pleasant change from work, a chance to learn something, and a long-range goal — and Ken, rummaging out the camera he got for Christmas, decides photography might fill all three and maybe even a job someday.
The only screen credit is the customary Coronet consultant title card: Educational Collaborator Paul H. Landis, Ph.D., Professor of Sociology at State College of Washington. The picture itself is copyrighted, per its titles, to David A. Smart, the Esquire publisher whose Coronet Instructional Films turned out these classroom shorts by the hundreds from its Glenview, Illinois studio. What sets this one apart from its stablemates is the framing device: rather than a flat classroom-camera address, an argumentative off-screen narrator walks Ken through a series of staged historical vignettes to make its point about work, leisure and the modern 40-hour week. The Prelinger Archives catalog note on the print, written by film historian Ken Smith, calls it "more imaginative than most" Coronet titles "when it comes to visual gimmickry" — a fair description of the back-in-time device carrying the argument.
Ken's mother, credited on no title card but identified in later filmography listings as "Mrs. Michaels," is an early and uncredited screen role for Hope Summers, long before she became a familiar television face as Clara Edwards on The Andy Griffith Show and Mayberry R.F.D. Smith's same catalog note records that the boy playing Ken went on to headline another Coronet short, appearing as "Chuck-of-the-future" in Good Table Manners — one small thread connecting two entries in Coronet's social-guidance run. The film survives today through the Prelinger Archives holdings at the Internet Archive, cataloged as one of the more visually resourceful entries in a genre usually content to let its narrator simply talk over a static scene.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole at the Zoo
programme.desc: Krtek tunnels blindly upward and breaks through into a zoo enclosure, where he proceeds to behave like a menace. He pesters ostriches, nearly drowns in the aquatic section — a pelican rescues him, but Krtek doesn't so much as nod in thanks — then antagonises baby chicks, climbs into their throats, and when a monkey pulls him to safety at the last second, he sticks out his tongue at the lot of them. But the zoo has a king with a toothache. Krtek finds a lion (or tiger — the distinction blurs in Miler's design) in terrible pain, reaches in, and yanks the rotten tooth. Instant friendship. The lion doesn't care about Krtek's earlier bratty behaviour; he only remembers the one who helped. Czech reviewers have noted the zoological impossibility of an ostrich sharing an enclosure with monkeys, and the Tom-and-Jerry-esque pacing of the chase sequences. One particularly sharp reading: Krtek is a krtek — near-blind, sensory-driven, not malicious but oblivious to social norms, a creature of impulse. His redemption at the end isn't moral growth but lucky timing: the right problem for the right skill set. Six minutes, scored by Vadim Petrov.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.desc: Krtek digs out of his burrow, naps, and wakes to a soaking — a garden hose has sprung a leak. He tries to fix it in a series of increasingly absurd attempts that Czech viewers have compared to the slapstick of Pat and Mat. A frog blocks what's left of the water flow, and the flower bed begins to die. The flowers — in one of Miler's most memorable flourishes — sing out in chorus: "Vodu, vodu, vodu!" (Water, water, water!). Mouse arrives to help, but neither of them can undo the plumbing disaster. So Krtek does what a mole does best: he digs. An irrigation canal, carved from the earth around the flower bed, solves the problem in a way that no hose ever could. As one ČSFD reviewer noted, "In one episode he fought with a gardener; here he becomes one himself" — a nod to the later television episode where the roles reverse. The episode's title is a joke: Krtek the Gardener is still a mole, solving a gardening problem with tunnels. Sharp-eyed viewers have catalogued two continuity errors: a sprinkler that vanishes and reappears between shots, and a leaf that regenerates after being picked. Music by Vadim Petrov.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Hedgehog
programme.desc: The rain stops and Krtek gets to work draining his waterlogged molehill. Meanwhile, a hedgehog struts past with fruit stacked on his spines, lounging in the grass, eating loudly, and not lifting a paw to help. Krtek invites him; hedgehog waves him off. Mouse arrives in a panic — danger. Krtek warns hedgehog, but hedgehog shrugs. Then a human hand reaches down, scoops hedgehog into a cage, and carries him away. Hedgehog wails. Krtek and mouse follow the tracks to a rural school and stand outside, bewildered — they don't know which door to try. They find hedgehog by his crying, squeeze through a crack in the wall into the natural history cabinet, and navigate past a skeleton and stuffed animals (Krtek pauses to swing on the whiskers of a stuffed tomcat, because he's Krtek). They rock the cage to the open window, tie it to the blind cord, lower it down like an improvised elevator — hedgehog screaming the whole way. On the ground, the cage springs open. Freedom. Then they meet a real cat, identical to the stuffed one. Krtek isn't worried — he's seen this before! — but this one moves. They run. Hedgehog saves them: Krtek and mouse hide in his spiny embrace, he curls into a ball, and the cat learns about consequences. The ball rolls all the way home. Eight minutes about the gap between who deserves rescue and who gets it. Krtek helps the friend who refused to help him, and the episode never comments on the irony.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: Gumby explores small planets — miniature worlds within worlds, a concept perfectly suited to a show built on tabletop sets where everything is already small. The episode is notable among Gumby collectors as a fan favorite from the syndication era, with a dreamlike quality that recalls the Vorkapich-influenced spatial experiments of the earliest episodes. The "walking into other worlds" premise reaches its most literal expression here: the planets are small enough to hold, yet contain entire landscapes.

programme.title: Marriage Is a Partnership
programme.desc:
Dotty rides an eastbound train alone and lets her mind drift back over the year just past. In flashback, Coronet reconstructs the small, cumulative friction of a first year of marriage: she and her husband Pete move into their first apartment together and work out, meal by meal, who does the dishes and who irons the shirts, redividing chores neither of them wanted the first time around. A furniture-buying trip turns into an argument about what they can actually afford; an older female relative arrives to help hang curtains and wash windows and, in the course of helping, quietly second-guesses how Dotty is keeping house; an afternoon spent minding a friend's baby gives the young couple an uneasy preview of a stage still ahead of them. The seasons turn — a yard filling with fallen leaves marks the year passing — and the flashback resolves the way Coronet's guidance shorts usually do: not with one partner winning an argument, but with Pete and Dotty at the kitchen table, going over the household budget together and deciding, out loud, as partners. The film closes back on the train, Dotty's face settled rather than troubled.
The card that opens the print reads "A Coronet Film," followed by a copyright date of MCMLI — 1951 — under the name of David A. Smart, the Chicago publisher who owned Coronet Instructional Films, and the RCA Sound System trademark Coronet ran on its negatives through the period. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance catalog, no director or performer is named on screen; the only credited contributor is the educational collaborator, Lemo D. Rockwood, Ph.D., billed as Professor of Family Relationships at the New York State College of Home Economics at Cornell University.
Rockwood's own class at Cornell, known on campus as the Marriage Course, was one of the most sought-after electives of the late 1940s, open to students across every college and taught with an unusual mix of historical and anthropological background alongside frank discussion of courtship, mate selection, and the daily mechanics of married life — an approach that, per Cornell University Library's own retrospective on Rockwood, drew real anxiety from more conservative faculty and administrators even as students filled her lecture hall. That same practical, unsentimental voice is what Coronet put on screen here: a Pete-and-Dotty story with no villain, only two people learning to negotiate. The film survives today through Prelinger Archives' donation of Coronet's negatives to the Internet Archive, where it continues to circulate in classroom-print form.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal has been busy in his laboratory concocting a hair-growth formula, and all he needs now is a willing — or unwilling — test subject. Brian obliges by accident: when the two collide, Dougal spots the snail's gleaming bald head and decides he has found his man. A few drops later, Brian is engulfed in a wild tangle of black hair so thick he can't see where he's going. Ermintrude, intrigued rather than alarmed, volunteers herself and emerges draped in luxuriant blonde locks to her considerable delight. Florence, unable to recognise either of them, summons Zebedee, who inspects the damage and mixes a corrective potion. He also finds Dougal and, by way of a lesson, pours the formula straight onto the dog's head, stripping the fur clean off his ears and scalp. A humiliated Dougal retreats to his lab to patch himself up — only to close the episode by suggesting Florence might consider going a little longer herself.
This episode was included on the 1984 VHS release "The Magic Roundabout" and the 1993 compilation "The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout" under the title "The Experiment".

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Lollipop
programme.desc: Two children leave a lollipop on a park bench — the same bench Krtek has been using as an adrenaline slide. He is thrilled by the find and utterly baffled by what it is. Over the next few minutes he tries it as a flag, a tennis racket, a shovel, and a traffic sign (the other animals refuse to stop at his intersection, which makes him cry). Eventually he figures out it's for licking. But wasps have been watching, and they want the sweet thing too. What follows is a running battle between a mole with a lollipop and a swarm with a plan. Voices by Jiřina Bohdalová — one of Czechoslovakia's most famous actresses — providing the non-verbal squeaks and exclamations. Hidden audio detail: in the scene where the children sit on the bench talking, the soundtrack plays reversed Czech dialogue — "kdepak já mám košíček, mám ho plný houbiček" (where's my basket, full of mushrooms) and "jen tam domů uháním" (I'm hurrying home) — run backwards as ambient chatter. Czech viewers have noted the structural rhyme with the chewing gum episode (found sweet object, failed attempts to understand it) and the green star episode (trying to return something to its proper place). The moral, delivered without a word: invention is just misidentification with confidence.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
The first Gumby episode ever broadcast — a three-part story that debuted on Howdy Doody on May 1, 1956 and launched a sixty-year franchise. Gumby discovers a spaceship in a toy store, flies to the moon, gets stranded when a meteorite destroys his ship, encounters strange rock creatures that sprout eyes, freezes in the lunar cold, and is rescued by his father via fire engine with an impossibly long extension ladder. It sounds like nonsense. It looks like nothing else ever made.
Animation Obsessive called this premiere "deeply alien" — and identified why. Art Clokey was applying his USC professor Slavko Vorkapich's kinesthetic film principles to children's television: using camera angles, cutting rhythm, and spatial relationships to create involuntary physical responses in the viewer. The slow approach of the moon "asteroid" feels more disturbing than it should. The match cut at 8:27 contrasts motion in two directions. Gumby's flight over abstract lunar geometry, the creatures moving in uncomfortable unison, the dolly shot down a hospital corridor where shadow and light play over Gumby's mother — Animation Obsessive called this last sequence "animated Kubrick."
The animation itself is crude. The sets are cardboard. But the filmmaking made people unable to look away. As Clokey explained: "Vorkapich got down to basics. His theory was that motion picture dealt only with motion and the illusion of three-dimensional objects created by the director's use of shapes, shadows, colors and motion. He said if you understand how to organize those things through camera angles, camera movement, pace and so forth, you could make any film more interesting. And it happened to me... people were fascinated with how I could make the screen come alive in ways that other people couldn't."
This three-part episode was preceded by an unaired pilot called "Adventures of Gumby: A Sample," produced January 29, 1955. NBC executive Thomas Warren Sarnoff ordered a second pilot after seeing it; that became this Moon Trip, which aired as a segment on Howdy Doody. The response was strong enough to warrant a full series. Bobby Nicholson hosted the earliest Gumby segments on Howdy Doody; Ruth Eggleston (wife of art director Al Eggleston, who invented Pokey) voiced Gumby in these first episodes before Dallas McKennon took over in 1957.

programme.title: Control Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Jeff Moore is seventeen and having a bad Friday. He's the designated driver for a triple date that night, and everything conspires against him along the way: the car won't start in the garage, his kid brother Roger is underfoot and easy to frighten, his mother and his sister Joan want things from him at exactly the wrong moments, and his friends needle him at the drugstore soda fountain while he waits on a stalled engine. A psychologist in a white coat keeps interrupting from behind a desk to sort Jeff's afternoon into three labeled blocks — RAGE, FEAR, LOVE — treating each flare-up as a case study in how those basic emotions get triggered, and how they can be managed instead of vented. By evening Jeff has stopped slamming doors and started thinking before he reacts; the film closes on the same picnic-ground bonfire it opened with, the whole group gathered around it roasting marshmallows, dates delivered and temper intact.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio on David A. Smart's estate in Glenview, Illinois — Smart, the Esquire magazine publisher, had set up Coronet in 1946 as a dedicated producer of 16mm classroom shorts — and copyrighted 1950 (the title card reads "Copyright MCML David A. Smart"). As with the rest of the line, the only person named on screen is the psychology consultant: the card credits Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College. Lauer's usual specialty at Iowa State was traffic safety — he headed the college's Driver Training Laboratory and is credited on Coronet's driver-education shorts of the same period — so his appearance here, consulting on temper rather than turn signals, is a small crossover into the studio's general social-guidance catalog. Letterboxd and TMDB both credit the direction to Ted Peshak, Coronet's regular postwar house director.
The film sits in Coronet's long run of postwar social guidance, or "mental hygiene," shorts made for classroom use, alongside titles like Are You Popular? and Shy Guy — all built on the same premise, that an adolescent's raw feeling is a problem to be labeled, explained, and brought under control rather than simply expressed. The Prelinger Archives, which preserved and catalogs this print, summarize it in a single line: well-balanced emotions help to create a well-rounded personality, especially in teenagers. Like most of Coronet's guidance output, the film has long since passed into the public domain and survives today chiefly through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
Three minutes of pulsating clay set to jazz. No characters, no story, no dialogue — just shapes expanding, contracting, morphing and splitting in stop-motion, choreographed to Mel Powell's "Don-Que-Dee." This is the film that started everything.
Art Clokey made Gumbasia in 1953 as a student at the University of Southern California, working alone in his father's garage on a ping-pong table. His professor was Slavko Vorkapich, a Serbian painter who'd arrived in Hollywood nearly penniless in 1921 and talked his way into becoming one of the industry's most influential film artists. Vorkapich had created the montage sequences in Mr. Smith Goes to Washington, Manhattan Melodrama, and Joan of Arc. By the time Clokey met him, Vorkapich had codified his ideas into a theory he called "kinesthetic film principles" — the notion that moving images create involuntary physical responses in the viewer. He described it as "massaging of the eye cells."
Vorkapich considered Clokey his protégé. "He turned my head around at USC as far as motion pictures are concerned," Clokey said. In the 1980s, Clokey elaborated: "It's similar to music. You build to a climax through use of timing and intensity of the stimuli — the duration, syncopation and so on. Vorkapich taught that it's more like poetry and music. He would refer to the shots and the definite cuts as notes. Visual notes to combine and use in various ways, to get across your feelings." Clokey called Gumbasia "an experiment in pure movement" — an attempt to strip away "the distraction of recognizable forms" and leave only the sensation of motion.
The title is a portmanteau of "gumbo" (the muddy clay from his grandparents' Michigan farm) and "Fantasia" (the Disney film it parodies). Samuel G. Engel, president of the Motion Pictures Producers Association, saw Gumbasia when his son — one of Clokey's students at the Harvard School for Boys — brought it home. Engel told Clokey to make a children's show. Gumby followed.
What makes Gumbasia extraordinary isn't the clay or the technique. It's that every Gumby episode afterward — all 233 of them, plus the movie — carries the DNA of this three-minute experiment. As Animation Obsessive noted, "People at home didn't register these as avant-garde techniques — they just found themselves unable to look away from the screen, because Clokey wouldn't let them." A seminary dropout working on a ping-pong table in a garage, applying a Serbian painter's theories about "massaging the eye cells" to lumps of colored clay, accidentally invented one of the most recognizable characters in American culture. The avant-garde became the vanguard. Three minutes of jazz and clay changed television.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Directed by Nikolai Serebryakov, who was evacuated from Leningrad as a child during the 900-day Nazi siege and grew up to become one of Russian animation's most distinguished and beloved figures.
Serebryakov was born December 14, 1928, in Leningrad, the son of a theatrical figure. After the siege, he trained as both an actor (graduating from the Bryantsev acting studio at the Leningrad Young Viewers' Theatre in 1948) and as a craftsman (graduating from the Vera Mukhina Institute of Applied Art in 1952, specializing in wood processing). He worked in restoration, theatrical design, and television before joining Soyuzmultfilm in 1960 as a production designer. His first collaboration was with Roman Kachanov on Little Masha and the Bear (1960).
He began co-directing with Vadim Kurchevsky — I Want to Be Brave (1963), Little Lazybones (1964), Neither God nor Devil (1965) — and was part of the generation of young animators who, during Khrushchev's "thaw," began pushing Soviet animation beyond pretty children's cartoons into more sophisticated territory. His contemporaries included Andrei Khrzhanovsky and Yuri Norstein, with whom he would later share a joint retrospective at the Edinburgh Festival.
Ball of Wool (1968), about an old woman who knits herself an entire life from a sheep's coat but falters when she tries to remake herself as a beautiful girl, was called "one of the masterpieces of Russian animated cinema" by Robin Buss in The Independent. He won prizes at Tours (1967), Grenoble (1976), and the Grand Prix at Tampere (1977).
His creative and personal life was inseparable from Alina Speshneva, a designer at the legendary Obraztsov puppet theatre in Moscow. They married — she was the sister of his first wife Nadia — and for sixteen years made everything together. They contributed the animation design for Elem Klimov's Sport, Sport, Sport (1970), a live-action/animation collage with an Alfred Schnittke soundtrack. In 1984, Alina died in an accident, and everything changed.
After her death, Serebryakov shifted from puppet animation to drawn cel work. He served as artistic director at Mosfilm's experimental "Debut" studio (1982–89), then won the Nika — Russia's Oscar — for The Parable about the Actor in 1989. He was named People's Artist of the Russian Federation in 1996.
For the Animated Tales he directed two episodes using cel animation: Macbeth and, in Series 2, Othello. The obituary noted that there were concerns about the violence of some scenes in his Macbeth — it was feared they might make it unsuitable for the target audience. But this is Macbeth; the violence is the point.
Brian Cox voices Macbeth. Cox was born in Dundee in 1946 to a working-class Catholic family — his father died of pancreatic cancer when Brian was eight, his mother suffered nervous breakdowns working in the jute mills, and he was raised by his three elder sisters. He started acting at fourteen at Dundee Repertory Theatre, trained at LAMDA, and narrowly avoided death in 1965 when a meeting with Laurence Olivier was cancelled, saving him from boarding a flight that crashed at Heathrow. He won two Olivier Awards — for Rat in the Skull (1984) and Titus Andronicus (1988, which he considers his greatest performance). Before this recording, Cox had spent time teaching and directing at the Moscow Arts Theatre School — a Scottish actor trained in Moscow voicing the Scottish king for a Russian animation studio. He was also the first actor to play Hannibal Lecter on screen, in Michael Mann's Manhunter (1986), and would later define television in the 2020s as Logan Roy in Succession.
Zoë Wanamaker voices Lady Macbeth. She was born in New York to a Russian-Jewish family, but her father Sam Wanamaker — an actor and director — was blacklisted during McCarthyism and fled to London, where he spent the last twenty-three years of his life on a single obsessive project: rebuilding Shakespeare's Globe Theatre on the South Bank of the Thames. He died in December 1993, four years before it opened. His daughter, voicing Lady Macbeth in a Russian-animated Shakespeare adaptation, carries both halves of that inheritance — the Russian and the Shakespearean — in a single casting choice that nobody planned but which resonates perfectly.

programme.title: Shy Guy
programme.desc:
Phil Norton is new in town and new at school, and he spends his lunch hours alone and his evenings in the basement, building radios and record players. His father — finding him down there again — puts the problem in Phil's own language: a component has to fit in, so it can work with all the other parts. So Phil goes back to school and does what an engineer would do. He observes. He watches the popular kids to work out what actually makes them liked, and the data surprises him: it isn't looks or money or noise, it's that they pay attention to other people. Phil tries it — asks questions, listens, offers to help a classmate fix a broken record player — and by the final reel the basement workshop is full of friends.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and directed by Ted Peshak, the house director behind many of Coronet's postwar guidance films. In keeping with Coronet practice, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Alice Sowers, Ph.D., director of the Family Life Institute at the University of Oklahoma. Released to classrooms in August 1947, it became one of the most widely shown of all the social guidance shorts — the genre's usual prescription of conformity delivered, for once, with a certain sweetness: the film never asks Phil to stop building radios, only to look up from the workbench occasionally.
Two people made their film debuts in these thirteen minutes, and both became fixtures of American television. Phil is a nineteen-year-old Dick York, then a busy Chicago radio actor, seventeen years before he became Darrin Stephens on Bewitched; educational and industrial films like this one were his bread and butter for years. And the narrator's voice belongs to a young Chicago announcer named Myron Wallace — who, as Mike Wallace, would spend nearly four decades asking harder questions on 60 Minutes.

programme.title: Mummenschanz: You & Me
programme.desc:
A full Mummenschanz stage performance, in a theater, in front of an audience — the thing the troupe almost never allowed onto film across half a century of touring. Two enormous grey hands meet and quarrel. A figure whose head is a lump of soft clay reshapes its own face to match its feelings. Creatures assembled from white blocks build and unbuild themselves. Masks made of toilet-paper rolls unspool to weep and to talk. Tube-worms in green and blue court each other across a bare black stage. There are no words, no music, and almost no light beyond what falls on the figures themselves; the theater's laughter and applause are the entire soundtrack, and the performers — visible only as black-clad suggestions beneath the shapes — never break the silence, not even at the curtain call.
You & Me was created for the company's 45th anniversary and premiered at Theater 11 in Zurich on December 1, 2016, under the creative direction of Floriana Frassetto — the last of the three founders still performing. Frassetto, Bernie Schürch, and Andres Bossard had formed Mummenschanz in 1972 and spent three years running on Broadway (1977–80) with a mask theater built from foam, clay, and household objects; Bossard died in 1992, and with You & Me Frassetto handed the vocabulary to a new generation of performers — Oliver Pfulg, Sara Francesca Hermann, Christa Barrett, Kevin Blaser, and company — while performing in the show herself. Around 130,000 people saw the production in Switzerland alone before it toured abroad.
This recording is Swiss television's cut of the show, broadcast by SRF, running just over an hour against the stage version's two forty-five-minute acts. A fuller 94-minute recording, taped by Swiss-Italian television at the Théâtre de Beausobre in Morges in 2017, exists only on the Mummenschanz foundation's own out-of-print video releases — making this broadcast cut the performance's one accessible form, and the only complete-in-spirit Mummenschanz show most audiences outside a theater will ever see.

programme.title: Improve Your Personality
programme.desc:
Improve Your Personality opens on a school walkway and quickly settles into the device it returns to for the rest of its ten minutes: a black silhouette head in profile, flanked by two labels, "OTHER PEOPLE" and "ENVIRONMENT," under the caption "YOUR PERSONALITY." The diagram states the film's whole thesis in one image — personality isn't something a person is simply born with, it's built out of how they treat others and how they answer to their surroundings — and the picture keeps cutting back to it between two contrasted case studies. A teenage boy who starts out sullen and closed-off is shown coming around: setting the table, hanging up the wash, pitching in at home instead of leaving the chores to the woman of the house. Cut hard against him is a teenage girl who does nothing in her scenes but admire her own reflection in a bedroom mirror, the diagram card reappearing each time to underline the moral. Along the way, one boy sizes up a girl walking past him on the same path from the opening and tells a friend, "Boy, has she got personality!" — about as flatly as the film could put its own pun. By the closing reel the same young people turn up dressed for a formal dance, in tuxedos and gowns, and a final card spells out the takeaway in script lettering: "Concentrate on the other person."
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films and copyrighted in 1951 (the opening card reads "MCMLI," credited to David A. Smart), the short follows Coronet's standard practice for the period: not one performer is named on screen, and the film's only title-card credit goes to its "educational collaborator," billed as Clifford R. Adams, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at the Pennsylvania State College. Adams held that post in fact as well as on the card — he was Penn State's real director of its Marriage Counseling Service and a member of the American Association of Marriage Counselors — and five years earlier had co-written the marriage-advice bestseller "How to Pick a Mate" with Vance O. Packard, then a staff writer for The American Magazine and later the author of "The Hidden Persuaders." Coronet drew on a small, recurring bench of writers, directors, and consultants across its guidance catalog — Melvin Waskin as house writer, Ted Peshak as its most frequent director among them — but this particular print names none of them; Adams alone appears on screen.
The film belongs to Coronet's postwar "mental hygiene" cycle, the run of guidance shorts the company produced through the late 1940s and 1950s for direct sale to schools. David Smart, who had toured Nazi Germany before the war, later told the Chicago Tribune that seeing Hitler's use of film as an "indoctrination tool" convinced him the same medium could be turned toward education instead, and Coronet ran with the idea hard enough to release a new title, on average, every three and a half working days. Against that backdrop, Improve Your Personality is a mild entry — no car crash, no scandal, just a civics-class gloss on manners dressed up as psychology, delivered with Adams' academic authority and Coronet's usual well-lit, tidy midcentury classrooms and living rooms. A 2010 Cineaste survey of the genre singled the film out as one of the era's less common entries not narrowly aimed at one sex, pitching its lesson at boys and girls alike.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Zebedee is waiting at the roundabout when Florence arrives in a slight rush, and after a brief reassurance he springs her off to the garden. Meanwhile, Dougal is motoring around with one eye out for Ermintrude, who has appointed herself traffic warden and has been making his life a misery with parking restrictions. His solution is a portable parking meter, which he plants beside his car to buy two hours of peace -- and it works, sending Ermintrude away satisfied. Florence turns up, finds the empty car, and sits down to wait while Mr McHenry falls foul of the warden himself. When Dougal returns and spots Florence, he quickly pockets the meter, takes her for a spin, and keeps replanting it wherever he parks. Brian catches him in the act but Dougal brazens it out. The scheme finally unravels when Ermintrude, despondent at a ticketless day, spots Dougal's car in what she believes is an unmarked space and writes him up -- only for Dougal to produce the meter and argue the point, to everyone's bemusement.
The Eric Thompson narration of this episode was released on the BBC Video VHS compilation Volume 1 (1984). The French version was adapted as a comic strip in issue 17 of Le Journal de Pollux magazine.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Television
programme.desc: A gardener moves into the plot next to Krtek's molehill. Krtek's friend mouse discovers the man watching a television programme about how to poison moles — the on-screen brand "ZNIČIT KRTKA" (Destroy the Mole), a substance so corrosive it dissolves soil to killing depth, eats through wooden carts with iron fittings, and would devastate any groundwater it touched. Krtek and mouse hatch a plan: sabotage the television set. What follows is a small-scale insurgency — two animals against a gardener armed with a spade and industrial pesticide. Czech viewers have called it the episode that teaches children about brainwashing, friendship, anarchy, and how dangerous home-improvement programmes are for their parents. ČSFD trivia contributors have noted that despite being nearly blind, a real mole's whiskers detect the faintest vibrations, allowing Krtek to dodge the gardener's retaliatory dawn spade attack with uncanny precision. When the gardener destroys the main tunnel, Krtek simply digs a parallel one while the man sleeps — moles sleep only three hours a day, so most repairs happen overnight. This is the episode that a ČSFD reviewer references when watching "Krtek zahradníkem" — "in one episode he fought with a gardener; here he becomes one himself." The television is the real villain: it radicalises the gardener into warfare against an animal that was minding its own business.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Umbrella
programme.desc: Krtek finds a junkyard full of treasures — an old boot, beads, a mirror, an alarm clock that sends him leaping — but the prize is a colourful broken umbrella. He fixes it in moments. Naps under it in the sun. Then the wind picks up and carries the umbrella away. Krtek grabs the handle just in time and is lifted into the sky — panic, then wonder, as the umbrella becomes a parachute. He lands in a river, where it becomes a boat. Frogs help him paddle to shore, but a pike attacks and a fierce underwater battle erupts (the umbrella doubles as a shield). Safely ashore, Krtek spots a melon stand, rolls one away, slices it up, and invites every animal in range to a feast. The furious vendor gives chase. Hedgehog pelts him with melon seeds; mouse throws rinds. Then rain and wind arrive, wrecking the vendor's stall — while the animals huddle dry and smug beneath their umbrella. The umbrella is shelter, aircraft, watercraft, weapon, and dining canopy across eight minutes. Indian viewer Mav Erick, writing years later on YouTube, called it one of the first cartoons he ever watched: "This brings a tear to my eye... I used to watch this when I was like 5-6 years old." That comment captures something about Krtek's reach — broadcast across the Soviet bloc, then pirated and shared worldwide, landing in living rooms from Mumbai to Baghdad to East Berlin.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.desc: Krtek digs up near some illegally dumped paint cans in the forest and immediately sees potential. He and mouse set to work: they paint every animal in the neighbourhood. The owl gets a checkerboard pattern. The frogs turn pink. Birds become kaleidoscopes. Trees go red, grass shifts colour, and the whole forest looks like a hallucination — Czech reviewers have called it "an animated drug trip." The purpose, it turns out, is self-defence. A fox has been hunting the forest's smaller residents, and the psychedelic camouflage terrifies it into retreat — the fox apparently suffers from chromophobia and cannot process a world this bright. Victory through paint. Then it rains, washing every colour into the soil. The forest returns to normal; the fox will presumably recover its nerve. Written by Ivan Klíma, scored by Miloš Vacek, and produced at the Bratři v triku studio. One reviewer noted the ecological reading: the "heroic" paint cans are illegally dumped industrial chemicals that, once washed into the groundwater, represent an environmental catastrophe far worse than one fox. Another pointed out that Krtek and mouse painted the plants too, which would kill them. Miler almost certainly didn't care — the gag works, the colours are gorgeous, and children don't think about runoff.

programme.title: Appreciating Our Parents
programme.desc:
Tommy comes home from school to a room that looks like magic: bed made, toys shelved, a torn cowboy shirt mended, a missing jacket button replaced. The film doubles back to show what he never sees — the mess he actually left that morning, and the hours of washing, ironing, mending, and dish-clearing that erased it while he was at school. That evening his father comes home with Tommy's weekly allowance, and Tommy, thinking only that he'd like more of it, follows his parents downstairs and sits in on their evening instead: his mother recounting a day of cooking, laundry, and straightening his room, his father working through the family budget at the kitchen table and then mending a broken chair rather than buying a new one. Tommy reframes the household as a football team that only wins if every player does his job, and sets out to do his: he fixes his own broken toy train track, keeps his room tidy without being asked, and banks his allowance instead of asking for more. His reward in the closing scene is not just his parents' approval but a bigger allowance, his mother and father agreeing he's earned a share of what his help has saved — appreciation paid out in cash as plainly as it is felt.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois and copyrighted 1950 (MCML) to Coronet publisher David A. Smart. As with other Coronet guidance shorts, the only credit on the print itself is the classroom consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Reuben Hill, Ph.D., Research Professor in Family Life at the University of North Carolina. Direction is attested elsewhere as Ted Peshak, who joined Coronet's Glenview studio in 1947 and, alternating projects with fellow staff director Gil Altschul, directed roughly half the company's output through the late 1950s, at his fastest turning out a finished one-reeler in a single day. Tommy is played by Skip Peshak, Ted's own son, one of several Coronet shorts in which the director cast his boy rather than one of the studio's regular Chicago performers.
Reuben Hill brought an unusually credentialed pedigree to the picture. By 1950 he had already co-written the marriage-education bestseller When You Marry (1945) and was partway through the University of North Carolina professorship (1949-1957) during which he developed what became the ABC-X model of family stress, drawn from his wartime research on military families; he went on to chair the International Sociological Association's family research committee and later served as the ISA's president. His name on the title card reflects a broader Coronet practice of enlisting university researchers to lend classroom authority to shorts on manners, thrift, and family duty. "Appreciating Our Parents" sits in that social-guidance cycle's domestic-economy strand, chores and thrift dramatized as filial love, and survives today through a 16mm print in the Prelinger Archives on the Internet Archive.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal has decided there is oil to be had in the Magic Garden, and sets about getting it. Among the trees he assembles an elaborate apparatus of pipes — a low pipeline snaking across the flowerbeds, fitted with a drilling head — and applies himself to the serious business of striking it rich, pausing frequently to lounge about as though the fortune were already made. Florence, sent along from the roundabout by Zebedee, comes to inspect the contraption, and Ermintrude and Brian gather round to see what the dog is up to. As with most of Dougal's grand schemes, the prospecting is conducted with enormous confidence and a thoroughly Dougal-ish result, leaving him with a great deal more mess than fortune.
The episode's French title is "L'or noir" ("black gold"). Eric Thompson's narration was released on VHS as Volume 1 by BBC Video in 1984, retitled "Oil"; the French version was dubbed into English for Nickelodeon's Pinwheel in the United States, and adapted as a comic strip in the 19th issue of Le Journal de Pollux (15 October 1974).

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon helps a pair of scissors which have accidentally cut a thread holding Button Moon in Blanket Sky. Through his telescope he sees two unusual dancers and Scruffy and Basil, two dogs which play hunt the bone. The scissors cutting the thread that holds Button Moon in the sky is one of those small details that reveals how carefully Allen thought about his world. Blanket Sky is literally a blanket — so of course a button hangs from it by a thread, and of course scissors could cut it. The internal logic is airtight because everything is what it actually is. Scruffy the dog became one of the show's most popular recurring characters, appearing across multiple series. In Button Moon's world, even the dogs are made from household objects — pipe cleaners, fabric scraps, buttons for eyes.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: It is Gumby's birthday, and he gets to choose his own present from the toy store. He picks a train, but while driving it home it escapes out the back of the van. The toyshop setting recurs here as the site of possibility — Gumby doesn't just receive a gift, he enters a world of choices. The runaway train is classic Clokey: objects have their own will, and controlling them is never as simple as owning them. The stop-motion train work, with its miniature tracks and landscapes, shows off what Clokey's team could achieve with the most basic materials when the filmmaking fundamentals were sound.

programme.title: The Fun of Making Friends
programme.desc:
Joey is a solitary boy, first seen alone at his own front window while the neighborhood kids have a snowball fight out in the yard; instead of joining in, he stays inside working quietly at a table with paper and scissors. Walking to school by himself down a snowy sidewalk, he keeps the same distance from his classmates. At home, though, his mother sits him down and reduces the problem to a checklist the film puts right on screen: Smile and Talk to People. Find Good Things in People. Tell Them the Good Things. Do This All the Time. Joey tries the rules out at his school desk, sharing a look and then a bag of something with a classmate, and by the next scene the two boys are paired off at a shared table; a girl is drawn into the circle outside in the snow soon after. The film closes back at Joey's house, now full of friends and a family dog sprawled on the rug — the boy who started the picture alone at the glass now has the room crowded around him.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films and copyrighted in 1950, the picture runs a little over nine minutes. The film's own catalogued production credits, preserved with the Prelinger Archives print, list Ted Peshak as director — the studio's regular hand on its postwar social-guidance line — with camera by Dale Sharkey, script by George Tychsen, and editing by Ace Moore. In keeping with Coronet's usual practice of naming only the outside expert who vetted the content, the credits identify the consulting authority as Elizabeth B. Carey, Ph.D., Supervisor of the Bureau of Instructional Supervision for the University of the State of New York.
The film belongs to the large body of social-guidance shorts Coronet supplied to classrooms through the late 1940s and 1950s: a simple problem, a numbered rule card, and a tidy resolution inside ten minutes. Distributed for decades on the 16mm educational circuit, it survives today through the Prelinger Archives and small footage libraries like A.V. Geeks, and it still turns up on retro-media blogs as an example of the genre's plain, unfussy way of talking to a lonely kid — reach out, the film tells him, and the loneliness just ends.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence meets Zebedee at the roundabout before heading to the garden, while Ermintrude drops by Dougal's new antique shop. The shop is a lively place, with its wares dancing about waiting for buyers. Dougal proudly presents his star item: an old cannon priced at 5,473 pounds, which he claims was used by Napoleon. The cannon, a bristling war veteran, furiously insists it is British, not French. Ermintrude takes fright at its outburst, so Dougal shunts the cannon aside and gives it a dusting, making it sneeze. Brian arrives in his usual breezy fashion, earning little patience from Dougal, who loads the cannon with a lump of sugar. When Florence turns up, the cannon continues bellowing war obscenities as Dougal lights the fuse. Florence observes it doesn't look happy; Dougal assures her there is no war on. The cannon duly explodes, leaving Dougal to lament he will never rise above the rank of Lance Corporal.
The cannon is destroyed in this episode, yet reappears intact at the start of the follow-up story "Dougal Sells the Old Cannon" with no explanation offered. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as Volume 1 by BBC Video in 1984, retitled "The Cannon." AB Productions recreated scene photographs for a book-and-audio-cassette edition released in 1990.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon sees a lazy grasshopper and some busy ants preparing for the winter. Aesop's fable of the grasshopper and the ants — the improvident musician who starves while the industrious workers feast — was one of the most frequently adapted stories in children's television. Disney's Silly Symphonies version from 1934 is the most famous. Button Moon's retelling through the telescope was necessarily simpler and stranger: the grasshopper and ants were household objects performing a moral lesson about work and play, narrated by Robin Parkinson in his warm, unhurried voice. Parkinson's narration was crucial to the show's tone. He'd been a working character actor since the 1960s, best known for playing the bumbling Herr Otto Flick's British contact in 'Allo 'Allo! His voice gave Button Moon a gentle authority — never condescending, never rushed.

programme.title: The End of the World in Four Seasons
programme.desc:
The apocalypse unfolds four times — once for each season — in four simultaneous panels. Spring's end is gentle, summer's is violent, autumn's is melancholy, winter's is inevitable. All four play at once in Driessen's signature split-screen, the viewer's eye pulled between parallel catastrophes that rhyme without repeating.
This is Driessen at his most formally ambitious: four complete narratives running simultaneously, each commenting on the others, the screen divided into quadrants. He animated each panel separately on paper, then handed them off for compositing. The result is a film you can watch four times and see something different each time — or try to hold all four in your mind at once and feel the vertigo of parallel doom.

programme.title: Date Etiquette
programme.desc:
A boy at the lockers works up to asking a classmate out, and the film follows the date start to finish exactly the way its own catalog description promises: the asking and the accepting, the call at her house, the evening out, and the goodnight at the door. He arrives to collect her properly and is walked into the parlor to meet her parents, seated and watching him make the right impression before he's allowed to take their daughter anywhere. The two of them join a crowd of classmates at a school affair built around a hallway soda fountain, all charm bracelets and small talk over paper cups, before pairing off to a restaurant booth, where the real lesson plays out in miniature: what to order, how to make conversation, who looks after the check. The night winds down the way it started, on a porch in near-darkness, with a goodnight exchanged in the same careful, rehearsed register as everything that came before it.
Coronet Instructional Films' only screen credit is its usual one: "Educational Collaborator Evelyn M. Duvall, Ph.D., Consultant, National Council on Family Relations," over the RCA Sound System card. The copyright record filed with the Library of Congress lists the short at 354 feet of 16mm, registered to David A. Smart on April 7, 1952 — a length that runs almost exactly the ten minutes Coronet built its classroom reels to fit. Duvall was no rented name for the title card: she had stepped down in 1951 after six years as executive secretary of the National Council on Family Relations and had just published Facts of Life and Love for Teenagers (1950), one of the first mainstream dating guides aimed at teenagers themselves rather than their parents. Date Etiquette plays like that book's table of contents staged with a cast of unbilled teenagers, each beat of the evening — invitation, parents, the affair, the restaurant, the doorstep — treated as a discrete skill to be gotten right.
It belongs to a run of Coronet dating shorts from the period, alongside titles like What to Do on a Date (1950), that walked the same courtship through in careful procedural order, with Duvall or another family-life consultant standing in for the studio's actual authorship. No director or performer is named on the print, and none has turned up attached to this particular title with any confidence — the film's teenagers are meant to be interchangeable models of correct behavior, not characters. The surviving print comes down through the Gordon Elgart Collection at Prelinger Archives, cataloged with its original one-line description from a 1953 Educational Film Guide entry, the same synopsis this note draws from.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
The series premiere, and the only episode animated outside Moscow — directed and designed by Robert Sahakyants (1950–2009) at Armenfilm in Yerevan, making this a Welsh-Armenian co-production within a Welsh-Russian framework.
Sahakyants was born in Baku, Soviet Azerbaijan, in 1950 — an Armenian family in a city that would later become dangerous for Armenians during the 1988–90 pogroms. His family relocated to Yerevan in 1964. He joined Armenfilm's animation department in 1970 and became a director at twenty-two. Over the next four decades he created some of the most beloved animated films in the post-Soviet world: Wow, a Talking Fish! (1983), In the Blue Sea, in the White Foam... (1984) — both based on Armenian and Caucasian folklore — and The Lesson (1987), which won prizes at the All-Union film festival. In 2002, he directed Yellow SubmarYAN, a loving Beatles homage transplanted to Armenia. He was named Honored Art Worker of the Armenian SSR in 1987 and Honored Artist of Armenia in 2008. He died in Yerevan in 2009 at fifty-nine. A memorial stands in his honor in the city since 2013.
For A Midsummer Night's Dream, Sahakyants brought cel animation in a style markedly different from the Moscow studios — the fairy world shimmers like illuminated manuscript pages, all jewel tones and liquid movement. The fairies' forest glows against the earthy, solid world of Athens, and the mechanicals' disastrous performance of Pyramus and Thisbe gets the full comic treatment.
The voice cast is quietly extraordinary. Bernard Hill — a decade before Théoden in The Lord of the Rings and Captain Smith in Titanic — plays Bottom, the weaver who wakes up with a donkey's head and takes it in stride. Peter Postlethwaite — whom Spielberg would later call "the best actor in the world" after In the Name of the Father (1993) — plays Peter Quince, the long-suffering director of the mechanicals' play. Daniel Massey (son of Raymond Massey, Oscar-nominated for playing Noël Coward in Star!) voices Oberon; Suzanne Bertish is Titania. Abigail McKern (daughter of Leo McKern, Rumpole of the Bailey) plays Hermia. Menna Trussler narrates Leon Garfield's bridging prose.
Script adapted by Leon Garfield, who compared the task of condensing Shakespeare to half an hour as "painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel on a postage stamp" — but found the comedies far harder than the tragedies: "In the tragedies, you have a very strong story going straight through. In the comedies, the structure is much more complex." Academic advisor: Professor Stanley Wells.

programme.title: Oh What a Knight
programme.desc:
A knight tries to rescue a princess from a castle, but both the quest and the castle keep folding in on themselves. The French title — "La Belle et la boîte" ("Beauty and the Box") — puns on the fairy tale while describing Driessen's technique: the screen splits and folds like an origami box, with multiple simultaneous panels telling parallel versions of the same story.
Driessen's split-screen technique became his most distinctive invention. He would animate each panel separately on paper, right in the center of the sheet, then hand the scenes to technicians who distributed them across the frame. "I would just animate my scenes right in the middle of my paper at a certain field-size and then at the Film Board they would distribute them over four panels." The result is a kind of visual fugue — several lines of action woven together, each commenting on the others.

programme.title: What To Do On A Date
programme.desc:
Nick and his friend Jeff are tossing a ball along the sidewalk when Nick spots a girl, Kay, walking home, and loses track of the game watching her go. Back at the house, her number is already penciled into the margin of Nick's notebook, right next to an unfinished book report on Nathaniel Hawthorne, and it's Jeff — leaning over the banister, needling him along — who finally gets Nick to pick up the phone and ask. Once Kay says yes, the two of them skip the expensive, ready-made idea of just taking a girl to the movies and instead throw themselves into the school's "Knick-Knacks" scavenger sale: painting signs, hanging a paper elephant from a ladder, stringing bunting and lanterns across the yard. Kay and her friend Phyllis turn up that afternoon to pitch in alongside them, sorting donated goods and tacking up notices on the club bulletin board, and by evening the sale has become a small carnival, the two couples working booths and finishing the night together over sandwiches and cold drinks — precisely the supervised, low-cost, group-built evening Coronet is holding up as the answer to the title's question.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films — the print's copyright card reads MCMLI, 1951, under founder David A. Smart, over the RCA Sound System mark. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance line, the only name in the picture itself is the consulting educator: the title card credits "Educational Collaborator Evelyn M. Duvall, Ph.D., Consultant, National Council on Family Relations," the family-life researcher whose dating and courtship studies underpin several Coronet guidance shorts of the period. No director or performer is named on screen. The Prelinger Archives catalog record for the film credits Ted Peshak as director, cameraman Dale Sharkey, writers George Tychsen and (George T.) Bradford, editor Dick Kirschner, and narrator George Stone — Peshak's credit for this specific title is echoed by Letterboxd's own listing, though, again, the print is silent on all of it.
The film sits alongside Are You Popular? and Date Etiquette in Coronet's cycle of postwar dating shorts, all pitching group activity and modest spending as the cure for an awkward date. Oddly, the Prelinger Archives catalogs this same title under 1950, a year earlier than the MCMLI copyright stamped on the print — likely a gap between production and the copyright's formal registration, but worth noting since it puts the film's actual copyright date a year later than its most common listing. Letterboxd and IMDb both credit Robert Casey as the lead of the teenage cast, though which of the two boys he played isn't attested anywhere reliable enough to print, and the film itself names no performers at all. It survives today as an unaltered classroom print, held and circulated through the Prelinger Collection along with dozens of other Coronet social-guidance shorts from the same run.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
The hunchbacked Duke of Gloucester schemes, seduces, murders, and manipulates his way to the English throne, dispatching brothers, nephews, and allies with equal ruthlessness — then loses everything at Bosworth Field when his own lords turn against him.
Directed by Natalya Orlova in paint-on-glass animation, her second contribution to the series after the Emmy-winning Hamlet. Where Hamlet was Rembrandt — dark, introspective, each frame etched in shadow — Richard III is more Goya: grotesque faces contorting with ambition, the oil paint itself seeming to curdle around Richard's twisted form. Orlova's paint-on-glass technique, in which each frame is a unique painting destroyed to create the next, gives the entire episode a quality of impermanence perfectly suited to a play about a man whose power dissolves the instant it's grasped. Born May 12, 1948, she studied under Sergei Obraztsov and works from Animos Film studio. Her career specialty is literary adaptation in the most labor-intensive animation technique that exists: before the 25-minute Hamlet, her longest paint-on-glass work had been a 10-minute Chekhov adaptation. The Christian Science Monitor called her Hamlet "a masterpiece... like watching a kinetic unfolding of the Hamlet story etched by Rembrandt." She later directed Animated Epics: Moby Dick (1999) with Rod Steiger as Ahab.
Antony Sher voices Richard. Born in Cape Town on 14 June 1949, the son of a South African Jewish businessman, Sher left for England at 19 and immediately began hiding everything about himself — his Jewishness, his South African origins, his sexuality. "Each of these things went into the closet until my entire identity was in the closet," he told The Guardian. He was rejected by both the Central School and RADA, trained instead at the Webber Douglas Academy, and cut his teeth at the Liverpool Everyman Theatre alongside Jonathan Pryce, Julie Walters, and Bernard Hill in a group where "anarchy ruled." He performed with the gay theatre group Gay Sweatshop before joining the RSC in 1982.
Then came 1984. His Richard III on crutches — the "bottled spider" — redefined the role for a generation. Taking Shakespeare's description of the "poisonous bunch-backed toad" literally, Sher used metal crutches to move like an arachnid, swinging between them with terrifying speed and grace. The performance won both the Laurence Olivier Award and the Evening Standard Award for Best Actor. His diary of the rehearsal and performance process, Year of the King (1985), illustrated with his own drawings and paintings, became arguably the greatest actor's memoir ever written about preparing a Shakespeare role.
The book reveals Sher was also a painter of real ability. Characters (1990) collected his portraits of roles. He wrote novels, plays, and directed — his play Primo (2004) about Primo Levi in Auschwitz was adapted into a film. He wrote The Giant about Michelangelo creating David. Cousin to playwright Sir Ronald Harwood (The Dresser, The Pianist). He played Ringo Starr in Willy Russell's John, Paul, George, Ringo... and Bert. He played Tamburlaine, Cyrano, Shylock, Falstaff, Lear's Fool AND King Lear (the only RSC actor to play both). He was Disraeli in Mrs Brown, the Chief Weasel in The Wind in the Willows, and Thrain II in Peter Jackson's Hobbit (Extended Edition only). Prince Charles called him his favorite actor.
He married RSC artistic director Gregory Doran in 2015, a decade after their civil partnership. Knighted KBE in 2000. Died of cancer at home in Stratford-upon-Avon on 2 December 2021, aged 72, with Doran at his side.

programme.title: Exercise and Health
programme.desc:
Three teenagers carry three different problems into the school gym: Ernie is run-down and out of shape, Jean is shy and withdrawn, Hal is tense and quick to snap. A physical-education instructor points all three toward the school's Acrobatics Club, and the film spends most of its ten minutes on the resulting workouts — spotted handstands and vaults off a partner's shoulders, tumbling on mats, chin-ups on a bar, badminton and archery out on the lawn. Two printed title cards carry the argument the pictures only illustrate: one notes that the sedentary worker, "bound by rules of business diplomacy," needs a physical outlet, and that the "pleasant tiredness" following exercise "promotes complete relaxation"; the other credits teamwork with building "balance and poise, along with skill, strength, and general physical fitness." By the last reel Ernie has traded the doctor's office for the tumbling mat, Jean is talking easily with the other girls on the archery line, and Hal has swapped his clenched jaw for a game of catch — three complaints answered by the same prescription of regular, cooperative exercise.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films, the picture opens with its only screen credit: educational collaborator Erwin F. Beyer of the Department of Physical Education at the University of Chicago, recorded on the RCA Sound System, with a copyright date of MCMXLIX (1949) under Coronet's founder David A. Smart. Coronet's house director Ted Peshak is credited with the film on Letterboxd and TMDB, consistent with his work on the studio's other social-guidance shorts of the period, though as with most Coronet one-reelers the on-screen credits name only the academic collaborator, not the director or cast.
The Prelinger Archives catalog summarizes the film in a single line — "How exercise will make you healthy and popular" — which is a fair, if blunter, restatement of the same argument the picture makes at length: that organized physical activity is a fix for the loosely related ailments of poor health, poor sociability, and poor nerves alike. It belongs to the same wave of postwar Coronet guidance shorts, tailored for physical-education classes rather than homeroom, and it survives today through Prelinger/Internet Archive prints rather than any particular later reputation of its own; no reliable cast credits have surfaced for Ernie, Jean, or Hal.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Matches
programme.desc: Krtek pops out of his molehill and takes a chestnut to the head. Searching under a fallen leaf, he finds a matchbox. Mouse arrives, and together they discover that matches are possibly the most versatile objects in nature. The box becomes a bed, a table, a little boat. Individual matches combine with chestnuts to form a tiny chair. They sail the matchbox-boat downstream and return with a carrot, which they slice into a carrot salad. After dinner, they accidentally strike a match — fire. Rather than panic, they build a campfire and warm themselves under the stars. Seven minutes of pure creative play that horrified at least one generation of Czech parents. As ČSFD reviewers have noted, this is not a cautionary tale about the dangers of playing with matches — it is an enthusiastic demonstration of what you can do with them. The matches burn impossibly long, which sharp-eyed viewers attributed to some kind of developmental prototype. Krtek's approach to fire is consistent with his approach to everything: unafraid, curious, and lucky enough to survive the consequences. Music by Vadim Petrov.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon finds a magic wand whilst travelling to Button Moon. Meanwhile, Mrs. Spoon plans a picnic for Egbert. This episode is sometimes listed online as "The Magic Totem" — a YouTube uploader's error. The correct title is "The Magic Wand." The introduction of a magic wand into the Button Moon world is a sly move. In a universe where everything is literally what it looks like — spoons are spoons, bottles are bottles — a wand that does magic is both the most natural and most disruptive object possible. It's the one prop that doesn't just look like what it is but actually does something impossible. Meanwhile, the domestic B-plot of Mrs. Spoon planning Egbert's picnic grounds the episode in the cozy family dynamic that kept parents watching alongside their children.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon, who lives with his family on Junk Planet, takes his daughter Tina Teaspoon to Button Moon. They find some talking umbrellas there and through a telescope see a hare and a tortoise having a race. Another Aesop fable through the telescope — and like The Grasshopper and the Ants two episodes earlier, one that Disney had already made definitive in animation. But Button Moon's version was something else entirely. The hare and tortoise were household objects racing each other while a spoon and a teaspoon watched through a telescope on a button hanging from a blanket. The sheer layering of abstraction — real objects playing characters in a fable viewed through an instrument on a celestial body made of a button — is the kind of thing that sounds insane written out but works perfectly when Robin Parkinson narrates it in his measured, matter-of-fact voice.

programme.title: Understand Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Mr. Brent, a high-school biology teacher, opens by springing a jack-in-the-box on his class to make a simple point: the same jolt doesn't hit everybody the same way. From there the lesson turns diagnostic. Working with three students — among them a boy named Larry — Brent lifts a plastic brain off his desk and traces the thalamus as the switching point where a stimulus becomes a feeling, then wires a student's fingers to a gauge to record the body's own evidence: racing pulse, tightened stomach, sweating palms, each mapped onto a cutaway silhouette on the wall chart. He walks the class through a wired maze holding a white mouse, using shock and cheese to demonstrate conditioning directly, then chalks the idea up as an equation: S¹, a dentist, produces only curiosity; S², his drill, produces fear. The blackboard closes the period the way it opened, as a formula — fear, rage, and love as raw material, conditioning as the process that shapes them, emotional maturity as the goal.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and copyrighted 1950 ("Copyright MCML David A. Smart," per the title card, naming Coronet's founder and the publisher of Esquire and Coronet magazines), recorded on the RCA Sound System. As with the rest of the line, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College — in real life the head of Iowa State's driver-research program and author of The Psychology of Driving, lending his credentials here to classroom emotion theory rather than his usual traffic-safety work. None of Coronet's young actors are named on screen; period research into the studio's stock company has since identified the boy playing Larry as John Galvarro, who played the same character, Larry, in Coronet's Are You Ready for Marriage? the same year and went on to small roles in Service and Citizenship (1951) and the Encyclopaedia Britannica short Drug Addiction.
The film belongs to Coronet's early-1950s run of shorts built around the vocabulary of behaviorist psychology — Control Your Emotions, made the same year, dramatizes the same three emotions through a teenager's bad Friday, while this one drops the story in favor of the lab: mice, wiring, and a plastic brain standing in for a plot. Ken Smith, whose capsule notes for the Prelinger Archives remain the standard reference for the genre, filed it as "even more Skinnerist than Control Your Emotions, and much less entertaining" — a fair verdict on a film that treats its teenage subjects less as characters than as case studies. Like most of the Coronet guidance catalog it has long since lapsed into the public domain and survives today through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon travels to Button Moon where he finds a wardrobe and helps to make a sad dress happy. Through the telescope, the fox and the hen. The penultimate episode of Series 1. The Button Moon adventure — making a sad dress happy — is pure Allen whimsy. A wardrobe contains dresses. A dress can be sad. Mr. Spoon can help. The emotional logic of very young children is taken completely seriously: of course a dress has feelings, and of course helping it is important work. This was the genius of Button Moon's writing. It never winked at the audience or played for adult irony. The objects were alive because the show said they were, and that was that. The fox and hen telescope story rounds out a series that drew heavily on classic fables — three Aesop adaptations, the Three Little Pigs, the Billy Goats Gruff — establishing the telescope as Button Moon's story-within-a-story engine.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon and his family watch a performance of the Paper Circus. Then through their telescope they see Scruffy the dog, whose best friend is moving away. The Series 1 finale, airing 2 March 1981. The telescope story — a dog losing his best friend to a house move — is Button Moon at its most emotionally direct. No fable, no fairy tale retelling. Just the sadness of someone you love going away. It's the kind of story that hits a three-year-old right in the chest because they understand it completely. The Paper Circus on Button Moon is another Allen invention: circus performers made from paper, performing in a circus made from paper, watched by spoons. Thirteen episodes in, the show had proven its format could hold anything — Aesop, Grimm, original stories, slapstick, gentle melancholy. Thames commissioned Series 2 immediately. Button Moon would return in December 1981 for another thirteen episodes, and then again, and again, for six more years.

programme.title: David
programme.desc:
A small boy tries to retrieve his ball from increasingly dangerous situations, each attempt triggering chain reactions of absurd consequences. Driessen's signature wiggling line style — delicate, ever-moving, never quite settling — is fully formed here.
Paul Driessen was born in Nijmegen, Netherlands in 1940. He studied graphic design and illustration at the Art Academy in Utrecht, then fell into animation by accident — making TV commercials in Holland with no animation training whatsoever. In 1967, George Dunning found him at the Cine Cartoon Centre in Hilversum while scouting talent and said "Whenever you want, come to England." When the Dutch studio collapsed, Driessen went — and arrived just as Yellow Submarine was starting production. Nine months, no script, Sgt. Pepper's had just come out. Dunning then helped him emigrate to Canada, where he joined the NFB's French animation studio in 1972. David was made back in Holland during a year-long break.

programme.title: How to Study
programme.desc:
Jim is a schoolboy handed a civics assignment: the teacher chalks up three current-events questions — should the federal government control medicine, should there be state control of radio and television, should labor unions be required to incorporate — and each student picks one to turn into a written report. Jim takes the labor-union question, and the film follows him treating the job like research rather than homework: he pencils a work schedule onto a wall calendar, then works through a stack of reference books — a general encyclopedia and a bound volume of the Readers' Guide to Periodical Literature — reading each one at a different speed depending on the job at hand, from a fast scan to find what's relevant to a slow, careful pass through the dense print on incorporation law and old court cases like Coronado Coal Company v. United Mine Workers. He boils what he finds down to three study questions, re-reads to check them, and writes the report up with time to spare on his pocket watch.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, the picture follows the house formula: the only credit on screen is the educational collaborator, here William G. Brink, Ph.D., Professor of Education at Northwestern University, named on the same title card as the RCA sound-system credit and nowhere else. Brink's own published work of the period concerned the study of classroom teaching materials, which tracks with the film's close attention to differentiated reading speeds — presented less as moralizing than as a plain set of techniques, the scan/skim/read-closely/re-read sequence that library and study-skills instruction would keep teaching for decades. As with much of Coronet's early-1940s output, the surviving print is black-and-white 16mm.
How to Study sits in the study-skills wing of Coronet's guidance catalog, a smaller cousin to the social-guidance shorts the company became better known for — the same brisk, under-ten-minute run time, aimed here at library and study-hall habits rather than dating or popularity. The Prelinger Archives catalog entry for the film describes exactly this: Jim preparing a civics report on labor unions using four kinds of reading — scanning, rapid reading, careful slow reading, and re-reading — to organize his research and write it up. Public domain since its educational-market rights lapsed, it now circulates chiefly through the Prelinger collection at the Internet Archive, alongside the rest of Coronet's postwar schoolroom output.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Mr Rusty asks Florence to keep an eye out for a very special carpet — large and quite out of the ordinary — and Zebedee bounces her along to the garden, where Dougal is busy beating exactly such a carpet over a wire and trying to pretend he isn't. He greets Florence with a barrage of unconvincing weather forecasts meant to send her home, until he backs into the carpet and knocks it loose; the moment he climbs aboard, it lifts off and sails away over the garden. Brian rigs up an improvised airport radio to talk the airborne dog down, reporting solemnly that Dougal is now in orbit. The carpet eventually settles, but when Florence sets a lump of sugar on it to test for magic, it promptly eats the sugar — a "cannibal carpet," Dougal decides — then sees off Brian before draping itself over Dougal entirely.
One of the few series-three episodes in which Ermintrude does not appear. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS in 1984 and on The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout in 1993, retitled "Magic Carpet".

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
At the roundabout, Mr Rusty admires Florence's new bob haircut and recalls that bobs were all the rage in his day. Zebedee pops up flourishing a walking stick, and Mr Rusty promptly returns with one of his own, presenting it to Florence and bidding her give it a twirl. She obliges. The pair later discover a whole crop of walking sticks scattered across the slippery ground and are happily twirling and skating when Dougal roars in on his special watering machine, furious to find his sugarcane plantation apparently pillaged. He rounds on Florence, Zebedee, and the freshly arrived Ermintrude — who, quite unbothered, plants herself in the soil and asks to be watered. Mr McHenry crashes the machine, earning a tart remark from Dougal. Peace is restored when Dougal magnanimously hands Florence a raspberry-flavoured sugar walking stick; she declares it lovely, and Zebedee quietly advises her to plant it so it can grow. Dougal dismisses Ermintrude's counter-proposals of sugar turnips and sugar carrots as undignified.
The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as part of BBC Video's Volume 1 in 1984, reissued in 1989 and 1992.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon takes Tina Teaspoon to Button Moon, where they encounter Charlie — a garden gnome whose nose has been replaced by a garden hose. The characters must find a way to help Charlie get his proper nose back while the Bottle Army stands guard on the castle walls. Through the telescope, they spy another adventure unfolding below. This episode comes from the show's sixth series, produced when Thames Television had refined Button Moon's distinctive handmade aesthetic into something close to art — every prop still fashioned from kitchen utensils and household junk, every set constructed from the contents of a drawer. By 1987, creator Ian Allen and his Playboard Puppets team had been building this world for seven years, and the craft shows: the characters move with an easy confidence that the earliest episodes lacked. The DVD source preserves the Thames Television production quality, including Peter Davison and Sandra Dickinson's iconic theme tune — the pair were married during Button Moon's early years, divorcing in 1990.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon and the family discover a new planet on their way to Button Moon — Planet Doughnut, a world shaped like its namesake. The episode showcases Ian Allen and Playboard Puppets at their most inventive, building an entire edible-looking celestial body from household objects. By the sixth series, Button Moon had become a quiet institution on ITV, airing weekly on Thames Television to a generation of children who accepted without question that a spoon could pilot a rocket made from tin cans through a sky made of blankets. Through the telescope, Mr. Spoon observes the familiar world below where another small drama plays out. Robin Parkinson narrates with the same gentle authority he brought to all 91 episodes across seven series.

programme.title: Social Courtesy
programme.desc:
Bill primps in front of his bedroom mirror, getting ready for a costume party with his girlfriend Carol, and grumbles that all this fuss over manners is old-fashioned. An unseen narrator disagrees, and makes Bill live with the consequences: every time the boy is rude, the narrator freezes the scene, "takes a picture" of it — the moment dissolves into a photograph hanging on the wall of the next shot — and rewinds Bill back to try again, a little more friendly this time. At the party itself, a teenage rec room dressed up as a hobo jungle, with hand-lettered signs reading "To Train," "Track 1," "Keep Out," and "Baggage Checked" strung up among the decorations, Bill argues under his breath with a voice nobody else can hear, until one of the girls asks if he's talking to himself. Bit by bit he tries doing what he's told — standing when an adult speaks to him, sitting up instead of slouching, actually listening to his friends — and by the last reel the chaperone is remarking on what a changed, courteous boy he's become; Bill leaves already holding an invitation to the next party.
The only screen credit belongs to the educational collaborator: the opening title cards name Mary E.
