Things go wrong almost immediately: Ermintrude can't be heard because the lid of her piano is closed on the keys, Dylan keeps missing his cue, and Brian somehow ends up stranded on top of the harp with a very long way down. Dougal, never short of a cutting remark, manages to infuriate Ermintrude and then break his own drum by hitting it too hard, leaving both the harp and drum sections hors de combat. Florence and Dylan try to keep things moving, Zebedee drops his baton mid-performance, and Brian eventually solves his predicament by sliding down the harp strings. Zebedee finally calls for a soothing lullaby to wrap things up, because it is, after all, time for bed.
Scenes from this episode were later combined with footage from "Piano Moving" and "Oil Wells" to create a new story, "Band Practice", narrated by Nigel Planer and broadcast by Channel 4 on 27 May 1993. The Eric Thompson script was also reprinted in the 1999 novel The Adventures of Dylan.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal and Florence stumble upon a life-sized Jack of Hearts who has gone AWOL from his pack, complaining he was getting a raw deal. He reveals that cards shuffle themselves and that the Queen of Spades in particular makes his existence miserable — reason enough, he insists, never to go back. Before long the rest of the pack arrives in force, demanding the runaway's return and promising a good walloping. After hearing both sides, Florence steps in with cool-headed logic: a pack short one card is simply useless, and the whole point of cards is to be played. The King and Queen are impressed enough to call for applause, the lost card reluctantly rejoins his suit, and the pack shuffles away. Dougal, inspired, suggests a game of Snap — but Florence decides it is probably time for bed.
The Eric Thompson narration version was released on BBC Video VHS Volume 2 in 1991.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: Gumby wants to bake a pie and jelly rolls for his parents. The dough, naturally, has other ideas. This is Gumby at its most domestic and its most playful — a clay boy working with dough, which is itself a kind of clay. The pun is structural: Gumby is made of the same stuff he is trying to shape. The episode trades adventure for kitchen comedy, but the stop-motion baking sequences required just as much painstaking frame-by-frame work as any dragon fight or moon landing. One of the highest-rated individual Gumby episodes on IMDb at 7.8, suggesting that viewers respond to simplicity done well. From the second year of the original NBC run, when the production had moved from Hollywood to a larger studio in Glendora.

programme.title: How To Be Well-Groomed
programme.desc:
Don and Sue are a well-scrubbed brother and sister whose entire day, it turns out, is organized around looking presentable. The morning starts with an alarm clock and a made bed, then moves through the sink and the mirror: washing, combing, cleaning fingernails. Sue skips red nail polish because, the narrators explain, it would only call attention to her stubby hands, and Don works through his own ritual of shaving and picking a tie in front of the glass, a Rice pennant tacked up on his wall behind him. Evenings run the same machinery in reverse — an iron on the board, shoes buffed to a shine, blouses and skirts hung with care in a closet barely large enough to hold them. The family sits down to breakfast together, mother included, and the dual narrators — a man and a woman trading lines — keep tallying the payoff: good habits that, they insist, make Don and Sue "the kind of people you'd like to know." The week's grooming builds to Friday night, when Sue chooses a dress and Don straightens his jacket, and the two head out the door turned out for their dates.
The film's title card carries a copyright date of MCMXLVIII — 1948 — under producer David A. Smart's name, though the Prelinger Archives and A.V. Geeks catalogs both list it under 1949, evidently the year the short actually reached classrooms. As was Coronet's standard practice, no director is credited on screen; the sole named contributor is the subject-matter consultant, billed on her own card as "Educational Collaborator Mary E. Weathersby, Head, Homemaking Education Department, Mississippi State College." Coronet Instructional Films, the Chicago-area studio David Smart built out of his Coronet and Esquire magazine ventures, supplied schools with hundreds of these shorts, and the recurring formula — an authority figure's name up front, an anonymous director behind the camera — appears here exactly as it does elsewhere in the catalog.
"How To Be Well-Groomed" belongs to the wave of postwar social-guidance shorts that scholar Michelle Boulé has dated to a 1947-1957 heyday, films built to model "preferred behaviors" for teenagers through tidy, repeatable rituals rather than drama. The two-narrator technique on display here — a man's voice and a woman's trading observations about Don and Sue's choices — was one of the genre's stock devices for making conformity sound like friendly advice. The film has been preserved and made publicly available through the Prelinger Archives, where cataloger Ken Smith (whose own reference book on the genre, "Mental Hygiene," draws on prints like this one) noted the shot list's small, telling details, and separately through the A/V Geeks 16mm Archive, which digitized its own surviving copy for continued classroom-history use.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon flies from Junk Planet, through Blanket Sky to shining Button Moon. There he meets Captain Large and the Bottle Army. Through his telescope he spies a witch's magic. This is the second episode, airing one week after the pilot on 15 December 1980 — ten days before Christmas. The show was already finding its rhythm: the journey through Blanket Sky, the adventure on Button Moon, and the telescope story became the three-act structure that would hold for all ninety-one episodes. Captain Large and the Bottle Army — a military commander made from a large bottle ordering around smaller bottles — were among the first recurring Button Moon characters beyond the Spoon family. Ian Allen built them all from real bottles. The telescope stories often retold classic fairy tales and fables, giving the show a double structure: the puppet adventure on Button Moon and the moral tale glimpsed through the lens.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
Gumby uses robots to do his household chores while he and Pokey play. The robots get out of control and Gumby has a frantic time trying to restore order.
The most famous individual Gumby episode — partly because in 1998 it was featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000, where Joel, Tom Servo, and Crow riffed on it as a short before their main feature. The MST3K treatment introduced Gumby to a generation that had missed both the original run and the Eddie Murphy revival. The Paley Center for Media includes it in their official Art Clokey compilation alongside Gumbasia. The premise — technology meant to help creates chaos instead — is evergreen enough that the episode works without any nostalgia filter. Clokey's robots are wonderfully clunky: boxy, purposeful, and completely indifferent to the havoc they cause. It's slapstick with an edge of genuine anxiety about automation, played out in clay on a tabletop in Glendora, California.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: The first episode of the syndication era. After two years on NBC as part of Howdy Doody, Gumby moved into syndication in 1960 with new episodes produced at Clokey's expanded Glendora studio. Dallas McKennon had taken over voicing Gumby in 1957, giving the character a warmer, more expressive sound than Ruth Eggleston's original. The Zoops are strange creatures Gumby encounters — Clokey never ran out of weird beings to populate his worlds. By 1960 the show had developed a much larger cast of recurring characters beyond just Gumby and Pokey.

programme.title: Dating Dos and Don'ts
programme.desc:
Alan "Woody" Woodruff gets a lucky break when his mother, laid up and told to stay off her feet for a week, hands down her own admit-one-couple ticket to Central High's Hi-Teen Carnival — it's too late to turn the ticket back in, so she tells him to make a night of it. Woody has to settle on the right girl and work up the nerve to phone her, and the film cuts between his own careful call and other boys fumbling the same moment, including his older brother Bob, a leather-jacketed member of Coronet's regular stock company, slouched over the receiver doing it the wrong way. Ann Davis says yes, and the picture follows both households getting ready — Ann having her hair set with her kid sister's help while her mother tidies the room, Woody waiting at the foot of the stairs in a coat and tie. At the carnival itself the couple work the midway games, stop at the refreshment stand, and take in the side-show tent before the evening winds down to a last, correctly executed good night at her door.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films and directed by Gilbert Altschul — listed in the studio's own paperwork as "Gil Altschul," the house director behind Coronet's run of postwar courtship shorts, including the direct sequel Going Steady two years later. In keeping with Coronet's practice of crediting only the academic consultant on screen, the picture's sole title credit belongs to its "authority," Reuben Hill, Ph.D., Research Professor in Family Life at the University of North Carolina. The studio's shooting credits additionally list Bruce Colling on camera, Harriette Smith and Hartley Pfeil as writers, George Wilbern editing, and Chicago radio announcer Ken Nordine narrating. Released in November 1949, the finished film runs just under twelve minutes; it survives today chiefly through an incomplete Kodachrome print, the version now held by the Prelinger Archives by way of A.V. Geeks.
Woody was played by John Lindsay, a Chicago-area teenager then attending North Park Academy; a 1952 alumni newsletter recalled that he had "made a movie about how to act toward a girl on your first date" before he went on to Northwestern University, an Army hitch, and a long career in securities investment management, eventually rising to vice president at McCormick & Co. His onscreen date, Ann Davis, was played by an actress who happened to share her name with the well-known television comedian — a different, unrelated Jackie Gleason, who later married and lived into her seventies. Dorothy Day played Woody's mother. Alongside Are You Popular? and Shy Guy, the film became one of the more widely circulated entries in Coronet's social-guidance catalog, kept in circulation now mainly as a plainspoken record of just how narrow the era's rules for a first date were.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence finds Dougal in the garden in a reflective mood, wondering whether either of them has achieved anything in life. The question is soon answered when Brian trundles past carrying drilling equipment on his shell, intent on sinking an oil well right there in the garden. Dougal watches with arch scepticism while Brian sets up his rig and declares himself a genius before starting to drill. The operation does not go quite as planned: Brian punches straight down into someone else's reserve, and an indignant oil lamp emerges from his underground den demanding to know what all the commotion is. Dougal recognises him as Florence's acquaintance from a previous visit, and the lamp makes clear that any oil in the garden is rightfully his before turning to greet Florence warmly. Brian, undeterred, cheerfully labels himself a misunderstood genius.
The trivia notes that scenes from this episode were later combined with footage from "Piano Moving" and "The Orchestra" into a Nigel Planer-narrated story called "Band Practice", broadcast by Channel 4 on 27 May 1993. The Eric Thompson narration was also released on VHS as part of BBC Video's Volume 2 in 1991.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
The growing ambition of Julius Caesar is a source of major concern to his close friend Brutus. Cassius persuades him to participate in a plot to assassinate Caesar, but they have both sorely underestimated Mark Antony.
Directed by Yuri Kulakov in cel animation, this is the most politically charged entry in the second series — a study in the mechanics of conspiracy, assassination, and rhetorical manipulation compressed into twenty-five minutes of Leon Garfield's razor-sharp script.
Kulakov was one of the least-known directors in the Shakespeare Animated Tales roster, but his career arc tells a story about survival in post-Soviet animation. He began work at Soyuzmultfilm during its late-Soviet period, then moved to smaller studios as the industry collapsed. In 1997, a year after completing Julius Caesar, he began developing his magnum opus: Prince Vladimir (Knyaz Vladimir), a traditionally hand-drawn animated feature about the Christianization of Kievan Rus'. The film took nine years to complete at the studio Solnechniy Dom-DM, finally releasing in 2006 — an act of pure stubbornness, producing a cel-animated epic in an era when every studio worldwide had gone digital. The result was a 78-minute film animated in a style deliberately evoking classic Soviet-era Soyuzmultfilm techniques and mid-century Disney, with voice work by Sergey Bezrukov. He also directed episodes of Testament: The Bible in Animation and Animated Epics: Beowulf for the same S4C/Christmas Films pipeline.
Joss Ackland voices Caesar. Born Sidney Edmond Jocelyn Ackland on 29 February 1928 — a leap-year baby who lived to 95 — in a basement flat in North Kensington, the son of an Irish journalist who'd been banished to England for seducing his parents' maid and then seduced his aunt's maid. Trained at the Central School of Speech and Drama under Elsie Fogerty, he left school at fifteen to act. In 1954, unable to find work, he and wife Rosemary moved to Nyasaland (now Malawi) to manage a tea plantation for six months before fleeing to Cape Town. Returning to London, he joined the Old Vic alongside Maggie Smith, Judi Dench, and Tom Courtenay. He created the role of Juan Perón in the original London production of Evita opposite Elaine Paige. His film career spanned 130-plus roles: the South African diplomat in Lethal Weapon 2, the Soviet ambassador in The Hunt for Red October, Jerry Westerby in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, C.S. Lewis in the TV Shadowlands, and the Black Rabbit of Inlé in Watership Down. He was a workaholic who freely admitted to appearing in "awful" films — he regretted Bill and Ted's Bogus Journey and the Pet Shop Boys music video (which he'd done purely because his grandchildren liked their music). In 1963, his house caught fire; Rosemary, pregnant, saved their five children but broke her back jumping from the bedroom window. Their eldest son Paul died of a heroin overdose in 1982. Rosemary died of motor neurone disease in 2002 after 51 years of marriage. CBE in 2000. He died in Clovelly, Devon, in November 2023.
Jim Carter voices Mark Antony. Born in Harrogate in 1948, Carter dropped out of law at the University of Sussex to join the Brighton Combination, a fringe theatre group, for five pounds a week. He later studied at an American circus school, learning juggling, unicycling, and tightrope walking — skills he still performs at cabarets. He met his wife Imelda Staunton during a 1982 National Theatre revival of Guys and Dolls. The world knows him as Mr Carson in Downton Abbey, which earned him four Emmy nominations, but his range runs from The Madness of King George to Shakespeare in Love to Tim Burton's Alice in Wonderland. In Julius Caesar, he had literal stage experience with the play — in 1980 he'd played Trebonius and Marullus in Peter Gill's Julius Caesar at Riverside Studios.
Hugh Quarshie, born in Accra, Gold Coast (now Ghana), in 1954, studied PPE at Christ Church, Oxford before choosing acting over journalism. A Royal Shakespeare Company member since 1981 and associate since 2005, he brought deep Shakespearean authority to his role. Film audiences know him as Captain Panaka in Star Wars: Episode I and Sunda Kastagir in Highlander. His ancestry traces to Ghanaian chiefs and a Dutch colonial official — revealed on Who Do You Think You Are? — making him a distant relative of Dutch actor Antonie Kamerling.

programme.title: Overcoming Fear
programme.desc:
At a busy municipal swimming pool, a teenage boy named Bill hangs back while the rest of the gang runs for the water. The opening shots track a crowd of kids racing past the diving boards and pool chairs, then settle on Bill alone at the water's edge and again by the locker-room doors, in his trunks but not going in. Mr. Barker, the pool's swimming coach, doesn't order him in; he sits down with Bill, first at poolside and then on a locker-room bench, and gets him to name what actually scares him about the water. The film then leaves the pool for a run of short vignettes on other, smaller fears — a backyard talk near the clothesline, a girl coaxing a small dog she's wary of, a scene in a book-lined room — before bringing Bill back to the water for a deliberately paced sequence of steps: standing in the shallow end, floating, finally diving from the board on his own. By the last reel he is swimming freestyle across the pool and crouching at the steps to help a smaller child in, one of the crowd he had been avoiding at the start.
Produced at Coronet's studio in Glenview, Illinois — the estate David A. Smart, the Esquire magazine publisher, converted into a 16mm production facility for his instructional-film business — and copyrighted MCML under the Coronet trademark, with the RCA Sound System credit that runs across the studio's postwar output. As with the rest of that catalog, no actors or director are named on screen; the only credit in the title cards is the educational collaborator, Herbert Sorenson, Ph.D., professor of educational psychology at the University of Kentucky and author of textbooks in the field, brought in to keep Barker's breakdown of Bill's fear grounded in contemporary psychology rather than simple reassurance.
Overcoming Fear belongs to the same run of Coronet social-guidance shorts as Shy Guy and Are You Popular?, made for classroom health units rather than theatrical release. The Prelinger Archives catalog description matches the print scene for scene: Bill's fear of the water, Barker's coaching, and the gradual buildup of swimming skill and confidence. No director or cast credits for this specific title turn up in any accessible filmography — Coronet's own credits stop at the consultant, and surviving catalog entries do not even agree on the running time of the print, some logging it under twelve minutes and others closer to thirteen. What holds constant across every source is the premise: fear treated as a nameable, solvable problem, worked through with the same brisk manner Coronet brought to its other studies of adolescent anxiety.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
At the roundabout, Mr Rusty excitedly introduces Florence to a bubble wand and soap, and the two are happily blowing bubbles when Zebedee bobs up and is persuaded to have a go himself, getting briefly startled by the result. Florence takes the wand into the garden to show Dougal, who is initially grumpy about the mysterious popping sounds before being won over enough to blow one himself — until the Train trundles through and delivers a withering remark about a grown dog playing with bubbles. Ermintrude arrives and is overcome with delight at the sight of them floating in the air, only to be crestfallen when Florence admits the soap has run out. Zebedee attempts a magical remedy but gets things slightly crossed: the Train begins puffing bubbles from its funnel while smoke billows from the bubble wand instead, sending Ermintrude into a burst of "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles" before the smoke makes her splutter.
This episode is among twelve made after the production of Dougal and the Blue Cat, using that film's updated character models; in the UK it was broadcast before the film's theatrical premiere. The Eric Thompson narration was released on the BBC Video VHS Volume 2 collection in 1991.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon flies from his home on Junk Planet to Button Moon. Through the telescope, the Three Billy Goats Gruff. Airing on 22 December 1980, this was the Christmas week episode of the first series. The telescope story retelling classic fairy tales was becoming the show's signature — and it gave Ian Allen a bottomless well of source material. The Billy Goats Gruff, with its bridge and its troll and its escalating sizes, was perfectly suited to the show's aesthetic of objects standing in for characters. Every prop in Button Moon was built from real household items by Allen's Playboard Puppets workshop in Norfolk. The troll under the bridge, the goats, the bridge itself — all kitchen scraps and junk drawer finds assembled with the conviction that imagination matters more than production value.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon lives with his family on Junk Planet. He has seen Button Moon shining in Blanket Sky and travels there in his spaceship. Airing on 29 December 1980, this was the last episode of the year — four episodes into what would become an eight-year run. The show's world was expanding. Beyond the Spoon family and Captain Large's Bottle Army, new characters were appearing on Button Moon and in the telescope stories. Every one of them was built from whatever Ian Allen could find in a kitchen drawer or a junk shop. The lo-fi aesthetic was not a budget constraint — it was the whole point. Allen had been performing puppet shows with household objects since founding Playboard Puppets, and Button Moon was the purest expression of his belief that a spoon with googly eyes is more alive than any CGI character, because a child can go home and make one.

programme.title: The Killing of an Egg
programme.desc:
A man tries to break a soft-boiled egg. The egg resists. What follows is an escalating war between human and breakfast that ends in mutual destruction. Three minutes, no dialogue, perfect.
Made during a "beautiful summer" back in Holland in 1977, the same year as David, after Driessen's first few films at the National Film Board of Canada. He rented a room and worked from home — "kind of fun, especially when you're young."
This tiny film changed the history of television. In 1977, a teenager named Stephen Hillenburg attended the International Tournée of Animation in California and saw The Killing of an Egg. It made him realize he could use animation to bring his own ideas to life. He went on to create SpongeBob SquarePants. Driessen's three-minute egg fight is the reason SpongeBob exists.

programme.title: How to Keep a Job
programme.desc:
Ed Blakeslee's job at Central Distributing Co. ends with a printed notice: his services are "no longer required due to business retrenching," effective immediately, over the signature of manager George Holman. Combing the classifieds afterward, Ed circles a promising line among the want ads: "Ambitious young man can make a place for himself in a well-established company. Attitude more important than experience. See Mr. Wiley at Star Products Company." At the interview, filling out an application and naming his expected starting rate, Ed meets a Mr. Wiley who is in no hurry to hire him outright. Instead Wiley lays out what the job actually asks for through a case in point: two nearly identical young men, Bob and Walter Anderson, working side by side in the Star Products shipping room. Split-screen photography sets the pair against each other shot for shot as the company's clock ticks overhead — one packs, tapes, and files with care and stays at his post, the other slouches through the shift, reads the newspaper at his desk, and treats the stockroom carelessly. Bob's diligence earns him a promotion; Walter's indifference earns him a termination notice much like the one Ed just received. Wiley's point isn't which twin looks better on paper, but which one makes himself worth keeping.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films and copyrighted in 1949 by publisher David A. Smart, the print carries only one credit besides the studio: an educational-collaborator card for John N. Given, Supervisor of Business Education for the Los Angeles City Board of Education, recorded on the RCA sound system. Unlike many black-and-white Coronet guidance shorts of the period, this one was shot in color, which lets the split-screen device separating Bob from Walter register clearly against the same shipping-room set.
The film belongs to Coronet's postwar run of classroom guidance shorts aimed at teenagers entering the workforce, and it leans on the "Goofus and Gallant" contrast — one exemplary figure, one cautionary one, presented side by side — that the studio used across the cycle to make its point without much subtlety. It has since passed into the public domain and circulates through the Prelinger Archives and the Internet Archive alongside its Coronet siblings.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence arrives in the garden to find everyone absent until Brian appears with news that Dougal has a musical problem requiring assistance. The trouble is that Dougal has been trying to load his piano onto Train's truck without success, much to Train's mounting irritation — she was supposed to be in Crewe the previous Thursday for the steam train reunion. When Florence and Brian pitch up, Dougal dryly informs them he is fishing off Brighton Pier. Train tartly compares Dougal's composure to an elephant stampede, and Florence calmly imposes order: Dougal must promise to keep calm, which he does at considerable volume. Together the three of them finally manhandle the piano aboard. Train announces that anything not loaded will be left behind, warns of further embarrassment at Watford Junction, and departs for Edinburgh — leaving Brian's miscellaneous whatnot firmly on the platform.
Scenes from this episode were later combined with footage from "The Orchestra" and "Oil Wells" to make a new story called "Band Practice", narrated by Nigel Planer and broadcast on Channel 4 on 27 May 1993. The Eric Thompson audio was retitled "The Piano Carrier" for its 1971 LP and cassette release, later reissued to CD. The episode script appears in the 1999 novel The Adventures of Brian.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
At the roundabout, Florence encounters Mr Rusty clutching a paper rollup — his contribution to the garden's new highway code project. Zebedee bounds in and the three head off to join the rest of the gang, who have each independently made their own road sign. Once everyone is assembled, Zebedee announces that Florence will sort through them all, and then springs off. The signs go up one by one: Penelope posts "Danger: Spiders at Work," Dylan (assisted by Florence) contributes "No Hooting, Rabbits Sleeping," Ermintrude insists on "Keep Off the Flowers," Dougal one-ups her with "Keep Cows Off the Flowers," Mr McHenry designates a "Scooters Only" lane, Train claims his own, the Twin Birds permit music, Brian sets a brisk limit of one mile per hour, and Mr Rusty crowns the display with "Flowers Are Best." As Dougal and Brian bicker over the results, Zebedee reappears — just in time for Mr Rusty to wonder whether the garden might now be slightly over-signed, except, of course, for his own.
This episode features the largest cast of named characters in the series, with twelve major and minor figures on screen. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as part of BBC Video's The Magic Roundabout Volume 3 in 1992, and again on The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout in 1993.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Car
programme.desc: Krtek pops out of his molehill to find the world has changed — loud, gleaming machines roar past, carrying dogs and geese. He wants one desperately. His chance comes when a spoiled boy named Karlík smashes his toy car and tosses it away. Krtek rescues the wreck — a pink Ford Thunderbird first generation, 1:12 scale, wind-up motor — and with help from his forest friends rebuilds it into something roadworthy. What follows is a layered dream-within-a-dream sequence: Krtek races through a city of soaring tower blocks that Czech audiences noted looked nothing like any socialist capital and everything like the West, cruises open highways, delights in speed. But exhaust smoke drifts over his meadow, and the episode's environmental message crystallises — the car that brings freedom also poisons the world it drives through. At fifteen minutes, this is the longest of the original Krtek shorts and the second ever made, following the 1957 Venice Film Festival debut. It established the template Miler would follow for decades: a found human object as the engine of wonder and trouble. The opening titles contain a typo — the orchestra credit reads FYSIO instead of FISYO (Filmový symfonický orchestr). Music performed by the Film Symphony Orchestra under direction not credited to a named composer, a holdover from the earliest production period before Vadim Petrov became the series' signature voice.

programme.title: Oh What a Nico
programme.desc:
A one-minute tribute film — Driessen's characteristic wiggling lines compressed into sixty seconds of pure gesture. "Nico" echoes his earlier Oh What a Knight, suggesting another variation on the same theme of quixotic struggle.
By 2004 Driessen had settled in a small village in the South of France, where he still animates on paper. He bought a Cintiq to modernize but never switched: "When I started my new film I still had paper sitting here. I need time to sit back and get used to the new computer programs but when you get older you want to get things done instead of spending time on technology. I'm still excited about the films I want to make and I don't want to delay it too much, so I'm still animating on paper. I scan them into the computer, though."

programme.title: Self-Conscious Guy
programme.desc:
Marty is a self-conscious high school student who freezes at the moments that matter most — reciting at the blackboard in English class, asking a girl out from a corner payphone, waiting through a tryout for the school play — because, as he explains it, he feels "as if there was a spotlight on me." Coronet gives the metaphor a literal form: a spotlight lands on Marty whenever his nerves take over, cutting him off from the room around him. He wants the play's leading role and loses it to nerves, ending up instead among the stagehands working the curtain. From the wings he starts noticing that his classmates — even Jack, the confident boy who won the part he wanted — carry the same private unease, and it's an ordinary game of ping-pong in the school rec room, not the stage, where Marty finally out-plays Jack and discovers the poise he'd assumed he didn't have.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films under founder David A. Smart and copyrighted in 1951 — MCMLI on the print's own title card — the film follows Coronet's standard practice of crediting only its outside expert on screen: the title card names Judson T. Landis, Ph.D., a family sociologist at the University of California, Berkeley, as educational collaborator. Landis was, by 1951, a familiar name to health and hygiene teachers; he and his wife Mary Green Landis had already co-authored the widely used high-school textbook Building Your Life, and Coronet leaned on that classroom credibility the way it leaned on university psychologists and sociologists across its whole social-guidance line.
Film historian Ken Smith, surveying the classroom-hygiene genre, judged it a lesser cousin of Coronet's own Shy Guy — "cheap, but effective" — singling out the spotlight device as the one inventive touch in an otherwise plain ten minutes, and noting that the young actor cast as Marty also turned up as the lead in Coronet's How to Say No the same year. That actor's name never made it onto any print or catalog card; cataloging Coronet's recurring faces at the Tralfaz blog, film historian Yowp lists him simply as "actor unknown" with "a specialty in big-lip anguish." Self-Conscious Guy survives today through the Prelinger Archives holdings at the Internet Archive, in the public domain like most of Coronet's postwar guidance shorts.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Mr Rusty cranks his barrel organ while Florence and her friends enjoy a spin on the roundabout. Zebedee appears, moved to joyful tears by the scene, and twirls about until everyone is quite worn out. He then invites the children to the garden — with the caveat that it may pour with rain. Mr Rusty kindly supplies umbrellas all round, and off they go. In the garden they find Dougal standing sentinel against the approaching weather, full of grim forecasts about storms on the way. The children are consoled to have their umbrellas, and Dougal pointedly asks whether they happened to bring a spare. They have — suitably modified. Brian saunters in, cheerfully pronouncing it a lovely day, earning Dougal's scorn; Brian, for his part, finds Dougal's improvised rain-hat worth a comment.
This episode is among a group of twelve made after the production of Dougal and the Blue Cat, reusing the updated character models from that film — all broadcast in the UK before the film's own premiere. The original slower, lower-pitched theme music can be heard at the opening. The Eric Thompson narration was released on BBC Video VHS Volume 2 in 1991.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Othello, a Moorish general in the service of Venice, has secretly married the senator's daughter Desdemona. His ensign Iago, passed over for promotion, engineers Othello's destruction through planted evidence and whispered insinuation, turning the general's love into a jealousy so absolute it becomes murder.
Directed by Nikolai Serebryakov in cel animation, his second entry in the series after Macbeth. Born in Leningrad on 14 December 1928, Serebryakov was evacuated during the wartime blockade as a child. He graduated from the Vera Mukhina Institute in 1952 and joined Soyuzmultfilm in 1960, becoming part of the Khrushchev-era "thaw" generation of animators alongside Khrzhanovsky and Kurchevsky. His Ball of Wool (1968) is considered a masterpiece of Russian animated cinema. He collaborated with his wife Alina Speshneva, a production designer from the Obraztsov puppet theatre — they won prizes at Grenoble and the Grand Prix at Tampere — until her death in an accident in 1984. He also contributed to Elem Klimov's Sport, Sport, Sport (1970, with a Schnittke soundtrack). Named People's Artist of Russia in 1996. The Independent's obituary described him as sweet-natured, with an appetite for "life, laughter, friendship, art and vodka." He died on 9 August 2005. A personal detail: he married first Nadia Speshneva, then her sister Alina.
Colin McFarlane voices Othello — his very first voice role. Born Colin Andrew Ignatius Peter McFarlane on 15 September 1961 in Upper Clapton, London, to Jamaican parents. His father Sidney McFarlane served in the RAF and was later awarded an MBE for voluntary service to the community. His mother Gwendolyn worked in the NHS. The family moved to Lincoln in the East Midlands, where McFarlane grew up. He attended the Perse School in Cambridge and read drama at Loughborough University, graduating in 1983. A decade after voicing Shakespeare's most famous Moor, Christopher Nolan cast him as Police Commissioner Gillian B. Loeb in Batman Begins and The Dark Knight — the corrupt official who stands in the way of justice in Gotham. He became the disembodied voice of The Cube on ITV (2009-2021), JJ in Bob the Builder, and has appeared in Doctor Who multiple times (the Heavenly Host in "Voyage of the Damned," Moran in Series 9, Colonel Pierce in Torchwood: Children of Earth). After voicing Othello for S4C, he went straight into the same production pipeline to voice God and Goliath in Testament: The Bible in Animation. From the Moor to the Almighty in two years.
Gerard McSorley voices Iago. Born on New Year's Day 1950 in Omagh, County Tyrone — a town that would become synonymous with the worst single atrocity of the Troubles when a Real IRA bomb killed twenty-nine people and unborn twins on 15 August 1998. McSorley went on to play the lead in the 2004 television film Omagh, portraying Michael Gallagher, a father who lost his son in the bombing, searching for justice. He won the Irish Film and Television Award for Best Actor. Playing Iago is one thing. Playing the grief of your own hometown is another.
He attended St. Columb's College in Derry — the same school that produced Seamus Heaney, John Hume, and Phil Coulter — and then Queen's University Belfast, where Heaney taught him. He is a descendant of John McSorley, the Irish immigrant who in 1854 opened McSorley's Old Ale House on East 7th Street in Manhattan, which remains the oldest continuously operating pub in New York City.
His career reads like a syllabus of modern Irish cinema: Cathal Brugha in Michael Collins, Chief Superintendent Lagan in Bloody Sunday, John Gilligan in Veronica Guerin, Sir Kenneth Curtiss in The Constant Gardener, the market auctioneer in War Horse. He was cast as Captain Queenan in Scorsese's The Departed but had to pull out — Martin Sheen took the role. He played Robert Aske in The Tudors and was decapitated by William Wallace in Braveheart. And millions know him as Father Todd Unctious in the Father Ted Christmas special — the priest who turns up uninvited and won't leave. He spent much of his early career at the Abbey Theatre and created Michael Evans in the original West End and Broadway productions of Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa.

programme.title: Family Life
programme.desc:
"Family Life" opens the way most Coronet council-of-family films do: with everybody a little frayed. The Miller household is a small chaos of overlapping errands — grocery bags fought over on the front step, a stalled car raising its hood in the driveway while father, mother, and their two teenagers crowd around it, a run out and back that solves nothing. Cut inside, and it's the mother who is left holding the kitchen together while the rest of the family goes its separate, quietly resentful ways. She decides the house needs running "like a business," and gathers everyone around the dinner table to lay out the plan on an actual placard: Guides to Home Management — Schedule, Responsibilities, Privileges, Finances. Chores get assigned (the daughter at the sink, the son drying and putting away), a weekly family council is scheduled to keep everyone honest, and by the last reel the Millers are eating together, laughing, and heading out the door as a unit — teenage son Harold, whose deadpan asides are the film's one real comic asset, getting the best lines along the way.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' Glenview, Illinois studio and copyrighted in 1949 to David A. Smart, the picture follows the house formula down to the credit block: the only person named on screen is the academic backing the script, here Florence M. King, M.S., Assistant Professor of Home Economics at the University of Illinois, billed as "Educational Collaborator." No director, writer, or performer receives a card — Coronet's postwar shorts routinely credited the consulting expert and nobody else, a practice meant to sell the film to school boards as sound applied psychology rather than as entertainment. The print carries the RCA Sound System mark seen on Coronet's 16mm classroom prints of the period and runs a lean nine minutes and forty-six seconds, per the Prelinger Archives' own cataloging of the surviving print.
"Family Life" belongs to the same wave of Coronet "systems" shorts that treated the household as a small enterprise to be managed with schedules and minutes, alongside titles like "Sharing Work at Home" and "Your Thrift Habits" — home economics extension thinking translated into 16mm melodrama for junior-high homerooms. It survives today through the Prelinger Archives and the Internet Archive, in the public domain like most of Coronet's late-1940s output, one of dozens of the studio's domestic-guidance shorts urging the same lesson: harmony at home is a matter of organization, not luck.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.sub-title: The Magic Roundabout (1965) - S02E097 - Let's Play At Cats

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Rocket
programme.desc: Krtek discovers a rocket abandoned on a children's playground and does what any reasonable mole would do — climbs in and launches it. The flight goes sideways almost immediately: the rocket crashes on a remote island, leaving Krtek stranded with the wreckage. Island animals help him piece it back together, and he flies home. Nine minutes of slapstick aeronautics, animated by Ota Kudrnáč, Bohumil Šejda, and Adolf Hamrlík, with a score by Milan Kymlička that replaced Vadim Petrov for this single outing. The episode gained an unlikely real-world sequel in May 2011, when astronaut Andrew Feustel — a NASA engineer with Czech roots — packed a plush Krtek in his personal kit aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour for mission STS-134 to the International Space Station. The toy had to meet full safety specs: lighter than a standard figurine, sewn from fireproof fabric, fitted with a velcro belt so it wouldn't float away in microgravity. Krtek celebrated his fifty-fifth birthday in orbit. He went up again in 2018, this time a smaller ten-centimetre version, spending 196 days and 18 hours in space — 3,152 orbits of the Earth. Distributed in the United States through Phoenix Films, Inc. as part of the Pennsylvania Public Libraries Film Center programme.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: Gumby encounters the Glob — an amorphous clay creature that can change shape at will. In a show made entirely of shapeable clay, a character whose defining trait is shapelessness is a sly joke about the medium itself. The Glob episodes play with the boundary between character and material in a way that anticipates decades of postmodern animation.

programme.title: The Writer
programme.desc:
A writer sits at his desk. Death arrives. What follows is a twelve-minute negotiation between creation and destruction, as the writer's stories come alive and intertwine with Death's attempts to claim him. The Dutch title — "De Schrijver en de Dood" — translates literally as "The Writer and the Death." Driessen's longest and most ambitious film to this point, using his split-screen technique to run the writer's inner life and outer reality simultaneously.
This was made after Driessen returned to Holland from a stint teaching at the University of Art Kassel. He split his career between Canada and the Netherlands for decades — "I've made many, many films at the Film Board and it's always really a nice environment for filmmakers like me to work. The Film Board is a good place for mixing with all the other animators also working on their own films, it's like a little family." But in Holland he would rent a room and work alone, which suited him just as well.

programme.title: Going Steady?
programme.desc:
Marie and Jeff are the couple everyone else has already decided is going steady — their friends assume it and their families discuss it, and the film opens by promising not to settle the question for either the characters or the audience. What follows plays out less as a story than as a string of conversations: Jeff works the question over by phone with a friend while his father hovers nearby waiting his turn to weigh in; Marie takes her own calls at home, then sits having her hair set by a girlfriend, turning the same question over out loud in front of a hand mirror; a parent on each side gets a scene alone with one of the teenagers, making a case neither Marie nor Jeff asked to hear. There is no crisis to resolve and no villain to blame, only the accumulating pressure of everyone around the two of them having an opinion about their relationship. The picture ends the way it began, on a title card handing the question back to the viewer: "What are the advantages -- and the disadvantages -- of going steady?"
Produced at Coronet's Glenview, Illinois plant and copyrighted MCMLI (1951) to Coronet founder David A. Smart, Going Steady? follows the studio's standard practice of naming only its academic consultant on screen: the title card credits Judson T. Landis, Ph.D., family sociologist at the University of California, Berkeley, whose survey work on adolescent courtship fed several Coronet scripts of the period. The Prelinger Archives catalog record for the surviving print — drawn from the production's own credit sheet rather than the screen titles — lists Gil Altschul as director, Hartley Pfeil as writer, Bruce Colling on camera, Ace Moore editing, and Sanford Singer in the role of Jeff. In place of a narrator, the film carries its exposition entirely on title cards, a structural choice the same catalog record notes explicitly.
Going steady itself was still a fairly new fixture of American high-school life in 1951, and a good deal of adult opinion regarded it warily, worried that pairing off early pushed teenagers toward premature marriage or worse. Coronet built much of its postwar catalog on that same anxiety, turning out dozens of comparable shorts on dating and getting along under its "social guidance" banner. Writing about the genre, film historian Ken Smith observed dryly that there would have been no need for these classroom mental-hygiene films at all if the young had actually behaved so pleasantly — and Going Steady? is typical of the type in refusing to resolve the argument it stages, closing on the same title card that opened it and leaving the discussion to the classroom rather than to the screenwriter.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
A passing remark from Florence about cats sets Dougal off into one of his contrary little disputes, which soon draws in the rest of the garden. Ermintrude pronounces cats jolly creatures, Brian declares he likes them, and when Florence mentions that cats climb trees the whole enterprise tips into action. Dougal and Ermintrude set about demonstrating their cat-like qualities up a small tree, watched by Florence and Brian, while Dylan drifts by only to announce that the very word "cats" makes him sleepy. The climbing becomes a contest; Ermintrude declares herself the winner and asks whether Dougal is wobbling — he insists he is perfectly stable, if a little sick. Asked how the two of them intend to get down again, they decide they will simply wait for autumn.
The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as Volume 2 by BBC Video in 1991.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Directed by Maria Muat using stop-motion puppet animation — and the Christian Science Monitor singled it out as the most enchanting of the series: "exquisitely crafted and articulated little puppets, shifted frame by frame in answer to scrupulous observation of human movement, give the action rare enchantment and wit."
Muat was born in Moscow in 1951 into a family of directors. Both her parents — Mariya Pavlovna Muat and Andrey Alexandrovich Muat — had studied under Maria Knebel, the legendary acting teacher who was herself a student of Stanislavski. Her father was the adoptive son of Boris Takke, a painter who had been the youngest participant in the 1910 "Jack of Diamonds" exhibition alongside Malevich, Kandinsky, and the Burliuk brothers — a key moment in Russian avant-garde history. Takke's work was then forgotten for decades, and Maria Muat would later spend eight years compiling an album to restore his reputation, calling it "a film on paper."
In 1975, Muat graduated from GITIS — the Russian Institute of Theatre Arts — from the workshop of Sergei Obraztsov. Obraztsov had founded the State Central Puppet Theatre in Moscow in 1931 and built it into the largest puppet theatre in the world, with over a thousand puppets in his personal collection. He essentially created the modern tradition of Soviet puppet art. Muat studied directly under him, then chose animation over live theatre.
She began at Multtelefilm in 1976 and debuted as director in 1979 with Uncle Au in the City. Moving to Soyuzmultfilm in 1988, she made The Loving Crow (1988) and Ancient Lyrics (1989) — lyrical puppet films that established her style. Twelfth Night was her international breakthrough. She later directed The Crown and the Scepter (1999) for another S4C series, and won the Nika Award — Russia's Oscar — for Snow Maiden (2006). In 2006 she co-founded Pchela Animation Studio with playwright Vladimir Golovanov, her husband and frequent collaborator, where she serves as artistic director. Over her career she has directed twenty-five puppet animated films. She holds the title Honoured Artist of the Russian Federation and is a Laureate and Academician of the Nika Academy.
Fiona Shaw voices Viola. Born Fiona Mary Wilson in Cobh, County Cork, Ireland — the daughter of a physicist and an ophthalmic surgeon — she trained at RADA, and on joining Equity discovered that a Fiona Wilson already existed. She took the name Shaw after her grandmother's maiden name and in tribute to George Bernard Shaw. By 1992 she had already won the Olivier Award for Best Actress for Electra (1990) and would win it again for Machinal (1994). She later played Richard II as a woman (1995), performed T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land as a solo show to astonished New York audiences, became Petunia Dursley in Harry Potter, Carolyn Martens in Killing Eve, and Maarva Andor in Star Wars: Andor. Her partnership with director Deborah Warner was described by the Daily Telegraph as "surely one of the most richly creative partnerships in theatrical history."
Hugh Grant voices Sebastian — Viola's twin. This was 1992, two years before Four Weddings and a Funeral would make him the most famous stammering Englishman on earth. He was still an indie and stage actor, best known for the Merchant Ivory film Maurice (1987).
Roger Allam voices Orsino. He originated the role of Inspector Javert in the first London production of Les Misérables (1985) — one of the most celebrated performances in West End history — and would later become beloved as Inspector Thursday in Endeavour, the Morse prequel. Two Olivier Awards. Born in Bow, East London, 1953.
This episode completes Series 1. The puppets were animated at Soyuzmultfilm's puppet department, the same tradition that produced Sokolov's Tempest and would later produce his Winter's Tale and The Miracle Maker. The comedy is harder to compress than the tragedies — Leon Garfield admitted the comedies were far more difficult to reduce — but Muat's puppet Malvolio, receiving his forged letter, is one of the series' most purely delightful sequences.

programme.title: Parents - Who Needs Them
programme.desc:
An ungrateful, sullen boy — alone in his room at night — flings his jester puppet to the floor in disgust. The puppet's grinning face comes eerily alive, and by the time the boy can see straight he has been rendered transparent: an invisible witness inside his own house. Trailing his mother down the hallway and through the kitchen, he watches her round of unglamorous chores — dishes, ironing, vacuuming, checking on him in the night — then follows his father through an equally unglamorous list: polishing the crystal chandelier, servicing the car in the driveway, sawing and mending furniture, tending the fish tank, working at the bench with a toolbox close at hand. It is a small, blunt reversal of the ordinary ghost story: instead of the dead observing the living, the ungrateful living observes what the living do for him without ever being seen doing it, and by the time his solidity returns, the boy has watched enough invisible labor to want back in.
Copyrighted MCMLXXIII to Coronet Instructional Materials, a division of Esquire, Inc., the film's own title card bills it as the "Second Edition of Appreciating Our Parents" — a refit of Coronet's 1950 short of the same message (directed there by Ted Peshak), trading that film's plainer before-and-after structure for the fantastical jester-puppet and invisible-boy device. As in the earlier picture, and per Coronet's long-standing house practice, no actor is named on screen; the only credit up front is the educational collaborator, Lucile Lindberg, Ed.D., Professor of Education at Queens College of the City University of New York. The end titles name the crew behind the camera: script by Larry Pont, direction by Dan McConnell, photography by Wayne A. Kolar, and editing by Paul K. Basten.
By 1973 Coronet's social-guidance genre — built in the postwar decades on films like Shy Guy and Are You Popular? — was well into a later, more theatrical phase, and this short shows the shift: the studio working the same appreciation-for-parents theme it had covered in 1950, but now reaching for a puppet-and-invisibility gimmick where the earlier film had simply set a boy's before against his after. It arrived only a handful of years before the 16mm classroom short gave way to videotape, one of the studio's last outings in the format it had spent nearly three decades supplying to American schools.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon goes to see Captain Large and his army. He also meets Bertie and Gertie, who have three wishes. On Button Moon, Captain Large orders the bottle army to build him a castle made out of pipes. This episode aired on 5 January 1981, crossing into the new year. The telescope story of the three wishes is one of the oldest folk tale structures in existence — it appears in cultures from Ireland to India to Japan, always with the same lesson: be careful what you wish for. Button Moon's retelling filtered it through kitchen-utensil characters, which somehow made the moral land differently than any illustrated storybook version. The pipe castle that Captain Large orders built is a perfect Button Moon detail — pipes are pipes, castles are castles, and no one questions why a bottle is commanding an army to build architecture out of plumbing.

programme.title: The Water People
programme.desc:
An ecological fable about water creatures whose world is gradually destroyed by pollution and human indifference. Driessen's longest film and one of his most narrative, running thirteen minutes with a clear environmental message underneath the signature wiggling-line absurdism.
Made after Driessen's return to the NFB's English animation studio in 1990, invited by producer Marcy Page. "All of a sudden, I was part of the English animation studio!" For his first two decades at the NFB he'd worked exclusively with the French studio — "a younger department, most of those films were non-narrative, based on expression and visual imagery which was much more interesting for me." The French studio had originally been seeded by Czech and French guest animators, while the English studio drew from the Zagreb school. By 1990 the two studios had begun to mix, sharing the same floor and technology.

programme.title: Hoppy the Bunny
programme.desc:
A teacher holds up a picture book to her class — "Once there was a little bunny" — and the film dissolves from the storybook page into a real rabbit in a real woods. Hoppy leaves his hollow tree on a fine morning, turns down breakfast with his neighbor Mr. Raccoon, and hops past a sleeping Mr. Owl and a favorite brook before wandering, without quite meaning to, out of the woods entirely and through a fence into a farm garden. He eats his fill of cabbage, carrot tops and green beans, tries to make friends with chickens too busy pecking to play, and gets laughed at by a fat white pig for worrying about overeating. Then he meets the farm's own rabbits, tame white bunnies living behind wire in houses the farmer built, fed daily by the farmer's children. Hoppy is tempted — no more foraging, no more danger — until the tame bunny tells him the trade: move in, and he can never again run loose in the woods with his friends. A bark from the farm dog, Rover, settles the question; Hoppy bolts for the garden gate and retraces his path home past the brook, the sleeping owl and Mr. Raccoon, glad of his adventure but gladder to be back in his own tree. The film closes on the same classroom, the children's own crayon drawings of Hoppy's day pinned up, and the teacher inviting them to say which part they liked best.
The short belongs to Coronet Instructional Films' "Background for Reading and Expression" line, a primary-grade companion series meant to be paired with a classroom read-aloud rather than a straight social-guidance lesson for teenagers. Its copyright, dated MCMLIII (1953), is held in the name of John Smart, who took over Coronet's Chicago-area operation with Jack Abraham after founder David Smart's death the previous year. As with Coronet's better-known guidance shorts, the only person credited on screen is the academic consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Ralph C. Preston, Ph.D., Associate Professor of Education at the University of Pennsylvania, with sound by the RCA Sound System. No director or cast is credited on this print, and unlike the studio's Ted Peshak-directed teenage dramas, "Hoppy the Bunny" is built almost entirely from nature footage of an unidentified live rabbit set against a storybook narration track, closer in kind to a classroom nature film than to a scripted guidance playlet.
Little has been written about the short beyond the archival record: it survives through the Prelinger Archives and has circulated among 16mm collectors via A/V Geeks, with no evidence of a theatrical or broadcast life of its own, and the print examined here carries a distribution stamp from the State of Georgia Department of Education Film Library, one of the many state and county film libraries that kept Coronet's catalog moving through classrooms long after initial release. It has no listing under its own title on IMDb. Its interest today is modest and specific: a small, unglamorous artifact of how mid-century reading instruction tried to marry a picture book to a nature film, using a tame-versus-wild rabbit's day to make an argument, gently, for the value of home.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence asks Zebedee what he has in mind for the day, and Zebedee announces he wants a photograph of everyone — cryptically adding that he'd like it "just in case", without saying just in case of what. Down in the garden, Dougal happens to have his camera and recruits a barely-containable Brian as his assistant. Mr Rusty is enthusiastic about the idea for the same unspecified reason, while Dylan is enjoying the rare peace and quiet before Ermintrude cheerfully warns him it won't last. Once the whole gang assembles, Florence asks where the birdie is — the traditional lure used to coax subjects to smile — and it turns out a small bird has been living inside the camera all along. It promptly flies away, leaving Mr Rusty fearing that without a photograph, prosperity will forget they ever existed. Brian solemnly announces he may cry.
A later version of this episode, narrated by Jimmy Hibbert, was combined with "School for Birds". This was the 100th and final episode of the series to be broadcast in the UK with Eric Thompson's narration.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
The Christian Science Monitor called this "the triumph of the series" and "a masterpiece" — "truly like watching moving pictures, a richly graphic rendering, in stony gothic settings, of a dark, dream-laden, haunted play." The critic compared it to watching "a kinetic unfolding of the Hamlet story etched by Rembrandt." It won two Emmy Awards in 1993.
Directed by Natalya Orlova using paint-on-glass animation — a technique so laborious that each frame is a complete painting, with figures adjusted by wiping and repainting directly on the glass surface, the background filled in anew each time. Nothing is saved between frames; every image exists only for the instant of its photography before being partially destroyed to create the next. Before Hamlet, the longest paint-on-glass film ever made in Russia was by the same director — a Chekhov adaptation that ran barely ten minutes.
Orlova was born May 12, 1948, and became one of the rare practitioners of this vanishing technique. For Hamlet she worked primarily in etching ink, creating a shadowy, tonal world close to actual etching in appearance, with color brought in for expressive suffusion of mysterious light. The movements have a different quality from cel animation — they rarely let you forget you are watching something painted. But as the Monitor's critic wrote, "Shakespeare is not lost. The medium serves the drama."
The paint-on-glass technique was virtually unpracticed in the West when Orlova made Hamlet. Its most famous practitioner, Alexander Petrov, would win the Academy Award in 2000 for The Old Man and the Sea — but Orlova was working in the medium years before Petrov's international breakthrough. After the Shakespeare series, she continued with paint-on-glass for Animated Epics: Moby Dick (1999) — with Rod Steiger voicing Captain Ahab in what would be one of his final roles — and Kashtanka (2004), a Chekhov adaptation. She also directed Richard III for Series 2 of this series, again in paint-on-glass.
Tilda Swinton voices Ophelia. This recording sits at the exact fulcrum of Swinton's career — between Edward II (1991), for which she won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress at Venice as Derek Jarman's muse, and Orlando (1992), the Virginia Woolf adaptation that announced her to the world. She was the daughter of Major-General Sir John Swinton, educated at West Heath school alongside Princess Diana, then Cambridge. She would go on to win the Academy Award for Michael Clayton (2007) and become one of the most singular presences in cinema — the White Witch in Narnia, the Ancient One in Doctor Strange, three characters simultaneously in Suspiria.
Nicholas Farrell voices Hamlet. He had already appeared in Chariots of Fire (1981) and would later play Horatio — Hamlet's best friend — in Kenneth Branagh's full-length Hamlet (1996). He went from voicing the prince to standing beside him. He also appears in The Iron Lady (2011) and Amazing Grace (2006).
The music was composed by Yuri Novikov, and the production design creates a world of stone corridors, candlelight, and creeping shadows that makes Elsinore feel less like a castle than a skull.

programme.title: One More Year on the Family Farm?
programme.desc:
"One More Year on the Family Farm?" opens on the shot it will return to at the end: an aerial pass over a two-lane road threading a green valley down past a cluster of barns and silos. Rather than following one family through a plot, the film is built as an issue-documentary — an entry in Coronet's Changing Scene Series — that lets members of two real dairy-farming households speak for themselves about whether to keep at it. One farm has modernized: cows stand in row after row of freestall housing, a milking parlor is threaded with steel line, and a bulk tanker truck idles in the yard, while a young man in glasses works through figures at an office desk rather than working a field. The other keeps to older ways — a man in a stocking cap forks manure out of a wood-sided barn by hand, walks cattle single file up a hillside pasture, and turns a narrow furrow behind a small tractor. Interspersed are direct-to-camera moments with the people themselves — an older farmer, a young woman, the men in caps and glasses — weighing the debt, the machinery, the hours, and the pull of a life some were born into and some are choosing to leave. The film never resolves which choice is right; it ends where it began, looking down at the valley from the air.
The on-screen credit is unusually specific for a Coronet short. Following the title card and its tag "(The Changing Scene Series)," a further title reads "©1977 Coronet Instructional Media, a division of Esquire, Inc." Two consultants are named — Content Consultant Jack L. Nelson, Ed.D., Professor of Education at Rutgers University, and Classroom Consultant William B. Stanley, Teacher of Social Studies at Cranford Senior High School in Cranford, New Jersey — followed by the studio's standard closing notice, "This film may not be copied or televised without written permission." As with Coronet's classic postwar shorts, no director, writer, or on-camera participant is credited; the film speaks in the voice of its consultants rather than its filmmakers.
The title card's own series tag marks this as part of a later, more issue-driven strand of the Coronet catalog, trading the scripted teenage leads of the studio's postwar shorts for real adults talking about their own livelihoods. The print survives today through the Internet Archive's educational-film holdings, part of the same circle of ephemeral prints preserved and scanned by collectors such as A.V. Geeks, and is cataloged there under a copyright still held by Phoenix Learning Group, Inc., the successor distributor of the Coronet library.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Transistor Radio
programme.desc: Krtek emerges one morning into his forest clearing — birdsong, bees drifting between flowers, the usual peace — and trips over an abandoned transistor radio. After fumbling with the dials he tunes into a football match, then weather reports, then music, and cannot stop. He plays it through the night, dancing and cheering alone while every creature in the forest packs up and leaves. When the batteries finally die the next day, Krtek tries to nurse the radio back to health with medicine and a woollen scarf, but nothing works. He kicks it, buries it in a little grave, and weeps. Only then do the animals creep back, and the forest sounds return. Written by Ivan Klíma and Zdeněk Miler, this is one of the rare Krtek episodes with actual spoken Czech — a radio announcer delivers weather forecasts and football commentary (voiced, according to Czech viewers, in the style of beloved broadcaster "strýček" Jedlička). The episode aired as part of Večerníček, the nightly children's programme that shaped generations of Czech childhoods.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: Mr. Spoon sees the stars playing a game. He also sees two strange birds and a camel who help to bring happiness to a sad princess. This is the halfway point of Series 1, airing 12 January 1981. The telescope story features storks — a departure from the Aesop and Grimm retellings of earlier episodes toward more original storytelling. The sad princess cheered by animals is a fairy tale archetype, but Button Moon's version was built from pipe cleaners and cotton wool rather than illustration. By this point Thames Television knew they had a hit. The show's ITV broadcast slot was attracting strong numbers for a ten-minute children's programme, and planning for Series 2 was already underway. The format — journey, adventure, telescope story, journey home — was proving infinitely flexible. Any story could be told through that telescope.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
On his way through the toyshop, Gumby passes several mirrors and loses a coin. Hunting for it inside the mirrors, he meets his own reflection — who tells him the only way to find the coin is to do everything backwards. Gumby eventually manages this and the hunt ends successfully.
An early showcase for the "walking into books and worlds" concept that would define Gumby. The episode demonstrates Clokey's willingness to play with spatial logic and visual paradox — Gumby doesn't just look in mirrors, he enters them. The backwards-logic puzzle inside the mirror is pure Vorkapich-influenced filmmaking: using the medium's ability to reverse and reorient motion as a narrative device rather than a trick. The toyshop, which would recur throughout the series as Gumby's gateway to adventures, was part of Clokey's intuition that play itself is a portal.

programme.title: Good Eating Habits
programme.desc:
Bill is always in a hurry. He bolts his breakfast, wolfs down his lunch, and grabs candy and soda between errands and after-school projects — a half-built radio here, a toy racetrack there — instead of sitting still for a proper meal. By dinner his stomach aches, and flashbacks lay out exactly the day that got him there: the rushed table, the gulped drink, the food eaten on the move. Sent to bed sick, he slides into a feverish nightmare of tumbling food and bursting light, his mother sitting up with him through the night. The morning after, the household models the corrected version of the same routine — juice sipped instead of gulped, food chewed slowly, breakfast eaten sitting down with the family — and Bill, pale but recovering, eats his way back to being not just well-fed but well-nourished.
The picture is a Coronet Instructional Films release, copyrighted in 1951 to David A. Smart, the Esquire publisher whose Chicago-area studio also put out a second magazine called Coronet that gave the film company its name. As with the rest of Coronet's postwar guidance line, the only credits on screen belong to the outside experts who vetted the material, not to any writer or director: educational collaborator Clifford J. Barborka, M.D., associate professor of medicine at Northwestern University Medical School, and special consultant James R. Wilson, M.D., secretary of the American Medical Association's Council on Foods and Nutrition and formerly associate professor of pediatrics at Syracuse University. The soundtrack carries the RCA Sound System credit standard on Coronet's 16mm classroom prints of the era.
Prelinger Archives, which preserves the film, catalogs it as a drama of "gluttony and hidden hunger" — the paradox, common to Coronet's health shorts, of a child who eats plenty yet malnourishes himself through bad choices and worse timing. The narration is voiced by James Andelin, a Chicago-based radio, television, and industrial-film performer; no director is credited on the print or corroborated in any outside record, in keeping with a house style that put the consulting physicians' names above any filmmaker's. It circulated to health classrooms through the 1950s and survives today through the Internet Archive's Prelinger collection.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal has decided to stand for parliament and is utterly convinced the electorate will vote for him. He plasters the garden with pictures of himself and races about in his car telling Mr Rusty of his plans, too busy to stop for anyone. Florence, fresh from having her hair done, finds Brian clinging to a tree after several near-misses with the campaigning dog; Brian compliments her new look before both agree that Dougal has gone quite dotty. The real blow comes when Dougal discovers that nearly every portrait of himself has been swapped out for a beaming likeness of Ermintrude, who has the full backing of the railway workers and the Train. Dougal confronts Brian up his tree with barely veiled menace, demanding his vote. Florence, more graciously, promises hers and hands over some sugar. Restored to his usual pomposity, Dougal delivers his parliamentary speech — and Brian concedes, drily, that the dog will go far.
This episode opens Series 3 and introduces a notable visual change: Florence sports a new, longer hairstyle, which Eric Thompson worked into the English script as something she cheerfully mentions herself.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Directed by Yefim Gamburg, a WWII veteran turned animation satirist who made this episode not at Soyuzmultfilm but at his own studio — the only director in the series to work independently.
Gamburg was born in Moscow in 1925 into a Jewish family. At seventeen he went to war, serving as a private and motorcyclist in the trophy brigade of the 39th Army — a unit tasked with capturing enemy military technology. He was wounded in action and awarded the Order of the Red Star in 1945. After the war he studied at the Art faculty of the Lenin Moscow State Pedagogical University, joined Soyuzmultfilm in 1955, and began directing in 1964.
He became one of the first Soviet directors to make animated parody films. Passion of Spies (1967) spoofed the spy genre; Robbery, ... Style (1978) sent up heist movies; Dog in Boots (1981) parodied Westerns. His 1976 musical Blue Puppy — about an outcast puppy whose blue color makes him different — used an innovative technique of drawing characters with spots of colored India ink, allowing for fluid shapeshifting effects. The songs were performed by Alisa Freindlich, Andrei Mironov, and Mikhail Boyarsky, three of the biggest names in Soviet stage and screen.
In 1989, he directed what may be the most symbolically significant cartoon in Cold War history: Stereotypes, the first-ever Soviet-American animated co-production, made with Laurien Productions of California. It ridiculed the mutual caricatures Americans and Russians held of each other — and it was made the same year the Berlin Wall fell.
By 1990, Gamburg had founded his own studio, Gamburgskiy Schot (renamed Renechans in 1991), and it was there — not at Soyuzmultfilm — that he animated Romeo and Juliet. The cel animation has a looser, more expressive quality than the Moscow studio house style, fitting for a man who'd spent his career puncturing conventions.
Felicity Kendal narrates — Britain's sweetheart from The Good Life (1975–78), the BBC sitcom about suburban self-sufficiency that made her a national treasure. Linus Roache voices Romeo. Roache is the son of William Roache, who has played Ken Barlow on Coronation Street continuously since the show's first episode in 1960 — the longest-serving actor in any television soap opera in history. Linus would go on to star in Antonia Bird's Priest (1994), play Thomas Wayne in Batman Begins (2005), and lead Law and Order (2008–10). Clare Holman plays Juliet; she would later become known for Inspector Lewis on ITV.
Gamburg died in Moscow in 2000 at seventy-five, three days after his birthday. His last film, an adaptation of Mikhail Bulgakov's The Fatal Eggs, was completed by his crew in 2003 and released posthumously. He is buried at the Donskoye Cemetery.

programme.title: Ways to Settle Disputes
programme.desc:
Two boys in a quiet suburban front yard come to blows over whose turn it is on the tricycle, and a knot of neighborhood kids pulls them apart — the film's first lesson, illustrated with a simple chalkboard-style cartoon of two riders sharing one trike, is COMPROMISE. From there the film moves to the schoolyard, where a shoving match breaks out during a pickup ballgame; the animated card this time reads OBEY THE RULES, with a batter squaring up beneath the words. Indoors, the same children — the film follows three of them by name, Alice, Jerry, and Eddie — argue over a mislaid notebook at their desks, settled once a teacher walks them through FIND THE FACTS. The last dispute is a classroom election for playground representative: the candidates' names go up on the blackboard with a tally beside them, and the lesson this time is FIND OPINIONS, weighing what classmates actually think rather than assuming it.
Coronet Instructional Films produced the short at its own studio outside Chicago, in the same house style as its other social-guidance shorts of the period. The only credit on screen, after the copyright card for company principal David A. Smart, is the educational collaborator: Carter Davidson, Ph.D., identified as President of Union College and Chancellor of Union University. Davidson was, in fact, president of Union College in Schenectady, New York, from 1946 to 1965, having previously spent a decade as president of Knox College in Illinois — a genuine academic credential lent to the studio's classroom-conduct pictures, in keeping with Coronet's practice of pairing its writer-director staff with an outside consultant's name for the title card.
"Ways to Settle Disputes" belongs to the wave of postwar Coronet social-guidance shorts distributed to schools on 16mm reels, teaching a single practical procedure — compromise, rule-following, fact-finding, opinion-gathering — through small, staged neighborhood and classroom conflicts rather than a single continuous story. Like most of Coronet's output from this period, the print carries no other on-screen cast credit; the child performers playing Alice, Jerry, and Eddie go unnamed. It has since passed into the public domain and circulates through the Prelinger Archives and the Internet Archive as an artifact of American classroom media, catalogued there by its Coronet reel description.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
King Leontes of Sicilia, consumed by sudden and baseless jealousy, destroys his family: he imprisons his pregnant wife Hermione, orders his infant daughter Perdita abandoned on a foreign shore, and drives his best friend Polixenes into flight. Hermione dies — or appears to. Sixteen years pass. The abandoned daughter, raised by shepherds in Bohemia, falls in love with Polixenes' son. When the lovers flee to Sicilia, Leontes is confronted with everything he lost. In the final scene, a statue of Hermione comes to life. It is Shakespeare's most beautiful miracle: the dead wife steps down from her pedestal and takes her husband's hand, and the only explanation offered is time and faith.
Directed by Stanislav Sokolov in stop-motion puppet animation, his second and final contribution to the series after The Tempest. Born in Moscow in 1947, Sokolov studied under Ivan Ivanov-Vano at VGIK — the grand master of Soviet animation — and joined Soyuzmultfilm in 1973. His directorial debut was Dogada in 1977. He worked at DEFA in East Germany and then at Christmas Films in Moscow, where his puppet work reached its fullest expression. Soviet censors had rejected his proposed Hoffmann adaptations as "too scary for children and too mystical for adults." He spent seventeen years making them anyway: Hoffmaniada, released in 2018, is a stop-motion feature that combines the biographical reality of E.T.A. Hoffmann — the office clerk who looked at his colleagues' noses and saw a mouse kingdom under their desks — with the fantasies he wrote. Between Hoffmann and Shakespeare, Sokolov also co-directed The Miracle Maker (2000) with Derek Hayes, a puppet-animated life of Jesus voiced by Ralph Fiennes. He won an Emmy for this Winter's Tale in 1996, and another for his contribution to the series as a whole in 1992. VGIK Professor, founding the Animation and Computer Graphics department in 1995. Honored Artist of Russia. He also made interfaith prayer films — Our Father (2001) and Shma Israel (2003) — puppet animation in service of the sacred.
Anton Lesser voices Leontes. Born in Birmingham on 14 February 1952, the son of David Lesser and Amelia Cohen, from a Jewish family. He earned a degree in architecture from the University of Liverpool in 1973 — he could have designed buildings — and then enrolled at RADA, where he won the Bancroft Gold Medal as the most promising actor of his year.
