The RSC spotted him immediately. As an associate artist, he played Romeo, Hamlet, Troilus, Petruchio, Brutus, Henry Bolingbroke, and Richard III. In 2006, twelve years after voicing Leontes in this animation, he returned to the role on stage at the RSC — one of the rare actors to inhabit the same Shakespeare character in both media across a career.
He was Troilus, Edgar, and Feste in the BBC Television Shakespeare. Thomas More in Wolf Hall (BAFTA nomination). Harold Macmillan in The Crown. Chief Superintendent Bright in Endeavour. Major Lio Partagaz in Andor — the ISB officer who delivered dialogue on Imperial bureaucracy with what Digital Spy called "powerful coolness." And Qyburn in Game of Thrones — Cersei's mad scientist, the last curious man in Westeros, whose abrupt death in the penultimate episode became a meme. His audiobook recordings of Dickens, Milton's Paradise Lost, Homer, and Rumi form a library in themselves; his Great Expectations won a Talkie Award. He has been cast as Garrick Ollivander in the upcoming Harry Potter television series.
Jenny Agutter voices Hermione. Born Jennifer Ann Agutter on 20 December 1952 in Taunton, Somerset — the same birth year as Lesser, two actors who grew up in different Englands meeting in animation's afterlife. Her father Derek was an entertainments manager in the British Army, so she spent her childhood in Singapore, Cyprus, and Kuala Lumpur before being sent to Elmhurst Ballet School at eight. She left school at sixteen to star in The Railway Children.
That film defined a generation's childhood — and then defined Agutter's career. She played Bobbie Waterbury in the 1970 Lionel Jeffries film, played the mother in the 2000 television version, and in 2022, at age sixty-nine, reprised her original role in The Railway Children Return — the same character, fifty-two years later. No other actor has played both child and elderly version of the same beloved role across half a century of British cinema.
At eighteen she starred in Nicolas Roeg's Walkabout, lost in the Australian outback. At nineteen, she won an Emmy for The Snow Goose opposite Richard Harris. At twenty-three she was Jessica 6 in Logan's Run, running from death in a world that kills you at thirty. She won the BAFTA for Equus. She survived the werewolf in An American Werewolf in London. She joined the World Security Council in The Avengers and Captain America: The Winter Soldier — the woman who sits in judgment of superheroes. Since 2012, she has played Sister Julienne in Call the Midwife. OBE for her charitable work with the Cystic Fibrosis Trust — two of her siblings died of the disease, and her niece carries it. She is a patron of the Shakespeare Schools Festival, the charity that puts school children on professional stages to perform Shakespeare. A fitting connection for the actress who closes this series.
Her husband Johan Tham, a Swedish hotelier she met at a Bath arts festival in 1989, died in 2025. Their son Jonathan was born on Christmas Day 1990 and became a physician.

programme.title: Are You Ready For Marriage
programme.desc:
Larry and Sue are a young couple who have all but decided to elope, since Sue's parents object to the match. Before they run off, they agree to talk it over with Mr. Hall, the marriage counselor at their church. Sitting across the desk from him, the two realize how little they actually know about each other, and Mr. Hall walks them through what he calls Cupid's Checklist: do they come from similar backgrounds, are they real friends, do they understand what marriage actually involves? He illustrates the point with props straight out of a classroom — a board of tiny wooden figures wired together at different "psychological distances," and a hand-drawn curve charting a couple's chance for happiness against how long they've been engaged and how old the groom is when he marries. By the end, Larry and Sue haven't been told no; they've just been shown how much groundwork a lasting marriage takes; the film closes on the two of them, warmer with each other than when they walked in.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films and directed by Gil Altschul, with camera work by Bruce Colling, script by Chuck Probst and Harriette Smith, and editing by George Wilbern. As with other Coronet guidance shorts, the only credential named on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: the title card introduces Reuben Hill, Ph.D., Research Professor in Family Life at the University of North Carolina, who also appears in the film itself playing the counselor, Mr. Hall. Hill was a genuine pioneer of family-life research — long affiliated with the National Council on Family Relations — and the checklist-and-chart approach on screen is a fairly direct translation of his academic work on courtship and marital readiness into a classroom short.
The trade press noticed the effort: Educational Screen's September 1950 review praised the picture for avoiding "stereotyped characters, stale and trite expressions" and judged it well suited to high-school counseling, in group settings or one-on-one. The Coronet catalog framed the film's purpose bluntly, as an attempt to stem what it called the postwar "epidemic of youthful, impetuous, and unsuccessful marriages." Whatever its era-bound charts and lapels look like now, the short is of a piece with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance line: a real family sociologist's checklist, dressed up as a date-night crisis, aimed squarely at the study hall.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal has grand ambitions: he is making a film — "Treasure Island", no less, shot in his own proprietary "Dougal-Vision" format — and he has press-ganged Brian into service as a very reluctant cameraman. Florence is cast as the star, but the production quickly unravels. Dylan wanders into the middle of a take, Ermintrude crashes the scene in Indian feathers convinced she is now a movie star, and Brian flatly refuses to film either sharks or man-eating butterflies. Florence and Ermintrude do eventually unearth a genuine treasure chest, which turns out to contain a large lump of sugar — filmed by nobody, because the camera was pointing the wrong way. Zebedee arrives hoping for a part, but Dougal has lost all enthusiasm for cinema and decides he would rather go to the pictures instead.
Dougal name-drops Ken Russell and Sergei Eisenstein at different points in the episode; Brian's reverent cry of "Antonioni Oni Oni" is a nod to Italian director Michelangelo Antonioni. The "Dougal-Vision" format parodies Paramount's VistaVision widescreen process of 1954. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as Volume 1 in 1984 and reissued in 1989 and 1992, then compiled on The Very Best of the Magic Roundabout in 1993 under the retitled name "Dougal - Film Director".

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal has decided to move his caravan, a plan that immediately goes wrong when he discovers he left the car keys inside it. Unable to get through the door, he climbs a ladder to the window, falls off, climbs back up, and finally tumbles inside — only for the caravan to start swaying alarmingly under his weight. Meanwhile, Florence waits on the roundabout for Zebedee, who arrives with a transparently flimsy excuse about traffic. Back in the garden, Dougal ropes the caravan down, retrieves his keys, and scrambles onto the roof before dropping into the car. When the car won't budge, Ermintrude cheerfully offers to push — then headbutts the front, sending Dougal and the caravan rocketing backwards into a rock. The wheels fly off into the flower beds. Dougal declares he'll stay exactly where he is, rejects a second offer of Ermintrude's assistance with considerable feeling, and eventually gets the car moving on its own. Florence arrives, Brian turns up to announce the stricken, wheel-less caravan is sitting in the greenbelt, and Dougal invites Florence in for a cup of tea.
The Eric Thompson narration of this episode was released on VHS as Volume 1 in 1984 (reissued in 1989 and 1992) under the title "The Caravan".

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: From the later syndication run, after production had paused for several years. By 1965, the show had been off the air since 1960 and Clokey returned to produce new episodes. The animation style had evolved — the sets were more detailed, the movements smoother, but the fundamental approach remained: clay figures on tabletop sets, one frame at a time, filmed in Glendora. The title is a neat double meaning: Gumby making geometric shapes, and a quiet joke about squareness itself in the mid-sixties.

programme.title: Noggin the Nog: Noggin and the Pie
programme.desc:
It is NogFest in the Northlands, and the centerpiece is to be a pie — an enormous one, hauled through the streets on a cart, big enough to feed the whole kingdom. Prince Knut, Noggin and Nooka's son, gets tangled up in the great pie's fortunes, and Nogbad the Bad, never far from anything valuable or edible, sees his chance. It ends, as the frames attest, with a pie floating in the castle moat, which is the sort of ending Noggin stories are unafraid of.
The story began as one of Oliver Postgate and Peter Firmin's Noggin picture books, published in 1971, and came to television as a new two-part story in colour when Smallfilms revived the series around the turn of the 1980s — the only fresh Noggin tale of the revival, alongside the colour remake of the Ice Dragon saga. This print presents the two parts as one continuous short. The colour work shows Firmin's later palette: the same pen line the series had carried since 1959, now over warm washes of gold and green, the characters' faces still recognizably descended from the Lewis chessmen that started it all.
Vernon Elliott's bassoon score and the narration of Postgate and Ronnie Stevens carry the tale, as they carried every tale of the Northlands. Dating the piece is its own small saga: sources variously file the television version under 1979, 1980, and 1982, the revival having been made and broadcast across those years — the book's 1971 date sometimes muddles catalogs further. What is not in dispute is that it was the Nogs' last new story, the final tale the Men of the Northlands told around their great log fires.

programme.title: How Do You Know It's Love?
programme.desc:
Nora is on the phone in her bedroom, turning over the same argument she's had all evening: this time, with Jack, it really is love. Her mother — reprising, almost word for word, the counsel Coronet had already handed down in Are You Ready for Marriage? — reminds her that conviction alone proves nothing, that most people fall in love more than once, and sometimes with more than one person at a time. Nora keeps seeing Jack anyway, and the two of them double-date with Jack's older brother Bob and Bob's fiancée Jean, out for dinner and back afterward to look through a photo scrapbook, where a joke snapshot turns up captioned "Whoops, caught you!!!" — a gag that only sharpens the contrast next to it. Measured against Bob and Jean, who share real interests, feel at ease together, take pride in each other, and have already worked out where they stand on religion, children and money, Nora's feeling for Jack starts to look more like a crush than the real thing. Common sense wins out, and, in the genre's usual fashion, everyone ends up happy.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films — copyright MCML under founder David A. Smart — and recorded on the RCA Sound System, the print carries a single credit: educational collaborator Reuben Hill, Ph.D., identified on the title card as a research professor in family life at the University of North Carolina, whose research on courtship and marital adjustment underlies the film's four-question test for "mature love." No director is named on screen; Letterboxd's listing for this specific title credits Ted Peshak, the house director behind most of Coronet's postwar guidance catalog, though the print itself is silent on the point.
Ken Smith, whose shot-list notes for the Prelinger Archives accompany the Internet Archive print, calls out the film as one of the few Coronet productions to carry a recurring background theme — a "wistful" musical cue used as a bridge between scenes — and rates it a film that "grows on you," a rare compliment inside a genre built mostly on cautionary conformity. It has circulated since as public-domain classroom ephemera through the Prelinger Collection, one of dozens of Coronet social-guidance shorts preserved there alongside it.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Directed by Stanislav Sokolov, the master Russian puppet animator who would go on to co-direct The Miracle Maker (2000, with Ralph Fiennes as Jesus) and spend seventeen years creating his magnum opus Hoffmaniada (2018). Designed by Elena Livanova, who would partner with Sokolov again for The Winter's Tale in Series 2.
Sokolov was born in Moscow in 1947 and studied at VGIK under Ivan Ivanov-Vano, a founding figure of Soviet animation. After military service, he joined Soyuzmultfilm in 1973 and made his directorial debut with The Guess (1977), a stop-motion folklore short. In the 1980s he crossed the Iron Curtain to work at DEFA-Trikfilm in East Germany — an unusual move that foreshadowed his later international collaborations. For years he had wanted to adapt E.T.A. Hoffmann's tales, but Soviet censors rejected the idea as "too scary for children and too mystical for adults." He finally got to make Hoffmaniada decades later, at Soyuzmultfilm, backed by the painter Mikhail Shemyakin — it took from 2001 to 2018.
The Tempest uses stop-motion puppet animation, the technique Sokolov would use for all his Shakespeare work. His approach was to differentiate human and supernatural elements through contrasting puppet styles — Prospero's weathered, heavy-browed face against Ariel's ethereal lightness. The island's isolation comes through atmospheric camera movements and textured miniature sets.
Between his two Shakespeare episodes, Sokolov also made an extraordinary series of interfaith prayer shorts — Our Father (Christian, 2000), Al-Fatihah (Muslim, 2001), and Shma Israel (Jewish, 2003) — three animated meditations on the opening prayers of three Abrahamic faiths. He has been a professor at VGIK since 1985 and in 1995 founded the Department of Animation and Computer Graphics, where he continues to teach.
Timothy West — one of the great British classical actors, married to Prunella Scales (Sybil in Fawlty Towers) — voices Prospero with the weight of a man who has spent twelve years on an island rehearsing his revenge and his forgiveness simultaneously. Alun Armstrong, who would become one of the most recognizable character actors in British film and television (Les Misérables, Braveheart, The Mummy Returns), plays Caliban. Martin Jarvis, celebrated as perhaps the finest audiobook narrator in the English language, provides the narration. The cast includes Ella Mood as Ariel, Katy Behean as Miranda, and Stephen Thorne as Stephano.
His Winter's Tale, also puppet animation with Livanova, would win the Emmy for Outstanding Individual Achievement in Animation in 1996.

programme.title: Spiegeleiland
programme.desc:
The Dutch title means "Mirror Island" but it's also a pun — "spiegelei" means "fried egg" in Dutch, so the title simultaneously reads as "Fried Egg Land." A tiny island where everything is reflected, doubled, and slightly wrong.
Made during the period when Driessen was teaching animation at the University of Art Kassel in Germany, succeeding the great Polish animator Jan Lenica. Two of Driessen's Kassel students went on to win Academy Awards: Christoph and Wolfgang Lauenstein for Balance (1989) and Thomas Stellmach and Tyron Montgomery for Quest (1998). Driessen himself would receive an Oscar nomination for 3 Misses in 1999.

programme.title: The Fun of Being Thoughtful
programme.desc:
Jane Proctor is a cheerful teenager who is, in archivist Ken Smith's later phrase, "slavishly devoted" to her family's happiness, and the film catalogues one evening of it: she tidies her room, helps get dinner on the table amid a bit of kitchen panic over the mashed potatoes, and — the plot's real engine — works to fix up her awkward brother Eddie with a date for the following night. Eddie, whose voice keeps threatening to crack, gripes along the way that he "hasn't a thing to wear" either. Jane's persistent thoughtfulness pays off in the last scene: she comes down the stairs in a new dress to her parents' and Eddie's evident delight, and the household settles back into its usual harmony.
Produced at Coronet's studio in Glenview, Illinois and copyrighted in 1950 (the title card reads MCML) by David A. Smart, who had founded the company with his brother Alfred as an offshoot of their Esquire magazine business. As with the rest of Coronet's postwar social-guidance catalog, the teenage cast goes uncredited; the only name in the titles belongs to the psychology consultant, credited on screen as Educational Collaborator Ernest M. Ligon, Ph.D., director of the Character Research Project at Union College in Schenectady, New York. Ligon had founded the Character Research Project in 1935 and would direct it for over four decades, building its work on ideas he had laid out in his earlier book The Psychology of Christian Personality. Directing credit likewise appears nowhere on screen, but Ted Peshak — the Glenview house director credited with roughly 350 educational films for Coronet — lists Fun of Being Thoughtful among his 1950 directing credits. The uncredited actor playing Eddie Proctor was a Coronet regular: a retrospective tracing faces across the studio's uncredited teen stock company notes that the same performer's voice had not yet finished cracking a year earlier in The Meaning of Pi (1949), and that he turns up again later in 1950 as Eddie in Developing Friendships and as Ed Parker in How to Get Cooperation.
The print survives through the Prelinger Archives on the Internet Archive, in the public domain along with the rest of that collection. Prelinger's cataloguer Ken Smith, whose notes on Coronet's output were later folded into his book Mental Hygiene: Better Living Through Classroom Films, 1945-1970, flagged the script's habit of chasing several morals inside ten minutes as "fun but a little hard to follow" — a fair description of a film that covers housework, dating, dress shopping, and hospitality all in one sitting. It belongs to the postwar "social guidance" genre Coronet all but defined for American classrooms, in which ordinary household courtesy is treated as a small-scale rehearsal for the larger civic virtues — responsibility, cooperation, good citizenship — that the studio's other shorts preached more directly.

programme.title: Noggin the Nog: Tales of the Northlands
programme.desc:
Two complete sagas on one tape, exactly as BBC Video released it in 1990. First, in colour, Noggin and the Ice Dragon: the Nogs' fire-squirting Firecake machine wakes Grolliffe, the great ice dragon, from his thousand-year sleep in the mountain, and Noggin must go up to face him — only to discover that a dragon, like most creatures in these stories, mainly wants to be understood. Then, in the original black and white, The Flying Machine: court inventor Olaf the Lofty attempts the impossible and builds a contraption that will carry a Nog through the air, with the mixed blessings of King Noggin and the active interference of gravity.
The pairing quietly tells the whole production history of the series. The Ice Dragon seen here is the colour remake from Smallfilms' 1979-80 revival, when Oliver Postgate and Peter Firmin returned to the Northlands two decades on and reshot the beloved saga with the same designs in paint and colour. The Flying Machine appears as it was made in the 1960s run — ink, wash, and Firmin's pen line, moved frame by frame under the rostrum camera at Smallfilms' Kent farm studio. Watching one after the other is a twenty-year time-lapse of the same two hands at work.
Both sagas carry the series' fixtures: Vernon Elliott's bassoon score, and narration by Postgate and Ronnie Stevens, who between them voice the whole court — Noggin, Queen Nooka, timid Captain Thor Nogson, Olaf the Lofty, Graculus the green bird, and the perpetually scheming Nogbad the Bad. The characters' faces descend from the Lewis chessmen in the British Museum, which Firmin had admired since 1952; the series they inspired first aired on the BBC in September 1959 and was still being repeated on Channel 4 in the mid-1990s, by which time the Nogs had passed into the permanent furniture of British childhood.

programme.title: How Quiet Helps at School
programme.desc:
The film opens in a school hallway lined with lockers, then pushes into a first-grade classroom where the ordinary business of the day — passing papers, moving chairs, calling out — plays as a small racket. Next door, under a teacher the narration calls Miss Bradley, the same tasks unfold in near-total silence: children whisper instead of talk, a boy sharpens a pencil and crosses the room to a supply closet without a sound, and the class works through an assignment while the wall clock ticks audibly in the quiet. Miss Bradley tells the room that keeping things this hushed is good practice because a classroom, like an office, runs better without noise, and that knowing when to be quiet is simply part of growing up. The film does not ask for silence everywhere — it closes on the same children loose and loud on the playground swings, the noise they were asked to hold indoors now given somewhere to go.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films on RCA's sound system and copyrighted MCMLIII to John Smart, the standard Coronet registration of the period. As with the studio's other social guidance shorts, the only credited collaborator on screen is the psychology consultant: the title card names Henry Bonner McDaniel, Ph.D., Professor of Education and Psychology at Stanford University. McDaniel was a real fixture of Stanford's education faculty in these years — Stanford's Graduate School of Education dates his work building out the university's guidance-counseling program to 1947–1968 — lending the film's classroom-management message the same applied-psychology backing Coronet leaned on across the genre. No director is credited on the print, and none is attested specifically for this title.
The film survives through the Prelinger Archives, whose catalog twice describes it in almost identical terms: a demonstration of "how a class can study and work better if the room is quiet," with noise given its proper place on the playground rather than banished outright. Later commentary on the Coronet social-guidance cycle has singled this one out as unusually serene even by the genre's own standards — one retrospective review calls the hushed classroom a room of "well-behaved, conscientious" children and notes the almost suspenseful quiet of watching a pupil cross the room without making a sound. Seen today, it reads less as an outlier than as a fairly ordinary specimen of the classroom-discipline instructionals Coronet turned out through the 1950s for use in American schools.

programme.title: Noggin the Nog: The Omruds and The Firecake
programme.desc:
Two complete black-and-white sagas from the mid-1960s, released together on tape by BBC Video in 1991. In The Omruds, strange tall figures appear in the Northlands and the Nogs must work out what they are and what they want — a story that turns, as Noggin stories reliably do, on talking to the stranger instead of fighting him. In The Firecake, court inventor Olaf the Lofty produces his most combustible creation, a cake that burns — to the fascination of the court, the alarm of Captain Thor Nogson, and the predictable acquisitive interest of Nogbad the Bad, who can smell an advantage from several fjords away.
These sagas come from the confident middle years of the original run, when Oliver Postgate and Peter Firmin had been telling stories of the Northlands since 1959 and the machinery of Smallfilms — Postgate writing, animating, and narrating; Firmin drawing everything; the pair working from Firmin's farm in Kent — was at full sail. The visual world is pure Firmin pen-and-wash, its faces still carrying their descent from the Lewis chessmen in the British Museum, the walrus-ivory Norsemen that had fascinated him since 1952.
Vernon Elliott's bassoon threads through everything, and Postgate splits the voices with Ronnie Stevens. The framing never changes: a tale the Men of the Northlands tell around their great log fires, in the dark night that is very long. It was a formula sturdy enough that the BBC kept the Nogs on air across two decades of repeats, Channel 4 revived them in the mid-1990s, and Smallfilms' next inventions — the Clangers among them, born from a Noggin story about a moon mouse — carried the house style to the moon.

programme.title: Am I Trustworthy?
programme.desc:
Eddie Johnson wants to be treasurer of his hobby club, and he's stung when the members nominate another boy instead and put him on the clean-up committee. He tells his father the other kids just don't like him, but his father redirects the question: trustworthy isn't the same thing as popular, it's whether people can count on you to do what you said you'd do. Pressed on it, Eddie has to admit the evidence is against him — a lamp he promised to fix sits forgotten in the corner, homework gets left to the last minute, a model kit lies half-built on the table. He draws up a chart to track himself against his word, then works through it scene by scene: fixing the lamp, finishing assignments on time, helping around the house and at the grocery store, and taking on a small job at the school library's book charge-out desk. By the end his kept promises have done what his campaign speech couldn't, and the treasurer's job he wanted looks within reach after all.
The only credit on screen, in keeping with Coronet's house practice of naming the classroom consultant rather than the filmmakers, is "Educational Collaborator Elizabeth B. Carey, Ph.D., Supervisor, Bureau of Instructional Supervision, The University of the State of New York," under a copyright dated MCML (1950) to Coronet's publisher, David A. Smart, with an RCA Sound System credit. A contemporary DVD review of the film corroborates that it was made for that same New York State office, meaning Carey's department was not just a lending credit but the body the film was produced to serve. No director is credited on the print, and none is reliably documented for this specific title elsewhere, so none is listed here.
"Am I Trustworthy?" belongs to the "social guidance" genre of postwar classroom shorts that Ken Smith catalogued in his 1999 book Mental Hygiene: Classroom Films 1945-1970, where he notes that trustworthiness in the film functions as something close to a synonym for obedience and conformity, and quotes its closing moral: "People have to show they can be trusted with little things if they want to be trusted with big things." A 16mm print was donated to the Internet Archive's Prelinger Collection in 2002 and remains in the public domain, and the film was later remastered for Kino Lorber's 2009 DVD anthology "How to Be a Man, Volume 1," drawn from Skip Elsheimer's A/V Geeks film library alongside eleven other classroom shorts of the era — a fairly ordinary, "stagey and confined" example of the genre, by one reviewer's account, but a representative one.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Green Star
programme.desc: Krtek finds a glowing green star lying in his meadow and decides it belongs back in the night sky. He enlists his woodland friends to help launch it upward, but nothing works — it is too high, and they are too small. A thieving magpie snatches the star and carries it to her nest. Krtek plants an acorn that sprouts into a towering oak in seconds, climbs to the nest, and retrieves the star — only to despair again, weeping, because he still cannot reach the heavens. Then the moon descends, takes Krtek aboard, and ferries him up through the darkness to set the green star in its proper place among the constellations. Written by Hana Sekyrková and Zdeněk Miler, the episode is pure fairy-tale logic: grief and persistence rewarded not by cleverness but by kindness from above. The instantly growing oak — a Miler signature — returns in later episodes whenever Krtek needs a quick miracle.

programme.title: Button Moon
programme.desc: When Tina gets a bump on her head, she cannot remember who she is. Maybe Mr. Spoon can help — but soon, things go wrong. The title is a play on Tina Tea-Spoon's name scrambled by her confusion: Tin-Who-Tea-What. This episode is sometimes listed online as "The Duck Who Forgot What He Was," but that appears to be a YouTube uploader's error conflating the telescope story with the episode title. The real title captures something genuinely clever about Ian Allen's writing — the wordplay works because all the characters ARE their objects. Tina is a teaspoon. Her identity crisis is literally about forgetting what kind of utensil she is. In a show where a spoon is a spoon is a person, amnesia becomes existential in a way that would make a philosophy student smile, even as a three-year-old just enjoys the slapstick of Tina bumping her head.

programme.title: Cat Meets Dog
programme.desc:
Four panels, four interweaving stories of cats and dogs — chasing, fleeing, befriending, betraying. The screen is divided into quadrants again, each animated separately by Driessen on paper, then composited at the NFB. The animals' stories intersect at panel borders, characters crossing from one reality into another.
Produced by Marcy Page and Maral Mohammadian at the NFB, co-produced in the Netherlands and Belgium. Screened internationally at HAFF, NFF, Sitges, and Animatou Geneva. This was Driessen at age 75, still drawing on paper in his French village, still shipping drawings to Montreal for compositing, still making the kind of films nobody else can make.
Paul Driessen's career arc: Dutch commercial animator with no training → found by George Dunning → Yellow Submarine (1968) → emigrated to Canada → thirty films at the NFB → fifty international prizes → Life Achievement at Ottawa and Zagreb → Oscar nomination for 3 Misses (1999) → two of his students won Oscars (Balance, Quest) → his three-minute egg film created the guy who created SpongeBob. All of it done on paper.

programme.title: More Dates For Kay
programme.desc:
Kay wants more dates than she's getting, and the film opens and closes on the same telephone in the front hall, bookending the lesson in between. Her older sister is the one setting her straight, walking her through what actually works while Kay tries it out: fixing her hair properly with a friend's help instead of letting it go, taking a real interest in what the boys around her care about — stopping to look at a classmate's book at the lockers, sitting in on the boys' after-school homework table instead of avoiding it — and putting herself where the boys are by taking on the unglamorous committee work, from typing up notices in the school office to organizing the cleanup crew nobody else wants. It doesn't all land right away; there's an awkward exchange in the hallway and a boy who walks off without her before the same habits, kept up patiently, start to change her luck. The picture ends where it began, on the phone, only now Kay is the one with news to report, and it's good news.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois — the operation Esquire and Coronet magazine publisher David A. Smart built to supply 16mm guidance shorts to American classrooms — the print carries his copyright credit, MCMLII, over the RCA Sound System card. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance line, the only name that appears on screen is the consulting educator: the title card credits "Educational Collaborator Mary E. Weathersby Pope, Formerly Head of Homemaking Education Department, Mississippi State College." No director or performer is named in the print itself. The film sits in the same run of Coronet dating shorts as Are You Popular? and Date Etiquette, all built around the studio's postwar conviction that dating success was a set of teachable habits rather than a matter of luck or looks.
At ten minutes, it's a tidy, single-period entry in that catalog, and one of its more memorable ones: Ken Smith's Mental Hygiene: Better Living Through Classroom Films, 1945–1970 catalogs Kay's habit of running the halls of her high school on one frantic ploy after another to land a boyfriend, and calls the results — watched from decades on — unintentionally hilarious, even though the film plays every scene perfectly straight for the classroom audience it was built for. It survives today as an unaltered Coronet print, held and circulated through the same ephemeral-film archives — Prelinger's collection among them — that preserve the rest of the studio's guidance catalog.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Rosalind, banished by her usurping uncle Duke Frederick, flees to the Forest of Arden disguised as the youth Ganymede, accompanied by her cousin Celia and the melancholy Touchstone. There she encounters the lovesick Orlando, and under cover of her disguise, offers to cure him of love by having him woo her as if she were Rosalind — which, of course, she is.
Directed by Alexei Karayev in paint-on-glass watercolors, this is arguably the most visually ravishing episode in the entire Shakespeare Animated Tales series. Karayev made a radical interpretive choice: he transplanted the Forest of Arden from medieval England to the world of Antoine Watteau's fêtes galantes — 18th-century French garden parties where aristocrats in silk and powder play at being shepherds. The guests wear fancy dresses and experience social freedom in painted gardens that shimmer and dissolve between frames, each one a painting destroyed to create the next.
Karayev had established himself as a paint-on-glass specialist before this commission. His 1986 short Welcome (Dobro pozhalovat), an adaptation of a story, won the Grand Prix at the Ottawa International Animation Festival — and it was animated by a young Aleksandr Petrov, who would go on to become the undisputed master of paint-on-glass animation and win the Academy Award for The Old Man and the Sea in 2000. Karayev effectively gave Petrov his breakthrough platform. Other Karayev paint-on-glass films include The Lodgers of an Old House (Zhiltsy starovo doma, 1987) and I Can Hear You (Ya vas slyshu, 1992). His filmography traces the full arc of Soviet-to-post-Soviet animation: Soyuzmultfilm in the late Communist era, then the S4C co-production pipeline that kept Russian animators employed through the 1990s collapse.
Sylvestra Le Touzel voices Rosalind. Born in Kensington in 1958 to a prominent Jersey family, she started acting at ten — her first role was a child who torments the Second Doctor in the 1968 Doctor Who serial The Mind Robber. As an adult she became one of Britain's most versatile character actresses: Fanny Price in the BBC's Mansfield Park (1983), Nina Khrushchev in Armando Iannucci's The Death of Stalin, Lady Dorothy Macmillan in The Crown (Season 2, described by The Telegraph as "magnificent"), and three different characters in the Wachowskis' Cloud Atlas. She's married to Welsh actor Owen Teale — they met during a production of Henry IV. Perhaps her most memorable moment came in a 1985 Heineken beer commercial parodying My Fair Lady, where she learned to speak Cockney: "The wa'er in Major'a don' taste like wot id ough' 'a." It placed 29th on Channel 4's 100 Greatest TV Ads.
Nathaniel Parker voices Jacques, the philosopher-melancholic who delivers the famous "All the world's a stage" speech. Born in 1962, the youngest son of Sir Peter Parker (British Rail chairman), brother of film director Oliver Parker. Trained at LAMDA, joined the RSC in 1986. He played Bassanio opposite Dustin Hoffman's Shylock in Peter Hall's 1989 Merchant of Venice. His first major screen break came as a Battle of France pilot in Piece of Cake (1988), followed immediately by playing Wilfred Owen in Derek Jarman's War Requiem — co-starring Laurence Olivier in his final screen role. Most famously Inspector Lynley for the BBC (2001-2007), then Henry VIII in the RSC's Wolf Hall, earning an Olivier Award and a Tony nomination. A painter himself, Parker brings particular sensitivity to the Watteau-inflected visual world Karayev creates here.

programme.title: Act Your Age
programme.desc:
Jim is working an algebra problem in a crowded classroom when the lead in his prized mechanical pencil snaps. He doesn't ask to borrow a spare; instead he takes the pencil to the top of his desk and starts carving his initials into the wood. That gets him sent to the principal, Mr. Edmonds, who confiscates the pencil but skips the lecture on vandalism and asks Jim to think instead about why he did it. Cutaways recast the outburst as childish rather than criminal: teenagers behaving badly dissolve into five-year-olds throwing the same tantrums, and a grown man on a sandlot diamond drops to the ground kicking and pulling his hair after a bad play, exactly like a scolded toddler. The school janitor adds his own complaint about kids "acting like babies," and Jim, talked into grading himself rather than just apologizing, builds a chart of his own: "How Old Am I?", rating his reactions when someone disagrees with him, pokes fun at him, or won't give him what he wants, scored against columns for today, next month, and next year, with his parents and friends filling in marks alongside his own. He gets the pencil back, and the film closes on Jim owning that the chart, not the excuse, is the honest answer.
Produced at Coronet's Glenview, Illinois studio and copyrighted in 1949 to the studio's founder, Esquire publisher David A. Smart, the picture carries the parenthetical subtitle "(Emotional Maturity)" on its own title card — the actual guidance-curriculum heading Coronet was selling to school boards under a catchier classroom title. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance line, the only credit on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: Wendell W. Wright, Ph.D., Dean of the School of Education at Indiana University, billed as "Educational Collaborator," with an RCA Sound System credit underneath. Coronet's regular postwar staff director, Ted Peshak, is credited with the film; the cast, in keeping with studio practice, goes unnamed on screen and unconfirmed elsewhere, so no actors are listed here.
Act Your Age sits in the same wave of Coronet "social guidance" shorts as Shy Guy and Are You Popular?, aimed at the same classroom hygiene-and-citizenship curricula, but working the material from the disciplinarian's side of the desk rather than the peer group's. Its "How Old Am I?" self-rating chart, turning an abstract scolding about maturity into a homework assignment Jim can fill out and hand back, is the device later viewers of the print have most often singled out as the quintessential Coronet touch — reducing a psychological problem to a worksheet with a solution built in. The film was preserved through Rick Prelinger's ephemeral-film salvage work, catalogued into the Prelinger Collection and digitized for the Internet Archive in 2002, and remains in the public domain today as the same plain classroom print Coronet released in 1949.

programme.title: Noggin the Nog: King of the Nogs
programme.desc:
The old King of the Nogs is dead, and before Noggin can take the crown he must take a queen. Guided by a talking green bird named Graculus, the gentle prince builds a longship and sails north to the Land of the Midnight Sun to find Nooka of the Nooks — while at home his scheming uncle, Nogbad the Bad, plots to claim the throne for himself. Storms, ice, a walrus, and Nogbad's treachery stand between Noggin and the wedding feast. This is the first saga, told across six ten-minute films, presented here as one continuous tale.
The look of the Nogs began in 1952, when a young Peter Firmin stood in the British Museum staring at the Lewis chessmen — the walrus-ivory Norse kings, queens, and glum little warders dug from a Hebridean beach — and caught what he later called "Nogmania." When Firmin and Oliver Postgate formed Smallfilms, working from Firmin's farm in Kent, those chess pieces walked off the board: Postgate wrote and animated, Firmin drew, and the BBC first broadcast the result on 11 September 1959. Each episode opens the same way, with the invitation to hear a tale the Men of the Northlands tell around their great log fires — words spoken over Vernon Elliott's spare bassoon score, which does for the frozen Northlands what a full orchestra couldn't.
Postgate shared the narration with actor Ronnie Stevens, the two voicing every king, inventor, and villain between them. The saga's stripped-down animation — cut-out figures moved frame by frame under a rostrum camera — was modest even by 1959 standards, but the storytelling was not: Postgate wrote the Nogs as a genuine Norse-flavored epic for small children, complete with dynastic peril and a villain whose name told you everything. Smallfilms went on to make Ivor the Engine, Bagpuss, and the Clangers — the last of which grew directly out of a Noggin story, "Noggin and the Moon Mouse."

programme.title: Are You A Good Citizen
programme.desc:
In the town of Midvale, the Civic Association has mobilized every community group behind its Annual Citizenship Day celebration, and the local paper carries the news that Alfred Heineman has been named First Citizen of the Town. As family and neighbors gather in his living room to congratulate him, the film turns the honor into an occasion for measuring Heineman — and the audience — against Coronet's own checklist for a good citizen: perform basic civic duties, take part in group activities, know and obey the law, keep informed on public affairs, be a good neighbor. Each plank gets its own small scene: Heineman serving his turn in a jury box; his own teenage son learning, mid-lecture, that a law broken through simple carelessness is still lawbreaking ("Look, ignorance of the law is no excuse. Whether you break a law through ignorance or carelessness or wickedness, it's all lawbreaking"); a mayoral campaign for one George Crane, run out of a storefront headquarters hung with "Crane for Mayor" placards and "Vote the Better Schools" bunting, offered as a model for staying informed; and a knot of neighborhood boys, shut out of the vacant lot they used to play ball on, learning to organize and petition the city rather than just resent the fence — a campaign that pays off when the Midvale Examiner reports the mayor dedicating a new playground.
Produced at Coronet's Glenview, Illinois studio and directed by Gil Altschul — paired, as on several of his Coronet assignments (Act Your Age, Going Steady?, Are You Ready for Marriage?, Why We Respect the Law), with cameraman Bruce Colling — the film was written by Dick Creyke, edited by George Wilbern, and narrated by Dick Thorne. Following Coronet's usual practice, the only credit beyond the production crew belongs to the academic consultant: Jerome G. Kerwin, Ph.D., professor of political science at the University of Chicago, whose presence lends the checklist its civics-classroom authority. The same credit card carries a small piece of in-house trivia: a "Juror in Box," identified in the lower right corner of the frame, is named as Ted Peshak — the director of several other Coronet guidance shorts, including Shy Guy, here turning up as an anonymous extra in someone else's picture.
At ten minutes, Are You a Good Citizen? belongs to the same question-titled cycle as Are You Popular? and Am I Trustworthy?, part of the roughly two hundred social-guidance shorts Coronet sold directly to schools through the postwar decades, typically for civics classes built around Citizenship Day and the between-exams calendar slots the genre favored. The surviving print circulates via the Prelinger Archives, uploaded by the A/V Geeks collection in 2013. Next to Coronet's more anxious dating-and-popularity titles, its brief here is almost technocratic — jury duty, ordinances, school-board politics, a won playground — a plain civics lesson delivered, as always, from a single family's living room.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Chewing Gum
programme.desc: Krtek emerges to find his meadow strewn with litter left by humans who drove off moments ago. He picks through the mess — some of it is actually fun to play with — until something sticky attaches itself to his body. Chewing gum. Sweet, yes, but it clings to everything. He tugs, twists, stretches; the gum only wraps tighter. Birds perch nearby and laugh. Mouse arrives and tries to help — no luck. The gum defeats them all until a curious cow wanders over, peels it cleanly off Krtek's fur, chews it experimentally, and blows a bubble that floats away and pops against the sky. Eight minutes of physical comedy with a moral that Czech audiences have noted stays fresh across decades: humans are slobs, nature has to deal with the consequences, and sometimes only a cow can solve your problems. One of Miler's sharpest environmental parables — the rubbish is both the inciting incident and the punchline, and Krtek's initial delight in playing with the garbage before the gum gets him adds a layer of ambiguity about complicity. Produced without dialogue, as all episodes from this era onward.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
Gumby meets Pokey. Promised a reward of 100 free ice cream cones, Gumby sets out to find a missing red pony. He finds Pokey with his hoof caught in a railroad track and frees him moments before the train arrives.
This is the origin of the most important relationship in the series. Art director Al Eggleston invented Pokey — the orange pony who became Gumby's permanent companion. Eggleston's wife Ruth had been voicing Gumby in the earliest episodes; now her husband gave Gumby a sidekick. Art Clokey himself would eventually voice Pokey, giving the character a distinctive, slightly dim quality that played perfectly against Gumby's earnest adventurousness. The ice cream cone reward is the kind of low-stakes, entirely sincere motivation that makes early Gumby so endearing — a green clay boy risks his life on train tracks for dessert, and it never occurs to anyone that this is absurd.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
Gumby visits a medieval kingdom and must fight in a jousting tournament against the Black Knight to save the realm. Just when defeat seems certain, a fire-breathing dragon comes to Gumby's aid.
A perfect example of Gumby's signature trick: walking into storybooks and becoming part of their world. Clokey built this concept from the beginning — the idea that fiction is a real place you can physically enter, that the boundary between reader and story is permeable. For a show made of clay, this is almost a philosophical statement: everything is malleable, including the wall between you and the adventure. The medieval sets, crude as they are, demonstrate Clokey's commitment to building complete miniature worlds for every episode, even at six minutes apiece.

programme.title: Better Use of Leisure Time
programme.desc:
Ken Michaels is flat on his bed doing nothing, and an unseen narrator won't let him get away with calling it rest — "moping" is the word used. Ken protests that there's nothing to do and no more free time than anyone else has, so the narrator takes him somewhere no ordinary Coronet short bothers to go: backward. First to a version of his own father a hundred years back, a farmer working a 72-hour week who orders young Ken off the bed to muck the stable and build new porch steps; then to a version fifty years back, a ten-hour-a-day, six-day-a-week father whose one indulgence is an evening with the stereoscope. Only then does the narrator return Ken to the present, where his real father works a 40-hour week, sneaks in a round of golf before supper, and is building a bookcase for the house in his spare time. The same time-trip is run on Ken's mother — scrubbing clothes, hauling water, baking bread and feeding chickens from dawn to dark fifty years ago, versus a washing machine and an evening spent planning the women's club program today. Sent to find out what his friends do with their own leisure, Ken discovers Dave identifying birds, Bill clerking part-time at the bookstore, Alice learning to sew, Marge at the piano, and a knot of boys in group sports. The narrator distills his father's bookcase hobby into a formula — a pleasant change from work, a chance to learn something, and a long-range goal — and Ken, rummaging out the camera he got for Christmas, decides photography might fill all three and maybe even a job someday.
The only screen credit is the customary Coronet consultant title card: Educational Collaborator Paul H. Landis, Ph.D., Professor of Sociology at State College of Washington. The picture itself is copyrighted, per its titles, to David A. Smart, the Esquire publisher whose Coronet Instructional Films turned out these classroom shorts by the hundreds from its Glenview, Illinois studio. What sets this one apart from its stablemates is the framing device: rather than a flat classroom-camera address, an argumentative off-screen narrator walks Ken through a series of staged historical vignettes to make its point about work, leisure and the modern 40-hour week. The Prelinger Archives catalog note on the print, written by film historian Ken Smith, calls it "more imaginative than most" Coronet titles "when it comes to visual gimmickry" — a fair description of the back-in-time device carrying the argument.
Ken's mother, credited on no title card but identified in later filmography listings as "Mrs. Michaels," is an early and uncredited screen role for Hope Summers, long before she became a familiar television face as Clara Edwards on The Andy Griffith Show and Mayberry R.F.D. Smith's same catalog note records that the boy playing Ken went on to headline another Coronet short, appearing as "Chuck-of-the-future" in Good Table Manners — one small thread connecting two entries in Coronet's social-guidance run. The film survives today through the Prelinger Archives holdings at the Internet Archive, cataloged as one of the more visually resourceful entries in a genre usually content to let its narrator simply talk over a static scene.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole at the Zoo
programme.desc: Krtek tunnels blindly upward and breaks through into a zoo enclosure, where he proceeds to behave like a menace. He pesters ostriches, nearly drowns in the aquatic section — a pelican rescues him, but Krtek doesn't so much as nod in thanks — then antagonises baby chicks, climbs into their throats, and when a monkey pulls him to safety at the last second, he sticks out his tongue at the lot of them. But the zoo has a king with a toothache. Krtek finds a lion (or tiger — the distinction blurs in Miler's design) in terrible pain, reaches in, and yanks the rotten tooth. Instant friendship. The lion doesn't care about Krtek's earlier bratty behaviour; he only remembers the one who helped. Czech reviewers have noted the zoological impossibility of an ostrich sharing an enclosure with monkeys, and the Tom-and-Jerry-esque pacing of the chase sequences. One particularly sharp reading: Krtek is a krtek — near-blind, sensory-driven, not malicious but oblivious to social norms, a creature of impulse. His redemption at the end isn't moral growth but lucky timing: the right problem for the right skill set. Six minutes, scored by Vadim Petrov.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.desc: Krtek digs out of his burrow, naps, and wakes to a soaking — a garden hose has sprung a leak. He tries to fix it in a series of increasingly absurd attempts that Czech viewers have compared to the slapstick of Pat and Mat. A frog blocks what's left of the water flow, and the flower bed begins to die. The flowers — in one of Miler's most memorable flourishes — sing out in chorus: "Vodu, vodu, vodu!" (Water, water, water!). Mouse arrives to help, but neither of them can undo the plumbing disaster. So Krtek does what a mole does best: he digs. An irrigation canal, carved from the earth around the flower bed, solves the problem in a way that no hose ever could. As one ČSFD reviewer noted, "In one episode he fought with a gardener; here he becomes one himself" — a nod to the later television episode where the roles reverse. The episode's title is a joke: Krtek the Gardener is still a mole, solving a gardening problem with tunnels. Sharp-eyed viewers have catalogued two continuity errors: a sprinkler that vanishes and reappears between shots, and a leaf that regenerates after being picked. Music by Vadim Petrov.

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Hedgehog
programme.desc: The rain stops and Krtek gets to work draining his waterlogged molehill. Meanwhile, a hedgehog struts past with fruit stacked on his spines, lounging in the grass, eating loudly, and not lifting a paw to help. Krtek invites him; hedgehog waves him off. Mouse arrives in a panic — danger. Krtek warns hedgehog, but hedgehog shrugs. Then a human hand reaches down, scoops hedgehog into a cage, and carries him away. Hedgehog wails. Krtek and mouse follow the tracks to a rural school and stand outside, bewildered — they don't know which door to try. They find hedgehog by his crying, squeeze through a crack in the wall into the natural history cabinet, and navigate past a skeleton and stuffed animals (Krtek pauses to swing on the whiskers of a stuffed tomcat, because he's Krtek). They rock the cage to the open window, tie it to the blind cord, lower it down like an improvised elevator — hedgehog screaming the whole way. On the ground, the cage springs open. Freedom. Then they meet a real cat, identical to the stuffed one. Krtek isn't worried — he's seen this before! — but this one moves. They run. Hedgehog saves them: Krtek and mouse hide in his spiny embrace, he curls into a ball, and the cat learns about consequences. The ball rolls all the way home. Eight minutes about the gap between who deserves rescue and who gets it. Krtek helps the friend who refused to help him, and the episode never comments on the irony.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: Gumby explores small planets — miniature worlds within worlds, a concept perfectly suited to a show built on tabletop sets where everything is already small. The episode is notable among Gumby collectors as a fan favorite from the syndication era, with a dreamlike quality that recalls the Vorkapich-influenced spatial experiments of the earliest episodes. The "walking into other worlds" premise reaches its most literal expression here: the planets are small enough to hold, yet contain entire landscapes.

programme.title: Marriage Is a Partnership
programme.desc:
Dotty rides an eastbound train alone and lets her mind drift back over the year just past. In flashback, Coronet reconstructs the small, cumulative friction of a first year of marriage: she and her husband Pete move into their first apartment together and work out, meal by meal, who does the dishes and who irons the shirts, redividing chores neither of them wanted the first time around. A furniture-buying trip turns into an argument about what they can actually afford; an older female relative arrives to help hang curtains and wash windows and, in the course of helping, quietly second-guesses how Dotty is keeping house; an afternoon spent minding a friend's baby gives the young couple an uneasy preview of a stage still ahead of them. The seasons turn — a yard filling with fallen leaves marks the year passing — and the flashback resolves the way Coronet's guidance shorts usually do: not with one partner winning an argument, but with Pete and Dotty at the kitchen table, going over the household budget together and deciding, out loud, as partners. The film closes back on the train, Dotty's face settled rather than troubled.
The card that opens the print reads "A Coronet Film," followed by a copyright date of MCMLI — 1951 — under the name of David A. Smart, the Chicago publisher who owned Coronet Instructional Films, and the RCA Sound System trademark Coronet ran on its negatives through the period. As with the rest of the studio's social-guidance catalog, no director or performer is named on screen; the only credited contributor is the educational collaborator, Lemo D. Rockwood, Ph.D., billed as Professor of Family Relationships at the New York State College of Home Economics at Cornell University.
Rockwood's own class at Cornell, known on campus as the Marriage Course, was one of the most sought-after electives of the late 1940s, open to students across every college and taught with an unusual mix of historical and anthropological background alongside frank discussion of courtship, mate selection, and the daily mechanics of married life — an approach that, per Cornell University Library's own retrospective on Rockwood, drew real anxiety from more conservative faculty and administrators even as students filled her lecture hall. That same practical, unsentimental voice is what Coronet put on screen here: a Pete-and-Dotty story with no villain, only two people learning to negotiate. The film survives today through Prelinger Archives' donation of Coronet's negatives to the Internet Archive, where it continues to circulate in classroom-print form.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal has been busy in his laboratory concocting a hair-growth formula, and all he needs now is a willing — or unwilling — test subject. Brian obliges by accident: when the two collide, Dougal spots the snail's gleaming bald head and decides he has found his man. A few drops later, Brian is engulfed in a wild tangle of black hair so thick he can't see where he's going. Ermintrude, intrigued rather than alarmed, volunteers herself and emerges draped in luxuriant blonde locks to her considerable delight. Florence, unable to recognise either of them, summons Zebedee, who inspects the damage and mixes a corrective potion. He also finds Dougal and, by way of a lesson, pours the formula straight onto the dog's head, stripping the fur clean off his ears and scalp. A humiliated Dougal retreats to his lab to patch himself up — only to close the episode by suggesting Florence might consider going a little longer herself.
This episode was included on the 1984 VHS release "The Magic Roundabout" and the 1993 compilation "The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout" under the title "The Experiment".

programme.title: Krtek
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Lollipop
programme.desc: Two children leave a lollipop on a park bench — the same bench Krtek has been using as an adrenaline slide. He is thrilled by the find and utterly baffled by what it is. Over the next few minutes he tries it as a flag, a tennis racket, a shovel, and a traffic sign (the other animals refuse to stop at his intersection, which makes him cry). Eventually he figures out it's for licking. But wasps have been watching, and they want the sweet thing too. What follows is a running battle between a mole with a lollipop and a swarm with a plan. Voices by Jiřina Bohdalová — one of Czechoslovakia's most famous actresses — providing the non-verbal squeaks and exclamations. Hidden audio detail: in the scene where the children sit on the bench talking, the soundtrack plays reversed Czech dialogue — "kdepak já mám košíček, mám ho plný houbiček" (where's my basket, full of mushrooms) and "jen tam domů uháním" (I'm hurrying home) — run backwards as ambient chatter. Czech viewers have noted the structural rhyme with the chewing gum episode (found sweet object, failed attempts to understand it) and the green star episode (trying to return something to its proper place). The moral, delivered without a word: invention is just misidentification with confidence.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
The first Gumby episode ever broadcast — a three-part story that debuted on Howdy Doody on May 1, 1956 and launched a sixty-year franchise. Gumby discovers a spaceship in a toy store, flies to the moon, gets stranded when a meteorite destroys his ship, encounters strange rock creatures that sprout eyes, freezes in the lunar cold, and is rescued by his father via fire engine with an impossibly long extension ladder. It sounds like nonsense. It looks like nothing else ever made.
Animation Obsessive called this premiere "deeply alien" — and identified why. Art Clokey was applying his USC professor Slavko Vorkapich's kinesthetic film principles to children's television: using camera angles, cutting rhythm, and spatial relationships to create involuntary physical responses in the viewer. The slow approach of the moon "asteroid" feels more disturbing than it should. The match cut at 8:27 contrasts motion in two directions. Gumby's flight over abstract lunar geometry, the creatures moving in uncomfortable unison, the dolly shot down a hospital corridor where shadow and light play over Gumby's mother — Animation Obsessive called this last sequence "animated Kubrick."
The animation itself is crude. The sets are cardboard. But the filmmaking made people unable to look away. As Clokey explained: "Vorkapich got down to basics. His theory was that motion picture dealt only with motion and the illusion of three-dimensional objects created by the director's use of shapes, shadows, colors and motion. He said if you understand how to organize those things through camera angles, camera movement, pace and so forth, you could make any film more interesting. And it happened to me... people were fascinated with how I could make the screen come alive in ways that other people couldn't."
This three-part episode was preceded by an unaired pilot called "Adventures of Gumby: A Sample," produced January 29, 1955. NBC executive Thomas Warren Sarnoff ordered a second pilot after seeing it; that became this Moon Trip, which aired as a segment on Howdy Doody. The response was strong enough to warrant a full series. Bobby Nicholson hosted the earliest Gumby segments on Howdy Doody; Ruth Eggleston (wife of art director Al Eggleston, who invented Pokey) voiced Gumby in these first episodes before Dallas McKennon took over in 1957.

programme.title: Control Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Jeff Moore is seventeen and having a bad Friday. He's the designated driver for a triple date that night, and everything conspires against him along the way: the car won't start in the garage, his kid brother Roger is underfoot and easy to frighten, his mother and his sister Joan want things from him at exactly the wrong moments, and his friends needle him at the drugstore soda fountain while he waits on a stalled engine. A psychologist in a white coat keeps interrupting from behind a desk to sort Jeff's afternoon into three labeled blocks — RAGE, FEAR, LOVE — treating each flare-up as a case study in how those basic emotions get triggered, and how they can be managed instead of vented. By evening Jeff has stopped slamming doors and started thinking before he reacts; the film closes on the same picnic-ground bonfire it opened with, the whole group gathered around it roasting marshmallows, dates delivered and temper intact.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio on David A. Smart's estate in Glenview, Illinois — Smart, the Esquire magazine publisher, had set up Coronet in 1946 as a dedicated producer of 16mm classroom shorts — and copyrighted 1950 (the title card reads "Copyright MCML David A. Smart"). As with the rest of the line, the only person named on screen is the psychology consultant: the card credits Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College. Lauer's usual specialty at Iowa State was traffic safety — he headed the college's Driver Training Laboratory and is credited on Coronet's driver-education shorts of the same period — so his appearance here, consulting on temper rather than turn signals, is a small crossover into the studio's general social-guidance catalog. Letterboxd and TMDB both credit the direction to Ted Peshak, Coronet's regular postwar house director.
The film sits in Coronet's long run of postwar social guidance, or "mental hygiene," shorts made for classroom use, alongside titles like Are You Popular? and Shy Guy — all built on the same premise, that an adolescent's raw feeling is a problem to be labeled, explained, and brought under control rather than simply expressed. The Prelinger Archives, which preserved and catalogs this print, summarize it in a single line: well-balanced emotions help to create a well-rounded personality, especially in teenagers. Like most of Coronet's guidance output, the film has long since passed into the public domain and survives today chiefly through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc:
Three minutes of pulsating clay set to jazz. No characters, no story, no dialogue — just shapes expanding, contracting, morphing and splitting in stop-motion, choreographed to Mel Powell's "Don-Que-Dee." This is the film that started everything.
Art Clokey made Gumbasia in 1953 as a student at the University of Southern California, working alone in his father's garage on a ping-pong table. His professor was Slavko Vorkapich, a Serbian painter who'd arrived in Hollywood nearly penniless in 1921 and talked his way into becoming one of the industry's most influential film artists. Vorkapich had created the montage sequences in Mr. Smith Goes to Washington, Manhattan Melodrama, and Joan of Arc. By the time Clokey met him, Vorkapich had codified his ideas into a theory he called "kinesthetic film principles" — the notion that moving images create involuntary physical responses in the viewer. He described it as "massaging of the eye cells."
Vorkapich considered Clokey his protégé. "He turned my head around at USC as far as motion pictures are concerned," Clokey said. In the 1980s, Clokey elaborated: "It's similar to music. You build to a climax through use of timing and intensity of the stimuli — the duration, syncopation and so on. Vorkapich taught that it's more like poetry and music. He would refer to the shots and the definite cuts as notes. Visual notes to combine and use in various ways, to get across your feelings." Clokey called Gumbasia "an experiment in pure movement" — an attempt to strip away "the distraction of recognizable forms" and leave only the sensation of motion.
The title is a portmanteau of "gumbo" (the muddy clay from his grandparents' Michigan farm) and "Fantasia" (the Disney film it parodies). Samuel G. Engel, president of the Motion Pictures Producers Association, saw Gumbasia when his son — one of Clokey's students at the Harvard School for Boys — brought it home. Engel told Clokey to make a children's show. Gumby followed.
What makes Gumbasia extraordinary isn't the clay or the technique. It's that every Gumby episode afterward — all 233 of them, plus the movie — carries the DNA of this three-minute experiment. As Animation Obsessive noted, "People at home didn't register these as avant-garde techniques — they just found themselves unable to look away from the screen, because Clokey wouldn't let them." A seminary dropout working on a ping-pong table in a garage, applying a Serbian painter's theories about "massaging the eye cells" to lumps of colored clay, accidentally invented one of the most recognizable characters in American culture. The avant-garde became the vanguard. Three minutes of jazz and clay changed television.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Directed by Nikolai Serebryakov, who was evacuated from Leningrad as a child during the 900-day Nazi siege and grew up to become one of Russian animation's most distinguished and beloved figures.
Serebryakov was born December 14, 1928, in Leningrad, the son of a theatrical figure. After the siege, he trained as both an actor (graduating from the Bryantsev acting studio at the Leningrad Young Viewers' Theatre in 1948) and as a craftsman (graduating from the Vera Mukhina Institute of Applied Art in 1952, specializing in wood processing). He worked in restoration, theatrical design, and television before joining Soyuzmultfilm in 1960 as a production designer. His first collaboration was with Roman Kachanov on Little Masha and the Bear (1960).
He began co-directing with Vadim Kurchevsky — I Want to Be Brave (1963), Little Lazybones (1964), Neither God nor Devil (1965) — and was part of the generation of young animators who, during Khrushchev's "thaw," began pushing Soviet animation beyond pretty children's cartoons into more sophisticated territory. His contemporaries included Andrei Khrzhanovsky and Yuri Norstein, with whom he would later share a joint retrospective at the Edinburgh Festival.
Ball of Wool (1968), about an old woman who knits herself an entire life from a sheep's coat but falters when she tries to remake herself as a beautiful girl, was called "one of the masterpieces of Russian animated cinema" by Robin Buss in The Independent. He won prizes at Tours (1967), Grenoble (1976), and the Grand Prix at Tampere (1977).
His creative and personal life was inseparable from Alina Speshneva, a designer at the legendary Obraztsov puppet theatre in Moscow. They married — she was the sister of his first wife Nadia — and for sixteen years made everything together. They contributed the animation design for Elem Klimov's Sport, Sport, Sport (1970), a live-action/animation collage with an Alfred Schnittke soundtrack. In 1984, Alina died in an accident, and everything changed.
After her death, Serebryakov shifted from puppet animation to drawn cel work. He served as artistic director at Mosfilm's experimental "Debut" studio (1982–89), then won the Nika — Russia's Oscar — for The Parable about the Actor in 1989. He was named People's Artist of the Russian Federation in 1996.
For the Animated Tales he directed two episodes using cel animation: Macbeth and, in Series 2, Othello. The obituary noted that there were concerns about the violence of some scenes in his Macbeth — it was feared they might make it unsuitable for the target audience. But this is Macbeth; the violence is the point.
Brian Cox voices Macbeth. Cox was born in Dundee in 1946 to a working-class Catholic family — his father died of pancreatic cancer when Brian was eight, his mother suffered nervous breakdowns working in the jute mills, and he was raised by his three elder sisters. He started acting at fourteen at Dundee Repertory Theatre, trained at LAMDA, and narrowly avoided death in 1965 when a meeting with Laurence Olivier was cancelled, saving him from boarding a flight that crashed at Heathrow. He won two Olivier Awards — for Rat in the Skull (1984) and Titus Andronicus (1988, which he considers his greatest performance). Before this recording, Cox had spent time teaching and directing at the Moscow Arts Theatre School — a Scottish actor trained in Moscow voicing the Scottish king for a Russian animation studio. He was also the first actor to play Hannibal Lecter on screen, in Michael Mann's Manhunter (1986), and would later define television in the 2020s as Logan Roy in Succession.
Zoë Wanamaker voices Lady Macbeth. She was born in New York to a Russian-Jewish family, but her father Sam Wanamaker — an actor and director — was blacklisted during McCarthyism and fled to London, where he spent the last twenty-three years of his life on a single obsessive project: rebuilding Shakespeare's Globe Theatre on the South Bank of the Thames. He died in December 1993, four years before it opened. His daughter, voicing Lady Macbeth in a Russian-animated Shakespeare adaptation, carries both halves of that inheritance — the Russian and the Shakespearean — in a single casting choice that nobody planned but which resonates perfectly.

programme.title: Shy Guy
programme.desc:
Phil Norton is new in town and new at school, and he spends his lunch hours alone and his evenings in the basement, building radios and record players. His father — finding him down there again — puts the problem in Phil's own language: a component has to fit in, so it can work with all the other parts. So Phil goes back to school and does what an engineer would do. He observes. He watches the popular kids to work out what actually makes them liked, and the data surprises him: it isn't looks or money or noise, it's that they pay attention to other people. Phil tries it — asks questions, listens, offers to help a classmate fix a broken record player — and by the final reel the basement workshop is full of friends.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and directed by Ted Peshak, the house director behind many of Coronet's postwar guidance films. In keeping with Coronet practice, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Alice Sowers, Ph.D., director of the Family Life Institute at the University of Oklahoma. Released to classrooms in August 1947, it became one of the most widely shown of all the social guidance shorts — the genre's usual prescription of conformity delivered, for once, with a certain sweetness: the film never asks Phil to stop building radios, only to look up from the workbench occasionally.
Two people made their film debuts in these thirteen minutes, and both became fixtures of American television. Phil is a nineteen-year-old Dick York, then a busy Chicago radio actor, seventeen years before he became Darrin Stephens on Bewitched; educational and industrial films like this one were his bread and butter for years. And the narrator's voice belongs to a young Chicago announcer named Myron Wallace — who, as Mike Wallace, would spend nearly four decades asking harder questions on 60 Minutes.

programme.title: Mummenschanz: You & Me
programme.desc:
A full Mummenschanz stage performance, in a theater, in front of an audience — the thing the troupe almost never allowed onto film across half a century of touring. Two enormous grey hands meet and quarrel. A figure whose head is a lump of soft clay reshapes its own face to match its feelings. Creatures assembled from white blocks build and unbuild themselves. Masks made of toilet-paper rolls unspool to weep and to talk. Tube-worms in green and blue court each other across a bare black stage. There are no words, no music, and almost no light beyond what falls on the figures themselves; the theater's laughter and applause are the entire soundtrack, and the performers — visible only as black-clad suggestions beneath the shapes — never break the silence, not even at the curtain call.
You & Me was created for the company's 45th anniversary and premiered at Theater 11 in Zurich on December 1, 2016, under the creative direction of Floriana Frassetto — the last of the three founders still performing. Frassetto, Bernie Schürch, and Andres Bossard had formed Mummenschanz in 1972 and spent three years running on Broadway (1977–80) with a mask theater built from foam, clay, and household objects; Bossard died in 1992, and with You & Me Frassetto handed the vocabulary to a new generation of performers — Oliver Pfulg, Sara Francesca Hermann, Christa Barrett, Kevin Blaser, and company — while performing in the show herself. Around 130,000 people saw the production in Switzerland alone before it toured abroad.
This recording is Swiss television's cut of the show, broadcast by SRF, running just over an hour against the stage version's two forty-five-minute acts. A fuller 94-minute recording, taped by Swiss-Italian television at the Théâtre de Beausobre in Morges in 2017, exists only on the Mummenschanz foundation's own out-of-print video releases — making this broadcast cut the performance's one accessible form, and the only complete-in-spirit Mummenschanz show most audiences outside a theater will ever see.

programme.title: Improve Your Personality
programme.desc:
Improve Your Personality opens on a school walkway and quickly settles into the device it returns to for the rest of its ten minutes: a black silhouette head in profile, flanked by two labels, "OTHER PEOPLE" and "ENVIRONMENT," under the caption "YOUR PERSONALITY." The diagram states the film's whole thesis in one image — personality isn't something a person is simply born with, it's built out of how they treat others and how they answer to their surroundings — and the picture keeps cutting back to it between two contrasted case studies. A teenage boy who starts out sullen and closed-off is shown coming around: setting the table, hanging up the wash, pitching in at home instead of leaving the chores to the woman of the house. Cut hard against him is a teenage girl who does nothing in her scenes but admire her own reflection in a bedroom mirror, the diagram card reappearing each time to underline the moral. Along the way, one boy sizes up a girl walking past him on the same path from the opening and tells a friend, "Boy, has she got personality!" — about as flatly as the film could put its own pun. By the closing reel the same young people turn up dressed for a formal dance, in tuxedos and gowns, and a final card spells out the takeaway in script lettering: "Concentrate on the other person."
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films and copyrighted in 1951 (the opening card reads "MCMLI," credited to David A. Smart), the short follows Coronet's standard practice for the period: not one performer is named on screen, and the film's only title-card credit goes to its "educational collaborator," billed as Clifford R. Adams, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at the Pennsylvania State College. Adams held that post in fact as well as on the card — he was Penn State's real director of its Marriage Counseling Service and a member of the American Association of Marriage Counselors — and five years earlier had co-written the marriage-advice bestseller "How to Pick a Mate" with Vance O. Packard, then a staff writer for The American Magazine and later the author of "The Hidden Persuaders." Coronet drew on a small, recurring bench of writers, directors, and consultants across its guidance catalog — Melvin Waskin as house writer, Ted Peshak as its most frequent director among them — but this particular print names none of them; Adams alone appears on screen.
The film belongs to Coronet's postwar "mental hygiene" cycle, the run of guidance shorts the company produced through the late 1940s and 1950s for direct sale to schools. David Smart, who had toured Nazi Germany before the war, later told the Chicago Tribune that seeing Hitler's use of film as an "indoctrination tool" convinced him the same medium could be turned toward education instead, and Coronet ran with the idea hard enough to release a new title, on average, every three and a half working days. Against that backdrop, Improve Your Personality is a mild entry — no car crash, no scandal, just a civics-class gloss on manners dressed up as psychology, delivered with Adams' academic authority and Coronet's usual well-lit, tidy midcentury classrooms and living rooms.
