Ray works back through the same round of situations correcting himself one by one, and the film closes with him at a piano surrounded by a room full of grinning classmates — the reward Coronet's guidance shorts always hand out for good behavior: being liked.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' Glenview, Illinois studio and directed by Ted Peshak, from a script by Robert Chapin and Dick Creyke, photographed by Dale Sharkey and cut by editor George Wilbern, with narration by George Stone. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance line, the only credit that appears on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Harl R. Douglass, Ph.D., director of the College of Education at the University of Colorado, a life-adjustment educator whose papers are held today in that university's own archives. Prelinger Archives, whose print of the film circulates today, catalogs the release as 1952; Letterboxd and IMDb's short-film index both list 1951 instead, a year's discrepancy common to Coronet's undated 16mm classroom prints.
Phil is played by Dick York — five years past his screen debut in the title role of Coronet's own Shy Guy (1947), and a dozen years before he became Darrin Stephens on Bewitched — while Mr. Martin, whose shop gives Phil his after-school job, is played by Carl Kroenke. Ray and the film's other roles went uncredited on screen, in keeping with Coronet's practice of naming only its academic consultant. The short is one of dozens Coronet turned out during its postwar guidance cycle and survives today as a plain, commercial-free classroom print through the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive.

programme.title: Shakespeare: The Animated Tales
programme.desc:
Petruchio arrives in Padua looking for a rich wife, and is pointed toward Katherina — beautiful, wealthy, and by universal agreement impossible. He declares he will marry her, tames her through a campaign of strategic starvation and sleep deprivation disguised as solicitous care, and ultimately wins her obedience. Whether she has truly been broken or is playing a longer game remains Shakespeare's cruelest ambiguity.
Directed by Aida Zyablikova in stop-motion puppet animation. Born in 1940, Zyablikova studied painting at the Yaroslavl Art School from 1958 to 1963, staying on as a teacher until 1967 before enrolling in the animator course at VGIK Film School. She joined Soyuzmultfilm as an animator in 1971, moved to Ekran (the Soviet TV animation studio) in 1974, and began directing in 1978, making twenty animated films there before Ekran closed in 1993.
Her first series was an adaptation of Tove Jansson's Moomintroll. But the work she became best known for was Kuzya the House Elf (Domovyonok Kuzya, 1984-1987), a beloved Soviet children's series about a young domovoi — a household spirit from Russian folklore — who moves into a modern apartment. The character became so iconic in Russian culture that the name "Kuzya" became virtually synonymous with domovoi for an entire generation.
Yet her most significant work may be her least known: Tell Us a Story, Doctor (1988), a puppet animation about Janusz Korczak — the Polish-Jewish pediatrician, children's book author, and pedagogue who ran the Dom Sierot orphanage in the Warsaw Ghetto. When the Nazis came to transport the children to Treblinka in August 1942, Korczak refused multiple offers of personal escape and went to the gas chambers with his two hundred orphans, leading them through the streets carrying the orphanage's green flag. Zyablikova chose to tell this story through puppets — the medium in which she could give Korczak's children faces.
After Ekran closed, she joined Christmas Films in Moscow, where this Taming of the Shrew was her first assignment. She stayed through 2002, directing Joseph for The Bible animated series (1996, BAFTA nominee) and three Canterbury Tales episodes (1998-2000), which won a BAFTA and earned her an Academy Award nomination. She has taught at VGIK since 2003. Honored Artist of the Russian Federation in 2014. Her final animations were The Rabbit from the Cabbage Garden (2006) and The Menu (2007), both at Soyuzmultfilm, both award winners.
Amanda Root voices Kate. Born in Chelmsford in 1963, she trained at the Webber Douglas Academy — the same school that produced Antony Sher. She joined the RSC straight out of drama school and was immediately cast in roles that would have been career peaks for any other actress: Juliet opposite Daniel Day-Lewis's Romeo, Cressida opposite Ralph Fiennes's Troilus, Lady Macbeth. She was "remarkably complete even in her early twenties, when physically she looked little more than a child," wrote one critic; "with her dark soulful eyes she could command a stage." In 1994, Emma Thompson asked her to play Marianne Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility, but Root had already committed to the title role in the BBC's Persuasion. Kate Winslet got the Sense and Sensibility part instead. Root's Persuasion won five BAFTAs. She voiced Sophie in the 1989 animated BFG. Tony Award nomination for Alan Ayckbourn's The Norman Conquests (2009).
Nigel Le Vaillant voices Petruchio. Born in Karachi in 1957, the son of a British father who had stayed in South Asia after the war and risen to Chief Executive of Brooke Bond's entire subcontinental tea operation. Le Vaillant was raised in Pakistan, returned to England at sixteen, attended Bryanston School and read at St Peter's College, Oxford. He then spent nine years unemployed trying to break into acting before finding fame as Dr. Julian Chapman in Casualty and the title character in Dangerfield. But the part that stayed with him was Volpone at the Oxford Playhouse in 1980, approvingly cited by William Slights in Ben Jonson and the Art of Secrecy. In the early 2000s, he abandoned acting entirely, uncomfortable with fame, and now regularly visits Southern India. He came back once — to play Edward Heath in the 2009 BBC drama Margaret — and then disappeared again.

programme.title: Lunchroom Manners
programme.desc:
A puppet theater dominates the front of an elementary classroom, flag hanging behind it, as a fumbling marionette named Mr. Bungle blunders in and out of a little door marked "BOYS ROOM," and the watching class laughs at exactly the behavior the film means to stamp out. The cartoonish object lesson gives way to a live-action follow-through: a boy scrubs his hands at the washroom sink, joins the line filing into the cafeteria, and works his way down a hot line loaded with cake, franks, and trimmings. Left to his own habits he eats carelessly — shoveling, slurping a straw, leaving his tray a mess — while a watching teacher looks on from the doorway unimpressed. A tidier classmate is held up as the counter-example, and the short closes on trays properly scraped and stacked, its lesson in "beginning responsibility" delivered the way Coronet always delivered it: gently, repetitively, and entirely without dialogue that isn't a teacher's.
The title card reads "Beginning Responsibility: Lunchroom Manners," placing it in the same Coronet strand as Shy Guy and its kin, and carries a copyright date of MCMLX — 1960 — a year later than the date this print is commonly catalogued under. As with the rest of the series, the only credit on screen is the educational collaborator: Ross L. Allen, Dr.P.H., Director of Education for the Division of Health, Physical Education and Recreation at the College of Education, Cortland State University of New York. No writer or director is named on the print itself, and none has been reliably attributed to this particular title elsewhere. The trademark card underneath identifies Coronet Instructional Films as, at the time, "a division of Esquire, Inc."
The film's afterlife has outrun its classroom career by a wide margin. Its puppet antagonist gave the experimental rock band Mr. Bungle, formed by Mike Patton and friends in Northern California in the mid-1980s, its name. Excerpts also turned up on an HBO Pee-wee Herman special, introducing the short to an audience of a very different age and temperament than the one it was built for. Coronet's straight-faced cafeteria etiquette lesson, uncredited actors and all, has proven considerably stickier than its intended nine-and-a-half-minute classroom slot.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence fancies a quiet stroll through the Garden, but it is Dougal who makes the first discovery: a rocking chair, which he immediately declares is exactly what he has always wanted. There is a snag, however — Brian is already sitting in it. Dougal tries to shift the snail with a cunning tip about a large lettuce nearby, only for Brian to clamber onto his back and demand a ride there. When Florence eventually finds the empty chair and settles in for a gentle rock, Mr. McHenry arrives, pronounces it just what he has always wanted, and wheels it off on Florence's own suggestion. Dougal returns, chairless and defeated, but brightens at Florence's hint that Mr. McHenry might also have sugar on hand. Zebedee pops up last and, on hearing the tale, delivers the inevitable verdict: "Just what I've always wanted."
The Eric Thompson script for this episode was reprinted in the novel The Adventures of Brian under the slightly altered title "The Rocking Chair". Both the English and French versions were included as a bonus feature on the Special Edition DVD of the 2005 CGI film.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence meets Dougal in the Garden, where he grumbles about being woken that morning by a "terrible jangling thing" that has left him thoroughly shaken. They soon track down the culprit: an over-eager alarm clock anxious about its ability to rouse sleepers. Brian is put forward as a test subject, but the snail's cheerful enquiry about whether everyone is up bright and early only deflates the clock further. Dougal then has an inspired idea — Dylan the rabbit is exactly the kind of deep sleeper the clock needs. While the clock sets off in search of the dozing Dylan, Dougal retreats to eat sugar lumps to cope with the excitement. Florence unwisely summons Zebedee, who promptly declares it time for bed, leaving her ruefully hoist by her own petard. The episode ends with the alarm clock noisily orbiting the still-sleeping Dylan, having accomplished nothing whatsoever.
The Eric Thompson narration of this episode was released on VHS as "Alarm Clock" on Volume 3 in 1992. AB Productions' 1990s remaster repeats a brief shot of Florence near the start, likely to cover a gap caused by deterioration of the original master.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
This episode survives only in its original French version; no Eric Thompson English narration was recorded for it. The action in the Magic Garden involves a crockery strike, with the usual cast of Dougal, Florence, Brian, Ermintrude, Dylan, and Zebedee caught up in the domestic unrest that the title implies.
The entire French version was broadcast on the BBC arts programme Late Night Line-Up on 13 December 1966, paired with the English version of "Large Hole in the Garden." That transmission marked the unofficial British television debuts of the revamped Magic Roundabout theme tune and of Dylan as a character.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal becomes convinced that a four-leaf clover is just the thing he needs, and Florence and Brian dutifully set about helping him find one. The search unfolds at the unhurried pace the garden demands, with Brian's cheerful incompetence and Florence's patient encouragement carrying most of the effort while Dougal provides the ambition.
Eric Thompson's script for this episode was later reprinted in the tie-in novel "The Adventures of Brian" under the retitled chapter "Brian, Vegetable Specialist". The English version has been repeated on BBC Four twice: 29 May 2007 and 27 November 2022.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence is in the garden when Dougal mysteriously leads her to a music box, which turns out to be a surprisingly self-important artiste. As the box's tune begins to wind down, Florence insists that everything has feelings and the music box warmly agrees, delighted to have found someone with such fine judgement. Dougal is considerably less impressed, muttering under his breath as Florence calls him the world's worst mutterer. Dylan arrives and plonks himself on top of the box, announcing that he is staging a protest against canned music — the curse of modern civilisation — before promptly winding the box up as tight as it will go, commanding it to play, and then falling asleep to the performance. Zebedee appears to declare bedtime, Florence bids everyone goodnight, and the music box departs wishing Dylan a good sleep.
The Eric Thompson narration of this episode was released on VHS in 1992 and on LP and cassette in 1971 alongside ten other second-series stories; the audio was later reissued on CD in 2005 and again in 2010.

programme.title: Your Thrift Habits
programme.desc:
Jack is broke, and he knows exactly why: a nickel here for a Berry Supreme sundae at the corner soda fountain, three dollars there for a ticket to the State College-All Stars game at Folger Stadium, and the rest gone to movies and odds and ends he can't quite account for. What he wants is a camera like the one his friend Ralph already owns, and he can't see how he'll ever get there on the money he has. Sitting down with an older advisor to work out where his allowance actually goes, Jack draws his income as a pie sliced into lunches, carfare, snacks, and personal spending, then writes himself a plain warning on a sheet of paper: "Watch these expenses!" From there it's a matter of engineering rather than willpower — a weekly budget, a savings line charted week over week, and a homemade progress gauge built around the shape of the camera he's saving for. The line climbs toward twenty-five dollars, and by the last reel Jack is signing his own name to the purchase.
Coronet Instructional Films copyrighted the picture in 1948 (MCMXLVIII, per the title card, under founder David A. Smart), produced with the company's usual RCA sound system billing. As with the rest of Coronet's guidance line, the only credit on screen belongs to the educational collaborator: Paul L. Salsgiver, director of the School of Business at Simmons College, whose academic standing was meant to give the budgeting lesson classroom authority. No actors are credited on screen, and no cast for this specific title could be corroborated in outside sources, so none is listed here.
Released to schools on 31 August 1948, Your Thrift Habits belongs to Coronet's long run of postwar social-guidance shorts, this one aimed squarely at consumer economics rather than manners or dating etiquette: a teenager's income, once it's actually itemized, turns out to be manageable if not exactly generous. It survives today through the Prelinger Archives, cataloged there as a lesson in budgeting and the choice between immediate and future satisfactions — a small, plainly made document of how postwar American schools tried to teach thrift to a generation raised on installment plans and drugstore sodas.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Train arrives in the garden and boasts to Brian that she is the fastest thing around, having just been running speed trials. Brian, not one to let that pass unchallenged, proposes a race — and Train, shaking with laughter, agrees. Dougal sets up the course while Florence, tipped off by Zebedee at the roundabout, arrives to start proceedings. She waves Dougal's flag and the contest is under way, with Ermintrude cheering loudly for Brian. Progress is limited: Dougal reports Brian is already four miles behind, though Florence urges patience and picks flowers for the winner. The race ends in anticlimax when both competitors grind to a halt, equally exhausted. Zebedee drops by to ask whether it is over; Dougal confirms it is and muses about entering them in the Monte Carlo Rally. Florence leaves her bouquet for Dougal to deliver to Brian and Train, and Dougal grumbles, as usual, that everything gets left to him.
This episode is one of the very few in the original run in which Train is clearly shown blinking. The Eric Thompson version was released on BBC Video VHS Volume 3 in 1992.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Mr Rusty frets about his chimney and enlists Zebedee to peer down it — Zebedee re-emerges black with soot, which reduces Mr Rusty to helpless laughter even as Zebedee tries to maintain his dignity. Meanwhile, Florence finds Dougal in the garden proudly displaying what he calls his patent chimney-sweeping device — a contraption he likens to a hedgehog. The whole gang converges on Dougal's house: Brian arrives with a ladder courtesy of Mr McHenry, but when Florence asks who will climb up, everyone flinches. Dougal flatly refuses, Brian pleads that he is legless, and Florence reconsiders after Mr McHenry helpfully notes that dogs can climb ladders. Mr McHenry eventually volunteers, scales the roof, and drops the sweeper straight down the flue, depositing a thick cloud of soot over Brian, then Dougal, and finally Florence herself. Zebedee arrives to find everyone begrimed, Mr McHenry proudly descends to report his progress, and Florence heads home to wash up — Zebedee reminding her, as ever, to bath before bed.
The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as part of BBC Video's "The Magic Roundabout: Volume 3" in 1992 and again on "The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout" in 1993.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal, sporting a tartan hat, has taken it upon himself to instruct Dylan in the noble art of bagpipes — a project Dylan finds both foolish and exhausting. Florence arrives to find the garden in musical chaos, and matters take a turn when Mr. McHenry wanders over demanding to know who is being tortured. He fetches his own bagpipes, only to reveal he has been using them as a watering-can, leaving a conspicuous hole. Florence calls on Zebedee for a needle, and the assembled cast settle on a strand of Dougal's fur as thread. Dougal is having none of it, fleeing around the garden and threatening to report everyone to the RSPCA — and to the head of BBC One — until Mr. McHenry quietly plucks a strand without him noticing. Florence patches the bagpipes, Zebedee calls time for bed and requests a lullaby, and Dougal stomps off muttering darkly.
This episode is one of the few instances in the Eric Thompson version where Dougal breaks the fourth wall by name-dropping the BBC. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as Volume 3 of The Magic Roundabout in 1992, where it was retitled "Dylan Plays the Bagpipes."

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Mr. Rusty cranks up his barrel organ at the roundabout, and Zebedee notes he hasn't played it in quite some time. Florence arrives, delighted, and urges him to play on — though the effort tires him out, and Zebedee promptly teleports her to the garden. There she finds Dougal, unusually subdued. The culprit is a bossy scarecrow who has declared the garden the exclusive preserve of scarecrows and is busy barring birds, dogs, and humans alike. Fed up, Florence calls Zebedee aside and whispers the problem; he conjures flower-patterned fabric and three pairs of scissors, and together they run up a smart new outfit for the scarecrow. Dougal trots back with a bow clamped in his teeth, Florence ties it atop the scarecrow's head, and the transformed figure promptly relaxes her prohibitions — the garden bursts into bloom, and Dougal slips off to chase a few snails to restore his dignity.
In Eric Thompson's version the scarecrow is female, and the original slower, lower-pitched theme tune can be heard at the episode's opening. The Thompson narration was later released on the BBC Video VHS collection Volume 3 in 1992.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence arrives at the roundabout to find Mr Rusty brimming with a splendid idea: a game of hide-and-seek before Zebedee turns up. When Zebedee does arrive, he obliges with a quick teleport to the garden, where the whole gang assembles in high spirits. Brian is elected seeker — over his own protests — and the rest scatter to hide: Dougal squeezes into a vase, Zebedee tucks behind a tree, Dylan settles behind a rock and promptly dozes off, Florence conceals herself behind a tall flower, Mr McHenry crouches behind his motorbike, and Mr Rusty lurks behind some poles. Brian slithers gamely around the garden but struggles to spot anyone, despite Mr Rusty and Mr McHenry being anything but invisible. Mr Rusty gives himself away by muttering aloud; Mr McHenry reluctantly concludes his hiding spot was never going to work; Dougal makes a break for it; Florence surrenders gracefully. Only Dylan remains — fast asleep and never truly in the running. Zebedee wakes him, declares it time for bed, and pronounces everyone thoroughly exhausted.
This is one of the few episodes in which Ermintrude does not appear alongside the main cast. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as part of The Magic Roundabout Volume 3 by BBC Video in 1992, and again on The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout in 1993.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
At the roundabout, Florence learns from Mr Rusty that the television has lost its announcer. Zebedee brings her to the garden, where Brian, Dylan, and Ermintrude all volunteer to fill the vacancy — Dougal cheekily proposes hiring broadcaster Robert Dougal, but Zebedee insists on equal auditions. Ermintrude goes first, advertising milk and delivering an imaginative weather forecast based on her own movements. Dylan settles in to share thoughts on flower power, promptly falls asleep, then shuffles off to find his spotted bowtie once Florence wakes him. Brian gives an earnest address on snail behaviour but is too small to poke his head out of the television set, drawing laughter from Dylan and Dougal. When Dougal's turn arrives he is struck dumb, steadies his nerves with sugar, and decides sugar is his subject after all. Finally, Florence — coaxed past her nerves — steps up and cheerfully tells viewers it is time for bed.
The Eric Thompson narration of this episode was released on LP and cassette in 1971 alongside ten other second-series stories, later reissued to CD in 2005 and 2010; it also appeared on the BBC Video VHS release The Magic Roundabout 4 (1992) and The Very Best of the Magic Roundabout (1993).

programme.title: Mind Your Manners
programme.desc:
A hand draws a cartoon on a blackboard — a couple bumping into each other, tempers fraying — under the chalked warning "Watch it! Your manners are showing!" That gag sets up the day the film then follows: a teenager named Jack moving from the breakfast table to school to the soda shop, with his manners tested at every stop. At home he minds his appearance before a hallway mirror and sits down to a family dinner with his mother, father, and sister. At school he waits his turn in a hallway lined with lockers, ducks into the library, and settles into a crowded classroom. After hours he catches a Glenview Bus Co. coach across town and lands with friends at a windmill-themed soda fountain, where a waitress in Dutch cap and apron works the booths while the kids talk, share, and needle a stalled car with its hood up out at the curb. The film's thesis is practical rather than moralizing: it drills the same short list of courtesies — greetings, waiting, sharing, tidy dress, table manners — through one ordinary day's worth of settings, trusting repetition over lecture.
Coronet Instructional Films of Glenview, Illinois copyrighted the picture in 1953 (the title card reads "Copyright MCMLIII, John Smart") and recorded it on the RCA Sound System, standard for the studio's output at the time. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance cycle, the only name that appears on screen belongs to the educational collaborator: Margaret M. Justin, Ph.D., Dean of the School of Home Economics at Kansas State College, who vetted the etiquette lessons for classroom use. No director is credited on the print, and none is attested for this specific title elsewhere, so none is listed here. The Glenview Bus Co. coach visible mid-film is a nice bit of incidental local color, consistent with the studio's home base outside Chicago.
Like Coronet's other manners-and-conduct shorts of the era, Mind Your Manners was built for classroom rental rather than theatrical release, one entry in a long run of social-guidance titles the company issued through the 1940s and '50s. It has since passed into the public domain and circulates through the Internet Archive and preservation outlets such as A/V Geeks, which catalogue it as a straightforward etiquette lesson built around a teenage character the site names Jack Connor. Seen today, it holds up as a plain, earnest artifact of postwar classroom instruction — a checklist of small courtesies dramatized rather than a story anyone would mistake for entertainment.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
At the roundabout, Florence notices that Zebedee has arrived without his familiar spring sound. He explains he is using his spare spring, so Florence sets off to track down the missing original. In the garden she asks Dougal, who cheerfully misunderstands and assumes she means the season. Ermintrude makes the same mistake and bursts into a song about spring flowers. Florence and Dougal move on to Dylan, who is asleep — Dougal reckons asking him is pointless, but Dylan stirs and insists he knows a thing or two about springs. Their surprise is short-lived when they find Brian the snail joyfully bouncing on what turns out to be Zebedee's spring. Florence scolds him; Brian is unrepentant, declaring he is setting a bold new trend in snail behaviour. He eventually topples off, bending the spring slightly, and shuffles away. Zebedee arrives, surveys the damage, and cheerfully puts everything right — then announces it is time for bed.
The Eric Thompson narration of this episode was released on VHS as part of BBC Video's "The Magic Roundabout Volume 3" (1992) and again on "The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout" (1993).

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.sub-title: The Magic Roundabout (1965) - S02E033 - Dougal's Adventure (Reconstructed)

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dougal runs into Brian in a fluster — he's been up since dawn with a tremendous list of things to accomplish and no time to deal with his untidy hair. Brian offers a barbed observation that a trim would indeed be in order, and Dougal sets off in search of what he insists on calling an "artiste." Meanwhile at the roundabout, Mr. Rusty and Florence admire the weather and exchange pleasantries until Zebedee arrives — late as usual, Florence notes — and the three of them make their way to the garden. There, Florence stumbles upon an impromptu hairdressing boutique, and inside, to her considerable surprise, Dylan is actually working: curlers, setting lotion, the full professional arsenal applied with the rabbit's characteristic mixture of drowsy intensity and near-crisis. When he finally whips the towel away, Dougal cannot see himself and Dylan patiently reminds him to remove the cloth. Florence pretends not to recognise the dog at all, greeting this curly-haired "stranger" with great politeness, before collapsing into helpless laughter. Dougal, spotting a poodle in the mirror and briefly finding it quite amusing, suddenly realises the poodle is him — and races off in a fury to track Dylan down.
The Eric Thompson narration of this episode was released on VHS as part of "The Magic Roundabout: Volume 3" by BBC Video in 1992, and the script was later reprinted in the 1999 book "The Adventures of Dylan."

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: A Christmas Carol adaptation, Gumby-style. Gumby walks into Dickens and encounters Scrooge. The episode aired December 10, 1960 — a holiday special disguised as a regular episode. By this point Clokey had fully developed the book-walking mechanic into the show's signature move: Gumby doesn't retell stories, he physically enters them and participates. Scrooge as a clay figure, hunched and miserly on a miniature set, has a tactile charm that no amount of CGI Christmas Carol adaptations can match.

programme.title: How to Say No
programme.desc:
The film opens on a bare stage behind a drawn curtain. A spotlight finds a teenager named Bill, who steps out to address the audience directly, the way a discussion leader might open a school assembly, then pulls the curtain back to show a living room set where his panel is waiting: Marty, Lucy, Nora, and Howie, sitting around as if the four of them had simply stopped by after school. Their conversation carries the rest of the picture. Marty starts things off describing what happens with "the fellows" after a game or practice, when the group usually stops somewhere and somebody starts passing bottles around; from there the panel works through a pajama-party scene where Lucy and Nora feel the pull to light up along with everyone else, and a couch scene about how far a date is allowed to go. Each vignette resolves the same way: know your own standards before the moment arrives, say no plainly instead of delivering a lecture to the group, and have something else ready to offer in its place — a sandwich and French fries after the game, a joke instead of a cigarette — so that turning something down doesn't cost anybody a friendship.
Coronet Instructional Films copyrighted the picture in 1951 under David A. Smart, and, as with the studio's other guidance shorts, the only name on screen belongs to the consultant rather than any performer: the title card credits Evelyn M. Duvall, Ph.D., of the National Council on Family Relations, as educational collaborator. Duvall was a working family-life researcher, not a studio hire in name only — she had published Facts of Life and Love for Teenagers the year before and would go on to a long career studying adolescent development. Rather than dramatize a single morality tale the way some Coronet shorts do, How to Say No is built almost entirely around the panel's own talk, staged as an informal living-room discussion in front of a studio audience implied by Bill's opening address — a format Coronet leaned on repeatedly in its early-1950s slate of teen guidance titles.
The film belongs to the cycle of "social guidance" shorts Coronet distributed to junior high and high school classrooms through the 1950s, teaching poise and peer resistance around drinking, smoking, and necking through calm, matter-of-fact talk rather than scare tactics. It survives today through the Prelinger Archives, which catalogued it under its full title, How to Say No (Moral Maturity), and the print is in the public domain.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Mr Rusty, Florence, and Zebedee organise a picnic in the Magic Garden, gathering the whole gang along the way. Each character — except Dougal — arrives with a contribution: Zebedee reminds Mr Rusty to bring a corkscrew, Florence supplies a tablecloth (which Dougal immediately worries may attract ants), Brian brings salt-and-pepper shakers and can't resist breaking into a chorus of "For He's a Jolly Good Fellow" about his own usefulness, Ermintrude contributes glasses, Dylan hauls along cushions and sets about napping on them at once, and Mr McHenry rounds things out with plates, cutlery, vases of flowers, and place mats — prompting Dougal to enquire pointedly about finger bowls. When Dylan finally asks where the food is, everyone falls silent: they've laid the most elaborately appointed table in the garden and forgotten to bring a single thing to eat. Brian sums up the situation by calling them all soppy.
The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as part of The Magic Roundabout 4 by BBC Video in 1992, and the script for this version is reprinted in the 1999 novel The Adventures of Dylan.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Dylan wakes from one of his customary naps and begins fretting about his direction in life — specifically whether he sleeps too much. Dougal, nearby and thinking along exactly the same lines, confirms the suspicion with relish. The anxiety tips Dylan over the edge: he lurches between sleepwalking and jolting awake, leaving Brian, Dougal, and Zebedee to watch bemusedly as the rabbit throws himself into a vigorous exercise programme — swimming over a stool, shadow boxing, and general sprinting. Florence, meanwhile, joins Zebedee at the roundabout for a few gentle exercises of her own. After the full exertion, Dylan collapses with exhaustion while Florence, Brian, and Dougal count down the seconds. When Florence asks whether the effort helped, Dylan cheerfully concludes that changing his natural way of life is simply not for him, and races off before Dougal can deliver a lecture. Zebedee calls time for bed; Dylan, sword in hand, replies "Touché!"
Although broadcast as a Series 2 episode, the production is actually a surviving colour Series 1 holdover, making it unusual in the run. Eric Thompson's narration was released on BBC Video VHS Volume 4 in 1992, and the accompanying script appeared in the published book "The Adventures of Dylan".

programme.title: Developing Friendships
programme.desc:
Bob McGraw used to walk home from school by himself, keeping to his own thoughts and not much minding the company. Then the other fellows start talking about the baskets Joe has been sinking, and Bob can't see what the excitement is about — after all, he'd been the one they used to call the best player, and he decides he doesn't need a rival crowding him out. But Joe keeps being decent in ways that are hard to resent: he credits his teammates instead of taking the bow himself, he goes out of his way for a floundering, awkward classmate named Eddie, and he treats a girl named Marie with the same plain courtesy he shows everyone else. Won over more or less against his will, Bob starts falling in with Joe and the circle of friends who gather around him, and when Joe enters — and wins — a statewide essay contest on Junior Citizenship, earning himself a trip to the capital, Bob is one of the gang who piles into a car and races to the station to welcome him home. That homecoming is the film's frame: the whole account of how the group came together unfolds as Bob's recollection while the friends wait together on the depot benches.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films out of Glenview, Illinois, and released to classrooms on August 19, 1950, with Ted Peshak directing, as he did much of Coronet's postwar guidance output. Coronet's usual practice was to reserve its one on-screen credit for the psychology consultant attached to a film, but the print circulating today opens directly on the station-platform scene, with no title or collaborator card surviving in it to transcribe; the young cast, drawn from the same pool of Chicago-area teenagers who turn up across the studio's other 1950 shorts, likewise goes unbilled on screen.
"Developing Friendships" belongs to a cluster of Coronet titles from the same year — Developing Leadership, The Fun of Making Friends, How Friendly Are You? — built around the same basic civics-class argument: that popularity and belonging are skills to be learned rather than traits you either have or don't, with a model classmate on hand to demonstrate the technique. Where a companion film like Are You Popular? measures its heroine against a cautionary rival, this one works by simple contrast between Bob's early standoffishness and Joe's easy generosity. The film survives in the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive, part of the large body of Coronet's classroom output that passed into the public domain and now circulates as the same plain print schools once rented by mail.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Florence arrives at the roundabout to find Mr Rusty at his barrel organ, then heads into the garden with Zebedee where she discovers Dougal in a state of high agitation. After much dithering, he finally confesses the awful truth: Ermintrude is flying a kite, which he considers thoroughly unnatural. Florence thinks it sounds delightful, and the two find the cow in a blissfully contented mood, string in hoof. Dougal gallantly offers her some flowers to nibble, and before he can politely decline Ermintrude's return invitation to have a go on the kite, he finds himself yanked skyward above the treetops, hollering for rescue. Florence is mildly concerned; Ermintrude is serenely confident he'll come down eventually. He does — straight into a pile of firewood, emerging even more agitated than before.
This episode is one of six series-2 episodes produced before the feature film Dougal and the Blue Cat, and features Ermintrude's updated character model, which was subsequently used in that film and carried forward into series 3. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as part of BBC Video's Volume 4 in 1992 and again on The Very Best of The Magic Roundabout in 1993.

programme.title: The Magic Roundabout
programme.desc:
Mr McHenry is searching the garden for something and enlists Florence's help, though he's oddly cagey about what it is. Dougal, Brian, Ermintrude, and Dylan are also hunting around — only Dougal knows the target. Before long a strange flying object descends from the sky, prods at the ground, then shoots back up again, giving everyone a considerable fright. When Mr McHenry returns still fretting about his missing contraption, Dougal confirms it: the culprit is the gardener's new automated flying planting machine. Dylan, who has been trying to sleep, complains that it has been buzzing over him and sowing primrose roots all over him in the process. Florence diplomatically suggests it might be time for bed, though Dougal is less than optimistic about a quiet night with a seed-planting saucer still on the loose.
The music composed for this episode was later reused in the original score for "Wild Western" in series 3. The Eric Thompson narration was released on VHS as part of Volume 4 in 1992, and the script was reprinted in the 1999 novel The Adventures of Dylan.

programme.title: Gumby
programme.desc: Gumby has a daydream adventure with a young dinosaur named Trixie, providing what the original synopsis calls "an authentic view of pre-historic times." The companion episode, "Egg Trouble," continues the adventure with volcanoes, earthquakes, and a dinosaur stampede. Clokey loved sending Gumby into other eras and worlds — dinosaur land was a natural destination for a character who could walk into any book. The "authentic" view of prehistory is, of course, cheerfully inaccurate, but Clokey's clay dinosaurs have a tactile charm that CGI will never replicate. You can almost feel the fingerprints on Trixie.

programme.title: The Golden Rule
programme.desc:
The film opens with the maxim itself rather than a single character: a carved relief accompanies the King James wording of Luke 6:31, "As ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise," and a teacher then chalks the plainer classroom version - "The Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you" - on the blackboard for a room of young pupils. A world map follows, with hands pinning flags marking the Holy Land and China, showing the same rule recurring in cultures on opposite sides of the globe. From there the lesson moves into ordinary childhood settings rather than a single continuous story: a family sits down to dinner together, two girls stop to talk at a backyard fence and then walk on down the sidewalk, boys play in the street on a bicycle and a tricycle, and in the closing minutes a boy folds and flies a paper airplane, then carries it down the block to share with a girl waiting at her door. Onscreen captions - "as you would have them," "what you would like" - punctuate the vignettes, restating the lesson each time the setting changes.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio on the Smart family estate in Glenview, Illinois, the picture is copyrighted 1953 to John Smart, who took over Coronet's productions after his brother and the company's founder, David A. Smart, died in 1952. The subtitle "A Lesson for Beginners" marks it as one of Coronet's primary-grade releases rather than the junior- and senior-high guidance shorts the studio is best remembered for. As on those films, the only credited participant is the educational collaborator named on the title card: A. M. Johnston, Ph.D., Associate Professor of Education at the University of Tennessee, recorded on the RCA Sound System. No director or cast is credited on screen.
The film belongs to the broad run of postwar "social guidance" shorts Coronet produced through the late 1940s and 1950s, which leaned on local nonprofessional performers rather than name actors to model behavior for classroom audiences. "The Golden Rule" is thinly documented outside its own print: it has no IMDb entry, and no Letterboxd or TMDb page could be located for it. The surviving copy has circulated through the stock-footage archive A.V. Geeks, whose catalogue description likewise characterizes the film as a series of everyday vignettes illustrating the rule - matching what the print itself shows.

programme.title: Carnival of the Animals
programme.desc: Joanna Lumley narrates Saint-Saëns' beloved musical menagerie with the London Mozart Players, set to animated illustrations by freelance designer Cat Fuller. Part of the LMP's "At Home with LMP" series launched during the COVID lockdown, this digital rendition pairs each of the fourteen movements with colorful animal animations while Lumley reads poetry written specially for the project by LMP violinist Martin Smith. The result is a pocket-sized masterpiece of family entertainment: the royal march of the lion, hens pecking in the barnyard, wild donkeys galloping across the steppe, tortoises performing the can-can in devastating slow motion (Saint-Saëns quoting Offenbach at funereal tempo), an elephant waltzing to Mendelssohn and Berlioz transposed to the deepest instrument in the orchestra (the double bass — his wickedest orchestration joke), kangaroos bouncing, an aquarium shimmering behind glass harmonica arpeggios, a cuckoo calling from the depths of the woods, birds fluttering in an aviary, pianists practicing their scales (Saint-Saëns classified pianists as animals — his wickedest taxonomic joke), fossils dancing a xylophone danse macabre, and the sublime swan, whose cello solo is the most famous piece he ever wrote and the only movement he allowed published in his lifetime. Saint-Saëns composed the whole suite in February 1886 in a small Austrian village after a disastrous German concert tour, writing to his publisher Durand that he knew he should be working on his Third Symphony but that this was "such fun" ("mais c'est si amusant!"). He premiered it privately at cellist Charles Lebouc's salon on March 3, 1886, with a lineup including Louis Diémer and Paul Taffanel. Franz Liszt himself requested a private hearing at Pauline Viardot's home. Subsequent performances featured musicians wearing masks of the animals they represented. Saint-Saëns was adamant the work never be published in his lifetime, terrified it would damage his reputation as a Serious Composer. He specified in his will that it should be published posthumously. He died in December 1921; Durand published the score in April 1922; the first public performance on February 25, 1922 by the Concerts Colonne under Gabriel Pierné was rapturously received — Le Figaro reported "cries of admiring joy" from the audience. Lumley, a self-confessed classical music fan, called the collaboration "thrilling" and noted that "music is more important than ever" in times of isolation.

programme.title: Social Courtesy
programme.desc:
Bill primps in front of his bedroom mirror, getting ready for a costume party with his girlfriend Carol, and grumbles that all this fuss over manners is old-fashioned. An unseen narrator disagrees, and makes Bill live with the consequences: every time the boy is rude, the narrator freezes the scene, "takes a picture" of it — the moment dissolves into a photograph hanging on the wall of the next shot — and rewinds Bill back to try again, a little more friendly this time. At the party itself, a teenage rec room dressed up as a hobo jungle, with hand-lettered signs reading "To Train," "Track 1," "Keep Out," and "Baggage Checked" strung up among the decorations, Bill argues under his breath with a voice nobody else can hear, until one of the girls asks if he's talking to himself. Bit by bit he tries doing what he's told — standing when an adult speaks to him, sitting up instead of slouching, actually listening to his friends — and by the last reel the chaperone is remarking on what a changed, courteous boy he's become; Bill leaves already holding an invitation to the next party.
The only screen credit belongs to the educational collaborator: the opening title cards name Mary E. Weathersby, Head of the Homemaking Education Department at Mississippi State College, in the standard Coronet slot for the psychologist or home-economics consultant behind the lesson plan. The copyright card reads MCMLI under the name of Coronet founder David A. Smart, and the print carries the RCA Sound System mark seen across the line. The finished film runs ten minutes sixteen seconds, and the Prelinger Archives catalog credits the camera work to Bruce Colling. No director or performer is named on screen, and none has turned up in any reliable secondary source for this particular title.
Social Courtesy belongs to the same wave of early-1950s Coronet social-guidance shorts as Are You Popular? and Shy Guy, but it handles the genre's usual show-and-correct formula more strangely than most: an audibly bickering, fourth-wall-breaking narrator, freeze-frames that turn into snapshots on a wall, and a scene structure that keeps backing up and starting over. Ken Smith singled it out in his 1999 study of the genre, Mental Hygiene: Classroom Films 1945-1970, as one of the most inventive films Coronet ever made. It has since passed into the public domain and is preserved in the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Graham Ralph of Silver Fox Films — a prolific British animation director whose career spans from the original Danger Mouse (1981) through Funnybones, Toucan Tecs, Cadillacs and Dinosaurs, William's Wish Wellingtons, The Forgotten Toys, and more recently Harry and His Bucket Full of Dinosaurs for Cartoon Network. In 1989, Ralph and Jerry Hibbert launched Hibbert Ralph Entertainment (HRE), with Ralph at the helm seeking creative challenges beyond the advertising work that had built their reputation. By 2005, he was directing The Magic Roundabout CGI TV series (following the 2005 feature film), advising young animators at Cartoon Master in Potsdam: "Give the audience something they have never seen before. They are hungry nasty things."
For Rhinegold, Ralph farmed the animation to Carlos Alfonso Animation in Madrid — a Welsh-Spanish co-production within the larger Operavox framework. Paul Shardlow designed it. The result was what Charles Solomon accurately described as trying "to turn Wagner's Das Rheingold into Heavy Metal, with Freya in a Frazetta-esque bikini." One DVD reviewer echoed: "What's with Freia wearing a string bikini? What crazy animator came up with that?"
The approach is maximalist fantasy illustration applied to the first opera of Wagner's sixteen-hour Ring Cycle. Gods, giants, dwarves, underwater Rhinemaidens — Ralph's drawn animation renders them with the visual vocabulary of 1980s pulp fantasy, which either suits or insults Wagner depending on your tolerance. The condensation of a two-and-a-half-hour opera into half an hour is inevitably brutal, but the same reviewer noted that "being a short opera by Ring standards, it worked okay being cut down" and that "Wagner's fantastic music is perfect for an animated fantasy film."
Sung by Phillip Joll, Penelope Walker, and Janice Watson, with the Welsh National Opera conducted by David Seaman. English translation by Amanda Holden, Welsh translation by Manon Williams and Wyn Davies. Executive producer Chris Grace, script editors Penelope Middleboe and Martin Lamb. IMDB 7.5.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Nina Simone's 1965 ten-minute tour de force from Pastel Blues, based on a traditional African-American spiritual. Simone recorded it in a single take. The song builds from a whispered plea to a full piano-and-voice storm.

programme.title: The Fun of Being Thoughtful
programme.desc:
Jane Proctor is a cheerful teenager who is, in archivist Ken Smith's later phrase, "slavishly devoted" to her family's happiness, and the film catalogues one evening of it: she tidies her room, helps get dinner on the table amid a bit of kitchen panic over the mashed potatoes, and — the plot's real engine — works to fix up her awkward brother Eddie with a date for the following night. Eddie, whose voice keeps threatening to crack, gripes along the way that he "hasn't a thing to wear" either. Jane's persistent thoughtfulness pays off in the last scene: she comes down the stairs in a new dress to her parents' and Eddie's evident delight, and the household settles back into its usual harmony.
Produced at Coronet's studio in Glenview, Illinois and copyrighted in 1950 (the title card reads MCML) by David A. Smart, who had founded the company with his brother Alfred as an offshoot of their Esquire magazine business. As with the rest of Coronet's postwar social-guidance catalog, the teenage cast goes uncredited; the only name in the titles belongs to the psychology consultant, credited on screen as Educational Collaborator Ernest M. Ligon, Ph.D., director of the Character Research Project at Union College in Schenectady, New York. Ligon had founded the Character Research Project in 1935 and would direct it for over four decades, building its work on ideas he had laid out in his earlier book The Psychology of Christian Personality. Directing credit likewise appears nowhere on screen, but Ted Peshak — the Glenview house director credited with roughly 350 educational films for Coronet — lists Fun of Being Thoughtful among his 1950 directing credits. The uncredited actor playing Eddie Proctor was a Coronet regular: a retrospective tracing faces across the studio's uncredited teen stock company notes that the same performer's voice had not yet finished cracking a year earlier in The Meaning of Pi (1949), and that he turns up again later in 1950 as Eddie in Developing Friendships and as Ed Parker in How to Get Cooperation.
The print survives through the Prelinger Archives on the Internet Archive, in the public domain along with the rest of that collection. Prelinger's cataloguer Ken Smith, whose notes on Coronet's output were later folded into his book Mental Hygiene: Better Living Through Classroom Films, 1945-1970, flagged the script's habit of chasing several morals inside ten minutes as "fun but a little hard to follow" — a fair description of a film that covers housework, dating, dress shopping, and hospitality all in one sitting. It belongs to the postwar "social guidance" genre Coronet all but defined for American classrooms, in which ordinary household courtesy is treated as a small-scale rehearsal for the larger civic virtues — responsibility, cooperation, good citizenship — that the studio's other shorts preached more directly.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Barnaby Dixon's puppet performs Merle Travis's 1946 coal miner's lament, later made famous by Tennessee Ernie Ford's 1955 version that spent eight weeks at #1. Dixon is a British puppeteer from southwest England who builds intricate finger puppets — his fingers control the feet while hinges, levers, and string mechanisms make the rest of the body move with startling naturalism.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Patti Page's 1950 hit performed as a puppet floor jam. 'The Tennessee Waltz' was one of the best-selling singles of the 20th century, spending thirteen weeks at #1. Page recorded it as a B-side; the DJ flipped it.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: The Beatles, Abbey Road (1969). McCartney found the lyrics to Thomas Dekker's 1603 lullaby on a piano at his father's house in Liverpool. He couldn't read music well enough to play the original melody, so he wrote his own.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Dixon's UV-reactive puppet troupe — skeletal figures that glow under blacklight. A completely different aesthetic from his naturalistic wooden puppets, these are pure spectacle designed for dark-room performance.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.sub-title: John the Revelator - HAIRY NEON BOYS
programme.desc: The Hairy Neon Boys perform the traditional gospel/blues song, recorded by Blind Willie Johnson in 1930 and covered by everyone from Son House to Depeche Mode. The blacklight puppet treatment gives the apocalyptic lyrics an appropriately otherworldly feel.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: A live-streamed puppet performance. Dixon occasionally does these to interact with his audience in real time, improvising puppet routines in response to chat.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Smokey Robinson and the Miracles, 1967 (released as single 1970, hit #1). Robinson wrote it with Stevie Wonder and Hank Cosby. Robinson said the circus-flavored melody Wonder brought him demanded sad-clown lyrics — he found the concept in the opera Pagliacci.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: The return of Dixon's Wick puppet character. Dixon builds ongoing narratives around his puppet characters, giving them personalities and arcs across multiple videos — a serialized puppet universe on YouTube.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Wick — another of Dixon's puppet characters — performs 'Into the Unknown' from Frozen II (2019), written by Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez. The puppet's small scale against the epic Disney ballad creates deliberate comic contrast.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Georgian folk song. The trio has had several lineup changes — past members include Irina Midelauri, Elene Nareshelashvili, Anuka Chincharauli, and Shorena Tsiskalauri — but the core sound remains: three women, a panduri, and centuries of vocal tradition.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A song from the Mtiuleti region in the mountainous center of Georgia, near the Georgian Military Highway. Mountain songs tend to be more austere and powerful than lowland songs — fewer ornaments, bigger intervals, voices that have to carry across valleys.

programme.title: Feeling Left Out
programme.desc:
Mike Hanlon is a popular type on paper — a football player with a letter jacket of his own — but the picture keeps returning to him standing at the edge of the same locker-lined hallway, watching a knot of letter-sweater boys trade jokes without him. He follows them into gym class, gripping the same chin-up bar, working the same jump rope, matching them stride for stride physically, and none of it earns him a way in; the group simply isn't built to admit one more. A coach notices him hanging back and makes the turn explicit: cliques form and close for reasons that have nothing to do with a boy's worth, and chasing one closed circle is a poor way to spend a school year. By the last reel Mike has stopped angling for the group and started talking to people one at a time — a girl bent over her books in study hall, a boy blowing a saxophone at a school function, a classmate he simply falls into step with in the hall. The film ends not with Mike joining the clique but with him no longer needing to.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films, Feeling Left Out follows the house formula of putting only one name in front of the camera — the collaborating academic. The distributor's own catalog credits Paul H. Landis, Ph.D., professor of sociology at the State College of Washington (today Washington State University), as the film's educational collaborator, the standard Coronet arrangement of borrowing a working social scientist to vouch for the lesson on screen. Coronet released the picture in 1951 as a classroom-rental 16mm sound short, part of the same wave of adolescent social-adjustment titles as Shy Guy and Are You Popular. As with most Coronet shorts of the period, the students playing Mike and his classmates went uncredited, and no director is named in surviving prints or distributor records for this title specifically.
The film survives through the A/V Geeks ephemeral-film collection, which placed its 16mm print on the Internet Archive under a Public Domain Mark; the distributor's own synopsis there — a boy who "wants friends but... concentrates on becoming friendly with a certain group of boys" rather than individuals — matches the picture beat for beat. It sits comfortably alongside Coronet's other clique-anxiety shorts of the era, all working from the same premise: that adolescent unhappiness is a solvable technical problem, and exclusion a symptom a level-headed adult and a change of strategy can fix before the closing titles.

programme.title: The Point!
programme.desc: In the Land of Point, everyone and everything has a point — except Oblio, the only round-headed boy in a kingdom of pointed heads, who has worn a pointed hat since birth to hide his difference. When the son of an evil count loses to Oblio at Triangle Toss (a game where you catch triangles on your head), the count demands enforcement of the law: pointless things must be banished. Oblio and his dog Arrow are sent into the Pointless Forest, where they discover that even the Pointless Forest has a point. They meet a man pointing in all directions who declares: "A point in every direction is the same as no point at all." They meet a rock man, dancing fat sisters, and a tree who helps Oblio see that everyone has a point. When Oblio returns and tells the kingdom what he's learned, the furious count rips off his hat — and finds a point on top of Oblio's bare head. Upon this revelation, the points of everyone else disappear and the pointed buildings become round. Harry Nilsson wrote, produced, and performed all the music. He was born in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn in 1941. His father abandoned the family when Harry was three — his song "1941" opens: "Well, in 1941, a happy father had a son / And by 1944, the father walked right out the door." Due to poverty, he dropped out after ninth grade and lied about graduating high school to get a job as a computer programmer at a bank. He worked the night shift on bank computers and spent his days writing songs. His uncle in San Bernardino gave him singing lessons. When his songs started getting recorded — by the Monkees, by Phil Spector, by Glen Campbell — Nilsson still didn't quit the bank. He never performed live concerts, one of the only major pop artists in history to achieve fame without touring. When the Beatles were asked at a 1968 Apple Corps press conference to name their favorite American artist, John Lennon said "Nilsson." Paul McCartney was asked to name his favorite American group. He also said "Nilsson." Lennon had listened to Nilsson's album Pandemonium Shadow Show for 36 straight hours. The two became close friends. During Lennon's "Lost Weekend" separation from Yoko in the mid-1970s, he and Nilsson were members of the Hollywood Vampires drinking club, notorious for alcohol-fueled incidents at the Troubadour. They made one album together, Pussy Cats (1974). After Lennon's murder in 1980, Nilsson left the music industry to campaign for gun control. He died of heart failure in 1994 at 52. The inspiration for The Point came to Nilsson on LSD: "I was on acid and I looked at the trees and I realized that they all came to points, and the little branches came to points, and the houses each came to a point. I thought, 'Oh! Everything has a point, and if it doesn't, then there's still a point to it.'" He wrote a twelve-page illustrated treatment and first pitched it to Hanna-Barbera, who passed. Fred Wolf of Murakami-Wolf Films took it on. Wolf skipped pencil tests entirely and went straight to ink-and-paint, giving the film its loose, handmade look. He worked nights and slept days through the entire production. The original story collaborator, Carole Beers, started steering the narrative toward science fiction; Nilsson, protective of his concept, was not pleased, so Wolf brought in Norm Lenzer to write the screenplay. Production began before a script existed. Mike Lookinland — Bobby Brady — voiced Oblio. In a waiting room before a recording session, young Lookinland was making car noises when his mother told him to be quiet. A man stood up, walked over, and said: "Lady, don't ever tell your kid to be quiet. I make my living on sound." The man was Mel Blanc. The film first aired February 2, 1971 on ABC's Movie of the Week — the first animated feature ever broadcast in prime time on American television. Dustin Hoffman, a friend of Nilsson's, agreed to narrate for $20,000 on the condition that his voice be used for one broadcast only. For later airings, the narration had to be completely re-recorded — first by Alan Barzman, then by Alan Thicke for cable, and finally by Ringo Starr for the home video release. Our version has the Alan Thicke narration, the third telecast restoration. The album's art director was Dean Torrance — of Jan and Dean ("Surf City"). Nilsson instructed that the design have points but no circles. The sales sticker on the shrink-wrap was a triangle. The cover illustration was hand-stitched in needlepoint by Torrance's wife Kathy. The album's arranger, George Tipton, was Nilsson's equivalent of George Martin — the last Nilsson album he arranged. Tipton had invested his life savings of $2,500 to finance Nilsson's first four recordings. The song "Me and My Arrow" became a hit single and, in the way of the early 1970s, ended up in a television commercial. The London stage adaptation at the Mermaid Theatre in 1977 starred Davy Jones and Micky Dolenz of the Monkees — who had been among the first artists to record Nilsson's songs, and who remained his close friends until his death. Nilsson also inspired the name Aerosmith: drummer Joey Kramer was listening to Nilsson's album Aerial Ballet, started riffing on the word "aerial," someone said "smith," and a band was born.

programme.title: Understand Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Mr. Brent, a high-school biology teacher, opens by springing a jack-in-the-box on his class to make a simple point: the same jolt doesn't hit everybody the same way. From there the lesson turns diagnostic. Working with three students — among them a boy named Larry — Brent lifts a plastic brain off his desk and traces the thalamus as the switching point where a stimulus becomes a feeling, then wires a student's fingers to a gauge to record the body's own evidence: racing pulse, tightened stomach, sweating palms, each mapped onto a cutaway silhouette on the wall chart. He walks the class through a wired maze holding a white mouse, using shock and cheese to demonstrate conditioning directly, then chalks the idea up as an equation: S¹, a dentist, produces only curiosity; S², his drill, produces fear. The blackboard closes the period the way it opened, as a formula — fear, rage, and love as raw material, conditioning as the process that shapes them, emotional maturity as the goal.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and copyrighted 1950 ("Copyright MCML David A. Smart," per the title card, naming Coronet's founder and the publisher of Esquire and Coronet magazines), recorded on the RCA Sound System. As with the rest of the line, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College — in real life the head of Iowa State's driver-research program and author of The Psychology of Driving, lending his credentials here to classroom emotion theory rather than his usual traffic-safety work. None of Coronet's young actors are named on screen; period research into the studio's stock company has since identified the boy playing Larry as John Galvarro, who played the same character, Larry, in Coronet's Are You Ready for Marriage? the same year and went on to small roles in Service and Citizenship (1951) and the Encyclopaedia Britannica short Drug Addiction.
The film belongs to Coronet's early-1950s run of shorts built around the vocabulary of behaviorist psychology — Control Your Emotions, made the same year, dramatizes the same three emotions through a teenager's bad Friday, while this one drops the story in favor of the lab: mice, wiring, and a plastic brain standing in for a plot. Ken Smith, whose capsule notes for the Prelinger Archives remain the standard reference for the genre, filed it as "even more Skinnerist than Control Your Emotions, and much less entertaining" — a fair verdict on a film that treats its teenage subjects less as characters than as case studies. Like most of the Coronet guidance catalog it has long since lapsed into the public domain and survives today through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Mario Cavalli through his company Pizazz Pictures (later known as pizazz, and later still absorbed into what became Studio AKA — now one of Britain's most respected animation houses). Cavalli has over 30 years of directing TV commercials and short films "in animation, live action, and in various innovative techniques of his own invention," as the Animate Projects archive describes him. His films — including Soho Square and The Cask of Amontillado (an Edgar Allan Poe adaptation) — have won major awards throughout the world.
For Carmen, Cavalli chose rotoscope: filming live actors performing Bizet's opera, then painting over the footage frame by frame with animator Ashley Potter handling the cinematography. The technique has a distinguished lineage — the Fleischer Brothers invented it in the 1910s, Ralph Bakshi built a career on it, and Linklater later elevated it in Waking Life and A Scanner Darkly — but it's polarizing. Charles Solomon called the result "singularly ugly — and barely animated." A DVD reviewer was kinder: "Some of it works quite well, but it's not quite as otherworldly as some of the other episodes (but then again, the Carmen story isn't quite as otherworldly either)."
The approach has a logic to it: Carmen is the most realistic opera in the series — no gods, no magic, no puppets. Seville tobacco workers, soldiers, smugglers, a bullfighter. Painting over real bodies preserves a groundedness that puppets or cel animation would lose. Whether that groundedness helps or fights the medium is the open question.
Sung by Jean Rigby (Carmen), Adrian Thompson (Don José), and Donald Maxwell (Escamillo), with the Welsh National Opera conducted by Julian Smith. Produced by Pizazz Pictures for S4C/BBC. IMDB 7.3 — the lowest-rated of the six, though Cavalli's technique has gained appreciation since. Contains animated nudity.

programme.title: Mind Your Manners
programme.desc:
A hand draws a cartoon on a blackboard — a couple bumping into each other, tempers fraying — under the chalked warning "Watch it! Your manners are showing!" That gag sets up the day the film then follows: a teenager named Jack moving from the breakfast table to school to the soda shop, with his manners tested at every stop. At home he minds his appearance before a hallway mirror and sits down to a family dinner with his mother, father, and sister. At school he waits his turn in a hallway lined with lockers, ducks into the library, and settles into a crowded classroom. After hours he catches a Glenview Bus Co. coach across town and lands with friends at a windmill-themed soda fountain, where a waitress in Dutch cap and apron works the booths while the kids talk, share, and needle a stalled car with its hood up out at the curb. The film's thesis is practical rather than moralizing: it drills the same short list of courtesies — greetings, waiting, sharing, tidy dress, table manners — through one ordinary day's worth of settings, trusting repetition over lecture.
Coronet Instructional Films of Glenview, Illinois copyrighted the picture in 1953 (the title card reads "Copyright MCMLIII, John Smart") and recorded it on the RCA Sound System, standard for the studio's output at the time. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance cycle, the only name that appears on screen belongs to the educational collaborator: Margaret M. Justin, Ph.D., Dean of the School of Home Economics at Kansas State College, who vetted the etiquette lessons for classroom use. No director is credited on the print, and none is attested for this specific title elsewhere, so none is listed here. The Glenview Bus Co. coach visible mid-film is a nice bit of incidental local color, consistent with the studio's home base outside Chicago.
Like Coronet's other manners-and-conduct shorts of the era, Mind Your Manners was built for classroom rental rather than theatrical release, one entry in a long run of social-guidance titles the company issued through the 1940s and '50s. It has since passed into the public domain and circulates through the Internet Archive and preservation outlets such as A/V Geeks, which catalogue it as a straightforward etiquette lesson built around a teenage character the site names Jack Connor. Seen today, it holds up as a plain, earnest artifact of postwar classroom instruction — a checklist of small courtesies dramatized rather than a story anyone would mistake for entertainment.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.sub-title: Can this VINTAGE SYNTH do Country？
programme.desc: Dixon pairs his puppetry with a vintage synthesizer to see if the instrument can handle country music. He's a multi-instrumentalist as well as a puppeteer — many of his videos feature him performing the music his puppets dance to.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.sub-title: Come Wayward Souls - recreated with Puppets
programme.desc: A puppet recreation of the haunting song from Cartoon Network's Over the Garden Wall (2014), sung by Jack Jones in the original. The show's autumnal folk-horror aesthetic translates perfectly to Dixon's handcrafted puppet world.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Dabchick — Dixon's signature puppet, a small bird with expressive head movements — performs a traditional spiritual. Dabchick was Dixon's breakout creation, the puppet that first went viral and established his YouTube channel. He later rebuilt Dabchick with a sleeker, more refined mechanism.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Second improvised puppet dance session. Dixon's approach to puppetry is kinesthetic rather than narrative — he's more interested in how a puppet moves than what it says, which is why his musical performances feel so alive.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: A puppet dance routine featuring one of Dixon's characters smoking — the kind of irreverent detail that separates his work from children's puppetry. His puppets are characters with vices.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Dixon's puppet performs an unnamed song in deliberately strange fashion — part of his ongoing experiment in seeing how far puppet performance can push a familiar tune into uncanny territory.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Manu is Dixon's warrior puppet — a humanoid figure with articulated limbs that Dixon controls with both hands. Manu was one of his first viral creations, demonstrating a new finger-puppet mechanism that allowed unprecedented range of motion.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A song from the Kakheti region of eastern Georgia — the country's wine country, where wine has been made continuously for 8,000 years. Kakhetian folk songs tend to have a more structured, formal quality than the wild polyphony of the western mountain regions.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Polish folk song ('Little Linden') performed by Georgian singers — a cross-cultural experiment that works because Polish folk melody and Georgian vocal harmony share an affinity for modal scales and open intervals. The video was a hit in Poland.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Georgian folk song. The title roughly translates as something about a young woman. Trio Mandili's achievement is making Georgian polyphony accessible to a global audience without diluting it — they don't add beats or synthesizers, they just sing in fields and kitchens and let the voices do the work.

programme.title: The Golden Rule
programme.desc:
The film opens with the maxim itself rather than a single character: a carved relief accompanies the King James wording of Luke 6:31, "As ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise," and a teacher then chalks the plainer classroom version - "The Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you" - on the blackboard for a room of young pupils. A world map follows, with hands pinning flags marking the Holy Land and China, showing the same rule recurring in cultures on opposite sides of the globe. From there the lesson moves into ordinary childhood settings rather than a single continuous story: a family sits down to dinner together, two girls stop to talk at a backyard fence and then walk on down the sidewalk, boys play in the street on a bicycle and a tricycle, and in the closing minutes a boy folds and flies a paper airplane, then carries it down the block to share with a girl waiting at her door. Onscreen captions - "as you would have them," "what you would like" - punctuate the vignettes, restating the lesson each time the setting changes.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio on the Smart family estate in Glenview, Illinois, the picture is copyrighted 1953 to John Smart, who took over Coronet's productions after his brother and the company's founder, David A. Smart, died in 1952. The subtitle "A Lesson for Beginners" marks it as one of Coronet's primary-grade releases rather than the junior- and senior-high guidance shorts the studio is best remembered for. As on those films, the only credited participant is the educational collaborator named on the title card: A. M. Johnston, Ph.D., Associate Professor of Education at the University of Tennessee, recorded on the RCA Sound System. No director or cast is credited on screen.
The film belongs to the broad run of postwar "social guidance" shorts Coronet produced through the late 1940s and 1950s, which leaned on local nonprofessional performers rather than name actors to model behavior for classroom audiences. "The Golden Rule" is thinly documented outside its own print: it has no IMDb entry, and no Letterboxd or TMDb page could be located for it. The surviving copy has circulated through the stock-footage archive A.V. Geeks, whose catalogue description likewise characterizes the film as a series of everyday vignettes illustrating the rule - matching what the print itself shows.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Nataliya Borisovna Dabizha (Наталья Борисовна Дабижа), one of Russia's most honored animators — Honoured Artist of the Russian Federation, Academician of the Nika Academy of Cinematic Arts, Emmy Award winner (Animator of the Year, Los Angeles, 1996), and recipient of the honorary prize at the San Marino International Film Festival for outstanding contribution to world animation (2012).
Dabizha graduated from the Moscow Theatre Art School as a puppetry artist in 1967 and spent two years at the legendary Sergey Obraztsov Central Puppet Theater before joining Soyuzmultfilm in 1969. She organized Soyuzmultfilm's animator training courses in 1979-80, became a director in 1982, and built a filmography of puppet films including The Mouse and the Cat (1983), Lonely Piano (1986), and the Bambr trilogy (1988-91). When Soyuzmultfilm collapsed, she moved to Christmas Films (1991-2000), where she animated The Tempest and The Winter's Tale for Shakespeare: The Animated Tales, and directed The Barber of Seville for Operavox.
She later returned to Soyuzmultfilm (2000-2008) before coming full circle: since 2012, she has been General Director of Christmas Films — the studio Babakhina founded, where the S4C pipeline was born. She teaches animation directing at the Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography (VGIK). Her late husband was the screenwriter D.S. Polonsky. Two documentaries have been made about her: One Role for Life (1997) and In Perfect Harmony (2005).
For Rossini's comedy, Dabizha brought traditional Russian puppet animation with a light touch — liveried servants wander around adjusting the miniature "sets" throughout the performance, breaking the fourth wall of an already farcical opera. Charles Solomon compared it to Gilbert and Sullivan. A DVD reviewer called it "a lot of fun" — the puppet servants stealing scenes from Figaro's scheming. IMDB 8.3 — tied with The Magic Flute for the highest-rated episode.
Sung by Donald Maxwell (Figaro), Peter Bronder (Count Almaviva), Patricia Bardon (Rosina), and Andrew Shore (Dr. Bartolo), with the Welsh National Opera conducted by Gareth Jones. Produced by Christmas Films and Renat Zinnurov.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A traditional Georgian song. Trio Mandili have released three albums: With Love (2015), Enguro (2017), and Sakartvelo (2021), all on EL Italia. Their vinyl was released on Merlins Nose Records in Germany.

programme.title: How to Study
programme.desc:
Jim is a schoolboy handed a civics assignment: the teacher chalks up three current-events questions — should the federal government control medicine, should there be state control of radio and television, should labor unions be required to incorporate — and each student picks one to turn into a written report. Jim takes the labor-union question, and the film follows him treating the job like research rather than homework: he pencils a work schedule onto a wall calendar, then works through a stack of reference books — a general encyclopedia and a bound volume of the Readers' Guide to Periodical Literature — reading each one at a different speed depending on the job at hand, from a fast scan to find what's relevant to a slow, careful pass through the dense print on incorporation law and old court cases like Coronado Coal Company v. United Mine Workers. He boils what he finds down to three study questions, re-reads to check them, and writes the report up with time to spare on his pocket watch.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, the picture follows the house formula: the only credit on screen is the educational collaborator, here William G. Brink, Ph.D., Professor of Education at Northwestern University, named on the same title card as the RCA sound-system credit and nowhere else.
