Brink's own published work of the period concerned the study of classroom teaching materials, which tracks with the film's close attention to differentiated reading speeds — presented less as moralizing than as a plain set of techniques, the scan/skim/read-closely/re-read sequence that library and study-skills instruction would keep teaching for decades. As with much of Coronet's early-1940s output, the surviving print is black-and-white 16mm.
How to Study sits in the study-skills wing of Coronet's guidance catalog, a smaller cousin to the social-guidance shorts the company became better known for — the same brisk, under-ten-minute run time, aimed here at library and study-hall habits rather than dating or popularity. The Prelinger Archives catalog entry for the film describes exactly this: Jim preparing a civics report on labor unions using four kinds of reading — scanning, rapid reading, careful slow reading, and re-reading — to organize his research and write it up. Public domain since its educational-market rights lapsed, it now circulates chiefly through the Prelinger collection at the Internet Archive, alongside the rest of Coronet's postwar schoolroom output.

programme.title: Peter and the Wolf
programme.desc: A boy, a bird, a duck, a cat, a grandfather, hunters, and a wolf — told entirely through Prokofiev's music and Suzie Templeton's extraordinary stop-motion animation, without a single word of narration. Peter lives behind a high wall with his overprotective grandfather. Beyond the wall is a frozen forest where a wolf hunts. When the duck wanders outside, the wolf swallows it whole. Peter climbs the wall, enlists the bird as a decoy, and lowers a rope to catch the wolf by its tail. The animation is breathtaking — snow falls with real weight, the wolf's eyes glow yellow in the dark, the duck's fate is genuinely distressing. In 1936, Natalya Sats — the director of the Central Children's Theatre in Moscow — commissioned Prokofiev to write a musical symphony for children. The intent was to cultivate "musical tastes in children from the first years of school." Prokofiev was given a rhyming libretto by the popular children's author Nina Sakonskaya. He hated it. He threw it out and wrote his own, in which each character is represented by a different instrument: the bird by a flute, the duck by an oboe, the cat by a clarinet in a low staccato register, the grandfather by a bassoon, the wolf by three French horns, Peter by the string quartet, and the hunters' gunshots by timpani and bass drum. He completed the piano score in under a week. The orchestration was finished by April 24. The premiere on May 2, 1936, at the Moscow Conservatory, was a disaster — Sats was ill, the substitute narrator was inexperienced, and the children paid no attention. A second performance later that month, with Sats herself narrating, was a triumph. By the time of the American premiere in March 1938 — Prokofiev himself conducting the Boston Symphony Orchestra at Symphony Hall — Sats was in the gulag. Her lover, Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, had been shot by Stalin in June 1937, and she was sentenced as his associate. She survived. Prokofiev's original first draft had been about a Soviet Young Pioneer righting wrongs against adults — the finished version still carries traces of Soviet ideology: the stubborn grandfather represents the un-Bolshevik older generation, and Peter's triumph over the wolf is Man taming Nature. But the music transcends all of that. It has been narrated by Eleanor Roosevelt (1950), Alec Guinness (1953), Boris Karloff (1957), Peter Ustinov with Karajan conducting (1956), David Bowie (1978), and Sting (1987), among dozens of others. Templeton's film strips away the narrator entirely. This was a radical decision — Peter and the Wolf had always been a narrated piece, the whole point being to teach children which instrument is which. But Templeton trusted the music and the images to do everything. She was right. Suzie Templeton was a science graduate from University College London who spent years travelling the world and teaching English at an Indian women's shelter before her mother showed her an image of Wallace and Gromit that changed her life. She enrolled in animation school at 28. Her student films Dog and Stanley won BAFTAs and international prizes. When producer Hugh Welchman and conductor Mark Stephenson asked her to animate Peter and the Wolf for a live orchestral performance, she began work alone in her own home. She quickly realized the scale of the project and moved to Se-ma-for Studios in Łódź, Poland — one of the oldest animation studios in Europe, where Zbigniew Rybczyński had made Tango. The production took over two hundred people and over five years. Every puppet was hand-built. Every snowflake was placed. The Philharmonia Orchestra recorded the score at Abbey Road Studios with Stephenson conducting. Gramophone magazine called it the best DVD version of Peter and the Wolf ever made. It won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film in 2008, the Grand Prix at Annecy, and the Golden Rose at the Rose d'Or Festival. Templeton's husband, the Dutch filmmaker and musician Rosto, died of cancer in 2019. She has two children. Her feature film Spitsbergen is in development. The duck is still alive inside the wolf. If you listen carefully at the end, you can hear it.

programme.title: Exercise and Health
programme.desc:
Three teenagers carry three different problems into the school gym: Ernie is run-down and out of shape, Jean is shy and withdrawn, Hal is tense and quick to snap. A physical-education instructor points all three toward the school's Acrobatics Club, and the film spends most of its ten minutes on the resulting workouts — spotted handstands and vaults off a partner's shoulders, tumbling on mats, chin-ups on a bar, badminton and archery out on the lawn. Two printed title cards carry the argument the pictures only illustrate: one notes that the sedentary worker, "bound by rules of business diplomacy," needs a physical outlet, and that the "pleasant tiredness" following exercise "promotes complete relaxation"; the other credits teamwork with building "balance and poise, along with skill, strength, and general physical fitness." By the last reel Ernie has traded the doctor's office for the tumbling mat, Jean is talking easily with the other girls on the archery line, and Hal has swapped his clenched jaw for a game of catch — three complaints answered by the same prescription of regular, cooperative exercise.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films, the picture opens with its only screen credit: educational collaborator Erwin F. Beyer of the Department of Physical Education at the University of Chicago, recorded on the RCA Sound System, with a copyright date of MCMXLIX (1949) under Coronet's founder David A. Smart. Coronet's house director Ted Peshak is credited with the film on Letterboxd and TMDB, consistent with his work on the studio's other social-guidance shorts of the period, though as with most Coronet one-reelers the on-screen credits name only the academic collaborator, not the director or cast.
The Prelinger Archives catalog summarizes the film in a single line — "How exercise will make you healthy and popular" — which is a fair, if blunter, restatement of the same argument the picture makes at length: that organized physical activity is a fix for the loosely related ailments of poor health, poor sociability, and poor nerves alike. It belongs to the same wave of postwar Coronet guidance shorts, tailored for physical-education classes rather than homeroom, and it survives today through Prelinger/Internet Archive prints rather than any particular later reputation of its own; no reliable cast credits have surfaced for Ernie, Jean, or Hal.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Gary Hurst, a journeyman of English-language animation whose career stretches from the original Danger Mouse (1981) through Challenge of the GoBots (1984), Toucan Tecs, Funnybones, Cadillacs and Dinosaurs, Rupert Bear, Free Willy: The Animated Series, Little Bear, Franklin, Faeries, Timothy Goes to School, The Berenstain Bears, 6teen, Johnny Test, Numb Chucks, Wander Over Yonder, and Chloe's Closet — an enormous list spanning four decades of children's television across BBC, ITV, Cartoon Network, Disney, and Nelvana/DHX Media.
Hurst also directed episodes of Testament: The Bible in Animation (1996), the S4C/Christmas Films series that followed directly in Operavox's footsteps through the same Welsh-Russian pipeline. So like Dabizha and Ugarov, Hurst was part of the extended S4C co-production family.
For Turandot, Hurst used drawn animation with elaborate chinoiserie backgrounds — Chinese silk-screen painting aesthetics applied to Puccini's mythical Beijing. Charles Solomon offered a double-edged assessment: the backgrounds "are more interesting than the animation in front of them." The Seattle Opera Blog featured the episode's "In questa reggia" as a notable animated rendering of one of opera's most demanding arias. One DVD reviewer couldn't follow the plot because Jane Eaglen's English diction was unintelligible, but praised the visual approach: "the hand-drawn animation, done in the style of Chinese silk screen paintings, was quite effective, and the ancient Chinese setting comes to life really well."
Puccini died before completing Turandot's final act — at the 1926 premiere, Toscanini stopped the orchestra mid-performance, turned to the audience, and said: "Here the opera finishes, because at this point the Maestro died." Franco Alfano completed the score from Puccini's sketches.
Sung by Jane Eaglen (Turandot), Edmund Barham (Calaf), and Janice Watson (Liù), with the Welsh National Opera conducted by Wyn Davies. IMDB 7.9.

programme.title: Ways to Settle Disputes
programme.desc:
Two boys in a quiet suburban front yard come to blows over whose turn it is on the tricycle, and a knot of neighborhood kids pulls them apart — the film's first lesson, illustrated with a simple chalkboard-style cartoon of two riders sharing one trike, is COMPROMISE. From there the film moves to the schoolyard, where a shoving match breaks out during a pickup ballgame; the animated card this time reads OBEY THE RULES, with a batter squaring up beneath the words. Indoors, the same children — the film follows three of them by name, Alice, Jerry, and Eddie — argue over a mislaid notebook at their desks, settled once a teacher walks them through FIND THE FACTS. The last dispute is a classroom election for playground representative: the candidates' names go up on the blackboard with a tally beside them, and the lesson this time is FIND OPINIONS, weighing what classmates actually think rather than assuming it.
Coronet Instructional Films produced the short at its own studio outside Chicago, in the same house style as its other social-guidance shorts of the period. The only credit on screen, after the copyright card for company principal David A. Smart, is the educational collaborator: Carter Davidson, Ph.D., identified as President of Union College and Chancellor of Union University. Davidson was, in fact, president of Union College in Schenectady, New York, from 1946 to 1965, having previously spent a decade as president of Knox College in Illinois — a genuine academic credential lent to the studio's classroom-conduct pictures, in keeping with Coronet's practice of pairing its writer-director staff with an outside consultant's name for the title card.
"Ways to Settle Disputes" belongs to the wave of postwar Coronet social-guidance shorts distributed to schools on 16mm reels, teaching a single practical procedure — compromise, rule-following, fact-finding, opinion-gathering — through small, staged neighborhood and classroom conflicts rather than a single continuous story. Like most of Coronet's output from this period, the print carries no other on-screen cast credit; the child performers playing Alice, Jerry, and Eddie go unnamed. It has since passed into the public domain and circulates through the Prelinger Archives and the Internet Archive as an artifact of American classroom media, catalogued there by its Coronet reel description.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: The theme song for Dixon's YouTube show Barnaby's Bailiwick — a variety format starring his puppet creations. 'Bailiwick' means jurisdiction or domain, which is fitting: Dixon's domain is a workshop in southwest England where he's been building puppet mechanisms since he was a teenager.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: A high-energy puppet dance number. Dixon's puppet designs allow for rhythmic hand-clapping, foot-stomping, and head-bobbing that would be impossible with traditional marionettes or rod puppets.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: From Jeff Wayne's 1978 Musical Version of The War of the Worlds, sung by Justin Hayward of the Moody Blues. One of the few prog-rock concept album tracks that became a genuine pop hit, reaching #5 in the UK.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: A traditional English folk song, collected by Ralph Vaughan Williams in 1908 from a singer in Sussex. One of the great songs of farewell and impossible return — 'fare you well, my dear, I must be gone, and leave you for a while.'

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: From the 1965 musical The Roar of the Greasepaint – The Smell of the Crowd by Leslie Bricusse and Anthony Newley. Tony Bennett's version is the standard. A torch song about loneliness that suits a solitary puppet perfectly.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Megrelian folk song from western Georgia. Trio Mandili are three women from Tbilisi who perform Georgian polyphonic singing — a tradition recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2001. Georgian polyphony is one of the oldest musical traditions in the world, with roots going back at least to the 8th century.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Georgian folk song. In 2017, Trio Mandili competed in Georgia's Eurovision national selection with 'Me da shen,' finishing 12th. They've also recorded songs in Hindi, Polish, Hebrew, Spanish, Italian, Ukrainian, and Russian — their Hindi cover of 'Goron Ki Na Kalon Ki' went viral in India.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Georgian folk song with a call-and-response structure. Georgian polyphonic singing isn't learned from sheet music — it's transmitted orally, generation to generation, in families and communities. Each region of Georgia has its own distinct polyphonic style.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Svan song from Svaneti, the remote mountainous region of northwestern Georgia. Svan polyphony is considered the most archaic form of Georgian singing — three-part harmony with dissonant intervals that sound alien to Western ears but follow their own ancient logic.

programme.title: How Friendly Are You
programme.desc:
Ray moves through a run of small social tests over the course of the film — wheeling his bike alongside another boy, brushing off a girl who's delighted to show him something wrapped in paper, working alongside his older brother Phil at Mr. Martin's shop, squaring off with another boy in the park over a piece of trash left on the grass — and gets nearly all of them wrong: offhand, closed off, quick to take offense. Phil eventually sits him down and talks through what friendliness actually costs and what it returns, the "responsibility of friendship" the film's own catalog description names directly. Ray works back through the same round of situations correcting himself one by one, and the film closes with him at a piano surrounded by a room full of grinning classmates — the reward Coronet's guidance shorts always hand out for good behavior: being liked.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' Glenview, Illinois studio and directed by Ted Peshak, from a script by Robert Chapin and Dick Creyke, photographed by Dale Sharkey and cut by editor George Wilbern, with narration by George Stone. As with the rest of Coronet's social-guidance line, the only credit that appears on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: the title card names educational collaborator Harl R. Douglass, Ph.D., director of the College of Education at the University of Colorado, a life-adjustment educator whose papers are held today in that university's own archives. Prelinger Archives, whose print of the film circulates today, catalogs the release as 1952; Letterboxd and IMDb's short-film index both list 1951 instead, a year's discrepancy common to Coronet's undated 16mm classroom prints.
Phil is played by Dick York — five years past his screen debut in the title role of Coronet's own Shy Guy (1947), and a dozen years before he became Darrin Stephens on Bewitched — while Mr. Martin, whose shop gives Phil his after-school job, is played by Carl Kroenke. Ray and the film's other roles went uncredited on screen, in keeping with Coronet's practice of naming only its academic consultant. The short is one of dozens Coronet turned out during its postwar guidance cycle and survives today as a plain, commercial-free classroom print through the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive.

programme.title: Trollflöjten
programme.desc: Ingmar Bergman first saw The Magic Flute at the Royal Swedish Opera when he was twelve. He went home and tried to recreate it in his marionette theatre but couldn't afford a recording. Around the same time, he wandered through an unlocked stage door at the Drottningholm Palace Theatre — an 18th-century court theater with hand-operated baroque stage machinery — and never forgot the chiaroscuro, the silence, the slanted stage floor. In his imagination, The Magic Flute always lived inside that wooden box. Decades later, when Swedish Radio chief Magnus Enhörning asked him for projects, Bergman answered immediately: "I want to do The Magic Flute for television." The Drottningholm scenery was too fragile for a film crew, so the stage — wings, curtains, wind machines, everything — was painstakingly replicated at the Swedish Film Institute studios. Recording began April 6, 1974 at the Circus Theater in Stockholm with the Swedish Radio Symphony Orchestra and Eric Ericson's Swedish Radio Choir. Ericson had initially refused; Bergman talked him into it. Filming started ten days later at Filmhuset and wrapped in July. Shot on 16mm by Sven Nykvist as an economy measure, blown up to 35mm for theatrical release — the first made-for-TV film with a stereo soundtrack. Sung in Alf Henrikson's 1968 Swedish translation, which Bergman altered: Sarastro becomes Pamina's father, trios in Act 2 are cut, Papageno wears ordinary clothes instead of plumage. Bergman frames the opera as a theatrical event, constantly reminding us we're watching a performance. A young girl's face in the audience becomes the film's emotional anchor — not Bergman and Liv Ullmann's daughter as critics assumed, but actress Helene Friberg. During intermission: the Queen of the Night and her Ladies smoke under a "Smoking Forbidden" sign, Tamino and Pamina play chess in their dressing room, Sarastro reads the score of Parsifal in glasses (Ulrik Cold was rehearsing the role), and a child slave reads a Donald Duck comic. Premiered on Swedish television New Year's Day 1975, reaching a third of the population. Pauline Kael in The New Yorker called it "a blissful present, a model of how opera can be filmed." Widely considered the finest opera film ever made.

programme.title: Good Eating Habits
programme.desc:
Bill is always in a hurry. He bolts his breakfast, wolfs down his lunch, and grabs candy and soda between errands and after-school projects — a half-built radio here, a toy racetrack there — instead of sitting still for a proper meal. By dinner his stomach aches, and flashbacks lay out exactly the day that got him there: the rushed table, the gulped drink, the food eaten on the move. Sent to bed sick, he slides into a feverish nightmare of tumbling food and bursting light, his mother sitting up with him through the night. The morning after, the household models the corrected version of the same routine — juice sipped instead of gulped, food chewed slowly, breakfast eaten sitting down with the family — and Bill, pale but recovering, eats his way back to being not just well-fed but well-nourished.
The picture is a Coronet Instructional Films release, copyrighted in 1951 to David A. Smart, the Esquire publisher whose Chicago-area studio also put out a second magazine called Coronet that gave the film company its name. As with the rest of Coronet's postwar guidance line, the only credits on screen belong to the outside experts who vetted the material, not to any writer or director: educational collaborator Clifford J. Barborka, M.D., associate professor of medicine at Northwestern University Medical School, and special consultant James R. Wilson, M.D., secretary of the American Medical Association's Council on Foods and Nutrition and formerly associate professor of pediatrics at Syracuse University. The soundtrack carries the RCA Sound System credit standard on Coronet's 16mm classroom prints of the era.
Prelinger Archives, which preserves the film, catalogs it as a drama of "gluttony and hidden hunger" — the paradox, common to Coronet's health shorts, of a child who eats plenty yet malnourishes himself through bad choices and worse timing. The narration is voiced by James Andelin, a Chicago-based radio, television, and industrial-film performer; no director is credited on the print or corroborated in any outside record, in keeping with a house style that put the consulting physicians' names above any filmmaker's. It circulated to health classrooms through the 1950s and survives today through the Internet Archive's Prelinger collection.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Valeriy Ugarov (Валерий Михайлович Угаров, 1941–2007), a Soyuzmultfilm veteran whose relationship with S4C predated Operavox by five years. In 1990, Ugarov directed The Quest for Olwen — an adaptation of Culhwch and Olwen from the Welsh Mabinogion — as a Soyuzmultfilm/S4C co-production. That film was one of the earliest sparks of the Welsh-Russian animation pipeline that would produce Shakespeare: The Animated Tales, Operavox, Testament, and Animated Tales of the World, all flowing through Yelizaveta Babakhina's Christmas Films studio in Moscow.
Ugarov's career at Soyuzmultfilm stretched back to 1971, contributing segments to the beloved Merry-Go-Round anthology series and directing the four-part At the Back of the Class (1978). His best-known solo work was Khalif the Stork (1981). He worked in cel animation, cutout, paint, and mixed techniques — a versatility that served the psychedelic demands of Mozart's Masonic fantasy.
For The Magic Flute, Ugarov used traditional cel animation in a style Charles Solomon compared to Yellow Submarine. Letterboxd reviewers noted Papageno flitting around as an actual bird, Sarastro ballooning in size as a billowing cape of a man, character designs with a "Peter Chung-ish" edge underneath traditional operatic costuming. The compressed half-hour format forces wrenching cuts to Mozart's two-and-a-half-hour score, but the animation exploits what no stage can: impossible spatial transformations, characters dissolving and reforming, the boundary between the human and the magical made literal.
The libretto was Jeremy Sams' English translation of Emanuel Schikaneder's original, sung by Neill Archer (Tamino), Alwyn Mellor (Queen of the Night), John Connell (Sarastro/Papageno), and Jennifer Rhys-Davies (Pamina), with the Welsh National Opera conducted by David Seaman.
Note: Amazon's Charles Solomon review incorrectly credits this episode to "Valeri Oganov." Every other source — IMDB, TMDB, FilmAffinity, animatsiya.net — confirms the director as Valeriy Ugarov. He continued working with S4C and Christmas Films until his death in 2007, directing episodes of Animated Tales of the World (2000) and Babka Ezhka and Others (released posthumously, 2008).
IMDB 8.3. Produced by S4C, BBC Bristol, and Christmas Films (Moscow).

programme.title: Improve Your Personality
programme.desc:
Improve Your Personality opens on a school walkway and quickly settles into the device it returns to for the rest of its ten minutes: a black silhouette head in profile, flanked by two labels, "OTHER PEOPLE" and "ENVIRONMENT," under the caption "YOUR PERSONALITY." The diagram states the film's whole thesis in one image — personality isn't something a person is simply born with, it's built out of how they treat others and how they answer to their surroundings — and the picture keeps cutting back to it between two contrasted case studies. A teenage boy who starts out sullen and closed-off is shown coming around: setting the table, hanging up the wash, pitching in at home instead of leaving the chores to the woman of the house. Cut hard against him is a teenage girl who does nothing in her scenes but admire her own reflection in a bedroom mirror, the diagram card reappearing each time to underline the moral. Along the way, one boy sizes up a girl walking past him on the same path from the opening and tells a friend, "Boy, has she got personality!" — about as flatly as the film could put its own pun. By the closing reel the same young people turn up dressed for a formal dance, in tuxedos and gowns, and a final card spells out the takeaway in script lettering: "Concentrate on the other person."
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films and copyrighted in 1951 (the opening card reads "MCMLI," credited to David A. Smart), the short follows Coronet's standard practice for the period: not one performer is named on screen, and the film's only title-card credit goes to its "educational collaborator," billed as Clifford R. Adams, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at the Pennsylvania State College. Adams held that post in fact as well as on the card — he was Penn State's real director of its Marriage Counseling Service and a member of the American Association of Marriage Counselors — and five years earlier had co-written the marriage-advice bestseller "How to Pick a Mate" with Vance O. Packard, then a staff writer for The American Magazine and later the author of "The Hidden Persuaders." Coronet drew on a small, recurring bench of writers, directors, and consultants across its guidance catalog — Melvin Waskin as house writer, Ted Peshak as its most frequent director among them — but this particular print names none of them; Adams alone appears on screen.
The film belongs to Coronet's postwar "mental hygiene" cycle, the run of guidance shorts the company produced through the late 1940s and 1950s for direct sale to schools. David Smart, who had toured Nazi Germany before the war, later told the Chicago Tribune that seeing Hitler's use of film as an "indoctrination tool" convinced him the same medium could be turned toward education instead, and Coronet ran with the idea hard enough to release a new title, on average, every three and a half working days. Against that backdrop, Improve Your Personality is a mild entry — no car crash, no scandal, just a civics-class gloss on manners dressed up as psychology, delivered with Adams' academic authority and Coronet's usual well-lit, tidy midcentury classrooms and living rooms. A 2010 Cineaste survey of the genre singled the film out as one of the era's less common entries not narrowly aimed at one sex, pitching its lesson at boys and girls alike.

programme.title: Hänsel und Gretel
programme.desc: Humperdinck's fairy tale opera, filmed for television with Georg Solti conducting the Vienna Philharmonic. Two children are sent into the forest by their desperate mother. They get lost. They find a house made of cake. The woman who lives there eats children. What makes this story remarkable begins long before the cameras rolled. In 1890, Adelheid Wette wrote a play based on the Grimm fairy tale for her own children to perform at Christmas. She asked her brother Engelbert to set five of her verses to music. The brother was Engelbert Humperdinck, who had spent the previous decade as Richard Wagner's personal assistant — he had helped produce Parsifal at Bayreuth in 1880-81 and tutored Wagner's son Siegfried. He composed four songs for a puppet show his nieces were performing, then couldn't stop. The four songs became sixteen. The sixteen became a singspiel. The singspiel became a full opera. He composed it in Frankfurt in 1891 and 1892 — a plaque still marks the house at Scheffelstraße 1 — and what emerged was the most audacious act of tonal sabotage in opera history: the entire Wagnerian orchestral apparatus — leitmotifs, through-composed structure, massive orchestration — aimed at a bedtime story about a gingerbread house. It premiered on December 23, 1893, at the Hoftheater in Weimar. The conductor was a twenty-nine-year-old named Richard Strauss. The audience went wild. Within eighteen months it had been performed across Germany, Switzerland, England, and the United States. It has been associated with Christmas ever since. The Evening Prayer — "Abends will ich schlafen geh'n" — where Hansel and Gretel fall asleep in the forest and fourteen angels descend to protect them, is one of the most beautiful things in all of music. The opera holds an extraordinary collection of broadcasting firsts. In 1923, the Royal Opera House chose it for the first complete radio opera broadcast. On Christmas Day 1931, it became the first opera transmitted live from the Metropolitan Opera. And on December 23, 1943, it became the first opera ever broadcast on television, on WRGB in Schenectady, New York — exactly fifty years after its premiere. This 1981 television film was directed by August Everding for Unitel, with Solti conducting the Vienna Philharmonic. The cast is a once-in-a-generation assembly. Edita Gruberová's silvery coloratura soprano as Gretel and Brigitte Fassbaender's warm dramatic mezzo as Hansel are the perfect sibling pair — Fassbaender brings a boyish physicality that makes you forget Hansel is a trouser role. Sena Jurinac plays the Witch, and this was her final role before retirement — one of the great sopranos of the twentieth century, born in Travnik in what was then Yugoslavia, who had reigned at the Vienna State Opera for over three decades, closing her career by cackling over a gingerbread oven. Hermann Prey sings the Father with his warm Bavarian baritone, and Helga Dernesch — who had been Brünnhilde under Karajan — plays the Mother. The Vienna Boys' Choir sings the gingerbread children. Solti drives the Vienna Philharmonic with his characteristic intensity; the overture alone — which Wagner himself might not have objected to — is worth the price of admission. Humperdinck died on September 27, 1921, at age 67. The night before, he had attended a performance of Weber's Der Freischütz in Neustrelitz — his son Wolfram's first effort as a stage director. He suffered a heart attack during the performance and died the next day from a second one. The Berlin State Opera performed Hänsel und Gretel in his memory. Among his other legacies: he invented Sprechgesang, the half-sung, half-spoken vocal technique that Schoenberg would later make famous. Kurt Weill was one of his students. And in 1965, a British pop singer named Arnold Dorsey stole his name, becoming "Engelbert Humperdinck" — a theft the composer, being dead, could not contest. Sung in German.

programme.title: Ways To Better Conversation
programme.desc:
Two teenagers trade an easy, back-and-forth conversation in a book-lined den, and the film uses them to set the baseline before it complicates the picture. The scene shifts to a workshop table where a foursome of classmates hammers together a wooden game board marked "First Prize, Picnic Camp Kit" for some coming school outing, and the building project pulls everyone into the talk — until one girl, chin on her hand and eyes down, visibly checks out while a friend chatters on beside her. The lesson sharpens further when a boy corners two listeners with a long, uninterrupted account of a pet project, illustrated by cutaway shots of a miniature tabletop landscape, its roads and toy houses standing in for whatever he won't stop describing, while his audience's attention visibly drains away. Coronet then makes its title metaphor literal: a full volleyball court of the same teenagers batting the ball back and forth, dissolving in and out of the talk scenes to argue that conversation, like the game, only works when the ball keeps moving between players. The reel closes on a spinning volleyball graphic that stamps out its rules one at a time — Respect Others' Opinions, Be Courteous/Include Everyone, Contribute, Stick to the Subject, Be a Good Listener — before gathering all five onto a single closing card.
Ways to Better Conversation was shot in color on Coronet Instructional Films' standard postwar formula: teenagers drawn from the Chicago area playing out a single behavioral checklist against the company's recurring den-and-bookshelf set, in place of a plotted drama with billed characters. Founder David A. Smart, who had already built Esquire and a magazine called Coronet before turning the latter's name into a classroom-film label, ran the operation out of the Chicago suburbs at a pace the Chicago Tribune once clocked at a new release every three and a half working days, staffed heavily by fellow WWII veterans. Across Coronet's social-guidance line, a credited "educational collaborator" — typically a psychologist, home economist, or family-life specialist — supplied the academic seal of approval that let schools treat the studio's etiquette advice as curriculum rather than propaganda.
The film survives in the public domain and circulates today chiefly through a color transfer donated to the Internet Archive's ephemeral-film holdings by the collector Skip Elsheimer of A.V. Geeks, cataloged there since 2013 under the same plain description Coronet itself might have used — "likens a good conversation to a volleyball game." It has since resurfaced in retrospective press as unexpectedly durable advice: a 2020s Upworthy piece revisiting the short judged that its checklist of turn-taking and listening "really does apply to today," even citing a flubbed line early in the reel as proof the print in circulation is an unvarnished classroom copy rather than a cleaned-up remaster.

programme.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed
programme.desc:
The Adventures of Prince Achmed is the oldest surviving animated feature film, and very nearly a one-woman invention. Lotte Reiniger had mastered the old folk art of the shadow-play as a child and was largely self-taught; for this film she perfected an animation form of her own, cutting figures from black cardboard and thin sheets of lead, jointing them with fine wire hinges, and repositioning each one a fraction at a time to be photographed frame by frame against backlit glass. The silhouettes are astonishingly expressive — every finger, veil, and flourish articulated — moving across luminous tinted backgrounds like a paper theatre brought to life.
It took three years, from 1923 to 1926. The Berlin banker Louis Hagen financed it by buying up film stock during the Weimar hyperinflation, when raw film held its value better than cash, and gave Reiniger the attic above his Potsdam garage as a studio. Her small team became a roll-call of the German avant-garde: her husband Carl Koch ran the camera and produced, while Walter Ruttmann and Berthold Bartosch — both major experimental animators in their own right — handled the magical effects, assisted by Alexander Kardan and Walther Türck.
The technical centerpiece was a homemade multiplane camera. Koch operated a rig of stacked glass layers lit powerfully from below, which let foreground figures and painted backgrounds sit on separate planes and gave the images a genuine sense of depth — more than a decade before Disney patented its own multiplane camera. Ruttmann conjured the flying horse and the story's transformations using wax, and Bartosch built oceans and night skies out of sand, soap, and transparent cutouts. Roughly 250,000 images were photographed over the three years, of which about 96,000 were edited into the finished film.
The story is drawn from the 1001 Nights: a wicked sorcerer tricks Prince Achmed onto an enchanted flying horse that carries him far from home, and his adventures take in battles with demons, his love for Pari Banu of the isle of Wak Wak, and an alliance with Aladdin and the Witch of the Fiery Mountain against the sorcerer's magic. Wolfgang Zeller composed the score in close collaboration with Reiniger as the animation took shape, and conducted it live when the film premiered at Berlin's Volksbühne on 2 May 1926.
The original negative was destroyed during the Battle of Berlin in 1945; the film survived through a print held in England, and in 1999 the BFI and the Deutsches Filmmuseum restored it — reconstructing the original scene-by-scene colour tinting and recording a fresh performance of Zeller's score.
This particular copy carries an alternative accompaniment: an original score by Brown Whörnet, composed and performed live at the Alamo Drafthouse on Lavaca Street in Austin, Texas in early 2004 and pressed in a small DVD run. This release is a 2020 remaster of that recording, with English subtitles burned into the print.

programme.title: Good Table Manners
programme.desc:
Fourteen-year-old Chuck is a disaster at the family dinner table: he reaches across his parents for the potatoes, talks with his mouth full, and answers his mother's corrections with a sarcastic grin. When his parents dress and go out for the evening, Chuck settles onto the sofa with a book — and finds tucked inside it an invitation to a boy-girl dinner party he has been dreading, embarrassed by manners he already half-knows are bad. That's when his older self walks in: a twenty-one-year-old Chuck, dressed in the identical sweater to make the point that the two of them are the same person, come back to coach his younger counterpart through a meal course by course. The lesson runs through a restaurant scene with a waiter and menu, three forks laid out and explained one at a time, a demonstration of cutting meat properly instead of stabbing at it, and a polite refusal of a dish he doesn't want — each swap of course, and each new point of etiquette, arriving with a snap of the future Chuck's fingers. By the closing scene, present-day Chuck is at the party after all, seated correctly among the other boys and girls, manners intact.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films and released in May 1951, Good Table Manners was directed by Ted Peshak, the studio's regular hand behind this run of postwar social guidance shorts. As with the rest of Coronet's classroom line, the only name on screen belongs to the outside expert who vetted the material: the title card credits educational collaborator Margaret M. Justin, Ph.D., dean of the School of Home Economics at Kansas State College, over the standard RCA Sound System card. The short was copyrighted that year (MCMLI) in the name of David A. Smart, the Esquire publisher whose company gave Coronet its name. Present-day Chuck was played by Stuart Sklamm, a Chicago juvenile performer who later hosted the local children's program Piano Pals — the fantasy device of the double, two ages of the same boy dressed alike and standing in the same room, is an unusually literal teaching gimmick even by the standards of a genre built on them.
Ken Smith, whose 1999 survey Mental Hygiene: Better Living Through Classroom Films catalogs the postwar guidance-film genre, singled it out as "the best of the table manners films," and preserved its own line of narration: "People judge many things about you just by the way you eat." The short circulated to home economics and health classrooms through the 1950s and survives today through the Prelinger Archives and the A/V Geeks Film Archive, both cataloging it from the same original synopsis: a bad-mannered boy meeting himself at twenty-one, and learning from him what he'll eventually already know.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.sub-title: A Creepy Song by an Unknown Writer
programme.desc: One of Dixon's longer-form puppet performances. His puppets aren't just lip-sync props — they're fully articulated characters with personality, built from scratch in his workshop. Dixon was featured on Deutsche Welle and Great Big Story, where he showed how to make finger puppets from Post-It notes and invisible tape.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Bart Howard wrote this in 1954 as 'In Other Words.' Kaye Ballard recorded it first, but it became Sinatra's signature after his 1964 version with Count Basie, arranged by Quincy Jones. It was the first song played on the Moon — Buzz Aldrin brought a cassette to the Apollo 11 lunar module.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: The opening number from Rodgers and Hammerstein's Oklahoma! (1943) — the first song in the first golden-age Broadway musical. Gordon MacRae sang it in the 1955 film. It was revolutionary: a musical that opened with a lone cowboy singing about corn, not a chorus line.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Pure improvised puppet dance — no specific song, just Dixon exploring what his finger puppet mechanisms can do. These improv sessions are where he develops new movement vocabulary that shows up in his more produced videos.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Pinkman — one of Dixon's puppet characters — performs Irving Berlin's most recorded song. Berlin, born Israel Beilin in Siberia in 1888, wrote it in 1940 at the Beverly Hills Hotel. Bing Crosby's 1942 recording remains the best-selling single of all time.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: A barbershop quartet arrangement of 'Sweet Adeline' (1903), originally written by Richard H. Gerard and Henry W. Armstrong. The song became the unofficial anthem of barbershop singing — the Society for the Preservation and Encouragement of Barber Shop Quartet Singing in America (SPEBSQSA) was practically founded on it.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Simon & Garfunkel's 1964 debut single, originally acoustic and ignored. Producer Tom Wilson overdubbed electric instruments without telling them — the remixed version hit #1 in January 1966. Paul Simon learned about the success while living in England.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: From Tim Burton's The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993), originally sung by Catherine O'Hara. Sally's longing ballad gets the puppet treatment — fitting, since the original film is itself stop-motion puppet animation.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.sub-title: THE HOUSE OF THE RISING SUN ☀️
programme.desc: The Animals' 1964 arrangement of the traditional folk song, recorded in one take at Kingsway Studios London for about £4. Alan Price got sole arranger credit — a source of lasting bitterness with Eric Burdon. Bob Dylan's acoustic version on his 1964 debut inspired the Animals' electric arrangement, which in turn inspired Dylan to go electric.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: Television performance on Georgia's Imedi TV of 'Erti nakhvit' — a Georgian love song. This is the broadcast version; they also have a standalone studio/field recording of the same song.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: The standalone version of 'Erti nakhvit.' Georgian polyphony uses three voice parts: the top voice carries the melody, the middle voice provides harmonic richness, and the bass voice anchors. It sounds nothing like Western harmony — the intervals are different, the tuning system is different, the aesthetic goal is different.

programme.title: One More Year on the Family Farm?
programme.desc:
"One More Year on the Family Farm?" opens on the shot it will return to at the end: an aerial pass over a two-lane road threading a green valley down past a cluster of barns and silos. Rather than following one family through a plot, the film is built as an issue-documentary — an entry in Coronet's Changing Scene Series — that lets members of two real dairy-farming households speak for themselves about whether to keep at it. One farm has modernized: cows stand in row after row of freestall housing, a milking parlor is threaded with steel line, and a bulk tanker truck idles in the yard, while a young man in glasses works through figures at an office desk rather than working a field. The other keeps to older ways — a man in a stocking cap forks manure out of a wood-sided barn by hand, walks cattle single file up a hillside pasture, and turns a narrow furrow behind a small tractor. Interspersed are direct-to-camera moments with the people themselves — an older farmer, a young woman, the men in caps and glasses — weighing the debt, the machinery, the hours, and the pull of a life some were born into and some are choosing to leave. The film never resolves which choice is right; it ends where it began, looking down at the valley from the air.
The on-screen credit is unusually specific for a Coronet short. Following the title card and its tag "(The Changing Scene Series)," a further title reads "©1977 Coronet Instructional Media, a division of Esquire, Inc." Two consultants are named — Content Consultant Jack L. Nelson, Ed.D., Professor of Education at Rutgers University, and Classroom Consultant William B. Stanley, Teacher of Social Studies at Cranford Senior High School in Cranford, New Jersey — followed by the studio's standard closing notice, "This film may not be copied or televised without written permission." As with Coronet's classic postwar shorts, no director, writer, or on-camera participant is credited; the film speaks in the voice of its consultants rather than its filmmakers.
The title card's own series tag marks this as part of a later, more issue-driven strand of the Coronet catalog, trading the scripted teenage leads of the studio's postwar shorts for real adults talking about their own livelihoods. The print survives today through the Internet Archive's educational-film holdings, part of the same circle of ephemeral prints preserved and scanned by collectors such as A.V. Geeks, and is cataloged there under a copyright still held by Phoenix Learning Group, Inc., the successor distributor of the Coronet library.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Barry J.C. Purves (born 28 August 1960), one of Britain's most celebrated stop-motion animators and, in the opinion of critics and DVD reviewers alike, the strongest episode in the Operavox series.
Purves came to animation through theatre — he still directs at the Altrincham Garrick Playhouse in Manchester — and his films are inseparable from performance. Next: The Infinite Variety Show (1989) had Shakespeare auditioning for Peter Hall. Screen Play (1992) retold the Willow Pattern story through Kabuki and Bunraku theatre, narrated simultaneously in British Sign Language and English — it earned an Academy Award nomination. Achilles (1995) depicted the Greek hero's story through the forms of ancient Greek theatre and sculpture. Every one of his six short films has been nominated for major international awards.
Beyond his own films, Purves was head animator on Tim Burton's Mars Attacks! (1996) — he animated the Martians in stop-motion before the fateful decision to switch to CGI — and served as previsualisation animation director on Peter Jackson's King Kong (2005). His models (Shakespeare, Achilles, Richard D'Oyly Carte) are displayed at the National Media Museum. His book "Stop Motion: Passion, Process and Performance" (Focal Press, 2007) is a standard reference.
For Rigoletto, Purves went dark. Verdi's tale of the hunchbacked jester whose mockery of wronged fathers returns to destroy his own daughter demanded it. One DVD reviewer wrote: "Everything, from the ugly hunchback jester to the rotting, creaking sets are amazing to behold. It won't make your day happy, but it's a spectacular example of what can happen when you combine classical music with animation." The puppet work captures the court of Mantua as a place of genuine menace — the Duke's seductions, Sparafucile's assassination, the sack in the storm.
Sung by Jonathan Summers (Rigoletto), Rosemary Joshua (Gilda), and Anthony Mee (Duke of Mantua), with the Welsh National Opera conducted by Wyn Davies. Produced by Glenn C. Holberton. IMDB 8.0.

programme.title: Snap Out Of It
programme.desc:
Howard Patterson has been ducking his history teacher, Miss Rogers, for two weeks about a report card he won't bring home. When the school finally corners him, the reason turns out to be almost funny: his grade climbed from a C to a B, and he's furious about it, because he'd set his heart on an A. Sent to see the counselor, Mr. Edmunds, Howard can't get past feeling cheated by a grade that any objective look would call an improvement. Edmunds walks him through the same pattern playing out all over the building — a boy in shop class who explodes when his first lamp isn't "perfect," a girl who sulks for days after losing the lead in the school operetta to a smaller part, a classmate named Bill who waits too long to ask a popular girl to the class party and is stunned to find she already has a date. Each case has the same shape: expecting too much, then reacting to an ordinary letdown as though it were a catastrophe. Using a basketball analogy — the different ways a benched player can respond to watching a teammate get blocked — Edmunds gets Howard to see that the goal isn't to stop wanting an A, but to aim high, accept the miss, and keep working. Howard takes the report card home, tells his father the real grade, and by the closing scene is back in Edmunds' office, steadier, and pleased with himself for keeping his emotions "in balance."
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and copyrighted in 1951 (MCMLI) under Coronet founder David A. Smart, whose Esquire and Coronet magazine money helped bankroll the postwar guidance-film boom. As was Coronet's practice, the only name that appears on screen belongs to the psychology consultant: the title card credits educational collaborator Clifford R. Adams, Ph.D., professor of psychology at the Pennsylvania State College. Adams was known to a wider public as the co-author, with journalist Vance Packard, of the 1946 marriage-advice bestseller "How to Pick a Mate," and as director of Penn State's Marriage Counseling Service and the Woman's Home Companion marriage clinic — credentials suited to coaching Coronet's teenagers through their feelings rather than their formulas. No director is credited on the print, and none is confirmed specifically for this title, so none is listed here.
"Snap Out of It!" — its full on-screen title carries the subtitle "Emotional Balance" — belongs to the mental-hygiene wave of classroom shorts that dominated homeroom film projectors through the 1950s, alongside Coronet stablemates like "Are You Popular?," "Overcoming Fear," and "Control Your Emotions." Its short running time still finds room for three separate cautionary vignettes orbiting Howard's central story, a structure typical of the genre's habit of restating one lesson across several interchangeable teenagers. Like most of Coronet's early catalog, the film lapsed into the public domain and survives today chiefly through the Prelinger Archives, which preserved and digitized the Coronet library, transcript and all, for research and reuse.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: The sea shanty that went viral on TikTok in January 2021 when Scottish postman Nathan Evans posted his version. Written about the Weller Brothers' supply ships that serviced whaling stations in 1860s New Zealand. Dixon's puppet version rides the wave of the shanty revival.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.sub-title: Tallulah is very DEMURE, very MINDFUL
programme.desc: Tallulah — one of Dixon's more elegant puppet characters — riffs on the 2024 'very demure, very mindful' meme. Dixon regularly incorporates internet culture into his puppet performances, keeping his centuries-old art form current.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A traditional Georgian song. The trio consists of Tatuli Mgeladze, Tako Tsiklauri, and Mariam Kurasbediani, who accompany themselves on the panduri — a three-stringed Georgian lute carved from a single piece of wood. 'Mandili' means woman's headscarf in Georgian.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: Title track from their 2017 album. They went viral in 2014 when they uploaded a video of 'Apareka' — a Georgian folk song — that gathered over eight million views. Three women singing in a field, no production, no gimmicks. The internet noticed.

programme.title: Carnival of the Animals
programme.desc: Joanna Lumley narrates Saint-Saëns' beloved musical menagerie with the London Mozart Players, set to animated illustrations by freelance designer Cat Fuller. Part of the LMP's "At Home with LMP" series launched during the COVID lockdown, this digital rendition pairs each of the fourteen movements with colorful animal animations while Lumley reads poetry written specially for the project by LMP violinist Martin Smith. The result is a pocket-sized masterpiece of family entertainment: the royal march of the lion, hens pecking in the barnyard, wild donkeys galloping across the steppe, tortoises performing the can-can in devastating slow motion (Saint-Saëns quoting Offenbach at funereal tempo), an elephant waltzing to Mendelssohn and Berlioz transposed to the deepest instrument in the orchestra (the double bass — his wickedest orchestration joke), kangaroos bouncing, an aquarium shimmering behind glass harmonica arpeggios, a cuckoo calling from the depths of the woods, birds fluttering in an aviary, pianists practicing their scales (Saint-Saëns classified pianists as animals — his wickedest taxonomic joke), fossils dancing a xylophone danse macabre, and the sublime swan, whose cello solo is the most famous piece he ever wrote and the only movement he allowed published in his lifetime. Saint-Saëns composed the whole suite in February 1886 in a small Austrian village after a disastrous German concert tour, writing to his publisher Durand that he knew he should be working on his Third Symphony but that this was "such fun" ("mais c'est si amusant!"). He premiered it privately at cellist Charles Lebouc's salon on March 3, 1886, with a lineup including Louis Diémer and Paul Taffanel. Franz Liszt himself requested a private hearing at Pauline Viardot's home. Subsequent performances featured musicians wearing masks of the animals they represented. Saint-Saëns was adamant the work never be published in his lifetime, terrified it would damage his reputation as a Serious Composer. He specified in his will that it should be published posthumously. He died in December 1921; Durand published the score in April 1922; the first public performance on February 25, 1922 by the Concerts Colonne under Gabriel Pierné was rapturously received — Le Figaro reported "cries of admiring joy" from the audience. Lumley, a self-confessed classical music fan, called the collaboration "thrilling" and noted that "music is more important than ever" in times of isolation.

programme.title: Social Courtesy
programme.desc:
Bill primps in front of his bedroom mirror, getting ready for a costume party with his girlfriend Carol, and grumbles that all this fuss over manners is old-fashioned. An unseen narrator disagrees, and makes Bill live with the consequences: every time the boy is rude, the narrator freezes the scene, "takes a picture" of it — the moment dissolves into a photograph hanging on the wall of the next shot — and rewinds Bill back to try again, a little more friendly this time. At the party itself, a teenage rec room dressed up as a hobo jungle, with hand-lettered signs reading "To Train," "Track 1," "Keep Out," and "Baggage Checked" strung up among the decorations, Bill argues under his breath with a voice nobody else can hear, until one of the girls asks if he's talking to himself. Bit by bit he tries doing what he's told — standing when an adult speaks to him, sitting up instead of slouching, actually listening to his friends — and by the last reel the chaperone is remarking on what a changed, courteous boy he's become; Bill leaves already holding an invitation to the next party.
The only screen credit belongs to the educational collaborator: the opening title cards name Mary E. Weathersby, Head of the Homemaking Education Department at Mississippi State College, in the standard Coronet slot for the psychologist or home-economics consultant behind the lesson plan. The copyright card reads MCMLI under the name of Coronet founder David A. Smart, and the print carries the RCA Sound System mark seen across the line. The finished film runs ten minutes sixteen seconds, and the Prelinger Archives catalog credits the camera work to Bruce Colling. No director or performer is named on screen, and none has turned up in any reliable secondary source for this particular title.
Social Courtesy belongs to the same wave of early-1950s Coronet social-guidance shorts as Are You Popular? and Shy Guy, but it handles the genre's usual show-and-correct formula more strangely than most: an audibly bickering, fourth-wall-breaking narrator, freeze-frames that turn into snapshots on a wall, and a scene structure that keeps backing up and starting over. Ken Smith singled it out in his 1999 study of the genre, Mental Hygiene: Classroom Films 1945-1970, as one of the most inventive films Coronet ever made. It has since passed into the public domain and is preserved in the Prelinger Collection at the Internet Archive.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Graham Ralph of Silver Fox Films — a prolific British animation director whose career spans from the original Danger Mouse (1981) through Funnybones, Toucan Tecs, Cadillacs and Dinosaurs, William's Wish Wellingtons, The Forgotten Toys, and more recently Harry and His Bucket Full of Dinosaurs for Cartoon Network. In 1989, Ralph and Jerry Hibbert launched Hibbert Ralph Entertainment (HRE), with Ralph at the helm seeking creative challenges beyond the advertising work that had built their reputation. By 2005, he was directing The Magic Roundabout CGI TV series (following the 2005 feature film), advising young animators at Cartoon Master in Potsdam: "Give the audience something they have never seen before. They are hungry nasty things."
For Rhinegold, Ralph farmed the animation to Carlos Alfonso Animation in Madrid — a Welsh-Spanish co-production within the larger Operavox framework. Paul Shardlow designed it. The result was what Charles Solomon accurately described as trying "to turn Wagner's Das Rheingold into Heavy Metal, with Freya in a Frazetta-esque bikini." One DVD reviewer echoed: "What's with Freia wearing a string bikini? What crazy animator came up with that?"
The approach is maximalist fantasy illustration applied to the first opera of Wagner's sixteen-hour Ring Cycle. Gods, giants, dwarves, underwater Rhinemaidens — Ralph's drawn animation renders them with the visual vocabulary of 1980s pulp fantasy, which either suits or insults Wagner depending on your tolerance. The condensation of a two-and-a-half-hour opera into half an hour is inevitably brutal, but the same reviewer noted that "being a short opera by Ring standards, it worked okay being cut down" and that "Wagner's fantastic music is perfect for an animated fantasy film."
Sung by Phillip Joll, Penelope Walker, and Janice Watson, with the Welsh National Opera conducted by David Seaman. English translation by Amanda Holden, Welsh translation by Manon Williams and Wyn Davies. Executive producer Chris Grace, script editors Penelope Middleboe and Martin Lamb. IMDB 7.5.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Nina Simone's 1965 ten-minute tour de force from Pastel Blues, based on a traditional African-American spiritual. Simone recorded it in a single take. The song builds from a whispered plea to a full piano-and-voice storm.

programme.title: The Fun of Being Thoughtful
programme.desc:
Jane Proctor is a cheerful teenager who is, in archivist Ken Smith's later phrase, "slavishly devoted" to her family's happiness, and the film catalogues one evening of it: she tidies her room, helps get dinner on the table amid a bit of kitchen panic over the mashed potatoes, and — the plot's real engine — works to fix up her awkward brother Eddie with a date for the following night. Eddie, whose voice keeps threatening to crack, gripes along the way that he "hasn't a thing to wear" either. Jane's persistent thoughtfulness pays off in the last scene: she comes down the stairs in a new dress to her parents' and Eddie's evident delight, and the household settles back into its usual harmony.
Produced at Coronet's studio in Glenview, Illinois and copyrighted in 1950 (the title card reads MCML) by David A. Smart, who had founded the company with his brother Alfred as an offshoot of their Esquire magazine business. As with the rest of Coronet's postwar social-guidance catalog, the teenage cast goes uncredited; the only name in the titles belongs to the psychology consultant, credited on screen as Educational Collaborator Ernest M. Ligon, Ph.D., director of the Character Research Project at Union College in Schenectady, New York. Ligon had founded the Character Research Project in 1935 and would direct it for over four decades, building its work on ideas he had laid out in his earlier book The Psychology of Christian Personality. Directing credit likewise appears nowhere on screen, but Ted Peshak — the Glenview house director credited with roughly 350 educational films for Coronet — lists Fun of Being Thoughtful among his 1950 directing credits. The uncredited actor playing Eddie Proctor was a Coronet regular: a retrospective tracing faces across the studio's uncredited teen stock company notes that the same performer's voice had not yet finished cracking a year earlier in The Meaning of Pi (1949), and that he turns up again later in 1950 as Eddie in Developing Friendships and as Ed Parker in How to Get Cooperation.
The print survives through the Prelinger Archives on the Internet Archive, in the public domain along with the rest of that collection. Prelinger's cataloguer Ken Smith, whose notes on Coronet's output were later folded into his book Mental Hygiene: Better Living Through Classroom Films, 1945-1970, flagged the script's habit of chasing several morals inside ten minutes as "fun but a little hard to follow" — a fair description of a film that covers housework, dating, dress shopping, and hospitality all in one sitting. It belongs to the postwar "social guidance" genre Coronet all but defined for American classrooms, in which ordinary household courtesy is treated as a small-scale rehearsal for the larger civic virtues — responsibility, cooperation, good citizenship — that the studio's other shorts preached more directly.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Barnaby Dixon's puppet performs Merle Travis's 1946 coal miner's lament, later made famous by Tennessee Ernie Ford's 1955 version that spent eight weeks at #1. Dixon is a British puppeteer from southwest England who builds intricate finger puppets — his fingers control the feet while hinges, levers, and string mechanisms make the rest of the body move with startling naturalism.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Patti Page's 1950 hit performed as a puppet floor jam. 'The Tennessee Waltz' was one of the best-selling singles of the 20th century, spending thirteen weeks at #1. Page recorded it as a B-side; the DJ flipped it.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: The Beatles, Abbey Road (1969). McCartney found the lyrics to Thomas Dekker's 1603 lullaby on a piano at his father's house in Liverpool. He couldn't read music well enough to play the original melody, so he wrote his own.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Dixon's UV-reactive puppet troupe — skeletal figures that glow under blacklight. A completely different aesthetic from his naturalistic wooden puppets, these are pure spectacle designed for dark-room performance.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.sub-title: John the Revelator - HAIRY NEON BOYS
programme.desc: The Hairy Neon Boys perform the traditional gospel/blues song, recorded by Blind Willie Johnson in 1930 and covered by everyone from Son House to Depeche Mode. The blacklight puppet treatment gives the apocalyptic lyrics an appropriately otherworldly feel.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: A live-streamed puppet performance. Dixon occasionally does these to interact with his audience in real time, improvising puppet routines in response to chat.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Smokey Robinson and the Miracles, 1967 (released as single 1970, hit #1). Robinson wrote it with Stevie Wonder and Hank Cosby. Robinson said the circus-flavored melody Wonder brought him demanded sad-clown lyrics — he found the concept in the opera Pagliacci.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: The return of Dixon's Wick puppet character. Dixon builds ongoing narratives around his puppet characters, giving them personalities and arcs across multiple videos — a serialized puppet universe on YouTube.

programme.title: Barnaby Dixon
programme.desc: Wick — another of Dixon's puppet characters — performs 'Into the Unknown' from Frozen II (2019), written by Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez. The puppet's small scale against the epic Disney ballad creates deliberate comic contrast.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A Georgian folk song. The trio has had several lineup changes — past members include Irina Midelauri, Elene Nareshelashvili, Anuka Chincharauli, and Shorena Tsiskalauri — but the core sound remains: three women, a panduri, and centuries of vocal tradition.

programme.title: Trio Mandili
programme.desc: A song from the Mtiuleti region in the mountainous center of Georgia, near the Georgian Military Highway. Mountain songs tend to be more austere and powerful than lowland songs — fewer ornaments, bigger intervals, voices that have to carry across valleys.

programme.title: Feeling Left Out
programme.desc:
Mike Hanlon is a popular type on paper — a football player with a letter jacket of his own — but the picture keeps returning to him standing at the edge of the same locker-lined hallway, watching a knot of letter-sweater boys trade jokes without him. He follows them into gym class, gripping the same chin-up bar, working the same jump rope, matching them stride for stride physically, and none of it earns him a way in; the group simply isn't built to admit one more. A coach notices him hanging back and makes the turn explicit: cliques form and close for reasons that have nothing to do with a boy's worth, and chasing one closed circle is a poor way to spend a school year. By the last reel Mike has stopped angling for the group and started talking to people one at a time — a girl bent over her books in study hall, a boy blowing a saxophone at a school function, a classmate he simply falls into step with in the hall. The film ends not with Mike joining the clique but with him no longer needing to.
Produced by Coronet Instructional Films, Feeling Left Out follows the house formula of putting only one name in front of the camera — the collaborating academic. The distributor's own catalog credits Paul H. Landis, Ph.D., professor of sociology at the State College of Washington (today Washington State University), as the film's educational collaborator, the standard Coronet arrangement of borrowing a working social scientist to vouch for the lesson on screen. Coronet released the picture in 1951 as a classroom-rental 16mm sound short, part of the same wave of adolescent social-adjustment titles as Shy Guy and Are You Popular. As with most Coronet shorts of the period, the students playing Mike and his classmates went uncredited, and no director is named in surviving prints or distributor records for this title specifically.
The film survives through the A/V Geeks ephemeral-film collection, which placed its 16mm print on the Internet Archive under a Public Domain Mark; the distributor's own synopsis there — a boy who "wants friends but... concentrates on becoming friendly with a certain group of boys" rather than individuals — matches the picture beat for beat. It sits comfortably alongside Coronet's other clique-anxiety shorts of the era, all working from the same premise: that adolescent unhappiness is a solvable technical problem, and exclusion a symptom a level-headed adult and a change of strategy can fix before the closing titles.

programme.title: The Point!
programme.desc: In the Land of Point, everyone and everything has a point — except Oblio, the only round-headed boy in a kingdom of pointed heads, who has worn a pointed hat since birth to hide his difference. When the son of an evil count loses to Oblio at Triangle Toss (a game where you catch triangles on your head), the count demands enforcement of the law: pointless things must be banished. Oblio and his dog Arrow are sent into the Pointless Forest, where they discover that even the Pointless Forest has a point. They meet a man pointing in all directions who declares: "A point in every direction is the same as no point at all." They meet a rock man, dancing fat sisters, and a tree who helps Oblio see that everyone has a point. When Oblio returns and tells the kingdom what he's learned, the furious count rips off his hat — and finds a point on top of Oblio's bare head. Upon this revelation, the points of everyone else disappear and the pointed buildings become round. Harry Nilsson wrote, produced, and performed all the music. He was born in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn in 1941. His father abandoned the family when Harry was three — his song "1941" opens: "Well, in 1941, a happy father had a son / And by 1944, the father walked right out the door." Due to poverty, he dropped out after ninth grade and lied about graduating high school to get a job as a computer programmer at a bank. He worked the night shift on bank computers and spent his days writing songs. His uncle in San Bernardino gave him singing lessons. When his songs started getting recorded — by the Monkees, by Phil Spector, by Glen Campbell — Nilsson still didn't quit the bank. He never performed live concerts, one of the only major pop artists in history to achieve fame without touring. When the Beatles were asked at a 1968 Apple Corps press conference to name their favorite American artist, John Lennon said "Nilsson." Paul McCartney was asked to name his favorite American group. He also said "Nilsson." Lennon had listened to Nilsson's album Pandemonium Shadow Show for 36 straight hours. The two became close friends. During Lennon's "Lost Weekend" separation from Yoko in the mid-1970s, he and Nilsson were members of the Hollywood Vampires drinking club, notorious for alcohol-fueled incidents at the Troubadour. They made one album together, Pussy Cats (1974). After Lennon's murder in 1980, Nilsson left the music industry to campaign for gun control. He died of heart failure in 1994 at 52. The inspiration for The Point came to Nilsson on LSD: "I was on acid and I looked at the trees and I realized that they all came to points, and the little branches came to points, and the houses each came to a point. I thought, 'Oh! Everything has a point, and if it doesn't, then there's still a point to it.'" He wrote a twelve-page illustrated treatment and first pitched it to Hanna-Barbera, who passed. Fred Wolf of Murakami-Wolf Films took it on. Wolf skipped pencil tests entirely and went straight to ink-and-paint, giving the film its loose, handmade look. He worked nights and slept days through the entire production. The original story collaborator, Carole Beers, started steering the narrative toward science fiction; Nilsson, protective of his concept, was not pleased, so Wolf brought in Norm Lenzer to write the screenplay. Production began before a script existed. Mike Lookinland — Bobby Brady — voiced Oblio. In a waiting room before a recording session, young Lookinland was making car noises when his mother told him to be quiet. A man stood up, walked over, and said: "Lady, don't ever tell your kid to be quiet. I make my living on sound." The man was Mel Blanc. The film first aired February 2, 1971 on ABC's Movie of the Week — the first animated feature ever broadcast in prime time on American television. Dustin Hoffman, a friend of Nilsson's, agreed to narrate for $20,000 on the condition that his voice be used for one broadcast only. For later airings, the narration had to be completely re-recorded — first by Alan Barzman, then by Alan Thicke for cable, and finally by Ringo Starr for the home video release. Our version has the Alan Thicke narration, the third telecast restoration. The album's art director was Dean Torrance — of Jan and Dean ("Surf City"). Nilsson instructed that the design have points but no circles. The sales sticker on the shrink-wrap was a triangle. The cover illustration was hand-stitched in needlepoint by Torrance's wife Kathy. The album's arranger, George Tipton, was Nilsson's equivalent of George Martin — the last Nilsson album he arranged. Tipton had invested his life savings of $2,500 to finance Nilsson's first four recordings. The song "Me and My Arrow" became a hit single and, in the way of the early 1970s, ended up in a television commercial. The London stage adaptation at the Mermaid Theatre in 1977 starred Davy Jones and Micky Dolenz of the Monkees — who had been among the first artists to record Nilsson's songs, and who remained his close friends until his death. Nilsson also inspired the name Aerosmith: drummer Joey Kramer was listening to Nilsson's album Aerial Ballet, started riffing on the word "aerial," someone said "smith," and a band was born.

programme.title: Understand Your Emotions
programme.desc:
Mr. Brent, a high-school biology teacher, opens by springing a jack-in-the-box on his class to make a simple point: the same jolt doesn't hit everybody the same way. From there the lesson turns diagnostic. Working with three students — among them a boy named Larry — Brent lifts a plastic brain off his desk and traces the thalamus as the switching point where a stimulus becomes a feeling, then wires a student's fingers to a gauge to record the body's own evidence: racing pulse, tightened stomach, sweating palms, each mapped onto a cutaway silhouette on the wall chart. He walks the class through a wired maze holding a white mouse, using shock and cheese to demonstrate conditioning directly, then chalks the idea up as an equation: S¹, a dentist, produces only curiosity; S², his drill, produces fear. The blackboard closes the period the way it opened, as a formula — fear, rage, and love as raw material, conditioning as the process that shapes them, emotional maturity as the goal.
Produced at Coronet Instructional Films' studio in Glenview, Illinois, and copyrighted 1950 ("Copyright MCML David A. Smart," per the title card, naming Coronet's founder and the publisher of Esquire and Coronet magazines), recorded on the RCA Sound System. As with the rest of the line, the only person credited on screen is the psychology consultant: Educational Collaborator A. R. Lauer, Ph.D., Professor of Psychology at Iowa State College — in real life the head of Iowa State's driver-research program and author of The Psychology of Driving, lending his credentials here to classroom emotion theory rather than his usual traffic-safety work. None of Coronet's young actors are named on screen; period research into the studio's stock company has since identified the boy playing Larry as John Galvarro, who played the same character, Larry, in Coronet's Are You Ready for Marriage? the same year and went on to small roles in Service and Citizenship (1951) and the Encyclopaedia Britannica short Drug Addiction.
The film belongs to Coronet's early-1950s run of shorts built around the vocabulary of behaviorist psychology — Control Your Emotions, made the same year, dramatizes the same three emotions through a teenager's bad Friday, while this one drops the story in favor of the lab: mice, wiring, and a plastic brain standing in for a plot. Ken Smith, whose capsule notes for the Prelinger Archives remain the standard reference for the genre, filed it as "even more Skinnerist than Control Your Emotions, and much less entertaining" — a fair verdict on a film that treats its teenage subjects less as characters than as case studies. Like most of the Coronet guidance catalog it has long since lapsed into the public domain and survives today through the Internet Archive and Prelinger Archives.

programme.title: Operavox
programme.desc:
Directed by Mario Cavalli through his company Pizazz Pictures (later known as pizazz, and later still absorbed into what became Studio AKA — now one of Britain's most respected animation houses). Cavalli has over 30 years of directing TV commercials and short films "in animation, live action, and in various innovative techniques of his own invention," as the Animate Projects archive describes him. His films — including Soho Square and The Cask of Amontillado (an Edgar Allan Poe adaptation) — have won major awards throughout the world.
For Carmen, Cavalli chose rotoscope: filming live actors performing Bizet's opera, then painting over the footage frame by frame with animator Ashley Potter handling the cinematography. The technique has a distinguished lineage — the Fleischer Brothers invented it in the 1910s, Ralph Bakshi built a career on it, and Linklater later elevated it in Waking Life and A Scanner Darkly — but it's polarizing. Charles Solomon called the result "singularly ugly — and barely animated." A DVD reviewer was kinder: "Some of it works quite well, but it's not quite as otherworldly as some of the other episodes (but then again, the Carmen story isn't quite as otherworldly either)."
The approach has a logic to it: Carmen is the most realistic opera in the series — no gods, no magic, no puppets. Seville tobacco workers, soldiers, smugglers, a bullfighter. Painting over real bodies preserves a groundedness that puppets or cel animation would lose. Whether that groundedness helps or fights the medium is the open question.
Sung by Jean Rigby (Carmen), Adrian Thompson (Don José), and Donald Maxwell (Escamillo), with the Welsh National Opera conducted by Julian Smith. Produced by Pizazz Pictures for S4C/BBC. IMDB 7.3 — the lowest-rated of the six, though Cavalli's technique has gained appreciation since. Contains animated nudity.

programme.title: Mind Your Manners
programme.desc:
A hand draws a cartoon on a blackboard — a couple bumping into each other, tempers fraying — under the chalked warning "Watch it! Your manners are showing!" That gag sets up the day the film then follows: a teenager named Jack moving from the breakfast table to school to the soda shop, with his manners tested at every stop. At home he minds his appearance before a hallway mirror and sits down to a family dinner with his mother, father, and sister. At school he waits his turn in a hallway lined with lockers, ducks into the library, and settles into a crowded classroom.
